en: Commentary on the Precious Mirror of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Pǔwěn of Gǎnglíng, a recipient of the Imperial Honor from the Great Qing Dynasty at Fǎjiè Monastery in Yúnnán. △ Ten: Separate Explanation of the Textual Meaning.

Following the usual practice, this is divided into three parts: (1) The Introductory Section; (2) [The Main Body]; (3) [The Conclusion]. (1) The Introductory Section. (2) Testimony to Authenticity. (1) [The First Part of Testimony to Authenticity]...
This clarifies the five meanings that authenticate the faith.
"Thus have I heard at one time the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Monastery.
These five meanings consist of faith, hearing, time, the teacher, and the location. If the subsequent chapter is included, they collectively form six kinds.

However, all are termed "testimonies of faith" (*śraddhā-pratyaya*). This means that whenever a Buddhist scripture contains such a testimony, it is then the word of the Buddha and must certainly be accepted with faith;
otherwise, it is a forgery and not worthy of belief. Such [terms] are words used to point toward the Dharma.
This refers to the ten volumes of sublime prose that follow. The phrase "I have heard" clarifies the basis of the transmission;
it means that such teachings as these were personally heard by me, Ānanda, directly from the Buddha—this being the speech uttered at the time of the compilation.
If one examines this according to the sixfold perfection, these two characters "evam" (thus) carry the meaning of faith and compliance; that is to say, one who has faith speaks thus.
It is so. Those who lack faith say it is not so; now that it is said to be "so," faith is perfected.
Therefore, the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable, yet faith is its primary foundation. Among the fifty-five stages, the stage of faith stands at the head;
among the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith comes first. Thus, one should know that the single word "faith" is the vanguard for entering the Way.
Furthermore, these two characters also serve to refute the doctrines of the two non-Buddhist schools, Ājīvika and Aulūkya.
By establishing them in this way, one refutes their inferiority and incorrectness. These are all explanations based on phenomena (*dharma*). As for the explanation based on principle (*tattva*):
Thus, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they reveal only True Suchness (*tathatā*), and it is this True Suchness alone that is the reality.
Furthermore, because the Buddhas speak in accordance with reality and sentient beings believe in accordance with reality, it is called "thus" (*evam*). This is a general discussion.

If one wishes to specifically point to the meaning of this very sutra, then the wondrous nature of the True Suchness of the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha is "thus," and all phenomena are ultimately [grounded therein].
This is the firm position. According to Qingliang (Chengguan), the five teachings are used to distinguish and extensively explain this matter;
thus, I shall not elaborate further here. "I have heard" refers to the accomplishment of hearing. This single word "I" (*aham*) is Ānanda’s own self-designation.
However, while the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*), there are four reasons why he now uses the term "I": first, [the conventional self]...

There are four [conceptions of self]: first, the pervasive conceptualization of ordinary beings; second, the sectarian tenets of non-Buddhists; third, the provisional self of the two vehicles; and fourth, the true self of the dharmakāya.
These are established in accordance with worldly conventions, provisionally positing the "self" of the guest and host as well as the true self of the dharmakāya.

It is not the self (ātman) as conceived by the pervasive conceptualizations of ordinary outsiders; rather, it is neither self nor non-self, yet it is conventionally designated by the worldly name "self.
"Hearing" refers to the nature of the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

while the ear is a specific among the six faculties, the "self" is the totality of the single body. By setting aside the particular and following the general, it is called "self. Thus, "hearing" is the very accomplishment of hearing.
This is indeed so. It is precisely the true self that is neither self nor non-self; it is the true hearing that is neither hearing nor non-hearing.

As for "at one time," this refers to the auspicious occasion when the Dharma King preached the Dharma. Success is achieved at such a moment. Even in worldly affairs, one must await a propitious period;
how much more so when the Great Dharma is widely proclaimed—how could it fail to coincide with such a glorious destiny? This must surely be excellent.

It is only at such a time that [the teaching] can be accomplished. However, no specific year, month, or day is fixed because calendars differ across various regions, and the durations of time—whether preceding or following, extending or shortening—are not uniform.
It is simply when the capacity of the listener and the response of the teacher coincide, and the act of speaking and listening is concluded, that it is collectively termed "at one time.
As for "Buddha," he is the master who expounds the Dharma; the full term is *Buddhāya*. This means "the Awakened One," referring to one who has awakened by himself.

Through initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), one realizes equality with original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), thereby achieving ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*). This is also called "self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening.

Thus, while the preceding three [aspects] pertain solely to self-benefit, these three encompass both self-benefit and the benefit of others. Therefore, "self-awakening" distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings; "awakening others" distinguishes [him] from those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);
and "perfection of awakening" distinguishes [him] from those still on the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). If one points to the person [who embodies this], it is Śākyamuni in the Sahā world.
The Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha—since none but this Most Holy One could expound such a Great Teaching—it is said that "the Master is accomplished.
The phrase "in Śrāvastī" below clarifies the location where the sutra was preached. Now, there are two types of locations:
first, the place of transformation, which is the city of Śrāvastī; second, the place of residence, which is the Jetavana Monastery. The word "in" [indicates]...

This refers to manifesting traces in this world; regardless of whether it has been long or short, all activities—coming and going, entering and exiting, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—are termed "being present.
It is fully called Śrāvastī, or alternatively Śā-véi (Shèwèi). These are variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit sound, like the dialectal differences between the "Chū" and "Xià" registers.
It is correctly translated as "Abundant Virtue" (Puṇyavat), also known as "Renowned for Wealth" (Śruta-vastu), or "Excellent Path" (Supathin). This is [the city of] Kośala.
"Guó" (國) is the name of the city. "Qí" (祇) is fully called Jītuó (祇陀), also known as Shìduō (逝多); this means "Victory in Battle.
It was given as a magnificent name to commemorate the joy when the Prince was born, coinciding with King Bimbisāra’s victorious return from battle.
"Huán" (桓) means "grove"; because the groves of trees belonged to him, it is called Jīhuán (祇桓). This refers to Prajñā; that is, Jī... [the text here is incomplete].

It signifies the meaning of "tree. As for the *vihāra*, it was established by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada for the Buddha, serving as a dwelling place where śramaṇas could dwell in tranquility to cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

According to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and other scriptures, the householder Sudatta wished to build a *vihāra* and invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma; having selected this garden, the Crown Prince said in jest: "Spread [the gold] sideways..."
When the gold was full, he sold it. The elder sent men to carry the gold on elephants and spread it across the park;
in a short while, it was nearly full, with only a small amount of ground remaining. The prince stopped them, saying, "The Buddha is a fertile field; one should sow the seeds of goodness therein."
"The garden belongs to you, but the trees belong to me. I shall personally construct a gate-tower for the Buddha’s entry and departure.
The elder then prepared a cave-dwelling for the Buddha over seven days, using exquisite sandalwood as fragrant plaster.

He provided one thousand two hundred separate rooms for the monks' residence, totaling one hundred and twenty locations, each with its own *ghanṭā* (gong) struck for the assembly. The Buddha told Ānanda, "These two have acted with a single mind."
Together they established a vihāra; it should be called the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The reason "Jeta" is mentioned first and "Anāthapiṇḍada" second is that the relationship between sovereign and subject must not be disordered, as propriety distinguishes the honorable from the humble.
Furthermore, the city is mentioned before the park because by naming the city, people from afar will know its location. Thus it is said:
In the case of a garden, one recognizes its location by what is nearby. However, this Dharma-gate of Great Samādhi cannot be proclaimed except in such an excellent place;

therefore, it is said that "the location is perfected. Regarding these five meanings above, the explanations of various schools either divide them into five sections or condense them into two or three;
not only do they fragment the text, but they also make the reading of the sentences inconvenient. For this reason, [I have now...]
This summarizes [the preceding] into one. △ Second, citing the great assembly as witnesses and proof (three parts): 1. The assembly of śrāvakas (two parts): 1.
Citing the types and indicating the number:
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty persons.
This is intended to lead the assembly to faith and conviction. The term "together with" (*sārdham*) carries the sense of "in common.
Thus, the compilers state that this *Dharmaparyāya* of the Definitive Nature was not heard by them alone; rather, it was heard in common with one thousand two hundred and fifty-five persons.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *Pratyekabuddhas* and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who likewise heard it together. For this reason:

This is cited to provide proof and inspire faith. Below this, the accomplishment of the great assembly is clarified. "Great" (大) is the Sanskrit term *mahā*; it is translated here as "great," "many," or "supreme.
This clarifies that these bhikṣus possess a vessel of profound capacity and respect, and are honored by great beings such as celestial kings;
therefore, they are called "great. They have thoroughly mastered both internal and external scriptures; therefore, they are called "many. They have transcended the nine... [text truncated]
Because there are fifteen kinds of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), it is said to be "superior. Now that it is designated as "Great" (Mahā), it is clear that it encompasses many such superiorities.
Furthermore, the term *bhikṣu* is one of the five cases where a word is not translated (*wu fǎn*), because it contains multiple meanings;

these include "one who terrifies Māra," "one who destroys evil," "a mendicant" (*qǐshì*), and "one who removes deficiency" (*chújìn*). First, regarding "terrifying Māra": this is because on the sixth heaven there is a Māra King.

The Palace. He, being attached to the desires of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and fond of worldly toil, fears that people will cultivate the Path and thus leave his domain, thereby diminishing his retinue.

Should there be men or women of right faith who possess the six sense faculties in full, are twenty years of age, and are free from the thirteen grave obstacles (*sthūlātyaya*) and sixteen minor prohibitions (*parivāsa*), and who obtain three preceptors and seven witnesses—or, in a border region—
In the midst [of the assembly], having obtained the three masters and two witnesses, one formally receives the bhikṣu precepts according to the Dharma.

At the precise moment of ascending the platform, once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is completed, this is called "attaining the precepts. One becomes a bhikṣu by nature and enters the number of the Saṅgha Jewel.
At that time, a terrestrial rākṣasa cries out in a loud voice: "In this place, there is a son of good family, or a daughter of good family, who has [received the precepts] according to the Dharma..."
"By going forth from home, we shall cause the devas to increase in excellence and the asuras to diminish.

When the *khecarī* yakṣas heard this, they also raised a great voice crying out "Excellent! The sound reached the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, where the devas likewise raised their voices crying out "Excellent!"

The sound was transmitted to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. In this manner, it was passed on successively to the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens, and even to the Brahma Heaven.
When the voice of this proclamation was heard within the palace of Māra, he gave rise to great sorrow and fear; thus, he is named "Terrifier of Māras" (Bhīṣmamāra). As for "Destroyer of Evil":

by leaving the household life and upholding the precepts, one gives rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through the precepts, and brings forth wisdom (*prajñā*) through concentration. Coarse [evil] is eliminated from the seven [paths of action] of body and speech.

It refutes what is not [the path]. It minutely destroys the evils of the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms; therefore, it is called "destroying evil. As for the "beggar" (*bhikṣu*):
having already left the household life, one is forever free from the four kinds of wrong livelihoods.

Externally, one begs for food to sustain the physical life; internally, one begs for the Dharma to sustain the life of wisdom. Regarding the four wrong livelihoods: the first is "looking upward" (*ūrdhvamukha*).

Regarding food: first, looking upward at the constellations and divining the winds and clouds; second, looking downward with the mouth, which refers to compounding medicines and observing the earth for planting in fields and gardens;
third, facing all directions with the mouth, which refers to serving as envoys for states and cultivating ties with the powerful and noble;

fourth, facing the four quarters with the mouth, which refers to astrology, divination, and the accumulation of wealth through commerce. These four types of sustenance are appropriate for worldly people.
Those who have left the household life must not enjoy such things; therefore, they are forever detached from them. As for the three types of false dharmas:
first is false precepts, namely the precepts of cattle, dogs, and so forth, up to all the worldly spells, incantations, and prohibitions of the various devas and rishis.

Those who cannot transcend birth and death are of two kinds: those of false concentration, namely ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists, who practice the four dhyānas and eight samādhis based on a mind of longing for joy and aversion;
and those of false wisdom, namely the two views of existence and non-existence, and the sixteen types of speculative views.
The sixty-two views, up to the one hundred and eight views and so forth—these are now all forever abandoned.
Seeking only the three higher trainings of the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are thus called "mendicants" (*bhikṣu*) or "those who remove hunger.

Purifying their observance of the precepts, they are able to serve as a field of merit for the world and are able to practice the vast gift of the Dharma, thereby removing from all sentient beings the two kinds of lack: the lack of merit and the lack of wisdom.
Regarding "the assembly": *saṃgha* in Sanskrit is translated here as "harmonious assembly" (*huohe zhòng*). There are two types of harmony:

first, harmony in principle (*lǐhé*), which refers to collectively realizing the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, harmony in practice (*shìhé*), which consists of six aspects:

harmony in precepts through collective cultivation; harmony in views through collective understanding; harmony in material benefits through equal distribution; harmony in person through dwelling together; harmony in speech through the absence of contention; and harmony in mind.
"Shared joy" refers to a group of four or more persons; thus, a single bhikṣu is not called a *saṃgha*, nor are two or three bhikṣus called a *saṃgha*.

Only when four bhikṣus dwell together may they perform all *dharmic* monastic acts (*saṃghakarma*), with the exception of the three types of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) consisting of the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the conferral of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), and the rehabilitation from an offense (*āpattivyutthāna*). If five bhikṣus dwell together...
One may then perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. Furthermore, one may confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) even in border regions.

If ten bhikṣus reside together, then in the five regions of India, the conferral of full ordination is permissible. If twenty bhikṣus reside together, then all formal acts (*karmavācanā*) may be performed.
Even if the number increases from this point on—reaching hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, or even the infinite—all who are likewise...
Those who reside in a single location and perform the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) together are collectively termed a "saṃgha.

Therefore, whenever a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed according to the Vinaya, one must first seek consent (*sāmīci*), thereby clarifying that it is a harmonious assembly. Having concluded this illustrative analogy, the phrase "the twelve hundred and fifty" below indicates the specific number.
This refers to the fact that the Buddha first ordained the five monks at the Deer Park, followed by the three Kāśyapa brothers.
The master had a thousand disciples. Next, he ordained Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with a following of one hundred.

Later, he ordained Yaśas and others, fifty people in total. These twelve hundred and fifty-five individuals had previously practiced heterodox paths, undergoing diligent and bitter asceticism without attainment.
Upon encountering the Tathāgata but once, they immediately realized the fruits of sainthood. Therefore, out of gratitude, they became his constant retinue.

Now, citing the general number, the five individuals are omitted for brevity. "Together" (*ju*) precisely clarifies the meaning that the master and disciples are like water and milk, always accompanying one another.

The above follows the ancient commentaries to establish the testimony of faith (*śraddhā*). Furthermore, there are two established meanings and three matters for dispelling doubt, which are fully recorded in various sub-commentaries; they shall not be described here at length.
△ II. Detailed Explanation of the Virtues of the Two Hairpins (2). 1. Narration of the Virtues.
All are untainted (*anāsrava*) Great Arhats... [omitted] ...who rescue the future and transcend all worldly burdens.
This enumeration of virtues contains two aspects: first, a general introduction regarding the identity of their names; second, a specific introduction regarding the distinctness of their virtues.

For now, we shall introduce the identity. To say "all are untainted Great Arhats" means that the word "all" generally introduces the fact that the names of the fruits of the one thousand two hundred and fifty persons are identical. "Outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to leaking; it arises because...
Delusion creates karma, which inevitably brings about bitter fruit, just as a broken vessel has leaks.

Now, although these leaks are of many kinds, to speak briefly, they do not exceed three types: first, the leak of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), which refers to all afflictions within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The second are the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), which consist of all afflictions in the two higher realms.

The third is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), which refers to ignorance beyond the realms. Since afflictions and karma constitute the causes of the outflows, and birth-and-death constitutes their fruit, they are now all completely severed;
thus, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, the three meanings of "Great" are as previously explained. Now, regarding the Arhat:
If one compares the fruit to the cause regarding a bhikṣu, it likewise contains three meanings: first, the meaning of being worthy of offerings (*arhat*), which is the fruit of the mendicant;
second, the meaning of slaying the thieves [of defilement] (*arhat*), which is the fruit of destroying evil; and third, the meaning of non-arising (*anuppāda*), which is the fruit of terrifying Māra.
One should know that those three apply to both cause and fruit, whereas these three pertain only to the fruit. Furthermore, there are another three types of Arhats.

There are three types: 1. Those who cultivate the *smṛtyupasthāna* of nature (*svabhāva*) sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*), attaining only the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) but not possessing the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

these are called persons liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*). 2. Those who cultivate the *smṛtyupasthāna* of concomitance (*sahagata*) sever the afflictions and realize the truth, becoming fully endowed with the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*);

these are called persons doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). 3. Those who cultivate the *smṛtyupasthāna* of conditions (*ālambana*) sever the afflictions and realize the truth, becoming fully endowed with...
He possesses the supernormal powers of the feet, the clear visions (*abhijñā*), and liberation (*vimokṣa*), and further has manifested the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*);

thus he is called one who has attained "unimpeded liberation. Because he now possesses this unimpeded liberation, he is titled a "Great Arhat. This is a general introduction concerning the identity of their names.

Below follows a detailed account of the distinctions in their virtues; that is to say, since their names are identical, their virtues likewise do not differ. However, this enumeration of virtues is brief.

There are two meanings. First is the virtue of self-benefit through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which refers to the aforementioned four lines. Second is the virtue of benefiting others through wisdom and precepts (*śīla*), which refers to the following eight lines.
The first clarifies self-benefit. Regarding "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*), this is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Born from the mouth of the Buddha."

They are born through transformation from the Dharma and have attained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma; they are capable of succeeding to the lineage of the Buddhas, and are therefore called "sons of the Buddha.

"Abiding" (zhu) means dwelling securely and immovably; "maintaining" (chi) means upholding without loss. This refers to abiding in the secret treasury of the three virtues and maintaining all wholesome merits.
It also means abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi while maintaining the Tathāgatagarbha. "Various" (zhu) means numerous.

The term "not one" refers to the state of not forgetting the cause-and-effect relationship. This refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), which are the places where one takes birth within the three realms (*tridhātu*).
To "transcend" means to not be bound by the conditions for birth in these various states of existence. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "excellently transcending":

although the noble ones of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) are able to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), eliminate the coarse分段 [births], and transcend the three realms, [this [term] distinguishes them from the superior state].
However, viewing the realms as a prison and regarding birth as a festering sore, one dares not enter them again; thus, although such a person has transcended, it is not yet "skillful.

Now, it is otherwise. What is called "transcending birth and death while remaining within birth and death," "transcending the three realms while remaining within the three realms," and "transcending all states of existence while remaining within all states of existence"—can this not be called "skillful"? As for the "land":
This refers collectively to the three realms. "Accomplishing dignified deportment" means that one accomplishes all three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle practices;
thus, there is dignity that is worthy of respect and decorum that may be emulated. As for the phrase "one who is able":
When ordinary lesser sages enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), their bodies are like withered wood and their minds like extinguished ashes;

they lack even the capacity for movement, so how could they possess dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*)? Now, it is revealed that by abiding in this Great Samādhi, one’s essence fills the Dharma-realm and its function pervades as many sands as there are in the Ganges;
thus, one can move and manifest within the Middle Way without abandoning dignified deportment—what is called "not arising."

In the samādhi of quiescent extinction, they manifest all modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). These four lines describe the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) and clarify the virtue of self-benefit.
Next, the benefit of others is clarified. Regarding "following the Buddha": it does not merely mean attending upon him as his retinue;

rather, because they can follow the Buddha’s regulations and assist in turning the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), they are so called. "Turning" means transmitting; that is, conveying it from oneself to others, hence the name.
It revolves. To proclaim, disseminate, and provide a model for emulation is termed a "transmission" (*zhuan*). Furthermore, the wheel possesses four meanings:

first, the meaning of perfection, referring to the hub, spokes, rim, and axle, as its substance and function are fully complete; second, the meaning of destruction, referring to the destruction of afflictions (*kleśa*).

First is the meaning of subduing, because it causes [afflictions] to be overcome. Second is the meaning of suppression, because once afflictions have been subdued, they are prevented from arising again. Third is the meaning of restriction, because once [afflictions] have been subdued, they are made not to arise again.
Fourth is the meaning of indeterminacy, because its flow proceeds without obstruction and its direction of movement is not fixed. Thus one should know the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Possessing both self-benefit and benefit for others, he is able to crush all subtle afflictions and transport sentient beings out of the perilous path of birth and death;
therefore, he is likened to a wheel. Since the Buddha has turned it, the various Venerable Ones have likewise followed in turning it;

this is precisely the teacher and disciple, as one breath, vigorously promoting the transformation of the Dharma. "Miao" (Wondrous) means wondrously attaining the Buddha’s wisdom and being capable [of turning the wheel].

This means being capable of performing the Buddha’s work. "Bequeathing" (*yi*) refers to bequeathing the Dharma to be transmitted; "entrusting" (*zhu*) refers to entrusting living beings to be transformed.

These two phrases describe the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). The single phrase "adorned and purified" pertains to self-benefit, namely the two accumulations of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃbhāra*) and the cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃbhāra*).
The single phrase "vast model" (*hiromoku*) pertains to the benefit of others; it refers to the assembly of sentient beings who are to be benefited.

*Vinaya* means "skillful treatment," signifying that one is well able to discipline and treat lust, anger, and ignorance. It is also called "subjugation" (*jōbuku*), meaning to refine the body and mind and to suppress transgressions and faults.

The direct translation is "discipline" (*ritsu*). "Discipline" (*ritsu*) means "dharma. It refers to the cutting and determining of what is grave or light, what is permitted or prohibited, and what is maintained.
These refer to the dharmas concerning transgressions and so forth. Regarding "rigorous purity": "rigor" refers to the observance through restraint, which is the cessation of all evils;

"purity" refers to the observance through performance, which is the cultivation of all virtues. Furthermore, rigor restrains the body and speech, while purity governs the mind and intentions. "Extensive" means to propagate and spread [the teachings].
"Model" (*fan*) refers to a teacher and model. "The three realms" (*sanjie*) are the realms of desire, form, and formlessness. This clarifies that the body is adorned and the mind is pure;

for this reason, it is said that one serves as a worldly law and acts as a worldly standard. Thus, one adorns the three clusters (*sanju*) to maintain oneself and purifies the single mind to serve as a model.
These two lines describe the training in morality (*śīla*). The four lines following "the response-body" (*yingshen*) correctly clarify the above.
These three studies do not merely save oneself, but further save others; they are beneficial not only in the present, but their benefits for the future are inexhaustible.

"Infinite responsive bodies" refers to the universal manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), responding humbly according to conditions, just as Avalokiteśvara manifests his body in every land. "Liberating sentient beings" refers to...
By means of the three types of untainted training (*anāsrava-śikṣā*), he delivers and liberates beings according to their capacities.

This is what is meant by crossing the river of afflictions and escaping the ocean of the wheel of suffering, just as a boatman ferries people across. Those mired in the mud of desire, he pulls out and frees;
those obstructed by the river of craving, he rescues and enables to cross. As for the phrase "the future," this indicates that it is not only the present that is thus.
Even throughout immeasurable kalpas in the future, one shall likewise rescue sentient beings by means of the Three Studies.
"Various defilements" refers to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), which entangle and cause sentient beings to fall into the realm of suffering within birth and death.

"To transcend" means to go beyond; that is, to manifest the body through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), to establish the model through the Vinaya, and to expound the teachings through Prajñā.
They transform all sentient beings so that they may all ascend together to the other shore and be liberated from the toils of worldly existence.
△ Second, the detailed enumeration of names:
Their names were Mahāmati Śāriputra (up to) Upānanda, who served as the leaders.
Śāriputra is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit Śāradvatīputra, which means "Son of Śārī.
He is so named because his mother’s eyes were as clear and sharp as those of that bird (the śāri). He is also called "Son of the Body" (Shenzi);

because his mother possessed a beautiful and upright physique, and the Venerable One was born from her very body, he was thus named "Son of the Body. These names both derive from his mother to establish his identity.
Furthermore, "Śā" is the name of his father and "ri" is the name of his mother; because it manifests both parents, he is named Śāriputra.
"Putra" means son. His formal name was Upatiṣya. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: He was a great master of treatises from South India named Tiṣya.
He walked alone in Rājagṛha, beating the drum of debate. The National Preceptor was defeated in argument, whereupon [the King] confiscated his fief and took him [as a disciple].
The husband became her wife. Śāri conceived, and the mother was immediately wise and highly skilled in debate.
Seven days after she gave birth, [the child] was wrapped in white woolen cloth and shown to his father. The father said, "My name is Tiṣya;
following my name, let him be named Upatiṣya. At that time, people, out of respect for the wisdom and eloquence of his parents, called him...
Śāriputra was the foremost in wisdom among the assembly of śrāvakas.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana—this is translated as "Great Maudgalya"—was his clan name. His personal name was Kolita, which means "knotless tree";
he was so named because he was born through a prayer made to the deity of that tree. Since worldly writing favors brevity, he was simply called by [his name].
Among all the śrāvakas, Mahākauṣṭhila—translated here as "Great Thigh"—was foremost in supernatural powers.
He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and was also known as the brahmacārin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail), who was foremost in his ability to answer difficult questions and challenges.
Pūrṇa is translated as "Full," which is his father's name; Maitrāyaṇī is translated as "Compassion," which is... [his mother's name].
Regarding his mother’s name: because he was named after both his father and mother, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra;
he is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. Subhūti is here translated as "Born of Emptiness," or "Wholesome," "Auspicious," or "Well-Appearing.
At the time of his birth, the storehouses and utensils in his home were all empty; the diviners said, "This child will surely bring about auspiciousness and goodness. This is "Wholesome" (Śubha).
Because auspicious signs appeared in his bowl, he received his name from this.

Thus, he was skilled in preaching the Dharma of emptiness, entered the samādhi of non-contention, and among the arhats, was foremost in understanding emptiness. Upānisaṭha means "the nature of dust" (rajo-dhātu).
It is because one attains the Way by contemplating that the nature of sensory objects is empty. The term "etc. refers to including the rest of the assembly.
The "leaders" are the senior elders and chiefs among the twelve hundred; they are those whom the assembly has honored and deferred to, following them in both movement and stillness.
They did not dare to arrive before him.
△ Second, the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *pratyekabuddha-asaikṣas* (until) belonging to the bhikṣus who, having completed their summer retreat, were performing the *pravāraṇā*.
In Sanskrit, *pratyekabuddha* is translated here as "Pratyekaja" (緣覺), which is also translated as "Solitary Realizer" (獨覺).

Those who appear during an era when a Buddha is present, who uphold the teachings on causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and who attain the Way through such practice, are called Pratyekajas. Those who appear during an era when no Buddha is present, who dwell in seclusion and contemplate the nature of phenomena, are called Solitary Realizers.

One who awakens to non-arising by oneself is called a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer). Those who have now arrived are the assembly of these Pratyekabuddhas. Regarding those "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*):

this means that their realization is ultimate and their delusions are exhausted, such that there is nothing further to learn. The inclusion of both characters [in the term *aśaikṣa*] clarifies the meaning of the principal and the retinue gathering together.

As for "beginners": this refers to those who, relying on the contemplation of dependent origination, investigate reality and sever delusions, having for the first time given rise to the supramundane mind.

This refers to the mind [of those in training]. This, then, encompasses the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) at the stage of those still in training (śaikṣa), but has not yet reached the stage of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
As for "coming together," it means that these two groups arrive simultaneously; this constitutes a "cloud-like assembly" and is not the same as being part of the regular retinue.
Therefore, the following two lines precisely clarify the reason for the gathering of the *pratyekabuddhas* and also serve as the cause for the Bodhisattvas to seek clarification and resolution.
To place these between the two pillars carries profound significance. "Belonging to" (*shǔ*) means to encounter, to meet, or to assemble.

"The end of the summer retreat" (*xiū xià*) refers to the fact that the Buddha ordained that bhikṣus observe the *śīla* of restricted movement for ninety days during a three-month period of *varṣā*; this day marks the completion of that time. What is... [text continues]...?
This means that during the summer, one rests here; because the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has been completed, it is called "concluding the summer" (*kṣayamāsa*).

As for *pravāraṇā*, it refers to the day when the period is fulfilled and the restrictions are lifted—namely, the three days of the seventh month, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth. It means that one recognizes within oneself the presence of transgressions.
To allow one to speak freely of oneself; to not recognize one's own faults; and to permit the Saṃgha to raise charges against one—therefore it is called *prātimokṣa* (self-indulgence).

This refers to the present-day *prātimokṣa-karman* performed within the Saṃgha, wherein each person makes a formal announcement, mutually seeks out [faults], confesses, and repents for transgressions.
The ritual for this is contained within the *Ekottara-karman* and is not detailed here. This is precisely the reason why the Pratyekabuddhas have gathered together.
...Thus. △ Third, the Assembly of Bodhisattvas (in two parts): 1. The preliminary gathering of the assembly through mutual exhortation;
the bodhisattvas of the ten directions resolve their doubts and inquiries (up to) the pure assembly at the Dharma feast attaining what they have never experienced before.
This directly follows the occasion of the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence).

Not only do the *pratyekabuddhas* assemble there, but bodhisattvas from the ten directions also come for the *pravāraṇā* in order to consult and resolve their doubts. As for "bodhisattva," it is fully called *bodhisattva*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Bodhi" refers to the Buddha-way; "sattva" refers to accomplishing sentient beings. This means that by employing the way of all Buddhas, one brings sentient beings to fulfillment.
Regarding the term "the ten directions," this refers to the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, as well as above and below.

Because these retreats for the rainy season (*varṣā*) are not restricted to a single location, they are called "the ten directions. "Consulting" (*tsu*) means to inquire; "resolving" (*chüeh*) means to decide or settle.
This refers to the bodhisattvas of the ten directions who, having doubts within their ordinary minds, were unable to reach a definitive resolution.
Now, encountering the day of *pravāraṇā*, they have all come to consult the Tathāgata, requesting that he resolve their uncertainties. Such are these mental doubts.
The "doubts within the mind" refers to those arising from seeing, hearing, or suspicion. "Reverently serving" means to attend with respect and comply without opposition.
"Kindly and stern" is a designation for one whose benevolence and majesty are both manifest, practicing both subduing and gathering.
Here, "reverently serving" represents the mind of the Bodhisattva, while "kindly and stern" reveals the Tathāgata.

This is its virtue. "Esoteric meaning" refers precisely to the definitive meaning of the esoteric cause. However, to say "about to seek" implies a desire to seek that has not yet been realized, as there is still something upon which one must wait.

Therefore, when the Tathāgata below speaks of the *Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Esoteric Cause*, it refers precisely to the wondrous state where the "beak" and the "peck" coincide—the subtle resonance of the meeting between the path and its response. If we consider this in terms of time...
Regarding this discourse: following this *prajñāpāramitā*, when he wished for them to hear the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he said, "Now, seeking the profound meaning.
From "At that time" onwards, it clarifies how the Tathāgata, according to the occasion and season, establishes the Dharma to transform sentient beings.
"To spread the seat" means to spread the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). "Calmly" (*yan*) refers to the state of being tranquil and still; "settled" (*an*) means to sit peacefully among the assembly.
This precisely describes the event when the Tathāgata, during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, personally prepared his seat and distributed voting sticks (*śalākā*) while sitting upon the grass.
Regarding the phrase "to proclaim the profound to the assembly": the word "various" (*zhū*) is an auxiliary particle;
"assembly" (*huìzhōng*) refers specifically to the *pravāraṇā* assembly. It was therein that he proclaimed and pointed out what is deep, subtle, and hidden.
"Method" (*dharma*) refers here to the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), which serves to eliminate the offenses arising from the views, hearsay, or doubts of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles.
"Assembly" (*sēn*) means a seat; it refers specifically to the Dharma-seat of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. "Pure assembly" refers to the ocean-like multitude of pure beings;
because these individuals possess the five virtues and are entirely free from the three types of offenses, they are called the "pure assembly. This is the explanation of this chapter.

This differs somewhat from what I have previously heard; moreover, the current explanation is entirely unlike what was taught in the past. Regarding this point, the old commentaries sometimes rely on meditative wisdom (*dhyāna-prajñā*) and sometimes speak of profound mysteries.
Although it is said that one thereby avoids falling into the trap of forgetfulness, it is like trying to prove a turtle is a soft-shelled turtle—it remains a matter of doubt that cannot be resolved.
Since there is no reliable basis for the esoteric meaning, I do not understand why the seats have been prepared and the assembly has gathered.
For what reason? Thus, at the outset you were full of pretension, yet in the end you were utterly abashed. I am indeed not clever; how would I dare to compete with you?

Nevertheless, as the meaning of the scriptures has been obscured, I dare not refrain from clarifying it. Herein, based on the Vinaya-piṭaka, I shall provide a detailed explanation of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination).
Thus, the intention behind the coming of the Pratyekabuddha can be understood, and the doubts in the mind of the Bodhisattva may be resolved.

Not only will the esoteric meaning find its proper place, but even the most profound matters will be made manifest. As it is said: "Principle returns to principle; phenomena return to phenomena. How could this be otherwise?
How could the confusion between phenomena and principle not be discerned?
△ Second, the assembly gathers after hearing the sound.
The kalaviṅka-like celestial voice pervades the worlds of the ten directions... (up to) with Mañjuśrī as the chief.
The full name is *kalaviṅka*, which means "bird of wondrous voice. It originates from the Snowy Mountains and cries within its egg; even then, it surpasses all other birds.
Its call is harmonious and elegant, such that listeners never tire of hearing it. This is used as a metaphor for the wondrous Dharma-voice of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the addition of the character "xian" (仙): it is intended to manifest the wondrous voice of the Buddha. If one were to use only "kalaviṅka," it would not suffice as a metaphor;
likewise, if one were to refer only to "xian-yin" (the immortal voice), it would also not suffice as a metaphor. Therefore, the two are combined.
This refers to the kalaviṅka’s celestial voice. It precisely reveals the meaning that the Buddha’s voice is subtle and wondrous, and its divine transformations are unfathomable.

Furthermore, the Buddha is named the Great Awakened Golden Immortal (Mahābuddha-suvarṇa-ṛṣi); thus he is called the "Immortal Voice. Indeed, the Buddha’s voice accords with the nature of reality and is all-pervasive;
wherever there are those with the conditions to encounter it, all may hear it. Now, desiring to awaken all the sages, for this reason—
It reaches everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions; thus, the perfect sound resounds clearly, encompassing the ten lands all at once.
How could the descendants of Lai Fu ever fathom it? Yet the Bodhisattvas speak of "counting as many as the sands of the Ganges" to emphasize its extreme abundance.
Because their mental hearing is unobstructed, they are able to hear the sound and gather from afar. This is the site of enlightenment.
This is the site for performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and practicing the Way. Mañjuśrī is here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*) and also as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*).
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he is the Fundamental Wisdom; in this present sutra, he is the Eye that Discerns Dharmas.

Therefore, below, he shall go to protect [the assembly] with mantras. As he selects the perfect penetration and judges the hearts of the multitude, there is none who does not submit with reverence. This is his wisdom-virtue.

Because of this honor, they are called the "foremost. The above constitutes the accomplishment of the assembly. Question: In various sutras, the descriptions of the assembly always include the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭau gaṇāḥ*);
why are they not listed here? Answer: The narration of events in various sutras differs from one another; therefore, there are cases where they are listed and cases where they are not.
However, in this particular sutra, they cannot be listed. Why? Because the manner in which the assembly is described in this sutra is as follows: [text continues].

During the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, those [beings] are specifically excluded; therefore, they are not listed. Thus, while only the Three Vehicles are enumerated, the Eight Divisions (*aṣṭakula*) are not included—there is indeed a sound reason for this.
It is precisely to manifest the meaning of this sutra: that concentration arises from precepts, and wisdom is elicited by concentration.
△ II. The Arising of the Occasion (4): 1. The King and His Ministers Present Offerings.
At that time, King Prasenajit, for the sake of his deceased father the king... [omitted] ...at the same time as he was feeding the Sangha, he waited expectantly for the Buddha’s arrival.
This explains that the king and his ministers invited [the Buddha] for offerings, thereby initiating the occasion for his erroneous fall. In the Sanskrit language he is called Prasenajit;

here it is translated as "Moonlight. He was born at the same time as the Buddha. When the father-king saw various radiant omens and auspicious signs, he declared them to be the result of his son’s power of merit, and thus gave him this name.
He was also called Vijitasena, because he had once been victorious in battle over all [his enemies].
Because he was the ruler of the kingdom, he was given this title; alternatively, he was named Vṛjiputra, which means "Harmonious and Joyful," and he was the sovereign of the city of Śrāvastī.
As for the term "time" (kāla), it refers to the day when the Tathāgata concluded the retreat, at the completion of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
Regarding the term "name" (*nāman*), it refers to the anniversary of the death of a parent—a day that a filial child cannot bear to utter, and is therefore called a "taboo name" (*ming-hui*).

On this day, the *Quli* (Book of Rites) states: "Upon the completion of the wailing, one observes the taboo [on the name]. This refers to the fact that after the burial of a feudal lord, seven months later there is a sacrifice in the courtyard of the ancestral temple called the "Completion of Wailing" (*zuku*).
Thereupon, an order is issued within the palace to abandon the old names and observe the taboo on the new ones; it is precisely as it says: "None dare to utter the personal name.
Now, the memorial day of the former king coincides exactly with the time of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) of the assembly of monks. All Buddhas rejoice...
On this day of joy, King Jayasena prepared offerings and personally invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide merit for the deceased spirit of his late sovereign.

"To prepare the fast-food" (yingzhai) means to arrange and provide the meals for the *poṣadha*. "The inner palace quarters" (gongye) refers to the left and right sides of the palace, known as the Yeting;
they are so named because they are situated at the left and right of the palace, like the armpits (*yexi*) of a person. "Delicacies" (zhenxiu) refers to the imperial...

"Meal" (*śan*) refers to the food; "inviting" (*yan*) means to welcome and request [the Buddha's presence]. Observing King Bimbisāra’s intention in honoring the Buddha, it is evident that there are six aspects:
namely, as for the location, it was within [his own palace]; as for the welcoming, it was personal; as for the arrangement, it was extensive;

as for the dishes, they were rare; as for the flavors, they were exquisite; and as for his companions, they were of equal status. One might say that his sincerity and reverence reached the ultimate limit of exhaustion. Within the city...

[This section] below clearly demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s holy transformation is impartial; thus, it moved the King to request [the teaching], while the ministers’ offerings also clarify that King Bimbisāra’s virtuous governance is worthy of observation.

This is what is meant by "the superior acts above and the subordinates emulate below. "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*) is a title for one who is honored both for age and virtue, and whose rank and emolument are equally esteemed;
he belongs to the class of ministers. A "householder" (*gṛhapati*), on the other hand, is one who delights in discussing names and principles and is pure...
"Pure" refers to those who occupy themselves with their own [virtues], namely the class of scholars, artists, recluses, and commoners.
"Feeding the Sangha at the same time" means that out of reverence for the Buddha-dharma, they provide food offerings to the Sangha simultaneously.

However, when both subjects and ministers desire to await the Buddha's response, they do so because they respect the primary host; once the host has come to respond, his companions must necessarily follow.
This clarifies the intention of these kings and ministers to revere the Buddha and make offerings to the Sangha.
△ Second, the Buddha and the Sangha attend the invitation.
The Buddha commands Mañjuśrī to lead the Bodhisattvas and Arhats to respond to the various hosts of the feast.
This clarifies the distribution of the Buddha and the Saṃgha. It was done so that the host of the invitation would not have his devotion frustrated.

For the Buddha is the Master of Transformation; having already accepted the King’s invitation and personally welcomed [the assembly] into the palace, he therefore commanded Mañjuśrī and others to lead the great multitude separately, universally responding to the host and comforting the hearts of the assembly. Nevertheless, both the sovereign and his ministers all desired to wait for the Buddha.

His coming to respond was indeed an act of impartial compassion and taking refuge; yet the Buddha personally went to the king’s location and commanded his disciples to distribute themselves among the ministers and the common people to respond to them—this too was an act of impartial benefit. This is what is meant by "the worldly dharma not being separate from the supramundane dharma."
△ III. Ānanda’s Mistaken Fall (2) 1. The Causes for Being on the Verge of Falling.
Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation... [until] he strictly regulated his deportment and solemnly observed the rules of the fast.
This refers to practicing compassion through wandering for alms without provisions; it is the cause for those who are about to fall [into lower realms].

The phrase "only one" (*kevalam*) is a subtle narrative technique of the sūtra author: among the great assembly, he singles out the single individual who is the appropriate recipient of the teaching, hence the term "only.
His full name is Ānanda, which means "Joyful One," so named because he was born when the Buddha first appeared in the world.
At home, Śuddhodana was filled with anxiety; yet upon hearing that his son had attained the Way, the Great King rejoiced greatly.

Furthermore, his younger brother Droṇodana announced the birth of a son, and the entire kingdom celebrated. The ministers and the common people were all delighted; for this reason, Śuddhodana bestowed this name.

It is also called "Joy" (Nanda), because his physical appearance was upright and handsome, and his speech, silence, movements, stillness, and deportment were such that the fourfold assembly [was moved].
This is because all who see it are filled with joy. "The Buddha’s younger cousin" refers to one who had previously accepted a separate invitation;
this means that before the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of mutual admonition), he had already accepted an invitation for a specific matter. "Huang" (遑) means leisure or opportunity.

"And" (*ca*) means "also. "Next" (*krama*) means "in order. Because he had gone beyond the boundary to travel afar and had not yet returned to the Jetavana, he was unable to attend the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, nor did he reach the ranks of those attending the meal.
The Sanskrit term is *sthavira*, which here is translated as "Elder" (*shangzuo*).
This is because there is no one superior to him. However, there are three types: first, the Elder by Age (*janma-sthavira*), namely—

1. The Preceptor of Seniority (*vṛddhataraka-ācārya*): one whose years of ordination (*śīla-varṣa*) are the highest. 2. The Preceptor of Merit (*puṇya-ācārya*): one who possesses great merit and wisdom and is esteemed and respected by the assembly.
3. The Preceptor of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-ācārya*): one such as an Arhat. The term *ācārya* means a "Preceptor" or "Model Teacher.
There are five types: 1. The Preceptor of Renunciation (*pravrajyā-ācārya*): the one from whom one receives the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*. 2. The Preceptor of Instruction...
1. The *ācārya* who, at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), questions the candidate in private and instructs them to request the precepts; 2.
The *ācārya* of the three *karmas*, who, at the time of receiving full ordination, performs the formal motion and the fourfold *karma* (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) on the ordination platform;
3. The *ācārya* of reliance (*niśraya*), from whom one receives reliance for even as little as one night; 4. The *ācārya* who teaches the recitation of the scriptures.

Lei immediately received the meaning of the sutra, even down to a single four-line verse. For this reason, the Vinaya regulations stipulate that whenever a monk travels far, his companions must number three:
first, an *upādhyāya* (preceptor); second, a *ācārya* (instructor). This is to strictly regulate conduct and prevent errors or omissions. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"When entering a village to beg for food, one shall be accompanied by another bhikṣu. This refers to the same principle. Now...
Since there is no one else, how can one avoid failure? As for returning alone:
because the Venerable One neither followed the Buddha to receive offerings nor joined the assembly for the midday meal; having departed alone in the past, he now returns by himself.
Having had no senior elder (upādhyāya) to accompany him, and lacking a teacher (ācārya) as a companion, he stands here truly solitary, his shadow alone.

This refers to a time when one is alone. Regarding "having no offerings," it means that since the king and his ministers were simultaneously holding a vegetarian feast (*śrāddha*) and both the Buddha and the Sangha had already accepted the invitation, on that day there was no one at Jetavana to present offerings. Thus, the Venerable One’s alms-round could not be avoided.
"At that very moment" means at the time he returned without having received any offerings. "Receptacle" (*saṃghāṭī*) refers to the alms bowl (*pātra*); in full, it is called [the *pātra*].
*Pātra*. This is translated as "vessel of proper measure. This means that its substance, color, and size all conform to the Dharma.
As for the substance, there are two types: iron and clay. As for the color, it is red-black, or colors such as pigeon-grey. As for the size, it corresponds to the capacity of one's own stomach;
at most it does not exceed three *sheng*, and at least it must hold one and a half *sheng*. "City" refers to Śrāvastī. Next...
"First" means to go from door to door to teach and transform others, practicing compassion with equanimity. "Circumambulating" (xún) means to follow in accordance;
that is, to practice begging in conformity with the rules and regulations of all Buddhas. Regarding "donor" (tányuè): "dāna" (tán) is giving;

it refers to practicing the giving of *dāna* to cross over the sea of poverty. Thus, it is called "seeking first. As for "last," it is because the Venerable One’s initial intention was that the king and his ministers [should come first].

Having already resolved to attain enlightenment, he invited the Buddha to provide a meal for the Sangha. He then said, "Among those who have now provided me with a meal, may this be the household that has never before offered a meal to the Sangha;
may they be the last lay donors to resolve upon the aspiration [for enlightenment], acting as the patrons who provide my meal.
This was because a "seeker" (yācaka) expresses a wish (prārthanā). Thus, the Venerable One’s intention was to cause those who had not yet resolved upon the aspiration to do so.
It causes those who are unwholesome to give rise to what is wholesome. This is why [the text] proceeds downward;

there are passages concerning "regardless of purity or impurity" and so forth, which clarify the intention of the initial seeking. *Kṣatriya* is translated here as "royal lineage," and is the most honored among the four castes.
This is what is called ultimate purity. A *caṇḍāla*—here translated as "killer"—is one whom the four castes do not even acknowledge;
this is what is called the most defiled. By citing these two extremes, the meaning of being "without question" regarding purity and defilement is clarified.
"Method" (*fang*) refers to the method by which the Dharma-Tathāgata practices impartial compassion. "Not choosing" means viewing all with the same eye; it is without discrimination.
He was noble, yet he did not discriminate against the lowly and humble. However, this single phrase became the condition for the arising of the teaching and the cause for falling into error.
Had the Noble One exercised even a slight degree of discernment, this teaching would not have arisen, and there would have been no cause for falling into error.
For Caṇḍālī was indeed impure, lowly, and humble. Because of the Noble One—
Since there was no discrimination, he could not avoid encountering an evil sorceress and falling into her chamber of lust.

The following two lines clarify the reason for this lack of discrimination: the Venerable One’s intention was to fully accomplish the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings, regardless of whether they were pure or defiled. "Ānanda already knew" and so forth; this clarifies—
Regarding the reasons for this equal alms-gathering: in the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, Śāriputra was once rebuked by Vimalakīrti for being partial, as was Mahākāśyapa.
Śāriputra had abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa had abandoned the wealthy to follow the poor; both were censured by Vimalakīrti.
Now, when it says "the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One," it is because Vimalakīrti is none other than the Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa; thus, Vimalakīrti...
What difference is there between this censure and that of the World-Honored One? Therefore, the titles "Tathāgata" and "World-Honored One" are presented together for a very specific reason.
In the past, Haiyan did not comprehend this principle and consequently made arbitrary deletions and alterations; thus, Leian’s rebuttal of his teacher was entirely appropriate.

"To open and expound the unobstructed" refers to what is called the opening and expounding of universal compassion (*samamaitrī*). It is "unobstructed" because it makes no distinction between the poor and the wealthy;
whereas the aforementioned two [types of compassion] each have their own limitations and thus fail to achieve equality, thereby not escaping suspicion and slander.

For those who are biased toward the poor, it gives rise to suspicion that they are seeking wealth; for those who are biased toward the wealthy, it gives rise to slander that they are being impoverished. "To measure" (*duó*; *dà* reversed) means to estimate or conjecture.
This is because, by being able to gauge the hearts of the poor and wealthy, one prevents them from giving rise to doubt or slander.
"City God" (Chéngxiáng) refers to the moat and ditch of Śrāvastī; "outer gate" (Guómén) refers to the city gates of Kauśāmbī. This clarifies entering from the outside.
"Majestic" (yán) means dignified and solemn; "orderly" (zhěng) means well-arranged. This ensures that one does not lose proper decorum (*īryāpatha*).

"Solemnity" means being reverently solemn; "respectfulness" means being reverent and cautious. This constitutes externally regulating one's physical demeanor while internally harboring respect and caution, thereby following the Buddha’s regulations as the ritual method for performing the *huazhai* (fasting and purification) ceremony.

Because this mind that loathes defilement and craves purity belongs precisely to the cognitive perspective of sentient beings, characterized by arising and ceasing."

This refers to the deluded mind. Therefore, he instructed them, saying: "You great assembly should understand that 'all sentient beings' here refers universally to the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms;
that is, it includes ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity, all of whom are contained therein."

There are two types of birth and death: first, *pariccheda* (segmented), which encompasses ordinary beings and non-Buddhists; second, *pariṇāma* (transformative), which includes both those of provisional and limited capacity.

Thus, for ordinary beings and non-Buddhists, there is the continuity of segmented [birth and death], while for those of provisional and limited capacity, there is the continuity of transformative [birth and death].

The phrase "continuity from the beginningless past" precisely clarifies that the accumulation of suffering has continued until now, and that one has never yet awakened to it. The phrase "all due to ignorance" means:
All those who are ordinary, external, provisional, or small are covered by the five abodes and entangled by the two deaths; for this reason, they do not know the true essence of the nature of mind.
Indeed, as for the truth of the nature of mind, it is not only ordinary beings and non-Buddhists who do not know it, but even those of the provisional vehicles and the small saints do not know it.
"Permanently abiding" is a designation for that which is neither born nor extinguished—the True Mind.
"Zhě" (the one who) refers to the meaning of being free from illusion and free from delusion. "Nature-purity-and-clarity" (*xing-jìng-míng*): nature (*xìng*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

Furthermore, the "ever-abiding true mind" is the function (*yòng*), while the "nature-purity-and-clarity substance" is the substance (*tǐ*). This clarifies the One.
The complete essence and great function of the mind are precisely the essence and function of the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama.

This is because this true mind and true nature is what the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) refers to as the "ever-abiding true mind" that is without change or variation, which is none other than the true *tathāgatagarbha*.
It is also what the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* calls the "non-associated mind."
This refers to that which is eternally abiding as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), where the noble and the ordinary are of one mark, and whose self-nature is pure.
This is precisely what the original sutra calls the "beginningless nirvana, the primordially pure essence.

These three phrases clarify delusion regarding one's own true mind. As for "functioning," it specifically reveals the process of deluding oneself regarding the truth and pursuing the false. "All deluded thoughts" refers to...

That which is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) refers to the associated mind (*samprayukta-citta*). This means the impermanent, deluded consciousness—the false discrimination that is associated with the various fetters (*saṃyojana*).

It is also what is termed in the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) as the "deluded mind of objective consideration. That is to say, it is the deluded mind that arises in accordance with defiled or pure conditions;

"Arising and ceasing" refers to this. Therefore, the original scripture says: "This is the false appearance and conceptualization of external objects that deludes your true nature.

Dust-like conditions are like shadows; they are illusory and false, and thus called "unreal. To grasp these as the mind is why one undergoes the cycle of birth and death.
These three phrases precisely clarify the recognition of others' deluded thoughts.

△ III. Grasping that the Mind Resides Within (2) 1. The Correct Grasping.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all in the world... [omitted] ...thus the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body."
This refers to the fact that the sentient being’s grasping mind resides within. "All worlds" refers generally to the three realms.
As for the "ten kinds," these are derived from the twelve categories by excluding those who are empty, scattered, extinguished, or submerged, as well as those without physical form.

In these latter two cases, the spirit and consciousness have been transformed into earth and wood, such that they lack thought and perception. Because these two types do not possess the faculty of mind and eyes, they are excluded.
The others, however, all possess them; therefore, they are said to be merely ten kinds. As for "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*):
because the karma created by ordinary persons varies from one to another, the resulting fruits they experience likewise differ; thus they are called "ordinary beings.
Although the "Observer"—that is, the Tathāgata with lotus-like eyes—is certainly not the same as an ordinary being, when one observes his state, he is [situated] among ordinary beings.
First: Regarding the "blue lotus eyes," because the petals of the blue lotus of India are long and broad, with the blue and white clearly distinguished, they possess the mark of a Great Man’s eyes;
therefore, it is used as a metaphor. "Floating roots" refers to the floating-dust roots (the physical sense organs).
Regarding the "four objects": namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. Because they belong to the ultimate sense as being invisible, they are not mentioned here.
This response implies that the Venerable One’s intention was this: if the ten bases have the mind residing within, then my mind must also reside within my body;
and since the Buddha’s eye is on the Buddha’s face, then my eyes must also be on my face. Such is the principle.
It is evident. What difficulty is there in debating this? Right here, upon the face and within the body, is the fixed location of the mind and eyes.
Therefore, it is resolved: such a conscious mind truly resides within the body.

One must know that this very point is precisely the essential passage where the Tathāgata, for the sake of those ready to receive the teaching, reveals the handle of his authority. For that which is recognized as the eye is...
[These are] floating dusts. Therefore, the subsequent refutation asks: "While you are inside a room, can the door see?
Thus, although those who have already died still possess eyes, why do they not see? That which you identify as the mind is precisely the consciousness-mind;

it is an impermanent, deluded consciousness, a false discrimination that properly belongs to the shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects. Therefore, the later sutra says: "A single delusion constitutes the mind."
It is precisely this that constitutes the delusion of taking the physical body as the inner self.

Thus, the reason all sentient beings transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death and are unable to attain liberation is entirely due to mistakenly identifying the cognitive mind as the true master.

"Ānanda, you gaze downward... up to "...you obtain far-reaching vision. This is the third round of question and answer.

In ancient translations, it was rendered as "right reception" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*), so called because one does not receive any [defiled] sensations; it is also translated as "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*). Because...

This is the great general dharma-gate expounded by this single sutra; it is the sovereign king of all concentrations.

It is not merely one of the three names requested by the interlocutor, for whereas those represent the particulars within the general, this represents the general within the particular. Nevertheless, it possesses...
There are many meanings. There are the samādhis of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the middle truth (*madhya-satya*).

Furthermore, there are the sequential samādhi of the three truths and the perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*) samādhi of the three truths. The present case refers to the perfectly integrated samādhi of the three truths.
It encompasses all phenomena, and all other samādhis enter into it; therefore, it is called the "King. This is seen in the ancient commentaries.
This [interpretation] is similar to the previous question and thus merely adds legs to a snake; by fragmenting and forcing connections, it frequently fails to accord with the intent of the sutra.

This is entirely due to a failure to understand that what was requested by the specific audience consists of particulars within the general, whereas what the Tathāgata revealed is the general within those particulars. Furthermore, this Samādhi of True Reality is precisely śamatha.
The samādhi of conventional truth is accomplished through *samāpatti*; the samādhi of the middle truth is accomplished through *dhyāna*.

Furthermore, the samādhi of ultimate truth ceases the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhava-āsrava*), while the samādhi of conventional truth ceases the afflictions of the sands of phenomena (*rajas-āsrava*).

The samādhi of the Middle Truth (madhyama-satya) ceases the delusions of ignorance; this is śamatha. The samādhi of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya) clarifies the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā).

The samādhi of the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya) clarifies the contemplation of the provisional (prajñapti-vipaśyanā). The samādhi of the Middle Truth clarifies the contemplation of the Middle Way (madhyamā-vipaśyanā);

these are the three samādhis corresponding to the principle of the Three Truths. There is no delusion to be destroyed and no contemplation to be established, yet through destruction there is establishment. This is...
It is *dhyāna*. The meaning of the *Śūraṅgama* at the Crown of the Buddha’s Head is seen in the title itself.

As for "King" (*rāja*), it is because this is the most honored and supreme among all *samādhis*; furthermore, upon entering this *samādhi*, one immediately governs and encompasses all other *samādhis*.
Thus, those who possess the ten thousand practices [are said to] mean that this self-nature is fundamentally settled, like the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels, and its six perfections...

There are no among the myriad practices that are not fully perfected therein. That the Tathāgatas of the ten directions "transcend through a single gate" precisely reveals that this samādhi is the essential path by which all sages travel together.

As for "wondrous adornment," it refers to using the two adornments of merit and wisdom—arisen in accordance with the nature—to adorn the self-nature itself; because nature and cultivation are non-dual, it is called "wondrous adornment."

"Path" refers to the fact that from the initial stage of *kandhūi* (dry wisdom) up to the final stage of *samyaksambodhi* (equal enlightenment), all rely upon this samādhi for their practice as the path by which they advance.
As for "touching the crown," it signifies affection; as for "bowing at the feet," it expresses reverence. When the superior shows affection to the subordinate, they touch the crown of the head;
when the subordinate shows reverence to the superior, they bow at the feet. This clearly illustrates the relationship between teacher and disciple within the Dharma assembly of that time.
Such was his love and respect.
△ Five: The Actual Refutation (2). One: Citing an Example.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... that one could see forests and springs—this is impossible."

△ 2. Refuting the Correct Conception (3). 1. The Correct Conception. Ānanda said:
"Among what I have taught, it is not these two kinds [of consciousness]. When consciousness arises therein, then the mind is present within."
This refers precisely to the middle between the faculties (*indriya*) and the objects (*viṣaya*). It is because those suited to the teaching cling to it, saying:

"That which I have spoken of as 'the middle' does not refer to the two kinds of middles—namely, that which is within the body and that which is in the location [of the object]. As the Buddha previously taught: "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
Now, the eye is the faculty; visible form is the object. When the eye possesses discrimination, it belongs to the internal faculty.
The sensory object of form is devoid of cognition; thus it belongs to the external realm. When the sense organ and the sensory object encounter one another, consciousness arises in between.
Since it performs the function of discrimination, is the mind not present therein?
△ Second, the direct refutation.
The Buddha says: "If your mind were within the sense organs and their objects" (up to) "...then being without intrinsic nature, what would constitute its characteristics?

This directly refutes the practitioner's current conception. Previously, the notion that the ordinary mind resides "in between" was treated as a general speculation; now, based on that general refutation, this specific causal conception is addressed.

This is the actual refutation. The meaning is as follows: If your mind were located between the sense organ and its object, then this essence of the mind would have to encompass both the organ and the object—would it be like a child born from the union of a father and mother?
Or would it not encompass both, being like something that arises spontaneously without depending on parents? If it were to encompass these two, then it would be...

The sense organs and their objects arise together through conjunction. If this were so, then these two entities—the organs and the objects—would be mixed with your mind-essence, making it impure and disordered rather than unified. Thus, one part would possess cognition while the other would lack it;
being diametrically opposed, existence and non-existence would stand side by side, falling into the two extremes. How, then, could this be called the Middle Way? For this reason...
I refute this. Your claim that the two meanings are established simultaneously is untenable.
If the Way were to arise spontaneously without encompassing both the sense organs and their objects, then—just as the mind does not know itself—the mind would not be capable of self-knowing;

it would necessarily depend upon the sense organs and their objects before it could have cognition. Were it to be separated from the sense organs and their objects, it could not know. Since it cannot know, then...

This is ignorance. Given such a nature, what use would there be for another? Furthermore, it must be spoken of as being "in the middle" by encompassing the characteristics of both the internal sense faculties and the external objects.
Now, since you do not encompass these, by what characteristic can you say it is "in the middle"?
This, then, combines both the partial and the universal; it is equally devoid of any middle characteristic.
△ Third, the conclusion of the refutation:
Therefore, one should know that to abide in the middle is impossible.
Thus, one knows that between your "floating calculation" and your "correct calculation," neither has any validity.
△ Seven: Refuting Non-attachment (3). One: A Shifted Calculation.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when I previously saw the Buddha... [up to] 'is this not my so-called mind of non-attachment?

This calculation takes non-attachment to be the mind. Regarding the occasion, since the previous six calculations involving specific locations had all been refuted, he was left with no other choice and thus calculated non-attachment to be it, even citing past teachings. He did not realize that the World-Honored One had [already responded].
In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is stated for the four disciples that "that which is manifested is neither internal, external, nor intermediate.

This precisely clarifies that the deluded mind has no substance, thereby revealing the original reality. It is as it is said: "If one seeks the mind throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not found;
where the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent. Where deluded mind is absent, that is itself Bodhi; birth-and-death and Nirvana are fundamentally equal."

How could it be said that there is a deluded mind while merely being without attachment? Furthermore, the Buddha’s words were interpreted as stating that the absence of all attachment is what is called "mind.
Moreover, [the interlocutor] did not dare to decide for himself, but simply said, "In that case, I am without attachment."

Is it not called "mind"? This is because one fails to understand that the nature of the mind arises and ceases in accordance with objects, having no substantial reality from the outset, yet instead falsely assumes it possesses a real substance. One merely claims not to be attached to external things;
