1. Aśvajit, here translated as "Horse-Winner. 2. Bāṣpa, here translated as "Little Wise One" (Kṣudrapanthaka). 3. Kauṇḍinya, who is Mahānāman. 4. Ājñātakauṇḍinya, here translated as "Fire-Vessel. 5.
Upatiṣya Kāśyapa, here translated as "Drinker of Light. The first three belong to the paternal lineage, while the latter two belong to the maternal lineage.
This was because when the Buddha first left the household life, his father, the King, dispatched these men to serve and protect him. And when the Buddha...
Previously, while he was practicing austerities on Mount Himavat, the three [companions] feared the ascetic and departed immediately.
Later, when he accepted the offering of milk-rice from a cowherd girl, the two who had delighted in his asceticism likewise departed and went together toward the Deer Park.

They had separately practiced heterodox paths. Only after the Buddha had attained enlightenment for five weeks did he go to deliver them. He turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths in three revolutions and twelve aspects;
Cunda was the first to attain understanding, and thus they were called the five bhikṣus beginning with Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya.
Bodhisattvas attain the fruit of the Mahāyāna, while Arhats attain the fruit of the Hīnayāna; this was the intent of the Buddha’s first turning of the wheel of Dharma.

The parable of the adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*) spoken at that time serves as a metaphor for the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), thereby implicitly revealing the primacy of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is merely an analogy for the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Here, we take only the analogy used for comparison and do not take the actual phenomenon being illustrated.

In this context, the "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*) illustrates only the body, its objects, and the mind that takes those objects as its conditions; both the "host" (the sky) and the "space" illustrate the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).
△ Second, the answer.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha... [up to] "...that which causes agitation is termed *rajas* (dust).
This Kauṇḍinya recounted his own realization and understanding as his response to the World-Honored One. Because his years were advanced and his age great, he was called "Elder" (*sthavira*).
When the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma, among the five disciples, Dignāga was the first to attain awakening. When the Buddha asked if he understood, he replied that he had understood;
thus, within the great assembly, he alone was first granted the name "The Understanding One" (*Ajñāta*).

Because he realized that the two delusions of views and thoughts are like guests or like dust, he attained the unconditioned, the *nirvāṇa* of the emptiness of persons, which is profoundly still and unmoving. Like...

The subject and emptiness: through these, one attains the fruits of sainthood. The above section indicates what has been realized; the following section describes what has been understood, which is twofold:
first, the explanation of the "guest," from "the World-Honored One" down to "is called the meaning of guest"; second, the explanation of the "object."
Furthermore, "ji" (即) means "down to"; "chen" (塵) signifies "dust" or "sensual objects. "Lvting" (旅亭) refers to a guest house where travelers stop.

"Chu" (俶) means "to prepare," referring to the arrangement of travel gear. "Huang" (遑) means "leisure," implying that one's appearance as a traveler is so hurried that there is no leisure for dwelling in peace.
"You" (攸) is equivalent to "suǒ" (所), meaning "that which"; thus, it implies that the host has nowhere to go. This serves as a direct metaphor for the host and the guest.
Arising and ceasing, as well as non-arising and non-ceasing, both come to rest within the pavilion of the five aggregates. Here, the traveler serves as a metaphor for the mind of arising and ceasing;

the overnight guest represents the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*). Because the afflictions of views are easily severed—being abandoned at the very moment of the Path of Seeing—they are like a traveler who departs after a single meal.
Because the afflictions of thought are difficult to sever—being removed only through the Path of Cultivation—they are like an overnight guest who remains until they have slept and rested.
"Departing. Packing one's bags for the journey ahead is a metaphor for completing what is old and hastening toward what is new;

the "way out" and the "way in" have no fixed host, which is a metaphor for the nature that is eternally abiding, unmoving, and beyond arising or ceasing. "A newly cleared sky" refers to the first clearing after the rain has passed. "Clear Yang" refers to...
The "morning sun" refers to the dawn. "Gaps" refers to holes or crevices. "Dust-phenomena in space" refers to the minute, floating particles that fly about when reflected by the sunlight.
This uses dust as a metaphor for the dust-like sands of ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is said to be hidden, subtle, and minute—just like dust entering a crevice.
Furthermore, this metaphor of adventitious dust has both a general and a specific application. Generally...
Thus, the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—and the two types of delusion—the conceptual and the innate—arise and perish according to their objects;

they do not possess a true, permanent nature and are all of the nature of "guests. Because they defile the wondrous clarity and turbidly disturb the emptiness of nature, they are equally of the nature of "dust.
Specifically, "guest" is a metaphor for the coarseness of conceptual delusion, while "dust" is a metaphor for the subtlety of the innate. Conceptual delusion is like a traveler.
Guests at an inn are easy to dismiss; those born together [as guest-dust] are as difficult to sweep away as dust in a dark crevice.

This is because, when the seeker requests instruction on the quiescent and eternally abiding, one borrows the metaphor of guest-dust to clarify the host-space, thereby enabling the recognition of the mind that is quiescent and eternally abiding.
△ Third Seal. The Buddha said: "So it is. This seal is acceptable.
Because the nature of adventitious dust arises and ceases, it disturbs both the host and emptiness; yet they remain tranquil."
It is immovable; such is its meaning, and it is indeed without error. This is precisely the Buddha’s intent:

he merely wished for Dignāga to clarify that the adventitious dust is the guest while the primary space is the host, and that arising-and-ceasing and movement-and-stillness are but the shifting of the body and its objects, whereas the nature of seeing within the eye remains eternally quiescent. Now, this analysis is precisely...
This accords with the Buddha’s mind; therefore, he confirms it by saying, "So it is.
△ Third, the actual manifestation of immovability (in three parts): First, manifesting immovability by contrast with external objects.
At that time, the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly... (up to)... "Who is the non-abiding Buddha? The Buddha said, "So it is."
This uses the Buddha’s hand as an external object to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is immovable.
Because Cenna had previously described the guest-dust as being subject to movement while the host-space remains still, the distinction between motion and stillness was clear.

The Tathāgata wished to cause the immediate disciple to realize the immovable host-space directly within the arising and ceasing of the guest-dust; therefore, in the midst of the assembly, he opened and closed his hand to pose the inquiry.
The Master said: "What did you see just now? The practitioner replied directly: "I saw the Tathāgata’s wheel-marked palms opening and closing among the assembly.

The World-Honored One then pursued him, saying: "When you say you saw the hands opening and closing, was it my hands that opened and closed, or was it your vision that opened and closed? The practitioner replied: "It was the Buddha..."
The precious hand opens and closes of its own accord; it is not that the nature of my seeing has opening and closing.

When the Tathāgata arrived here, he saw that the student appeared to have attained realization, yet it was not true realization; therefore, he exerted all his strength to uplift him, saying: "Look at that which moves—what is it?"
"Who, then, is this one who is still? Regarding such words, you should have directly accepted them at once, realizing that where there is the guest, there is the host;
where there is dust, there is emptiness; that movement is itself stillness, and delusion is itself truth.
Alas, Venerable Sir, you merely make your livelihood upon the fist and the palm, thereby creating a division between mind and境 (objects/conditions). Thus, you have split them into two.
This is like being stuck on a stake; both guest and host fall into the two extremes, which is truly to be lamented.

You merely say that the Buddha’s hand moves and does not abide, yet you claim that my nature of seeing has no stillness—how then could it have movement? It is simply that the Buddha’s hand moves without abiding;
who can say whether my nature of seeing is abiding or non-abiding? This is precisely the awakening to the nature of seeing that accords with the occasion.
The nature abides and is unmoving. One must know that these two characters, "seeing-nature," were at the corners of the World-Honored One’s mouth;
one must realize the two characters, "movement and stillness," by searching beneath the feet of Dharmapāla.

Although this does not yet constitute great penetration or great awakening, compared to what came before—when one mistook the floating sense-roots for the faculty of seeing and took dark appearances as the object—it is a vast improvement.
It was not seen; yet, one has now caught a glimpse of a single fragment. Therefore, the Buddha permitted it, saying: "The term 'hundred jewels' is a designation for what is precious.
As for the 'wheel-palms,' these are the hands and feet of the Buddha, each of whose centers possesses the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel."
Generally, the World-Honored One’s three instances of pointing with his hand each have their own symbolic significance.
In the first instance, he clenches his fist, symbolizing the desire to shatter delusion and reveal the truth. In the second, he extends his hand to demonstrate that the truth is not delusion.

In this [third] instance, whether opening or closing [the hand], it precisely symbolizes the clear distinction between truth and delusion, while foreshadowing their mutual integration. This is what is meant by the principle—
It is difficult to know. The Sage must demonstrate it; this is what is meant by "characteristics. II.
Revealing immovability by means of the internal faculties:
Thereupon, the Tathāgata [extended his hand] from the wheel-marked palm... (until) "who could cause it to shake? The Buddha said, "So it is."
This uses the head of the interlocutor as the internal faculty (*indriya*) in order to demonstrate that the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is immovable.
Having previously distinguished between movement and stillness in relation to external objects, there was a concern that a distinction between "internal" and "external" might arise;

therefore, the Tathāgata caused light to fly from his palm to the interlocutor’s left and right, causing him to look around. He then questioned him with respect to the internal faculty, saying: "Your head..."
"Why are you shaking today? The Venerable One replied, "I saw the Radiance of Jewels coming toward my left and right;
therefore, as I looked to the left and right, my head moved of its own accord. To say that the head moved of its own accord at the very moment the occasion arose is already an error.
If the head could move of its own accord, how would it differ from the eyes being able to see of their own accord? Furthermore, even a dead person...
"There is a head here; can it move? Yet the World-Honored One did not attend to this, but merely relaxed his grip for a moment and pursued him, saying:
"You are gazing at the Buddha’s radiance. When your head moves to the left or right, is it your head that moves, or is it your seeing that moves?
The practitioner immediately replied: "It is my head that moves of its own accord; as for my seeing, it is still non-existent."
"Movement! How could there be stillness? It is merely that the head moves of its own accord. Who would say that my seeing-nature is either moving or not moving?
In the preceding passage, the objects moved while the seeing remained still, which was easy for people to discern.

Here, however, it is within a single body that the head moves of its own accord while the seeing remains unmoving; this is truly difficult for people to discern. And yet, I, the Tathāgata, because..."

What he says should likewise be confirmed with the response: "So it is. The World-Honored One had Ājñātakauṇḍinya describe the two terms "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*) and "host sky" (*mukhya-ākāśa*);
this was intended for the listener to recognize that adventitious dust does not exist apart from the host sky. Thus, the purpose of the teaching was fulfilled.
Who would have known that upon reaching this point, one merely understands the distinction between the movement of adventitious dust and the stillness of the host sky, yet fails to realize—
Guang shook his head and moved; all this was movement of his own mind. Thus, he betrayed Gautama not a little.
△ Third, because he clearly knew it was false, he admitted the deluded movement.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly (until): "In this cycle of birth and death, they themselves take up the flow and turn."
This reprimand is directed at those who are ready for it. Since they clearly know that [the nature of reality] is immovable, yet they recognize false movement;

furthermore, regarding "those sentient beings," this is a veiled reference to Ānanda and others. Since that which wavers is designated as "dust" (*rajas*), one should know that dust does not exist apart from space.
Since that which does not abide is designated as a "guest," one should know that wherever there is a guest, there must be a host. You all—
"O assembly, simply observe Ānanda’s head as it moves back and forth; when you see that there is nothing moving, you will then be able to identify the host by means of the guest.

Furthermore, simply observe my hand as it opens and closes; when you see that there is no expanding or contracting, it is only logical that you should perceive emptiness through the dust. Why is it that until this day, although you have [perceived] movement..."
This is to know that what moves is the guest-body; why then do you not recognize the eternally abiding host?
Since you take that which oscillates to be the realm of objects, you continue to lose yourself in the tranquil void. In sum, you fail to penetrate the One Mind.
Therefore, within these phenomena of sense-faculties and objects, from the beginning of birth until the end of death, you cling to this [body] in every thought-moment. Thus, life arises.

To extinguish deluded thoughts and mistake them for the mind, while conversely neglecting and losing the birthless, deathless, eternally abiding true nature—is this not a case of placing one's crown upon one's shoes, acting with inverted priorities? It is because they have lost the truth regarding their original nature and mind.

One inevitably recognizes external objects as oneself; thus, one falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristics of one’s own body and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one’s own mind.
Consequently, when the nature of the faculty loses its true essence, one mistakes the floating sense-organs for the capacity to see;
when the mind loses its true essence, one conversely clings to the faculty of discernment as one's own mind. All of these are instances of recognizing external objects as oneself.
This is a clear proof. "Within this" refers to being within the midst of these two: the deluded body and the deluded environment.
"Taking it for oneself" means that this cycle of saṃsāra and its wandering are not created by Heaven or established by Earth, nor are they bestowed by humans;
they are all taken up by oneself. So who else could one blame?

△ III. Manifesting that Vision is Undestructible (III) A. Inquiry (I) 1. The Assembly’s Request with Mindful Intent.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [requested] the nature of the two luminous manifestations of arising and non-arising/non-extinction.
This passage describes the state of confusion and awakening among the great assembly. Their intention was to seek the Buddha in order to clarify the two natures.
As for "composure" (*tai ran*): because they had previously heard the Buddha reject the capacity for mental deduction as being non-mind, their bodies left their seats and their minds became startled.
Furthermore, hearing that there is no substance apart from sensory objects, although their mouths remained silent, their hearts were already lost. Thus, whether in body or in mind—

Neither of us felt at ease. Now, having heard the Buddha’s eloquent exposition on adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*) to clarify that the mind is fundamentally empty, and knowing that the nature of seeing is immovable—this being the wondrously luminous true mind—and further receiving two successive confirmations, our alarm and doubt have somewhat subsided;
thus we have attained composure of body and mind. With the thought "since beginningless time," etc., I acknowledge the benefit of the previous refutation of delusion and reflect upon it.
"I regret my past errors. "Today I have attained awakening," and so forth—this refers to receiving the benefit of the manifestation of the Truth above.

"To rejoice that today is right" means that the fundamental mind is precisely the originally existing true mind, while "discriminatory shadow-events" refer to the aforementioned mind capable of deliberation;

this clearly explains how one has been consistently deluded regarding the Truth and has identified with the false. "Attaining awakening" means realizing that the previously mentioned deliberating mind is but a shadow.
Matter. Now, seeing one's nature as the true mind—this clarifies the distinction between the true and the deluded, so that the eye of wisdom and the mind are opened and enlightened.
Previously, identifying with the deluded was like a child who has lost its mother; the life-force of wisdom was on the verge of extinction.

Now, having attained the vision of one's nature, it is like encountering a compassionate mother; the life-force of wisdom can be restored. How fortunate this is! For this reason, he joins his palms and bows to the Buddha.
And so he thanked him. However, this single ritual of thanks not only expresses gratitude for what has preceded, but also requests what follows;
thus, he wishes to hear about "body" and "mind. Based on the previous words of the Buddha, [the questioner] asks: "Why do you now take movement as the body and movement as the object?
Why do thoughts arise and perish moment by moment, causing you to lose the true nature and act in delusion? Therefore, there is this request. The underlying meaning is: "How is it so?"
Regarding the truth of the mind: what constitutes the falsity of the body? What is empty and what is real?
Please point these out directly before my very eyes in the present moment. What is subject to arising and ceasing, and what is not subject to arising and ceasing?
Based on the natures of these two—truth and falsity—I earnestly entreat your compassion to explain them clearly and in detail. For falsity is itself emptiness.
Arising and ceasing. "True" means real, which is precisely non-arising and non-ceasing.
△ Second, the King’s departure and inquiry.
At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha... (up to)... all those with outflows wish to hear this.
This king personally confessed his nihilistic views and heterodox doubts, inquiring about the correct principle of neither arising nor ceasing.

Because the king had formerly served non-Buddhist teachers, he had long harbored nihilistic views; now, having encountered the appropriate occasion, he heard that the Lord is empty, eternally quiescent, and that the nature of seeing is immovable.
For this reason, he harbored doubts and requested the Buddha to resolve them for him. Those who have not yet received the Buddha’s instruction are thus pointed out.
This was during the time when the Buddha had not yet appeared and the Dharma had not yet been heard.

At the time of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, there were six heterodox teachers who, throughout the various large and small kingdoms of the five regions of India, each used false teachings to convert kings and ministers. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
In the city of Rājagṛha, there were six teachers, including Pūrṇa, who claimed, "We are omniscient ones," and thus stood as rivals to the Buddha.
Kātyāyana—*Kātyāyana* being his clan name (*gotra*)—was named Kālābudha, meaning "Ox-Neck";
he was the fifth of the six teachers. That man asserted that one should kill all living beings if one lacks shame and remorse.
One does not fall into hell; it is like empty space, which receives neither dust nor water. Those who possess shame and remorse fall into hell.
All sentient beings are created by Īśvara. When Īśvara is angry, sentient beings suffer;
when Īśvara is pleased, sentient beings find peace and happiness. Pūraṇa Kāśyapa says that [the mother] is not to be called "mother."
His own name was Śaṅkha, which means "Righteous Victory" (Zhengsheng). He was the third of the six heretical teachers.
That man claimed that all sentient beings were created by a Sovereign (Ruler), who is as autonomous as the earth, which carries both the pure and the impure; the three great elements are likewise so.
Just as one might wash, burn, or blow [upon] them, they are like a withered tree stump in autumn that grows back again in spring; because it grows back, one should cut down the stump.

"What fault is there? [They claim that] one dies here and is reborn here again; that the retribution for suffering and pleasure is experienced here not through the manifestation of karma, but because there is no cause in the past or present and no fruit in the future. Both of these individuals take annihilationism as their tenet.
This is truly because they do not understand that the ālayavijñāna, which precedes death and follows birth, is the root of saṃsāra."

This constitutes the realization of wisdom; it is the primordial essence of nirvana. Yet, one instead falls into erroneous calculation, asserting that the annihilation of this body is itself nirvana—is this not a grave error?
Furthermore, "nir" signifies non-arising and "vāṇa" signifies non-ceasing; thus, it is non-arising and non-ceasing.
This is called "nirvāṇa. Yet they falsely and erroneously claim that after death there is annihilation, where neither suffering nor pleasure exists, nor even the nature of seeing or hearing;
this they call the "quiescent nirvāṇa. Furthermore, they repudiate the causes and effects of the three periods of time.
How could this not be false view? It is exactly like the calculations of those in this land who hold that the *hun* ascends to heaven and the *po* descends to earth;
all such views belong to this same category. How could they know of one who dies yet does not die? My thought is this:
although I have encountered the Tathāgata, I still harbor doubts. I do not yet know how the World-Honored One will manifest the truth for me and provide instruction.
I strike [the drum] to cause them to personally realize and know that within this body of birth and death, there exists a state that is neither born nor extinguished.
If this is clearly understood, not only will false calculations be eliminated, but the true mind may also be made manifest.
This ground of non-birth and non-extinction is precisely the eternally abiding true mind. By means of this principle of true permanence, it is not...
"I alone wish to hear it. Indeed, among the present assembly of those still subject to outflows (*āsrava*), there is none who does not likewise wish to hear it.
The fox is a beast of doubt; generally, those among humans who possess much doubt resemble it.
△ II. The Exposition (2) A. The Exposition that the Body Undergoes Transformation (1) 1. A Brief Explanation of Transformation and Extinction.
The Buddha addressed the Great King: "Your body exists at present... [up to] "...it shall eventually reach total extinction. The Buddha said: "It is so."
This Buddha, wishing to demonstrate that within birth and destruction there exists non-birth and non-destruction, first scrutinized their nature of birth and destruction. His intention was this:
"You claim that after this body dies, it is annihilated. For now, I shall not inquire about what happens after death; I ask only about the present."
"Is this physical body of yours identical to a vajra, indestructible? Or will it ultimately undergo decay?
He replied, "This body of mine will eventually return to transformation and extinction. The Buddha questioned him further, "Your body is currently present and has not yet perished;
how do you know that it will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction? He replied, "Although this impermanent body..."
It has not yet ceased. However, as I observe its thoughts arising and thoughts ceasing, they pass away without stopping; what was just new becomes new again, continuing on without abiding.
This movement of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flows like fire turning to ash—gradually diminishing and gradually perishing.
Because of this perishing, there is no cessation. For this reason, I am certain that this body is impermanent. It is fixed.
"It shall cease only after it has been extinguished. Because this cause does not abide in the present, one knows that it must necessarily cease in the future.

Why wait until death to know this? The Buddha said, "It is so. Since the King has described impermanence as shifting and passing away from moment to moment, its principle is necessarily thus. Therefore, I confirm it, saying: 'Truly so; truly it is.'"
△ Second, the detailed exposition on transformation and destruction.
"Great King, your current age has already reached old age" (extending to) "therefore you know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and destruction.
This is the sequential exposition on the transformation and destruction of youthful and aged appearances. From "Great King" downwards, up to "the state of full vigor."

At that time, [the Buddha] distinguished their appearances from youth to old age; from the words spoken by the Buddha down to the end of their transformation and cessation, he then analyzed the gradual stages of that transformation and cessation.
Therefore, the Buddha asked: "In your current age of life, you are certainly already decayed and aged.
As for your countenance and features, how do they compare to when you were a youth? The King then replied:
In the past, when I was a mere infant, my skin and its textures were moist, supple, and radiant.
As I grew into adulthood, my essence was complete and my spirit sufficient; thus, my vital energy was abundant and my blood was full.
Now that my age has declined, constrained by decrepitude and senility, my physical form is withered and parched, my complexion is haggard and emaciated, and my essence...
Then one’s physical resources are exhausted and the spirit becomes dark and obscure. One reaches the stage where the skin is like that of a chicken and the hair is white as a crane;
walking is unsteady and decrepit, and life is pressed against the setting sun, such that one will not last much longer.

How can this be compared to the time when the vital energy was overflowing, the blood full, and one was in the prime of youth? This is a disquisition on the differing appearances of the three stages of youth, maturity, and old age.
Next, the gradual process of transformation and destruction is explained. The Buddha then asked: "The appearance of your body must not have decayed all at once;
it must have reached this state by degrees. The King replied: "Worldly transformations shift subtly and imperceptibly.
I truly do not notice them, yet I see only the passing of days and months and the alternating succession of cold and heat until I have gradually arrived here. For what reason..."
The manifestation of light and shadow involves both extension and contraction. Let us consider this for a period of ten years.
When I was twenty, although I was called young, my countenance already showed signs of aging. By the time I reached thirty from being ten, I had further declined compared to when I was twenty.
Now, at sixty-two, if I look back upon my fiftieth year, it appears as if...
Yet, even for the strong and robust, is it not the case that they undergo a transformation every ten years?
As for me, seeing this subtle shifting, though my youthful complexion fades day by day, I call it "passing away"; as the signs of old age press upon me daily, I designate it as "falling.
However, because these transitions and changes occur within that interval, to limit the discussion to a period of ten years is merely to speak in broad strokes.

If I were to further engage in subtle reflection and investigate its transformations to their ultimate limit, would it be only that there is one transformation every twelve years, or two transformations every twenty-four years? In truth, there is indeed one transformation every year; yet how could it be limited to annual change?
There is also a transformation every month. Not only does it transform monthly, but it also shifts every single day. If one were to sink even deeper into this...
When one reflects and examines with careful discernment, one finds that within this single thought-moment there are ninety *kṣaṇas*.

From moment to moment, throughout every succession of thoughts, all are in a state of flux, never remaining still for an instant. Thus, one knows that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and perish.

At first born, one is called a child (*hái*); as one grows slightly older, one is called a youth (*rú*). The outer layer of skin is called the epidermis (*fū*); the texture of its lines is called the pores (*còu*).
At twenty or thirty, one is said to be in full maturity; at seventy, one is said to be in decline; at eighty or ninety, one is said to be in senility.
Now, at sixty-two, one is approaching decline; hence it is called "pressing. "To reach" (*dai*) means to arrive;
it signifies that the time of death is drawing near. As for "years" (*ji*), this refers to twelve years. Having reached sixty-two now and looking back to fifty, this constitutes...
One *kṣī* (a period of twelve years). Thus, it is reduced by approximating it to a *kṣī*. A *kṣaṇa* is the shortest unit of time;

since one thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) comprises ninety *kṣaṇas*, and because a sharp blade can pierce through ninety sheets of paper in a single thought-moment, one thought-moment contains ninety *kṣaṇas*.
This clarifies that the body undergoes transformation.
△ Second, clarifying that the nature is without arising or ceasing (II). 1. Questioning, establishing, and consenting to the explanation.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "You have seen these transformations... (until) I shall now show you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished."
This inquiry establishes that within the process of arising and ceasing there exists that which neither arises nor ceases, as it is so taught.

When the Buddha met King Ajātaśatru, he recounted the sequence of arising and ceasing with such meticulous detail that it could demonstrate the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, he asked him:
"Since you already know that within this momentary body arising and ceasing ceaselessly continue until they finally reach total extinction, can you know this momentary body..."
"Is there anyone among them who has not perished? Upon hearing these words, the king was suddenly struck with awe. He joined his palms and replied, "I truly did not know this;
it is something that even a righteous king has long been ignorant of. Had I known this earlier, how could I have been deluded by the heretics?
The Buddha said, "Since you do not know, I shall now point it out to you. [The Buddha] said: "As for your..."
Prior to the nature of arising and ceasing, the King requested the ground of non-arising and non-ceasing; here, the Buddha granted the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
This is the correspondence between the request and the grant.
II. Manifesting Non-Cessation (2): 1. Manifesting that what is seen is unchanging.
"Great King, at what age did you see the waters of the Ganges? [The King replied: "At the age of sixty-two, they were no different.
This passage uses the waters of the Ganges to demonstrate that the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is unchanging.
The Buddha first restated the words of King Amara, and subsequently examined whether the Ganges water seen at age three was the same as that seen at age thirteen.
"How is the water of the Ganges? The King replied, "It is exactly as it was when I was three years old;
there is not the slightest difference, even now that I am sixty-two years old. From this one can know that although the seasons have changed, what is perceived remains unchanged.
Thus, 'unchanging' means 'immutable. Jīva—here translated as 'Longevity'—is the custom in the land of India."
They all serve the deity of Longevity. Whenever a child reaches the age of three, they visit that temple to express gratitude for having been granted life and to pray once more for longevity.
△ Second, clarifying that the seer does not perish.
The Buddha said: "You now [observe] your own aging—hair turning white and face wrinkled... (omitted)... you all claim that after this body dies, it is completely extinguished."
This is precisely the nature of seeing, demonstrated to show that it is neither born nor extinguished. Therefore, he restates it, saying: "Now you yourself suffer from white hair and wrinkled face;
compared to your time as a youth, you are certainly different. Yet, does this seeing of yours when observing the river change with age?
The King replied, "No. The Buddha then pointed out: "Though your face is wrinkled, this seeing within remains the same."
The essential nature of the river’s manifestation has never been wrinkled. That which is wrinkled undergoes change, whereas that which is not wrinkled does not change.
That which changes is subject to extinction; that which does not change is fundamentally without birth or death.
Since there is neither birth nor death, how could it again undergo your birth and death within your body of birth and death? It is already present before you.
If they do not even admit its arising and ceasing, yet claim that after death it undergoes total annihilation, is this not utterly erroneous?
How much more so when they cite Makkhali Gosāla and others, asserting that the complete extinction of this body after death is called *nirvāṇa*;
this is the height of error. Makkhali did not even recognize the word "Dharma" (the Way). As for Kūṭadanta, his mother’s name was...
Furthermore, that person claims that the defilements and stains of sentient beings have neither cause nor condition;

this is the second of the Six Heretics, all of whom take annihilation as their primary tenet. Because this chapter follows the King’s contemplation within his own body, it results in [the view of] annihilation.

The Buddha, however, elucidates from the perspective of insight, and thus there is neither arising nor ceasing. This precisely means not departing from the path beneath the flowers, leading [the way].

"Entering the Cave in the Middle of the Sky. This not only dispels the King's doubt regarding annihilationism, but also fulfills the request of the one present to clarify the nature of the mind through the two kinds of illumination.
△ Third, the realization and understanding.
Upon hearing these words, the king came to believe in what occurs after death; he leaped for joy with a delight such as he had never experienced before.
This concludes the benefit specifically for the king: whereas previously he was confused by the view of annihilation and harbored doubts, he now understands the process of rebirth and rejoices.
These words refer to the aforementioned statement that the body does not perish nor remain unchanged when crossing a river.
As for "casting off birth and proceeding toward birth," it means that one casts off the preceding aggregates (*skandhas*) and is subsequently born with the succeeding aggregates.
Regarding "attaining what was never before attained": in the past, because one had not yet seen one's nature, one thought it would be annihilated;
now, having attained the vision of one's nature, one finally knows it is not extinguished. Thus, what is attained today is precisely what was never before attained in the past.
△ 4. Manifesting that Vision is Not Lost (2) 1. The Question.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, [and said: "I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements."

This refers to the practitioner who, having heard the preceding passage stating that "that which is unchanging is fundamentally without arising or ceasing," consequently gave rise to doubt and requested clarification.
Thus it is said, "If this seeing and hearing are necessarily without arising or ceasing. This is precisely the point where doubt arises.
Now, while the preceding section mentioned only "seeing," the present one adds "hearing"; this demonstrates that by citing a single instance, all four modes of being are encompassed.
"The six are the essence. I mean that if the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth were subject to arising and ceasing, they could be called lost or forgotten.
Since this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither arising nor ceasing, they are quiescent and eternal; they are thus equal to those of all Buddhas, without any distinction.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One say only of us that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion, while [saying nothing of] the Buddhas?"
"Is this not also called the loss of the inverted nature? Yet I am entangled by the two obstacles, like being stained by dust and grime;

I pray that the Buddha will arouse his compassion and wash me clean once and for all. How could I have known that when the Buddha speaks of the 'loss of the true nature,' he speaks of it as 'lost' only because of inversion, and not in the sense of a total annihilation?"
△ Second, the demonstration (in two parts): first, using the analogy of turning the arm downward without fault.
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm (until: all people of the world gazed upon it with double the intensity.
This refers precisely to the inversion of the arm; it serves as a metaphor for non-loss. Since the Buddha’s birth is of one essence, there has fundamentally been no loss from the beginning;
it is merely due to inversion that they appear different. However, the inversions within the mind have no form or color, making them inherently difficult for people to know.
Therefore, the Buddha manifested images to demonstrate them, so that people might easily see and easily understand. Thus, by means of—
With his thousand-spoked wheel hand hanging down and pointing downward, he asked Ānanda, "Do you see my hand as upright or inverted?
Having once encountered this "spicy hand," Ānanda did not dare decide for himself; yet, he could not remain silent.
He thus shifted the blame onto others, saying, "The sentient beings of the world consider this to be inverted. Then, seeking to clear himself completely, he added, "But as for me..."
[The monk] did not know. [He thought,] "Who is upright and who is inverted? The World-Honored One followed his words and pursued him, saying:

"If people of the world consider this to be inverted, then by what standard would they consider something to be upright? At that moment, the disciple was caught by the hook of the Tathāgata’s single word;
he could not escape it and was forced to reply: "If the Tathāgata were to point upward toward the sky with his hand..."
This is what is called "correct. The World-Honored One, taking a mistake as a mistake, raised his arm and said:
"If this were so, it would be upside down; there is but one arm. Therefore, pointing upward is called 'correct';
when has it ever increased by even a single thread? Pointing downward is called 'upside down'; when has it ever decreased by even a hair's breadth? Even if one were to turn it upside down,"
It is simply one hand; there is nothing other than the exchange of head and tail. It is merely taking the head that was upright above and exchanging it for the tail that hangs below.
This clarifies that although there is an inversion, the arm has never been lost.
As for this appearance of the inverted head and tail, you and the people of the world alike look up at it while looking down.
It is manifest and evident, and exceedingly clear. Why, then, do you speculate that worldly beings take this to be inverted, while you yourself do not know who is right and who is inverted?
*Bai* (倍) means "similar" or "of the same kind," and also "intimate.
*Mudrā* is translated here as "seal" (*yin*), which refers to the hands forming a seal. It involves the movements of the Buddha’s hands, turning them over and up and down.
Reclining and stretching like a lotus flower, opening like the act of bestowing and receiving, its form subdues demons and outsiders—there is nothing that is not a seal.
Therefore, it is called "Seal-Hand" (Mudrāhasta).
△ Second, the analogy of the mind being inverted yet without loss (three parts): First, citing the Dharma to directly apply the analogy.
Thus you know that your body and those of all Tathāgatas—[omitted]—the nature of your bodies is inverted.
This directly cites the dharmas of the two bodies of the born and the Buddha, using the metaphor of joining two hands to illustrate the relationship between the upright and the inverted.
This follows from what was said above: since the hand is thus, you should know that your body and the Buddha-body can likewise be understood through analogy.
This has been elucidated. The body of the Tathāgata is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

It is like a hand that, though it does not increase in size, points upward toward the sky; then the head is truly the head and the tail is truly the tail, and the whole world considers this to be correct.
Your bodies, which are termed "inverted by nature," are like a hand that, though it does not decrease in size, hangs down with its arm extended and fingers pointing downward.
Then the head becomes the tail, and the tail becomes the head; the whole world considers this to be an inversion.

This is merely the natural alignment of phenomena as they have not yet emerged, which is why they appear in such an inverted manner. Therefore, the subsequent passage instructs one to contemplate this with careful attention.
△ Second, causing one to contemplate perversion.
"Follow your careful contemplation of your own body and the Buddha-body" (up to) "...you do not know where the perversion of body and mind resides.
This [passage] regarding causing one to contemplate perversion is as follows: while the perversion of the hand is easily known by people, the perversion of nature—
People are inherently difficult to enlighten; therefore, I have commanded you to contemplate with meticulous attention, wishing to cause you to attain sudden self-awakening.
Thus it is said: "Let you examine and observe with thorough discernment: if your physical body is compared to the Buddha’s golden body, then your body is called 'inverted.
Since there is the name 'inversion,' there must necessarily be the reality of inversion."
From what actual basis do these names and designations arise such that they are called "inversions"?
Yet Ānanda and the great assembly, confronted by this single question, were as if carved from clay or wood; they stood dazed, not knowing where these inversions lay.
This was truly because they had not realized that all phenomena are mind-only. Had they known that all phenomena are mind-only...
As for the mind, both body and mind are nothing other than objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind; thus one knows the locus of the inversion of body and mind.
It is for this reason that my previous refutation of those who have lost the true nature is fundamentally based on this point.
"Following" (sui) means to allow things to be as they are. "Name" (mingzi) is like a designation or label. "Staring fixedly" (dengzhishi) describes a state of being dazed;

"blurred" (meng) refers to a state of mental confusion and lack of clarity, where the eyes are not bright. "Blinking" (shun)—also written as "xun"—refers to the movement of the eyes. To say "not blinking" means that the pupils are fixed and motionless.
△ Third, the comprehensive demonstration of the correct and the inverted (3): 1. Citing past teachings to clarify what is correct.
From "The Buddha gave rise to compassion and pity for Ānanda" to "the objects manifested within the true, essential, wondrous mind."
This citation introduces the teachings commonly expounded to clarify the meaning of "Right and Universal.

As for the term "Ocean Tide Sound," it clarifies that [the teaching] issues forth in response to the capacity of beings and speaks when the time has arrived; it is like the tide of the great ocean, which never fails its appointed hour.
Furthermore, its sound is perfectly pervasive, just like the ocean tide, being universally complete and all-encompassing. This is because it accords with the capacities of those present.
To fail to realize that the single thought-moment of the present is the nature of seeing and hearing, which is unmixed with sounds and forms, is precisely the true mind.

Its substance pervades the Dharma-realm and its magnitude is equal to empty space. Yet, to delusively identify this wretched body composed of the four elements and this mind that is but a shadow following the conditions of the six sense-objects as one's own self is no different from abandoning the great ocean to cling to a floating bubble. Therefore...
The Buddha, pitying their inverted views and lamenting their ignorance, did not wait for them to inquire, but out of unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*), spoke directly to them, saying:
"I have always taught that phenomena such as form and mind are manifestations of mind alone.
That which you call the body of the four great elements, and that which you call the mind that sees and hears, are both this present single thought-moment, unmixed with anything else."
Sounds, forms, seeing, and hearing are merely objects manifested by the true mind.

Because the nature of our present seeing and hearing in this very moment is free from names and transcends all signs, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). Because it is penetratingly clear and vacuous yet responsive, it is called "luminous" (*ming*).

Because its essence is without falsehood or delusion, it is called "true" (*zhen*). Because its nature is without defilement or admixture, it is called "refined" (*jing*). Unifying these four meanings, it is inconceivable.
Therefore, it is called the "wondrous mind. "Form" refers to the eleven types of form-dharmas; "mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings;
"various conditions" refer to the arising of mind—where four conditions give rise to form—and the two conditions that govern the mental concomitants, which are the fifty-one mental factor dharmas;
"various objects of cognition" refers to the twenty-four types of non-associated formations, the six types of unconditioned phenomena, and so forth.

These are all phenomena—mundane and supramundane, defiled and pure, including both the environment and its inhabitants. The aforementioned phenomena constitute the five stages of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), which comprehensively encompass everything;
yet they all arise as manifestations of the true mind, like objects reflected in a mirror, inseparable from the mirror and devoid of any substantial essence that can be apprehended.
[The text] asks regarding the six kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena: can the first five be said to be non-existent?
[Question: Its substance is ultimate suchness (*tathatā*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, its name is provisional while its substance is real. How can you say it has no substance?
Is it not like the images of objects in a mirror? [Answer: This fundamental scripture is the perfectly complete and substantial Great Teaching.

The suchness spoken of therein is established in contrast to the delusory. Since it arises through such opposition, it itself becomes a delusory dharma. Therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "By speaking of the delusory, the various truths are revealed."
"Delusion. Both 'true' and 'false' are equally delusions. That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), without arising or ceasing, and unreal—like a flower in the sky—is this very thing.

He asked again: "Previously, it was stated that the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*) is the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* and acts as the manifestor. Now, according to this statement, the *ālayavijñāna* is itself the manifested object.
Does this mean that apart from 'Mind-only,' there exists another True Mind? The answer was: "The preceding seven [consciousnesses]..."

The Dharma is merely that which is manifested by the true mind, which alone acts as the manifestor. Because the *ālayavijñāna* functions as both the manifestor and the manifested, when contrasted with the purely true mind, it is demoted to the status of the manifested;
yet when contrasted with the phenomena of the preceding seven consciousnesses, it is elevated to the status of the manifestor.
However, this is not of two distinct entities from the perspective of the true source; thus it is said that they are "neither one nor different.

That the ālayavijñāna is thereby established is precisely due to this. Therefore, when a Tathāgata awakens to this mind, the beginning is truly the beginning and the end is truly the end—just as the index finger on a hand, though it has not increased in any way, is universally regarded as being upright. This is the [realization] of the Tathāgata.
The body is that by which one becomes a Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
△ Second, the reprimand for acknowledging delusion as the cause of perversion:
"How is it that you have lost the original wondrous [nature]... (until)... all are things within the wondrously luminous true mind?"
This rebuke concerns the neglect of the true and the recognition of the delusory. Its meaning is:

"How is it that you all have lost your own wondrous mind and wondrous nature, instead falsely recognizing the state of delusion within that which is fundamentally devoid of both delusion and enlightenment?
Thus, Wénlǐng says: "Fundamentally wondrous" means it is inherently wondrous from the very beginning, not requiring cultivation or effort. Now, as for the mind and its nature—

The essence and its function are designated differently. As for the mind (*citta*), it arises from the wondrous as clarity; it is perfectly integrated and illuminating, fundamentally without movement, like the light of a mirror.
Therefore, it is called the "perfectly wondrous and luminous mind. This is the subtlety of its function. As for its nature (*prakṛti*), it is wondrous precisely because of this clarity;
it is凝然 (quiescent) and profoundly still, beyond comparison with any thing, like the substance of a mirror. Therefore, it is called the "precious, luminous, and wondrous nature."
This essence is wondrous. Yet this mind and this nature—their total substance and great function—are originally and inherently possessed by you yourself;
how could you have lost them? Why, then, within your awakening, do you mistake it for delusion? For all phenomena arise from this.

All that appears is manifested by the mind alone; this is primordial awakening. Failing to realize that one’s own mind is this primordial awakening, one instead falsely identifies the four elements as the body and conditioned reflections as the mind.
This is precisely what the practitioner does when taking movement to be the realm of the body and the capacity for deliberation to be one's own mind;
these are all instances of falsely identifying deluded sentiments within the heart of primordial awakening.

This is precisely what is meant by taking an object to be oneself; is this not delusion within enlightenment? Nevertheless, if one explains this enlightenment and delusion in terms of the correct and the inverted, they become perfectly clear.
For there is fundamentally no mind of delusion or enlightenment, just as a hand fundamentally has no "correct" or "inverted" side.
Yet, we speak of delusion and enlightenment because sentient beings distinguish between the correct and the inverted. Therefore, one awakens to this.

Because this mind is inherently correct, the Buddhas are called "Perfectly All-Knowing. Because one is deluded regarding this mind, it is called "inversion," and thus sentient beings are said to have "inverted natures.
Yet, correctness and inversion exist only within the palm of a single hand; likewise, delusion and awakening reside solely within a single mind.
Now, while abiding within the originally awakened mind, one instead identifies with deluded sentiments; therefore, it is said: "to identify with awakening."
This is delusion within awakening. Therefore, the following section uses body and mind to clarify the reason for this delusion within awakening.
Now, this wondrously luminous mind-nature is fundamentally devoid of both delusion and awakening; the characteristics of body and mind all arise from the luminous essence of the nature of mind.

At the very beginning, failing to awaken, one suddenly gives rise to delusion. Originally, there was neither confusion nor enlightenment; the true mind and the true mark are the emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Yet, through obscurity and darkness, they became the insentient and unawakened "stubborn emptiness" (*jaḍa-ākāśa*). This is what is called the arising of ignorant craving;
from this arising, universal delusion is produced, and thus the nature of emptiness comes into being. Because one is confused regarding the luminosity of the nature, ignorance (*avidyā*) is formed.
Therefore, it is said that "obscuration" (*huìmèi*) is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). From this ignorance, a stubborn void (*wánkōng*) arises;
thus it is said to be "voidness. This is what the Sūtra means when it says, "Due to delusive confusion, there is empty space.
Because the two dharmas—the manifested void and the manifesting ignorance—conjoin, it is said: "Within the obscuration of the void. Now, this "darkness" is itself ignorance.
Within the state of karmic entanglement, there arise the external forms of the four elements, mountains, rivers, and the world-system as the environmental retribution (*pratyaya-āśraya*).
Therefore it is said: "The binding of *asmitā* (ego-consciousness) becomes form. This is what the Sūtra means when it says: "When *saṃjñā* (perception) becomes clear and settled, it forms the land.

Because the false conceptualizing mind mingles with the characteristics of the four great elements, there arise the internal forms of sentient beings—the five aggregates and six sense organs—as their primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*). Therefore it is said: "The characteristics of *saṃjñā* [become form]."
Regarding the body: "conception" (*saṃjñā*) is the deluded mind, and "form" (*nimitta*) is deluded matter. When matter and mind combine, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are complete.
As the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings are nothing but cognition. This is precisely how the body recognizes delusion within its own awakening.
Since there is thus the root-body internally and the vessel-world externally, the deluded thought and the conditioned mind— [End of excerpt]
Accumulating within, it then internally conditions reflected images, oscillating without ceasing; externally conditioning actual forms, it rushes forth without end.
Worldly people do not realize that this is originally the mark of ignorance’s successive coarse agitation.
Furthermore, they mistake this internal oscillation and external flight—the state of delusion and turmoil—for the very essence of reality.
This is one's own true nature of mind; it is precisely within this self-awakening of the mind that delusion is recognized.

Once one has become deluded regarding this, one takes that which is darkly turbulent to be one's own mind, and remains resolutely unchanging, asserting, "My mind is within the physical body," dwelling therein upon the lump of flesh. This is utterly not so.
Know this: both the physical body within and the deluded mind without, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are all merely images manifested within my wondrously luminous mind.
Therefore, what was said previously—that "your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the true mind"—is precisely correct.
This is because you have lost sight of the vast and pervasive mind that permeates the entire Dharma-realm.

Yet, on the contrary, one identifies with the mind of arising and ceasing within this insignificant body. Is this not a case of recognizing delusion within awakening, thereby creating one's own inversion?
△ Third, the analogy: though inverted, it does not lose its essence.

For example, from "a clear and tranquil ocean of hundreds of thousands of miles" to "the Tathāgata calls them pitiable," although this metaphor is inverted—like a hand hanging downward—it serves to clarify that the nature is never lost.

Indeed, the hundreds of thousands of oceans are a metaphor for the true mind, which is precisely the present moment of thought; it is the nature that is not intermingled with form, sound, seeing, hearing, and so forth.

That which is not pervasive yet appears pervasive refers to the substance of a single bubble; this serves as a metaphor for the nature of the sensory perceptions, discriminations, and views of the object-conditions grasped by the practitioner.

That which is not localized yet appears localized refers to abandoning the Truth and identifying with the delusion—like discarding the ocean while identifying with a bubble—and grasping the delusion as the Truth—like seizing a single bubble and calling it the entire tide. To identify with the bubble while abandoning the ocean is already a state of deluded inversion.
How much more so for one who clings to a single bubble, believing it to exhaust the entirety of the ocean’s expanse, and designating the whole as the "Great Ocean" or the "Small Bo Sea.
Is this not a person who, amidst delusion and inversion, adds yet another layer of double delusion? This precisely clarifies the meaning of being inverted from beginning to end:
it is like my hanging my hand downward; although nothing is diminished thereby, the entire world [perceives it otherwise].
Because you regard this as inverted, your bodies are thus of an inverted nature.
Furthermore, when you say that you do not know the location of the inversion of body and mind, that very statement is itself the location of the inversion of your body and mind.
Moreover, you originally have nothing lost; it is only because of this inversion that you speak of loss. The Tathāgata calls this "recoverable."
This refers to those who possess compassion. If one has truly lost [the truth], they are not worthy of pity;
however, because people are now constantly as if they have lost it due to their inversions, they are deeply pitiable and objects of compassion.
△ Section Five: Revealing that Vision Has No Source (2) 1. Requesting Instruction Out of Doubt.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction... [until] "...uprooting my roots of doubt and returning to the Unsurpassed Way."

This describes raising doubts in order to seek instruction. Regarding "the profound instruction of compassionate rescue": the meaning is that while one was formerly submerged in total perversion, one now receives compassionate rescue;
while one was formerly utterly lost regarding the wondrous mind, one now receives profound instruction. Thus, one is moved by the Buddha’s deep compassion.
Therefore, I shed tears as a token of my gratitude. Yet, I still harbor doubts; thus, I join my palms once more and say:
"Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and awakened to the wondrously luminous nature of the mind, which is my own original, perfect fulfillment,"
Encompassing the ten voids and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it neither arises nor ceases; fundamentally, there has been no loss.
It is the ground of mind that is eternally abiding and unchanging. Yet we have always neglected this mind, mistakenly identifying the subjective faculty of cognition as the mind;
thus, it is only fitting that we are called those whose nature is inverted. Nevertheless, today we hear it manifest before us.

Regarding the sound of the Dharma: when manifesting the realization of the true mind, one invariably employs the conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*). Thus, this conditioned mind is precisely that which we look up to for reliance and upon which we depend.

Although the World-Honored One did not wish for us to recognize it as such and instead rejected it as "not the mind," if it were merely some other kind of conditioned mind, it might indeed be discarded.
However, as for the sound of the Buddha-Dharma, it is only by means of this [conditioned] mind that one can receive, listen to, and comprehend it. Only then...
It is currently being employed; how could one suddenly abandon it all at once? Because its function is being realized, one cannot help but acknowledge it.
What the World-Honored One requires me to acknowledge is the perfect, wondrous mind. Although it is vast and great, its function is not yet manifest at present;
I have merely obtained it in vain. Therefore, I still do not dare to acknowledge it as my original, fundamental ground of mind.
This is so. If one recognizes this, then one ought to discard that; yet now, since you cannot bear to discard that, you likewise do not dare to recognize this.
Why? It is said: if you discard the mind of causal conditions, what will there be to receive and uphold the Buddha-Dharma hereafter?
Even if you do not begrudge that causal mind, would you not alone hold the Buddha-Dharma in high esteem? This is why you hesitate, unable to settle upon a definitive choice.
I take my leave. I pray that the Buddha will uproot the roots of my doubt and enable me to return to the Unsurpassed Way.
The Perfect Sound possesses three inconceivable qualities: first, those from different regions and diverse species all hear it as their own original voice;

second, whether their capacity be great or small, shallow or deep, they all receive benefit according to their understanding; third, even those separated by distance who possess the karmic affinity perceive it as if it were right before their eyes.
"Those who pull out the root of my doubt" refers to the doubt concerning the mind that takes objects as its condition. Its roots are deep and its foundation firm; it cannot be removed by oneself.

I pray that you rely upon the Buddha's power to pull it out for me. This reveals that the practitioner’s habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from extensive learning are profound and difficult to eliminate.

It is precisely at this juncture—when the provisional mind and the true mind are both maintained yet one cannot decide between them, and while they waver in a state of instability—that one must simply wait.

At the end of the third fascicle, each person knows for themselves that their mind pervades the ten directions; having attained the original wondrous mind and the ground of the eternally abiding mind, they finally dare to let go and take full responsibility.
△ II. Exposition (2) A. Refuting that the mind which perceives conditions has a point of return (1) 1. General statement of the Dharma and the analogy.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You and others still [regard]... because there is nothing to be cognized; you are also like this."
This is a general metaphor for clinging to the teachings while losing the mind. It is because the previous passage stated: "I have awakened to the Buddha’s manifest preaching of the Dharma-sound;
I now employ my conditioned mind to respectfully gaze upon it. Thus, one knows that the practitioner values the Dharma-sound as the ultimate truth.
Failing to realize that one is merely becoming attached to the words and迷失 (losing) the principle, one loses the intended meaning of the teaching. Therefore, the Buddha established this metaphor.
I enlightened them, intending that I had expended so much speech and effort solely to eliminate this discriminating mind and thereby accord with true nature.
Who would have known that until now you all still listen to the Dharma I preach with a discriminating mind?
Since you listen to my teaching on the perfect and wondrous mind-dharma with a deluded, discriminating mind, then this mind—
The Dharma also becomes a false object of perception; one cannot thereby attain the truth of its *dharmatā*.
Since the teachings are used to expound the truth, and that truth is the very mind of sentient beings, how can one cling to the teachings while losing sight of the mind?
One must realize that the one who preaches the Dharma is like a person pointing at the moon, while the listener who hears the Dharma is the one looking at the moon. This...
The finger is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s vocal teachings; the moon is a metaphor for the mind of one who grasps the Dharma in its entirety.
If one claims that by means of my vocal teachings one illuminates one's own mind, this is like looking at the moon by means of the finger.

To hear the teachings and contemplate the mind while disregarding the finger is to be merely turned by the sensory object of sound. To cling solely to language and written characters is to mistake the finger for the moon.
Not understanding how to reflect back upon one's own mind and thereby losing the lunar disc—this is not merely the loss of the moon; it is also the loss of the finger.
This is a direct metaphor for not only failing to realize one's own mind, but also being ignorant of the intent of the teaching. Why is this so?
Because they mistake the pointing finger for the bright moon, this metaphor illustrates taking the external voice of the teaching as one's own mind;
since self and other are not distinguished, they lose sight of the finger alone, but furthermore fail to recognize the moon itself.
Thus, they not only fail to understand the meaning of the teaching, but also fail to know its principles and its essence, for the essence consists of the phrases, names, and sounds.

Because it belongs to the realm of sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Darkness is the principle that is our own true mind, and therefore it is luminous. As for the phrase "Why is this? below, it interrogates the luminosity in order to point to the essence:

while darkness is the finger, the nature of the moon is luminous. If one were to mistake the finger for the moon, then the two natures of light and dark could not be distinguished. This serves as a metaphor for teaching:
because it belongs to the realm of sound-objects (*śabda-viṣaya*), it cannot perceive or illuminate, just like the finger. The mind is fundamentally spiritual awareness; it is endowed with...
There is cognitive illumination, like the moon. If you cling to the teachings while losing sight of the mind, then you will mistake the dust of non-illumination for the mind of illumination.
Consequently, the two aspects of illumination and non-illumination become muddled, and you can no longer distinguish between them; how foolish this is!
Now, you take the sound of the Dharma as the object of cognition and give rise to a mind that cognizes it; thus, you have lost your way.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā)—how is it different from observing a finger and taking it for the moon? It is like a person who, placing a finger where the moon should be, cannot distinguish between light and darkness.
Therefore, it is said in summary: "It is also thus."
△ Second, the specific demonstration of that which is subject to return (in two parts): First, a brief clarification of the absence of intrinsic nature.
If one discriminates my teaching through the sound of the Dharma (up to: how can there be a non-discriminative nature apart from sound?
This clarifies that the mind which perceives conditions is not of a permanent nature. Above, the objects of perception were eliminated;

here, the perceiving mind is eliminated. The intent is this: if the mind that discriminates the sounds of the Dharma were your true mind, then this mind should naturally possess a self-nature capable of discrimination even apart from the sounds of the Dharma that it discriminates. This would be possible.
Now, that which lacks intrinsic nature is like a guest who stops for a time and then departs; it never remains permanently.
That which possesses intrinsic nature is like a host who goes nowhere at all—just as with the keeper of a pavilion. Thus, while guests come and go, the host remains constant.
The same is true for the true and the false aspects of the mind. If you take that which is able to discern the sounds of the Dharma to be the true mind, [you are mistaken].
In that case, this mind should abide eternally by its own nature apart from the sensory object of sound.
Why then, when separated from the sound of my preaching the Dharma, does it lack your discriminating nature?
△ Second, the detailed demonstration that there is a place of return.
This is not merely a matter of the mind discriminating sounds (up to the point where it is said that each has its own place of return); rather, how can [the mind] be the master?
This detailed demonstration that there is a place of return is intended to clarify the true master, who has no place of return—just as with the original substance of an object.
Since these are your own possessions, there is nothing that can be returned. Therefore, following the previous statement, it is asked:

"Is it only the mind conditioned by hearing the Dharma that is free from the sound-dust and the nature of the mind capable of discrimination? Even your mind that discriminates my appearance is likewise free from my physical color, marks, and signs;
the nature of the mind capable of discrimination is also absent. In this way, it is not only because of the arising and ceasing of sensory objects [that the mind is empty].
The mind that perceives and hears through conditions is not your true nature;
even the mind that smells, tastes, and cognizes—once it is separated from the objects of fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental phenomena—is likewise entirely devoid of the nature of true mind.

Reaching this point, both the discriminating mind and the objects discriminated by it are universally quiescent; therefore, it is said that they are "entirely non-existent. This extends even to the internal guarding [of the mind].

"Secluded and tranquil": this is a realm that is neither form nor emptiness. It merely suppresses the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the preceding six consciousnesses so that their discrimination no longer functions;

it is like the waters of a river or lake which appear level from afar, yet in reality flow on without ceasing. This precisely refers to the seventh consciousness taking the eighth consciousness as its object;
because it is detached from the five external sense-objects, it is said to be "not form. Because it clings to the internal [consciousness] as a self, it is not emptiness.

Therefore, it is said that this is not emptiness. Thus, those such as the Kauśīlīs conceive of this as the *ātman* (self); being deluded and ignorant, they establish it as the "Lord of the Primordial Darkness" (*ādikāra-pradhāna*).
This is still not true, let alone the active engagement with objects and the blazing proliferation of conceptual discrimination.
Hence, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists extend to eighty thousand kalpas; beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is pitch black."
They do not know [the truth], and thus they call it the "Primordial Darkness" (*ādikāra*). From this, consciousness first arises; therefore, it is called the "Primal Truth" (*pradhāna*).

It is also called the "Nature of the World" (*prakṛti*), meaning that the sentient beings of the world possess this nature by virtue of the Primordial Darkness; it is, in other words, the fundamental nature of the world.
It is also called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*). This means it exists spontaneously, having no origin. Thus, from the obscure (*amita*) arises awakening (*buddhi*);

this is also termed "the Great" (*mahat*), which is the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava-vijñāna*). From awakening arises the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the "divine self" (*puruṣa*).

From the I-consciousness arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); from the subtle elements arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and from the gross elements arise the eleven faculties (*indriya*). By means of the divine self...

It is the Lord. Abiding in the center, it is immutable and indestructible, encompassing all phenomena. There are twenty-four principles (*tattva*), which constitute "that which belongs to me" (*mama*);
these all depend upon the *puruṣa*, and are thus called the "Lord Principle" (*īśvara-tattva*). When the subject and object are discussed together, they form the twenty-five principles.

One who is detached from the conditions of all phenomena [realizes] that through this *pradhāna* (the Unmanifest), the objects of cognition (*viṣaya*) are extinguished, and the *puruṣa* is the subject.
The deluded mind takes as its object the so-called "spiritual self" (ātman). Apart from the dharmas that serve as its objects, it likewise lacks any inherent nature of discrimination.
From this it follows that when one discriminates sound, one returns it to sound; when one discriminates form, one returns it to form;
and even when one discriminates primordial matter (prakṛti), one returns it to primordial matter. If you recognize these discriminations...
They are distinct. Since you consider them to be the nature of the mind, each has already returned to its own source;
how then can they be the master that does not return? Kuśārī is simply another name for Maskarī Gośālīputra.
△ Second, revealing that the nature of seeing has no place of return. (iii) First, seeking instruction on its lack of return.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature each had a place of return... [until] I only pray that you will compassionately deign to explain this for me."

This is because, having heard that there is something to be returned, one seeks to demonstrate what is not to be returned. "To return" is like borrowed property, which must necessarily be returned to its owner;
if it were an object belonging to one's own household, there would be nowhere to which it could be returned. Therefore, the interlocutor said:
"If my faculties and the nature of the mind each have something to be returned, then as for the wondrous clarity and original [nature] spoken of by the Tathāgata..."
Mind. Why is it called "without returning"? I pray that you will take pity on me and explain this for my sake.
If the stainless one were to inquire with skillful means and pure questions: "Is it not the case that every person has a share in this, and each individual is perfectly accomplished? Is this so?
Qing said, "Indeed. The Official asked, "Why is it that there is no point of entry? Qing took a rosary from his sleeve and showed it to him, saying, "Whose is this?
The Official lowered his head and had no reply. Qing put it back in his sleeve and said, "If it were yours, you would have taken it;
as soon as one engages in thought, it is no longer yours. The Official was struck with awe. Thus it is said.
Know that as soon as there is discrimination, there is something that can be returned.
△ Second, the actual demonstration of that which cannot be returned (three parts): First, clarifying that the nature of seeing is itself the Truth.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Furthermore, when you see me... [up to] "...it is like a second moon; it is not the reflection of the moon."
This is intended to demonstrate that there is no returning. First, it clarifies that this very nature is the Truth.

Because the audience, upon hearing the preceding analysis, perceived that there is a "returning," they subsequently sought the wondrous mind that is without returning. Therefore, the Buddha showed them: "That which has no returning exists precisely within the place where there is returning;
one need not leave the waves to seek the water. Furthermore, as for you here before me, when you see me—first...
When thought has not yet arisen, there is an absolute absence of discrimination, unmixed with form; this nature of seeing is the true essence.
This radiance has been fundamentally present from the beginning, yet this essence of seeing has its substance permeated by delusion.

It divides itself into the six sense-fields, unable to turn back the six and lose the one, merging the profound with the profound; therefore, it is merely called the "Essential Source of the Clarity of Seeing."
Yet it is not called the "wondrously brilliant mind. This indicates that its substance already possesses brilliance and clarity; it merely lacks the "wondrous" quality.
Nevertheless, it is not identical to the wondrously brilliant mind, just like a second moon or a moon beside [the real one], produced by pressing on the eyes.
Although it is no different from the true moon, it merely has one extra "pressing"; it is not like the reflection of the moon in water.
The true moon and [its reflection] are as far apart as heaven and the abyss.

This is because the wondrously luminous mind-nature is vast and boundless, perfect and formless, and thus difficult to point out directly. Therefore, it relies upon the essence of seeing as a skillful means to indicate it.

If one awakens and enters through this essence of seeing, then the entire body and its great function are right here. Thus, there are three moons: first, the pure moon in the heavens; [the others being its reflections].

There are three moons: first, the moon itself; second, the moon produced by pressing the eyes; and third, the moon reflected in water. Now, the first moon is used as a metaphor for the wondrously luminous nature of the mind;
the second moon is a metaphor for the fundamental essence of seeing-clarity; and the third moon is a metaphor for the discrimination of objects.
Thus, one who has not yet attained the first moon should urgently recognize the second moon—just as one who has not yet attained the wondrous essence [must rely on its reflection].
