One who seeks to clarify the mind should urgently recognize the fundamental source of the clarity of seeing.

Although these two moons are not the pure moon, if one were to depart from the pure moon, these two moons could not possibly exist. Although the clarity of seeing is not the wondrous mind, if one were to depart from the wondrous mind, this clarity of seeing could not possibly exist.
Thus, one can see that seeing arises from the mind and is in its entirety identical to the mind; one should simply proceed from this point.
The seeing-essence enters into the true mind; however, one must not cling to the seeing-essence as being the true nature itself.
By removing the delusion within the seeing, that which remains is the true mind. It is like removing the pressure from the eyes—the true moon is revealed.
Certainly, it cannot be divided into two, yet it cannot be conflated into one either.
△ Second, showing that which is returnable is not the true [nature].
"You should listen attentively; I shall now show you" (up to) "everything that exists does not fall outside this category.
This is intended to demonstrate the vision that is non-returnable, and thus first marks out the characteristics of that which is returnable. Therefore, he warns him, saying: "You..."
Listen attentively. I shall now show you the ground from which there is no returning. This means that it is not a state characterized by return;
therefore, do not manifest a view of non-returning. For this reason, I first clarify that which can be returned from. Ānanda, do you see this great lecture hall?
When it is wide open and the morning sun rises in the east, you perceive the appearance of light; at midnight, during the dark of the moon or the new moon, [you perceive darkness].
When it is dark, one perceives the characteristic of darkness; through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives the characteristic of openness;
between walls and buildings, one perceives the characteristic of obstruction. By distinguishing these various locations, one perceives the characteristic of conditions (*pratyaya*).

That which is solid yet void and spacious is the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that which is turbid and murky is the characteristic of dust (*rajas*); and that which is clear and settled is [the characteristic of stillness].
"Vapor" refers to the appearance of purity. Yet, within these eight appearances, there is a distinction between the subject and the object.
Discursive, deluded vision belongs to the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*). The remaining seven types do not transcend light and darkness;

both form and emptiness pertain to the domain of the eye, and thus belong to the objective perceived (*ālambana*). Each of these subjective and objective appearances has its own cause; appearances depend upon causes.
Once they have formed, they are identical to transformations. You all observe these various transformed phenomena; I shall now each return them to their original causes.
As for what the original cause is, and from what substance it came, it likewise departs following that same substance.
Yet, each of these transformed phenomena has its own cause of origin; I shall now clarify how these appearances return to their source.
The solar orb returns to its original state as the dark phase of the black moon; the characteristic of pervasion returns to its original state as windows and doors;

the characteristic of obstruction returns to its original state as walls and buildings; the perceiving vision returns to its original state as conceptual discrimination; the characteristic of rigid emptiness returns to its original state as the vast void;

the characteristic of dense turbidity returns to its original state as fine dust; and the characteristic of clarity and purity returns to its original state as a clear, cloudless sky. Thus one knows that all phenomena in the world are...
All possible characteristics do not fall outside this category; they are all false and not real. Apart from sensory objects, they have no substance;
they all belong to that which can be returned.
△ Third, revealing that which cannot be returned is the truth.
"You see these eight kinds of objects; as for the luminous nature of seeing (the faculty of sight), it does not revert to them—if it were not you, who would it be?
This clearly demonstrates that the nature of seeing has no place of return, and thus it is the true master. The meaning is this:

when you see these eight kinds of phenomenal characteristics, your seeing remains distinct from the objects before it; within these eight appearances, the luminous nature of seeing must necessarily [remain].
At which sign (*nimitta*) do you wish to return? Why is this? If you were to return at the sign of light, there would be no time of darkness;

when the sign of darkness appears before you, with what then would you see? Although the various distinctions of signs such as light and darkness change incessantly, your essence of seeing perceives them all simultaneously; from this, it is sufficient to know that [the nature of seeing is constant].
These characteristics arise and perish of their own accord within your visual essence, and their individual forms undergo transformations;

yet your visual essence remains clearly manifest and unclouded, steadfast and unchanging. How could it possibly be the same as the deluded perceptions of discrimination that return along with light, darkness, form, and emptiness?
If both the subject and object and all such characteristics were capable of returning, then by nature, this would not be your true self.
"Nature. You should abandon it. Since this is your essence of seeing (*darśana-vijñāna*), it cannot be returned to various external forms;
it is your own true master. Suppose you say, 'It is not you,' then tell me, who else could it be? In this passage, the "essence of seeing" alone is pointed out as that which is non-returnable.
This is because the essence of seeing is not separate from the true nature; therefore, the text mentions the essence of seeing while simultaneously clarifying the nature itself.
Moving forward, this leads to the two kinds of false views—those of identity and difference.
Below this, one dispels this essence of seeing so that the true nature alone is revealed, just as when one removes a second moon to perceive the pure moon.
△ Third, the reprimand for self-immersion:
"Thus you know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, bright, and pure... therefore the Tathāgata calls you pitiable.
This reprimands the deluded recognition of the conditioned mind while mistaking it for the essence of seeing. The intent is that if one could know this essence of seeing, then—
I know that your true mind is fundamentally wondrous without depending on cultivation; it is fundamentally luminous without depending on polishing;

and it is fundamentally pure without depending on washing away defilement. It is only because you cling to this deluded mind of the perceiving subject that you have become confused and distressed by yourself, losing what was originally possessed and suffering in vain through the cycle of rebirth. Therefore, between these two states of birth-and-death...
Long subjected to攀緣 (parikalpa) and妄想 (vikalpa), you have drifted and sunk, with no time of emergence in sight; all this is what you yourselves have brought upon yourselves.
Therefore, the Tathāgata now says: "You are indeed to be called pitiable and worthy of compassion."
△ 6. Revealing that Vision is Not a Material Object (2) 1. The Appropriate Audience Poses a Question:
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of vision is without anything to be returned, how can I know it to be my true nature?"
This is an inquiry presented to resolve a doubt. The intention is this:

although I have received the Buddha’s instruction that this seeing does not return along with various phenomena, it nevertheless remains constantly mixed and indistinguishable from objects such as light, darkness, form, space, water, and land.
Now, among these various objects, how can one discern and know that this very seeing is my own self?
Is this its true nature?
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s correct revelation (in four parts): First, identifying the subject and object (in two parts). First, clarifying the nature of the seer.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “I now ask you... [down to] ...sentient beings see through their eyes, yet it does not exceed the breadth of a few inches.”
This clarifies the nature of the five kinds of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that can be seen.

It specifically describes how the practitioner in question, although he had not yet attained the pure divine eye through untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), was nonetheless able to see the first dhyāna by relying on the power of the Buddha, thereby obtaining unobstructed vision free from all hindrances.
Aniruddha said, "It does not perish"; because in the past he offered alms, he received merit that does not perish.

It is further said that he was never poor and constantly enjoyed celestial blessings; thus, when this younger half-brother of the Buddha was rebuked for sleeping during the day, he consequently abandoned his rest and eventually lost his sight.
Later, by cultivating the *sudarśana-vairocana-vajra-samādhi*, he attained the "half-head" divine eye (*ardha-śīrṣa-divya-cakṣus*).
Therefore, in response to King Brahmā Śuddhavāsaka, he said: "I see this Śākyamuni Buddha."
The three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is like an *āmala* fruit held in the palm of one’s hand.
The present mention of Jambudvīpa is because every great thousandfold world-system contains a Jambudvīpa; this particular instance is cited to reveal the general principle.
Thus, it is as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In all Jambudvīpas, it is said that the Buddha is therein. The *āmala* fruit is shaped like a betel nut (*pūga*).

Eating it dispels wind and cold. This is called "difficult to distinguish," for because the peach and the *nāi* fruit resemble one another, it is difficult to differentiate whether they are raw or ripe.
It is the local custom of that land to always hold this fruit in the hand; thus, it is taken as a metaphor. Regarding the bodhisattvas who perceive hundreds of thousands of worlds:
those of the first stage (*bhūmi*) perceive one hundred worlds, those of the second stage perceive one thousand worlds, and so on up to the tenth.
The Buddhas of the ten directions behold immeasurable world-systems as numerous as the atoms within unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, for there is nothing they do not gaze upon.
This is because the Buddhas possess the five eyes and exhaustively penetrate the entire Dharma-realm.

Yet, when it comes to sentient beings, although they see with perfect clarity, their vision does not extend beyond a mere fraction of an inch. This is what is meant by the saying: "If separated by a layer of paper or film, one cannot see external objects."

If separated by the skin, one does not see the five viscera. Nevertheless, to say that these five kinds possess the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is because seeing the first dhyāna is the nature of direct perception for the wisdom-eye of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Seeing Jambudvīpa is the nature of direct perception for the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Seeing hundreds of thousands [of worlds] is the nature of direct perception for the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) of a Bodhisattva.
This is the nature [of perception]. To see fine dust is the nature of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-eye as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
To see a mere fraction of an inch is the nature of the ordinary sentient being’s flesh-eye as direct perception. Because these five eyes differ, their five modes of direct perception likewise differ.

Nevertheless, they are all the direct perception manifested by the eight consciousnesses, which are what the seeing-nature illuminates; for the essence of seeing takes direct perception as its object-condition.
The objective realm (*viṣaya*)—the state where no discrimination arises—is itself true nature (*tathatā*). This reason is intended for those whose capacities correspond to the teaching.
As the previous question asked: "How can one know that this is my true nature? This is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of seeing nature; it is your own true nature.

Now, these five kinds [of objects] range widely up to the *dharmadhātu* and narrowly down to a mere fraction of an inch. Although their dimensions differ, the nature that is able to see them remains without distinction.
This is different.
△ Second, clarifying the objects perceived:
"Ānanda, furthermore, when you and I observe the Four Heavenly Kings... [down to] ...there is nothing that is not a prior object of the environment, a conceptual distinction, or a hindrance."
This refers exclusively to the objects perceived by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of those who are ready for the teaching.
My intention is to set aside the other four views for the moment; rather, let us speak based on your own direct perception of the nature of seeing.
For instance, when you and I observe the palaces where the Four Great Heavenly Kings reside, they are situated only at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru; yet, above...
Equal to the sun and moon, extending downward to the great earth, one surveys everywhere within this interval.
As for sentient beings, there are those dwelling in water, those dwelling on land, and those moving through the air; this refers to the locations where all categories of beings reside.
As for the characteristics of insentient things, there are those that are shrouded in darkness and murky, and those that are clear and bright.
As for "clear and bright," this refers to the appearances of morning and evening, sunshine and shade.
Yet these various sentient and insentient things, with their diverse forms and distinct images, are none other than objects distinguished by the external environment;
they are all that which confronts the eye, the realms that obstruct and hinder, and they are precisely what your vision perceives.
△ Second, the selection from within this context:
"You should, in this regard, differentiate between self and other (until) 'who is my own essence and who are external objects?
This is intended for the specific practitioner, to select the intrinsic nature from among the aforementioned subject and object of perception. Therefore, it says:"
"You should, regarding what I have said above concerning the seer and the seen, carefully analyze and distinguish between self and other.
'Self' refers to the nature of seeing; 'other' refers to objective phenomena. Yet, as for leading the practitioner to choose for themselves, this is precisely what is meant by the saying:
'One cannot walk another by taking them by the hand; only when the person is willing will they move forward. Therefore, I say now:"
"Regarding what you call 'leading' and 'following,' who is it that leads, and who is it that follows? My intention is this:
for now, I shall not reveal the truth to you. I wish instead to cause you to personally develop the eye of wisdom.
Within these two—subject and object—discern and examine them minutely: which of these is my Ānanda’s own essence of the nature of seeing that acts as the subject?"
It is that which sees. What is it that is seen? It is the forms and images of external objects.
By making such a distinction clearly and distinctly, you will naturally come to know your own nature. This is because of the previous question: "How can one know this as my true nature?
Therefore, the Buddha had him discern and select for himself; once he is able to select it, [he shall realize it].
Through this seeing-nature of mine, I naturally come to know my own true nature.
△ Third, the clear distinction between objects and seeing (4): First, the direct clarification that objects are not seeing.
"Ānanda, exhaustively trace the source of your vision from the palaces of the sun and moon down to blades of grass, shrubs, people, and animals—none of these things are you.
This was because, although the Buddha had previously instructed the disciple to personally examine and select for himself, he was unable to discern the distinction.

Therefore, from this point downward, the Buddha proceeds with four successive rounds of inquiry to clarify the matter. This section specifically clarifies that external objects and phenomena are not the seeing-nature itself.
This is the nature (*prakṛti*). It is the ultimate limit. To see the source is to see the nature. The meaning is this: exhaust the power of your eyes and exhaust the essence of your vision;
observe this most supreme object from the palaces of the sun and moon. This is the object, but it is not you.
Furthermore, he went to the surrounding Seven Golden Mountains and surveyed them thoroughly, observing these most inferior objects and phenomena.
Although they possess various kinds of light, they are nonetheless material things and not you. Not only those at the highest and lowest points, but even those far away gradually draw near.
He further observed the clouds rising in the midst, the birds flying, and the winds blowing.
From the arising of moving dust, up to trees, mountains and rivers, blades of grass and weeds, and humans and livestock—these are the appearances of objects situated in the midst or nearby;
they are all merely objects and are not your seeing-nature. As for what is meant by "who is the appearance of objects," it is these very things.
In Sanskrit, *Meru* means "light" or "radiance"; this refers to the [Mount] Meru, the seventh...
These are the Golden Mountains (*Suvarṇaparvata*). Because they possess golden radiance, these mountains encircle Mount Sumeru, standing in separate ranges between the seven seas;
all are composed entirely of pure gold. Their names are: first, Yugaṃdhara (Holding the Pair); second, Īṣādhara (Holding the Axle);
third, Kakuda (Carrying the Wood); fourth, Sudarśana (Good to Behold); fifth, Aśvakarṇa (Horse-Ear); sixth, Vinataka (Elephant-Trunk); and seventh, Nimindhara (Fish-Mouth).
Among these, light is most abundant; therefore, it is called "various.
△ Second, the correct clarification that what is seen is not an object:
"Ānanda, as for all these natures of objects, whether near or far... (up to)... this subtle, wondrous, and luminous clarity is truly your nature of seeing."

This correctly clarifies that the nature of seeing is not a material object. Since the preceding section pointed out that all material objects are not the nature of seeing, the nature of seeing itself should naturally be distinguished and extracted. However, because Ānanda does not understand this, [the Buddha] shows it again, saying:
"Ānanda, what you see now—whether near or far, large or small—all these various material forms and phenomena with their myriad states and ten thousand appearances."
They are arrayed before your eyes, yet your nature of seeing illuminates them all without omission.
Although these objects differ from one another in their various forms, they are all gazed upon by the single essence of seeing; they do not interfere with or confuse one another.
You should know that while the categories of objects possess their own inherent distinctions, there is no differentiation within your nature of seeing. This very essence of seeing remains unmixed.
That which is intermingled with objects is your wondrous, pure, and luminous mind. Therefore, know that this mind is truly not separate from the nature of seeing within your eyes.
Why, then, are you unable to discern it amidst these various objects? That which is called "Who is my own essence?"—this is it.
This precisely answers the question: "How can one know that this is my true nature?"
This is the question.
△ Third, the counter-argument that seeing is not an object:
"If seeing were an object, then your seeing would also be [an object]... (up to) ...it is naturally not an object; how could it not be you?"
This serves to clarify, by contrast, that the nature of seeing is not a material object. Continuing from the above, it says: "Is it only that objects are not seeing?
Seeing, too, is not an object. The intent is this: if your seeing were a material object, then my seeing would likewise be a material object;
in that case, you would also be able to see my seeing. Fearing that he might erroneously calculate that we both observe the four heavens equally, [the text continues].
When the royal palace and all other objects and phenomena are being perceived by the Blessed One, his vision is present within all those things.
Why then should I not also perceive them? Therefore, it is restated: "If you say that when you and I see the same object..."
"One who claims to see my seeing— when I withdraw my gaze and look inward, and do not see external objects—
why do you not likewise see my 'not-seeing' and point out exactly where it resides?
If, when I withdraw my gaze and look inward and do not see objects, you are unable to see my [not-seeing]..."
When you do not see that which is not seen—that is, at the very moment I am seeing an object—how could you possibly see my seeing of that object?
Fearing further erroneous calculation, [the text] states: "The time when I do not see is precisely the seeing of my not seeing the Buddha.
Therefore, it is refuted by restating: "If you claim that the time when you do not see is precisely the seeing of my not seeing, then if that were so..."
This is simply a place that you yourself do not see. Thus, it is not a characteristic of seeing that the Tathāgata does not see.
How could you, with your deluded mind, conjecture that what you call a "place where one does not see" is actually the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s seeing that he does not see?
If you truly do not see the ground where the Buddha does not see, then this seeing—
Nature is spontaneous; it is not a thing possessing characteristics. How could this not be your own self-nature seeing?
△ Fourth, a counter-argument that things are not seeing.
Furthermore, when you now perceive objects, [the text continues] until: "The nature of seeing is all-pervasive; if it were not you, who else could it be?
This is an inverted clarification that objective phenomena are not the nature of seeing. Continuing from the above:
if your nature of seeing were an object, then the object would also be your seeing. Yet, at this moment when you perceive an object, since you have already perceived the object...

If objects possessed vision, they would likewise see you; thus, the visual essence of sentient beings and the forms of insentient things would become hopelessly entangled and indistinguishable. Furthermore, your seeing and my seeing would both become objects of sight.
If this were so, one would not know who is "you" and who is "I," who is the agent and who is the object, or who constitutes the primary retribution.
Who constitutes the environment of support? Who constitutes my own substance? Who constitutes material phenomena?
If you, I, and all the worlds were thus indistinguishable as one, intermingled and impossible to separate, then no stable establishment could be achieved. Could such a principle truly exist?
Now, at the time you see objects and see me, if it were certainly your seeing alone and not my seeing, then you and I would be clearly established as distinct entities;
yet in that case, the sentient and the insentient, the self and the other, and the environment and its inhabitants [would all be separate].
Objects and phenomena are distinct from my body; they are clearly separate and unmixed. Thus, you should know that the nature of seeing is detached from all objects and phenomena.
Even as you now look at the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, down to blades of grass, shrubs, people, and things—all these are pervaded by your own nature of seeing.
None of them belong to objects, nor do they belong to me. Is this not your own nature of seeing? To whom else could it possibly belong?
"Worldly" (*loka*) refers here to the sentient and insentient realms. In Sanskrit, *naya* means "method" (*vidhi*) or "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*).
This is because various sutras and śāstras describe conventional truth as "established truth" (*prajñapti-satya*).
Now, "establishment" means that all mundane phenomena each have a fixed nature and cannot be confused; it refers to the established positions and the order in which they are set forth.
This is the boundary of their strength.
△ Fourth, rebuking doubt regarding one's own nature:
Why do you doubt your own true nature, thinking your nature is not true, and instead take me as the object to seek reality?
This reprimand is directed at the person present, who doubts their own nature. The passage beginning with "How could it be... is the formal expression of this reprimand. Its meaning is:
why do you not have confidence in yourself, but instead doubt yourself? This true nature is inherently yours;
the nature is fundamentally within you, yet you do not regard it as real, but instead take my words to seek its reality. Nevertheless, he continues to ask:
"How can it be known that this is my true nature? Is this not an error? △ 7.
Revealing that Vision is Unobstructed (3): 1. The Audience Doubts Obstruction Due to Objects.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing [is as you have described]... I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me.

This was to clarify that the nature of seeing is unobstructed. Because the audience had heard the preceding statement that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, they consequently suspected it might be obstructed.
Thus, giving rise to doubt, he posed the question: "If this nature of seeing is originally..."
If my true nature were necessarily not mixed with external objects, it should remain unchanging wherever I am.

Now, when I and the Buddha observe the jeweled palaces of the heavenly kings, or dwell within the two palaces of the sun and moon, looking down upon a single four-continent world-system, this vision extends throughout the entire realm; how vast is the Sahā world! And yet, when [the vision] withdraws...
Returning to the vihāra, he beheld only this garden; yet upon entering the hall of the Pure Mind, even as he looked upward and downward, he saw nothing but the eaves and corridors. How small it was!
World-Honored One, if the essence of this seeing-nature has from the beginning pervaded the entire Sahā world, then its greatness should certainly not become smaller; why is this?
Since it is now within this room, it fills the room entirely; yet its dimensions are so indeterminate.
Is it that the nature of seeing itself contracts its greatness to become small? Or is it that it is partitioned and severed by these walls and buildings, unable to continue?
Whether it is contracted or severed—the meaning must surely lie herein. I do not know what the principle of this is.
Therefore, I pray that you will deign to show compassion and expound upon it for me.

As for the "Victorious Treasury" (*jaya-garbha*), it is called the Victorious Treasury because the palaces of the celestial kings are a gathering place for all manner of jewels. The solar palace, moreover, is composed of fire-maṇi jewels.
The sun palace is fifty-one *yojanas* in size and is composed of water-mani jewels; it is forty-nine *yojanas* in height.
Within both, there are palaces, terraces, and ponds, filled with devas and humans. Although the sun palace is composed of fire-mani jewels, it is likewise cool like the moon;
it is only because its radiance is superior and descends below that it produces heat. Ānanda followed the Buddha.
At times he dwelt there. "Saha" means "endurable" (堪忍) or "able to endure" (能忍); in the Han language, it is called the "Realm of Endurance" (忍界) or the "Land of Endurance" (忍土).
It is named "Endurance" because all sentient beings therein endure the three poisons and various afflictions.

It is also called "Sahā," which means "Mixture" (雜會), for the six destinies and four modes of birth, as well as the holy and the ordinary, are intermingled therein. [The full name is]... (text incomplete)
"Sanghārāma" is translated here as "Garden of the Assembly. This is because "saṃgha" refers to the community of those who dwell there, while "ārāma" refers to the garden where they dwell;
thus, in the Western Regions (the lands to the west), temples are called *saṃghārāma*.
△ Second, the Tathāgata reveals that the nature is unimpeded (2): First, the formal explanation of non-obstruction.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "In all worlds... [down to] ...the nature of reality is thus; how could it have a location?"
This clarifies that both large and small are obstructions left behind by external objects; it is not that the nature of seeing itself expands or contracts according to size.

The meaning is this: as you have asked, regarding all worldly things, one may see the vastness of a single realm or the smallness of a single room, such as the interior and exterior partitioned by walls and buildings. These aforementioned phenomena, characteristics, and functional activities—
Each belongs to the sensory objects before one's eyes; one should not say that the seeing itself expands or contracts, or is interrupted or continuous.
For your nature of seeing is like empty space, while all sensory phenomena are like vessels.

Although the sensory phenomena have size, interior, and exterior, the nature of seeing has no expansion, contraction, interruption, or continuity. It is just as when a vessel is square or round, yet the space within it remains unchanged.
It has no fixed characteristics. You do not currently know the nature of seeing in relation to the characteristics of objects;
you need only observe an empty vessel, and then you will understand. Suppose there were a square vessel here: within it, one would see only square space. Let me ask you this:
Regarding this empty space within a square vessel: is its direction fixed or unfixed?

If it were fixed in direction, then when the vessel is replaced with a round one, the space should not become round; yet since the space becomes round because the vessel is round, its direction is unfixed.
If it were unfixed, then while inside a square vessel, there would have to be no "square space"; yet since [the space] conforms to the squareness of the vessel...
Space is also square; this, too, is a fixed direction. You must understand that both the fixed and the unfixed do not reside within space;
it is simply because the vessel exists that such is the case. As for your statement that you do not know where this principle resides:
regarding the nature of this faculty of vision—its expansion and contraction, its fixed and unfixed qualities—it is also like empty space in this regard.
This is precisely because the nature of seeing has no fixed location, yet it is not absent from anywhere.
Why do you now stubbornly cling to fixed principles like one who restrains the strings while playing the lute, insisting on seeking a single, definitive place where it resides?
△ Second, the successive explanation of the unimpeded nature.
"Ānanda, if you further wish to cause [the nature] to enter into that which is neither square nor round" (up to) "how could there be no trace of continuity?"—this meaning is not so.
This successive explanation demonstrates that the nature of seeing is unimpeded. Therefore it is said: "Ānanda, if you further wish to cause it to enter into emptiness..."

Regarding the nature of space entering into that which is neither square nor round: one merely removes the squareness and roundness of the vessel, whereas the essence of emptiness fundamentally lacks any characteristic of being square or round.
One should not say that after removing the vessel, one must further remove the location of the square or round characteristics of empty space itself.
The meaning is this: if one wishes to cause the nature of seeing to enter a state where there is neither large nor small, one must simply exclude the external objects;
for the nature of seeing itself is fundamentally without size. One should not say that after excluding the external objects, one must further exclude the location of the nature of seeing.
As for your question regarding entering a room, where the seeing contracts to become small—if that were so, then when looking up at the sun, [the seeing would have to expand].

It might also be possible to stretch it evenly toward the side of the sun. If walls and buildings could obstruct the view so as to cause it to be severed, then when a hole were pierced through them, one might likewise draw the view through to restore its continuity.
Now, observing that the sun cannot be pulled back to extend it into the room, how could it possibly be contracted to become smaller?
Since no trace of continuity can be found once the hole is pierced, how could walls and buildings ever obstruct it?

It causes [them] to be severed. Therefore, one knows that this interpretation is certainly not the case. "Entering non-existence" (rurū) refers to penetration and understanding. "Sin" (竇) refers to a hole or cavity.
"Wan-yin" (挽引) means to pull or draw forth. "Qi-deng" (齊等) means equality. "Ri-mian" (日面) is equivalent to the vicinity of the sun.
△ Third, the penetration of obstruction and non-obstruction.
From beginningless time, all sentient beings [have been] able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
This passage clearly elucidates the reason why sentient beings encounter obstructions while the Tathāgata is without obstruction. All sentient beings...
"Those who are born" refers collectively to ordinary worldly beings, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity within the Lesser Vehicle.

This is because ordinary worldly beings and non-Buddhists mistake external objects for the self, while those of provisional or limited capacity mistake the self for external objects; thus, they become obstructed. Now, objects are inherently incapable of obstructing, and seeing is inherently incapable of being obstructed.

Yet, that ordinary worldly beings, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity ultimately encounter obstruction is not due to the obstruction of objects. It is truly because of [the lack of... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated here].

At the outset, one loses track of one's own *tathāgatagarbha* mind, which transforms into the *ālayavijñāna*, manifesting as the two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*).
These appear as material and mental phenomena; thus, ordinary people and non-Buddhists do not realize that these material and mental phenomena are but bubbles and shadows of the true mind.
They grasp them as being substantially real and identify with them—this is what is meant by "mistaking objects for oneself."
Even those who provisionally employ the Lesser Vehicle and are sages do not know the subtlety of the *ālayavijñāna*, and thus they regard all phenomena as truly existing outside the mind.
Failing to realize that the myriad dharmas are mind-only, they become deluded regarding their own nature and treat themselves as objects.

Having lost the Tathāgatagarbha—the mind in which subject and object are one—they are not only unable to transform objects so they return to the mind, but rather allow the mind to be [enslaved] by them.
Objects undergo transformation; thus they shift and migrate according to external conditions and are obstructed by movement.

Consequently, regarding these sensory objects, one perceives them as large or small, calculating their contraction or expansion, entirely lacking any sense of autonomy. Thus we know that objects are fundamentally the mind;
when one is deluded and takes them to be objects, they then obstruct the mind. It is just as ice is fundamentally water; when it freezes, it becomes ice.
Thus they are obstructed by water; all this is to be self-deluded and self-obstructed.
For this reason, being turned by objects is what is called "birth"—that which is termed "the self-mind grasping at the self-mind, whereby non-illusion becomes illusory phenomena.
If one can turn objects, one is identical to a Buddha; this refers to turning the objects of the two divisions of appearance and seeing, namely form and mind. By means of these two...
It is like the two horns of a snail: when they emerge, they appear as a pair; when they retract, they become a single entity.

Now, simply by not following the conceptual discriminations of the world, the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) dissolves. Once the perceived aspect has dissolved, one is free from all grasping of body and mind.

Being free from such grasping, the perceived aspect naturally transforms—this is what is called "the profound entry merging with the profound," returning to the limit of consciousness (*vijñāna-paryanta*).
At this juncture, the essence of consciousness becomes perfectly luminous; when it is transformed into wisdom, it constitutes the Tathāgata-garbha mind.

Thus, one is immediately identical to the Tathāgata. As it is said: "If one does not grasp at anything, there is nothing that is not illusion. Since even non-illusion does not arise, how could illusory phenomena be established?
This is because, in a state of delusion, the body is but a tiny thing, confined and stagnant within its shell, while the mind is turbid and distracted, pursuing [objects].
When objects are partial and restricted, one is consequently turned by them and becomes obstructed. Now, at the time of awakening, all things are of one body; they are perfect and not partial.
Realizing that objects are but mind, one is luminous and not obscure. Therefore, both body and mind attain perfect clarity;
this is because one has turned objects into non-obstruction. Thus, one knows that mind and objects are quiescent and extinguished.
This is precisely the immovable site of enlightenment (*acala-maṇḍala*). Because the primary and secondary retributions are mutually interfused, a single hair-pore contains the entire realm.
Now, a single hair-pore is the smallest unit of the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while the ten directions constitute the largest unit of the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
That a hair-pore contains the ten directions means that the small subsumes the large; this is the integration of phenomena into principle, whereby all things are realized as one's own self.
This is because self and others are not separated by even a hair’s breadth. That the ten directions exist within a single hair is the entry of the great into the small;
it is the realization that phenomena are fused with principle. Thus, one uses the mind to fuse with the myriad dharmas, whereby a thousand differences are subsumed without obstruction.
Therefore, when being transformed, one observes the "great" as being encompassed by the "great," and observes the "small" as being encompassed by the "small. One recognizes form...
The mind is the substance of form; it transforms the perceived and the supporting, becoming the transformation of the supporting and the supported.

Now, when transforming objects, the one and the many are without obstruction, the small and the large are mutually contained, form and mind are non-dual, and the supporting and the supported are interpenetrating. Reaching this point, principle and phenomena are as one;
therefore, the body is identical to the mind, and there is no body apart from the mind. Thus it is said that the body and mind are perfectly luminous and one.
It is utterly motionless; this is precisely the site of attaining the Way. It universally constitutes one great treasury of radiant light (*mahā-avabhāsa-garbha*).

How, then, could there be any expansion or contraction, or any distinction of large and small? This is the very crux regarding whether birth and Buddhahood, or delusion and awakening, are obstructed or unobstructed.
△ 8. Revealing that Vision is Only the True (2) 1.
A Question. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision... [please] deign to bestow great compassion and reveal what I have not yet understood."

This summarizes the preceding meaning, as it gives rise to a doubt and difficulty. Having heard the Buddha say that this subtle, wondrous, and luminous clarity is truly your seeing-nature, and having further heard that this seeing-nature is all-pervasive—asking "if it is not you, then who?"—one thinks:
"If that which is currently pervasive throughout the myriad things is my essence of seeing, then this essence of seeing must necessarily be my wondrous, subtle, and luminous nature."
If this were so, then this wondrous nature would now be before my very eyes, yet it would be separated from my body.
This would mean that the pervasive seeing-essence—which I suspect must be my true nature—is instead outside of me.
If the seeing-nature is thus outside the body, then the mind within the body ought to...
"It is not the self. Furthermore, what kind of thing is this? For now, the mind within the body is truly able to discern that nature of vision;
yet, as for that nature of vision which pervades the exterior of the body, it has never separately distinguished itself.
It is able to differentiate my own body. Observing it in this way, that which is capable of discernment—"
"It seems to be within my own body, yet it is not that seeing-nature which pervades all things.
If that which pervades all objects were truly my mind, then it would mean that my own body is now being seen by it."
Since that [seeing-nature] is able to see, it is its pervasive seeing-nature; truly, truly, it is the self, whereas the body is not the self.
However, if that seeing-nature is outside the body and yet can see my own self, then it is the same as an external object being able to see me.
That an external object can see me was already refuted by the Buddha previously; why do you not [accept this now]?
Is this erroneous? Having investigated and pursued the matter through successive stages, I truly do not understand it. Therefore, I pray that you will bestow your compassion and further enlighten me.
Little do I realize that what the Buddha pointed out is the nature of seeing which is neither capable nor objectified—yet this is precisely what the practitioner clings to.
This is the state of mind and its objects, characterized by the duality of subject and object; there is no small amount of fundamental misunderstanding here.
△ Second, the definitive answer (in two parts): First, the simultaneous rejection of both paths (in three parts): First, the direct rejection of this view.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said... [up to] the Buddha saying, 'So it is, so it is.
This demonstrates that there is no seeing apart from objects, thereby dispelling this notion of 'seeing.

Although many points are refuted within the text, it is solely because the word 'prior' (*qian*) stands at the forefront as the root of that error. By refuting only this single word 'prior,' all doubts will dissolve. Such is the intended meaning.
What you have just said—that this which you see is right before you—is truly a mistaken and preposterous statement;

it does not accord with the principles you have established, nor is it a true principle. If this essence of seeing were actually present before you, and you truly saw its form and characteristics, then since it possesses form and characteristics, it must certainly have a specific location. Since it has a specific location, it would necessarily not be...
"It can be pointed out. Since it can indeed be pointed out, why do you not identify and demonstrate it to me?
Furthermore, as we sit here now in the Jeta Grove, observe the groves, the channels, and even the grasses and trees.

Although they differ in their minute details and sizes, whatever possesses form can all be observed with the eyes and pointed out with the finger to others. If this seeing-essence were necessarily located [within the body],..."
You should now come forward and, with your hand, definitively identify its characteristics. Point precisely to that location among all these objects;

clearly and without error, demonstrate to me which one is "seeing. Ānanda, you should know that whatever currently possesses form is nothing other than a material object, while that which is formless is empty space. Apart from these, there is nothing else.
There is nothing else to point to. If space were the essence of seeing, then since it has already become the essence of seeing, what else could be pointed to as "space"?
If material objects were the essence of seeing, then since they have already become the essence of seeing, what else could be pointed to as "objects"?
However, by raising the issue of emptiness in relation to phenomena, the myriad images are fully present. You should apply a further degree of subtle effort to these myriad images:

strip them away to reveal their opening, peel them back until they fall away, and dissect and analyze them to extract the clear, bright, and essential source of seeing—the pure and wondrous essence of vision.
This essence of seeing is fundamentally unstained by objects. It is not...
"Intermingled with phenomena, it is therefore said that purity is fundamentally neither identical to the myriad forms nor separate from them; hence it is called 'wondrous.
Furthermore, it must transcend the realm of things; one must not allow it to be covered or concealed, but point directly to it.
To present something resembling 'me' or the various appearances of objects, though clearly manifest, would still leave room for delusion. The practitioner replied:
Now, receiving the Buddha’s definitive command to peel away and analyze, I shall provide a thorough dissection of these myriad phenomena.
From the lecture hall nearby to the Ganges River afar; from the sun and moon above down to the Jeta Grove below.
Whatever can be observed by the eyes and pointed out by the fingers is entirely a material object; none of these possess this essence of seeing.
It is just as the Buddha taught: even a Bodhisattva cannot immediately extract the essence of seeing from the myriad phenomena to make it stand apart from objects and reveal its own nature.
If even a Bodhisattva cannot yet do so, how much less can I, a mere beginner?
This is precisely the meaning of what preceded; it is truly not the ultimate reality. Therefore, the Buddha granted his approval, saying, "So it is, so it is.
This was an acknowledgment that there is not a single thing, yet there is seeing.
However, while the World-Honored One’s question lay in non-identity, the disciple’s response lay in non-separation. This is the subtle excellence of the dialogue between teacher and disciple.
"Pei" means to open wide; "bao" means to strip away; and "xi" means to analyze and discern. As for the lion, it symbolizes fearlessness.
Just as the lion’s majesty subdues all beasts, the Buddha’s majesty shakes all malevolent forces.
△ Second, the refutation of that which is not seeing.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda, [saying] as you have stated... (up to) the Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
This reveals that apart from seeing there is no object, thereby refuting that which is not seeing. The preceding text clarifies that not a single thing exists.
If one sees, then it is clear that the nature of seeing inherently lacks the meaning of being "in front.
Here, it is clarified not only that this is so, but that there is not a single thing that is not seeing; how, then, could the nature of seeing possess the meaning of being "in front"?
The Buddha feared that the interlocutor would understand only that the nature of seeing is detached from all characteristics, without realizing that the nature of seeing is itself all phenomena.
Therefore, this is stated first. Those words serve to cite and confirm his intention, as if saying:
"If we rely on what you have said, among these myriad phenomena, there ultimately is no such thing as 'seeing. Now I shall further inform you:
even when you and the Tathāgata sit in the Jeta Grove, it does not hinder you from further observing the groves and gardens, as well as all manner of distinct and diverse phenomena. If...
It is certain that there is no essence of seeing within your clarity that can be pointed out for you to grasp.
How could it be that all material phenomena are truly not your seeing? You should, moreover, look further into the midst of these myriad phenomena.
Each and every one must be clarified. Furthermore, you should point out, among these various objects and phenomena, which one is not your seeing.
The disciple replied: "I have indeed observed the myriad phenomena extensively, yet I do not know which among these myriad phenomena is not my seeing.
Why is this? Although the myriad phenomena are many, let me now cite one or two as examples to illustrate the point."
This can be understood. If you claim that the tree is not the self and yet you see the self, then how do you see the tree?
If you say that the tree is itself the seeing of the self, then since the tree has already become seeing, why is it still called a "tree"?
In this manner, one may examine all phenomena exhaustively, pointing them out one by one, even unto empty space. If you claim that space is not the self and yet you see the self...
Furthermore, how can one perceive emptiness? If one says that emptiness itself is a view, then since emptiness has already become a view, how could it still be called "emptiness"?

I have further reflected that, within these myriad phenomena, upon subtle investigation, there is not a single thing that is not a view. Therefore, the Buddha also granted this, saying: "So it is, so it is."

This grants that there is not a single thing that is not seeing. Yet, while the World-Honored One’s question lies precisely in "neither being nor non-being," the disciple’s response, however, lies in "neither being nor non-being.
This too is the subtle artistry of the dialogue between teacher and disciple.
△ Third, the assembly is comforted by the Buddha.
At this, the Great Assembly—consisting of those who are no longer learners (*aśaikṣa*) [up to] you—should contemplate this with earnest attention so as not to disgrace our sorrowful longing.
Both of these reasons are affirmed; yet, because the hearts of the assembly were bewildered, the Buddha comforted them out of his compassion. This is truly due to...

Beginners, being provisional and limited, do not realize that the physical body and the objective world are both merely the laborious manifestations of one’s own mind, yet they cling to them as real entities existing outside the mind.
Consequently, they argue over what is right and what is wrong. Now, hearing the Buddha reveal this wondrous nature that is neither right nor wrong, they feel even more lost and find no foothold;
yet they fail to realize that from within the midst of right and wrong, one returns once again.

One must grasp this within the midst of "is" and "is not. Therefore, upon hearing the two successive approvals, one remains茫然 (máng rán—perplexed) and fails to understand the two meanings of being neither the view of "is" nor the view of "is not.
This is because at first one takes it to be the view of "is," and yet it is again the non-view of "is."
In the end, one must say that it is neither seeing nor non-seeing. Thus, if one traces back from the front, its beginning cannot be found;
if one measures forward from the rear, its end cannot be fathomed. It is truly difficult to find fault with this, yet it is indeed something to be alarmed by and indeed something to be terrified of.

Because right and wrong cannot be distinguished therein, one loses what they hold fast to. [The practitioner] thinks that if "this is so" or "that is not so" were determined with certainty, then one could remain steadfastly fixed;
but now, there is neither "so" nor "not so," as both are equally validated, and there is never any single certainty.
This is why people are struck with alarm and trepidation, thereby losing their composure.

Thus, the Buddha, knowing that their spirits were unsettled and their doubts manifold—whereby their minds were as bewildered as a wandering spirit, and their hearts were cowed with fear and unease—gave rise to a heart of compassion and comforted them, saying: "O sons of good family, do not be alarmed."
I am the unsurpassed Dharma King. Whatever I have spoken is entirely words of truth, corresponding to the reality of suchness as I have realized. It is not deceptive, erroneous, or false;
nor is it the claim of the Makkhaliputtas that there is an "Immortal Heaven" where one remains undisturbed for a lifetime and is reborn when answering others.
That deity established four kinds of evasive and confused discourse: namely, that "existence is non-existence" and "non-existence is existence";

"both existence and non-existence" and "neither existence nor non-existence. All of these maintain both possibilities and ultimately lack any certainty, serving only to delude and confuse the minds of people.
Now, to have neither this view nor that view is indeed the definitive [resolution].
Both are definitively dispelled, and neither is established. How could this be the same as the deceptive and indeterminate arguments of those sophists?

It is simply that your minds are coarse and your reflections shallow; you have not contemplated with careful discernment. If you would but contemplate with earnest attention, there will surely be a resolution.
I shall certainly not fail the heart of your sincere longing. For the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is subtle and its eloquent analysis is inconceivable. If [the previous...]
By using a single "Tut," the practitioner is made to startle with immediate realization. By using both [the negative and positive], the entire assembly is left bewildered.
Because delusion must be shattered instantaneously, it is swept away with a single stroke that cuts through both ends.

Because the Truth is difficult to state directly, it is clarified through a process of winding maneuvers—capturing and releasing. Herein, "true speech" refers to speech that accords with reality; it is definitively not...
This is an error. "As it is" (yathā-tathatā) means speaking of the True Suchness (*tathatā*) as it was realized by me.
"Without failing" means not being remiss.
△ Second, the correct elucidation of the One True [Nature] (2): First, Mañjuśrī’s request.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, [arrived] and questioned [the Buddha] regarding what is not this and what is not that.
Because the great assembly was bewildered and unable to pose such questions, Mañjuśrī took pity on the multitude and requested [the teaching] on their behalf.
Thus, with the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in devout sincerity, he petitioned, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Buddha has previously..."
I have clarified for the assembly that within the two categories of form and emptiness, there is fundamentally no such thing as "seeing" or "not seeing.
Yet, observing this great multitude, they not only fail to awaken to this truth, but harbor doubts. They think to themselves:
"If these manifestations of form, emptiness, and so forth were indeed my own seeing, then among all myriad phenomena, there should naturally exist..."
One can point [at things], yet one receives what is pointed out by me; why then can you not point now?
If these forms, emptiness, and other such phenomena were indeed not objects of my seeing, then among the myriad phenomena, there should be nothing at all that could be seen.
Why, then, can you still see them? Therefore, you do not understand the ultimate resolution regarding the two meanings of "there being no seeing" and "there being no non-seeing."

Therefore, there is alarm, doubt, and fear. Yet, although this great assembly still possesses outflows (*āsrava*), they are not like those of the past during the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* periods, when their roots of goodness were meager and insufficient to receive the Dharma.

I only pray that the Tathāgata, in his great compassion, will once again clarify for us: what are these various objects and phenomena, and what is this essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*) fundamentally and originally?
Regarding such objects: since the essence of seeing is found within these myriad phenomena, and yet there is neither a "seeing" nor a "non-seeing," what does this mean?
△ II. The Tathāgata’s Compassionate Instruction (II) A. Clarifying that the True Mind is Beyond Relativity (I) 1.
The Direct Exposition. The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: "...How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within this?"
This answers the preceding question, precisely revealing that the true mind is beyond all relativity, thereby clarifying that it is neither "is" nor "is not.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī because of his prior inquiry; he spoke thus so as to extend the teaching universally to the great assembly.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are those who have attained the ultimate fruit. As for "Great Bodhisattvas," this refers to those from the eighth stage upward who are able to abandon the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) and attain the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi).

"Abiding spontaneously" specifically distinguishes this from the concentrations of the provisional vehicles and the Śrāvakas; their contemplation of vitarka and vicāra involves emergence and entry, and thus they cannot abide spontaneously. This is *samādhi*.

This is precisely the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*. What is now called "abiding in oneself" means that by means of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvid-āryajñāna*), one dwells eternally in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
This is what is meant by the statement: "The *nāga* is always in meditative absorption; there is no time when it is not in absorption.

It is not like the provisional or limited concentrations that involve entering and emerging from samādhi. "Seeing" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and "the object of seeing" refers to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Thus...

It is the objective condition (*ālambana*) for seeing. "Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the deluded mind associated [with consciousness], while "characteristics" (*nimitta*) refer to the deluded objects of the external environment.

To discuss these collectively, they do not exceed two divisions. When ordinary beings, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas abide in this samādhi, they are able to transform the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Even the name "Ālayavijñāna" cannot be found; how much less so its objects!

Since even the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing faculty (*darśana-bhāga*) currently manifest cannot be found, how much less so can the deluded mind and deluded objects that arise from them?
Therefore, they are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally, they do not exist at all.
Below, I shall directly answer your question. Your previous inquiry to me concerned material phenomena and the essence of seeing.
What was its original nature? Why would there be right or wrong? Therefore, it is shown:
"This seeing and its objects are originally Bodhi, the wondrously pure and luminous essence. How could there be right or wrong within it?

This is because these two parts—subjective seeing and objective appearance—both rely upon the eighth consciousness and are of one and the same substance. Only if they possessed two distinct substances could one speak of right and wrong between them.
This seeing is non-seeing. Since they are now of one essence, how can one distinguish between what is seeing and what is non-seeing?

Furthermore, the substance of this consciousness is originally the bodhi of self-nature; it is inherently wondrous without depending on cultivation, inherently pure without requiring cleansing, and inherently luminous without needing polishing. Therefore, wonder is itself the Dharma.

The body is purity, which is liberation; clarity is *prajñā*. This is what is meant by being three while being one, and being one while being three—neither identical nor separate, neither vertical nor horizontal. It transcends all dualities and is far removed from subject and object;
it is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), the single true *dharmadhātu*. How could there be such views as "is" or "is not" within this?

"Do you see it? You should know that this manifestation of vision has reached its limit; this is precisely the Tathāgata exhausting all he possesses and presenting it as a gift, even including his own boat.
△ Second, the illustrative explanation.
"Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: as for you, Mañjuśrī [up to] 'in between there is neither this moon nor that non-moon.
This uses the provisional Mañjuśrī as an analogy to clarify that the single true Dharma-realm is fundamentally devoid of the two characteristics of being and non-being.
Therefore, he asks: 'As for you, Mañjuśrī, you are but a single essence; are you this true Mañjuśrī? [Is it so?]
Suppose we add another Mañjuśrī to this existing Mañjuśrī; would it be permissible to call him "this Mañjuśrī"?
Furthermore, suppose we subtract one Mañjuśrī from within this existing Mañjuśrī; would it be permissible to call him "not-Mañjuśrī"?
It is neither, for he is not so. Mañjuśrī is a person of great wisdom; therefore, with a single nudge, he turns. Thus it is said:
This very "I" is the one true Mañjuśrī. Beyond this, one must not further add another who is Mañjuśrī.
Why? If one were to further add another who is Mañjuśrī, then I would become two Mañjuśrīs.
However, since there is already this one true Mañjuśrī present today, it is also not permissible to call him non-existent.
Mañjuśrī, regarding the fundamental substance (*dharmatā*): if there were something further beyond it that could be described as "together with" the fundamental substance, then one might speak of it;

however, since there is absolutely nothing that can be described [as such], how could there be the two characteristics of "is" and "is not" within this present, singular fundamental substance? This is the correct analogy:
to remove the single true substance and then add the myriad phenomena (*dharma*) externally is a failure of vision; to subtract even one [phenomenon] is likewise a failure.
These myriad phenomena are not seen, yet they cannot be said to be unattained; for within the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), there is neither a single dharma added nor a single dharma lacking.
It is perfectly identical to the Great Void, being without deficiency and without surplus. The Buddha said:

"Since you know that in the original state, the sublime Mañjuśrī is fundamentally free from right and wrong, then this wondrously luminous essence of seeing, regarding the myriad phenomena of space and dust, is likewise [free from them]."
It is likewise so. This view [regarding] phenomena is, in essence, the wondrous principle that is neither form nor mind, the primordial luminosity that is neither born nor extinguished;
it is the very root of bodhi and nirvana, the true mind that is pure and perfect.
Due to its initial lack of awakening, a single thought of delusion arises, which, as the evolving karmic consciousness, constitutes this view.

The two aspects—the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). That which is subsumed under the objective aspect consists of the physical body, the sensory organs, the environment, and the myriad phenomena of form and emptiness.
That which is subsumed under the subjective aspect consists of the natures of smelling, tasting, sensing, knowing, seeing, and hearing.

This is because these two aspects—form and emptiness, and hearing and seeing—arise based upon the Truth (*tathatā*), like a second moon. Since they are like a second moon, one knows that they are fundamentally non-existent.
How can one, based on the second moon, give rise to false conjectures and produce notions of right and wrong, asking, "Which is the true moon, and which is not?
Thus, all such assertions of right and wrong arise solely from not having seen the true moon.
Mañjuśrī was simply able to perceive that the single moon is the reality; he did not falsely give rise to right and wrong within it.
This has been seen. Within this, the second moon differs from the former; the former was merely a metaphor for seeing, whereas this one also serves as a metaphor for both seeing and its object.
△ Second, concluding on the distinction between delusion and awakening.

Therefore, when you now observe the seeing and the objects (up to "is thus able to cause you to transcend 'pointing' and 'not pointing'"), this "knot" returns to the distinction between delusion and awakening. This is because, through delusion, "is" and "is not" arise;
through awakening, one transcends beyond "is" and "is not. Here, the word "you" (汝) refers back to the person addressed (*dengji*), and does not refer to Mañjuśrī.
Therefore, it is said that because you have not today awakened to the wondrously luminous true mind, you observe this essence of seeing amidst various sensory objects.
Within these two divisions, you employ all manner of clarifications, asserting what is right and what is wrong, what belongs within the sphere and what belongs outside it:
taking the internal as the root-body, the external as the vessel-world, and that which is between them as the consciousness-mind. If this were so...
Such categories as these are all termed empty, false, and floating thoughts; they are by no means real. For this reason, one cannot transcend the dichotomy of "this view" and "not this view.
It is just like pressing on the eye and seeing a second moon, then vainly engaging in conjecture, ultimately never escaping the deluded debate over whether it is that moon or not.
Suppose, however, that through this one could achieve a single moment of pure truth.

Severing both extremes and not establishing a middle, then throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is only the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity—neither true nor false—which is my own essence. This very substance is the one true dharma-realm;
thus, both the perceived object and the perceiving subject are but empty flowers. Therefore, it enables you to transcend the realm of right and wrong.
How could one, moreover, within the midst of the myriad phenomena, designate something as "seeing" that can be pointed out, or something as "not seeing" that cannot be pointed out?
It is just as when one knows the reality of the single moon, false conceptualizations completely vanish and the distinctions between right and wrong naturally subside.

These two instances of the character "pointing" (zhǐ) correspond to the "pointing" in the preceding passage, referring to the two cases of pointing to what is seeing and pointing to what is not seeing.
"Pointing" refers to words. Because one is deluded regarding the single true Dharma-realm, "pointing" becomes the finger and the non-finger.

If one awakens to this principle, one transcends both the finger and the non-finger; thus, one can emerge from the finger of the view of "is" and further emerge from the finger of the view of "is not.
It is evident that delusion and awakening, truth and falsehood, depend solely upon a single thought-moment. If for a single thought-moment there is false movement, one is deluded.
Then the mind and its objects will become chaotic, and right and wrong will arise like sharp blades.

If one awakens through a single thought of pure sincerity, then wondrous enlightenment is profound and still—transcending names and free from dependence, utterly beyond the reach of thought and speculation. How, then, could the dualistic views of right and wrong have any place within it?
△ 9. Manifesting that Vision Transcends Sentiment (3) 1. Transcending the Sentiments of Non-Buddhists (2) 1.
A Question. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma-King has said... [until] ...one attains the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind.”

Regarding the phrase "transcending conceptual thought": because natural causes and conditions all belong to the deluded attachments of non-Buddhists and those of provisional or limited capacity, this present seeing-nature is entirely distinct from them;
therefore, it is said to "transcend conceptual thought and perceive conditions," which is precisely the seeing-nature.
By means of this, one perceives nature. Whether perceiving light or darkness, perceiving obstruction or emptiness, one is able to awaken and illumine, universally taking all as objects;

therefore, it is termed "awakened objects. Because of the Buddha’s instruction, the practitioner realized that the essence of the refined vision of form and emptiness is fundamentally the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant body of Bodhi;
only then did he attain the understanding of the principle that the perception of nature is eternally abiding and all-pervasive.
Nevertheless, a doubt arose, for he feared that this might be conflated with the heterodox schools and thus contradict the True Dharma. Therefore, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Truly, as the King of All Dharmas has taught regarding the conditions of awakening—if it is indeed all-pervasive, indeed eternally abiding, and indeed its nature is neither arising nor ceasing—then would it not be identical to the 'Golden-Headed' heretics of the former Brahmans?"

Among the twenty-five principles established by their school, the *pradhāna* (primordial nature) is eternal, as are the various ascetics who smear themselves with ashes and so forth, who reckon that there is a *puruṣa* (spiritual self) pervading the ten directions.

Now, regarding this "condition for awakening" taught by the Buddha which pervades the realms of the ten directions—what difference is there between this and the *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* reckoned by them to pervade the ten directions? Furthermore, [it is the same].

In the past, the World-Honored One also dwelt upon Mount Laṅkā and extensively distinguished for Mahāmati and others the reasons why the internal teachings differ from those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
For those non-Buddhists constantly assert spontaneity (*svabhāva*), claiming that things are naturally so by their very nature.
As they say: "Who opened the rivers and seas and heaped up the mountains? Who pruned the thorns and painted [the world]?"
Among birds and beasts, there is not a single thing in the world that can give birth [to itself]. Therefore, all phenomena are spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
This, however, negates cause and effect and fails to establish cultivation and realization; thus, the Buddha extensively taught dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to refute it.
The principles explained in our own inner teaching are not the same as the realms clung to by those external paths. I now observe this...
Awakening to the nature of seeing through its conditions also constitutes spontaneity. Why? Because it is inherently present and never lost, it is said to be "not born.
Because it is ultimately indestructible, it is said to be "not extinguished. As the single true Dharma-realm, it is far removed from delusion;
as neither form nor mind, it is far removed from inversion. Therefore, within the myriad differences, it is manifested and perfected everywhere throughout the ten thousand phenomena.

Within this, each and every thing is uniquely revealed. If one infers from this principle, it seems not to accord with the former teaching on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), but rather resembles the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) clung to by those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

I do not yet understand how the World-Honored One distinguishes and reveals to us the difference between what the Tathāgata has taught and what those non-Buddhists have conceived, so that we may know they are indeed distinct.
The point of distinction is that only then will one not enter among the various heterodox paths.

Were it otherwise, should one fall into a heterodox way and again produce empty delusions, one would then be failing the sacred teachings of the past. This is why one harbors doubts and cannot reach a decision.
This is precisely for the purpose of attaining the true nature of the mind, as well as the complete essence and great function of subtle awakening and clarity.
Regarding "causes and conditions": "cause" refers to the seed that gives rise to birth; "condition" refers to the auxiliary factors that support and trigger development.

Just as with various grains and the like, they must take the root-seed as the cause and soil and water as the conditions before they can produce sprouts and develop stalks, continuing until [harvest].

It also flowers and bears fruit. This is because, in the past, the Buddha frequently spoke of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the sake of provisional and inferior practitioners who were ordinary beings, in order to refute the non-Buddhists' doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
As for the "former Brahmin" (*pūrva-brahmaṇa*): "Brahmin" means "pure lineage," referring to those who claim to be descendants of Brahmā;
"former" refers to an ancient person. He is Sāṃkhyakāra. According to the *Saptati-śāstra*, he is said to be this—

The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) arose from emptiness; they spontaneously produced four virtues and composed one hundred thousand verses, serving as the progenitor of the Six Teachers, and are thus called the "Ancient Brahmins" (pūrvavādin).

Those who "throw ash upon themselves" and so forth include such practices as going naked, plucking out hair, lashing oneself with thorns, and observing the precepts regarding cows, dogs, and other animals, as well as the "five heats" (pañcatapa) that scorch the body. This is because the Sāṃkhyas formerly practiced the consumption of milk.
The flight of the pigeon: all these various ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are their remaining lineages.
As for the "True Self" (*ātman*), it is precisely the mark of a self clung to by the non-Buddhists; yet there are three types: first, the large; second, the subtle;
and third, the vast. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "It cannot be reached, and its giving is similar to that [of others]. As for "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), it is...
What is called "originally natural" refers to their reckoning that all internal and external phenomena, from beginning to end, are without cause, without cultivation, and without realization.
This is because they do not know that within the *ālaya-vijñāna* both defiled and pure seeds are contained together;

thus, these seeds give rise to karma and moisten rebirth, serving as the very root for abandoning one life and receiving another. Yet, they instead falsely reckon that a true self exists inherently within the body.
They are constantly born in various realms, pervading the ten directions, yet this nature does not perish—is this not a contradiction? "Obtains" (huò) means "to acquire.
△ Second, the decisive answer.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If I were now as you have described—[from 'until']—how could one see light if the nature of seeing were severed and extinguished?
This decisively refutes [the notion of] spontaneity (*svabhāva*) in order to answer his question. Therefore, he first addresses the disciple suited for this teaching and reprimands him, saying:
I have now, as described above, analyzed and revealed these various matters in order to shatter deluded consciousness and manifest true insight.
I have exhausted my lips and tongue and employed every possible expedient, all of which was nothing other than to inform you of the path of ultimate reality.
Yet I did not know that you still do not awaken; you remain in confusion, claiming this to be the self of an externalist.
Is that so? Furthermore, whatever is called "spontaneous" (svabhāva) must be inherently such, eternally abiding and unchanging, to be described as spontaneous.
If it is not eternally abiding but shifts and changes according to conditions, then it is not spontaneous.
Suppose you, Ānanda, insist that the pervasive and immovable nature of awareness—which is not subject to arising or ceasing—is spontaneous. If...
"You and I must first distinguish this for ourselves. Observe clearly this awareness and its objects: is there indeed a single, eternally abiding, unchanging essence?
Only if such exists can it be called 'spontaneous. Furthermore, observe this wondrously luminous vision;
this is precisely what you call the 'capable of awareness' and the 'capable of perceiving. Brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness—these are what you [perceive]."

This refers to that which is awakened to and that which is taken as an object. Now, regarding this nature of awakening (*bodhi*), among the four conditions (*pratyaya*), by which condition would you take it to be its natural essence?

If you take the condition of light to be the natural essence of this nature of awakening, then when perceiving the appearance of light, it would be an inherently natural essence that remains fixed and immovable; yet, such is not the case for this awakening.
The nature of seeing can only be perceived when light is present. When darkness arrives, this seeing-nature has already departed along with the light;

it should not, therefore, continue to perceive the characteristic of darkness. If you further take the perception of emptiness to be the natural essence of this awakened nature, then when perceiving the characteristic of emptiness, it would be an inherently natural essence that is fixed and immovable. If that were so—

This awakened nature can only perceive the characteristic of emptiness. When it reaches a place of obstruction where there is no emptiness, this seeing-nature would already have become extinguished along with the characteristic of emptiness; it should not be able to further perceive that obstructed place.
Thus, from the characteristics of light and so forth above, down to the two characteristics of light and darkness below—omitting the condition of obstruction herein—it is said: "Then..."
This reaches the ultimate in brevity. The meaning is that even taking darkness as a condition, this nature of awareness is its natural essence;
thus, the perception of the appearance of darkness is taken as the fundamentally innate, natural essence, which is eternally fixed and immovable.
Thus, this nature of awareness can only perceive the characteristic of darkness. When light arrives, this seeing-nature has already vanished along with the darkness;
it should naturally cease to exist and ought not to further perceive the characteristic of light. Why, then, do you still see that characteristic of light?
Observing from this perspective, your nature of awareness sees light when light comes and sees darkness when darkness comes, following after space.
This is emptiness. Because you see obstruction when there is obstruction, you know that your seeing-nature manifests in accordance with conditions.

Why, then, do you delude yourself into thinking it is the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) of non-Buddhist schools, falsely claiming it to be eternally abiding and all-pervasive? You ask: "The teachings of our own school speak of eternal abiding and all-pervasiveness;
the external systems also speak of a 'dark nature' (*prakṛti*) that is eternally abiding and a 'divine self' (*puruṣa*) that is all-pervasive. How do they differ?"
