[Question: "How so? [Answer: The difference between the internal and the external is more than that between heaven and abyss.

For when the Buddha speaks of the "ever-abiding true mind" (*nitya-citta*) that pervades the *dharmadhātu*, he clarifies that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is unchanging while its wondrous capacity is able to follow conditions.

Thus, its unchanging nature constitutes its "ever-abiding," and its following of conditions constitutes its "pervasion. This precisely elucidates the entire substance and great function of the One Mind. [The views of] the non-Buddhists...

Those who falsely conceptualize a "spontaneous nature" (svabhāva), regarding it as an eternal, pervasive divine self (ātman), hold that this ultimate principle (tattva) and divine self are the producer, while all phenomena are the produced.
Thus, they claim the producer is eternal and pervasive, whereas the produced is neither eternal nor pervasive;
this is like a son who does not resemble his father. Since both cause and effect are thus untenable, how much more so [the rest]?

The Buddha taught that all phenomena are but mind. Yet they mistakenly claim that within a realm which is neither form nor emptiness lies the ultimate principle, taking it to be the primordial source of all dharmas.
They establish this as the "Dark Truth" (tamas-tattva) and the "Divine Self" (ātman), asserting that each possesses its own intrinsic nature.
Little do they realize that *pradhāna* (the primal principle) is their own mind; it is the half-extinction of dust. The *puruṣa* (the self) is also their own mind;
it is the subduing of deluded consciousness. Originally, there is but one mind, and both lack inherent substance.

Yet they remain ignorant of this, asserting that *pradhāna* is the producer and material objects are the produced; that the *puruṣa* is the enjoyer and all else is the enjoyed. [This distinction between] object and self—
To hold that the subject and object each possess their own intrinsic nature is to fail to realize the single mind; it is to maintain that there exists a path of a hidden nature external to the mind.
For this reason, they are called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthikas). Furthermore, what they call "eternal" is merely a false conceptualization of eternity within the midst of impermanence;
it is entirely the pervasive calculation and speculation of their conscious minds and possesses no actual reality. Therefore, it is not the same [as our teaching].
The Buddha taught that this is eternally abiding and all-pervasive.
△ Second, transcending the conceptualizations of our own school (in two parts): First, the shift in reasoning.
Ānanda said: "If this wondrous nature of seeing is not self-originated... how can this principle accord with the nature of causes and conditions?"
This transformation and relinquishing are spontaneous, yet they are reckoned as dependent origination. The intention is that since it is not spontaneous, it must belong to dependent origination;
furthermore, dependent origination is the true Dharma of our own school, not the false attachment to spontaneity held by non-Buddhists.
Therefore, I have now revealed and clarified that this nature of seeing is a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions.
Yet, there may still be doubt. Why? Because phenomena born of causes and conditions cannot abide permanently or remain unchanging.
Now, it is said that this seeing and its conditions are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi—immovable, all-pervading, and perfect. However, [this] meaning...
It resembles the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), yet it does not accord with the nature of phenomena arising from causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Therefore, this mind of mine remains unclear; I am in doubt and have not reached a resolution. I must certainly consult and inquire of the Buddha:
how may this seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*) come to accord with the nature of that which arises through causes and conditions?
△ 2. Refutation by Logical Analysis.

The Buddha said: "Regarding your statement concerning causes and conditions, I shall question you further" (extending to): "Light as a condition and darkness as a condition are identical to space and obstruction.
This refutes both the cause and the condition; it is because the preceding passage [discussed] True Suchness following conditions.
This refutes their notion of "nature. Herein, by means of the unchanging nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the [notion of] causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is refuted.
Now, "cause" refers to the direct cause, while "condition" refers to the auxiliary condition. Therefore, the Buddha said: "As for your statement that this view arises from causes and conditions..."

I shall further insist on questioning you thoroughly. If it is as you say—that this seeing-nature of yours first arises and manifests before you because of your current perception of light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction—then does this seeing-nature exist because of light?
Does it exist because of darkness? Does it exist because of emptiness? Or does it exist because of obstruction? Ānanda.
If you hold that light is the seed for the arising of vision such that vision exists, then light must be the cause capable of producing the nature of vision.
When darkness arrives, the light is extinguished; since vision exists because of light, it must likewise be extinguished because of light.
It is like hair growing dependent upon skin: once the skin is no longer present, the hair has nothing to which it can adhere. This, then, is vision...
The nature [of seeing] should naturally cease and perish; it ought not to perceive darkness. How then can it again perceive that darkness?
The same applies to the cause of darkness. This may be understood by analogy with everything from emptiness and obstruction to light and darkness.

Now, since this seeing-nature is able to perceive light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction alike, it does not rely on dharmas such as light and darkness as its generative cause. It may be concluded thus.
"You already know this. Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding this nature of your seeing: within brightness, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction, by what conditions does seeing exist?
Does it exist conditioned by brightness? Does it exist conditioned by darkness? Does it exist conditioned by emptiness?"

"Does it depend on obstruction for its existence? Ānanda, if emptiness serves as the auxiliary condition for the arising of seeing, such that seeing exists because of it, then emptiness must be the condition capable of producing the nature of seeing. Yet when one reaches a place of obstruction, the emptiness ceases to be."

Since this vision depends upon emptiness for its existence, it should perish along with that emptiness. Just as fire arises dependent on fuel, once the fuel is consumed, the fire also perishes accordingly;
so too, this nature of vision should naturally cease and be extinguished, and it would not be logical for it to perceive obstruction.
Why, then, do you still perceive such obstruction? The same applies to obstruction. This principle may be extended by analogy to light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction alike.

Now that you have clearly perceived each of these characteristics, such as light and darkness, it can be understood that this nature of seeing does not rely on dharmas such as light and darkness as its conditions for arising. This is why it can see both light and darkness, and can see both emptiness and obstruction;
this is precisely the unchanging essence of True Suchness (Tathatā), and therefore it is not produced from causes.
It does not exist in accordance with conditions.
△ Third, transcending internal and external objects:
"One should know that such a wondrously bright, essential awareness... (up to)... how could empty space be subject to your grasping?"
This clearly reveals the nature of awakened awareness: it simultaneously transcends both internal and external conditions and stands far beyond the realm of right and wrong.

It demonstrates that the nature of luminous awareness remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging. Therefore, the non-Buddhists cling to the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Failing to understand the wondrous function of following conditions while failing to grasp the unchanging essence, the provisional and the small vehicles cling to causes and conditions;

thus, there arises the distinction between the internal and the external. Indeed, this principle of the unchanging following conditions and the following of conditions without changing is the guiding framework for the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his entire life and the essential discourse for entering into the ultimate truth. Therefore, this—
He concluded by saying: "You should understand that this nature of subtle, awakened, wondrous clarity is, from the beginning, one in its essence and function.
It possesses the subtlety of remaining unchanging while following conditions. Because its subtle essence does not change, it is said to be neither cause nor condition;
because its wondrous function follows conditions, it is also said not to be a spontaneous function. Since it follows conditions,"
It is not that there are no causes and conditions; yet, since its essence does not change, it is not that it is not spontaneous.
With this essence of subtle, wondrous, and brilliant pure awareness, which is like the great void, there is fundamentally no "not" within "not-not," and originally no "is" within "is-not.
If one relies upon the gate of the True Suchness of the Mind, one is detached from all marks; therefore, as for "non-being," everything is non-being. Even if...
Based on the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind, it is identical to all phenomena; therefore, everything is thus.

Generally, the preceding clarification of causes and conditions and spontaneity belongs to the category of "existence" (yu-jù); this clarification of neither causes and conditions nor spontaneity belongs to the category of "non-existence" (wu-jù).
That which is neither not-causes-and-conditions nor not-spontaneous belongs to the category of "both existence and non-existence. There is nothing that is not non-existent and not non-not-existent.

There is neither "is" nor "is not"; this belongs to the category of "neither being nor non-being. However, these four propositions of existence and non-existence, as well as the four propositions of "is" and "is not"—all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane, whether sacred or profane, defiled or pure, down to a single speck of dust—each possess these four propositions.
If one were to enumerate them, there would be infinite sets of four propositions; yet upon reaching this point, none of them are applicable.
Therefore, it is directly swept away by saying: "Detached from all marks. This is the precise intent for eradicating traces and entering the profound mystery (*xuan*).

Yet, fearing that one might become detached from marks and sink into emptiness, one must instead strike the dead to bring forth the living. Thus, it is turned and swept away again by saying: "Identical with all dharmas.
This is further a subtle word for returning to the path and entering the wondrous. Therefore, know that this sutra transcends the four propositions and is beyond [conceptualization].
This is the secret scripture that directly points to the human mind for the realization of Buddhahood through seeing one's nature. As it is truly said:
"To deliberate upon it is to err; to stir a thought is to deviate. It transcends the realm of thought and calculation, and utterly surpasses the path of emotional and intellectual reckoning.
How is it that you, within this wondrously enlightened nature, apply your minds and exert your intentions, employing what is called of the world...

Are these causes and conditions, spontaneity, duality, conceptual proliferation, and all names and marks that can be distinguished, the essence of this subtle, wondrous, and luminous refined awareness?
It would be like using one's hand to grasp or rub empty space; not only is it of no benefit, but it merely results in exhausting oneself.
How could empty space ever comply with your grasping? Since it is impossible to place a hand upon empty space, [how can you grasp its essence?]

How could the wondrous clarity admit the application of the mind? In this context, the phrase "not non-natural" (*fei bu ziran*) must be supplemented with the phrase "not non-conditional" (*fei bu yinyuan*);

only then will its meaning be complete. O Wise One, please examine this carefully: "all worldly beings" refers here to what the *lakṣaṇa*-school (the School of Characteristics) calls the world of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the world of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is because "naturalism" (*ziran*) is the doctrine followed by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
That which is not for the practitioner is the worldly proliferation (*prapañca*) of causes and conditions; this is what is followed by those of provisional and limited capacity.
That which is for the practitioner is itself the worldly proliferation. Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "Causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), are all worldly discourses;

existence and non-existence, the ultimate and the conventional, are entirely the discriminating consciousness-mind. If one does not see the reality of things as they truly are, yet wishes to understand them through intellectual interpretation..."
This refers to the following: it is like holding a bow made of rabbit horns, mounting an arrow of tortoise hair, and attempting to shoot Mount Sumeru with a handless person;
one will only exhaust oneself in vain toil, for such a thing can never happen. This is what that means.
△ Ten: Manifesting Seeing as Free from Seeing (3). 1. Citing Teachings to Pose a Question.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One... [down to] ‘is it caused by the mind or by the eyes? What is the meaning of this?’”
This citation of past teachings has given rise to present doubts, prompting this inquiry. The intention is as follows:

while it may be acceptable to say that the wondrously enlightened nature does not belong to the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) of the non-Buddhists, it seems unacceptable to say that it is not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, how is it that the World-Honored One constantly proclaims to the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions? Namely:
Is it because of emptiness, because of light, because of the mind, or because of the eyes? For if what is before one’s eyes were neither empty nor bright, then seeing could not occur;
likewise, without the mind and without the eyes, one could not see either. Therefore, it is only by depending on these factors that seeing can be accomplished;
this meaning of dependent origination (pratyaya) is perfectly clear and evident. Now, you say that the nature of seeing does not depend on these at all—is this not so?
Is it that what is right now was wrong in the past? Or is it that the principle is the same for both now and then, yet I have not attained realization?
Herein, that which is cited as the appropriate response is precisely the Tathāgata manifested through eye-consciousness; it is the nature of seeing itself.

Thus, in the Mahāyāna, eye-consciousness arises only through nine conditions, whereas in the Hīnayāna teachings, it is said to roughly possess four conditions, none of which may be lacking. However...
All these are conditions for the arising of visual consciousness. This "mind" also refers to the six consciousnesses of the Hīnayāna;

because they do not realize the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, mental phenomena are considered to be only one. Little do they realize that the World-Honored One now relies upon the visual essence (*kāyendriya-śuddha-rūpa*) to reveal the nature of seeing, so that one may, by means of the nature of seeing, realize the wondrously enlightened luminous nature. Yet [the practitioners] instead mistake the nature of seeing for...
Visual consciousness—how different is this from mistaking a peacock for a mountain fowl, or viewing the jade of Hebo as a mere block of dull stone? Is this not foolish?
Nevertheless, within the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, it is taught only that visual consciousness arises from four conditions;

it has never been said that the four conditions give rise to the nature of wondrous enlightened clarity. This is because the nature of wondrous enlightened clarity is not something produced by productive causes.
Furthermore, to now identify the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature as being produced from causes and conditions is to be profoundly mistaken.
As for the nine conditions: first, space; second, the sense organ; third, illumination; fourth, the object; fifth, attention; sixth, the seed; seventh, discrimination; eighth, defilement and purity;
ninth, the fundamental [consciousness]. If one adds the equal and immediate condition, they become ten.
△ II. Clarifying through Reasoning (2) 1. Explaining that Previous Teachings were Provisional.
The Buddha said: "Ānanda, when I spoke of the various marks of worldly causes and conditions, that was not the ultimate truth."
This clarifies that the former teaching was a provisional expedient for a specific time, and cannot be compared to the present teaching. Therefore, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, when I spoke of consciousness arising from the four conditions, it was nothing other than a provisional and skillful means to guide those of the Lesser Vehicle.
This was specifically because non-Buddhists falsely speculate on 'spontaneity'; therefore, I borrowed the concept of causes and conditions to refute them."
This is what is meant by "using a wedge to extract a wedge" or "using poison to counteract poison.

It is not the same as the teaching on the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization spoken of today. How could one use the eye-consciousness of the past to conflate with the nature of seeing of the present?
△ Second, the explanation that what is currently being discussed is not a condition (*pratyaya*).
Ānanda, I ask you again: regarding all people in the world... [up to] ...both are called "seeing," so why do they not see?
This analysis now explains the reasons why this teaching differs from what was previously taught. Therefore, it says: "Ānanda, I ask you again:
Just as people in the world each say for themselves, 'I am able to see,' by virtue of what do they say they see?
And by virtue of what do they say they do not see? Ānanda replied: "People in the world, because of..."
When there is the light of the sun, moon, or lamps, one perceives various forms and characteristics; therefore, it is called "seeing.

Furthermore, because of the absence of the light of the sun, moon, or lamps, one does not perceive these various forms; therefore, it is called "not seeing. Thus, both seeing and not seeing belong to causes and conditions.
For this reason, you, who are responding to the occasion, cling to the nature of seeing as arising from causes and conditions. Therefore, the World-Honored One followed your words and questioned you.
He refuted this, saying: "Ānanda, if this seeing-nature is called 'not seeing' when these three kinds of light are absent, then it should likewise not be possible for it to see darkness.

How is it, then, that you still see darkness? If you claim that although one does not see brightness, one must necessarily be able to see darkness, then this is merely the absence of the sun, moon, and lamps; how can it be said that [the seeing-nature] is non-existent?"

Do you see it? Ānanda, if you say that when in darkness one does not see the appearance of light and therefore calls it "not seeing," then now, when in brightness one does not see the appearance of darkness, one should likewise call it "not seeing.
If this were so, then when seeing darkness there would be no appearance of light, and when seeing light there would be no appearance of darkness.
To see light and to see darkness—both are called "not seeing. Is there such a principle? However, these two characteristics cannot coexist;

yet within them, the nature of seeing has never for a moment been absent. Furthermore, if one knows that light comes and darkness departs, and darkness arrives and light vanishes, it is simply that these two characteristics of light and darkness mutually suppress and displace one another; it is not [the nature of seeing].
You perceive that the nature of seeing exists for a moment and does not exist for a moment in both light and darkness.

If this is so, you should know that whether in light or in darkness, it is equally called "the ability to see. Why, then, do you claim that when there is no light, one does not see? It is not that the seeing itself is absent.
You should understand that worldly people recognize seeing as residing in the eye and fail to realize it is the mind; therefore, they acknowledge only the presence of light.

[The Master] said: "I see. [The student] does not allow for seeing in the dark, yet he does not realize that seeing within darkness fundamentally does not employ the eyes, nor does it depend upon empty clarity or the discriminating mind.
This, then, reveals the seeing within darkness, whereby the four conditions are simultaneously subverted.
Although this is the same as the "blind man seeing darkness" discussed in the first fascicle regarding the nature of seeing, the method of subversion differs from what preceded. It reveals—

The nature of seeing is the mind; it merely breaks through the visual faculty’s capacity to see. Now, by revealing that the nature of seeing is not "light," one further breaks through the capacity to see as being produced by causes and conditions.
△ Third, the formal revelation of the transcendence of seeing (in two parts): First, the formal revelation.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should now know [the passage from] "conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of their conjunction.
This correctly reveals true seeing, which is still distinct from the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddhi*).
Herein, the seeing that is free from conditions is precisely what was previously revealed as the essence of seeing, as it was said: "This mind is unmoving, undying, and does not lose its nature."
Returning [to the source], it is not that things lack non-obstruction; rather, all that is revealed in the eight chapters on the True [Nature] is this very essence. Therefore, it was said previously:

"Although this seeing is not the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant essence, it is like a second moon. Now, what is revealed is the seeing that is apart from seeing—this is precisely what was previously called the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant essence.
Furthermore, the reason for discarding this "seeing-essence" is precisely to eliminate the second moon.

This clarifies the pure moon. Therefore, following upon the above, it says: Since you know that seeing light and seeing darkness are both called "seeing," by this principle you should now understand that when you see light, this essence of seeing does not belong to the light;
likewise, when you see darkness, this essence of seeing does not, of its own accord, belong to the darkness. It is thus.
When seeing emptiness, this essence of vision is certainly not produced by emptiness; yet when seeing obstruction, this essence of vision is likewise not produced by obstruction.

Since this essence of vision is neither produced by light, darkness, emptiness, nor obstruction, it is clear that it does not belong to causes and conditions. Therefore, the conclusion is stated: the four principles are established.
That is to say, these four meanings—light, darkness, space, and obstruction—are sufficient, when investigated, to establish the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*).

It does not depend on causes and conditions; it exists inherently, apart from external objects. This concludes the preceding point that the essence of seeing is independent of external objects and does not belong to causes and conditions.

For light, darkness, obstruction, and space are all equally objective manifestations (*nimitta-bhāga*), whereas the essences of seeing, hearing, and so forth all belong to the faculty of seeing (*darśana*).

[The division of] the two parts—the perceived and the perceiver—originates from within the essence of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*). Now, wishing to manifest this essential body of self-realization, one must necessarily eliminate these [two parts].
Were these two to remain, they would ultimately obscure the essential body; it is like falsely seeing two moons when there is but one moon.
If those two moons were retained, one could not avoid the conflict of "is" and "is-not. Now, having removed the two moons, there remains only the single, pure moon. Thus...
Thus, subject and object are extinguished. Therefore, the text below further eliminates the "essence of seeing" (*darśana-bīja*) in order to reveal the true seeing (*bhūta-darśana*). It declares:
"Although you already know that the essence of seeing is detached from conditions, you must further understand that the nature of true seeing is likewise detached from the essence of seeing.
Hence, it speaks of "seeing the seeing," and so forth. The first instance of the word "seeing" refers to the wondrously luminous true mind, like a pure [mirror].
The "moon" refers to the first instance of the word "seeing," which is the luminous essence of seeing (*jian-jing-ming-yuan*).

The "second moon" refers to the meaning that when this nature of true seeing illuminates and perceives that aspect of the divided seeing, this seeing of the true seeing is not the seeing of the divided aspect belonging to the luminous essence of seeing.
Thus, one knows that the nature of true seeing remains as it is, transcending [the former].
The seeing that constitutes the fundamental source of the clarity of vision—even this seeing of the "seeing-portion" (jien-fen) cannot be reached by ordinary seeing.

Yet, even this clarity of vision is accompanied by delusion; it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneously formed through combination. How much more so is this truly pure nature of seeing?

Why do you still persist in this? Furthermore, you claim that the wondrously enlightened, luminous nature belongs to the category of phenomena produced by causes and conditions, as taught for those of provisional or limited capacity.
Is that the inherent nature of those externalists, or the characteristic of the conjunction of consciousness arising from the four conditions?
This is truly but a single moon; in reality, there is no question of whether there is a second moon or not. This is because seeing belongs to the eight consciousnesses;

since the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) within the true nature carries delusion, there are two kinds of delusion: the same as [the delusion of] discrimination and the delusion of karma. This is what is discussed in the following text.
This refers to the fact that both the shadow and the vision are equally cataracts. True vision, however, is the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature;

it belongs to the fundamental substance of self-realization, being purely true and devoid of delusion. This is precisely what is meant in the following passage as "that essence of the seeing-spirit is the true nature, not a cataract.
Therefore, it is not called "seeing. Thus, one should know that the "true vision" herein is the vision of "knowing-seeing without seeing"; this constitutes Nirvana.
This is the true essence of the *pātra*. Herein, "leaving behind" (or "separation") refers to transcendence;
it must by no means be understood as a separation involving disjunction.
△ Second, the concluding exhortation.
"You disciples, being narrow-minded, inferior, and ignorant... [up to]... you shall not attain weariness on the wondrous path to Bodhi.

This concludes the previous section and exhorts one to grasp true vision. It is truly because you Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle possess such limited and shallow capacities that you are confined and submerged by what you have previously heard;
hence, they are called "narrow. Your realization of the Truth is not genuine, and you consider a small attainment to be sufficient. This is...
Because its name is inferior—being both narrow and base—it lacks knowledge and discernment;
even this essence of seeing cannot know [it], let alone be able, through that very essence of seeing, to penetrate the subtle and true reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the pure true mind.
For the reality-mark is markless, which is to say that true seeing is seeinglessness. Having now already instructed you...
"You should thoroughly understand this for yourself. Reflect upon it deeply and contemplate it with diligence.
Strive to swiftly abandon the fundamental source of the clarity of seeing, and quickly attain the wondrous, enlightened nature of clarity.

Do not allow yourself to be negligent, drifting along in indolence, claiming you are weary and thus giving rise to laxity, so that you must stop halfway. This is because to achieve Bodhi, one must..."
This single path of the nature of seeing is the most essential and subtle. Within this, true seeing is precisely the mark of the Great Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa;
it is the seeing of non-seeing, which is also the true substance of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
This is what is meant by "exiting through one gate onto the path of wondrous adornment. Indeed, this manifestation of seeing may be called ascending the peak.

This forms the summit. It is like entering the sea to reach its source. Now, since the Tathāgata has already caused the essence of vision to be eliminated, this further exhortation is precisely intended for those who are ready;
it is to let go of one's hands at the edge of a precipice and advance further upon the tip of the staff.

△ 2. Distinguishing the False to Clarify the True (in two parts): A. Generally Clarifying the Request for Permission (in two parts): 1. Describing Delusion and Requesting Instruction. Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One... [up to] "...with tears of compassion, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and received the holy instruction."
This describes the inquiry made out of confusion. The intention is this: "The Buddha has proclaimed for us the doctrines of causality (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*);
these are what I have already heard. As for the concepts of conjunction and non-conjunction, these are what I have not yet heard.
Furthermore, having heard of causality and spontaneity, I still do not know how this essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddhi*) can be 'neither of the two. Now, once again..."
"Having heard this regarding the essence of seeing, although it can perceive those four marks, it does not belong to them; yet this is still not the true seeing.
It only causes us to become even more bewildered within our state of confusion; it serves to further increase our delusion."

However, while the characteristics of such combinations may not yet be clearly understood, they can still be awaited for a short time. As for the delusion regarding the "seeing of seeing," one must not delay even for a moment.

Furthermore, since it was previously stated that "this seeing and its objects are originally Bodhi, the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant essence," it follows that this essence of seeing is none other than the nature of wondrous enlightenment. Why, then, do you speak again of the "seeing of seeing"?

At that time, was it not seeing that saw? Yet the nature of seeing is one; how can it suddenly be true and suddenly be false, now suppressed and now exalted, fluctuating and unstable to such an extent?
Now my confusion and distress increase all the more, precisely because I do not know why this is so.
I prostrate myself and pray that the Tathāgata will extensively manifest his great compassion and unfold the eye of great wisdom.

By opening the way and providing instruction, you have caused our minds to open and our intentions to be resolved; we have suddenly cast off our state of confusion and distress, directly attaining the nature of enlightened clarity.
This is truly because when clouds of delusion stack upon one another, the ocean of enlightenment is difficult to illuminate;

when mists of distress layer upon layer, the true mind is not pure. If you would graciously brush away these clouds of delusion and suddenly sweep away these mists of distress, then this enlightenment—

The mind may thus be clarified and purified. Yet, once the ritual of confession (bai) has concluded, those who rise to offer mournful condolences and shed tears do so out of pain at the deep-seated entrenchment of deluded passions;
whereas those who prostrate themselves in worship and receive the teaching do so by looking up to the holy intent to bring forth illumination.
△ Second, the reprimand for lingering attachment and the permission to proclaim.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda... [down to] ...those with outflows shall attain the fruit of Bodhi.

This is intended to explain the luminous purity of the awakened mind; yet, prior to that, he first reprimands those who are deluded and lingering. From "At that time" down to "wondrously cultivating."
In the "Traveling" section, the author first explains the Buddha’s intention: out of compassion for those who have not yet awakened, he intends to bring them to realization.
Regarding *dhāraṇī*, it is called "total retention," meaning it encompasses all phenomena and sustains immeasurable meanings.

However, there are distinctions between single-syllable, multi-syllable, and wordless forms. Now, following Guifeng’s *Brief Commentary*, we shall not adopt the multi-syllable or single-syllable versions, but rather the [wordless] one.
To take the word "non" (wu) is to grasp the pure, perfect *bodhi* mind; one should now likewise take the word "non," which refers to the presently so-called luminous and pure awakened mind.

Furthermore, the addition of the single character "great" (*da*) precisely reveals that this *dhāraṇī* is the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm. It is just as [the subsequent] four sections and seven elements are all like this.
The wondrous true suchness-nature of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is precisely this.

As for the various *samādhis*, they refer to the twenty-five sages who each described their own perfect penetration; when they all say "entering *samādhi*," it is indeed because none of them transcends the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
Therefore, Wu Jiang stated: "The Great *Dhāraṇī* is total retention, while the various *samādhis* are universal inclusion. Both are one.

This serves as a gateway to the universal characteristics of all phenomena; indeed, there is a profound reason for this. "Wondrous" refers to the wondrous mind, which constitutes the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha and is that which transcends through a single gate to the state of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
As for the "path of cultivation," it refers precisely to the subsequent "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ."

This is, among all practices, the most concise and wondrous essential path. According to the root scripture, it involves generating faith and opening understanding to establish the cause for sublime cultivation;
proceeding through the arousal of practice and realization to achieve the fruit of sublime cultivation.
Thus, the entire scripture serves as a level path leading toward the Tathāgatagarbha.
Yet, when the Buddha was about to expound this meaning, he first rebuked those who merely possess much learning. This was precisely because he intended to speak now of the Way that transcends words;

he feared that although you may have a powerful memory, it would only increase your extensive learning and further reinforce the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and phrases, rather than benefiting your *śamatha*.
You have not yet clearly understood the principle of subtle and profound contemplation. Therefore, you must now listen with earnest sincerity.

Because this teaching instructs one to contemplate the mind and accords with the ultimate truth, if you can act accordingly, I shall distinguish the true from the false for you, providing guidance and instruction, so that all future beings subject to outflows may likewise rely upon this.
One cultivates *śamatha* through subtle and profound contemplation in order to attain the fruit of Bodhi. "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means to distinguish it from that which is coarse;

for to employ discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), to direct the mind toward objects, and to engage in conceptualization and grasping through observation is coarse rather than subtle.
To restrain the body while sitting in stillness, yet with the breath coming and going, is lax rather than profound. This [practice] distinguishes itself from...
Therefore, it is called "subtle and secret" (*mīmāṃsā*). This specifically designates the essence, which is the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*.

However, when the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) perceive this *garbha-citta*, it is as if viewed through a fine gauze; for this reason, it is called "subtle. Only Buddha after Buddha can realize it to the ultimate extent; thus, it is termed "secret.
Know that since this samādhi is called "subtle and secret," it is by no means characterized by emerging or entering.
This samādhi is the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi, which is inherently and primordially possessed by one's own nature.
Herein it is stated that even those with future outflows (āsrava), by relying on this to practice, shall yet attain Bodhi;
it can thus be known that for those currently free from outflows, it goes without saying that they will do so if they rely on this to practice.
△ Second, the specific exposition (in two parts): First, the clarification of the false and the true (in two parts). First, a detailed demonstration of the two types of falsity (in two parts).
First, the direct indication of their names (in two parts). First, the general indication.
"Ānanda, all sentient beings transmigrate through the world... (up to) 'second, the commonality of sentient beings' is false seeing.
This indicates that within the essence of seeing (*darśana-sāra*), there are generally two kinds of false seeing.

Therefore, when the Buddha addressed the disciple, saying, "What I call the 'seeing of seeing' is not [ordinary] seeing," was it not for a reason? For within the essence of seeing, there still exist these two delusions, which must not be overlooked.
This is not to be debated. However, "all sentient beings" refers generally to ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity.

"Wandering in the mundane world" refers to ordinary people and non-Buddhists who undergo the cycle of birth and death within the shared world, as well as those of provisional vehicles and lesser sages.
The experience of the provisional means, the true retribution, and the transformation of the cycle of rebirth all arise from the initial single thought of non-awakening.

Through the deluded movement of ignorance, this awakened nature is turned about, thereby forming the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). Based upon this karmic consciousness, the illusory manifestations of subjectivity (*darśana*) and objectivity (*nimitta*) are produced;
thus, there are two kinds of inverted, discriminative, and false views. As for the combination and distinction of these two kinds, they constitute the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*).

This refers to individual karma. Regarding the statement that both are "inverted": because they do not realize that the perceived object (*nimitta*) and the seeing subject (*darśana*) are fundamentally one mind, ordinary worldlings and externalists mistake objects for the self, while those of the provisional and lesser vehicles mistake the self for objects; thus, both are inverted.

Furthermore, individual karmic deluded vision corresponds to discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*), while collective karmic deluded vision corresponds to co-emergent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*); both are...

These are the delusions, namely what are called the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the dust-and-sand (*rajas*) [delusions], and ignorance (*avidyā*). "Arising in their respective places" means that where there are delusions, there must necessarily be karma:
specifically, the views and thoughts give rise to the various karmas of outflowing good, evil, and imperturbability;

the dust-and-sand delusions give rise to the karma of the partial truth of the outflow-free; and ignorance gives rise to the karma of both the outflowing and the outflow-free, which pertains to the two extremes.

Regarding the revolving of karma: because there is karma, there must be suffering. There is the karma of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), which constitutes the revolving of the Shared Residence (*sahā-vāsa*).

There is the karma of the sands of *dharmas*, which constitutes the revolving of Expedient Means (*upāya*). There is the karma of ignorance (*avidyā*), which constitutes the revolving of True Reward (*bhūta-pāka*).

These three—delusion, karma, and suffering—are like the clusters of the akṣa fruit; they do not separate from one another even for a moment. Furthermore, these two kinds of false views arise from delusion.
The awakening mind suddenly arises; there is only the manifestation of delusion, which has not yet been summoned by karma. Therefore it is said that it "occurs in its own place.
Within the very sphere of delusion, one grasps and creates karma, receiving retribution according to that karma, flowing on in successive stages.
Therefore it is said that while one undergoes the cycle of karma, this essence of vision possesses such delusions;
how can one not examine and debate them in order to clarify them? Now, as for what are called the "two views," what constitutes these two?

The first is the deluded vision of the individual karma of sentient beings, which refers to what is seen uniquely by a single person’s single consciousness regarding their own root-body and the vessel-world. The second—

This refers to the deluded perceptions of the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) among sentient beings; it speaks in terms of the root-body and the vessel-world perceived in common by many individuals and many consciousnesses.
Nevertheless, although the common and the particular differ, their falsity is one and the same.
Therefore, within every thought-moment, all sentient beings fully possess these two types—the common and the particular—and for this reason, they undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain. However...
Throughout the day, one remains within two kinds of delusive views, yet the nature [of the mind] does not change. This is "seeing the non-seeing" through right view;

if one awakens to this, saṃsāra will cease. Question: Since the interlocutor has already doubted whether seeing is non-seeing, why did the World-Honored One not answer directly, but instead extensively clarify the two kinds of delusive views?
Answer: If one does not extensively demonstrate that there are delusive views, [the doubt cannot be resolved].

[The text] says: "To see" does not mean manifesting true seeing or non-seeing. One should know that all ordinary beings who have not yet abandoned the eye-disease of ignorance—including ordinary people, followers of external paths, those of the provisional and small vehicles, and even those up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment—are likewise called those with false seeing or having-seeing.

Only the Buddha alone has completely eliminated the eye-disease; only then is it called true seeing or non-seeing. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "That essence of seeing is true; therefore, it is not..."
This is called "viewing"; it refers precisely to this intention.
△ Second, the specific explanation (in two parts): First, explaining the deluded vision of individual karma.
What is meant by "deluded vision of individual karma"? (From here until: "How much more so regarding the distinction between what is not the lamp and what is not the seeing?"

This uses a metaphor to clarify the deluded vision of individual karma (*bipakṣa-mithyā-darśana*). Therefore, he interrogates [the audience], saying: "What is meant by the 'deluded vision of individual karma'?

From the passage beginning with "Ānanda" down to "the five colors layered together," all belong to the metaphorical section. The phrase "one person" serves as a general metaphor for ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Within this context, the "clear eyes" metaphorize the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, while the "pure lamp" metaphorizes purity.

The "pure true realm" refers to the true nature and true realm within one's own essence. The "red cataract" is a metaphor for the deluded vision of karmic consciousness, encompassing the entire *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).
The "perfect reflection" is a metaphor for the deluded realms of the four great elements, universally subsuming the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect).

Furthermore, it is said that the "layered five colors" serve as a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or Lesser Vehicles, which collectively subsume all phenomena of both form and mind.
Because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is the pure, true realm, it is fundamentally devoid of a single thing and transcends all subject and object.
It is like a clear eye or a pure lamp, which fundamentally lacks such phenomena as the four elements, the five aggregates, form, or mind.

It is solely because of a single thought following conditions that the karmic consciousness is formed, giving rise to the perceived and the perceiver; thus, form and mind falsely appear, just as [diseased vision appears] within the eyes.
When one has an eye ailment, one sees circles of hair and five colors. This is established as a standard example to demonstrate the deluded vision resulting from individual karma.
What do you think? Is this circular shadow manifested by the lamp the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the vision?
This bright circular shadow is fundamentally neither the lamp nor the vision, yet it is also not separate from the lamp or separate from the vision.

This analogy illustrates the five aggregates of appearance and perception (*nimitta-skandhas*). Although they are delusions and certainly not real, they nonetheless do not exist apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Ānanda, if you claim that this circular shadow is a color inherently present upon the lamp itself, then why would those whose eyes are free from cataracts not see it as well? It is, for example, like the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
When viewed through the lens of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, then that which is seen, its conditions, and all perceived forms are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.

This perfect reflection is merely the perception of one with a cataract; it serves as a metaphor for all sentient beings, who, through deluded vision, differentiate the objective realm (*viṣaya*) from the subjective field (*bhājana-loka*), taking them to be truly existent outside the mind, and thereby giving rise to the cycle of causes and conditions.

This is indeed their tenet. If they claim that this circular reflection is simply the color already inherent within the faculty of vision, then once this nature of the seer has become the color of the circular reflection that is seen, for that person who wears the cataract—
Furthermore, as for that which is able to see the circular reflection: since it is not itself the act of seeing, what kind of thing could it be called?
This metaphor illustrates that the fundamental substance of the *tathāgatagarbha* is unchanging. The meaning is this:

if this capacity to see were already established as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the perceived, then those ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and followers of the provisional or limited vehicles who perceive such objective aspects would no longer be [capable of true seeing].

As for the mind, what else might it be called? You should know that although the objects of the perceived portion are the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna), they manifest through conditions; yet its unchanging essence is inherently and originally tranquil.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if the circular reflection upon a lamp were something existing separately apart from the lamp, then it would necessarily exist all around, above, below, to the left, and to the right.
Look to the right side: it would only be plausible if there were a circular shadow upon a screen or curtain, or amidst a table and seating arrangement, emerging from that very place.
This is a metaphor for the objective realm of the *nimitta-bhāga*.

If this existed separately, apart from the true realm of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it would be like seeking a shadow away from its form, or searching for waves while discarding the water; such a thing is utterly impossible.
In principle, if this circular shadow were something existing separately, apart from the seeing, then since it would be detached from the seeing, it should not naturally be perceived by the eye.
How then could the eye of a person with cataracts see that circular shadow? This metaphor illustrates the deluded mind of the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*);
if it were to exist separately from the true essence of the "store-nature" (*ālaya-dhātu*), then there would be a mind external to that nature.
Unless one is among those of provisional capacity or small realization who still possess delusions, the object of perception cannot be perceived by the mind itself, just as the eye cannot see itself.
This preceding inquiry and refutation serves to reveal that [the perceived object] is empty and illusory.
Therefore, you should know that these five colors of the floating hairs actually reside within the lamp; yet, they do not arise from the lamp itself.
It forms its shadow; yet it is only because one sees it that there is illness, and the lamp is the cause of this shadow.
This metaphor illustrates that the objective realm of the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) originally manifests from the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). However, the object alone does not arise;

it is primarily due to the perceiving *darśana-bhāga* (seeing aspect) of the mind that the objective realm of the *nimitta-bhāga* is manifested. "The shadow and the seeing are both cataracts" intends to clarify that...
The two divisions of the seeing and the seen—the seeing that acts as the subject and the reflected image that serves as the object—are both the delusive cataracts of the true mind.

To say that "seeing the cataract is not itself a disease" is a precise metaphor for the fact that the true mind is not delusive; it serves to reveal that at the moment of seeing the seeing, there is the true seeing which is not [merely] the seeing [of objects].
For both the seeing and the seen divisions arise equally based upon self-realization, and neither possesses [independent existence].

Because it is the self-substance, it is said that both the shadow and the vision are equally a cataract. However, this self-realization is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha* as the "self-verifying portion" (*svasaṃvittibhāga*);
therefore, it is able to perceive the cataract without being afflicted by it. One must ultimately not apply the metaphor of the sixteen characters below;
one must not differentiate between what is the characteristic and what is the vision. If even this should not be differentiated, how much less so in this case?
In the middle [of the text], it further states that it is "neither a mark nor a vision. This precisely reveals the meaning that true vision is neither "is" nor "is not.

However, these two divisions—vision and mark—are just like a second moon. This secondary moon is neither the true essence of the pure moon itself, nor is it a reflection of the moon separated from the water. Why is this? Because the perception of the second moon is produced by pressing [the eye].
Therefore, the analogy of the perceived and perceiving aspects illustrates how the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) exists through the conditioning of conditions.

Yet, the ignorant do not understand this fundamental distortion of the sense organs; they thus give rise to false conjectures, wondering whether it is the form of the true moon or not the form of the true moon.
This is just like the circular reflection: they wonder whether it is separate from the lamp, separate from the vision, or neither the lamp nor [the vision]. It is not [any of these].
Do you see? This metaphor illustrates how ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity fail to realize that the two divisions of seeing and seen are but one mind;
they instead falsely give rise to various discriminations, asserting "internal" and "external," or "mind" and "object.
If one is a wise person who already knows the fundamental source, they will naturally not speak of whether a form is real or unreal—just as one who is apart from both the lamp and the seeing.

The statement that "it is neither the lamp nor the seeing" is a metaphor for how all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, while abiding in their own samādhi, realize that this seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. Like flowers in the sky, they have never existed at all;
thus, they naturally do not speak of whether this is true seeing or not true seeing, until they reach the state of being free from both mind and objects. It is not...
The mind is not something that can be described as an object. Now, this perception of the circular shadow is likewise so.

Since those who possess wisdom already know it to be produced by a cataract of the eye, if they now wish to clarify what constitutes the lamp and what constitutes the seeing, even that cannot be said;
how much less could one differentiate them as being "neither lamp nor seeing"? This precisely illustrates the realization of self-attestation (*svasaṃvedana*).

Regarding the fundamental substance, even the single character "mind" cannot be found; how much less can one speak of it as having characteristics or views, or as being without characteristics or without views?
In this context, the word "pressing" serves as a metaphor for the red cataract, the act of pointing, and the object of seeing.
△ Second, explaining the deluded vision shared by those of the same class (*sabhāga*).
What is meant by "deluded vision shared by those of the same class"? (From: "That which was originally neither seen nor heard.
This clarifies the deluded vision shared by those of the same class. Why is it called "shared," Ānanda? Here, to the south of Mount Sumeru, there is...
In the continent of Jambudvīpa, excluding the waters of the great ocean, there are three thousand islands in total among the vast plains and lands where sentient beings dwell.

Specifically, regarding the one central great island from east to west, including all its constituent parts, there are two thousand three hundred large kingdoms; the remaining [islands] number two thousand nine hundred.
There are one hundred and ninety-nine small continents within the various oceans.

Within these continents, there are lands numbering three hundred, two hundred, or at the very least, only one or two countries, up to thirty countries, forty countries, or fifty countries; all of these are set aside and not discussed here. Arhat.
Furthermore, if one were to consider among these various continents that which is the smallest, what would constitute its smallness?
It is because within this continent there are only two kingdoms;
yet, among these two kingdoms, if the people of only one kingdom collectively encounter adverse conditions, then that small continent—
When the sentient beings of that land behold all manner of inauspicious omens—whether they see two suns or two moons;
or between those suns and moons, halos of malevolent vapors; or the sun and moon eclipsing one another;
or when baleful mists approach the sun and moon, appearing in shapes like pendants or jade rings—all these are...

The sun and moon possess omens of calamity. When the rays of a star point in one direction alone, it is called a *keta* (comet). When its radiant vapors spread out in all directions, it is called a *pō* (boomerang-shaped comet).

When it moves crosswise with no visible trace, it is called a *fei* (flying comet). When its light descends in a stream, it is called a *liu* (flowing comet). These are all omens of calamity among the stars.

As for the "back-ear" (*fu-er*) phenomenon, it is the excessive vapor of yin and yang. That which bends like the back of a bow while facing the sun is named "back" (*fu*). It is like a jade ring (*jue*).

That which embraces the sun is called an *ear* (a halo). That which reflects the sun and appears at dawn is the *hong* (rainbow). That which faces the sun and appears at dusk is the *ni* (comet/secondary rainbow).
Furthermore, the male is called the *hong* and the female is called the *ni*. These are all omens of calamity arising from the interplay of yin and yang.
Thus, the various phenomena of the sun, moon, stars, and planets, as well as these transformations of yin and yang and their manifold signs of misfortune—all of these are merely...
The sentient beings of a single country are summoned by common karma; therefore, they are able to see this together. This is what is called the deluded vision of common karma.
If, within that country on the primary continent, there were originally no such common karma, not only would they not see it, they would not even hear of it.

Herein, those who "see" serve as a metaphor for ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or limited vehicles, who do not penetrate the five aggregates of form and mind—the characteristics of seeing and being seen.
They falsely give rise to notions of right and wrong. Thus, ordinary beings and outsiders perceive the分段生死 (pǎnduàn shēngsī—segmented birth and death) of the Land of Common Residence as an evil sign;
those of the provisional and limited vehicles perceive the 變異生死 (biànyì shēngsī—transformative birth and death) of the lands of Expediency and True Reward as an evil sign.

Although there is a distinction between the holy and the ordinary, they are equally lands characterized by evil signs. Those who do not see them are, by metaphor, the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
Abiding within the samādhi of self-mastery, one perceives that both the seer and the objects of seeing are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
There is only pure clarity, as if no country were being seen. Thus, the Treatise cites the *Spring and Autumn Annals*:

In the sixth year of Duke Ai of Lu, there were clouds in the state of Chu resembling red crows, flying alongside the sun for three days. The Lord of Chu sent someone to inquire about this from the Zhou court.
The Grand Historian said: "Does this portend for the person of the King? Du Yu’s commentary states: "The sun represents the sovereign;
