Excellent. The above concludes the section on "Revealing the True through Perception.
II. Harmonizing the Categories to Clarify the Nature (2): 1. General Statement that Delusion is Identical to Truth.
Ānanda, you have not yet clarified that all floating dust-like phenomena... [until] ...delusion and awakening, birth and death, are utterly unobtainable.
This serves as a general outline of the four sections, clarifying the essential meaning that delusion is itself truth. It begins from this point with what was previously mentioned:
"I wish now to expound upon the path of wondrous practice for the various samādhis of the Great Dhāraṇī.
This follows because, up until now, we have only used the faculty of the eye to reveal the nature of true seeing, which is neither cause nor condition.
Nor is it spontaneous. It reaches the point where both harmony and disharmony are transcended. Although this is but a brief summary, it is called "the seeing and the conditions for seeing.

Originally, these are the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant essence of Bodhi. This passage merely clarifies that within the eye, both the subjective seeing that perceives and the objective dust that is perceived, when brought together, return to the Truth.
At this point, the Buddha feared that the practitioner might only know what lies before them...

Upon seeing the nature, one recognizes the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet fails to realize that all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms—whether defiled or pure—are none other than the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Therefore, he synthesizes the four categories and traverses the seven elements.

I wish to cause those who encounter this teaching to realize that, in every dharma and at every point, there is not a single root, not a single speck of dust, not a single consciousness, and not a single great element that is not the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, following the preceding, it says:
"Ānanda, although you know that these two aspects of the seeing-nature—its false differentiation and its true essence as revealed through the tenfold demonstration—are as follows..."
The nature of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is thus beyond doubt.

Yet, it remains unclarified that all the empty and unreal bodies and sense organs of the world, as well as the objective realms that obscure the true mind, are manifold and diverse—both the internal body and its faculties and the external environment.
Therefore, they are called "various illusory manifestations. The meaning is that although these manifestations are numerous, [they are all of one essence].
If one discusses illusion and transformation, they are one and the same. Because these are mere borrowings and fabrications, established in vain as empty names, they are called "illusion" (*māyā*).
Being non-existent yet suddenly appearing, and ultimately not real, they are termed "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).
They are just like a mirage or flowers in the sky, formed in vain within a dream; that is to say, the deceptive appearances of a shimmering heat haze and dust motes. However, this...
The faculties, the body, and the vessel-world—these illusory manifestations originally have no basis; they merely arise suddenly through delusion regarding the Truth.
Thus, when they come, there is nowhere from which they come; hence it is said, "they are born where they are. Being born, they are unborn; they are primordially quiescent.
Thus, when they depart, there is nowhere to which they go; hence it is said, "they are extinguished wherever they are. This is precisely what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "All..."
Phenomena are unborn; I speak of the meaning of the momentary (kṣaṇika). That which arises at the very first moment is simultaneously subject to cessation;

this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both, nor without a cause;
therefore, it is said that they are unborn. This so-called "unborn" is precisely what I mean by "cessation. Now, regarding these phenomena:
All are illusions and not real; they are delusions and not substantial, being merely designated as "characteristics.
The above clarifies that characteristics are false, as the present sutra says: "Observing that characteristics are fundamentally false, there is nothing that can be pointed out or described.
Below, the true nature is correctly revealed. Because all phenomena lack inherent nature and arise based upon the True [Nature], their nature is entirely...

The nature of wondrous enlightenment and luminosity constitutes its essence. This is precisely what the present sutra states: "Contemplate that the fundamental nature is originally true; it is solely wondrous enlightenment and luminosity.
The term "thus" (*rúshì*) is a word used to point to a phenomenon, here referring back to the preceding meaning that while appearances are false, the nature is true.
The phrase "and so forth" (*nàizhì*) is a term of abbreviation, implying that the names and categories of all phenomena cannot be fully enumerated; however—
Taking the various worldly dharmas discussed in ordinary life, they are briefly explained in four categories; hence the phrase "up to and including. These are:
the five aggregates (skandhas) of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the six sense bases (āyatanas) of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;

the twelve spheres (āyatanas) consisting of the six faculties and their six corresponding objects; and the eighteen elements (dhātus) consisting of the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses. Such are the four categories.
Everyone knows that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is illusory birth; through the separation of causes and conditions, there is what is called illusory extinction.
Regarding these four propositions, I shall now explain in detail only the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); the others may be understood by analogy.

For instance, the five sense organs and six sense objects constitute the eleven factors of form, which are termed the aggregate of form. One must, in a previous life, have perceived these various phenomena...
The perfumed seeds are deposited within the ālayavijñāna; this is what is called the "cause.

When one reaches the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and seeks out parents, the parents then become the object, triggering feelings of aversion and attraction; this is what is called the "condition.
Finally, through the union of warmth, breath, and consciousness, the embryo is formed; this is what is called "conjunction. Thus, it is the conjunction of cause and condition.
Thus, while in the womb, the five sense organs are formed; upon emerging from the womb, one encounters the six sense objects—this is called birth.

If one investigates this birth, it is fundamentally illusory and false; hence it is said that "empty falsehood gives rise to existence. Yet these causes and conditions are, by their very nature, phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
According to the power of prior karma, there is a limit to the duration of life, whether long or short; when this limit is exhausted, one naturally departs.
It disperses; this is the separation of causes and conditions. Thereby, the five faculties and the six objects are simultaneously lost, which is termed "extinction.
If one investigates this extinction, it too is illusory and false; therefore, it is said that what is called "extinction" is empty and false.
One is utterly unable to know where this extinction goes, nor from where birth comes. Furthermore, how could one know that this birth is an illusion, and this extinction likewise?
Fundamental delusion—whether arising or ceasing—is entirely illusory and false, lacking any inherent reality;
yet, that which is able to manifest this is precisely the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature). Now, "garbha" (*zàng*) carries the meaning of being concealed or covered.
Because the *Tathāgata* is concealed within the minds of sentient beings, it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha*. This is the same as the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*.
It is the mind. Because this single mind has two gates: first, the gate of the True Suchness (tathatā) of the mind;
second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind. Sentient beings follow the flow of birth and death; therefore, arising and ceasing are fully manifest while True Suchness is entirely hidden.

Yet, arising and ceasing have no inherent substance, and their very substance is entirely True Suchness. Thus, the Buddha clarifies that this coming and going of arising and ceasing is precisely the sentient being.

This is the Tathāgatagarbha inherently possessed from the beginning. Thus, as its essence (*tattva*), it remains unchanging and unmigrating throughout the cycle of birth and death, and is therefore called "eternally abiding" (*nitya*).
Yet, as its function (*vṛtti*), it is unobstructed and undimmed even while situated upon the path of delusion, and is thus termed "wondrously luminous" (*prabhāsvara*).
Because the fundamental essence is immovable, its wondrous function is all-pervasive. Therefore, essence and function are one and the same; thus—
The wondrousness of all things reaches the nature of the Supreme Spirit; it is entirely without differentiation. Therefore, it is called the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

If you, Ānanda, were truly able to personally realize this principle, yet still sought within that wondrous, eternally true nature for matters of coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, these would likewise be merely illusory and false designations, utterly devoid of reality.
The ultimate reality can be attained; yet even awakening does not exist—how much less so delusion?
Moreover, since both delusion and awakening are unattainable, how could there be room for causes and conditions to harmonize, or for arising and ceasing, coming and going, to occur within it?
△ Second, specifically clarifying that the delusive is identical to the true (in four parts). First, uniting the five aggregates with their nature (in two parts). First, the general inquiry:
Ānanda, how is it that the five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true suchness-nature?
This is a general inquiry that serves to explain the five aggregates (*skandha*). Although they are illusory and false in their appearance, their nature is fundamentally real.
In Sanskrit, they are called *skandha*; this is translated here as "aggregates" (*yun*). In ancient translations, they were rendered as "shadows" (*yin*). "Aggregate" takes the sense of accumulation.
"Skandha" (aggregate) is a term meaning "to cover" or "to conceal. Taken collectively, it refers to the accumulation of conditioned phenomena that conceal the true nature.
The five are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. As the preceding Buddha said:

"Thus, and so forth," up until the point where he speaks of the wondrous true *tathatā* nature of the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*. The intended meaning is that all these things which I have described...
Regarding the statement that "dharmas—whether illusory or false—are all real": how could this be so without cause? Therefore, each of these points is examined and explained to clarify it.
For this reason, first the dharmas of the aggregates (*skandhas*) are clarified. What are the five aggregates of birth and extinction in the world?
These are merely illusory and false designations. Why is it that I also describe them as the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Therefore, the following provides an analogy to clarify this.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (five parts). First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as its own nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person with clear and pure eyes... [up to] ...it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
These eleven factors—the sense organs and their objects—combine to form the single aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). This analogy clarifies that it is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, it is said: "For example, suppose there is a person in this world who originally possesses excellent eyes, meaning they are clear and free from cataracts."
With eyes that are clear and free of impurities, one gazes upon the bright, cloudless void of a clear sky.
Thus, the clear void is vast and remote, possessing nothing else at all.
That person, for no reason, fixes their gaze without moving, staring wide-eyed and gazing directly into the void until they become fatigued; then, within the void, they suddenly perceive a delusion.

Flowers arise in profusion, swirling and shimmering above and below. Furthermore, there appear all manner of signs such as flying flies, hanging locks of hair, black moons, golden stars, and various forms of chaotic, non-floral phenomena.
One should understand that these are the characteristics of this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
This is just like the case of one who, with eyes fixed in a stare, perceives flowers in the empty sky; it is exactly so. Within this context, it is as if there were...
"Person. These are the characters for "person. If one follows the original sutra and examines the explanations provided throughout, this precisely illustrates the substance of the subsequent passage:
"the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening" and "the fundamental awakening that is clear and wondrous. The "pure and clean eyes" metaphorize the body endowed with correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*);

the "clear and bright sky" metaphorizes the body endowed with true reality (*tattva*). This is precisely the correct wisdom and true reality in which stillness is ever-illuminating and illumination is ever-still.
It is utterly non-existent. This is a metaphor for the oneness of principle and wisdom (*jili*), wherein no dharma can be apprehended.

Because that person has no external cause, he does not move his eyes; this is a metaphor for the essential awakening being inherently luminous. When one falsely creates "luminous awareness," then this true mind follows conditions and moves delusively, thereby forming the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
His staring causes fatigue; this is a metaphor for establishing an objective realm based upon luminosity. This, then, is dependent upon the storehouse consciousness.
When consciousness possesses the two divisions of seeing and appearance, then "empty space" serves as a metaphor for the absence of both identity and difference.

"Seeing distinct floating flowers" serves as a metaphor for the active manifestation of difference. Now, regarding these two phrases: the "empty space" above is a metaphor for the nature of the storehouse (ālaya), which fundamentally lacks all phenomena of form and mind;
the "distinct seeing" below is a metaphor for the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga); and the "floating flowers" are a metaphor for the appearing-part (nimitta-bhāga).
This refers to what was previously called "the seeing and the conditions for seeing. Furthermore, there are all manner of delusive and disordered non-characteristics;

these collectively metaphorize the deluded mind and the deluded objects. That is to say, internally, the mind of discursive thought, and externally, the realm of the sense-faculties and the physical body—this is precisely what was previously called "along with the characteristics of that which is conceived. "It is also like this" correctly corresponds to what preceded it.
It is like flowers in the sky, which fundamentally do not exist at all. All of the above serves as a metaphor for how delusion arises from the True.

The subsequent passage, beginning with "If they were to come from space," etc., analyzes how delusion is unreal. The section following "Therefore," represents the realization that delusion is itself the True.
Hereafter, all instances follow this pattern. The intended meaning is: if such wild flowers, Ānanda, were to come from space...
Since these [lotuses] have emerged by drilling out from empty space, they should likewise enter back into empty space by drilling in.
If these lotus-forms both emerge and enter by drilling, then this empty space must also have an interior and an exterior.
If it has an interior and an exterior, it is a substantial phenomenon (*bhāva*) and is therefore not empty space. Indeed, if empty space were...
That which possesses substantial reality is not empty space. Since it is real and not void, it cannot accommodate the appearance of delusory flowers.
Within it, there would have to be an emergence that "drills out" and a disappearance that "drills in.
Just as within your body, Ānanda, how could there possibly be another Ānanda who emerges by drilling out from within?
Does it penetrate and then vanish? This makes it clear that these flowers do not come from space.
If you claim these flowers do not come from space but emerge from staring with wide-open eyes, then since they emerged from the eyes, when they return, they should likewise enter through the eyes.
Even if we were to grant that there is such emerging and entering, this would still not refute your position; however, [it is as follows:]...
As for the nature of these flowers: if they truly emerged from the eyes, then these delusive flowers would belong to what is produced by the eyes and receive the influence of the eyes;
just as a child must resemble its mother, they should likewise possess the capacity for seeing.
If that which possesses the power of seeing were to go out [with the flowers], then since it could produce the flowers, it should naturally see them as they swirl back into empty space.
The eye is that which is capable of seeing. If you claim that it is without vision and can only serve as an obstruction, then depart!
Since it can obstruct and veil the empty space, when it returns, it should naturally obstruct and veil the eye itself.

Furthermore, if these flowers and fruits emerged from the eye, then once the flowers have emerged, at the very moment the eye sees them, the eye should be free of any obscuration. But since this is not the case—
If the cataracts are removed, one may then be called one with clear and bright eyes. Why must one see a cloudless sky devoid of flowers before being designated as having clear and bright eyes?
Thus, the calculation that [the flower] originates from the eye is also incorrect. The above argument refutes the falsity and lack of reality;
by stating that the flower does not come from space, it is illustrated that it does not arise spontaneously without a cause.
That it does not emerge from the eye is a metaphor for its lack of existence through the combination of causes and conditions.
This clarifies that the illusory and false appearance of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is neither the principle of suchness (tathatā), nor is it the unmoving true wisdom;

rather, it arises solely through the movement of a single thought-moment of delusion. Therefore, it is concluded that delusion is itself the truth, saying: "It does not come from emptiness, nor from the eye."
Therefore, one can know that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is fundamentally empty, lacking any intrinsic substance; it is a delusion manifested falsely in accordance with karma.
Since it does not emerge from itself, it is not produced by causes and conditions; since it does not come from emptiness, it is not something that exists spontaneously.
If this is so, then what is it that manifests? This is the knowledge that arising is itself non-arising;
it is not a manifestation through the causes and conditions of combination. It is arising from non-arising, yet it is not a spontaneous occurrence through non-combination.
For its essence is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
△ Second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is itself the nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease... [continues] ...it is neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
From this point downward, the single mind-dharma is divided into the four aggregates; here, the aggregate of sensation is specifically clarified as being the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is its nature. "Feeling" (vedanā) has the meaning of experiencing and receiving.

This refers to the arising of the three feelings—suffering, pleasure, and equanimity—in response to objects that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neutral. If distinguished individually, it consists of the first five consciousnesses; if taken collectively:

This constitutes the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). However, it necessarily requires the five sense organs to encounter the five sense objects, thereby giving rise to the five consciousnesses, which are then able to experience objects that are either adverse or favorable, or separated or joined;
only then does it constitute the aggregate of sensation. Yet, this is not like the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which calculates in terms of internal and external;
here, one merely calculates in terms of substantial existence. Now, this too is shown to be empty by means of the two points from which [sensation] has no origin.
This is not the reality. Ānanda, what is meant by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)?
It is like a person whose four limbs—hands and feet—are tranquil and at ease; whose five limbs and hundred bones are harmonious and pleasantly relaxed;

who is so faintly oblivious as to forget that he has life, and who does not even perceive that he has a body—how could he know that there is sensation? This is because both [body and mind] have been relinquished.
This is due to the nature of opposition and compliance. Yet, that person has no cause and no reason;
with the palms of both hands, they rub against one another in empty space, whereupon within those two hands, false appearances arise—such as sensations of roughness or smoothness, coldness or heat.
You should understand, however, that this is merely the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
This is also like that which arises when one rubs empty space; such is the case. This person represents the *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse nature).

Its tranquility and harmony represent the unmoving fundamental substance. Rubbing empty space without cause represents the sudden movement of a single thought, wherein the two types of grasping arise together.
Obstructing true emptiness, they give rise falsely to various sensations; thus, they are like roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat.

Roughness is used as a metaphor for the painful sensations of the three miserable realms; smoothness, for the pleasurable sensations of humans and devas; cold, for the withered sensations of the two vehicles;

and heat, for the flourishing sensations of the provisional vehicles. The above clarifies how delusion arises from the truth; what follows distinguishes that delusion has no reality. Therefore, it says:
Ānanda, these illusory sensations of cold, heat, roughness, and smoothness do not emerge from empty space, nor do they drill out from within the palms of the hands.
This passage correctly opens up two paths to demonstrate that the illusoriness of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exactly like this.
Ānanda, if you were to say that these illusory sensations come from space, since—
"It can touch your palm; why does it not touch your body? Furthermore, space is originally without discrimination and without selection.

It should not be that space also discriminates and selects, such that it does not touch the body but comes alone to touch the palm—is this reasonable? It is clear, then, that this does not come from space. If...
If it is claimed that this contact emerges from the palm, then even a single isolated palm should be able to produce it without depending on the joining [of two hands].
Yet, before they have joined, why are the various characteristics such as cold and heat absent? Why must it wait for the rubbing together of the palms before emerging?
Furthermore, since [the sensation] has already emerged from the palm, when this palm closes, the palm knows that the contact has emerged;
likewise, when the palm opens, the palm should also know that the contact has entered.
Since the palm knows the entry, it should also know the traces of this contact as it enters into the arm, the wrist, the marrow, and the bones connected to the palm. Why is this so?

I do not know. If one were to mistakenly claim that within the marrow of the arms and wrists there truly exists a conscious mind that knows its own emergence and also knows its own entry, then it would follow that there is a distinct entity that travels back and forth within the body.
Yet it touches itself; why must one wait for the palms to join together to know its emergence before insisting that this alone constitutes "touching"?
It is thus clear that [the sensation] does not emerge from the palm. The former passage refutes the falsehood of its lack of reality; the latter clarifies that falsehood is itself the truth.
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false, fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor uncaused.
The nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is also as explained previously.
△ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is itself the nature:
Ānanda, it is like a person talking about sour plums... (up to)... fundamentally neither through causes and conditions nor by way of spontaneity.

This analogy clarifies the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which is in essence the *tathāgatagarbha*. For "perception" (*saṃjñā*) takes the meaning of conceptualization; it refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

When this consciousness corresponds with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), the six perceptions are formed. Because they are combined and accumulated, they are called the aggregate of perception. As for the six perceptions:
this means that the mental consciousness clings to the perception of form and perceives form; it clings to the perception of sound and perceives sound, and so on, up to [clinging to]...
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the faculty of perceiving. Furthermore, it is called "perception" because it discriminates, contemplates objects, and grasps their images;

it belongs entirely to the sixth consciousness and is also termed the "deluded thought of pervasive interpenetration. Therefore, [the Buddha] said: "Ānanda, what is meant by the aggregate of perception?
For example, suppose there is a person who happens to hear someone else speak of the sour taste of plums; immediately, water flows from his mouth. Suddenly, of its own accord—"
Contemplate this: when one steps upon a precipice, a sense of aching numbness arises in the feet.

You should understand that this aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise like the salivation caused by hearing of a sour plum, or the aching of the feet from thinking of stepping on a cliff.
It is so. This metaphor illustrates how the thought-aggregate (saṃjñā-skandha) arises from a single moment of deluded movement.
Ānanda, as in this analogy of the sour plum, the water that is cited does not arise from the sourness of the plum, nor does it enter the mouth and then emerge.
This correctly opens up two paths to clarify that the perception of water is illusory and not real.
If one were to claim that this water arises from the plum vinegar, then the plum vinegar itself should produce it;
why would it wait for a person to speak of it before the water emerges from the mouth? Since the plum vinegar does not speak, this water certainly does not arise from it.

It is clear that the "water produced by the sour plum" arises from the ear. If one were to claim that this water enters through the mouth and exits from it, then the one who hears of the sour plum should already have the water in their mouth;
why then wait for the report of the sour plum to be heard by the ear before the water emerges from the mouth?
Since the mouth has not yet heard this report, this water certainly does not enter or exit through the mouth.
This is clear. If one were to hear this teaching with the ears alone, such that there actually were water [there], why would this water not flow from within the ears?

Why, instead, does it flow from the mouth? By analogy, this can be understood through the comparison of imagining oneself treading upon a precipice with the description of the sour plum. If one says this—
This astringency does not arise from the foot, nor does it enter through the foot. If it arose from the foot, the foot itself would have the perception; why wait for the perception of the mind?
If it entered because of the foot, the foot should have the perception itself; why wait for the perception of the mind?
If this astringency were produced solely by the perception of the mind, why does it not arise within the mind itself, but instead arises within the foot? If one knows this...
Since this water is absent from both that [acidic] place and the astringent one, it is clear that these are illusory, false appearances. The above has distinguished their falsity and lack of reality;

what follows is the realization that the false is itself the True. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false, being neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously;
it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. This may also be understood by analogy with the explanation of form (rūpa).
△ The four aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are themselves the nature.
Ānanda, it is like a torrential stream where waves succeed one another... (up to) "originally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This metaphor clarifies that the aggregate of formations is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. For "formation" (*saṃskāra*) takes the meaning of shifting and flowing; thus, [it is the nature].

This is the *cetanā* (volition) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*). Because it is able to drive and employ one’s own mind to create what is wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, it is itself karmic action (*karma-saṃskāra*).

Among the hundred dharmas, it subsumes the greatest number of categories; therefore, it is said that "matter (*rūpa*) comprises eleven in their entirety, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) each comprise one, seventy-three are included in the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and eight are gathered within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). As for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)...
It is that which is without accumulation and is not subsumed under the gateway of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Although all eight consciousnesses possess a nature of flux, it is the *manas* whose flux is most predominant, because its continuity is uninterrupted from moment to moment.

Although all eight consciousnesses possess volition (*cetanā*), the volition of the *manas* is most predominant, because its intrinsic nature is that of deliberation (*manana*). This aggregate (*skandha*) should therefore be assigned to the seventh consciousness.

This is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Ānanda, what is meant by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)? It is like a violent torrent of water, with thousands of waves and ten thousands of billows, continuing day and night.
Yet, the wave at the preceding limit and the surge at the succeeding limit do not overstep one another, nor do they cross each other.
This illustrates that the former does not wait for the latter, and the latter does not reach the former; it flows on day and night, ceaselessly.
"Intermittent. Regarding the statement that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) should be understood as being like a torrential flood:

this refers to the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) undergoing deluded movement, thereby forming the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). When this is further stirred by the winds of objects, it becomes the manas;

thus there is a subtle, continuous flow, characterized by arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, which does not cease for even a single moment. The state of the aggregate of formations is just like this. This...
The first part clearly explains how delusion arises from the truth; the latter part distinguishes that delusion has no reality.
Ānanda, the nature of this torrential flow does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water. Yet, it is not the fundamental nature of water;
thus, it is neither identical to space or water. Nor is it something that exists apart from space or water.

This torrential current is not separate from the water of space. Here, space is used as a metaphor for *tathatā* (suchness), and the water is a metaphor for the *garbhadhātu-svabhāva* (the nature of the storehouse).
This clarifies that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is neither identical to the *tathatā-garbhadhātu-svabhāva*, nor is it separate from the *tathatā-garbhadhātu-svabhāva*.
Thus, Ānanda, if one were to say that this torrential current arises because of space, then throughout the ten directions there would be—
If this were to exhaust the entirety of space, it would result in an inexhaustible torrent;
yet the world would naturally be swept away and submerged by its current. However, while this space is inexhaustible, the torrent is finite;
thus, it is clear that the torrent is not produced from space. This metaphor illustrates the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is eternally abiding and immovable, tranquil and inexhaustible.
This clarifies that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) undergoes moment-to-moment transformation and, being intensely active, is subject to exhaustion.
If one were to claim that this torrent exists because of water, then the nature of this flow would not be the nature of water.

Why, then, is the nature of water taken as the characteristic of the possessor (*svāmī*), while the nature of the flow is taken as the characteristic of the possessed (*svabhāva*)? Now, these two characteristics should be clearly distinguished.
It must be stated that [the stream] exists in the present; only then can it be said to exist by reason of water. It should be like a fruit existing because of a tree:
when one perceives the tree that possesses the capacity and the fruit itself, they are clearly distinguishable, and only then is it said to exist because of the tree.
If, however, one were to claim that the nature of this torrent is identical to the nature of water, then this water—
Since turbid flow is taken as its nature, then at the time of clarity, it would naturally not be the inherent nature of water.
This metaphor illustrates that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) arises following conditions based on the *ālaya-vijñāna* (store-consciousness);

it does not possess a fixed single nature, nor does it possess a fixed dual nature. If one were to claim that the nature of this flow exists apart from emptiness and apart from water, and is something else entirely...
Thus, space originally has no interior or exterior. Furthermore, apart from water, there is no such thing as the nature of a violent torrent.

Nor is this [torrent] separate from space and water. This metaphor illustrates that apart from the *tathatā-garbha* (the treasury of true thusness), there is no *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) to be found.
If one knows that the violent torrent does not arise from space or water, then...

Not being separate from emptiness and water, delusion is fundamentally without cause; it is merely a phantom, falsely designated as a characteristic. The above section has distinguished that delusion lacks reality;
the following clarifies that delusion is itself the nature. Therefore, it is said: "For this reason, one should know that it is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously;
its original state is the *tathāgatagarbha*-nature. This may also be understood by applying the same explanation used for form (*rūpa*).
△ The five consciousness-aggregates (*vijñāna-skandha*) are themselves the nature (*dharmatā*).
Ānanda, it is like a person taking a *pingala* jar (up to) "originally neither through causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature.
This analogy clarifies that the consciousness-aggregate is none other than the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. For consciousness takes "discernment" as its essential meaning; although...
While all consciousnesses are capable of discernment, this consciousness encompasses the eight seas and seven waves; therefore, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
It is that which receives perfuming and maintains seeds, and is the master who abandons one life and enters another, departing after and arriving before.
This is because True Suchness possesses two aspects: following conditions without changing, and remaining unchanging while following conditions.

When True Suchness follows conditions, it constitutes the *samskāra-avidyā* (formative ignorance) that brings about phenomenal existence; yet, the essence of this ignorance is empty, which is precisely the unchanging True Suchness.

Thus, being neither identical nor different, they together constitute this *ālayavijñāna*. Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) belongs to the eighth consciousness.

What is called the aggregate of consciousness? It is like a person who takes a bottle shaped like a *piṅgala* bird, plugs its two openings, fills it completely with empty space, and carries it for a journey of a thousand li, making use of that empty space.
Sending provisions to another country: one should know that this consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is likewise like this. It is like someone carrying empty space to send it afar.
Herein, "the person" is a metaphor for the power of good and evil karma; "the jar" is a metaphor for the root-body of ignorance (avidyā);

and "the space" is a metaphor for the immutable True Suchness (tathatā) existing within this root-body of ignorance. This collectively serves as a metaphor for the union of the true and the false, which constitutes the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

This refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). As for "blocking its two apertures": when True Suchness (*tathatā*) has not yet followed conditions, it possesses both the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*);
once it follows conditions to become consciousness, these two wisdoms are obstructed and transformed into the two hindrances (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).

"A person traveling a thousand li while carrying a vessel full of air" is a metaphor for karma dragging consciousness along as it wanders through the three realms, going nowhere among the six destinies and four modes of birth that it does not reach.
"Using it to provide provisions for another country" is a metaphor for casting off the preceding *skandha* (aggregate) to proceed toward the succeeding *skandha*.
Such is the characteristic of the *vijñāna-skandha*. This above clarifies how delusion arises from the True.
The following section clarifies that what is false lacks reality. What is discussed below does not refer to the person or the jar, but rather to the space within the jar;
it states that this space neither comes from that direction nor enters from this direction.

This precisely opens up two paths, serving as a direct metaphor for the nature of this consciousness, which possesses the characteristic of being neither going nor coming—just like the space within the jar mentioned above. Ānanda...

If it is argued that this emptiness comes from that other direction, then since the original bottle has already departed carrying its emptiness with it, there should now be one less volume of emptiness at that location where the original bottle was placed.
Why, then, would there not be a deficiency of emptiness in that direction? If this is the case, it is clear that it did not come from that direction. If...
That which is called the space within the jar is what enters this location. Since there is entry, there must necessarily be exit.
If one were to open a hole in the jar and turn it upside down right now, one should see the space emerge.

Yet, since one does not see the space emerge even when the jar is opened and turned upside down, it is clearly certain that this space is not something that enters this location. This space within the jar neither goes nor comes.
The characteristic of "coming" is a direct metaphor for the true nature (*tathatā*), the immovable essence.
Although it follows conditions within the root-body of karmic consciousness, there is never anything to be found of arising or ceasing, or coming and going.
Nevertheless, this limited space within the small vase and the vast, inexhaustible space outside the vase are fundamentally not two; they have never been distinct.
Though there are obstructions, there is neither deficiency nor excess. If one can simply shatter this jar with fierce power, it will become entirely one vast and inexhaustible void.
It is just so with all sentient beings: if they sever the karmic force of ignorance, [they likewise become the great void].

Once one discerns that the conditioned root-body is empty, then the wondrous principle of true emptiness realized by the Buddhas of the ten directions stands in direct confrontation with it—non-dual and without distinction. How, then, could there be any difference between the sentient being and the Buddha?
If one knows that the space within a vase has never come or gone, then one knows that the space outside the vase is likewise neither deficient nor redundant; thus one knows the Truth.
In its fundamental nature, there is originally no arising or ceasing, nor coming or going.

That which appears to have arising, ceasing, coming, and going is merely the power of ignorance and karma, which falsely identifies with the faculties, the body, and other phenomena; thus, there is the false birth of their conjunction and the false death of their conjunction.
One should know this: this aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is fundamentally without arising, ceasing, coming, or going.

That which appears to have arising, ceasing, coming, and going is nothing other than a phantom and delusion designated as a "mark" (lakṣaṇa). Its nature is fundamentally neither conditioned by causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) nor spontaneous;
it is the wondrous true suchness (tathatā) of the Tathāgatagarbha. Nevertheless, within the daily activities of us ordinary people, with every single movement...

Movement: merely giving rise to a single thought causes one to fall into the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). This obstructs and isolates the true nature; this is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Receiving and experiencing [sensations] within the mind is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). The mind taking this principle as its object is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Its continuous, uninterrupted succession is... [the aggregate of formations].
That which is vividly distinct is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). That which is clearly manifest is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

These five aggregates, in their entirety, are a single thought-moment; this single thought-moment, in its entirety, is the five aggregates. If one contemplates and observes according to this subtle and profound principle:

When one clearly perceives that the characteristics of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are empty, then the form of the gathered foam is merely void; how could there be sensation (*vedanā*) like a water bubble?

Perception (*saṃjñā*) like a mirage is not real; mental formations (*saṃskāra*) like a plantain tree are only emptiness; and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is illusory and false, has no abiding place.
If this is so, then the ultimately firm and solid essence does not depart from its present location.

△ Second, the unification of the six sense bases with the nature (2). 1. General inquiry:
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the six sense bases fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true suchness-nature?
This collectively interrogates the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which are precisely the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

In Sanskrit, they are called *praveśa*, which is translated here as "entry" (*rù*) or "locus" (*chù*). However, there are two meanings: first, that the faculties and objects mutually enter one another;

that is to say, when the six faculties encounter their respective objects, each is able to draw in (*xīrù*) the object it confronts. Second, that the six faculties are the loci where the six objects enter.
This is because both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) serve as the entry points for consciousness.
For this reason, various sūtras refer to them as the twelve bases (*āyatana*). However, in this fundamental sūtra, only the six sense faculties are designated as "bases" (*āyatana*).

This is because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they are capable of directly producing consciousness, and furthermore, they can receive objects and grasp the external sensory fields; therefore, they alone are specifically termed "bases. Nevertheless, these six factors...
Because they are intimately connected [to consciousness], they are called "internal" (*ādhyātmika*). Because they can produce consciousness, they are also termed "faculties" (*indriya*).

Now, faculties are distinguished as being either superficial (*tuccha*) or ultimate (*paramārtha*); here, only the ultimate is taken. This refers, for example, to what is called the primordially existent, unchanging *tathatā*.

This clarifies the fundamental substance of immovability. "Coming" refers to True Suchness (tathatā) coming in accordance with conditions, thereby manifesting its wondrous function that is all-pervasive.

"Treasury" (garbha) means that this true mind can contain the immeasurable wealth of merit and dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms, just like a treasure trove. "Wondrous True Suchness-nature" refers to this Tathāgatagarbha. At...

In every faculty and every object, phenomena manifest according to their inherent nature (*dharmatā*). Like a mani jewel reflecting the sun, it does not linger in a single color yet manifests everything;
therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). Being fundamentally free from all delusions, it is called "true" (*zhen*).

Being fundamentally free from change or variation, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). This is the essence shared equally by sentient beings and Buddhas; for this reason, it is termed "nature" (*xing*).
△ Second, the detailed explanation (six parts): 1. The eye-entrance is itself the nature.
Ānanda, that very eyeball which you stare fixedly until it produces fatigue... [up to] ...is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*), which is the very nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is precisely for Ānanda to exchange his grape-like [physical] eyes for the locus of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The intention is this:

Ānanda, this sense-base of the eye is exactly what was previously described in the section on the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)—namely, "as when a person, for no reason, does not move their eyeballs, and through staring, the signs of fatigue arise. This is it. For, as mentioned before...
The eye is used as a metaphor for the True; fatigue is a metaphor for the delusory; and the flower is a metaphor for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Thus, it is through deluded vision that one perceives the frantic flowers, which constitute the appearance of fatigue in the eye.

Now, it is said that not only is the perception of frantic flowers the appearance of fatigue in the eye, but even the pure eye that does not see those frantic flowers is likewise so. If one discusses this according to correct principle, it is also Bodhi.
Because it is the characteristic of fatigue, it is said that both that pure eye and the characteristic of fatigue are equally within the true mind of Bodhi;
they are all alike like the illusory flowers produced by staring with fixed eyes. This is precisely what is meant by "the reflection and the vision are both defects.
Furthermore, both the seeing and the objects of sight are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. Nevertheless...

As for this faculty of the eye, it does not exist apart from its dependence on the two kinds of false objects—light and darkness—which mutually confront one another and adhere to the tranquil essence;
thus, it causes the visual faculty to become active and consequently dwells amidst these two objects of light and darkness.
It immediately draws in the images of these two objects—light and darkness—just as a magnet attracts iron;

therefore, this seeing is called the "nature that enters. However, if this seeing that enters were separated from those two objects of light and darkness, it would ultimately lack any essential nature of entering. This is the meaning of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

Thus it is, Ānanda. According to worldly sentiments and false reckonings, one might say that this seeing emerges from the floating sense-organ, or else from the objects, or otherwise from empty space.

You should know that this seeing which enters [the field of perception] does not come from light or darkness, nor does it emerge from the floating sense-organ; yet it is also not born within empty space.

Why is this? If one claims that this seeing which enters [the object] comes from light, then when the appearance of darkness manifests, this seeing would perish along with the light, and one should not perceive the darkness. The same would apply if it came from darkness.
However, this seeing which enters perceives light when encountering light and perceives darkness when meeting darkness; therefore, it does not arise from the sensory objects.

Now, if you claim that this seeing-faculty and its penetrating essence arise from the floating root, then there would be only a single floating root, and necessarily no two objects of clarity and darkness.
Thus, this seeing-faculty and its penetrating essence cannot be said to "enter" except in relation to an object;
it must face the two objects of clarity and darkness before it can be called "entering. Now...
Since there is no dust to enter, this faculty of seeing likewise has nothing with which to enter; thus, its original self-nature is lost.
For there must be an object for there to be a subject; now that there is no object to enter, how can there be a subject that enters?
This means it does not arise from the sense-faculty. If one were to claim that this seeing which enters is [merely] within the void...
As for "empty space emerging": since empty space lies outside of both the sense organs and their objects, both the organs and the objects should be visible.
If, moving forward, one can perceive the various forms of objects, then upon withdrawing, one should likewise be able to see one's own floating organ.

Even if one were to see the organ upon withdrawing, that would still be empty space observing itself; what connection would that have with your faculty of sight? Thus, it does not arise from [the eye].
Śūnyatā-born, it is clear. Therefore, this eye-āyatana is void and lacks substantial reality; it is illusory and has no place from which it comes.
Thus it is said that "illusory falsehood is designated as a mark. Yet its nature is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous.
Now, regarding this passage on the "greatness of the sense-bases" (*āyatana-dhātu*), if one follows the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, each chapter—
There are four [stages]. Now, from the first stage up to what is called "seeing the nature," these are dharmas produced by causes and conditions;
they are the general designation for that which is both delusory and true, namely, the various illusory and transformative appearances of the floating dust.
Next, from "departing from this seeing" up to "what has to do with your entry," this is what I call "emptiness"; it is the general designation for that which is truly so.

They arise in dependence on conditions and perish in accordance with those conditions. Within the true and eternal nature, if one seeks for coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.
Therefore, you should know that the eye-faculty is false and illusory;
it is also termed a "provisional name. This refers to what was stated in the general summary: "When causes and conditions combine, there is illusory arising; when causes and conditions separate..."

That which is false and illusory is called "extinction"; that which is phantom-like and illusory is termed "characteristics. These four are neither produced by causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature;
this is also termed the meaning of the Middle Way. This is the general indication of the Middle: namely, that their nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightenment and clarity.
This extends even to the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*. Even according to the ancient exegesis, the clarification of the four kinds of non-arising is as follows:
since it does not arise from light or darkness, it is not "arisen from another. Since it does not emerge from the sense organs (*indriya*), it is not "arisen from itself.

If it were impossible for it to arise from the conjunction of the organ and the object (*viṣaya*), it would not be "arisen from both. Since it does not emerge from space, it is not "causeless. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena do not [arise].
It is not self-arisen, nor does it arise from another; it is neither co-existent nor causeless. Therefore, it is said to be "non-arising.
Know that this sutra is the wondrous Dharma of non-arising. Based on these two meanings, all subsequent chapters shall be explained accordingly.
△ Second, the ear-faculty is itself the nature.
"Ānanda, it is as if someone were to use two fingers... (up to) "...it is neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the ear-faculty is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, the Great Being Avalokiteśvara used fresh rolled leaves to [substitute for]...

"Perfectly penetrating" refers to the sense-faculties. The phrase "Ānanda, it is like... is a figurative expression; it borrows a mundane matter to illuminate the principle so that it may be easily understood.

This is not the same as the meaning of a formal analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). All subsequent instances follow this pattern. Previously, [it was mentioned that Ānanda] had been staring fixedly for a long time.
Yet one falsely perceives floating flowers in the air; now, because you have urgently plugged your ears, you falsely hear sounds within your head.
This is merely a sign of the exhaustion of the ear. You might think: "Is it only sound that is a sign of the ear's exhaustion? This [hearing] involves both the ear and its exhaustion;
furthermore, they are equally signs of exhaustion produced within the Bodhicitta. However, this is like staring with wide-open eyes...
When fatigue arises, one sees only empty flowers. When the Bodhi-mind becomes fatigued, then seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing all arise simultaneously.

Yet this faculty of hearing has no inherent nature of its own; it merely depends on the floating root [the physical ear]. When there is movement, there is sound; when there is stillness, there is no sound.
In contrast to these two kinds of delusive objects, the clarity of the mind becomes "stuck," giving rise to the act of hearing, which dwells within movement.
Within stillness, one immediately absorbs these two types; this is called the nature of the faculty of hearing that is capable of entry.
However, if this hearing were separated from both movement and stillness, it would ultimately lack any essential nature capable of entry.
Such is the meaning of the ear-faculty’s entry. Ānanda, you should know that such is the hearing-faculty’s capacity for entry.
This nature does not come from stillness or motion, nor does it emerge from the physical sense organ, nor is it produced within empty space.
Why is this? If one were to say that this hearing arises from a state of stillness, then when a state of motion is present before one, [it would cease].
This hearing should then immediately cease along with the state of stillness, and one should no longer hear movement;
yet, who is it that can still hear the roaring of the myriad apertures? Thus, this hearing does not come from stillness.
If you claim that this hearing arises from the state of movement, then when the state of stillness manifests before you, this hearing should immediately follow the state of movement and cease.
It ceases and vanishes; one should not perceive stillness again. Furthermore, who is it that can hear that which is silent and soundless?

This, then, does not come from movement. If you claim that this hearing arises from the floating sense-organ (the ear), then this single floating organ must necessarily lack both the two objects of movement and stillness. If that is so, how could such a faculty of hearing enter [into the state of silence]?

The essence of this [hearing] is such that there is nothing that does not enter through the medium of objects; it must encounter the two types of objects—movement and stillness—in order for "entry" to be spoken of.
Now, since there is no object into which one enters, this hearing has, from its very origin, lacked the self-nature of being an "enterer.

For there can only be an "agent" (the ability to enter) when there is an "object" (that which is entered). Since there is here no object to be entered, how could there be an agent who enters? This is so.

Then it would not arise from the sense organ. If you claim that this hearing emerges from empty space, then empty space must possess the capacity for hearing and inherently constitute the nature of a sense organ.
Since it would already possess the nature of a sense organ, it would no longer be empty space.
Furthermore, if empty space were to hear for itself, what connection would that have to your own auditory faculty? Thus, it does not arise from empty space.
For this reason, all three locations are equally non-existent. One should know that the ear-faculty is a phantom and a false appearance;
its essence is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ Third, the nose-faculty is itself the nature.
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who suddenly pinches their nose... (until) "it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the nose-faculty is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. This was [demonstrated] by Cūḍapanthaka using his two hanging fingernails.
This is also the place to lift up the nostrils that reach the heavens.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, for no reason, suddenly holds their breath by inhaling deeply and drawing it inward, refusing to let it out.
If they hold it for a very long time, it becomes a state of exhaustion; consequently, within the nostrils, they perceive a cold breath and are touched by it. Because of this cold contact—
Furthermore, they make distinctions: they take the unobstructed flow of the breath as "void" (*śūnya*) and the blocked cessation of inhalation and exhalation as "solid" (*bhāva*).
Thus, based on the sensory objects (*viṣaya*), they distinguish between the open and the obstructed; based on the sense organs (*indriya*), they differentiate between the void and the solid.
Therefore, when the organ is void, the object is open; when the organ is solid, the object is obstructed. Such openness and obstruction, voidness and solidity, extend even to all fragrances.
Foul odors—all these are but signs of exhaustion belonging to the nose-faculty.
Not only this, but even this nose-faculty together with its signs of exhaustion are likewise merely signs of exhaustion produced by the staring of the Bodhi-mind.
Yet, this nose-sphere (*ghrāṇāyatana*) originally has no self-nature; it is only because of the floating root that there is hearing when it is open, and none when it is blocked.

I have heard that when the two kinds of false objects correspond, they adhere to the profound stillness and give rise to smelling. Abiding within the midst of penetration and obstruction, it immediately absorbs these two kinds;

this is called the nature of the smelling-faculty that is able to enter [the objects]. However, if this smelling-faculty were separated from those states of penetration and obstruction, it would ultimately lack any essential nature capable of entering. You should know that such is the case with this smelling-faculty.

The nature that is able to enter [the sense-field] does not come from the opening or closing [of the faculty], nor does it emerge from the floating root-faculty, nor is it produced within empty space.

Why? If one were to say that this act of smelling arises from the opening of the faculty of hearing, then when it reaches the state of the closing where there is no hearing, this smelling should likewise perish along with the opening of the objective field. It should...
If one does not hear again when there is an obstruction, how can it be known that there is hearing despite the obstruction?
Since one is able to know the obstruction, it is known that this hearing does not come from the unobstructed state.

If this hearing were to exist because of the obstructed state of non-hearing, then at the time of reaching the unobstructed state of hearing, this hearing should immediately perish along with the object of the obstruction. From [this point]...

If there were no hearing, there should likewise be no smelling. How then could these odors—whether fragrant or foul—be clearly manifested, distinct and unmistakable, as they come into contact with the nose?
Since one perceives fragrance and stench, it must not be that they come while the organ itself is blocked.
If you claim that this faculty of smelling and hearing arises from the floating sense-organ (the physical root), then it would be solitary...
The single faculty of the nose-organ necessarily lacks both the objects of "penetration" and "obstruction.

Thus, regarding such faculties of smelling and hearing, their nature as "entrances" is nothing other than being described in relation to their objects; one must encounter the two objects of penetration and obstruction before they can be called entrances.
Now, since there is no object to be entered, these faculties of smelling and hearing are fundamentally devoid of the capacity to enter.
It is of the nature of self-existence. Only because there is an object can there be a subject; since here there is no object to enter, how could there be a subject that enters?
This, then, does not arise from the sense organs. If you claim that this hearing emerges from empty space, [it would be as follows:]
If this emptiness were capable of hearing and, having emerged, were then to smell various fragrances and stenches, then when it turns around, it should naturally also smell your nasal faculty.
Even granting that the smelling faculty exists, since it is emptiness itself that possesses the power of hearing, how could it be related to your nasal sense-base?
Thus, one knows that [hearing] does not arise from emptiness. For this reason:
Since these three locations are all absent, one should know that the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇāyatana*) is a phantom and a false appearance;

its fundamental nature is the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously. "Trigger" (*ji*) refers to the barb of a crossbow; it is like the superior sense-organ (*indriya*) which possesses the function of producing hearing.
△ The fourth is the tongue-sphere (*jihvā-āyatana*), which is itself the nature.
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who licks his lips with his tongue... [up to] "...it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the tongue-sphere is itself the *tathāgatagarbha* nature; this refers to the place where Kauṇḍinya formerly ate his meals.
This is the Dharma-gate for attaining [realization]. Ānanda, it is like a person who finds no meaning in anything and exhausts himself by repeatedly licking his own lips with his tongue.
By licking incessantly, he causes his tongue to become fatigued. If that person is ill, then because of this licking, he falsely perceives a bitter taste.
If that person is not ill, then because of this licking, he faintly experiences a sweet sensation. From this...

When one tastes something thoroughly, false notions of sweetness and bitterness arise; this precisely reveals that the faculty of the tongue capable of entering [objects] possesses the nature of neutrality (*madhura*) which remains constant before the tasting occurs and while it is unmoving.

Above this, combining all various flavors—sweet, bitter, pungent, and sour—into a single object (*viṣaya*), the nature of neutrality is separately established as another object in order to clarify [the principle].
The tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*), whether encountering moving or unmoving flavors as objects, is entirely a state of exhaustion belonging to the tongue.

Not only are these things the exhaustion of the tongue-root (*jihvendriya*), but even this tongue-root together with its states of exhaustion are likewise merely states of exhaustion produced by the staring of the Bodhi-mind. However, this tongue-faculty originally has no self-nature; it is merely...
Due to the floating sense-faculty, it encounters two kinds of delusory objects: the sweet and bitter of movement and the blandness of non-movement.

Adhering to the profound stillness, it gives rise to tasting. Abiding amidst the sweet and the bland, it immediately absorbs these two; this is called the nature that is capable of entering through the discernment of flavor.
However, as for this discernment of flavor, even if it were separated from those sweet and bitter flavors, as well as from the bland, [it would still persist].
Ultimately, there is no essential nature that can enter [the sense-sphere]. Such is the meaning of the tongue-sphere (*jihvā-āyatana*).
Ānanda, you should know that this cognition which can taste sweetness, bitterness, and even blandness—this is the cognition of flavor.
It does not come from sweetness or bitterness; it does not exist because of the flavorless. Furthermore, it cannot emerge from the floating sense-organ, nor does it arise from empty space.

Why? If one were to say that this nature of knowing taste arises from movement and originates from flavors such as sweet and bitter, then when it encounters the unmoving nature of the flavorless, [it would cease].
If this cognition were to follow that movement, then once the sweet and bitter flavors have ceased, it should no longer perceive the neutral taste;
how then could it perceive the neutral taste of non-movement? Since it is able to perceive the neutral taste, this cognition does not arise from the sweet and bitter flavors.
If one claims that the nature of this cognition of flavor arises from the ordinary, unmoving neutral taste—

As for "emerging": when one moves and perceives the flavors of sweet and bitter as they manifest before one, this nature of cognition should follow the unmoving neutrality and perish along with it; thus, one should no longer perceive that sweetness or bitterness.
Furthermore, how could one then be able to know the two characteristics of sweet and bitter? Since one does know them, it follows that cognition does not emerge from neutrality. If you say:

This faculty that is capable of knowing [taste] arises from the "floating root" (the tongue). If it were a solitary floating root alone, there would necessarily be no two objects of perception—sweet and bland.
Thus, this faculty that perceives taste and its nature of entering [the object] cannot be called "entering" except in relation to an object;
one must encounter the two objects of sweet and bland before it can be called "entering. Now, since there is nothing for it to enter, how can it be called "entering"?
As for this dust, so too this faculty that perceives taste fundamentally lacks the self-nature of being an agent of entry.
Since there must be an object in order for there to be an agent, and since here there is no object to enter, how could there be an agent of entry?
Thus, it does not arise from the faculty. If one were to claim that this cognition emerges spontaneously from space, then [it would be] space...
It is [the tongue] itself that knows the taste; it is not your mouth that can know the taste. Furthermore, it is empty space itself that knows the taste;
what connection does this have with your faculty of the tongue? For this reason, all three locations are entirely non-existent.
You should know that the faculty of the tongue is a phantom and a false appearance; its essence is the Tathāgata, who is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is he spontaneous.
This is the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha). △ Fifth, the sense bases are themselves the nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person who has one hand that is cold [up to] "it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature."
This clarifies that the sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is the Dharma-gate realized by Pilindavatsa when he reached the limit of enduring pain. For touch is the object-field corresponding to the body.
Herein, the two hands are a portion of the sense-base of the body. Thus, by clarifying the deluded perception of the two hands, the deluded perception of the entire body is understood by analogy.
This can be understood through an analogy. Ānanda, suppose there is a person with nothing else to do who places his own cold hand against another’s hot hand.
If the power of the cold hand prevails, then the hot hand will likewise become cold.
If the efficacy of the heat is superior, then the cold hand will also become hot. This...
The body and its contact are both devoid of intrinsic nature. It is like two hands, one cold and one hot, coming into mutual contact;
neither possesses a fixed state, and thus it is known that both are illusory.

Since a single palm does not constitute contact, it is said that such sensations of cold and heat must depend on these two hands joining together for them to be perceived as contact; hence, it is called "contact perceived through conjunction. However, this conjunction...

They do not combine spontaneously; rather, one must first separate them before their subsequent combination can be known. Thus, it is said that "separation makes the knowledge [of combination] manifest.
Regarding "interpenetrating forces," this refers to the forces of cold and heat mutually interpenetrating.

As for "if they are established," this means that if the force of heat prevails, then the cold becomes hot; if the force of cold prevails, then the heat becomes cold. All of these endure for a long time.
Contact results in fatigue; thus, within the sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*), one falsely gives rise to this contact. This means that it is not only this;
even the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) together with this fatiguing contact are likewise but manifestations of fatigue arising from within the Bodhi-mind.

However, this entry of the body is fundamentally devoid of self-nature. It arises merely because the floating sense-organ encounters two kinds of false objects—those perceived through contact and those known through separation—which cause the clarity of consciousness to become "sticky" and give rise to awareness.
Abiding between these states of contact and separation, it immediately absorbs these two kinds of objects;

this is what is called the nature of the faculty capable of entering through awareness and cognition. Yet, if this awareness and cognition were to depart from those [objects], [it would cease to exist].
Regarding the two objects of separation and conjunction, as well as opposition and compliance, there is ultimately no essential nature that can enter [the sense-field].

This is because both separation and conjunction possess the two conditions of opposition and compliance. For example, in the case of a pleasant touch, conjunction is compliant while separation is opposed;

in the case of an unpleasant touch, conjunction is opposed while separation is compliant. Thus, one speaks of "separation and conjunction, opposition and compliance" in relation to the meaning of the body-sphere (*kāyāyatana*).

It is thus. Ānanda, you should know that this nature of awareness and cognition which is able to enter [the body] does not arise from the joining or parting [of the hands], nor does it exist through compliance or opposition.
Furthermore, it does not emerge from the physical sense-organ (the "floating root"), nor is it produced from empty space.
Why? If one were to say that this awareness comes when the palms join, then when the palms separate—
At the time when they are not in conjunction, this cognition should likewise perish simultaneously with that conjunction;

it should not continue to perceive their separation. Why, then, does it perceive their separation? Since it perceives their separation, it follows that this cognition did not arise from the conjunction itself.
The same applies to the two aspects of opposition and conformity. If one were to claim that this cognition...
That which arises from a single sense organ is, by itself, a solitary sense organ; it necessarily lacks the states of separation or union, opposition or compliance.
These are the four characteristics. Thus, this nature of awareness capable of entry is nothing other than "entry" as described in relation to sensory objects.
One must have the four marks [of the sense objects] before one can speak of "entering.
Now, since there are no objects to be entered, this root of cognition fundamentally lacks the self-nature of an agent who enters. Since there is an object, there is an agent;
but since there is here no object to be entered, how could there be an agent who enters? Thus, it does not arise from the sense organs. If it were necessarily...
If this perception arises from empty space, then empty space itself must possess perception;
what, then, would it have to do with your body’s sense-base? Thus, it does not arise from empty space.
For this reason, you should know that the body’s sense-base is fundamentally without origin; it is a delusive illusion designated as a "mark," and its nature is non-causal.
This is because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is not produced by conditions nor is it spontaneous.
△ Sixth, the sense-base of mind is itself the nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep... (up to) fundamentally neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor spontaneous in nature.

This clarifies that the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is the very nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, Subhūti realized this "vision within the dark chamber" and entered the ocean of the jewel-luminous void.
Because the mind-base manifests through the signs of weariness, it cannot be seen as clearly as the first five [bases].

This is extremely subtle and hidden; therefore, the following passage uses waking and sleeping, remembering and forgetting, to elucidate the entry into the mental sphere (*manas-āyatana*), so that people may easily understand and know it.
Thus it says: "Ānanda, suppose there were such a person. Beneath his mental ground..."
Because of excessive exertion, one reaches a state of fatigue and exhaustion, and thus desires to sleep.
Once the sleep has become deep, one immediately awakens from it. Therefore, during the time of waking, one perceives external objects and remembers them;
however, while actually fast asleep, one loses memory and forgets them. Furthermore, within sleep there are dreams.
To remember is to recall; to wake up and not remember is to forget. These are all manifestations of the mind’s recollection and oblivion regarding perceived objects.
Thus we may observe that throughout our days, we sleep and then awaken, and having awakened, we sleep again, even to the point of forgetting and then remembering once more.
To remember and then forget again; to sleep and then wake; to remember and then forget—these are all merely the inverted and laborious characteristics of the entrance of the mind (*manāyatana*).

Yet, this sleeping, waking, remembering, and forgetting each possesses the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-nirodha*), through which they shift and pass away.

For example, initial falling asleep is "arising"; being in the midst of sleep is "abiding"; being about to wake is "changing"; and having already woken is "ceasing. This is just as with initial waking.

Awakening from sleep is arising; being fully awake is abiding; becoming weary is change; falling asleep is cessation. As with the first recollection, it is arising; the act of recollecting is abiding;
being about to forget is change; having forgotten is cessation. As with the first instance of forgetting, it is arising;
the state of having forgotten is abiding; the desire to remember is change; the completion of remembering is cessation. Thus, arising, abiding, change, and cessation do not exceed these.

Because they continue from beginning to end, revolving back and forth in a cycle, they are called "perversions. Furthermore, these four characteristics all arise from beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
thus, moment by moment they shift and flow, absorbing the marks of habituation and returning inward to the faculty of mind (*manas*).

These four characteristics do not pause for even a single kṣaṇa; the former does not wait for the latter, and the latter does not reach the former. Therefore, it is said that they are not mutually related.
Transgressing [the truth], the mental faculty enters into deluded cognition; such is its nature. Therefore, the mental faculty is called the root that is capable of knowing.

Generally, worldly people know only that sleep and waking, memory and forgetfulness, are the laborious manifestations of the mind, yet they fail to realize that these, along with the mental faculty and the faculty of knowing, are likewise laborious manifestations upon the Bodhi-mind.

However, this faculty of mind (*manāyatana*) originally lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It merely arises in conjunction with the floating sense-organ and those two kinds of delusory objects of arising and ceasing.
Thus, it clings to the profound stillness and gathers cognition, dwelling amidst these two types of objects of arising and ceasing.
It then draws in and seizes these internal objects of the two kinds of arising and ceasing. Although it draws in these internal objects, it nevertheless does not [become one] with the former...
