The five sense-faculties (*pañca-āyatana*) are the same in this regard. That is to say, when the first five faculties take present objects as their conditions, it is called "flowing with the current.

If they instead take the internal [mind] as their object, it is called "flowing against the current. Furthermore, even if they were to flow against the current, they would still not reach their own internal sense-fields (*viṣaya*).

Therefore, that which the first five faculties cannot reach while flowing against the current is designated as the nature of the cognizing faculty that is able to enter [the object]. However, this cognition—

As for its nature: even if one were to depart from those two kinds of delusive objects—waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing—there would ultimately be no essential nature capable of entering. Such is the meaning of the "entrance of the mind.
Ānanda, you should know that this faculty of the root which is capable of perceiving and entering does not come from waking and sleeping, nor does it exist because of arising and ceasing. However...
Nor does it emerge from the physical sense organs, nor is it produced from empty space. Why?
If one were to say that this nature of cognition capable of entering [the body] comes from the waking state, then at the time of sleep, it would have already perished along with the waking state.
Furthermore, by what means does one sleep? Tell me: who is it that is currently slumbering in this state of profound darkness?
And who is it that can dream? If [sleep] arises from this state of slumber, other instances may be inferred accordingly.

If you claim that this nature of awareness capable of entering [sleep] must exist from the very moment sensory objects arise, then at the moment those objects cease, it should likewise [cease] along with them.
It does not exist. How then can it go on to experience the cessation of sensory objects and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness?

This would mean that it does not arise from the existence of birth. If you claim it arises from the cessation of sensory objects, then when those objects arise again, it should likewise cease along with them and be non-existent.
Who then could be called the conscious awareness and discrimination capable of knowing the arising of sensory objects? This—

Nor does it arise from cessation. If one claims that this nature of awareness capable of entry emerges from the floating sense-roots and has no relation to waking or sleeping, one fails to realize that this very state is like a red lotus upon a lump of flesh:
it is bright when open and dim when closed; it opens when one wakes and closes when one sleeps. Therefore, this waking...
Sleep has two aspects: it constantly opens and closes in accordance with the physical form.

If one were to depart from these two types of substantial characteristics—waking and sleeping, opening and closing—then this conscious subject capable of entering [samādhi] would be like a flower in the sky;
ultimately, there would be no nature capable of entering. This, then, would not arise from the sense faculties. If one were to claim that this consciousness...
If it were produced from space, then space itself would possess sentience; what, then, would it have to do with your mental faculty?
Thus, it is not produced from space. For this reason, all three locations are non-existent. You should know that the mental faculty is a phantom and a delusion, a mere designation for its appearance;
its essence is the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is the nature.
△ Third, the reconciliation of the twelve bases with the nature (in two parts): First, the general inquiry.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true thusness-nature?
This collectively interrogates the twelve bases (*āyatana*), which are themselves the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

For the first five aggregates (*skandha*), metaphors are employed to illustrate the Dharma in order to shatter clinging to false conceptions. Next, the six sense bases (*āyatana*) borrow from worldly phenomena to reveal their illusory and delusive nature.
These twelve bases, continuing through to the final seven elements (*dhātu*), are all things presently perceived by the eyes and heard by the ears.
That which is commonly known by all people is shown to be their inherent nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). This proceeds from the distant to the near, and from the remote to the intimate;
it is precisely like the Tathāgata’s gradual and skillful guidance, his compassionate heart (*pobin*) that artfully brings about awakening.

"Twelve" refers to the six internal sense faculties and the six external sense objects. "Place" (*chu*) means location or spatial position; it also implies being fixed or determined. By means of the internal faculties and the external...

Dust (objects) each has a fixed location and spatial position. Now, because one wishes to dissolve them back into the nature of the treasury [the *ālayavijñāna*], one therefore refutes and eliminates their fixed locations and positions.
Furthermore, although within this context both faculties and objects are mutually refuted to reveal the true, the primary intent lies in the refutation of the objects.

This is because the six internal sense organs have already been refuted and clarified previously. Indeed, since the organs and their objects depend upon one another, their relationship is like that of two bundles of reeds leaning against each other;
therefore, they must be cited together and refuted as a pair.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in six parts): 1. The nature of the eye and visible forms.
Ānanda, you should first observe this Jeta Grove forest... [up to] ...it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two bases of eye and form are themselves the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
this is the point realized by Upāliśata. Therefore, the World-Honored One raised both the eye and form together to interrogate him, saying:
"Ānanda, you usually know only that all dharmas rely on causes and depend on conditions, as when it is said that the eye and form serve as conditions. However—"
As for this eye-faculty that is able to observe, and these objects of observation— the colors of the Jeta Grove, its springs, and its ponds—
since that which observes is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and that which is observed is the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*),
how do you understand these phenomena that arise from such faculties and objects? Are they not external forms that give rise to your visual perception?
Is it within the internal sense-base? Or does the internal eye-faculty arise at the external location of that visible object?

These two questions correctly open up two paths. Ānanda, if you further claim that it is the internal eye-faculty arising at that external appearance of form which constitutes the place where seeing first occurs, then this is form...
The nature belongs to the eye. Suppose the visual faculty were to see only empty space;

at a time when it does not see the characteristics of form, this nature of form should naturally perish along with those characteristics of form. Once the nature of form has perished, the characteristics of form would also be non-existent.
Even if your seeing were to persist, what would there be to manifest? Since there is nothing to manifest, then both the characteristics of emptiness and form—
All things are non-existent; for both the characteristics of space and form must depend on one another to be manifested.

Since the characteristic of the substance of form has already been shown to be non-existent, who then could manifest the characteristic of the substance of space? Thus, the calculation that the eye produces the characteristic of form is erroneous.
If it is claimed that the visual faculty produces the characteristic of space, this is likewise just like its producing the characteristic of form.

If it is further claimed that this external dust of form gives rise to your internal visual perception, such that only then does the locus of seeing exist, then this nature of seeing would belong to form.

Should you then encounter empty space—at a time when no visible forms appear before you—this nature of seeing ought likewise to perish along with form. If the nature of seeing has perished, then who [is it that sees]?

If one analyzes empty space and form, they would both be utterly non-existent. Since objects are manifested by means of the sense organs, and the organs are now absent, by what could one manifest the objects that are distinguished as either empty space or form?
This calculation—that form arises from the visual faculty—is also incorrect. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should understand that internally..."
The eye that sees and the external forms and space—these two have no location.

This very appearance of form and the faculty of seeing are both merely false designations for these two locations. If one seeks their source, they are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ Second, the ear and sound are themselves the nature.
"Ānanda, you listen further to this [sound] within the Jeta Grove" (up to) "...is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two locations—the ear and sound—are themselves the Tathāgatagarbha-nature; it is the point understood by Kauṇḍinya.
Ānanda, listen further to this: within the Jeta Grove, the drum is struck because vegetarian food has been prepared, and the bell is tolled because the great assembly wishes to gather.
Now, these sounds of the bell and the drum, whether preceding or following one another, arise in continuous succession.

In your view, how do you understand this? Do these sounds come to the vicinity of your ears so that you hear them, or does your faculty of hearing go to the place where the sounds are so that you hear them?
Ānanda, if it were the case that the sound of these bells and drums comes to the location of the ears, then when I enter the city to beg for alms...
If there were no self within the forest, then I certainly would not hear the bells and drums in that forest.
However, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa must not have heard them at the same time. Why is this? Because the sound of these bells and drums must necessarily reach the vicinity of Ānanda’s ears.
Even if one were to grant that the assembly heard them together, how could a single bell and a single drum [be heard by all simultaneously]?
Are there multiple sounds? This is like a single person who cannot simultaneously attend to two places; thus we know that a single sound cannot reach all ears at once.
How much more so is this evident in the following example? Since it is not even heard when [the conditions] are few, how could it be heard when they are many?
How much more so when there are many? Yet, this is not the case now; for upon hearing the sound of a bell, they all come together to the place of eating.

Thus, one can know that it is not the sound that comes to the side of the ear. If you further claim that it is your faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) that goes to the location where the sound of the bells and drums is, then it would be as if I were returning to dwell in the Jeta Grove and consequently no longer existed within the city. Therefore—

I certainly do not hear the bells and drums within the city. Just as when you are in the city and hear the sound of those drums, your ear has already gone to the place where the drums are being struck.
Even if the sound of the bell and the resonance of the drum were to emerge simultaneously, they should not be heard at the same time. Why?
Because this single sense-organ has already gone to the location of the drum; therefore, when the sound of the bell emerges, it necessarily cannot be heard [simultaneously].
[The opponent] replies: "They are heard together. [The author] says: This is like how a single body cannot simultaneously reach two places;

thus one knows that how could a single sense organ possibly go everywhere to multiple sounds? If both the bell and the drum are heard together, this would imply the existence of multiple sense organs.
Is such a principle even possible? How much more so when the subsequent examples clarify this! The intention is: not only are the bell and drum produced and heard simultaneously, but...
Within that city, elephants trumpet, horses neigh, oxen bellow, and sheep bleat; the various sounds of both sentient and insentient beings emerge all at once and are heard simultaneously.

This makes it clear that the ear does not travel to the location of the sound. If one were to claim that the faculty of hearing and the object of sound each remain in their own respective positions without any movement between them, then the sound would not come to the ear, nor would the ear go to the sound.
If sound does not travel, then since the two do not reach one another, there should likewise be sound where there is no hearing;
yet this is not the case. Wherever there is sound, the ear immediately hears it. Thus, we know that there is indeed a movement [of sound].
Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should understand that the internal faculty of hearing and the external..."
Regarding the auditory faculty and the object of sound, both are devoid of a fixed location. Therefore, these two—the faculty of hearing and the object of sound—are both illusory designations.
If one seeks their fundamental source, it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous.
△ Third, the nose and fragrance are themselves the nature.
Ānanda, when you again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... (up to)... it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two locations—the nose and fragrance—are themselves the Tathāgatagarbha-nature. This is the entry into Perfect Penetration of the youth Aromatic Adornment.

This is the locus. The Buddha, wishing to clarify the characteristics of the sensory objects of the nose, first pointed to a rare fragrance to manifest its excellence, and then questioned him, saying:
"Ānanda, you should now smell with your nose; smell this sandalwood in the incense burner.
Yet, as soon as a mere *liang* (one-tenth of an ounce) has been ignited, throughout the forty *li* within the city of Rājagṛha, everyone simultaneously [perceives it]."
Upon smelling this fragrance, what do you think? How do you interpret it?
Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree itself? Does it arise from your faculty of the nose? Or does it arise from empty space?
Ānanda, if you say that this fragrance arises from your nose, then since you claim this fragrance is produced by the nose, it should follow that...
This fragrance ought to emerge from the nose; however, the nose is merely flesh and is not sandalwood.
How, then, could the scent of sandalwood exist within the fleshy nose?
Even if one were to concede that the nose produces it, to claim that you can smell it would still contradict reason. Why is it said that the fragrance enters the nose?
Only then can it be called "smelling. Since the fragrance has already emerged from the nose, to say that you are able to smell it is not at all the true meaning.
Thus, [the fragrance] is not produced by the sense organ. If you claim that this fragrance is produced by space, then the nature of space, which is its producer, is immutable and eternal;
consequently, the fragrance produced by it ought likewise to be immutable.
Since it exists constantly, why must one rely on burning this withered wood in an incense burner for there to be fragrance?

One can thus know that it does not arise from emptiness. If you claim that this fragrance must arise from the wood, then the substance of this extraordinary fragrance is produced by the burning as smoke, which allows the nose to perceive it. If it is perceived by the nose, it ought to be [the nose] that receives it.
Regarding its smoke and vapors: one might say that fragrance arises from the wood;

yet, as that smoke rises into the void, it has not traveled far before the fragrance is already perceived within a distance of forty li. How could this be if the fragrance were produced from the wood?
Therefore, the conclusion is drawn below: "For this reason, one should understand that external fragrance [is not produced from the wood]."
The olfactory faculty within and the fragrance as the object—both of these have no fixed location.
Thus, this smelling faculty and that fragrant dust: these two locations are equally false designations of appearances.
If one seeks their source, they are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously. Sandalwood, too...
Regarding "ox-head" (gokhura): sandalwood originates from Mount Ox-Head in the northern continent of Uttarakuru. Thus, it is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

"This incense, six *zhu* in weight, is worth the entire Sahā world. The *Bowu zhi* states that during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, envoys from the Western Garden presented four pieces of incense, each as large as a chicken egg.
According to Han regulations, incense weighing less than one *jin* was not permitted [to be offered].
Later, when Chang’an was afflicted by an epidemic, a messenger submitted a petition requesting that one pellet be burned as incense.

Within a radius of forty li, all those suffering from the plague were cured. This is clear evidence of the extraordinary excellence of this wondrous fragrance. The *Lilizhi* (Annals of Calendars) states:
"Twenty-four *zhū* constitute one *liǎng*. What is now called one *zhū* is [calculated as] one-quarter, one *lí*, six *máo*, six *sī*, and six..."
Suddenly! △ Fourth, the nature of the tongue and its flavors:
"Ānanda, when you are constantly holding your almsbowl among the assembly during the two meal times... (up to) "...it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature."
This clarifies that the two bases of tongue and taste are themselves the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
this is the place where the tongues of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata drag upon the ground. For there are none among humanity who do not eat and drink, yet few are able to know the true flavor.

Therefore, he causes the one present before him to seek out the news by directing his attention toward the very edge of the bowl where the spoon is lifted and the chopsticks are set down, and to inquire of him, saying: "Ā—"

I challenge you: when you partake of the two sustenances of Dharma-joy and the delight of dhyāna during ordinary times, and hold your alms-bowl to eat amidst the great assembly, your tongue-faculty may at times encounter ghee, curd, and clarified butter—these are all called "superior flavors.
Surely these must pass through your mind; yet, how do you interpret this in your own mind? Regarding these superior [flavors]...
Does this flavor arise from empty space? Does it arise within the tongue-faculty? Or does it arise within the food and drink?

If you claim that this exquisite flavor arises from your tongue-faculty, then since there is only one tongue within your mouth, that which produces it should likewise be only one, and the flavor produced should also be only one. Its...
It can produce the faculty of the tongue. At the moment it is produced, the flavor of ghee has already been formed; thus, it should perceive only the flavor of ghee.
Or, if it encounters black rock honey, it should not shift or change its perception, yet it would also know it to be the flavor of honey.
If the fruit were not subject to inference, transformation, or change, yet one could still perceive the taste of ghee alone, then it would no longer be called the "faculty that perceives taste.

How could there be a tongue-faculty that does not know taste? If you claim that the tongue-faculty is capable of inference, transformation, and change, and thus allows for the perception of many tastes—since taste arises from the tongue and is manifold in kind—then [the following applies]:
Your tongue does not possess multiple entities; therefore, it would be inconsistent for that which produces [the sensation] and that which is produced [by it] to be distinct. Thus it is asked:
"How can various kinds of flavors all arise from a single tongue-faculty capable of cognizing them?
It is evident that the notion that flavor arises from the faculty is incorrect. If one were to claim that this flavor arises solely within the food itself—
It does not depend upon the tongue-faculty. Now, food is fundamentally an insentient object; it is not a consciousness capable of discrimination.
How, then, could it know of itself whether it is sweet or bitter? Furthermore, if food were able to know for itself, it would be the same as another person eating and perceiving the flavor;
what business would that have with you? How, then, can your tongue-faculty be called that which "tastes" flavors?
Is this knowledge [produced] by the tongue? To say that this perception of flavor arises from the food is also incorrect.
If you claim that this flavor arises from space, then you might as well try tasting space yourself; what kind of flavor does it have?
Even if you insist that space possesses a salty taste, then it would follow that the entirety of space is salty.
Salt. Since it can salt your tongue, it should likewise salt your face; thus, the people of the world would all be like fish in the salt sea.
Once they have experienced this saltiness, they would naturally fail to perceive its sweetness.
If they truly do not recognize sweetness, they will naturally not be aware of saltiness either, until both the flavors of salt and sweet become indistinguishable.
[The Buddha] said: "Know this. How could empty space be called that which knows taste? This calculation that taste arises from space is even more incorrect.

Therefore, he concludes below by saying: "For this reason, one should understand that the external object of taste and the internal faculty of the tongue, as well as the act of tasting and that which is tasted—both of these are without location. That is to say:
This capacity of the tongue to taste and that which is tasted by the flavor—both are illusory designations.
If one seeks their fundamental source, it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

Regarding "black stone honey" (*kṛṣṇa-phāṇita*), the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states that it is simply sugarcane syrup; because its color is black and its consistency is firm, its flavor is [extremely]... [sweet].
It is sweet; therefore, it is called black stone honey (*kṛṣṇa-phāṇita*).
△ Fifth, the nature of bodily touch:
"Ānanda, when you regularly rub your head with your hand in the early morning... [up to] ...it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature."
This clarifies the two bases of body and touch, which are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. This is precisely the spot that Bhadrapāla touched while bathing.

Generally speaking, what is called "touch" must be established through the union and separation, or the opposition and conformity, of the sense organ, the object, the subject, the capacity for cognition, and the lack thereof.
Here, touch is specifically elucidated by means of the single body alone. This is correct.

This reveals that all phenomena are of one essence; fundamentally, there is neither subject nor object, neither union nor separation. It is only because the sensory objects and the mind are separated by deluded emotions that they falsely appear to exist.
Therefore, the Buddha questioned him, saying: "Ānanda, suppose I were to command my disciples to stroke their heads three times a day, and they themselves recite:
'Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let not the body transgress. A practitioner who acts in this way will attain..."
Dushi, you too should practice according to these instructions. Always, at dawn, rub your head with your hand.
At the moment of this rubbing, the hand knows there is a head, and the head knows there is a hand. Now tell me: who is the knower? Who is the known?
Furthermore, who is that which is touched, and who is the toucher? Yet, as for this capacity...
As for that which knows touch: does it reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head?
If one claims that the knower of touch resides solely in the hand, then the knowledge of touch would be located in the hand, while the head would become an insentient object.
How, then, could the head know the touch of the hand and experience that sensation? If one claims that the knower of touch...
If [the sensation] were located solely in the head, then one would perceive the touch as being in the head, and the hand would become a useless object.
How then could one know that the touch of the head is on my hand and call it "touch"? If you claim that the head and the hand...
If each [part] has its own cognition, then you, Ānanda, must have two bodies.

If you claim that the head and the hand share a single cognition, then the sensations produced by them must also be a single touch. If this were so, then the hand and the head would constitute a single entity.
If they were indeed a single entity, then touch could not be established. Why? Because it is only when there are two distinct things that [touch can occur].
One might say it is "contact. But now that there is only one [entity], how can there be contact?
If you claim that the head and the hand are still two cognitions and two entities, tell me then: where does this contact reside? Does it belong to the subject that touches?
If [the capacity] belongs to the subject, then wherever there is contact—whether in the hand or in the head—it would all constitute the capacity to touch;

yet these are not themselves the object touched. Since that which is touched is not established, how could space be established for you as the object touched? If, on the other hand, contact belongs to the object...
Whether it be in the hand or in the head, all become that which is touched; yet this is not the same as being the toucher itself.
Since there is no such thing as a "toucher," how could empty space possibly become the toucher for you? Thus, both the "toucher" and the "touched" are equally unestablished.
Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should understand that the touch which is perceived and the perceiver [are likewise unestablished]."
These two—the body and its object—both lack a fixed location. This very faculty of the body and the sense-object of touch are both illusory designations.
If one seeks their origin, they are neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; they are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
To whom does "touch" belong? Who is it that touches? Only when these questions are addressed can the meaning be fully elucidated.
△ Sixth, the mental faculty and its objects are themselves the nature.
"Ānanda, that which you constantly take as objects within your mind—whether good or evil... (up to) "...is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two locations of the mental faculty and its objects are the Tathāgatagarbha-nature; this is how Mahākāśyapa attained perfect penetration.
It is a locus. Ānanda, that which you ordinarily take as the objective dharma-dust within the mental faculty belongs solely to the internal;
it is merely the shadow-activity of the arising and ceasing of the first five sense-objects, and even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it possesses no separate substance.
If one wishes to discern this nature, it does not exceed three categories: first, the nature of goodness; second, the nature of evil.
This refers to the nature of all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas possessed by the sixth consciousness.

Third is the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), which refers to the nature of all that is neither unwholesome nor wholesome within the sixth consciousness, characterized initially by a lack of recollection.
All arise from what is perceived by the mental faculty (*manas*) and spontaneously establish a fixed principle; therefore, they are called "nature" (*svabhāva*).

This is what is meant by being capable without being taught. Since all conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and all contaminated phenomena of arising and ceasing are produced through the activity of these three natures, they are said to be "generated and formed. However, as for these various phenomena...

It does not take the three natures as its standard; therefore, it is called the "Dharma-standard. For this reason, whatever the mental faculty (*manas*) of ours takes as its object is either good or evil.
If one does not discern between good and evil, one falls into the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Apart from these three natures, there is no other mental dharma to be found. Yet, as for this dust of dharmas (*dharmaviṣaya*), is it indeed you?
Is it produced from the mind of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*)? Or does it exist in a separate location apart from the mind of your mental faculty?

Ānanda, if you claim that this dharma-object (*dharma-viṣaya*) is identical to the mind of the mental faculty, then since the dharma-object is thus the mind of the mental faculty, it should not be a dharma-object.
Since it would not belong to the objects of perception, it would by its own nature not be [a dharma-object].
Regarding the objects perceived by the mind-faculty (*manas*), how can they constitute the objective domain of that mind-faculty?

If one were to claim that these mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) exist as distinct directions or locations separate from the mind-faculty, then those mental objects would necessarily possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Yet, is the nature of such objects conscious or is it non-conscious?
Is there cognition? If you claim there is cognition, then it should be designated as the mind of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*);

it should not be further renamed an internal object-field (*dharmāyatana*). Since it differs from your mental faculty, and furthermore, since it is a cognition that is not an object-field, it would be yet another mind.
Would this not be identical to the mental capacity of another person? Even if you insist on maintaining that it is distinct—
It has a specific location. Even if it were not a sensory object (*viṣaya*), it certainly could not be the mental measure (*citta-mātra*) of another person;
rather, it must be yours. If it is indeed your own mental measure, why would your mind not be united with it as one, instead being separated from it as two?
Thus, it can be seen that the calculation that the dharma-object exists apart from the faculty of thought (*manas*) and yet possesses cognition is erroneous.
If you claim that this mental object (dharmāyatana) is a mind separate from the faculty of the intellect (manas), yet lacks cognition, then this mental object must still belong to the internal.

Since it is not external forms, sounds, odors, or tastes, nor is it the tactile sensations of contact, cohesion, cold, or heat, nor is it the characteristics of space and so forth—if separated from all these objects, where could it possibly exist? For now, let us consider...
Within this space between form and emptiness, there is nothing at all that can be manifested or pointed out.
Is it not the case that within the human world, there is yet another "emptiness beyond emptiness," which serves as the locus where the objects of the dharma-realm (dharmas) are contained?
Furthermore, since this dharma-object (dharma-āyatana) is not possessed of consciousness, it cannot in itself be the faculty of mind (mano-indriya) that acts as the perceiving subject.
Moreover, being situated outside of the sense-faculties in empty space, it certainly cannot be the dharma-object that serves as the perceived object.
Since it is neither the perceiving faculty nor the perceived object, both subject and object are unattainable. Now tell me: from where does this locus of dharmas arise?
Who, then, stands [as the knower]? To claim that one can perceive mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) apart from the mental faculty (*manas*), yet there is no cognizer, is likewise erroneous.
Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should understand that these are merely the dharmas which serve as objects of perception."
Thus, both the faculty that serves as the object of cognition and the mind that cognizes it are devoid of any location.

Consequently, this mental faculty (*manas*) and its corresponding mental objects (*dharmas*) are both illusory designations. If one seeks their fundamental source, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they spontaneous;
rather, they are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Within this context, the character "mind" (*xin*) uniformly refers to the mental faculty of cognition (*manovijñānendriya*).
△ Four: The Four Assemblies on the Eighteen Dhātus as Being Nature (2). 1. General Inquiry:
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the eighteen dhātus fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true *tathatā* nature?
This is a general inquiry. In the Sanskrit language, it is *dhātu*; here it is translated as "element" (*jie*).

This carries the meaning of "cause," referring to the fact that the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—are mutually causes for one another. Furthermore, it carries the meaning of "genus" or "lineage," referring to the fact that each of the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—possesses its own seeds.
Because each has its own distinct category. The eighteenth refers to the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, "realm" (*dhātu*) means a boundary or limit. That which is internal and capable of cognition belongs to the boundary of the sense organs;

that which is external and serves as the object of cognition belongs to the boundary of the objects; and that which is intermediate and capable of clear discernment belongs to the boundary of consciousness. Hereafter—

Although the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are presented together, the primary refutation lies in consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is because the two categories of faculties and objects are first refuted by way of making them manifest.

For if the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) is established, then the faculties and objects are established in mutual dependence; if the realm of consciousness is not established, then the faculties and objects are mutually quiescent.
This is like a single room divided into three sections by internal walls; now, those intermediate walls have been demolished.

The walls originally constituted a single room; thus, there was no separate designation for three bays. Therefore, this not only breaks through consciousness (*vijñāna*), but also breaks through boundaries (*dhātu*).
Since there are no distinct divisions of territory, consciousness, the sense faculties (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*) do not even require the application of names to be integrated.
This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in six parts): First, that eye, form, and consciousness are themselves the nature.
Ānanda, as you have understood, the eye and form serve as conditions... [down to] fundamentally neither being the nature of causes and conditions nor the nature of spontaneity.
This clarifies that the triad of eye, form, and consciousness is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is the locus where Śāriputra’s mental vision emits light.
For the Buddha wished to shatter Śāriputra’s realm of consciousness, he first questioned him regarding what the disciple had previously understood, saying:
"Ānanda, according to what you have explained before, the eye possesses discrimination, while the objects of form are devoid of cognition; as for consciousness..."

It arises therein. Thus, with the eye-faculty and the object-field as internal and external conditions, visual consciousness arises in between, thereby establishing the threefold boundary. Now, is this consciousness produced by the eye-faculty as its cause?
Is it that the eye alone constitutes the boundary of this consciousness? Or is it that because it is produced by the object-field of form, the object-field of form constitutes its boundary?

Ānanda, if you say that this consciousness arises solely from the faculty of the eye and thus the eye-faculty constitutes its boundary, then since the defining characteristic of consciousness is the cognition of objects, yet there would be neither the objects of form nor emptiness—how could it arise?
Then there would be no object to be distinguished. Even if you possessed visual consciousness, what would you have it employ?

Since there is no sensory object (*viṣaya*), consciousness is not employed. If you claim that the sense faculty (*indriya*) is perceived as the limit of consciousness from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and if your ultimate sense faculty is composed of the eight pure substances (*śubha-dravya*), even so—
The function of this faculty is to illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness, yet its essence belongs to that which is invisible.
Thus, this faculty is not the same as the color-phenomena of blue, yellow, red, or white, which manifest clearly within, without, or in between, and possess distinct indications.
Furthermore, since the essence of this faculty is invisible, there is no location where it can be found.
It has been demonstrated that since there is no location—neither internal, external, nor intermediate—it follows from where your visual consciousness establishes its boundaries?
To calculate the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) by positing the eye-faculty as its basis is erroneous.

If you claim that this consciousness arises solely from the object of form and takes form as its boundary, then when the appearance of space manifests—that is, at the time when there is no form—your consciousness arising from form should perish along with the form and would not be able to cognize space.
How, then, could it cognize this as the nature of emptiness rather than the nature of form? If you say:
When the characteristics of form undergo transformation, your consciousness also perceives that transformation of the characteristics of form;

thus, your consciousness does not itself undergo transformation along with those characteristics of form. However, when that form ceases while your consciousness does not migrate, this consciousness exists alone.
Being without further counterparts, with what other dharma could it demarcate boundaries? And on what basis could it establish its own realm?
Suppose one were to argue: "If consciousness changes when matter changes, then it is possible to establish a distinct realm for consciousness alongside matter.

To refute this, it is said: If consciousness changes in accordance with matter, then both matter and consciousness would change and perish together, and the defining characteristic of consciousness as a realm (*dhātu-lakṣaṇa*) would naturally vanish.
Since the characteristic of a realm no longer exists, how can one say that consciousness has matter as its realm?
If one were to calculate dualistically that both consciousness and form are equally unchanging, then the realm of consciousness could be established based on form.
To this, it is refuted: if both are unchanging, then their two essences must exist eternally. Since this consciousness arises because of form, it would likewise be devoid of cognition;
it should naturally be unable to discern or know the location of empty space. This being so—

If one can know the location of emptiness, how could one possibly know the location of form? Since the location of form cannot be known, from what basis could the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) be established?
Thus, it is evident that the calculation which establishes the element of consciousness based on the object-field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*) is also erroneous.
If it is argued that neither the sense organ alone nor the object alone can produce consciousness, [then...]
If you claim that it must depend upon both the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and the object-field (*rūpa-viṣaya*) to be able to arise together, tell me:
do they arise as a single unified mass, or do they arise separated in two distinct locations? If you say they form a single unified mass, then there would be no intervening gap;
even if consciousness were to arise, it would necessarily exist apart from and beside [the sense organ], so how could it be established?

Is it the boundary within which consciousness arises? If you claim it exists apart from both locations, then even the consciousness that arises would have to split into two parts to join them—one half joining with the eye-faculty and the other half joining with the visual object.
If this were so, how could it serve as the boundary within which consciousness arises? Furthermore, the two...

If they were to combine, the essential nature of consciousness would become further confused. Why? Because if it combined with half of the sense organ, it would belong to that which possesses cognition;

if it combined with half of the object, it would belong to that which lacks cognition. Thus, cognition and non-cognition would be intermingled and mixed, such that its essential nature would be inherently chaotic from the outset.
How, then, could the boundaries of consciousness be established? One may observe and deliberate upon this consciousness.
To establish the *dhātu* (elements) based on both the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is even more erroneous. Therefore, the conclusion below states:

"By this principle, one should understand that when the eye-faculty and the form-object serve as conditions to produce the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), these three locations are entirely without arising. Thus, it is known that the eye-faculty, the form-object, and the eye-consciousness-element—these...
Third: fundamentally, it is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ Second, the ear, sounds, and consciousness are themselves the nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the ear and sounds acting as conditions (extending to): fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

This clarifies that the triad of ear, sound, and consciousness is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is precisely the locus where the Great Being Samantabhadra’s mental hearing is manifested.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the ear-faculty that you habitually recognize as functioning in conjunction with the object of sound to produce ear-consciousness:
does this consciousness arise because of the ear-faculty, taking the ear-faculty as its cause? Or does it take the ear-faculty...
Is it the boundary of consciousness? Or is it produced by the sense-object of sound, such that the sense-object of sound itself constitutes the boundary of consciousness?
Ānanda, if you say this discussion arises solely from the faculty of the ear, then you are merely taking the faculty as the producer;
yet you fail to realize that there is the movement of sound and the stillness of no-sound—these two characteristics of the sense-objects.
Since it does not manifest before one, the supreme sense-faculty (paramārtha-indriya) cannot function as a knower.

Thus, there would necessarily be no object to be known, and the faculty that knows it would likewise not exist. If this were so, there would be nothing to be known externally and no knower internally.

Since the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are likewise unestablished, what shape or appearance could the consciousness produced by the organs possess, and from whence would it arise?
Furthermore, if you should argue: "The ultimate sense organs (*paramārtha-indriya*) are invisible and therefore cannot constitute the spheres (*dhātu*) of consciousness;
however, the superficial sense organs (*sāmantaka-indriya*) are visible—could they not then establish the spheres? Thus he refutes [this position].

He said: "If you claim that the fleshly ear can hear—that is, if you maintain that the peripheral sensory organ (*bāhyendriya*) can also produce consciousness—then since there would be neither the movement of sound when it is heard nor the stillness of silence when there is no sound, the assertion that the fleshly ear can produce hearing and consciousness is likewise unestablished.
Furthermore, even the primary sensory organ (*pradhānendriya*) cannot produce consciousness."
How can it be said that the physical ear-organ (*māṃsa-śrotra*), which has the shape of a rolled leaf, gives rise to consciousness?

All the more so, since this physical ear is intermingled with the color-form (*varṇa-saṃsthāna*) of the body-organ (*kāya-indriya*). Since the organ already belongs to the body, its object must be the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), unless it is the sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*).
Even if one wished to establish a sense-field (*dhātu*) based on this, it could only be called the "body-consciousness field" (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*). Thus, as for the ear—

Regarding the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*): furthermore, from what is it established? It is not correct to maintain that the element of consciousness is established by means of the supreme ultimate and the physical sense organ (*mūla-indriya*).

If one were to claim that this consciousness arises solely due to the object of sound, then this auditory consciousness would exist independently of the sound-object alone, without any relation to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) which performs the act of listening. One fails to realize that, since [the faculty] is absent...
If the faculty of the ear that is able to hear were itself extinguished, then the characteristics of the sounds heard would also vanish. From what location, then, could consciousness arise?

If you claim that consciousness takes sound as its objective sphere (*viṣaya*), then even granting that consciousness arises from sound, one must also grant that the auditory faculty exists because of the auditory object;
for there are two kinds of sound-characteristics: movement and stillness. Thus, this consciousness and the sound [are related].

First: when the ear-root hears a sound, it should also hear the consciousness. If it does not hear the consciousness, then sound and consciousness would both fail to be the "element" (*dhātu*) that gives rise to consciousness.
If, however, it does hear the consciousness, then consciousness—just like the sound—would be entirely devoid of cognition.
Since consciousness is already being heard by the ear and thus lacks cognition, who then is it that knows the hearing of consciousness? If...
This means that if there were no further cognition—no knowing, hearing, or perceiving—then for the rest of your life you would be like grass and trees, possessing not a single bit of awareness;
is such a principle possible? Therefore, the calculation of the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) as being established by the object-field of sound is also incorrect.

Since the sense organ does not arise alone and the object does not appear in isolation, it should not be that the sound-object and the hearing-organ intermingle with one another to constitute the middle element within consciousness. For if they are said to intermingle, they cannot constitute an element.

Yet there would be no intermediate position. Since an intermediate position must exist for internal and external to be distinguished, if there were now no intermediate boundary, from what boundary could the two aspects of internal and external be established?

Thus, the calculation that the consciousness-element is established by the commonality of the sense-faculties and their objects is even more incorrect. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should..."

One should understand this: that which is called the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and sound-objects (*śabda-viṣaya*) as conditions giving rise to the sphere of auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*)—these three locations are all, in their entirety, non-arising.

Thus, one knows that these three—the auditory faculty, sound-objects, and the sphere of auditory consciousness—are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ Third, the consciousness of nose-odor is itself the nature.

Ānanda, furthermore, as for the nose and odors that you understand to be conditions (up to the point where it is said): fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the triad of nose, fragrance, and consciousness is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is the very object of contemplation for Sundarananda.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the nose and fragrance acting as conditions to produce olfactory consciousness:
does this consciousness arise because of the nasal faculty, such that the nasal faculty constitutes the boundary of the consciousness? Or does it arise because of fragrance?
Is it that the olfactory object (*gandha-viṣaya*) produced from dust serves as the boundary for consciousness?

Ānanda, if you say that this consciousness is produced because of the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), and thus the nose-faculty serves as the boundary for consciousness, then within your own mind, what would you take to be the nose?
Would you take the hanging flesh on the face, shaped like a pair of claws?

Is the "floating dust-root" (the physical organ) the nose? Or is it the "ultimate reality-root" (the sensory faculty), which possesses the nature of initiating the cognition of smelling and the movement of inhalation and exhalation, that is the nose?
If one takes the fleshy form to be the nose, then that fleshly substance belongs to the body-root (*kāyendriya*), not the nose-root (*ghrāṇendriya*).
Furthermore, that which performs the cognition is the tactile cognition of the body; it does not belong to the olfactory cognition of the nose.

Furthermore, that which is known is the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) and does not belong to the object of fragrance (*gandha*). Since it is called the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it is not the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*);
since it is called the object of touch, it is not the object of fragrance. If this is so, then even the nose-faculty and the object of fragrance would lack a name;
how then could the nose be established as the realm of consciousness? This calculation takes the floating root (*mūla*) to be the realm of consciousness.
This is delusion. If you take the nature of that which perceives by smelling as the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), then within your own mind, what do you consider to be the knower?

If you say that the flesh at the tip of the nose is the knower, then that which is known by the flesh fundamentally belongs to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*);
it is not the nose-faculty and the object of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*). Therefore, the knower would belong to the body, not the nose.

It is the nostrils that are involved. If you consider the emptiness within the nostrils to be the faculty of cognition, then emptiness itself would possess cognition, and the flesh at the tip of the nose would be devoid of awareness.

Furthermore, if the emptiness within the nostrils already possesses the nature of cognition, then by such analogy, all empty space ought to be the flesh at the tip of your nose; yet, [in reality], it lacks the nature of cognition.
Then all the flesh of your entire body would likewise not be that which knows emptiness.
Since you yourself are thus empty space, which fundamentally has no location, today Ānanda himself should likewise have no location.

Furthermore, if the body is not that which knows, then even though the body exists, it should not perceive where it is located. Suppose you then formulate this further argument: "This is the ultimate truth..."
This knowledge does not originally depend on the flesh, nor does it depend on space; rather, it arises in dependence upon fragrance and stench.

He then refuted this, saying: "If you claim that fragrance and stench themselves constitute the nature capable of producing the faculty of olfactory cognition, then this olfactory cognition would belong inherently to the fragrance and stench.
Since the fragrance and stench possess their own olfactory cognition, what concern is it to your sense organ?"
[The opponent] says: "It is not that fragrance and stench give rise to cognition; rather, it is because of fragrance and stench that cognition arises.

[The author] refutes this as well, saying: "If you claim that the two gases of fragrance and stench must arise because of your nose’s smelling and cognizing, then those two kinds of moving gases—fragrance and stench—would not arise of their own accord."
The stinking iranda tree and the sandalwood tree are, in the ultimate sense, the very sources from which your sense organ arises.
If these two substances do not come into contact with you, you should simply smell your own nose and see for yourself whether it is fragrant.
Is it the nose that is the stench? If the nose were the stench, then it could not perceive fragrance.
If the nose were fragrance, then it should not be able to perceive stench. How could there be a faculty of the nose that does not know fragrance and stench?
If you claim that your nasal faculty can smell both fragrant and foul vapors, then it would follow that you, as a single person, must possess two distinct cognitions.
"One who perceives fragrance" and "one who perceives stench"—if this were so, there would be two noses.
For a single person has but one nose; if there were two noses, then when I question him, there ought to be two [answers].

Ānanda, between these two, which one is your true self? If you claim that the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), which is capable of producing [perception], is a single entity, then the odors produced—whether fragrant or foul—would necessarily not be two distinct things.
If what is foul can already be considered fragrant, then that foulness lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If what is fragrant can further become foul, then that fragrance lacks intrinsic nature.

However, since these two kinds—the fragrant and the foul—are not present as the nature of the faculty that perceives through smelling, from what could the sphere of olfactory consciousness (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) be established?
This calculation that the ultimate reality constitutes the sphere of consciousness is also false.

If it is argued that this consciousness arises because of the fragrance-object (gandhaviṣaya), and that the fragrance-object itself constitutes the boundary of the consciousness, then it is as follows:

Consciousness exists because of fragrance. Just as the eye has the capacity for seeing, yet cannot perceive the eye itself, so too consciousness exists because of fragrance and should therefore not know that fragrance.
If it can know the fragrance, then it is not produced by means of fragrance.

If one does not know fragrance, and the consciousness that is capable of knowing it likewise does not exist—should the result be that fragrance is not known? It would not be merely a matter of the consciousness being absent;
rather, both the realm of fragrance and the realm of consciousness would necessarily fail to be established. Why is this? For fragrance is not perceived by smelling alone;

were it not for the existence of such fragrance, it would necessarily be manifested through consciousness. Now, since consciousness itself is not consciousness, [then fragrance cannot be established either].
Since fragrance has no counterpart, its boundaries naturally do not exist. Once the realm of fragrance is not established, consciousness likewise does not know where the fragrance resides.
Even if one were to concede that the realm is established by virtue of consciousness, the realm would still not be established because consciousness itself lacks a counterpart.
Why is this? Because it is not established from the objective dust of fragrance. If this is so, then...

To claim that the destruction of consciousness constitutes its realm is an error without end. This calculation that the fragrance-particle constitutes the realm of consciousness is even more delusory.
Now, since this intermediate realm of consciousness does not exist, then both the internal faculties and the external objects fail to be established.
If neither the internal nor the external are established, then that which arises through their coexistence lacks reality.
If the intermediate realm is not established, then that which is co-arisen is not true. How could the nature of those consciousnesses of smelling and hearing not be ultimately false?
Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should understand that the olfactory faculty and olfactory objects serve as conditions."
Regarding that which arises as the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna-dhātu*), there is, in fact, no sense of arising within these three locations.
Thus, the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), the fragrance object (*gandha-viṣaya*), and the nose-consciousness— these three— are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha-nature,
which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ Fourth, the consciousness of tongue and taste is itself the nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, that which you understand as the conditions of the tongue and taste (up to: "fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature").
This clarifies that the tongue, flavors, and gustatory consciousness—these three—are the very nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;

this is the point of entry into perfect penetration through the sound of the Dharma as realized by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, gustatory consciousness arises.
Is this consciousness produced solely by the tongue-faculty, such that the tongue-faculty itself constitutes the boundary of the consciousness?
Or is it produced by the object of taste, such that the object of taste itself constitutes the boundary of the consciousness?
Ānanda, if you say that this consciousness is produced solely by the tongue-faculty without depending on external objects, and can cognize on its own—then...
Regarding the tongue being the boundary for consciousness:

if that were so, then all things in the world—such as the sweetness of sugarcane, the sourness of the *āmla* plum, the bitterness of *hāridrā*, the saltiness of rock salt, and the pungency of *śuṇṭhī*, ginger, and cinnamon—would have no taste at all, because taste depends upon the tongue. Since taste resides [in the object],...
"Your tongue, try it yourself. Is that tongue sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, then your tongue would already be a bitter flavor.
Furthermore, who comes to taste your tongue and perceive its bitterness?
For the tongue does not taste itself; who, then, performs this knowing and perceives that the tongue has become [bitter]?"
Is it the taste that is bitter? If you claim that the nature of the tongue is not bitter, then taste would not arise within the tongue of its own accord;
how then could a sense-field (dhātu) be established for the arising of consciousness? Therefore, it is incorrect to establish the consciousness-element based on the tongue-faculty.
If you claim that this consciousness arises solely from the object of taste without depending on an internal faculty, such that consciousness itself constitutes the taste—yet, since consciousness...
If [taste] arises because of flavor, then the very substance of consciousness would be that flavor itself.
If this were so, flavor would not be tasting its own flavor; it would be the same as the tongue-organ, which likewise should not taste its own tongue.
Since it does not taste itself, how can consciousness know what is flavor and what is not flavor? Furthermore, all flavors are originally not the property of a single entity.
[Consciousness] arises. Since the flavor that produces it already consists of many substances, the consciousness produced by it should likewise possess multiple entities;
just as a mother with many children must have many [children]. This uses the multiplicity of flavors to refute the singularity of consciousness.
Suppose it were argued that the essence of consciousness is indeed one; yet its essence must necessarily arise dependent upon flavor. Since the consciousness produced...
If they were one, then the tastes produced by them should also be one. That being the case, the saltiness of salt, the blandness of water, the sweetness of sugarcane, the pungency of ginger,
as well as the harmony formed by the combination of various flavors, their innate and unchanging co-arising natures,
and their extraordinary transformations through burning and boiling— whether raw or cooked— all such diverse tastes would necessarily be identical.
If they were of a single flavor, there would likewise be no differentiation; just as the child is one, the mother must also be one.
This uses the oneness of consciousness to refute the multiplicity of flavors. Furthermore, the very name "consciousness" is derived precisely from its capacity for differentiation.
If, in the case of the fruit, differentiation is absent, then it cannot be called consciousness. When even consciousness has no name, how [can there be flavor]?
Furthermore, can it be said that this consciousness is established by not relying on the internal faculty of the tongue, but depending solely on the external object of flavor?
If so, then the claim that the element of consciousness is established because of the object of flavor is also incorrect.
Since this conscious mind is produced neither from the faculty nor from the object, it cannot be that empty space is able to produce your mind.

As for tongue-consciousness, it establishes the boundaries of consciousness by depending upon space; is there any such principle? It is evident that those who calculate that [consciousness] arises without a cause are even more mistaken.
If one were to claim that a single faculty alone or a single object alone cannot establish the boundary of consciousness, [it would be untenable].

If it must be the case that consciousness arises only when the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) and the taste-object (*rasa-viṣaya*) come together in mutual conjunction, then consciousness cannot arise even within that conjunction itself.
Why? Because the faculty and the object are distinct and difficult to merge into one; thus, from the outset, neither possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since they lack intrinsic nature, how could they give rise to the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*)? This can be seen.
The notion that they arise together is also incorrect. Therefore, the conclusion below states:

"For this reason, one should understand that what is called the tongue-consciousness element, which arises with the tongue-faculty and taste-object as conditions, consists precisely of these three locations."

There is no meaning of arising whatsoever. Thus, these three—the tongue faculty, the flavor object, and the tongue-consciousness element—are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha nature, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ The fifth is the nature of body-tactile consciousness itself.
Ānanda, furthermore, as you have clarified that body and touch serve as conditions [up to] "it is fundamentally neither a causal condition nor a spontaneous nature."
This clarifies that the body, touch, and consciousness—these three—are themselves the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; this is the point of entry for Upāli’s awakening.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood—that the body and touch serve as conditions to produce body-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the body-faculty, such that the body-faculty constitutes the boundary of the consciousness? Or does it arise because of the object of touch?
"Is it that the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) constitutes the boundary of consciousness?
Ānanda, if you claim that this consciousness arises solely from the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), then there would necessarily be no two objects—namely, contact and separation.

Thus, although there is the body-faculty capable of sensation and observation, if there is no objective condition (*ālambana*) for such sensation and observation, even if a body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) were to arise, what would it cognize?"

To calculate that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) alone can produce consciousness is erroneous. If you claim that this consciousness is produced solely by the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), then necessarily your own body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) would not exist. If that were the case, even if the object of touch were present, who would know it?
How could there ever be a person without a body who is able to perceive contact and separation? This calculation [that] touch alone can produce consciousness is thus mistaken.
This is again erroneous. Ānanda, objects do not touch themselves, nor do they inherently possess cognition. It is only because the body possesses cognition that one perceives contact.
That which knows within the body is the object-field of contact (spraṣṭavya), while that which is able to know the object-field of contact is the faculty of the body (kāyendriya).
If you were to say that cognition itself is contact, then it would no longer be the faculty of the body. If you claim that cognition...

This is precisely the body, yet it is also not the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Therefore, this cognition resides between the two aspects of the internal and external—the body and the object of touch—and fundamentally has no fixed location.
If one were to say that this cognition is separate from the object of touch and conjoined with the body, then this cognition would be the very self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the body;
in that case, it would certainly not be the object of touch. If, however, one were to say that this cognition is separate from the body...
Contact is precisely this cognition belonging to the characteristics of space and so forth; it is certainly not the body itself.
Thus, regarding this cognition of contact, the principle of its co-arising with the internal body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the external object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) cannot be established.
If even that which is capable of co-arising cannot be established, how can the consciousness that arises from such co-arising be posited? [End of Middle Section]

This refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*), for it is produced within them. Since consciousness itself cannot be established, the nature of these internal faculties and external objects is entirely empty.
Thus, even if your consciousness were to arise, from whom would it establish its constituent element (*dhātu*)?
This calculation that body and touch arise together is even more erroneous. Therefore, [the text] concludes below:

It is said: For this reason, one should understand that what is called the body-consciousness element, which arises with the body-faculty and tactile objects as conditions—these three locations are entirely devoid of the meaning of "arising.
Thus, these three—the body-faculty, the tactile objects, and the body-consciousness element—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

This is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Regarding vitarka (initial application) and vicāra (sustained application): coarse seeking is called vitarka, while subtle investigation is called vicāra; this is precisely the body-consciousness.
It takes the conjunction and separation of the two objects as its conditions. If there were no conditions, there would be no consciousness. Thus, it is caused by the object, not by the body.
△ The sixth consciousness, which cognizes mental objects (*dharmas*), is itself the nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, that which you understand as the mind taking mental objects as conditions (up to: "is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature").

This clarifies that the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are themselves the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; this is the locus where the heart-light of Maudgalyāyana was perfectly bright and clear.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand—that the mind takes mental objects as conditions to give rise to mental consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the mind-faculty (manas-indriya), such that the mind-faculty itself constitutes the boundary of this consciousness? Or does it arise because of mental objects?
"It is produced by the dust; is it then that the dharma-dust serves as the boundary for consciousness?

Ānanda, if you say this consciousness arises solely from the faculty of mind (*manas*), then within your faculty of mind there must be some dharma-dust upon which it reflects, before your faculty of mind capable of reflection can manifest. Thus, when the dust exists, the faculty exists."
If the mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*) previously contemplated do not exist, then the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) likewise has nothing from which to arise;

thus, when the object perishes, the faculty perishes as well. Since one is separated from the mental objects that serve as its objective support, the mental faculty cannot even be found to have any form or appearance.
Even if the mind were able to produce consciousness, what would it have to use? For without an object, it is of no use.

It is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, regarding your sixth consciousness-mind and the faculty of thought (*manas*), which both take discernment as their nature—tell me, is this consciousness-mind identical to that faculty of thought?
Are they different? If the consciousness-mind were identical to the mental faculty (manas), then the consciousness-mind would be the very same as the mental faculty;
how then could the mental faculty be the producer and the consciousness-mind the produced?

If the consciousness-mind were different from and not identical to the mental faculty, then consciousness would be the same as external objects and should thus belong to the insentient, having no capacity for cognition. If...
If consciousness has no object of cognition, it would not be of the same category as the mental faculty (*manas*).

How, then, can one say that this conscious mind is produced by the mental faculty? If it is claimed that this conscious mind does have an object of cognition, then both consciousness and the mental faculty would share the nature of discernment (*vijñapti*). In that case, what is the discerning nature of consciousness, and what is [the nature] of...?

Is it the nature of the mind to discern? Since even these two natures—the commonality and the difference—of the sense organ and consciousness cannot be established, how then can this element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) be established by means of a sense organ?

It is erroneous to take the mental faculty (manas-indriya) as the element of consciousness. If you claim that this consciousness arises solely from the object-field of phenomena (dharmālambana), then...
All phenomena in the world do not depart from the five sensory objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. You should now observe these five factors;

each has its own distinct characteristics, clear and vivid. When they are contrasted with the preceding five sense organs, none of them are subsumed under the sixth organ, the mental faculty (*manas*).
If your conscious mind were definitively produced in dependence upon these mental objects (*dharmas*), it would not be problematic.
"Today you should examine this dharma-object (dharmāyatana) with careful attention: to what kind of form does it belong?

You do not realize that this dharma-object, even if separated from the five preceding objects—the forms seen by the eyes, the movements heard by the ears, the openness and obstruction smelled by the nose, the sweetness and blandness tasted by the tongue, and the contact and separation felt by the body—this..."

The shadows of arising and ceasing—were one to transcend these aforementioned characteristics, one would ultimately find no form, shape, or location of the *dharmāyatana* (mental objects) to be obtained.
Fearing that one might insist, "In this context, arising and ceasing themselves are the *dharmāyatana*; are they not indeed forms?
[the author] refutes this, saying: "For while form, emptiness, and the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are like the physical body of a person, the *dharmāyatana*..."

This is the shadow that follows the form. Therefore, when it is said "at the time of arising," it means that [the mind] arises in accordance with those dharmas such as form and emptiness, just as the shadow arises when the form arises;
it does not mean that there is an actual shape within the sensory objects (dharmas) from which it arises.
Likewise, when it is said "at the time of ceasing," it means that [the mind] ceases in accordance with those dharmas such as form and emptiness, just as the shadow ceases when the form ceases.
It is not that the dharma-object (dharmāyatana) possesses a real form that then ceases; rather, it is the dharma-object itself that arises and ceases.
This arising and ceasing of the dharma-object does not exceed that of the preceding five objects (pañca-viṣaya). If one were separated from the five objects, no distinct dharma-object could be found.
Furthermore, since the dharma-object which serves as its cause lacks any form, how much more so the consciousness that arises dependent upon that object? How could it [possess]...?
What kind of shape or appearance could it have? Since even the characteristics of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) do not exist, how could the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) arise from them?
To claim that mental objects constitute the realm of the conscious mind is, moreover, erroneous. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "For this reason, one should understand that..."
That which is called the consciousness element arising with the mental faculty and mental objects as conditions—
these three bases are entirely devoid of the meaning of "arising. Thus, these three— the mental faculty, the mental objects, and the consciousness element—
are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which is neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor produced spontaneously.
△ III. The Threefold Traversal of the Greatly Fused Characteristics (3) 1. The Question of the Appropriate Audience.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has constantly taught the Dharma of the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).”

This question arises because the interlocutor clings to the notion that worldly illusory appearances are produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions, while the wondrous nature of awakening alone is not so produced.
Failing to realize that the nature and its manifestations are non-different, he falls into the two extremes; hence this inquiry.
In order to clarify the seven great elements, the Buddha first demonstrates the meaning of their nature and characteristics as being neither conjoined nor non-conjoined.

If one were to say they are conjoined, then the nature would be identical to arising and ceasing; if one were to say they are not conjoined, then the nature and the characteristics would be two separate things.
The reason why both conjunction and non-conjunction are negated is that the nature is like water, while the characteristics are like ice. As it is said:
Water becomes ice, and ice returns to water. Previously, we only brought the characteristics back to their fundamental nature to specifically reveal the *tathāgatagarbha* nature;

therefore, it was called "Converging the Categories. Here, however, we use the nature to dissolve the characteristics to perfectly demonstrate the *garbha* nature; therefore, it is called "Traversing the Seven Greats.
This causes one to realize that things and self share the same root and that nature and characteristics are of one body—this is the great purport of the Seven Greats. What follows...
Because these exist, the myriad dharmas are generated and sustained; they do not depart from the four great elements, yet they are established upon emptiness.

This is because sensation arises due to seeing, and cognition arises due to consciousness. Within this context, the intended meaning for the practitioner is that the essence of awareness is wondrously luminous.
That nature is neither arising nor ceasing is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); it does not belong to causes and conditions. I have already heard and accepted this.

As for the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), these are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; they are not the ultimate truth and certainly belong to causes and conditions.
Why, World-Honored One, do you categorically reject them all? Furthermore, I have heard that the Dharma commonly taught by the Tathāgata throughout the various periods of his lifetime teachings—

The thesis is that all things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions. That is to say, throughout the entire world—whether sentient or insentient, internal faculties or external objects—though there exist various manifested forms, none fail to be revealed through the conjunction of the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind.
Is it not therefore the case that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all the result of the conjunction of causes and conditions?
And appear in the world? If it were merely a matter of natural rejection, I would have no doubt; for that would not belong to our own teaching.
However, as for the convergence of causes and conditions, that indeed belongs to our own teaching. How then could the Tathāgata ultimately [teach] causes and conditions...?
Is it that both are equally natural, such that both are to be equally set aside and cast out? This doubt deeply contradicts our own teachings and deviates from our fundamental school.
Therefore, today I do not know where this principle of setting aside and casting out is to be subsumed, nor to which school or teaching it belongs.
Although I have already received the Buddha’s clarification on this matter previously...

Please show us this. You have taught that the conjunction of causes and conditions constitutes the conceptual designations and names of the mundane world, and not the true nature of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Thus, since these mundane names and forms and the ultimate truth each represent one extreme, they do not seem to be the Middle Way;
