they cannot avoid being mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and ultimately fail to provide a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*). We only pray that the Tathāgata will graciously bestow his compassion upon us.
He reveals to us and to all sentient beings the principle of the Middle Way, as well as the definitive teaching (nītārtha)—the true Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
To repudiate is called "rejecting" (pai); to cast out is called "banishing" (bin).
△ Second: Rebuking and Admonishing, then Granting Permission to Proclaim.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, [saying]... (until) "Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s holy command.

This rebuke was directed at the delusions and parsimony of those present, serving as an admonition to listen and a permission to proclaim. The intent is this: previously, because you were possessed by Māra...
Having gathered [these thoughts], he then sought to become weary of and detached from all the teachings of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and other Hīnayāna vehicles that he had previously heard.
For this reason, he resolved his mind and earnestly entreated for unsurpassed Bodhi.
Therefore, today I shall instruct and point out for you the most supreme and primary Truth (Paramārtha-satya), which is why I set aside the conventional causes and conditions of harmony.
This is precisely because I wish to cause you to discard the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the Hīnayāna and instead grasp the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Middle Way.

Why, then, do you again take these unreal worldly conceptual proliferations and false delusions (*vikalpa*) to be the harmony of causes and conditions, constantly harboring doubts and entangling yourself, refusing to let them go? Why is this?
Yes. However, Ānanda, although you are widely learned and know the teachings of all Buddhas, now that you hear of the *tathāgatagarbha*—the ultimate truth—you repeatedly give rise to doubt.
This is just like one who has memorized the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia) and can merely describe medicines, yet is not a gatherer of herbs;
when genuine medicinal substances are placed before him, he is unable not only to distinguish the real from the counterfeit, but cannot even identify them.
Furthermore, they instead give rise to doubt and abandon [the teaching]. For this reason, the Tathāgata says that they are truly to be pitied.
Immediately following, he exhorts and grants permission, saying: "Listen attentively now;
I shall, for your sake, analyze and reveal the reasons why there is neither union nor non-union. Not only for you and the great assembly here in the present..."
By means of penetrating the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), may those who practice the Mahāyāna in future ages also all attain to this true reality and together roam the ocean of the Tathāgatagarbha.

For this reason, the one addressed remained silent and spoke no word, quietly receiving the instruction and reverently upholding the holy intent of our Buddha. As for "true reality," it refers to the *bhūtalakṣaṇa*.
It is signless; even signlessness is non-existent—only then is it called the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). This is precisely the three Tathāgatagarbhas of the original sūtra.
To speak of "thorough penetration" means that they are three while being one, and one while being three; this is the meaning of what is termed "harmonious penetration."
△ III. Correctly Expounding the Teaching (2) A. General Demonstration of the Great Nature.
Ānanda, as you have said, when the four great elements combine... [up to] ...just as water becomes ice, and ice returns to water.
This provides a general demonstration of the false nature of appearances and the true nature of reality, clarifying the framework of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*).

Therefore, he first restates their doubt, saying: "Ānanda, if it is as you previously stated—that the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind must combine and harmonize in order to manifest all the various transformations of the world—then you do not realize that these four..."

The essential nature of the great elements is the Tathāgatagarbha-mind. Fundamentally, it is neither a composite nor non-composite, because it possesses the quality of remaining unchanging while following conditions, and following conditions while remaining unchanging.
Ānanda, if one were to claim that the essence of those great elements is necessarily not a composite, then each individual great element would be unable to intermingle with the other great elements.
He then provides an analogy, saying: "It is like empty space, which does not mix with various forms. If that were so, then the functions of the great elements would be lost;

for instance, if the nature of earth were always solid and did not become moist upon meeting water, or if the nature of water were always cold and did not become hot upon meeting fire, how could they produce and sustain the myriad things?
This clarifies that True Suchness possesses the function of responding to conditions. It stands apart...
It differs from the characteristic of discordant, stubborn emptiness; therefore, it is not a state of non-harmony.

If one were to claim that the nature of the great elements is such that their substance must necessarily be a composite, then they would be identical to various transformations that exist from beginning to end.

The end causes the beginning to arise again, and thus the beginning and the end mutually complete one another. From birth to extinction, and from extinction continuing to birth, birth and extinction are thus continuous.
This means that having been born, one dies again; having died, one is born again. Therefore, speaking in accordance with this sequence, it is called "birth-and-death" and "death-and-birth.
Thus, from the present life to a future life, and from the present death to a future death. Therefore...
Discussing this with intervals, it is said: Birth after birth and death after death proceed like a whirling firebrand, without any rest.
In this state, the essential nature of the great elements is lost; just as earth loses its solidity when it encounters water, or water loses its moisture when it encounters fire.
Once their own essence is lost, by what means could they then generate and sustain the myriad things? This...
The clarity of True Suchness possesses a body of immutability, which is utterly distinct from the changing phenomena of a whirling firebrand;
therefore, it is not a composite. Ānanda, the nature of the various great elements is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

When arising in accordance with defiled conditions, the nine realms and the seven great elements are formed within the Buddha-dharma realm, analogous to water forming ice. When arising in accordance with pure conditions...
Thus, within the nine dharma-realms, the Buddha-realm constitutes the seven great elements, just as ice returns to become water.

There is but a single nature of moisture; yet ice and water differ in appearance. This is called "the unchanging following conditions. Although ice and water differ, the nature of moisture is non-dual.
This is called "following conditions without changing. Because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, all...
The Great Elements are non-dual with the nature of reality, truly perfect and harmonious, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Because their unchanging essence is identical to their capacity for adaptation to conditions, all the Great Elements manifest in accordance with the mind, in response to measures, and following the course of karma.
△ Second, the specific manifestation of the greatness [of the elements] (7): First, the element of earth is itself its nature.
You should observe that the nature of earth—whether coarse as the great earth (up to) ... is merely a verbal expression and entirely devoid of substantial reality.
This clarifies that the earth element is the very nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is the Dharma-gate realized by the Bodhisattva Sthitamati.
The meaning is this: you have not yet penetrated the nature of the great elements—that which is neither a composite nor non-composite.

It will not hinder you; simply take this nature of the earth and investigate it repeatedly using the analytical method of discerning form to reveal emptiness used by ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the Hīnayāna.
Through this, you will know for yourself: that which is coarse constitutes the great earth, while that which is subtle constitutes the minute atom (*paramāṇu*).
By gradually analyzing from the coarse toward the large, one proceeds through successive stages until reaching the *paramāṇu*. Now, as for this *paramāṇu*...

"Emptiness" (*kha*) is established by analyzing that atom (*paramāṇu*) into its constituent parts, specifically one-seventh of the ultimate limit of the characteristics of material form (*rūpadharma*).
Once this point is reached, it can no longer be analyzed. Even if one were to attempt to further analyze this "neighboring-emptiness atom" (*pratyupasthita-paramāṇu*), [it would be impossible].
This is precisely the nature of empty space; it is truly not the color-nature of the earth element. Ānanda, as for what you call "conjunction":
if these neighboring atoms of dust were further analyzed, they would become empty space.
You should know that only when empty space is able to conjoin and give rise to material forms can it be called a true characteristic of conjunction. However, you now...

Day after day, he asked again: "Since all the various manifested phenomena of the world arise through combination, consider this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom): by how much empty space must it be combined to exist?"
If they do not join with space, then these atoms must transform; would they then recombine to form further atoms?
However, while we have heard that by joining with another, one becomes itself, we have never heard of something becoming itself by joining with itself.

Since you claim that all characteristics are in combination, these atoms must likewise be in combination. If, as a result, these atoms were in combination, they would necessarily be joined with space.

Only when this is accomplished can it be called true integration (*saṃghāta*). If form were formed without integrating with space, then it would be clear that it is not the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that integrates to produce the characteristics of the four great elements. Fearing that you might further argue:
"Although space cannot integrate to form a minute atom (*paramāṇu*), a minute atom can be analyzed and dissolved into empty space; is this not the integration of form that produces [space]?"

"Is it empty? Therefore, he refutes this, saying: "Furthermore, as for 'breaking down the neighboring atom-dust and entering into emptiness,' this is merely called 'analyzing form to produce emptiness';
it is not called 'uniting form to produce emptiness. If you say it is 'uniting form to produce emptiness,' then tell me:
how many forms and appearances must be combined to constitute a single void? This would be called 'unifying form-and-appearance' to produce the void."

Is it empty? If emptiness were formed by combining with form, then it would clearly not be the nature of the four great elements (mahābhūta) formed from the characteristics of the combination of those four elements.

If you say that at the time of combining with form, one merely perceives the combination of form—and that it is not the case that emptiness is formed by combining with form—then you should know that when emptiness combines [with something], it is merely called the "combination of emptiness."

It is not that emptiness combines with [matter] to form the characteristics of matter. Furthermore, matter possesses physical substance; thus, one can still speak of analyzing it and dissolving it into empty space.
However, emptiness lacks physical substance; how, then, could one say it combines to form the characteristics of matter?

If one understands that emptiness cannot combine, then one knows that even the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom) is not formed through the combination of *paramāṇus*. Since it is not a combination...
By combining them, one observes the small to understand the large; thus, it can be known that the nature of the earth does not originally exist through combination.
Therefore, the notion of combination is erroneous. For you have hitherto only known how to analyze form to return to emptiness, and how to combine emptiness to form form.
The original source does not know this suchness that is unchanging while following conditions, nor the coming of that which follows conditions while remaining unchanging.
Because its nature inherently possesses the functional capacity for the ten realms of both defilement and purity, it is called the "Treasury" (garbha).

Since there is no phenomenon, mundane or supramundane, that is not contained within it, it is called the "Middle" (madhya). This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrous luminosity of quiescent illumination.
This is the essence. Because this nature-inherent form is itself true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it does not require the analytical disintegration of form to return to emptiness.
This clarifies that the conventional and the ultimate are identical, being free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). However, this emptiness is not the same as a partial or insentient emptiness;
because it is the emptiness inherent in nature, it is itself true form, and it does not require the conjunction with emptiness to constitute form. This...
"Clarity" (*ming*) is precisely the ultimate (*zhen*), the conventional (*su*), and all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Because the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional is itself the Middle Way, they are both termed "nature" (*xing*). This refers to the perfect fusion of the three truths—neither identical nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal—which elucidates the *tathāgatagarbha*-nature.
Since all ten realms of existence possess this nature, it perfectly encompasses both form and emptiness. From...
Because it is free from defilement and turbidity, it is called "pure. Because it is subject to no change, it is called "primordial.
Because it can encompass all phenomena and subsume the entirety of the ten voids, it is called "pervading the Dharma-realm. This clarifies the unchanging essential body.
By means of this essential nature, it merely accords with the deluded or awakened minds of sentient beings within the ten realms;

according to the measure of their perceived defilement or purity, there is nothing that does not follow their respective outflowing or non-outflowing karma to manifest the coarse or subtle forms of the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—which they enjoy according to their respective capacities. How could there be any limit?

How profound is this! This clarifies the wondrous function of responding to conditions. Yet, all those in the world—ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or limited vehicles—who are ignorant and lacking in insight, fail to comprehend this principle that responding to conditions is non-changing and non-changing is responding to conditions, and that phenomena manifest according to karma.
Consequently, they are deluded into regarding them as causes and conditions of conjunction, or as those of non-conjunction.

These constitute the two kinds of false conceptualization based on nature. Thus, they are all merely the consciousness-mind that clings to objects, engaging in deluded discrimination and pervasive calculation;
how could they know the ultimate principle that the immutable follows conditions, wherein the essence is empty yet manifests phenomena?
Even if one were to apply this analogy by extension, regarding all conventional worldly discourse—such as [the notion of] causes and conditions arising from themselves...
However, such notions as "conjunction" or "non-conjunction" are merely conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*); ultimately, no true meaning can be found therein.

The following sections should all be interpreted according to this same principle. Herein, the text clearly reveals the *tathāgatagarbha* nature—neither changing with conditions nor remaining unchanged—which constitutes the true nature of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*). This is what is called the "dharmas intrinsically possessed by nature."

This is the Gate. It is precisely the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena. One must know that the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are identical to the aforementioned aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);

they differ only in their horizontal and vertical arrangements, and in their opening and closing. If one vertically opens a single aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it constitutes the six preceding elements;

when the four aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth are combined, they constitute the single element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*). Furthermore, if one horizontally combines the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), they constitute the five preceding elements.

By combining the six sense organs into the Great Element of Sight and combining the six consciousnesses into the Great Element of Consciousness, one knows that the seven elements originally possess no distinct dharmas.
Thus, one first unifies the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), all of which are subsumed within the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.

This clarifies that the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha inherently possesses the seven great elements, aggregates, bases, and elements. Therefore, the preceding section was the unification of characteristics into the nature, thereby elucidating the identity of phenomena with reality.

This principle constitutes the particular within the universal; it clarifies how phenomena are integrated by their nature (*dharmatā*), precisely demonstrating the events that are identical with reality (*tattva*).
As the universal within the particular, this is what is meant by the doctrine of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*). Thus, the wondrous principle of the mind-nature—

The fundamental purport of the Great Samādhi is only now fully elucidated; therefore, because previous commentaries failed to reach this point, their discussions have been muddled and contentious, with each author displaying their own cleverness while anxiously attempting to bore holes into the primordial chaos (*chaos*).

Whether they distinguish between the three stages of cessation and the three contemplations, or discuss the three truths and the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, such instances are all like the redundant appendages of a snake; we shall not adopt them here.
△ Second, the fire element is itself the nature.
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it relies upon various conditions... (until)... "there are only words, but no real meaning.
This clarifies that the fire element is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature; it is the object of contemplation for Aghnyasmarā. Ānanda...
Difficult. It is simply that the nature of fire originally has no self (*ātman*) and no fixed essence; it takes form by dwelling within things, merely depending upon various conditions (*pratyaya*).
For example, it arises by relying on the sun, dry grass, and a mirror. Thus, it has no substantial entity of its own that can be grasped.
You need only observe that in the city of Śrāvastī, [fire] has not yet been produced this morning.
In a household where food is prepared, when one intends to cook and lifts the cauldron over the fire, it is necessary to seek fire.
The *yangsui* (sun-stone) is what the *Huainanzi* calls the "fire-square pearl. It is made of copper and is shaped like a mirror;

when it reflects objects, their images appear inverted, and when directed toward the sun, fire emerges from it. Furthermore, the *Lunheng* states that on the day of Bingwu during the hour of wu in the fifth month, [it should be sought].
The "five-direction stones" that are smelted and refined are the essence of copper. They are circular like mirrors with a depression in their centers;
these are what we call fire-mirrors today. When the weather is clear, one holds this toward the sun to seek fire. These are all matters easily understood by those present before you.
Ānanda, if you claim that the nature of this fire is produced through a combination [of causes], then it would be as follows:
Present before me are you and these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus;
although we are now called a single assembly and designated as a harmonious community, even though this multitude is harmonious and termed a single group,
if one were to investigate their fundamental origins, each possesses his own body, and each has a clan name born of his respective parents.
Lineages, clans, and personal names differ. For example, Śāriputra is called "Son of the Vulture Peak" (Gṛdhrakūṭaputra), as he is of pure descent from that lineage.
Upatiṣya is called "Original Melon Forest" (Mūlakośambaka) because he lived near this forest; he is also called "Melon Tree" (Kauśambaka).
Because his neck was hunched like a papaya fruit, he belonged to the Great Tortoise clan. Thus, from "even Ānanda is of my Solar clan" down to this point:
these various divisions, each possessing its own body, name, and lineage, are collectively termed a "community.
Although they constitute a true assembly, each ultimately returns to its own root; thus, even the name "assembly" is but an illusory fabrication. Ānanda.
Difficult. If you claim that the nature of this fire exists because of the combination of causes, could the fruit then be identical to Śāriputra and others, each born from their respective clans?
Yet, when he holds a mirror and tinder in his hand and seeks fire toward the morning sun, tell me: does this fire emerge from within the mirror? [He] then uses the mirror...
Is it the tinder that is the root? Or does it emerge from within the tinder?
If you say the tinder is the root, is it from the sun that it comes? Or is the sun itself the root?
Ānanda, if you were to say that this fire comes from the sun, then since it has come from the sun, it should also be able to burn your hand.
The moxa is applied in the center. Yet, from the sun down to the hand, across forty-two thousand yojanas, this fire would have to descend from above and below.
At all points where it passes, every tree and forest ought to have been consumed by the flames first.
Since the trees remain as they were and are not burned, we know that the fire does not come from the sun.
If you claim that the fire emerges from within the mirror, then since it has already emerged from the mirror, it must be capable of burning the tinder while still within the mirror;
such would indeed be a fierce fire. If so, the mirror before the tinder should have melted first.
Why, then, does this mirror not melt? Fearing such an error, one might say: "Fire can overcome metal; how could it fail to cause it to liquefy?"
Is this not the meaning? Therefore, he refutes it, saying: "If that were so, why not bend your hand and grasp this mirror?
Try it once and see; there is not even a trace of the appearance of heat. How then could this mirror melt?
Since it does not melt, we know that the fire does not emerge from the mirror. If you claim that the fire arises from the tinder..."
Then it would follow that fire could be produced from the tinder alone. Why must it depend on the light of the sun and the clarity of the mirror—these two factors meeting together—for fire to arise?
Since it depends upon both the sun and the mirror, we know that the fire is not produced from the tinder alone.
Furthermore, you should carefully and attentively observe the mirror: it is truly because the human hand holds it that the sunlight descends from the heavens.

The mugwort herb originally grows underground. If those three things each have a place from which they come, from what direction does this nature of fire alone emerge to travel here? Since it has no origin, [how can it be said to come?]
Thus, it is clear that [the fire] cannot be explained by the principle of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Furthermore, whatever is called "conjunction" necessarily involves multiple objects meeting in a single location before it can be termed a conjunction. Now, the sun and the mirror are separated by the vast distance of heaven and earth;
they are certainly neither conjoined nor combined. It follows that the nature of this flame cannot arise from nowhere.
Is it something that exists inherently? Yet, it must depend upon the presence of those three substances before it can exist;
furthermore, it is not the case that they do not harmonize. However, this nature of fire is a harmony that does not mean "conjunction.
You still do not understand this within the *tathāgatagarbha* (and so forth). For this nature of fire is fundamentally empty; it is the nature-endowed (*xingju*) that follows conditions (*suíyuán*).
The unchanging essence is thus able to respond to the mind and accord with conditions, manifesting according to karma;
this is precisely the wondrous function of the unchanging following conditions, which gives rise to the various distinctions of the ten dharma realms.
From here on, all follows the previous explanation; the text is easy to understand. To cause vapor to rise is called "cooking" (*chui*); to apply fire is called "stewing" (*cuàn*).
△ Third, the water element is itself the nature.
"Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are not constant" (up to) "...there is only verbal expression, and it is entirely devoid of real meaning.
This clarifies that the water element is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature; it is the Dharma-gate realized by the youth Candraprabha.
Ānanda, as for the nature of water: if it is directed, it flows; if it is obstructed, it ceases. Furthermore, if it is sought out, it flows;
otherwise, it ceases. Thus, it flows at times and ceases at others, lacking any fixed, constant nature.
It is just like the one in the city of Kapilavastu who was called Kapila—meaning yellowish-red, or "yellow-haired," or also "yellow-headed."
This refers to those whose heads are golden, namely those who today bind their heads with copper rings and wear yellow crowns.
*Cakravāḍa* means "wheel" (*cakra*) or "mandarin duck" (*vāḍa*); it is also translated as "Wheel Mountain" (*cakravāḍa-parvata*), meaning it is named after its reliance upon mountains.
*Padma* means "red lotus. According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it says: "For example, the forms of the sun and moon are like the deep and perilous *padma*.
This is precisely the name established by non-Buddhists based on their meditative objects (*samādhi-viṣaya*).
*Hāsata* is sometimes called "water-seeker," though this remains unclear. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes various masters of great illusion who seek the Great Yin (*tàiyīn*).
This essence is the water within the moon. It is used to harmonize the elixirs of illusionary arts;
that is to say, one gathers the quintessence of the moon to cultivate and refine the primordial pneuma (*prāṇa*).

These illusionists, therefore, act on the night of the waxing moon prior to the full moon—taking the period before the full moon as the "white moon" and the period after it as the "black moon"—for when the moon...
At noon, when the light was like that of broad daylight, he then took up the *fangzhu* (square-jade) to receive the water descending from the moon.
Thus, the *Huainanzi* states: "When the *fangzhu* beholds the moon, it exudes moisture and becomes water.

This means that *fang* refers to the stone of the five directions, and *zhu* refers to the "yin-divining mirror," which is like a large clam; this refers to the water-gathering pearl. This is based on the treatise.
Heng said: "On the night of the *renzi* day of the eleventh month, at the hour of midnight, I refined stones from the five directions in the north to create this object.
It is shaped like a cup or a basin; when exposed to the moon, it exudes moisture.
Now, does this watery nature emerge spontaneously from within the bead itself? Does it arise naturally from within empty space? Or does it descend from the moon?"
Ānanda, if you say that this water comes from the moon, then even when the pearl is at a great distance—
since the moon is as far from the human world as the sun is— it is still able to cause the pearl to emit water.
If that were so, then all the mountains, forests, trees, and woodlands through which it passes while near the moon should likewise be made to gush forth flowing water.
It is like this: when the moon is directly to the south, all the mountains, forests, and trees to the south of the pearl are places near which the moon has passed;
or, if the pearl is on level ground, then the tall groves and great trees above the pearl [are likewise so situated].
All [these] are locations near which the moon passes; therefore, they should all discharge [water].

If trees and forests discharge [water] when the moon shines upon them, then wherever the moonlight falls, water would flow there—why then wait for the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror used for lunar distillation) to produce it?
If trees and forests do not discharge [water], then even the trees and forests near which the moon passes would likewise [not discharge it].
If it does not emit a flow, how could it cause water to emerge from a *fangzhu* mirror located in a distant land?
Thus, it can be clearly understood that this water does not descend from the moon.
If one were to claim that this water emerges from the *fangzhu*, then water should also flow out from this pearl during ordinary times; why then must it wait for the middle of the night?
If you say that water arises after the bright fortnight of the month, then it can be seen that this water does not emerge from the jewel either.
If you claim that this water is produced from space, then wherever there is empty space, there should be water;
since the nature of space is boundless, the nature of water would likewise be limitless. In that case, from the human realm up to the heavens—
All become one vast, immense ocean, and all are equally submerged by this water.
How, then, could there still be any distinction between those dwelling in the water, those on land, and those moving through the air?

Since there are those on land and those moving through the air, we know that this water was not produced from space. You may continue to observe this with earnest attention; the moon has always been...
It ascends to the heavens. The pearl is held in the hands of a person; it is placed upon a basin filled with water, which was originally prepared by a conjurer.
These three things each have their own origin, yet from what direction does this water alone come to flow into this place?
Since it has no point of origin, it cannot be harmonized [with the other elements].

The meaning of "conjunction" (saṃyoga) is thus clear. Furthermore, whatever is called "harmony and conjunction" (saṃghāta) must involve multiple objects meeting together in one place before it can be termed "conjoined.
Now, the moon and the water-jewel are separated by a distance as vast as that between heaven and earth; they certainly do not constitute harmony, nor do they constitute conjunction.
It is therefore unreasonable to claim that the water within this moon is the essence of the Yin (the lunar spirit), for such a thing has no source from which it could have arisen.
If it were inherently present, yet necessarily waited for the moon-jewel to appear in opposition before emerging as water, then it would not be the case that they are not in conjunction.
However, this nature of water is a "conjunction" in the sense of non-conjunction. You still do not understand this [as explained in the passage] regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*.
For this nature of water is fundamentally empty; it is the inherent nature (*prakṛti*) manifesting in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*).
The unchanging essence is thus able to respond to the mind according to its measure and manifest in accordance with karma;
this precisely constitutes the wondrous function of the unchanging following conditions, which results in the various distinctions among the waters of the ten dharma realms.
From here on, all shall be explained in accordance with the preceding interpretation; the meaning may be understood by analogy. *Zhé* (陟) is pronounced *zhí*; it means "to ascend."
△ The fourth, the wind-element, is itself the nature.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant... (until) there are only words, but no real meaning.
This clarifies that the wind-element is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature; it is the Dharma-gate realized by Vairocana. Ānanda.
Difficult. That which is called "wind," though its nature is characterized by movement and agitation, if one seeks its reality, it fundamentally lacks a fixed essence.
Why is this? Because it arises when there is movement and ceases when there is stillness. For example, when one waves a garment, it arises upon that movement.
When the robe is draped, it is still and thus ceases. What is called movement and stillness, or arising and ceasing, is entirely impermanent.

This can be understood by observing a single present instance. For example, when you habitually adjust your robes upon entering the assembly, the corner of this saṃghāṭī robe may happen to move for a moment—and likewise...
Suppose there is a person standing nearby, and a slight breeze brushes against that person's face.
Now tell me: does this wind come from the corner of your *kāṣāya* robe? Does it arise spontaneously from empty space?
Or does it originate from the face of that person standing nearby? Ānanda, as for the nature of this wind: if it were to emerge from you...
As for the corner of this *kāṣāya*, the robe itself is wind; you are not wearing a robe, but rather wearing wind.
Furthermore, since the nature of wind is agitation, and this robe is already wind, it ought likewise to fly about and flutter like wind.
"It should have departed from your body; why does it not leave now? This is to test non-arising through movement.
Furthermore, since your robe is moved by the wind, my robe must also be moved by the wind.
As I preach the Dharma today amidst this assembly, with my great outer robe draped over me, look at the robe I am wearing—this wind [is moving it]."
As for this nature, where does it reside? If it cannot be seen, there must be another hidden space within the garment that renders it invisible.
Were there no such place to hide it, [it would be visible].
Thus, it is clear that the wind does not arise from clothing; this is precisely using stillness to verify non-arising.
If one were to claim that this wind arises from empty space, there are many among the world who hold such a view, as in the saying: "When space exists, wind arises."
That is so. Since you say wind arises from space, it ought to arise spontaneously; why then must it depend upon the movement of clothing to exist?
Furthermore, when your clothing is not moving, by what cause is there no wind to brush against a person’s face?
Moreover, the nature of space is eternally abiding; if it can produce wind, it should produce it constantly. For...
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is without cessation. Since wind arises constantly when combined [with emptiness], why is it that no wind emerges when a garment does not move?
This implies that since wind is produced from emptiness, if emptiness is eternal, then wind should also be eternal.

Furthermore, if empty space were truly able to produce wind, then at times when there is no movement and no wind—during periods of stillness and extinction—empty space itself would likewise [be subject to cessation].
When the wind ceases, since the wind does not arise, it would follow that emptiness arises where there was none; how then could this not be a cessation?
This implies that because emptiness can produce the wind, when the wind ceases, emptiness should also cease. Yet, in reality, neither is the case;

therefore, the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding while the wind is not eternally arising. Furthermore, at the time the wind ceases, empty space does not cease; thus, one can perceive the wind [within space].
Emptiness is a separation; it is ultimately divergent and not something that can be produced.
The following two lines correctly clarify the error of [claiming] the extinction of emptiness, thereby demonstrating that emptiness is without arising or ceasing. The intended meaning is as follows:
when wind ceases, it is something that all people in the world can see and hear—such as the silence of myriad pipes, the stillness of grasses and trees, and the non-arising of ripples on water.
These are all the characteristics of the extinction of wind, which can be known through seeing and hearing.
Yet, what kind of characteristic could the emptiness of extinction possess that might be manifested and known?
Furthermore, if one were to grant that empty space has arising and ceasing, it would be a conditioned thing and could not be called unconditioned emptiness. This is because...

Regarding the six kinds of unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): since that which is called "empty space" has the unconditioned as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can it be said that wind arises from space?
If it could produce wind, it would become a conditioned entity (*saṃskṛta-vastu*); how then could it be the unconditioned empty space?
Thus, it is clear that the nature of this wind does not arise from space. If one were to claim that this wind is...
As for that which arises spontaneously on the face of the person being brushed: since it has arisen from that person’s face, it must have traveled from there to here;
thus, it ought to brush your face in the direction of its movement. Yet now, this wind arises from your own adjustment of your robe and is currently brushing that person.
Since the wind has arisen from that person’s face, why does it not brush your face in the same direction?
Yet it instead brushes against that face; thus, it is clear that the nature of this wind does not arise from that face.
You should now examine and contemplate this with careful scrutiny, adjusting your robes: it is truly upon your face, which is being brushed, that [the wind arises].
That which belongs to such a person—space and the unconditioned—is quiescent in its essential nature and does not itself participate in the movement of the wind.
Thus, these three each have their own fixed location; from what direction, then, does this nature of wind alone arise and stir here?
Since it has no point of origin, it cannot be explained through the principle of conjunction.
Furthermore, that which is called "harmony and union" must necessarily involve no difference between this and that to be termed harmony and union.
Now, as for wind and space, their essential natures are distinct: one is quiescent and eternally abiding, while the other arises and ceases without constancy.
Thus, movement and stillness are each separate; they are certainly neither in harmony nor in union. It should not be that this wind—
"Is this nature something that arises from nowhere and exists of itself? Yet, when we observe the straightening of a robe, there is wind in the air;

furthermore, it is not the case that they do not come together in harmony. As for the meaning of whether this nature of wind is in harmony or not, you still do not understand it at all—it resides within the Tathāgatagarbha (and so forth).
For this nature of wind is fundamentally empty; it is rather the nature-inherently-present (xingju)."
The fundamental substance that remains unchanging while following conditions is thus able to respond to the mind according to its measure and manifest in accordance with karma;
this is precisely the wondrous function of the unchanging following conditions, which gives rise to the various distinctions among the winds of the ten dharma realms.
The following sections are all explained as previously; they may be understood by analogy. *Saṃghāṭī* has no direct equivalent in Chinese.

In the Tang language, it is called the "repeated-layered robe" (*chóngfù yī*). Qingliang states that new cloth is double-layered while old cloth is single-layered; because it must be made by layering, it is called "repeated-layered.
It is also called the "harmonized robe," because it combines new and old materials. It is further named the "variegated or fragmentary robe" (*zásuì yī*), because—
Because it consists of many strips, it is the *saṃghāṭī*, the largest of the three robes (*tricīvara*). "Kāṣāya" is the general term for these three robes.
It is also called the "Dust-Removing Garment" because it severs the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); the "Emaciating Garment" because it cuts through the afflictions (*kleśa*);
the "Lotus Garment" because the wearer becomes free from defilement; or the "Discarded Color Garment," because—

Because the Vinaya regulations establish three types of dyed colors as being in accordance with the Dharma, Master Qingliang states that these are "improperly colored robes," as they do not employ the five primary colors.
They are also called "dyed colors" (rañjana) to signify that the mind is stained by color; thus, one must remain unstained.
Fang said: "It means that while within defilement, there is no defilement.
△ Fifth, the Great Emptiness is itself the nature.
Ānanda, the nature of emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form (until: ...but there are only words and explanations, and no real meaning).
This clarifies that the great element of space merges with the preceding four elements and returns to the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha;
it is precisely the point realized by the Ākāśagarbha. Ānanda, the nature of space is fundamentally formless, yet its squareness, roundness, largeness, and smallness are not fixed from the outset;
they are manifested only because of substantial forms. For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, far from the river—

In a distant place, from the Kṣatriyas down to the Caṇḍālas and other such castes, because they had newly established their dwellings and settled there, they were intent on digging wells to seek water.
When they first dug out one foot of earth, they saw one foot of empty space within the well.
In this manner, as they gradually dug further and deeper, until they had dug out ten feet of earth, the well—
In the interim, one obtains a space of ten feet. Thus, the depth of this space corresponds to the amount of earth excavated:
if much is removed, it is deep; if little, it is shallow. Although there is a difference in depth, the space itself is one and the same.
Now, is this space produced by the earth? Does it exist because of the excavation? Or does it arise spontaneously without cause?
"Ānanda, suppose it were further claimed that this empty space arises spontaneously without cause.
Then, before the well had been dug and the earth excavated, why was this unobstructed space not seen?
Instead, one would have seen only a vast expanse of obstructed earth, entirely devoid of even a trace of openness. From this, we know that this space..."
It is evident that [the earth] exists because of excavation; it does not arise spontaneously without a cause.

Generally, non-Buddhists mostly cling to the doctrine of causes and conditions regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), while they mostly cling to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) regarding the element of space (*ākāśa*). Therefore, [the text] first refutes the absence of a cause in order to clarify that [space] is not spontaneous.
If one were to claim that this space is produced by excavating the earth, then when this soil is moved out of the well—
At that time, one should subsequently see empty space entering the well, just as when a pond is dug and water is drawn in.
This would be reasonable. Furthermore, while the earth emerging can be seen, what is the appearance of empty space entering?

If it is merely observed that the earth emerges first and there is no subsequent entry of empty space into the well, how can you say that this empty space is produced by digging the earth and subsequently emerges? This...
To calculate that space exists only after the earth has been excavated is erroneous.

If you say that space and earth are no different, except that the earth can be brought in or taken out while space cannot, then it follows that space must have existed even before the earth was excavated.

Thus, space and earth would both occupy the same location and constitute a single entity, fundamentally lacking any cause for their distinction. Since there is no difference [between them], [the claim of their distinctness is false].
If space were the cause, it would be of the same substance [as the earth]; thus, when [the earth] emerges, space should likewise emerge.
Now, when the soil is moved and the well is emptied, why does space not emerge along with it? This further demonstrates that the calculation that space emerges because of the earth is erroneous.

If you say that this emptiness is produced by digging and does not arise from the earth, then it would follow that empty space is produced by digging and is unrelated to the removal of earth from within a well that results in the formation of empty space.
Why is it that we observe that when one foot of earth is removed, one foot of space is obtained, and when ten feet of earth are removed, ten feet of space are obtained? If...
This means that this emptiness does not arise because of the digging; it has no connection with the digging.
It is the digger who brings forth the earth himself, yet he should not perceive the existence of empty space. If that were so, how could one see empty space as soon as one digs?

Thus, one knows that both [theories]—that it arises because of the digging or that it does not arise because of the digging—are erroneous. You should, for now, take the trouble to examine this more thoroughly.
This is the reality. Regarding this reality, one should further investigate and examine it with thorough discernment.

For instance, when a well is dug, it emerges from the earth due to human effort; as it is operated and turned according to the direction of the labor, the soil is moved and brought out from within the ground.
Thus, each has its own source of emergence. Now, as for this void within the well, by what cause does it arise?
From where would it emerge? Since there is no place from which it emerges, the principle that it cannot be produced through combination is clear.
Now, generally speaking, for something to be called a "combination," the two factors involved must not be distinct; only then is a combination established.
If one were to perversely insist that space emerges from the digging of the earth, then while the nature of the dug earth is solid and real, the nature of space is void.
Penetration can only be said to apply to digging the earth; it cannot be said to apply to digging empty space.
Since the two dharmas of earth and emptiness—one belonging to solidity and the other to vacuity—are fundamentally distinct, their respective natures do not function for one another.
It is certainly neither a state of harmony nor a state of conjunction. Should it not be that the nature of this emptiness emerges of itself from nowhere?
Yet, the fact that one must wait for the earth to be excavated before emptiness is revealed means that it is also not the case that they are not in conjunction.
Below, he uses the element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*) to dissolve the preceding four elements, saying: "If this empty space is such that its nature is perfectly interfused and all-pervading..."

Furthermore, you should know that that which has been unshaken by birth and extinction from the very beginning is such that the present earth, water, fire, and wind—these four great elements—are equal to space;
thus they may be called the five great elements. They are termed "equal" because their essential nature is impartial.
To discuss them in terms of characteristics is delusion, yet it is not that there is no distinction between them. When one contemplates their original true nature, there is nothing [to grasp].
If they were not perfectly interfused, then these five great elements would all be the wondrous nature of True Suchness, the Tathāgata-garbha mind;
from the very beginning, there would have been no birth, death, movement, or fluctuation to be found therein.
Ānanda, it is only because your own mind is obscured and not luminous, deluded and not awakened, and because its movements provoke doubt that you are unable to realize this.
The four great elements are fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Even if you do not yet understand that the preceding four are themselves this nature, you should observe by analogy:
Is the empty space within this well produced in the well because of the digging of the earth?
Or does it enter the well after the earth has been removed? Is it that the earth has coming and going while the space neither comes nor goes? If...
The nature of Great Enlightenment is perfectly pervasive; it neither emerges nor enters, yet it is not that which neither emerges nor enters.
This means that one awakens to the fact that the nature of the four great elements is perfectly pervasive, being neither joined nor conjoined, yet not unjoined or unconjoined.
However, as for this meaning of "conjoined yet not conjoined," you do not yet fully understand it to be the awakening inherent within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. It is...

This is the emptiness inherent within the nature of true emptiness; it is the very essence of true awakening. This clarifies that the ten dharma realms are empty within the nature, and both emptiness and awakening are the nature and are true.

Indeed, ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or limited vehicles know only that the five great elements are insentient dharmas and thus designate them as "non-awakening," while they regard the sense organs and consciousnesses as sentient dharmas and designate them as [awakening].
Awakening! One must realize that both the sentient and the insentient are equally the nature and equally the truth; they share the same essence of awakening.
This is precisely what is meant by "the sentient and the insentient are one body," where everywhere is entirely the true Dharma-realm.
This is the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena, the ultimate discourse of the Nature School (Xingzong). These ten dharma-realms—both the primary and the derivative—are each...
There is nothing that is not originally pure and all-pervading throughout the Dharma-realm; this is the fundamental substance that remains unchanging while following conditions.

Because it can follow the minds of sentient beings within the ten realms, responding to the magnitude of their respective capacities and conforming to their various wholesome and unwholesome karmas, it manifests as the emptiness of the ten dharma-realms. This is the wondrous principle of the unchanging following conditions.
It is used [as such]. Yet all the ordinary people of the world, as well as those of provisional and limited capacities among outsiders and followers of the Lesser Vehicle, lack knowledge and wisdom;
they are deluded by this emptiness and take it to be either the causal conditions for digging a well or causeless spontaneity.

All of these are the conceptualizing and calculating of a deluded, false consciousness. Such statements—whether concerning causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the union and non-union of things—are all merely...

Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is that which possesses no real meaning whatsoever. *Kṣatriya* in the Sanskrit language is translated in the Qin language as "Lord of the Fields"; these are those of the royal lineage.
*Brāhmaṇa* is called "Pure Conduct" (*śuddhacaryā*), and is also called "Pure Resolve" (*śuddhāśaya*); these are the gentlemen who preserve the Way and abide in rectitude.

The Vaiśyas are merchants; the Śūdras are farmers. These constitute the four castes of the noble and the lowly in the Western Regions (India), corresponding to the four classes of society here [in China]. The Pāṭalas are said to have sharp faculties, or alternatively, to be swift;
they are one of the eighteen clans of the Brāhmaṇas, comprising those such as astrologers, physicians, and diviners. The Caṇḍālas...
They are called the "Slaughterers" (Kuài) or the "Austere Banners" (Yánzhì). This means that their evil karma adorns them of its own accord;

as they travel, they shake bells and carry banners to warn others to take different paths and not to travel with them. These are the butchers and wine-sellers. Furthermore, these constitute two classes: the wise and the foolish.
△ Sixth, the Greatness of Seeing is the very nature itself.
Ānanda’s seeing-awareness lacks intrinsic knowledge; it exists because of form and space (and so forth, until) there is only verbal expression, entirely devoid of real meaning.

This clarifies that the Greatness of Seeing universally encompasses the six sense organs, harmonizes and integrates the five great elements, and returns them to the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, [it is said] of Śrī-Prabhāketu: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific verse regarding Śrī-Prabhāketu (Potulight) from the source text.*
To realize this is to attain the perfect penetration of mindfulness of the Buddha. This is because the great nature of this seeing is identical to the great nature of the sense-faculties;

here, by citing the single faculty of seeing, one may infer the remaining five faculties. This refers to the non-conceptual nature within the faculty that reflects upon objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It does not refer to the two faculties of the ear or the nose. It correctly belongs to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which, while relying upon the gates of the six sense-faculties, takes as its object the six sensory realms through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it is spoken of simply as "seeing" and not as the "eye-faculty" and so forth;

there is indeed a profound reason for this. Nevertheless, the various sacred teachings clarify only the six elements (*dhātu*) in their sequential order and do not establish a separate "seeing-faculty."

This is because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fully subsumed within matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Since the first five [elements] are all matter and the last one belongs to mind, they are not established separately.
However, there are three reasons why this "Great" [element] is established in the root sūtra: first, to include the preceding; second, to accord with what follows;
and third, for the sake of perfect penetration. Regarding the first point, to include the preceding: as for the ten [elements] in the previous text...

The preceding sections all borrowed the essence of seeing (*jian-jing*) to reveal the nature of the storehouse (*zang-xing*). Now, I shall further clarify that the essences of seeing, hearing, and so forth are themselves the nature of the storehouse.

Thus, the previous indications that "seeing is the mind," that "seeing is immovable," that it "is neither extinguished nor lost," that "it has no source of return and is not a material object," and even that it is "unimpeded and solely true"—the intent of these points, which transcend emotion and leave behind views, reaches its ultimate fulfillment here.

This is clear. Second, regarding "conforming to what follows": as the subsequent text states, the cycle of birth and death and the wondrous permanence of bliss are both the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and nothing else.
Since he intends to expound this Dharma-gate, he first establishes this "Greatness. Third, regarding "perfect penetration" (*pariśuddha-vyavahāra*):
as with the six objects, the six sense organs, and the six consciousnesses, all are for the purpose of the perfect [penetration] of the various sages discussed in the text that follows.

This serves as the foundation for the "Universal Penetration. If this Great Root were not established, the "Perfect Penetration" of Avalokiteśvara’s mindfulness of the Buddha would lack a basis to rely upon;
therefore, it is necessary to establish this Great Root. Ānanda, that which perceives is the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*).
One speaks of "perception" (*bodha*) rather than "nature" because perception is itself the nature. Thus, the subsequent text says: "The seeing-nature is luminous through perception."

This refers to the awareness of clarity and brilliance. Originally, there was one unified essence of clarity and brilliance, which through delusion was divided into the six harmonious functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
Now, when we speak only of "seeing" and "awareness," we are discussing this solely from the perspective of the eye.

The meaning is that the act of seeing as an awareness is fundamentally the substance of one unified essence of clarity and brilliance; originally, it possesses neither a knower nor a known object, but rather [arises] because of...
Form is empty, yet there exists that which knows and that which is known. This clarifies that the sense organs have no intrinsic nature and exist only in dependence upon their objects;

this is precisely what is meant in the following passage by "the consciousness arising from the dust. By this principle, it is evident that the same applies to hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognition.
Thereupon, he again takes up the preceding sensory object and asks: "Suppose you, at this moment, are in the Jeta Grove, as is your usual practice..."
As for what is observed: at dawn it is bright, and by evening it becomes dark; this refers to the brightness and darkness of the day.
Furthermore, if one dwells in the middle of the night or at midnight during the waxing moon (the white fortnight) prior to the fifteenth day, there will be light.
From the sixteenth day onwards, during the dark fortnight, it is dim; this is the brightness and darkness of night.
Thus, whether bright or dark, these characteristics that fill space can only be discerned by means of your seeing-nature.
This dust of light has no self-nature and manifests because of the faculty; take this as an analogy for movement and stillness, fragrance and stench, sweetness and blandness.

The dust of arising and ceasing through union and separation is without exception like this. This is precisely what was meant previously by saying that "seeing and the conditions of seeing are fundamentally non-existent," and it is also what was said later regarding "the sense organs and their objects sharing the same source, and bondage and liberation being non-dual.
Therefore, these four propositions are presented once more: first, identity; second, difference; third, both identical and different; and fourth, neither identical nor different.
Revealing that there is no inherent nature, he examined it closely and said:
"As for this seeing-nature—is it identical in essence with the forms of light and darkness, as well as the empty form of the great void?
Is it not identical in essence? Is it both identical and different? Or is it neither identical nor different? Ānanda, this seeing-consciousness..."
Furthermore, if light, darkness, and space were fundamentally one entity, then these two entities—light and darkness—would mutually negate one another.
Why is this? When there is darkness, there is no light; is this not the negation of light?
When there is light, there is no darkness; is this not the negation of darkness? Because of this light...
Darkness and form incline toward one another, mutually encroaching and seizing; thus, the two entities are mutually extinguished.

Yet, with what could this nature of seeing be unified? If you claim that this seeing is of the same substance as darkness, then when light arrives, since darkness and seeing are already of one substance, they ought naturally to perish together. If you claim that this seeing must...
Regarding the claim that light and seeing are of one and the same substance: when darkness arrives, since light and seeing are of one substance, they ought to both perish along with the darkness.
If this seeing indeed perishes together with the darkness and is extinguished along with the light, then it is further said:
Furthermore, how can it be said that when light comes one sees light, and when darkness comes one sees darkness?

If you claim that while the two characteristics of light and darkness inherently possess the distinctions of arising and ceasing, this nature of seeing and awareness is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, then there would be that which arises and ceases and that which does not arise or cease.
How, then, could the principle of being a single essence be established? This cannot be seen as possible.

It is clear that they are of one and the same substance. If you claim that this nature of seeing is not of one substance with light, darkness, and so forth, then set aside light, darkness, and empty space for a moment, and observe the original essence of this seeing that is capable of discernment and analysis:
what kind of shape or appearance does it have? You do not realize that if one is separated from...

If the nature of seeing were distinct from light, darkness, and empty space, it would be fundamentally the same as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare—merely possessing a hollow name while lacking any substantial reality.
Furthermore, does this nature of seeing truly exist apart from light, darkness, and empty space?
Regarding these three things, which are distinct and not the same: apart from these three things, from where else could your nature of seeing be established?
Thus, it is clear that they are neither different nor a single entity.
If you claim that this nature of seeing can likewise be both bright and dark, then the two characteristics of brightness and darkness would [be mutually...]
They are mutually contradictory. If they were identical in being bright, then darkness would have to cease; if they were identical in being dark, then brightness would have to perish.
If they were identical in one state, they would lose the other. How, then, can it be said that they are identical?
If you claim that the nature of seeing might also be distinct from light, darkness, and empty space—such that it is perhaps distinct from light, it should not see light;
or perhaps distinct from darkness, it should not see darkness; or perhaps distinct from emptiness, it should not see emptiness.
Furthermore, apart from being distinct from these three things, there is fundamentally no such thing as the nature of seeing. How, then, can it be said that it is "perhaps" [distinct]?
It is different. It is evident that being both the same and different is not the case.
If you claim that the nature of seeing is not the same as these three things, it should be possible to analyze where the boundary of emptiness lies and where the boundary of seeing lies;
only if emptiness and seeing could thus be divided would they be called "not the same. However, emptiness and seeing are fundamentally—
This is a single entity; fundamentally, it has no boundaries or limits that can be analyzed. How, then, can it be said not to be identical?

If you claim that the nature of seeing is not different from the three factors [the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing], then when one sees darkness and sees light, while light and darkness mutually undergo change, the nature of seeing does not undergo alteration. Thus, while the object seen undergoes transition, the subject that sees—
They do not change; how could they be conflated? How, then, can it be said that they are not different?
Thus, it is clear that they are neither identical nor different. When the analysis reaches this point, it may be said that the Tathāgata has emptied his treasury to bestow his gift.
Therefore, those who subsequently attain clarity and give rise to faith through the appropriate occasion all do so by means of this. Nevertheless, they are not a single entity.
That which is "not self-arising" clarifies that phenomena produced through causes and conditions do not arise from themselves.

That which is "not of a different nature" is what I call emptiness; it does not arise from another. That which is "neither identical nor different" is also termed the provisional name; it does not arise from both together.
That which is "neither non-identical nor non-different" is the meaning of the Middle Way; it does not arise without cause. This is precisely the departure from [extremes].
The four propositions cut off the hundred negations. To reveal and clarify the nature of seeing is the wondrous true *tathāgatagarbha* nature of *tathatā*;
this is the definitive meaning of non-arising and the ultimate sense of the Middle Way.

It is precisely the "dharma free from frivolous proliferation" requested by the disciple at the outset, and it is what is later referred to as "receiving the jeweled mansion bestowed by the Heavenly King. Below, [the text] intends for the disciple...
Pay close attention. You must not hastily let this nature of seeing pass by. Therefore, I exhort you:
for now, do not hesitate to examine it even more minutely—not merely minutely, but with further subtlety; not merely examining, but adding thorough scrutiny.
Until you have reached a state of precise and authentic examination, you must scrutinize and observe it once again; you must, by all means, [proceed thus].
Only when one has reached the ultimate limit and seen the source does one finally come to rest. One must know that the clarity perceived before one is derived from the sun;
the darkness perceived comes with the dark moon; what is perceived as openness belongs to space;
and what is perceived as obstruction returns to the great earth. Thus, these phenomena of clarity, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction each have their own origin.
Thus it is. From what source do you thus perceive these four kinds of essences?
Since they have no source from which they emerge, the principle that they cannot be combined is clear.
Furthermore, whatever is called "combination" must consist of multiple natures becoming one to constitute a combination. Yet the present faculty capable of seeing possesses a conscious nature.
The light, darkness, emptiness, and solidity that are perceived belong solely to the realm of inert dust; thus, the nature of awareness and the nature of inert matter are distinct from one another.
They are certainly neither in union nor in conjunction. Since this is the case for the faculty of sight, it is likewise for the other faculties.
How could this essence of seeing possibly emerge of its own accord without a source? Yet, it must necessarily depend upon light, darkness, obstruction, and space.
Thus it is revealed. For one who possesses this vision, there is likewise no lack of harmony. Below, [the text] speaks of the great fusion of the five previously mentioned elements, saying:

"If you can awaken to the sixfold nature of the faculties—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—and realize that their essence is perfectly interfused, universally pervasive, and from the very beginning has never been shaken by arising and ceasing, then..."

One should know that this boundless, limitless, unmoving, and unshakable space, together with the earth, water, fire, and wind that arise, perish, move, and shake—these five great elements—are equal to seeing; thus they may be called the six great elements.
Because the essence of their nature is equal, they are called "uniform. Although their characteristics are illusory, it is not that there is no distinction between self and other.

When one contemplates that their nature is fundamentally true, everything is seen to be perfectly interfused. Thus, these six elements are all the wondrous *tathatā* (suchness) of the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature).
From the very beginning, they have never known arising or ceasing, nor any movement or fluctuation. Ānanda, merely...
Your nature is submerged in the depths of ignorance and mired in the remote and biased.

Lacking supreme wisdom and deficient in the eye that discerns the Dharma, you are unable to realize that the six faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, along with the five great elements mentioned previously, are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Even if [you were to] further...
If you do not realize that the preceding five are themselves the nature, you should examine them by analogy:

Are these six types of sensory faculties—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—subject to arising and ceasing? Are they identical or different? Are they not subject to arising and ceasing?
Are they not identical or different? If you claim that the nature of the faculties definitely belongs to arising and ceasing, then apart from this, by what means could one...
Is this the eternally abiding true nature? If you claim that the six sense organs are of one and the same substance, how can there be the distinction between the six locations?
If you claim that the six sense organs are each of a different substance, then how could a single person possibly possess six natures?
If you claim that the nature of the six sense organs is non-arising and non-ceasing, then [how do they function] when currently encountering objects?
Then there is cognition; when separated from objects, there is no cognition. Is this not arising and ceasing?

If you claim that the nature of the six faculties is neither identical nor different, then since they are originally one unified clarity, how could they not be identical? Yet they are divided into six harmonious combinations—how could this not be difference?

If one can awaken to the fact that the natures of these six clarities, such as seeing and the rest, are perfectly pervasive and circular, then [arising... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "生", which corresponds to the beginning of the character for "arising" (*sheng*). The translation reflects the available portion.)
Cessation is not the cessation of arising; sameness and difference are neither the same nor different.

Thus one awakens to the nature of the five great elements as being perfectly pervasive, neither joined nor conjoined, yet neither disjoined nor unconjoined. However, you have not yet been able to understand this principle of "conjunction that is not conjunction.
This seeing, which is inherently possessed within the Tathāgatagarbha, is precisely the luminosity of original enlightenment.
This essence of true original enlightenment is precisely the vision of intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). This luminosity perceives the ten dharma realms;

both this vision and enlightenment are the intrinsic luminosity of nature. It is because ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or limited vehicles know only the vision that forms the sense organs from conditioned matter (*rūpa*) that there are those who perceive a mere fraction of a field of vision, those who perceive the four continents, and those who perceive the great trichiliocosm.
Regarding "realms" (*dhātu*): they all possess boundaries. Yet, one does not realize that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively pervade even the pure lands within a single mote of dust.
This is precisely the vision of the fundamentally pure and original nature; it is that which enables them to circumscribe and fill the entire *dharmadhātu*.
This is the very essence of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), which remains unchanging while following conditions. Because—
It can accord with the minds of sentient beings across the ten realms, responding to the scope of their respective understandings, whether great or small.
Just as this faculty of sight perceives its nature as being all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, one knows that the hearing of the ear,
the smelling of the nose, the tasting of the tongue, the tactile sensations of the body, and the cognitions of the mind are all the wondrous nature, whose virtuous functions are luminously pure.

However, being empty, luminous, and unobscured, all equally realize the nature of seeing; pervading the entire Dharma-realm, how could there be any spatial directions or locations that could limit it?

Yet, as for the fact that the nine realms perceive with varying degrees of distance and proximity, this is nothing other than the manifestation of their respective outflowing and non-outflowing karma.
All of these are the wondrous functioning of the nature of seeing, which remains immutable while conforming to conditions.
Use your ears. Yet all the ordinary people of the world, as well as those of external paths, provisional teachings, and the Lesser Vehicle, lack knowledge and discernment;
they are deluded regarding this nature of seeing, taking it to be either a single cause and condition, or a natural state of identity and difference.

All such views are merely the conceptual calculations of the deluded, discriminating consciousness. These various expressions—whether concerning causes and conditions, nature, harmony, or non-harmony—are all [mere constructs].
Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is entirely devoid of real meaning.
△ Section Seven: The Great Consciousness is Identical to Nature.
"Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises from the six [sense-objects]... (up to) "...there is only verbal expression, entirely devoid of real meaning."
This clarifies that the great aggregate of consciousness subsumes the six consciousnesses and, through universal integration, merges with the six elements to return to the Tathāgatagarbha;

this is precisely the perfect penetration realized by the Compassionate Honored One in his position as the Regent. Ānanda, this sixth consciousness takes "discriminating cognition" as its essential function.
However, as for its nature, it originally has no source or course. It arises and perishes in an instant, resembling a wild fire;

it emerges solely from the illusory and false interaction between the six faculties and their objects. Now, by using visual consciousness as a model for inference, the others may be understood by analogy.

Just as you do today, surveying all the assembly of sages and worthies within this Śūraṅgama gathering with your eyes—circling them all around and examining them universally—this is precisely the faculty of the eye that performs the observing.
These are the objects (dharmas) being observed. Although the faculty and the object stand in relation to one another, at the moment when not even a single thought has yet arisen, this—

Within the primary faculties (*indriya*), the nature of seeing grasps objects of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is like tongs grasping an object, or like the sun radiating its light;

there is no analytical discernment whatsoever. It is merely like an image appearing in a mirror, wherein from the outset there is no analytical distinction between the beautiful and the ugly, or the good and the bad.
Yet, your consciousness suddenly arises in a single thought-moment within the midst of the faculties and their objects, and thus subsequently—
The mere indication of names gives rise to conceptual discrimination; that is to say, "This is the name Mañjuśrī, 'Wondrous Auspiciousness';
this is Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, 'Full Compassion'; this is Maudgalyāyana, 'Bean-Eater'; this is Subhūti, 'Born of Emptiness';
this is Śāriputra, 'Son of the Vulture Peak. This refers precisely to the visual consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness.

This visual consciousness is merely termed "recollection-based discrimination" (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). It arises for only a single moment in relation to an objective reality (*vastu*), yet it has not yet engaged with names and phrases.
At the same time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions solely as "conceptual discrimination" (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*);
in relation to that same objective reality, it arises for a second moment, calculating and grasping at names and words, such as "Mañjuśrī" and so forth. This is because...

Visual consciousness—by analogy with the other four—is no exception to this. As for mental consciousness, which, apart from the five sensory consciousnesses, functions independently to perceive its own object as a mere mental image, it is likewise included in this category.

Now, regarding this cognition that discriminates through visual consciousness: does it arise from the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*), or does it arise from the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), or does it arise...?
Is it in empty space? Or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?

Ānanda, if you claim that the nature of this eye-consciousness which performs discernment arises solely within the seeing-faculty, then in the absence of those four things—light, darkness, form, and space—it would necessarily not exist. Thus, apart from the objects of sight, [it could not arise].
Originally, there was no "seeing" by which you could see. Since the very faculty of seeing lacks intrinsic nature, from what could consciousness possibly arise?
Thus, it is clear that the sense organ alone cannot produce consciousness.
If you claim that the nature of this visual consciousness of yours arises independently within the perceived object itself, that certainly would not be so.
Regarding that which arises from the faculty of seeing: since there is no faculty of seeing, one does not perceive the appearance of light, nor does one perceive the appearance of darkness.
Thus, when neither light nor darkness is beheld, this is precisely the absence of the faculty of seeing.
Then the various marks of form and emptiness would likewise all be non-existent.
Furthermore, since those objective dust-marks that produce [consciousness] lack intrinsic nature, from what could this produced eye-consciousness possibly arise?
It is thus clearly known that the dust alone cannot produce consciousness. If it is claimed that eye-consciousness arises from space and is not related to [the dust],...
Regarding the characteristic of objects (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*): it is also not the seeing faculty (*darśana-indriya*). If it were not the seeing faculty, it would lack the nature capable of discernment;
naturally, it could not know light, darkness, form, or space. This means that apart from the faculty, there are no objects.

If it were not the characteristic of objects, the objective realm (*ālambana-viṣaya*) would cease to exist, and seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing would have no place to be established. This means that apart from objects, there is no faculty.

Thus, abiding in this state is neither between characteristic nor perception. If one were to say that this emptiness is without substance, then being non-existent would be the same as the absolute non-existence of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns;

if even the self-substance of emptiness is thus fundamentally non-existent, how could it have the capacity to give rise to consciousness? If one were to say that this emptiness has a substantial body, then furthermore—
