Furthermore, since this [emptiness] is neither a characteristic nor a view, it cannot be distinguished from other things;
if even its own nature cannot be distinguished, how could it give rise to a consciousness that performs discernment?
Even if insentient and ignorant emptiness were able to produce your visual consciousness, it would likewise be insentient—what use would you have for such a thing? It is not so.
Can consciousness that is inert and dull truly be capable of discernment? Thus, to claim that consciousness arises from emptiness apart from the sense organs and their objects is even more untenable.

If you say that visual consciousness has no cause and emerges suddenly of its own accord, why does it not suddenly produce another consciousness during the daytime when the bright moon is absent? [This is because] consciousness...
When the bright moon first appears, one might say it emerges suddenly without cause.
Now, since there is no moon at midday, the consciousness that recognizes the moon certainly does not arise separately from that [moon]. Thus, to claim it emerges without cause is even more untenable.
I command you to investigate this nature of consciousness with precision; do not be careless or superficial. Therefore, I exhort you, saying:
Examine this matter minutely; do not hesitate to examine it even more minutely.
Thus, it is "subtle" because it is subtle within the subtle, and "thoroughly examined" because it is examined within the thoroughly examined.

You must understand that this faculty of ultimate reality relies upon the superficial root of the physical eye, while the various appearances of form and emptiness are projected as the objective realms appearing before one.
If that which is seen and its characteristics can be described by form and named, it constitutes a substantial entity (*sabhāva*).

However, that which, like space, cannot be discussed in terms of shape or characteristics, constitutes a lack of substantial entity (*asabhāva*). Although existence and non-existence differ, each has its own source and development.
Your ability to thus discern and recognize them—what is the underlying cause for this, and from what does it arise?
It does not emerge. Since there is nothing that emerges, it is clear that the principle of "harmony and integration" (*saṃghāta*) cannot apply here.
Furthermore, whenever one speaks of harmony and integration, it must be a case where the essence and nature mutually follow one another; only then can it be called harmony and integration.

Now, in the present state, consciousness possesses discrimination, which is termed "movement," while seeing is without discrimination, which is termed "clarity. Thus, movement and clarity are certainly not in harmony, nor are they integrated. Nor are they [identical].
Combined. Since it is so for eye-consciousness, the same applies to the other five. It should not be that this discerning eye-consciousness is without cause;

how could it arise spontaneously without a reason? Yet, since it must depend upon the meeting of the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) before arising, it is certainly not the case that they do not combine.
Below, the Great Consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*) integrates the preceding six elements, saying: "If one can..."
Awaken to this conscious mind as being neither a union nor a separation, yet not a non-union and non-separation. From the very beginning, it has fundamentally no point of origin.

One should also know that these various consciousnesses of discernment—the eye seeing, the ear hearing, the nose smelling, the tongue tasting, the body feeling, and the mind cognizing—these six consciousnesses, in their essential nature, are each complete and perfect, serene and eternally abiding.

Therefore, as for their nature, none of them arise from conditions. Thus, these two great elements—sight and consciousness—along with the great element of space, together with earth, water, fire, and wind, are equal in their nature and may be termed the "Seven Great Elements. Although their characteristics are illusory, they are not without distinction;
yet when one contemplates that their nature is fundamentally true, there is nothing that is not perfectly interfused. Thus, these Seven Great Elements are all immediately [identical to the One Mind].
The Tathāgatagarbha-mind, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā), has from the very beginning been fundamentally devoid of any obtainable arising or ceasing.
Yet you, Ānanda, are coarse regarding the mind and have not yet realized the subtlety of the *ādāna-vijñāna*;

you are superficial regarding vision and do not know its profound depth in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For this reason, you have hitherto reckoned that the eye resides on the face and have reckoned [the location] of the mind.
Within [the body], etc., you are unable to realize that the six sense organs (ṣaḍindriya) through which you possess seeing and hearing,
as well as the six consciousnesses (ṣadvijñāna) that manifest cognition, together with the aforementioned six elements (ṣaḍdhātu), are fundamentally your own self-nature—
the originally inherent Tathāgatagarbha. If you still do not awaken, you should contemplate these six locations of the mind of consciousness.
Is it identity and difference? Is it emptiness and existence? Is it neither identity nor difference? Is it neither emptiness nor existence?
If one says they are identical, yet the six faculties are distinct; if one says they are distinct, yet their source is a single, brilliant essence.
Thus, one knows that this consciousness cannot be described in terms of identity or difference. If one says it is empty, yet there is still discernment. If one says...
Since it exists, yet lacks form and color, one knows that this consciousness cannot be described as either empty or existent.
If one says they are not the same, their fundamental essence is originally one; if one says they are not different, the six sense bases appear distinct. Thus, one truly knows this consciousness.
Furthermore, it cannot be described as being either non-identical or identical. If one says it is not empty, it is apart from the sense organs and their objects, and fundamentally lacks self-nature.
If one says it is not existent, it is currently able to discern all forms and emptiness. Thus, we know that this consciousness can no longer be described as being either non-empty or non-existent.
If one can awaken to the fact that the six sense-bases, consciousness, and mind are neither identical nor different, [one realizes the truth].

As for the statement that "there is existence distinct from emptiness, yet not existence apart from emptiness," this is the realization that the six elements of the past and the element of consciousness of the present are neither combined nor non-combined.
Yet, you do not fundamentally know that these six consciousnesses are originally the intrinsically true consciousness within the Tathāgatagarbha;
that which is wondrously luminous awareness is precisely the fundamentally enlightened, wondrously luminous, true nature.
This consciousness refers to the consciousnesses of the ten dharma realms. Both this consciousness and its nature are the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*).

Because it is able to remain unchanging while following conditions, and to follow conditions while remaining unchanging, it is called "wondrously illuminating yet eternally quiescent" and "quiescent yet eternally illuminating";
therefore, it is named "enlightenment" (*bodhi*). Being originally pure, it is called "tranquil. Yet, by means of this nature of consciousness, there is nothing that does not...
It encompasses all; therefore, it is said to pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Regarding "containing and emitting," this refers to what is later stated:

"Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. This means that emptiness exists within the storehouse nature (ālaya-vijñāna), capable of being contained and emitted;

it is used to emphasize how exceedingly minute it is. This is truly because ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacities falsely identify the six consciousnesses as their own mind. Therefore...
Movement was previously restricted by its conditions; now that it has been revealed, it is seen to pervade the preceding six great elements, all of which constitute the nature of the treasury.
Thus, its substance encompasses the ten voids—how could there be any cardinal directions or locations capable of limiting it? This is precisely the fundamental substance of the unchanging.
Nevertheless, the reason it momentarily manifests as the six consciousnesses is none other than following along with the outflowing and non-outflowing [dharmas].
It is merely that karma manifests it; this clarifies the wondrous function of following conditions (*pratyaya*).
Yet all worldly ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity lack knowledge and discernment.

They do not understand that this consciousness is the causal condition for the mutual production of the faculties and their objects, nor do they realize it is a "spontaneity" that emerges abruptly—all such things are but the deluded, discriminating, and calculating mind of false consciousness.
[The Buddha] said: "There are only causes and conditions that naturally harmonize; they are not [truly] joined. Such discourses are all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
they possess no real meaning whatsoever. Indeed, the form and mind of the ten dharma realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are nothing other than the light and shadows of self-nature.
This is truly because a single thought-moment of deluded movement gives rise to ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences. Therefore, the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) does not cease."
Birth and death continue without rest. Therefore, I, the Tathāgata, out of necessity, have spoken of nature and characteristics;

I have spoken of the true and the false; I have spoken of the four divisions; and I have spoken of the seven elements. Yet, when speaking of nature, it does not go beyond the one mind and its two gates;

when speaking of characteristics, they do not go beyond the eight consciousnesses and their four parts. For this reason, this sutra first speaks of the four divisions to subsume characteristics back into nature, and subsequently speaks...

The Seven Elements: by means of their intrinsic nature, they dissolve into one another. This clarifies that nature and characteristics are non-dual, and that phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused.

Furthermore, within these seven elements, first bring the four gross elements back to the element of space. One wishes for people to understand that empty space neither emerges nor enters, neither does it not emerge or enter;
it is fundamentally without movement and pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Thus, one knows that the four gross elements likewise have no [independent existence].
Arising and ceasing, yet without coming or going, it pervades the entire dharma-realm. This is such that it is identical to illusory form and identical to true form;

identical to inert emptiness and identical to true emptiness. Because true emptiness is identical to form and true form is identical to emptiness, one is able to be identical to both form and emptiness, and thus identical to true awakening.
In this way, the myriad phenomena are all true. Although the six sense organs exist, they are utterly transcended.
All such discriminations are, in fact, the six sense organs themselves and are identical to true nature; therefore, they are called "nature-vision" (*xing-jian*).
Now, this nature-vision is the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (*ben-ju*). Thus, while it follows conditions to illuminate objects, it is not altered by those objects;

hence it is called "the clear and brilliant vision of enlightenment. Since the sense organs are thus, the consciousnesses are likewise so. Consequently, the six consciousnesses are united as the Tathāgatagarbha.

This nature is precisely the cognitive nature (*xing-shi*). It is also able to clearly comprehend all things while remaining transcendent in every circumstance; therefore, it is called "clear knowledge" (*ming-zhi*).
Since it is termed clear knowledge, it is the very essence of the fundamental clarity of true awakening. How could it not be called true consciousness (*zhen-shi*)?
For this reason, the four categories are extensively integrated to reveal the purity of the single nature, and the seven elements are universally fused to correctly elucidate the myriad dharmas.
This is the fundamental nature. Thus, while the Buddhas of the three periods realize Great Bodhi within ignorance, all sentient beings undergo birth and death from within True Suchness.
That there is a distinction between the holy and the ordinary is nothing other than the difference between delusion and awakening.
To be deluded is to wander in the cycle of saṃsāra through vast eons; to awaken is to attain liberation in this very place. Therefore, it is said:
It merely manifests according to the karma of sentient beings, in accordance with their mental states and the extent of what they are capable of knowing.

The above concludes the Tathāgata’s refutation of the false to reveal the true. Question: In this context, the discussion of consciousness refers only to six types; why are the seventh and eighth not mentioned?
Why is this? The answer is: because the eighth [root] is included within the six kinds of faculty-natures (*indriya-gotra*), and the seventh is the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Therefore, they are not distinguished separately.
△ Second, Ānanda clarifies the arising of faith (in two parts): 1. The narrator describes the benefits.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [from] before the Tathāgata spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.
This clarifies that the Venerable One had fully realized the Great Matter and possessed deep faith in his own mind;
for this reason, the compiler of the sutra recounts in detail the benefits he attained. Indeed, at the beginning of the second fascicle, it is stated that his body and mind were at ease.
In the initial refutation of delusion, the seven locations were shown not to be the mind; yet, one had not yet escaped alarm and doubt.

Upon hearing the revelation of the True, wherein it was pointed out that the seeing itself is the mind and that this seeing is immovable, alarm and doubt were suddenly stilled, and one felt somewhat at ease. Only then did one realize that within the body there exist two natures, the true and the false;
however, as this was still not fully understood, it was said: "I pray that the Tathāgata will reveal and bring forth the nature of body and mind."

Regarding the distinctions between the real and the false, the empty and the substantial, the Buddha subsequently used King Prasenajit as an occasion to manifest that [the mind] is indestructible, proceeding through ten successive demonstrations.
Yet even those present were still unable to comprehend it; therefore, the Buddha later extensively synthesized the four categories of phenomena back into the single *tathāgatagarbha* nature.

By using this single *tathāgatagarbha* nature to universally integrate the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), he demonstrated that when the false is shattered, even the visual essence (*cakṣur-vijñāna*)...
[The text] refutes [dualistic views]. To manifest the truth, the myriad phenomena are all true; to harmonize them, essence and appearance are non-dual.
When mind and matter are equalized, this is the Tathāgata’s thoroughgoing instruction for humanity, proclaiming the ultimate reality within the supreme meaning.
It may be called a most subtle, profound, and unsurpassed revelation. Therefore, the compiler of the sutra records: "At that time..."

Then Ānanda, who was present at that moment, and the great assembly gathered for the Dharma, all received from our Buddha Śākyamuni Tathāgata the subtle and profound essence of the seven locations where delusion was exposed and the ten instances where the truth was revealed; they thus realized that all phenomena are ultimately returned to their fundamental nature.
By means of the profound subtlety of using nature to dissolve appearances, he provided various such exhortations and gave detailed instructions.
Consequently, both body and mind became completely purified and expansive. Thus, the body attained non-obstruction, and the mind attained non-hindrance.
Because one awakens to the Dharma-body precisely through the illusory body, one no longer falsely identifies the illusory manifestations of the four elements as the body;

thus, one is not entangled by delusive objects. Because one awakens to the true mind precisely through the deluded mind, one no longer erroneously clings to the shadow-like reflections of the six sense-objects as the mind; thus, one is not obstructed by the deluded mind. This...
Then body and mind will be perfectly luminous. This is not like the former state of taking external objects as oneself and regarding movement as the body, whereby one is entangled by the body;
nor is it like mistaking oneself for an object and identifying the capacity for inference as the mind, whereby one is obstructed by the mind.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Consciousness and the sense faculties emerge and enter momentarily, like a deer caught in a net."

It is like a bird in a cage, pecking at one thing and abandoning another, circling back again and again without a moment’s rest. Consciousness dwelling within the cage of the sense organs is just like this;
it is because one has not yet awakened to the fact that the nature of the storehouse (ālayavijñāna) possesses both unobstructed and obstructed aspects.
Now that you have realized that the aggregates, bases, elements, the great faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are fundamentally one—the nature of the storehouse—then the deer and...
A bird cannot be caught by either a net or a cage; there is only the single nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha), which encompasses and gives forth the ten voids.

As it is said, it is richly endowed with myriad virtues and is vast and free from even the slightest speck of dust. What further body could there be to be entangled? What mind could there be to be obstructed?

For this reason, whether body or mind, there is no obstruction or hindrance; everything is utterly open and expansive. This [section] above generally indicates that both body and mind are expansively open, without obstruction or hindrance.
Below, the text specifically analyzes and describes this. There are three points according to their meaning:

first, the description of the mind; second, the description of the body; third, the conclusion regarding the benefits. Now, for the first, the description of the mind, the intention is as follows: not only did those present at the assembly realize...
Illuminating body and mind, one attains freedom from obstruction; this refers to the great assembly of those who heard the teaching together.
They, too, each individually attained self-confidence and self-knowledge that their own minds pervade the entire Dharma-realm and fill the ten directions.
Herein, the two characters "self-know" (*zìzhī*) represent the detailed narration of the scribe; they must be carefully distinguished. If [this were not so], when facing...

Regarding the phrase "one who knows for themselves" (*zhijīn*): it refers to the fact that after the delusions were shattered, the practitioner presented himself with tears of sorrow, saying, "I did not know that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable," and further, "This was truly because I did not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal."
Furthermore, he asked, "How can one know that this is my true nature? and so forth. These were all instances where the person concerned was unaware of their own state.

Had he been addressing the great assembly, he would have said, "I myself know it. Thus, because King Bimbisāra was present while the truth was being revealed, he rose from his seat and declared, "How do you manifest and realize this mind as the ground of non-arising and non-ceasing? Now, this great assembly..."
All those with outflows (āsrava) wish to hear this; yet it is that the great assembly does not know for themselves.

Thus, from the time the formal rules were established and passed down through the ages until this very day, the fruit has ripened and fallen from its stem, the clouds have dispersed and the moon shines bright.

This is what is meant by "when a person drinks water, they know for themselves whether it is cold or warm. As for the phrase "each and every one," this refers precisely to those who are ready to receive the teaching.
Unlike those others who deeply believe in their own nature and understand that this mind is inherently pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm,
my previous field of vision— relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power— only reached as far as the First Dhyāna, where I took the boundlessness of space to be ultimate.
Now, seeing the empty space of the ten directions, how insignificant it appears, like looking at the space within one's own hand.

One merely holds them upon objects such as palm leaves. Previously, one did not know that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—all such objects of perception—are things manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind.
Now, one clearly understands that all things existing within the mundane world are none other than my own self-nature bodhi; this nature-awareness is wondrously luminous.
The primordial awakened mind follows the mind and responds to conditions, manifesting in accordance with one's karma.
Previously, you mistakenly grasped at the shadows of the six sense objects, which were moved and obstructed by external things; thus, you perceived the world as either vast or small.
Now, for the first time, you know that your own mind is pure and unmixed, all-pervasive and perfect, containing the entire Dharma-realm and encompassing it.
Enveloping the ten directions—this is such that there is nowhere it does not go, yet it is the ever-abiding true mind;
there is no place that is not the essence of nature-purity and luminosity. The above correctly describes how the mind is vast and expansive, attaining non-obstruction. Next, the body is described:
previously, one erroneously believed that the ten kinds of distinct beings all possessed a consciousness-mind residing within the body; now, one looks back upon this.
The essence of the father and the blood of the mother give rise to this impermanent, illusory, and deluded body.

Within this emptiness of nature, it is like a single speck of dust stirred up by the wind within the vast void of the ten directions—seemingly existent yet seemingly non-existent, as if present yet as if vanished.
Although this illusory body exists, it is like a spark from a flint or a flash of lightning.
In the end, it is not eternally existent. Although it appears to exist, it is ultimately not eternally existent; therefore, it is said to be "as if existing.
Yet, although this illusory body has not yet perished, it is like dew on a leek or a wind-blown lamp—it must inevitably perish. Although it appears not to have perished, it must ultimately perish;
therefore, it is said to be "as if perishing. Previously, one was deluded and took this [illusory state] as the mind with absolute certainty.

Delusion lies within the physical body. Now I have realized that this physical body exists within the ocean of the mind, like a single bubble floating upon the surface of a vast, tranquil, and clear sea—suddenly arising and suddenly vanishing.
Fundamentally, there is nowhere from which it arises; how could there be any obstruction? It is nothing more than following the mind, responding to conditions, and manifesting according to karma.
This precisely describes how the body attains freedom from obstruction. Regarding the third point, the summary of benefits, the meaning is as follows:

previously, one did not know where the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) leads, one did not know the location of the inversion of body and mind, and one did not know that the nature of seeing is the mind. Not...
I previously knew that the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are the Tathāgatagarbha, yet I did not know that the seven great elements pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

Now, I clearly know this for myself and am entirely free from doubt. Previously, when the Buddha revealed the wondrous nature of precious clarity, I still said that I had merely obtained this mind and did not dare to recognize it as my original ground of the heart-mind. Now, without even needing to recognize it, it is of itself...

I have attained the wondrous mind that has been inherently present. Previously, I did not know that body and mind are true and false, real and illusory, or that they are subject to arising and ceasing before one's eyes or are beyond arising and ceasing.
Now, I clearly understand that body and mind are perfectly luminous, eternally abiding, and indestructible.

This which is known and believed is precisely the belief in the principle of the Great Samādhi—the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of purity and luminosity—as first revealed by the Tathāgata.
It is what is referred to in the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) as "the first single mind being the source.
Now, regarding the two instances of the phrase "knowing for oneself" (*zizhi*) within this text: although they are recorded by the compiler of the sutra, in reality...

The intention here is subtle and profound. Those of limited capacity generally know only that within empty space there are the myriad things, that within the myriad things there is the body, and that within the body there is the mind-nature.
Thus, they hold that nothing is as vast as empty space and nothing is as minute as the mind-nature.
Now it is not so; one must personally realize that the measure of the mind-nature pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Regarding the realm (*dhātu*): one first realizes that emptiness resides within the nature of things. It is no larger than a leaf held in the hand;
thus, the minuscule state of all objects contained within that emptiness becomes even more evident. At this time, one surveys all phenomena universally.
Since the entire nature of the One Treasury is thus, what further thing could there be to obstruct it? Hitherto, one has only known that the mind dwells within the body; now it is not so.
When one looks back upon the physical body, it resides within the ocean of the mind like a single floating bubble;

thus, birth and death, existence and non-existence, are no longer worth taking to heart. At this time, when observing the vastness of the aggregates, there is only the single true mind. Furthermore...
What body could there be that is subject to attachment? That which was previously unknown is now entirely clear and known by oneself.

This concludes the preceding meaning. If one were to introduce what follows: if one does not know this for oneself, how could one develop understanding, initiate practice, and realize this Great Samādhi?
Therefore, we know that the two characters "self-knowing" (自知) serve as the conclusion.
The preceding section clarifies the structural framework of the sutra.
Having reached this point in the narrative, it is precisely like a traveler who suddenly finds a magnificent mansion. Thus, what is attained today is that which was never previously attained.
What exists today was indeed unprecedented in the past. Since we have now gained this benefit within our hearts, how could we fail to offer our thanks to the Buddha?
Therefore, with hearts inclined and palms joined before the Tathāgata, we reverently compose these brief verses to praise and express gratitude for his profound kindness.
All of this is the narrative of the sūtra compiler regarding the benefits obtained by the assembly of practitioners present at that time.
This is merely the intended meaning [of the preceding]. △ Second, the praise and description by the audience (six parts). First, praising the Buddha-dharma:
"The Wondrous, Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One, the Śūraṅgama King, is rare in the world."
In this passage, the interlocutor speaks these verses of his own accord to praise the Buddha and the Dharma. Specifically, the first phrase praises the Buddha alone;
the next four characters praise the Dharma alone; and the final three characters praise both the Buddha and the Dharma as being equally rare and marvelous.
It is because the interlocutor has profound faith in his own mind-nature that he has come to realize the Buddha’s three [bodies].
The body is no different from oneself; therefore, it is praised as "wondrously profound, universally sustaining, and immovable.
These six characters all praise the three bodies (*trikāya*). Thus, the first two characters praise the *dharmakāya*.

Because the *dharmakāya* is signless, profoundly still, eternally quiescent, unconditioned, non-active, and neither arising nor ceasing, it is called "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*). The next two characters praise...

This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*. Because it has cultivated the various *pāramitās* throughout immeasurable eons, it comprehensively gathers all untainted merits (*anāsrava-guṇa*) and maintains them without loss until the end of the future;
therefore, it is called "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*). The latter two characters praise the *nirmāṇakāya*.

By responding to conditions through sympathetic resonance, clouds of manifested bodies appear everywhere; yet because they have never moved from their fundamental source, they are said to be "immovable.
Furthermore, these two characters for "Wondrous Honored One" (Miaozun) apply universally to both the superior and the inferior. This refers to what is called the three bodies as one essence:
they are three while being one, and one while being three. Thus, the three are not three, and the one is not one; this does not hinder [their manifestation].
It is three yet one; therefore, it is called "wondrous. Since these three bodies are fully present, the ten titles are completely manifested.
Thus, among the celestial beings, he is called the "God among Gods," and among the sages, he is called the "Sage among Sages."
Within all the worlds and the nine realms of existence, there is none who does not revere them; for this reason, they are called "Venerable" (Zun).

Furthermore, "Wondrously Profound" (Miaozhan) praises the virtue of *prajñā* according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Total Retention" (Zongchi) praises the virtue of liberation according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Immovable" (Budong) praises the virtue of the Dharma-body according to the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). Because these three are one, it is called "Wondrously Profound."
It is one yet three; therefore, it is called "total retention" (dhāraṇī). It is neither three nor one, yet it is both three and one;
therefore, it is called "immovable. This praises the Buddha for possessing the three virtues and realizing the three truths.
As for Śūraṅgama, it refers to the Dharma taught by the Buddha when his practice has reached ultimate perfection; it is the general name for Great Samādhi, as revealed throughout this sutra.
This one samādhi alone is the most honored and supreme among all samādhis;
because it attains great mastery over all dharmas, it is called the "King," for it is able to govern and encompass all samādhis.

Previously, when the recipient of the teaching had not yet attained realization, he requested [instruction] using the specific names within the general category; now that he has clearly understood for himself...
Having understood this, one takes up the general name from within the specific and praises it, saying: "This is called the Perfect and Wondrous Great Samādhi.

This signifies the non-duality of the general and the specific. Indeed, the Buddha is rare because he appears in the world having realized the three virtues through his possession of the three bodies;
he appears as rarely as the udumbara flower blooms once in an age. How could he not be rare? The Dharma is rare.

This is because, while the teachings of the various periods were all given according to the capacities of sentient beings, none compare to this sutra, which exclusively discourses on the perfect and subtle, elucidates the Great Samādhi, points directly at the human mind, and enables one to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Is this not indeed a rarity among the Dharmas? Thus, both the Buddha and the Dharma are truly extraordinary and rare phenomena within both the mundane and supramundane realms.
...Thus it is.
△ Second, the exposition clarifying the mind:
"To eliminate my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas, I shall attain the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*."
This is precisely the opportune moment for the practitioner himself to describe his own clear realization of the mind-ground. His meaning is this:

from time immemorial, I have mistaken the false for the true, and my mind-nature has been inverted. Now that I have obtained the hearing of this sutra, the inverted deluded thoughts of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas will all be like melting ice and snow in boiling water.
For these inverted thoughts are precisely what was previously described as "mistaking the false for the true."

They take external objects as themselves, and in their delusion, they take themselves as objects. They falsely identify the four great elements as the characteristics of their own bodies, and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of their own minds.
Whether regarding what is internal or external, large or small, they cling to causes and conditions or calculate them to be spontaneous;
this extends even to views of harmony or lack of harmony. All of these are the inverted,攀缘 (pān-yuán) consciousness-minds of billions of kalpas.
"Delusive thoughts! Today I have finally realized that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is unchanging while following conditions, and it follows conditions while remaining unchanging.
Thus, all these various frivolous discourses and false conceptualizations are simultaneously eliminated. This single sentence describes the Tathāgata’s achievement in destroying delusion.
The Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable" in Chinese. The Sanskrit term *kalpa*— [end of excerpt]
This is called "time-period" (*kāla*). Since anyone who attains Buddhahood must necessarily pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"One cultivates the practices of the six *pāramitās* for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, plants the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred *kalpas*, and thereafter attains the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "One passes through one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), from the first stage to the seventh stage one completes two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and at the eighth stage..."

Up until the attainment of Equal Enlightenment, these three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* lead to the acquisition of the ultimate *dharmakāya*. All of this is the provisional discourse of skillful means (*upāya*).

It clarifies that while there is a sequential progression, it is not a case of merely passing through stages. Regarding the view that there is no such sequential progression, the various commentaries from antiquity offer differing interpretations:
some maintain it is the discourse of skillful means; some maintain it is a manifestation through supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); and others maintain...
To briefly describe those who have attained realization: some claim it does not refer to a single individual, while others speak of gradual cultivation and sudden enlightenment.
If one relies on the established doctrines of various commentaries to judge right and wrong between them, how can later practitioners of the Great Samādhi reach a state free from doubt?
There are two reasons for this resulting confusion: the first is attachment.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the provisional teachings of Vijñaptimātra represent an incomplete understanding of this meaning.

Second, regarding the passage concerning the aspiration to eliminate afflictions through inferior causes and the subsequent realization of the two fruits: now, if we speak according to the true purport of the original sūtra, all doubts will naturally be resolved like melting ice.
For the "Dharmakāya" mentioned herein refers to the Dharmatākāya (the body of the intrinsic nature) that is inherently possessed by us.
Furthermore, the ten dharma realms equally uphold the substance of existence; this is not the meaning of "partial realization" or "ultimate realization" as commonly understood.
This is precisely the ontological essence of the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, namely what is called the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
Regarding the term "attainment," "attain" means to obtain; it is also not the sense of "obtaining a portion" as commonly understood.

This is the realization of the ultimate. It is precisely when the capacity of the practitioner is met that they thoroughly perceive their own nature and gain conviction in the principle of this *dharmakāya*.

As for the statement "without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*," it means that one has faith that one's own mind is the Buddha, that one's own mind becomes the Buddha, and that the *dharmakāya* is accomplished without being obtained from another; therefore, it is said that there is no need to pass through further *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. And...

This is the initial attainment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This refers to what was stated in the preceding passage: "clearly knowing for oneself that one has attained the fundamental, wondrous mind.
It clarifies that the mind as cause and the awakening at the stage of fruition are non-dual and without distinction; this is the direct attainment of the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*).
However, because this Dharma-body is obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*) and entangled by deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), it remains in a state of confusion and lacks awareness.

It was as if I had lost something only to find it again. Now that coarse delusions have been briefly shattered and inverted perceptions have just begun to dissolve, I finally realize that having attained this principle is like catching a glimpse of a leopard through a tube—already seeing one of its stripes. Reaching this point, I now believe that my own mind is none other than the *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb of the Tathāgata).
Since this *garbha* is the true reality of the *dharmakāya*, it is said that I have "attained the *dharmakāya*."

This refers merely to attaining through faith; it does not mean attaining through realization. Therefore, there is the removal of delusions, and only when one's vows are fulfilled does one realize the two fruits.
This is precisely why [the teachings] extensively expound the perfect and sudden doctrine, using parables to seek the gateway and demonstrating the meaning of practice, clarity, and realization.
What cause for doubt could there be? As this very sutra states: "Although the principle is suddenly awakened to, that which is mounted upon awakening is eliminated all at once. As for phenomena..."

"It is not removed instantaneously; it is exhausted through successive stages, whereby one attains clear realization. This single sentence describes the benefit of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the truth.
△ Third, the making of great vows.
"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King... (up to) "...this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.

This refers to having previously attained the Dharma-body, yet being characterized by inherent endowment rather than having completed cultivation and severance. Therefore, one now arouses the mind and establishes vows, desiring to seek ultimate perfection.
The opening phrase describes the mind of wisdom; that is, the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way, which simultaneously encompasses the afflictions.
The first vow is to sever afflictions; for only by definitively severing afflictions can one attain Buddhahood.

The next phrase describes the mind of compassion, which is the vow to deliver sentient beings, while simultaneously encompassing the vow to study the Dharma-gates; for only by definitively penetrating the Dharma-gates can one deliver sentient beings.
These are precisely the Four Great Vows. The intent is that while the great kindness of the Buddha is indeed difficult to repay, one merely wishes—
From this day forward, until they attain the fruit of Bodhi and accomplish the Way of all Buddhas— being called Kings of All Jewels and liberated just as I, the Buddha, have been—
they shall take this profound mind that unifies wisdom and compassion to serve,
above, the Buddhas of lands as numerous as motes of dust, and to liberate, below, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Among all sentient beings, one who possesses even this single point of profound resolve is called "superior," for they repay the great kindness of our Buddha’s subtle and wondrous instruction.
As for the "Precious King": the Buddha is one of the Three Jewels and is thus the king of all jewels, both mundane and supramundane.
△ Fourth, the request for testimony.
"I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness" (up to) "I shall never enter *nirvāṇa* here.
This request for testimony is to seek the Buddha’s protection, so that one may ultimately not deviate from one's original vow. Because...
In his previous life, he was like Śākyamuni; therefore, it is said, "I vow to deliver beings such as these. Now, he vows to take up this land just as Śākyamuni did;

therefore, it is said, "I vow to enter the five turbidities. The five turbidities are the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
This is because in an age of turbid evil, sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform through spiritual instruction. As for people...

Those who are fearful and avoidant; whereas now, knowing that the nature of the treasury is impartial, and that defilement and purity, good and evil, are fundamentally not two different things, one enters first with courage and without timidity—this is precisely the mind of valor. *Nirvāṇa* is the same as *niehuan*;

these are merely differences in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit (Brahma) sounds. In the language of Qin, it is called "unconditioned" (*wuwei*), and also "extinction and deliverance" (*miadu*). This [term] is not to be grasped.
There are two [aspects]: first, not seeking the solitary nirvana of the two vehicles; second, not seeking the ultimate nirvana of the Buddhas.
This is just like Kṣitigarbha-rāja, who is said to realize bodhi only after all sentient beings have been saved. This is the vast mind.
It is the desire that "only when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted shall I enter extinction. This vow is most profound; therefore, I entreat you.
He placed his hand upon [the disciple's] head to administer the oath of testimony.
△ Fifth, the hope for further instruction:
"The Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion" (extending to) "...sits in the place of enlightenment throughout the ten directions."
The above concludes the formal request; hereafter, I hope that the Buddha will once again provide further instruction. The intent is this:
my ignorance and deluded thoughts cannot be shattered except by the Buddha, the Great Hero; the mire of my craving and desire cannot be pulled me from it except by the Buddha’s great power.
Yet, as for the bliss of the four virtues, who other than the Great Compassionate One could bestow it? [Regarding] the two deaths...

Who other than Great Compassion can extract one from such suffering? Therefore, I look up to you with compassion and pray that you will examine my case even more thoroughly, so as to eliminate my subtle delusions.
For what was previously called "eliminating inverted conceptions" is precisely what the subsequent text describes:

The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. You have already extinguished the afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) among sentient beings in the three realms;
these are precisely the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the three realms, which are coarse afflictions.

As for what is now called 'subtle,' it refers to what is stated in the subsequent text: 'Yet you still do not know that within the faculties there has been accumulation throughout successive births.'"

It begins with empty cultivation. That cultivation must depend on what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) to be attained. This also refers to the eighty-one grades of volition (*cetanā*) within the three realms;

when contrasted with [afflictions] associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), these are called "subtle. Furthermore, it is said: "How much more so regarding the divisions and categories of arising, abiding, change, and cessation within this?
This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) outside the realms; when contrasted with [afflictions] associated with views and cultivation, it is even more subtle.
Furthermore, it is subtle—precisely what is meant by so-called "subtle afflictions" (*mṛdu-kleśa*).

This means that while the inverted thoughts spanning billions of kalpas belonging to my coarse afflictions have already been eliminated under your grace, the thought-afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) accumulated within the root-faculties since beginningless time as empty habitual tendencies, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the specific categories and numerical divisions of the various realms, have not yet been exhausted. I pray that the Tathāgata will further bestow [his grace].
Please examine this in detail and provide an exposition to eliminate my subtle delusions.

If you would allow me to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment and realize the Dharma-body at an early date, and thereafter, arising from that essence, manifesting through various forms and reflections, appearing in bodies according to the capacities of beings, and sitting everywhere upon the site of enlightenment throughout the worlds of the ten directions—would that not be most joyful? Indeed...
The first two lines clarify the praise of the Buddha and the request for instruction; the subsequent two lines clarify seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.
It can be seen that what the dragon’s son did was indeed extraordinary compared to ordinary people; yet when a tiger is but three days old, it already possesses the spirit to devour an ox.
△ Sixth, expressing profound faith:
"The nature of Śūnyatā may perish, but the Śakraka-citta does not waver.
This is precisely for the sake of the practitioner, borrowing emptiness as a metaphor to express the profound faith in one's own mind. Regarding "Śūnyatā": [it refers to] space.
"Empty. *Śakara* means "solid" or "firm. This implies that empty space is not a material substance and, by its very nature, cannot perish;
yet, even if it were possible for it to perish, my present heart of profound faith and all the great vows I have thus generated are firm and unshakable. This signifies—
If one’s vows are firm, they cannot be shaken; if one’s faith is firm, there shall be no regression.
This is what is meant by "this single faith" and "eternal faith. The above section concludes the first part, which clarifies the false and the true in order to engender faith.
The Precious Mirror Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume Three;
The Precious Mirror Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume Four.
Composed by Fǔyuǎn of the Fǎmén School at Yún’ān Fǎjiè Monastery, Imperially Honored by the Great Qing Dynasty.
△ 2. Distinguishing Characteristics and Nature to Open Understanding (2) 1. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra States His Doubts and Requests Instruction.
At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra... [up to] ...eagerly yearned for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
This is precisely because Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, having heard that the four aggregates and the seven elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha, failed to realize the non-duality of nature and appearance.

For this reason, he gave rise to doubt and requested instruction. This is truly because although the Venerable One had attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) and had already realized the emptiness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya), his ignorance (avidyā) had not yet been destroyed and his attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) still remained; thus, he had not yet realized that all appearances are entirely the nature itself.

Therefore, not knowing the source from which the myriad dharmas arise and continue, and failing to understand that the entire nature is itself form, they do not know the principle of the perfect fusion of the seven elements.
For this reason, they give rise to doubt and inquire further; thus, with bodies bowed in reverence and minds full of respect, they address the Buddha and offer words of praise, saying:
"Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses such sternness in subduing others, yet is able to..."
It causes deluded thoughts to be instantly extinguished; truly, it possesses great majesty. Possessing a compassion that embraces all, it is able to cause right faith to arise deeply within people;
it is indeed a true Great Virtue. It may be called one who skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma and is adept at its manifestation.
Furthermore, all that has been expounded above is the self-realization of the Tathāgata, the foremost definitive meaning.
The realm of the perfect fusion of the three truths transcends the reach of thought, mind, speech, or deliberation.
Now, for the sake of sentient beings, [the Buddha] points out the *tathāgatagarbha* nature within the great enemy of the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and elements (*dhātus*).

By enabling people to eliminate the inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas and attain the *dharmakāya* of their own intrinsic nature, the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma for humanity can truly be called—
Excellent! Yet this ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is of an extremely profound and subtle principle, difficult to comprehend.

Even though I have long been esteemed by the World-Honored One and, amidst his preaching, was granted the seal of approval as being foremost among all people, today, upon hearing the subtle and wondrous Dharma-voice spoken by my Tathāgata, I am as if deaf.
As for those who have ears, they can hear the sound of a mosquito from more than a hundred paces away.
One might think that if a deaf person cannot hear a mosquito even when it is nearby, how much less could they hear it from more than a hundred paces away?
Even a loud voice might not be heard by them, let alone the faint sound of a mosquito. Furthermore, their actual physical form is still...

They do not see it; how much less could they hear its sound? If one considers the nature of things, those of the Two Vehicles are of narrow and inferior faculties, their meaning being like that of a deaf person.
The small fruits and the Great Enlightenment are worlds apart, like a distance of over a hundred paces.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is a principle of extreme subtlety, like the sound of a mosquito. Such is the ultimate truth.
If one cannot even perceive the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha through clear understanding, how much less can one attain silent resonance by hearing it without comprehension?
Although the Buddha previously proclaimed this with extreme clarity, his original intent was to cause us to eliminate our delusions;
yet now, not only are we unable to sweep away our former confusions, we still do not understand this in detail.
The meaning of "news" (or "newspaper") is that old delusions have not yet been eliminated while new doubts arise once more;
thus, neither can be brought to ultimate resolution, until one finally reaches a state where there is neither doubt nor delusion.
As for those like Ānanda, the Śrāvakas still in training, although they have received the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous instruction and have already awakened to their own [nature],...

Although this is so, within our very faculties there remain habitual tendencies from beginningless time and the various outflows (*āsrava*) of conditioned existence that have not yet been entirely eliminated.
We still look to the Buddha to further scrutinize and remove them; it goes without saying that we ourselves harbor doubts.

Even those among us who have attained the rank of the four fruits and whose merit surpasses that of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), such that they are entirely free from all outflows—even they [have doubts]. However...
Even now, having heard the subtle sound of the Dharma of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) spoken by our Tathāgata, we are still thus:
hesitant and unable to reach a decision, with doubts and regrets still arising. It is as if the business of the donkey has not yet been finished when the business of the horse arrives;
we repent for what we formerly practiced while still hearing the new teaching. Furthermore, we are still entangled by hesitations and doubts that we cannot resolve. We remain just like this.
How much more so for those who have not yet exhausted their habitual outflows (*vāsanā-asrava*). For this reason, I have two doubts and pray that you resolve them.

The first is the doubt regarding the arising and continuity of the myriad dharmas. World-Honored One, if it is as previously stated—that all conditioned worldly phenomena, including the sense organs, objects, aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and even the seven great elements, all belong to the unconditioned *tathāgatagarbha*—then [how can there be arising and continuity]?
This refers to that which is fundamentally pure and quiescent (*viśuddha-prakṛti*). If this is so, then since it is already pure, it should not further admit of defilement;
since it is already fundamental and quiescent, it should not further undergo flux and change. This being the case, I ask:

how did these insentient objects—the mountains, rivers, and great earth—which serve as the environmental retribution (*bhājana-vipāka*) for sentient beings, suddenly arise at the very beginning? And...

The defiled forms and minds of all sentient beings mean that both the sentient and the insentient, as well as the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—are all characterized by defilement and are not pure; this is clear.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "original suchness" (benran), it is inherently natural, without fabrication or transformation. Now, as for the root-body and the vessel-world, the insentient [portion]...
The phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; the birth, aging, sickness, and death of sentient beings—these shift in succession, flowing on without ceasing.
From beginning to end, and from end back to the beginning, they circulate through arising and ceasing, transforming and migrating.

Thus, it is clear that this is not the primordial nature. This is evident because, failing to comprehend the principle of following conditions, one uses these phenomenal appearances to raise objections.
This is the nature [of things]. Second is the doubt regarding the perfect interfusion of the five great elements.

Furthermore, I have heard the Tathāgata say that these four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—are from the beginning in their nature perfectly interfused, all-pervading, profound, and eternally abiding.
World-Honored One, if the nature of earth were all-pervading, it should consist purely of earth. Moreover, since earth can overcome water, water should consequently not exist.
[The opponent] says: How can there be room for water to exist [within fire]? If the nature of water were all-pervasive, it would follow that everything would be purely water.
Furthermore, since water can extinguish fire, fire ought not to arise at all.

Moreover, how can you explain that these two natures—water and fire—are both pervasive throughout space, yet do not overcome or extinguish one another? World-Honored One, [you have said that fire] covers the earth...
The nature of obstruction belongs to hindrance; the nature of emptiness belongs to vacuity and penetration.
That which is obstructed does not penetrate; that which penetrates is not obstructed. How can these two natures coexist and both be called "pervading the dharma-realm"?
This arises from failing to understand the principle that "the unchanging follows conditions," and thus using the nature to challenge the characteristics. However...
While the Blessed One certainly possesses the true meaning, and I too possess the truth, we are both ignorant of the ultimate destination of these two meanings.
I pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim the secret intent and disseminate the subtle words;
may you manifest great compassion, explain the source of the *tantras*, point out the meaning of their perfect integration, and guide me, so that—
The clouds of delusion were suddenly rent asunder, and the moon of the mind became perfectly bright; thus they reached the ultimate stage where there is no doubt.
Having spoken these words, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and the entire assembly each prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed instruction.
△ 2. The Tathāgata Dispels Doubt and Grants Permission to Teach (3): 1. Granting Permission and Admonishing to Listen.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa... [until] ...reverently listening to the Buddha’s Dharma-voice in silent compliance.

This is an announcement to the assembly, exhorting them to listen attentively. The intent is that although previously, for the sake of Ānanda and others, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*),
and elements (*dhātu*) were explained as being identical to the *tathāgatagarbha*— thereby causing them to shatter delusion and return to reality, which is the supreme among all supreme truths—
now it is for the sake of you all and those in this assembly whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and who have attained the [highest] stage.
For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), he further elucidates how delusion arises from the truth, so that they may know that the myriad dharmas arise from the single nature—
the fundamental one mind— and reach the realization that appearance and nature are identical, and delusion and truth are identical. This principle that nature and appearance,
truth and delusion, are neither identical nor separate, is what is called the true ultimate within the ultimate.
However, as for "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*), it is the object traversed by the most supreme path. Thus, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are briefly four types:

first, the worldly ultimate (*loka-paramārtha*), which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); second, the ultimate of reasoning (*yukti-paramārtha*), which refers to suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), its cessation (*nirodha*), and so forth;

third, the ultimate of realization (*adhigama-paramārtha*), which refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness; and fourth, the ultimate of the ultimate (*paramārtha-paramārtha*), which refers to—

The One True Dharma-realm: according to the later passages of the sutra, when it speaks of the arising and continuity of the myriad dharmas, they originate from the two types of awakening inherent in the nature;
when it speaks of the perfect fusion of the seven elements, they converge in the one mind and the threefold treasury. This is precisely the One True Dharma-realm.

Therefore, this belongs to the fourth ultimate truth. The meaning is that I now cause those in this assembly who are of a fixed nature and do not turn their minds—the dull-facultied śrāvakas—and all others who have not yet realized the two kinds of emptiness regarding persons and phenomena, to immediately turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.
As for those with sharp faculties, such as arhats and so forth: the term "and so forth" (等) includes the remaining four natures.
Furthermore, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, there are five natures: first, the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle; second, the nature of the Pratyekabuddha;
third, the nature of the Tathāgata vehicle; fourth, the indeterminate nature; and fifth, the nature of no-nature, which refers to the icchantikas.
Now, however, regardless of whether one possesses a fixed or indeterminate nature, or whether one turns the mind [toward enlightenment] or does not turn the mind, all shall universally obtain this.
The single Buddha-vehicle leads directly to the site of the Bodhimanda and into the great ocean of nirvana.
*Āraṇya* is said to mean "free from clamor and contention," and it is also called a "place of stillness.

Since all ordinary arhats receive this name, yet their freedom from contention and stillness are not called "true," for they remain attached to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, having not yet realized all dharmas.
Because it is inherently quiescent from the very beginning, the path of cultivation that diverges from this is but a byway or a detour; it is not the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood.

If one attains the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, then regardless of whether the faculties are sharp or dull, or whether the environment is moving or still, both phenomena and principle will reach ultimate realization;
only then can it be called true quiescence and correct cultivation. It is said that this alone—

One reality is true; the other two are not real. This refers to those śrāvakas of fixed nature and icchantikas who lack the potential [for awakening] and cannot attain Buddhahood—those like scorched sprouts or rotten seeds. Now, they all equally obtain the One Vehicle and shall all become Buddhas.
Ultimate nirvana—is this not the discourse on the supreme pinnacle of the Mahāyāna? He then cautioned them to listen, saying:

"Now you must listen attentively; I shall analyze and explain it for you. Fumai and the others, reverently admiring the Dharma-voice of our Buddha, cleared their minds and stilled their breaths, listening in silent reverence.

△ Second, the actual refutation of doubts (divided into two): 1. Directly addressing Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra (divided into two): 1. Refuting the doubt regarding the continuous arising of various marks (divided into three):
1. Directly refuting what is doubted (divided into three): 2. Generally distinguishing between the real and the delusive (divided into two): 1. Citing and establishing true awakening.
The Buddha said, "Pūrṇa, as you have said... (up to) 'I have always heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.

Here, the Buddha wishes to clarify the origins and details of the continuity of birth; therefore, he first restates and confirms their doubt, specifically seizing upon true awakening to interrogate them.
The phrase "As you [have said]" below is the restatement and confirmation. He then interrogates them by saying: "In your ordinary [experience]..."
Have you not heard that which the Tathāgata has proclaimed: that True Suchness (tathatā) accords with conditions yet remains unchanging as it accords with conditions?
Thus he taught the meaning of the wondrous clarity of the awakened nature and the luminous wonder of original awakening.

This question regarding the fundamental nature is based on the fact that the single essence of True Suchness possesses the function of acceding with conditions while remaining unchanging, and of remaining unchanging while acceding with conditions; therefore, it is said that the awakened nature is wondrously clear.
This means that the nature is fundamentally self-awakened; it is fundamentally wondrous and inherently luminous.

"Fundamental awakening is luminous and wondrous" means that the fundamental nature is self-awakened, and this nature is inherently luminous and inherently wondrous. Originally there is no duality; all subject and object are transcended.
This precisely clarifies the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) dharma-gate of the one true *dharmadhātu*, which is none other than the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. By means of...
The essence remains unchanging while its function accords with conditions; it is quiescent yet illuminating, and thus called "wondrously luminous" (miao-ming).
Because its function accords with conditions while its essence remains unchanging, it is illuminating yet quiescent, and thus called "luminously wondrous" (ming-miao).

This is the mutual fusion of essence and function, where quiescence and illumination are both transcended, leaving only the single True Dharma-realm. This is precisely the principle that intrinsic nature and phenomenal characteristics are non-dual. And [this is] full...
When Maitreya was caught on the single hook, he said, "I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.
At that moment, his nostrils had already fallen into the hands of the World-Honored One.
△ Second, the clarification of deluded awareness. The Buddha said:

"That which you call 'awareness-illumination'—is it the illumination of the nature... (down to)... 'the nature-awareness is necessarily luminous; it is through delusion that it becomes 'illumination-awareness.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s simultaneous opening of the two paths of the real and the delusive, in order to clarify the delusion that has been mistakenly identified. The meaning is as follows:
Regarding what you said—"Your mind is inferior; it calls this 'the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous' and 'fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous"—what is your understanding of this?
Does it mean that the nature is inherently luminous and spiritually unobscured, and is thus designated solely as "awareness"?

Or does it mean that awareness was originally not luminous and is made luminous through its function, and is thus designated as both "luminosity" and "awareness"? For if it were designated solely as "awareness," [it would be incomplete].

That which does not require the addition of "illumination" (ming) is true awakening (*tathatā*). That which is designated as both "illumination" and "awakening" and necessarily requires the addition of "illumination" is deluded awakening (*bhrānti-bodha*).
Yet the World-Honored One presents both the true and the deluded together, desiring to lead Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to personally determine what to adopt and what to reject.

Who would have known that the Venerable One was unable to grasp the true and instead identified with the deluded? Therefore it is said: "If you claim that this does not require the addition of illumination..."
To designate it merely as "awakening" (jue) implies that this awakening possesses only the capacity for obscure awareness, yet lacks the clarity of manifest illumination.
What benefit is there in adopting such an unilluminated awakening?

It appears that the Venerable’s intention is to reject, through explicit negation, the true awakening that has nothing to illuminate, while tacitly adopting the deluded [state] that has something to illuminate.
"You have awakened, yet you do not realize that as soon as there is subject and object, you are far removed from the fundamentally pure nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
For this reason, the Tathāgata follows your words and establishes two barriers to refute them, saying:
'If there were no object of illumination, then there would be no illumination. Your intention must be to take for granted that there is an object of illumination; you simply do not understand."
If one knows that there is something illuminated, then it is no longer the fundamentally pure and original awakened nature (*bodhi*).
Fearing that they might instead calculate that because illumination is refuted, non-illumination (*avidyā*) must be grasped, he therefore refutes this further, saying:

"Suppose you were to say that this absence of illumination is not 'having illumination,' but rather 'non-illumination. Furthermore, this non-illumination is also not the fundamentally awakened, tranquil state."
This is the wondrously luminous true nature. Insofar as there is something that is not "awakening," it reveals this awakened nature to not belong to "having-luminosity.
Insofar as there is nothing that is not "luminosity," it reveals this awakened nature to not belong to "non-luminosity.

This is truly because the original awakening of self-nature must always be accompanied by the true luminosity of self-nature; this luminosity is neither the deluded luminosity of "having-something" nor is it "nothingness."
This is ignorance. It is simply that True Suchness (tathatā) possesses the function of responding to conditions;

due to non-awakening for a single thought-moment since beginningless time, it has become the deluded awakening that is the object of illumination. Thus, through this lack of awakening, ignorance is formed.
△ II. Specific Explanation of the Continuum of Birth (2) 1. Explaining the Reason for Sudden Arising.

Awareness is not an object of illumination; it is by means of illumination that objects are established. (Up to: Therein, neither similarity nor difference exists, for truly conditioned phenomena [are empty].
This clarifies that the karmic fruits of sentient beings in this world all arise from a single thought of ignorance;

they exist through non-awakening. This answers the question of how they could suddenly come into being. The meaning is that the nature of awakening is fundamentally not something that can be made an object of illumination.

Because of this deluded illumination, a deluded "object" is established. Once the object has been falsely established, your deluded "subject" (the capacity to perceive) is thereby produced. Thus, the subject is originally non-existent.
Within the dharma-nature where subject and object are identical or different, they blaze forth as subject and object in identity and difference;
this is the reason why the world suddenly arises. Furthermore, distinct from that difference of the "differentiated," one falsely establishes identity based on difference;
this is the reason why empty space suddenly arises. Moreover, since there is both identity and difference, they mutually...

This is the revelation. Therefore, one further establishes that there is neither identity nor difference; this is because sentient beings give rise to these notions suddenly. Now, if ignorance does not arise, it remains as it is;
once it arises, it inevitably creates the distinction between subject and object. Where there is difference, there must necessarily be identity.
Since there is both difference and identity, there must necessarily be neither identity nor difference. Thus do all phenomena flourish.
However, when the true nature is suddenly disturbed, subject and object stand in opposition; how can weariness and anxiety not arise?
Once weariness and anxiety have persisted for long, how can delusory objects not manifest? Since delusory objects exist, how can the pure, spontaneous characteristics of the mind remain unmuddied?
From this single thought, one unconsciously gives rise to the three subtleties and six coarsenesses—the dust and toil of affliction.

That which moves is the world; that which is still is empty space. Thus one knows that the empty space of the ten directions is the common characteristic within the deluded mind. That which moves without being still constitutes the world;
thus one knows that the worlds of the ten directions are the particular characteristics within the deluded mind. This insentient realm of empty space all belongs to delusion.
The mind is thus clarified. If there were neither sameness nor difference therein, then as for sentient beings: to call them "the same" refers to their shared nature;

yet since their bodies and lives are each distinct, it is called "no sameness. To call them "different" refers to the fact that the four great elements are entirely uniform and the mind-consciousness is likewise uniform;
therefore, it is called "no difference. Thus, this dharma of neither sameness nor difference arises precisely because of sameness and difference.

To establish [distinctions] based on this is truly a method of conditioned activity; it is certainly not comparable to the awakened nature (bodhi) which, as mentioned above, is fundamentally free from both sameness and difference.
Thus, we can see that sentient beings are likewise merely the appearances of neither-sameness-nor-difference within the deluded mind.
This passage was formerly interpreted as referring to ignorance, non-awakening, the three subtle states, and the six coarse states.
As for the commentator’s interpretation, its intent is indeed profound; however, it causes the flow of the text to be interrupted, thereby making the meaning of the sūtra difficult to clarify.
For this reason, I have not adopted it. Should one wish to correlate it [with the present passage], there would be no objection. It is because the preceding chapter stated:

"The nature of awakening is inherently luminous, yet through delusion it becomes the 'awakening of luminosity'. Here, the first phrase pertains to the True, while the second phrase pertains to the Delusive; that is to say, proceeding from the True...
The arising of delusion is precisely the True Suchness (tathatā) following conditions to form fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā). "Awakening is not that which is illumined;

because of illumination, an object is established"—these two phrases constitute the phase of karma (karma-lakṣaṇa). "Once the object has been falsely established," and so forth, for the four phrases, constitutes the phase of transformation (vipariṇāma-lakṣaṇa).
From "it differs from that object" up to "neither identical nor different" constitutes the phase of manifestation (nirbhāsa-lakṣaṇa). The above.
These are the three subtle [states]. Next, the arising of weariness through mutual dependence corresponds to the "characteristic of cognition" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) among the six coarse states.

Long-term weariness corresponds to the "characteristic of continuity" (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*). The stirring up of dust corresponds to the "characteristic of grasping" (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*). The turbidity of one's own characteristics corresponds to the "characteristic of calculating names" (*nāma-saṃkhyā-lakṣaṇa*).

Dust, weariness, and afflictions correspond to the "characteristic of initiating karma" (*karma-pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*). From the self-initiation of the world up to the truly conditioned phenomena, these are the bonds of karma.

This is the characteristic of suffering. Therefore it is said: "Nescience, through non-awakening, gives rise to the three subtle states; with objective realms as conditions, they grow into the six coarse states.

Thus we know that if one does not rely on fundamental awakening, how could there be nescience? If one does not rely on nescience, how could there be objective realms? If one does not take objective realms as conditions, how could there be the six coarse states?
To subsume the six coarse states is to reduce them to the perceived and the perceiver; to subsume the perceived and the perceiver is to reduce them solely to karma.
Regarding consciousness: since the karmic consciousness is solely ignorance, and ignorance is solely original enlightenment, it is as it is said:
"When deluded, the entirety of the true becomes false; when awakened, the entirety of the false is the true. This is precisely that point.
△ Second, explaining the cause of continuity (3): 1. The continuity of the world.
From "The clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness interact to form agitation" (up to) "by these causes and conditions, the world continues."
The above explains how, based upon true awakening, deluded movement arises and transforms into the characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth;

this, in turn, depending on ignorance, transforms into the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), whereby the continuity of the world-systems comes to be. This is the direct answer to the question regarding the sequential migration of phenomena as they end and begin again.
It is because the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally pure and inherently such, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*, and is by nature immovable.
Fundamentally, there is no continuity of birth; it is only because of the unfolding of karma that the appearance of movement and the continuity of birth arise.
From the very essence of the original self-awakening (*pratyātmabodhi*) of all sentient beings, deluded luminosity arises, whereby the darkening of true emptiness becomes a state of inert emptiness.
Thus, they take this deluded awakening for luminosity and this inert emptiness for darkness. These two dharmas contend with one another. That...

This alternation of change falsely gives rise to vibration; that is to say, movement produces wind. Thus, above the wheel of space (ākāśa-maṇḍala), there is a wheel of wind (vāyu-maṇḍala) which sustains the world.
One thereby knows that the solidification of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is entirely sustained by the power of the wind of ignorance (avidyā-vāyu), so that it does not disperse.
It can be seen that the seed of the great element of wind is none other than the deluded mind of ignorance.
It is merely the moving aspect of thought. Since it arises from the mutual usurping of luminous awareness and dark ignorance, it becomes a state of agitation.
Because movement must have its opposite in stillness, within this deluded luminosity, a kind of solidified false conception is established.

It is like a person who, while overcome by sleep and tormented by a nightmare, experiences a state of delusion and distress; though this is fundamentally unobstructed, they falsely perceive it as obstructed.

Just as in the midst of such a dream, one stubbornly clings to the desire for release and falsely perceives that some object is pressing down upon them, thereby giving rise to the appearance of all manner of solid obstructions.
One should know that the great earth—what is called the precious golden wheel—is likewise so perceived.
This is precisely the characteristic of solidity and obstruction established by the essence of your own deluded luminosity and awareness.

Therefore, upon the wind-circle, there arises the great golden wheel of earth, which sustains the lands. Thus, one should know that the seed of the great golden wheel of earth is merely the solid aspect of a single thought-moment of the deluded mind of ignorance;
for within the deluded mind, the solid aspect is none other than ignorance itself.
