Once the gold and jewels have formed, ignorance is shaken. Furthermore, a wind arises; with this shaking wind, it rubs against the solid and obstructed gold.
As they move and remain firm, rubbing and churning against one another, they evoke the appearance of fire in the world, which undergoes transformation, birth, and maturation.
This is the nature of transforming existence into non-existence. Thus, one knows the seed of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*).
This is merely the appearance of ignorance’s delusion, wherein the movement and stillness of a single thought rub against one another.
When the jewel of true awakening is taken by the deluded mind, it contains luminosity and generates moisture, like a pearl emerging from water.
Furthermore, the fire of the deluded mind’s transformations causes the vital energy to become parched and ascend in flame, like an object being steamed and emitting vapor. Therefore...
One perceives that there is a water-wheel which encompasses the worlds of the ten directions.
It can be seen that the seed of the great element of water is produced by the steaming heat of the two delusions of gold and fire within a single thought-moment of the ignorant, deluded mind.
In sum, because of the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*), one perceives the wind-wheel; because of the grasping at solidity and obstruction, one perceives the gold-wheel; because of friction...
Because of dryness, one experiences the fire element; because the love of the heart is deep, one experiences the water element.
Thus, it is known that the seeds of the four great elements all arise from a single thought of ignorance. The above has explained how the four great elements are formed based on ignorance.
The following statement explains that the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is formed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The meaning is this:

once ignorance has established the nature of the four great elements, although they are each mutually contradictory, they nevertheless assist one another. For instance, the nature of fire is inherently to ascend, while the nature of water is inherently to descend;
through this alternating ascent and descent, they interact to produce all things, establishing various solid obstructions to form the vessel-world.

Regarding the elements: if the water of craving prevails within the deluded mind, it becomes low-lying and marshy, forming a vast ocean; thus, there are watery realms in the world such as the four great oceans.
If the fire of anger prevails within the deluded mind, that which is dry and extensive becomes a continent (*dvīpa*), while that which is small becomes a sandbank (*taraṅga*);
thus, there are terrestrial regions in the world such as the four great continents. This is due to the element of water.

Because they have formed [a bond], within that great ocean—which was originally a low-lying, marshy watery land where fire should not exist—there arise flames from the mutual establishment of the fire of anger within their hearts; thus, a light of fire constantly arises on that continent.
The sandbars (*tàn*) were originally dry land and should not have water;
yet, because the mind’s craving for water establishes itself there, water can exist and flow constantly into the rivers.
If within the deluded mind the power of water is inferior while the power of fire is superior, then it solidifies into high mountains; therefore, when mountain rocks are struck, they produce flames.
The seed-nature of fire still persists therein. That which melts and transforms into water is because the seed-nature of water has not perished.
If within the deluded mind the power of earth is inferior while the power of water is superior, then it emerges as grasses and trees;
thus, when forests of myriad trees and thickets of various plants encounter a conflagration, [they transform accordingly].
It forms earth; thus we know that the seed-nature of earth still persists. Or, through the condensation of matter, it forms water;
thus the seed-nature of water does not perish. It can be seen, therefore, that the four great elements are nothing other than objects manifested by the deluded mind.
This is because a single thought of deluded movement stirs up ignorance to form the element of wind. Solidity...
Obstructed by ignorance, the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) is formed; through the friction of movement and stillness, the fire element (*tejo-mahābhūta*) is formed;

and through the mutual steaming of metal and fire, the water element (*ap-mahābhūta*) is formed. Thus, there are the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*), which arise through the interaction of the objects of the deluded mind.
Furthermore, due to the harmonious union of water and fire, they become the seeds of continents and oceans. Then, the force of the water is diminished, following the force of the fire.
They become the seeds of mountains and rocks; furthermore, descending to the level of the earth, they follow the course of the waters to become the seeds of grasses and trees.
Thus, acting as seeds for one another, they coalesce to form the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

For these causes and conditions, worlds undergo the phases of formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness, ending and beginning again in succession so that the cycle continues without interruption. There are those who have borrowed from the ancient commentaries.

Regarding the generation and overcoming (sheng-ke) of the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) as explained by commentators: although there are arguments based upon them within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), I do not accept them here.
Since this sutra primarily reveals that all things are but mind (*citta-mātra*), how can one allow it to be conflated with those worldly false conceptualizations?
Furthermore, consider such things as mountains and stones striking fire, or ice melting into water; how could these be reconciled with the theory of the five elements?
Commentary: If one classifies stone as belonging to the metal element (*kāya*), then metal can produce water; how could it also produce fire?
If one classifies stone as earth (*pṛthivī*), then neither water nor earth should be produced from it. Furthermore, when a forest burns and turns to ash, one might say that fire produces earth;
yet when wood is twisted and squeezed, water is produced—is this not simply wood producing water in reverse? Therefore, the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*) of the world are fundamentally...
This has no real meaning; one should not use that to explain this.
△ Second, the continuity of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa clarifies that delusion is not from another [source]... (up to) ...by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
This clarifies that the continuity of sentient beings all arises from the "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*). The Buddha’s intention is this:
what Pūrṇa calls the falsity of "clarity" is not due to any other cause; it is simply the fault of falsely adding the capacity for illumination (*neng-ming*) upon the essence of true awakening.
Because there is the capacity for illumination, there is the object of illumination (*suoming*). Since the falsity of the object of illumination [already exists],...
However, once established, the principle by which they are made manifest cannot be transcended;
thus, from the single essence of pure spirit, they are divided into the six harmonious aggregates. For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not transcend form.
These are the six kinds of delusive objects of perception: form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental phenomena.

Once these have been accomplished, one thereby distinguishes the six kinds of deluded faculties—the seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—that constitute the subjective capacity for perception.
These faculties necessarily grasp at objects, giving rise to delusions and creating karma, which leads to the manifestation of forms within the four modes of birth.

Regarding the phrase "sharing the same karma," it means that one must depend upon the three—oneself, the father, and the mother—sharing a common karma; through either conceptualization or desire, they mutually...

Because there is entanglement, there are the two categories of womb-born and egg-born. As for "conjoining and separating," this refers to those who do not depend on parents but arise solely through their own karma;
they either conjoin with moisture to form a body or separate from ease to undergo transformation. These are the two categories of moisture-born and transformation-born.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Due to craving for sexual desire, there are egg-born and womb-born; due to craving for fragrance and flavor, [there are moisture-born and transformation-born]."
Therefore, one undergoes moisture-birth (*saṃsvedaja*). According to one's desire, one undergoes transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).
These are the origins of the four modes of birth (*yoni*) and the six destinies (*gati*). Now, for instance, regarding the beginning of womb-birth (*jarāyuja*):

due to that illusory intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), at a place where conditions are met, a luminous sign and desirable forms appear before one. Relying upon this luminous sign, one then...
Perceiving false objects, one gives rise to thoughts of desire; thus, when a male perceives his father as distinct, and a female perceives her mother as distinct, aversion is formed.

When a male perceives his mother as identical [to himself], he falsely conceives the thought of her being his wife; when a female perceives her father as identical, she falsely conceives the thought of him being her husband, and thus love is formed.
It is from this very thought of love that the flow pours into the parents' two drops—the red and the white—thereby forming [the embryo].
Regarding the seeds of rebirth: when the two drops of red and white [semen and blood] receive this notion of affection, they become established as a fetus.
Thus, although its occurrence is due to sexual union, it actually arises because the three karmas of the parents and those of the self are identical.
It enters the womb like a stone attracting iron or a needle drawing thread. Therefore, through this notion of affection—
Due to the conditions of sexual union, within seven days of being in the womb, the *kalala*—known as the "coagulated slime"—is produced.
After two weeks, it becomes the *arbuda*, known as the "bubble," and so forth; "and so forth" refers to the remaining three stages:
after three weeks it is called the *peśī*, known as "flesh-mass"; after four weeks it is the *ghana*, known as "solid flesh"; and after five weeks...
This refers to the *praśākhā* stage, known as the "stage of form," when, at the completion of ten months, one emerges from the womb.

Now, among these four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—there is none that does not correspond to the delusions and karma experienced by each being through these four types of birth.
Thus, those born from eggs possess only indeterminate perceptions; those born from wombs generally arise due to feelings of attachment and longing. When [the conditions] combine...

The "moist-born" (saṃsvedaja) cling to odors and flavors out of craving, never departing from what they have been drawn to. Those who "depart through transformation" (upapāduka) crave superior objects;
they abandon this place and hasten toward that. All these are summoned by the four types of karma, and thus there are four modes of birth corresponding to their respective conditions.
However, it does not stop at this; from this point onward, forms are changed and retributions shift, and the cycle of birth and death has no end.
Cease! Sometimes emotion transforms into thought, and sometimes thought transforms into emotion; sometimes union changes into separation, and sometimes separation changes into union.
As they mutually alter and transform one another in various ways, there is karma that can induce experience, and there must be retribution that is received.
Following one's wholesome karma, all four modes of birth possess the possibility of ascending flight.
Pleasure follows its evil karma; thus, within the four modes of birth, there is the suffering of sinking and falling.

When one seeks the cause of this, it is none other than the fault of awakened clarity that constitutes the primary cause. Therefore, sentient beings bring about one another’s continuity as conditions.
△ The continuity of the results of the three karmas.
Pūrṇa, because perception and craving are bound together as one, one cannot be separated from craving; by these causes and conditions, the results of karma continue in succession.
This clarifies that the continuity of karmic results arises entirely from craving.

Pūrṇa, due to the two perceptions of aversion and attraction within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), becomes greedily attached to the objects of desire; as his three types of karma correspond [to those of his future parents], he is bound and enters the womb.
Once inside, he feels affectionate attachment and joy, unable to leave of his own accord. For this reason, when parents in the world give birth to a child, the child in turn...
Grandsons are born; sons and grandsons are produced and succeed one another without interruption.
If one seeks the cause of this, it is that these things take greed and attachment as their root. Because there is greed and attachment, there must necessarily be body and life.
All who possess body and life must alike be nourished; since they crave nourishment, they will inevitably consume meat.
Thus, the intent to harm living beings cannot be restrained by even the most compassionate person.

Consequently, among the four classes of birth, according to the power of their karma, the strong coerce the weak and the weak serve the strong; they swallow one another and devour each other in succession. To seek...
As for the origin of this: such beings take the killing of creatures and the proliferation of greed as their fundamental basis.
It is just like when humans eat sheep; when the sheep dies, it becomes a human, and when the human dies, they become a sheep, coming to devour one another in turn.
This is what is meant by "eating his eight liang and returning him half a jin. Is it only between humans and sheep that this occurs? It is thus for all ten classes of beings.
Sentient beings die and die again; they are born and are born again. Revolving through cycles of retribution, they prey upon one another.
Due to these evil karmas, they are born together life after life, dwelling in the same world, encountering one another as enemies and vengeful adversaries, repaying each other in turn.
Reaching to the furthest limits of the future, they devour one another without ceasing. If one seeks the origin of this, it is rooted in theft and greed.
Question: This concerns only the eating of meat; how can it be called theft? Answer: Generally, taking what is not given and taking it secretly are both termed theft.
For instance, when a person eats a sheep, does the sheep ever willingly consent to being eaten by that person?
This is taking what is not given. When sheep die, they become humans; they come to devour one another in turn. This is "shady taking" (*yin-qu*).
Therefore, all are called theft—is this not appropriate? By observing this, one knows that the source of killing and stealing arises from eating meat.

For example, when the eighty thousand Śākyas were slaughtered by Virūḍhaka, they recognized the immediate conditions of his insults and abuse, yet they did not realize that it was due to their eating fish.
As for remote causes: it is like the times of peace in this world when people kill and eat animals at will.

How could they know that as days pass and years deepen, those among humans who enjoy blessings will find their merit exhausted and their karma manifest, while those animals who have been slaughtered will receive their retribution by being reborn as humans?
All carry the enmity of killing, which ultimately results in an eon of slaughter. Therefore, the Buddha established the prohibition against taking life and the precept against eating meat;
this is precisely to stop killing and restrain chaos, so that peace may be constantly enjoyed and all may ascend together to the foundation of benevolence and longevity.
The above has clarified the root of karmic retribution; below, the sequence of its continuity is described. If one acts out of greed for killing...
To speak of it in terms of life: you owe me my life; I return your life. I owe you your life; you return my life.
To speak of it in terms of theft and greed: I owe you a debt; I repay your debt. You owe me a debt.
"Return my debt to me! Because of this karmic debt of life, even after passing through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of births, the repayment will never cease.
Due to this continuity, one remains constantly within birth and death and is unable to escape it. This is as when speaking of sensual craving."
Thus, you love my mind, while I cherish your form; I love your mind, while you cherish my form.

Because of these causes and conditions of mutual love and affection, even though we may encounter and meet one another throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, we will always remain within the bonds of attachment, never reaching a day of liberation.
If one were to discuss the fundamental cause, it is solely these two characters—“greed” and “love”—that act as the executioners.

Theft, sexual misconduct, and the three [other non-virtues] are the roots. Due to these causes and conditions of craving and attachment, karmic causes and their suffering fruits arise and continue in succession without end.
△ Third, the conclusion on the continuity from end to beginning:
"Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted states continue in succession (until) because of this delusion they end and then begin again."
This passage generally concludes by summarizing the three kinds of continuity, in response to Pūrṇa’s sudden request concerning the beginning and end [of existence].
The meaning is that these three continuities—the world, sentient beings, and karmic retribution—have no other underlying principle;

because they are illusory and false, they circulate in inversion, mutually generating and continuing one another. In short, it all originates from the first moment of non-awakening, which is delusion.
Recognizing and awakening to clarity, it subsequently becomes the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). Once the karmic consciousness exists, the two views suddenly arise.
Thus, at the beginning, because there appears to be a world, there are sentient beings; because there are sentient beings, there is karmic retribution.
Later, because that karmic retribution is uninterrupted, the characteristics of sentient beings continue; because sentient beings are not severed, the world continues.
However, these are not real; they are nothing other than the deluded luminosity of the essence of awareness, which takes on the blame for its own faults.

Because of this delusion, the nature of clear cognition arises as the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-portion). Because of this act of cognizing, the manifestation of objective appearances becomes the *nimitta-bhāga* (the appearing-portion).
As to your question, "How did the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise? you should know that they proceed from—
This illusory awakening and clarity suddenly gives rise to the two divisions of the perceived and the perceiver. It then undergoes successive transformations and cycles of transmigration;
there is nothing that does not arise from this karmic consciousness of awakening and clarity, wherein the perceived and the perceiver are empty and unreal, false and not true.
Therefore, from beginning to end, and from end back to beginning, they continue in succession without interruption.
△ Second, an explanation that simultaneously addresses the raised objection (2): First, Pūrṇa’s objection based on the cause grasping the effect.
Pūrṇa said: “If this wondrous awakening... [as it continues] ...how could the outflows of conditioned existence ever arise again?”
This Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra clings to the nature of the cause while challenging the realization of the fruit. His intention is this:

if one relies on the Buddha’s teaching, then these sentient beings currently possess the essence of wondrous enlightenment within their entanglements. By nature it is primordially wondrous; enlightenment is primordially luminous.
When compared with the mind of the Tathāgata, it does not increase in the Buddha, nor does it decrease in the sentient being. It is only because of the sentient being...
Upon the essence of wondrous enlightenment, one forcibly imposes deluded luminosity; because it was originally non-existent, the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth suddenly arise.

This is certainly true. I venture to ask: when the Tathāgata, now at the site of enlightenment, beheld the morning star at night and realized wondrously enlightened true emptiness and the fundamentally enlightened wondrous luminosity—seeming as though he and sentient beings were identical from the beginning—is this not the same as the original state? Or do you not understand?
The world of mountains and rivers, the conditioned sentient beings, and the karmic fruits of habitual outflows—when will these ever arise again?
△ Second, the explanation through the analogy of the Tathāgata’s true and false natures (in two parts): First, the analogy that the false does not arise again.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "For example, it is like a person who has lost their way... (up to) "...when will the mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever emerge again?
This was because Pūrṇa had erroneously clung to the dharmas; therefore, the Buddha raised this analogy to cause him to resolve his doubts by means of the facts at hand.
Within the text, two analogies are presented in succession: the first clarifies that delusion is without cause, and the second clarifies that the characteristics of the objective world are not real.
This is merely to clarify the meaning that delusion does not arise again. Therefore, he poses a question, saying:
"Suppose there is a person who becomes confused in a certain village and suddenly mistakes south for north.
Do you think this person’s confusion exists because of a pre-existing confusion? Or does it arise from awakening because of a state of being originally unconfused? Man!
Cizi said, "The delusion of this person does not arise because of delusion, nor does it arise because of awakening. Why?
Because prior to being deluded, there was originally no root from which delusion could arise. How, then, could awakening exist because of delusion?

Furthermore, since the opposite of delusion is not the root that gives rise to delusion, how could [awakening] exist because of awakening? The Buddha said, "Since you already know that delusion is fundamentally..."
There is no fundamental basis for this. Suppose that person, while being in the midst of confusion, mistakes south for north;
yet, if there should suddenly be one who awakens them by pointing it out, then even though this person has long been deluded, once they have attained awakening, regarding this village—
"Would they fall back into delusion? He replied, "No, World-Honored One. Once one has attained awakening, one no longer falls into delusion.
Therefore, the Dharma principle states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions do not fall into delusion after their awakening; it is likewise so.
This is truly because this delusion of ignorance does not take self-nature as its basis, nor does it take the essence of awakening as its basis. When one investigates its substance...
The nature is ultimately and originally empty. This precisely accords with the previous point that the delusion of losing one's direction has no cause.

That is to say, even in the past, there was originally no delusion to be found. It is like one who has lost their way: even while in the state of delusion, the directions themselves have never actually shifted.
Not only is delusion unfindable, but awakening (*bodhi*) is likewise unfindable; it is only when viewed from the perspective of the time of delusion that awakening is posited.

At that time, it seems as though there is delusion and awakening. Just as when one is deluded and takes south for north, compared to the moment of realizing that it is south and not north, it seems as though there has been a shifting or a change. Now, once awakening realizes delusion, delusion is forever extinguished;
yet even the single word "awakening" cannot be found—how much less could delusion arise again? It is also like a person with cataracts seeing empty space.
The flower in the sky is not originally a real existence; yet when the cataract is removed, the flower vanishes from the void, nor is it truly non-existent.

Suppose there were a foolish person who, in that empty space where the flower had vanished, waited further for the flower to arise again. Do you consider this person foolish or wise? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"In the void, there was never a flower to begin with; how could there be arising or ceasing? It is merely a false perception that the void has ceased."
"This is a perversion. To instruct you to emerge [from it] again is truly madness. How can you further ask about the difference between the ignorant and the wise?
The Buddha then followed his words and questioned him, saying: "As for this person who waits for the flowers, he is indeed as you say—utterly foolish and mad.
Since you already know this, why do you ask me about the wondrous, enlightened, luminous emptiness of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas?"
When will mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever appear again? You must know that the Buddha is like one who removes a cataract, while you are like those waiting for flowers [to appear].

Once you realize that the void originally has no flowers and that it was only through deluded vision that birth and death arose, you will understand that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning;
there has never been delusion or enlightenment. To cling to the Buddha as being truly existent, and to seek to extinguish the false to realize the true, is already a perversion.
How much more so when one further awaits the Buddha? If the false arises from the true, then what difference is there between this and that which further gives rise to the flowers of waiting?
△ Second, the analogy that the true does not change again.
Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold—[the passage continues] up to "bodhi and nirvāṇa are also like this.
This clarifies the meaning that once one has realized the Truth, there is no longer any delusion. Therefore, it is illustrated by the following analogy:
"It is as if gold exists within ore, and ore is mixed with gold. At that time, the two substances are blended together, and the refined gold cannot be distinguished. If...
As for that mineral gold: once it encounters the fire of a furnace and undergoes smelting, it becomes pure gold, no longer mixed with ore.
It is like a tree that has been burned to ashes; once it has become ash, it can never again become a tree.
If one were to seek ore within gold or seek wood within ash, would this not be erroneous? This is by way of the analogy of gold.
The metaphor for the merit of bodhi-wisdom is its immutability, comparable to pure gold that is not mixed with ore or soil.
Once bodhi is attained, afflictions no longer arise again, just as refined gold cannot once more become ore. Ashes serve as a metaphor for the merit of nirvāṇa’s cessation and non-arising;
thus they are like wood-ash. Having entered nirvāṇa, one does not sink back into the cycle of birth and death again.
It is just as wood ash can never again become wood. Therefore it is said, "it is likewise.

These two chapters clarify that while the former explains how delusion is fundamentally unarisen and thus unrelated to attaining Buddhahood, this latter section clarifies that the true source is immutable;
how could one hope for Buddhahood to arise anew? Although the four preceding metaphors each differ, they all reveal [the same truth].
Once awakened, one shall never again fall into delusion.

△ Second, refuting the doubt regarding the perfect interfusion of the great nature (in two parts): First, directly refuting the doubt; second, clarifying nature and characteristics through a metaphor.
(First, citing the doubt and presenting the metaphor.)

Pūrṇa, as for your question regarding earth, water, fire, and wind—up to "why do you further ask about their mutual non-inclusivity"—this is because you, Maitreya, have not yet realized that the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) manifests according to karma.

Therefore, previously you raised questions concerning the continuity of various phenomena and the perfect fusion of the great elements. Since the former [section] has already refuted their continuity, this section shall now refute their perfect fusion as well.
Because they are fused, I shall cite their words to resolve the difficulty regarding their mutual non-overpowering and non-containment. My intention is this:

you previously asked how it is that the two natures of water and fire do not overpower or extinguish one another, given that earth, water, fire, and wind are all-fusing and all-pervasive; furthermore, you questioned the relationship between space and the great earth.
Their natures are distinct; they cannot coexist. How, then, can both be all-pervasive? Now I shall clarify this for you through an analogy.
It is like empty space: vast and boundless, open and unfathomable; it can only be designated by name, for no object can serve as its equal.
Therefore, its essence is not identical to the various characteristics; yet it does not reject those characteristics either, allowing them to manifest as they may.
Thus, when the sun shines upon the sky, it manifests the characteristic of brightness; when clouds gather in the sky, it manifests the characteristic of darkness;
when the wind blows and sways, it manifests the characteristic of motion; and when the sky is clear and serene, it manifests the characteristic of purity.
When the yin energy coalesces, it manifests the appearance of turbidity; when wind and soil accumulate together, it manifests the appearance of gloom;
when the light of water is clear and transparent, it manifests the appearance of reflection.

Thus, in each case, whether bright or dark, clear or turbid, moving or obscured by gloom and reflection—all these conditioned phenomena—are they produced because of the sun and other such factors, or rather because of empty space?
Yet it exists of its own accord. If you claim that this [space] arises dependent upon those [conditions], let us for now take the sun as one example to illustrate the exclusion of the other six.

When the sun shines upon the sky, since it is the light of the sun, then all the empty space throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whenever there is a place of illumination—is of the same solar color; thus, the entire world should become filled with a single [solar] form.
Regarding the substance of the sun: how could one see a bright, round sun like a basin or a bowl within the sky?
Since a round sun is seen, there must be a luminous appearance beyond the substance of the sun that does not belong to the sun itself; it must naturally belong to space.

How can it be said that light arises because of the sun? If you claim that this appearance of light is not produced by the sun but exists inherently within space, then since space is ever-present, light should be constantly illuminating. Why, then, is there darkness at midnight amidst heavy clouds and black mist?
When there is no sun, one perceives only the appearance of darkness; does light not arise?

You should know that this brightness belongs neither to the sun nor to space, yet it is not different from space, nor is it different from the sun. If this single characteristic is thus, so too are the six characteristics.
Therefore, you should know that when the primary elements are examined according to their own characteristics, they are fundamentally and originally false, just as [the following].

The appearance of light is neither sun nor sky; it cannot be pointed out or described. If one were to falsely claim that it can be pointed out or described, it would be like grasping at flowers in the sky and believing them to be real—an act of delusion.
To further interrogate its characteristics regarding their mutual sublation and extinction would be even more so.
This is like seeking to retain empty flowers while expecting them to further produce empty fruit; it may be called the most deluded among the deluded.

If one contemplates the original, fundamental truth through the self-nature of the great elements, it is just like the appearance of light, no different from the sun in the sky—it is solely the wondrously enlightened mind of the Tathāgata-garbha nature. Yet, as for this wondrous mind:
It is originally self-awakened; it is originally self-luminous. It is the singular essence of the treasury, fundamentally not water, fire, empty space, or the great earth.
Why do you not know this, yet still ask me whether these things do not mutually sublate one another but rather coexist?
△ Second, applying the Dharma to the analogy:
"The true, wondrous, awakened clarity is also like this" (up to) "...revolving in delusion with nothing to rely upon.
This applies the Dharma to the analogy to clarify in detail the characteristics of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*): they are none other than the *tathāgatagarbha* nature following karma.
This is the discovery. The meaning is that you have hitherto known only that deluded awareness can be luminous, yet you were fundamentally unaware of the true awareness that is wondrously luminous.
This true awareness, wondrously luminous, is precisely the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Nevertheless, it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognition, manifesting in accordance with their karma.
Manifestation is like space: its essence is not comprised of manifold characteristics, yet it does not obstruct them. It is the same for the manifestation of all phenomena.
This is the general application of the analogy of space to clarify that the fundamental reality of the nature of contemplation is solely wondrous enlightened clarity.
What follows is the specific application regarding the manifestation of various phenomena; the intent is to say that even if your mind were to take emptiness as...
If you illuminate it through the characteristics [of the elements], then the Tathāgatagarbha, responding to the karmic conditions, will appear as emptiness within your mind.
Even if you were to illuminate it individually through earth, water, fire, or wind, the Tathāgatagarbha, responding to the karmic conditions, would appear within your mind in each respective form.
If you were to illuminate it by means of all seven elements together, the Tathāgatagarbha, responding to the karmic conditions, would likewise appear within your mind.

Then they both appear together; this precisely accords with the analogy. Just as when the sun shines upon the great void, it becomes bright (and so forth), until the water becomes clear and reflective—how can one say that these two appear together? It is like the case of a single body of water.
The reflection of the sun appears within it. At that time, there are two people who both look at the sun in the water together.
However, these two people go their separate ways, one toward the east and one toward the west; thus, each sees a sun following after them.
The one traveling east says the sun follows him to the east, while the one traveling west says the sun follows him to the west.
Thus, this reflection of the sun has no fixed standard from the outset; it is fundamentally not real, as can be easily inferred. This precisely accords with the analogy. What do you think?

In such a case of different locations (and so forth), up to the point where no radiance is produced—it should not be further objected that "this water and the sun's reflection are originally one and the same; why is it that two people [see them] in the east... and so on.
As each person walks toward the west, they each perceive the sun following them as they go. Since there are already two suns, how could there be a reflection of a single sun appearing in the water?
This precisely accords with the analogy. One should know that this light is neither the sun nor the sky, yet it is not different from the sky and the sun.
For this reason, when one investigates and analyzes thoroughly, it is found to be fundamentally illusory, entirely lacking any real trace. It may serve as...
This is precisely what is meant by the statement that the so-called "observing of appearances" is fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out or described.

△ Second, the correct elucidation of nature and appearance (in three parts): First, distinguishing nature and appearance through delusion and awakening; (Second, one part: Elucidating that delusion is itself worldly appearance.
"Pūrṇa, because you allow the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and supplant one another, you give rise to the dust of affliction and the appearances of the world.
This [passage] distinguishes between nature and characteristics through the lens of delusion and enlightenment;

it is intended to prevent Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra from thinking that since the Tathāgatagarbha-nature is inherently pure, perfectly interfused, and unobstructed—without one subduing or extinguishing the other—how is it that the world currently appears before us?"
Why is it that they mutually oppress one another and encounter obstacles? Therefore, before these conditions had even sprouted, the Buddha showed them this, saying:
"Pūrṇa, this mutual oppression and mutual obstruction—what else could it be? It is truly because you all are deluded regarding the nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna)."
As fundamental ignorance remains unbroken, the dualistic perception of form and emptiness is difficult to forget.
Consequently, one discriminates between form and emptiness, causing them to compete with and usurp one another within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha follows defiled conditions and manifests according to karma as form or as emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm like the great void, yet without rejecting those various phenomena.

They manifest and interact with one another. Therefore, within this, false perceptions arise, appearing as if there were mutual differences between the movement of wind and the clarity of space, or the brightness of the sun and the darkness of clouds, which clash so violently that earth and space become obstructive to one another. When water and fire contend, worldly afflictions fill the eyes and hindrances crowd before one.
All these faults stem from being deluded regarding the nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) and being stifled by ignorance (avidyā). At this point—
The fundamentally existing awakened nature is contrary to it, yet one turns away from it; the illusory appearances of sensory objects are not conjoined with it, yet one joins with them.
For this reason, worldly toil and afflictions are aroused, resulting in the phenomena of the world such as form and emptiness, water and fire.
Thus, the complete nature becomes phenomenal form, and through movement, it comes to be obstructed by barriers.
△ Second, revealing that awakening is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*.
"By means of my wondrous clarity, which is neither extinguished nor born" (up to) "...therefore I give rise to the wondrously enlightened nature of *tathatā*.
This is the Tathāgata’s own self-praise and self-proclamation, clarifying the reason for the perfect fusion and non-obstruction [of the three natures]. The meaning is as follows:
The reason I have attained this perfect interfusion and non-obstruction is that it could not have been through any other method;

it is none other than having awakened to the truly wondrous, enlightened clarity—the eternally abiding true mind that neither perishes nor arises—and thereby harmonizing with the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha, following pure conditions, becomes solely a single body of wondrous enlightenment and clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm.
For this reason, within it, the one and the many are unimpeded, and the small and the large are mutually contained; therefore, it manifests as one.

This is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature manifesting as the immeasurable. This is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature manifesting as the small. This is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature manifesting as the large. This is...
The nature of the treasury is the site of enlightenment; it is the world of the nature of the treasury; it is the physical form of the nature of the treasury;
it is the space of the nature of the treasury; it is the tip of a hair of the nature of the treasury; it is the jewel-adorned land of the nature of the treasury;

it is the atom of the nature of the treasury; it is the wheel of Dharma of the nature of the treasury. Because it is the nature of the treasury, each and every manifestation does not become diminished.
Manifesting immeasurable and immeasurable [forms], yet they are not many; even when seated upon a single mote of dust, that mote of dust is not constricted.
Pervading the ten directions, yet the ten directions are not expansive. Why is this so? It is entirely because the Tathāgata has realized that motes of dust are not dust.

He speaks of extinction from within non-extinction; he understands that motes of dust are themselves awakening. He speaks of conjunction in a place where there is no conjunction. For this reason, he brings forth [this manifestation].

The suchness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-tathatā*). Thus, whether one or many, small or large—even down to the bodies and minds, the worlds, the jewel lands, and the atoms of dust—there is nothing that is not my wondrously enlightened and luminous nature. This is because the entirety of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself the nature;

therefore, it attains perfect fusion and non-obstruction. If we follow the perspective of Qingliang, there are six types of non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).

The phrases are as follows: first, based on internal manifestation; second, correctly internal manifestation correct; third, correctly internal manifestation based; fourth, based on internal manifestation correct;

fifth, based on internal manifestation based-correct; sixth, correctly internal manifestation based-correct. These may be inferred by analogy; therefore, I shall not trouble you with further elaboration.
△ Second, the correct demonstration of the perfect interfusion that reveals the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* (in three parts). First, the correct demonstration of the nature of the empty *garbha*:
"The *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally the wondrous, perfect, and circular mind" (up to) "because it is neither mundane nor supramundane."
This perfect interfusion correctly points to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. One name encompasses three meanings, serving as the entire substance and great function of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
This is because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha possesses a substance that remains unchanging while following conditions.
There is the function of the unchanging following conditions, which, by following the causes of delusion and enlightenment, forms the conditions of defilement and purity.
Following the conditions of delusion, there are the six realms of ordinary beings and their defiled dharmas, like water forming ice.

Following the conditions of enlightenment, there are the four classes of noble ones and their pure dharmas, like ice returning to water. Although ice and water differ, they share the same nature of moisture; thus, these three chapters [are presented].
This clearly elucidates the meaning. Herein, we first reveal the fundamental essence of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which remains unchanging while following conditions.

Although this garbha-nature manifests the two aspects of defilement and purity by following the two conditions of delusion and enlightenment, the mind of the Tathāgatagarbha is from the beginning primordially subtle, perfectly complete, eternally abiding, without deficiency or lack, neither ceasing nor arising, and pure.
It is pure by its very nature; it is fundamentally neither the conscious mind nor vacuous emptiness.

The seven elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as well as the eighteen realms and three categories of sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses, are likewise not the dharmas of the mundane world. By contemplating this, one knows that it is not a worldly phenomenon.
It is neither illumination nor ignorance; it is the exhaustion of both illumination and ignorance. And so on, up to: it is not the exhaustion of old age and death.
This is not the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas regarding the circulation and cessation [of dependent origination]. It is not suffering or its origin, up to and including neither wisdom nor attainment.
This is not that which belongs to the two vehicles—the Śrāvakas—nor the mundane and supramundane Four Noble Truths, the four fruits, or even the wisdom capable of emptying them.
This is the principle [of suchness]. It is not *dāna*, nor even up to *pāramitā*.
This is not the dharma of the six perfections of a bodhisattva—giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—which reach the other shore.
By observing this, one knows it is not a supramundane dharma. Thus, it continues up to: it is not the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha...

These three designations do not refer to the four virtues of Great Nirvana—permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Observing this, one knows that they also do not refer to the supreme supramundane Dharma.

Because it is neither a mundane dharma, nor a supramundane dharma, nor a supreme supramundane dharma—since it is non-existent in all three respects—it is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha. This clarifies the Tathāgata...

Regarding the meaning of "emptiness in reality": the reason the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not mentioned in the text is that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) subsume the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), while the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) subsumes the latter four aggregates;
therefore, they are not treated separately.
△ Second, it further demonstrates the nature of non-emptiness:
"That is, the Tathāgatagarbha is the primordial luminosity of the wondrous mind" (up to) "...because these are both mundane and supramundane.
This reveals the wondrous function of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which remains immutable while conforming to conditions. [This is] because the substance of the Tathāgatagarbha...

Although it is unchanging, its wondrous function accords with conditions; thus, it can respond to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition and manifest in accordance with their karma.

Therefore, regarding all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds, when one contemplates their appearances, they are fundamentally illusory, but when one contemplates their nature, it is fundamentally true.
Thus, one knows that this is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha mind, which is fundamentally and originally luminous. It is without...
Delusion has no awakening; from the very beginning, the source is inherently wondrous. It is neither defiled nor pure.

For this reason, it is precisely the dharmas of the seven elements and three aggregates of the mundane world; it is precisely the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas that transcend the world;

and it is precisely the dharmas of the three titles and four virtues within the stage of the Buddha-fruit, which transcends the world beyond the world. Because of this, the worldly dharmas are themselves...
The supramundane dharmas are themselves the supreme-supramundane dharmas; because these three are identical, it is called the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
This clarifies the meaning of the "non-emptiness" of reality as it truly is.
△ Third, the perfect demonstration of the nature of both emptiness and non-emptiness:
that is, the wondrously luminous fundamental mind of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither identical nor different, and is both identical and not identical.

This precisely and perfectly reveals the entire substance and great function of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging.

Based on the principle that essence and function are non-dual and stillness and illumination are mutually integrated, it is clarified that the Tathāgatagarbha is neither "all" nor "not all," yet is both "all" and "not all," ultimately transcending both identity and difference. Thus, being both "is" and "is not" is extinguished;
this is why it is the primordial source of the wondrously luminous true mind. Because it belongs neither to "is" nor to "is not," it is said:
"Detached from both 'is' and 'is not'": this refers to the perfect interfusion and dual quiescence. Furthermore, it is not detached from "is," nor is it detached from "is not.
Therefore, it is said: "This is both 'is' and 'is not. This phrase should be understood by carrying the character "is" (是) through to the subsequent clause;

only then will the meaning become fully clear. This precisely elucidates the perfect interfusion and dual illumination. Because it is both dual-quiescent and dual-illuminating, it is called "empty and non-empty."

This is the Tathāgatagarbha. This clarifies the meaning of being empty yet not empty according to reality. If one were to explain the Tathāgatagarbha solely by means of "not being all dharmas," one would stagnate in emptiness.
If one were to explain the Tathāgatagarbha merely by means of "being identical with all dharmas," one would again stagnate in existence.
However, if one explains the Tathāgatagarbha by means of "neither departing from identity nor departing from non-identity," then one abandons the two extremes.

To be attached to the Middle Way—whether by asserting that "this is it" or "this is not it"—is to clarify the *tathāgatagarbha* while abandoning the Middle Way, thereby remaining stuck in the two extremes.
One must understand that within this Middle Way, there is total non-identity yet identity, total identity yet non-identity;

it is separate yet not separate, and not separate yet separate. This is precisely the severing of both ends so that the middle remains unestablished, thereby transcending words and cutting off all conceptualization.
This refers to the perfectly interfused and subtle true mind. It is precisely what was previously called "the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity.
Furthermore, this true mind is the very substance and function of the Great Buddha’s Crown Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

For this reason, this samādhi is able to encompass the three types of cessation (*śamatha*), subsume the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and include the *śamatha* of the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
The third name is "The Dharma Gate of Universal Characteristics. Because this is the samādhi inherently possessed by the self-nature *tathatā*, it is called "Perfect" (*yuan*) and "Sublime" (*miao*);
it is for this reason. Thus, the title refers to this when it says "The Great Buddha-Crown"; it points to this.

When it says "The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization," it refers to the realization of this; when it says "The Myriad Practices Cultivated by All Bodhisattvas," it refers to the cultivation of this.
All sentient beings who are deluded are deluded regarding this. As stated in the preceding three fascicles, those who give rise to faith believe in this;
those who subsequently attain understanding comprehend this; and that which the practitioners in the assembly are confused about is precisely this.
That which Pūrṇa doubts is this; that which the Tathāgata reveals is this. This refers to the text spanning six and a half fascicles below.
The "celestial king’s flowered mansion" is a metaphor for this. Pointing to the perfect penetration and clarifying the primary and auxiliary practices is the cultivation of this.
The transformation of sentient beings and the realization of the stages of sainthood is the verification of this. Therefore, I have composed this commentary here.
This is why various schools do not separately list the three contemplations. It is as the Buddha himself said:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices; it is that which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions call 'surpassing through a single gate.
This refers precisely to this. Regarding the first of the three preceding chapters, it says: "The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind..."

"Body" refers to the essence (*tī*). Next, "primordial luminosity" (*yuánmíng*) refers to the mind’s wondrous self-functioning. Here, "wondrous luminosity" (*miàomíng*) refers to the mind’s primordial essence as the union of essence and function.
△ Third, exhorting progress in cultivation through dharma and analogy.
"How do the sentient beings within the three realms of existence (up to) cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a little attainment sufficient?
This passage universally rebukes delusions and stagnations regarding both the Dharma and its metaphors, urging one toward authentic cultivation.

The intent is that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha consists of three names for a single essence; speaking of three, it is one, and being one, it is three—neither vertical nor horizontal, like the sky.
The King’s eye neither unifies nor differentiates; its form is like that of Brahmā. It transcends the paths of mind and speech, subtle and inconceivable.

How could the sentient beings within the three realms of existence—desire, form, and formlessness—as well as the minor sages of the two vehicles, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have transcended the world, possibly fathom it through their respective objects of knowledge and their knowing minds?
How could it be the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realization of unsurpassed bodhicitta? How much less so when one uses the discriminating consciousness and worldly language to inquire about it?

To claim that mountains and rivers suddenly arise, or that they mutually obstruct and perish, and to cling to such false conceptualizations as being capable of entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision—is this not utterly erroneous? Indeed, your bodies are like lutes.
The musical instruments of the *śīrṣaka-vīṇā* and *kōng-hóu*—your minds are just like the sounds within these instruments.
Although the sounds exist, if there are no fingers, they can never be produced. Just so, although the *tathāgatagarbha* nature exists, if there is no *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, one can never realize it.
Thus we know that "wondrous sound" refers to the wondrous mind; the "wondrous fingers" refer to the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
This refers to wondrous concentration (*samādhi*). Without wondrous concentration, your wondrous mind will ultimately never be awakened.
Therefore, it is said that you and all sentient beings alike possess this mind; it is just like the sound of those lutes and other instruments—it is likewise so.
Although the precious awakened true mind is inherently possessed by everyone, and each person lacks nothing as it is perfectly complete,
without deficiency or impairment, yet because one does not possess this samādhi, one ultimately cannot awaken to it— this is truly a pity.
Since I have realized this wondrous samādhi and awakened to this treasury-mind, the moment I press my finger, it immediately becomes the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, emitting a great light.

"O Bright Ones! You lack this wondrous samādhi and are deluded regarding this true mind. Therefore, as soon as you raise your minds for a moment, worldly afflictions arise, and your former obstructions immediately reappear.
Is this not because you lack the wondrous pointing-out and thus fail to produce the wondrous sound?
Is it not because you lack the wondrous samādhi and thus fail to awaken to the wondrous mind? Although you all possess this mind, you are unable to attain its full realization."
As for the reason why its essence is great yet its function is limited, it is truly because their faculties are subtle and their aspirations are inferior;
they are unwilling to diligently seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, but instead merely cherish and cling to the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna.

They consider themselves satisfied with having obtained only a small portion of the Buddha-dharma. "Qin" means "to restrain"; it refers to restraining all that is deviant in order to establish what is correct.
It is the mind of man. If one follows the ancient construction, it is three chi and six cun in length, symbolizing the three hundred and sixty days [of the year].
It employs twelve [frets] to represent the twelve pitch-pipes (*lǜ*). There remains one additional fret to symbolize the ruler;

thus, it is circular at the top and square at the bottom, following the patterns of Heaven and Earth. However, it originally has only five strings to clarify the five musical tones. This is why Emperor Shun played it.

There was a five-stringed *qín* lute upon which the verses of the "Southern Wind" (*Nánfēng*) were sung. By the time of the Zhou dynasty, King Wen and King Wu each added one string, so that there were seven in total.
The largest string represented the ruler, being broad, harmonious, and warm; the smallest string represented the minister.
It is clear and pure; this embodies the virtue of both ruler and minister. As for the *se*, it signifies density and compactness.

Regarding the twenty-five strings, as for the *konghou*, according to the *Baihutong* (Explanations According to the White Tiger Hall), Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty commissioned the court musicians Hou Hui and Hou Tiao to create it.
Its sound was "kan-kan," yet it responded to the musical rhythm; therefore, it was called *Kanhou*.
Later, it was eventually corrupted and called *kōng hóu* (箜篌). The character *hóu* (候) was derived from the name of that particular musician.
Some say that for instruments such as the *qín*, *sè*, and *Qin-zhēng*, the distance between the strings and the wood is all less than an inch;

only for the *kōng hóu* are the strings and the wood far apart, with the sound emerging from the void (*kōng*). The name *Kōng-hóu* may have been established for this reason. It now has fourteen strings.
As for these two characters, it is said that they do not necessarily require the "bamboo" (竹) radical; however, fearing this may not be certain, I have retained them here for future investigation.
Regarding the *pipa*: pushing the hand forward is called *pi*, while withdrawing the hand backward is called *ba*. It possesses sounds produced by striking, plucking, hooking, and picking.
As for the four-stringed version of today, it originated when a princess was sent during the Han dynasty to marry the Kunmi king of the Wusun.

Reflecting on his long journey, fearing that he might harbor thoughts of his native land and remain unable to escape the sorrow of separation, [the Emperor] commissioned skilled musicians to expertly craft the *zither* (*zheng*) and *dun* (*zhu*) for the pleasure of travel, intending to provide him with diversion along the way. Regarding the "Ocean Seal" (*haiyin*):
the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that all forms and images within Jambudvīpa are like the ocean, each bearing an impression; this is analogous to the nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
The ocean universally manifests all mundane and supramundane phenomena, both defiled and pure.
△ Second, further explaining the resolution of the objection (in two parts): First, Pūrṇa accepts the question.
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata... [have] obscured our own wondrous clarity and thus suffered this immersion.
Thus, Pūrṇa (Maimayi) took up what had been previously stated and asked again: "The cause of delusion is desire; one seeks the True by extinguishing the delusive."
"I and the Tathāgata" below refers to the preceding meaning that the precious awakened true mind is fully perfected in each and every one.

"In the past, when I encountered" below refers to the preceding meaning from "establishing the reason through the luminosity of the cause" up to "the three types of continuity where the great elements mutually oppress one another."
Now that one has attained the Noble Vehicle, it is still not yet ultimate. This summarizes the previous meaning of being satisfied with a small attainment due to attachment to the Lesser Vehicle.

That all delusions are perfectly extinguished summarizes the previous four metaphors as well as the meaning that the characteristics of contemplation are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out.

"Exclusively wondrous, true, and eternal" summarizes the meaning of the preceding contemplation on the nature of the mind as fundamentally true, solely wondrously enlightened and luminous, and the perfect fusion of the three aspects of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
From "I venture to ask" below, he formally inquires into the cause of the arising of delusion;

the intent is that we followers of the Hīnayāna know only the six consciousnesses and the three poisons as the basis for establishing defilement and purity, and thus have not yet [realized] the *dharmatā*.
Having reached this conclusion, I do not yet know the cause of this delusion; from what does it further arise? I venture to ask the Tathāgata:
for what reason do all sentient beings possess this cause of delusion, whereby they lose their own precious awareness and obscure its wondrously luminous function?
Having lost both this essence and its function, why do they undergo this continuous immersion in the cycle of birth and death? This is due to my previous question.
The Buddha replied that they arise due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, [the interlocutor] asks again:
"From what does this ignorance itself arise? This is precisely a question that exhaustively seeks the ultimate source.
△ II. The Tathāgata’s Definitive Response (II) 1. Clarifying that Delusion is Fundamentally Without Cause.
The Buddha addressed Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts... [the nature of delusion is thus]; for what reason does it exist?"

This arose because Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra asked how delusion could have a cause, noting that the World-Honored One had stated that all delusions are completely extinguished and that only the wondrous, true, and eternal remains.

This seemed to imply that there was a cause for delusion and that delusion could be extinguished. Therefore, the Buddha told him that delusion fundamentally has no cause, in order to eliminate his doubt regarding the extinction of delusion and the pursuit of truth.
His intention was to convey that although you have heard it said that one should contemplate appearances...
Fundamental delusion cannot be pointed out or described. When one contemplates that the nature is fundamentally true, there is only wondrous, enlightened clarity;

thus, the delusions regarding the arising and continuity of the myriad dharmas and the doubts concerning the mutual containment of the great elements have already been eliminated. Nevertheless, residual delusions remain, and one has not yet realized that this ignorance is without cause;
therefore, one forcibly seeks it out in an attempt to extinguish it. One must know that delusion is fundamentally without cause, and furthermore—
There is no such thing as extinction. Even if you do not yet understand this clearly, I shall now question you again regarding a matter before your eyes;

try to explain it, and you will naturally see it for yourself. Have you not heard of the incident in the city of Śrāvastī, where the youth Yaśoda looked into a mirror at dawn, became terrified of his own reflection, and ran about wildly like a shapeless demon? At that time—
"What do you think? This person’s head is originally present, yet he reproaches himself for having no head;
he was originally not a *chīmèi* (a mountain sprite), yet he calls himself one. What is the cause of this? From what does it arise? Should he not be running about madly without reason?
When the Venerable One was thus questioned by the Buddha, he immediately understood clearly and replied: "This person is merely his own mind..."

He was deranged; his aimless wandering was due to nothing else. What cause could there be for this? One must understand that while the Venerable One understood the parable, he remained confused regarding the Dharma.
Therefore, the Buddha took the point at which he had attained understanding and used it to clarify the essential meaning of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that this wondrously enlightened, perfectly luminous mind is equally possessed by Buddhas and sentient beings alike. As for its essence, it is fundamentally complete;
as for its function, it is fundamentally luminous and wondrous, inherently pure and natural. From the beginning, there is neither reality nor delusion.
Since you have already labeled it "false and illusory," how can you seek for it a real cause? If it were truly and substantially existent, [it would not be called false].
That which serves as the cause is itself the reality. How, then, can it be called delusion? If one investigates its cause, it is originally that the mind gives rise to various false thoughts;

these thoughts arise from one another in succession, having no substantial essence from the start. It all originates from a single moment of confusion, where confusion accumulates upon confusion throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes.
Thus, the habits have become deep and the tendencies thick; even though one may hear the Buddha’s various teachings, [one remains bound].
Though enlightened, you remain thus deluded and unable to turn back; you continue to seek a false cause.
How could you know that such a cause for delusion arises from the delusion of one's own mind? It seems as if it exists, yet in reality it is fundamentally empty.

If you can simply realize that the arising of delusion has no cause, then your discursive thoughts will have nothing upon which to rely. From this, you should know that even ignorance and discursive thought are likewise [empty].
There is no cause capable of producing it; what, then, would one wish to grasp? What delusion would one seek to extinguish as something produced?
Therefore, for one who attains Bodhi, there is nothing other than the realization that delusion is fundamentally without cause, and thus their task is complete.
How could there be a "causeless cause" to be shown to others? It is just like a person who has awakened recounting the events of a dream; even if the mind [continues to function],...
"Though you are clever and discerning, for what reason would you wish to take those objects within a dream and show them to others?
Yet, even though the objects of a dream seem vaguely present as if they could be grasped, they cannot be taken;

how much less so for these delusive thoughts, which from the beginning have no cause and fundamentally do not exist? How could one possibly find a cause for them when attempting to explain it? Thus [he spoke of] this delusion.
It is without cause. It is like that man in the city, Yan Rudata, who, resembling one possessed by madness, fled in terror from his own head.
How could there be any causal conditions? No one taught him to run madly, nor was there any madness inherent in his head from the beginning.
One need only cease this madness to realize that this head is not obtained from without. Even if you have not ceased your madness, the head remains as it is;
what loss could there be? Pūrṇa, your deluded thoughts and the mad nature of Rāhula are just like this.
They are fundamentally without cause; how can you vainly seek them, wishing to extinguish them as if they were something existing somewhere?
Yes. Yan-rudatuo (Yajñadatta) is translated as "Obtained from a Shrine" because he was obtained through a request made at a spirit shrine.
Chi refers to a monster of the mountains and marshes; it is a mountain deity with the form of a tiger. Mei refers to the deity of a residence;
it has the head of a pig and the body of a human. Both belong to the class of ghosts.
△ Second, revealing that the true is not obtained through acquisition:
"You need only not follow after the discrimination of the world... [until] you will realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
This clarifies that not only is the false cause fundamentally non-existent, but even when one awakens to it, the truth is not something separate that exists elsewhere. The meaning is this: you...
Seeking after delusion is merely a means to seek the truth. It is simply a matter of resting the mind; there is no other method.

If one can thoroughly understand that worldly karma and its fruits, as well as the threefold continuity of sentient beings, are like eyebrows and eyes reflected in a mirror—originally not truly existent, yet appearing to exist through delusion—then by investigating this delusive thought, one finds that even delusion has no cause. Thus, one will naturally no longer follow the world.
One falsely gives rise to discrimination regarding the three—realms and so forth. When this mind comes to rest for even a moment, the conditions for the arising of these three are suddenly severed;
thus, the continuity of the three types of phenomena has no further cause from this point on. This is what is meant by "the tree falls and the roots are cut," such that they will never grow again.
This is called the natural subsiding of the madness of the *Rāvaṇa* within your own mind.
If one can truly act in this way, then at that very moment, it is precisely the original *tathāgatagarbha*, the bodhi-mind of true suchness.
Upon reaching this state, one finally realizes that one’s own nature is inherently sublime, inherently pure, and inherently luminous;
that it is primordially pure and naturally pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. It is originally one's own true mind, not something obtained from another through artifice. By virtue of this—
Observe this: what need is there for the toil and hardship of scriptural study? What use is there for the cultivation and realization of the knotty and difficult?

This principle is just like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within their own garment, yet remains in a state of confusion, neither perceiving nor knowing it, while wandering abroad in poverty and exposure, running about begging for food. Although they suffer such distress, they are in truth destitute. Furthermore—
He rejoiced that his pearl had never been lost. Suddenly, by a stroke of fortune, he encountered a wise person who pointed it out within his garment and showed him the precious gem.
Thus, all the aspirations of his life were fulfilled according to his heart's desire. Having obtained this rare treasure, he attained great wealth and abundance.
Only upon reaching this point did he realize that such a divine pearl was merely an old object already within his own clothing—namely, his very self.
The family treasure is inherently possessed; it is not something obtained from others. "Ken" refers to the joints between flesh and bone, and "qing" refers to the knots of muscle and sinew.
Although these two characters appear in the "Nourishing Life" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, their meaning here is actually different.
This passage takes the sense of not requiring the laboring of sinews or the suffering of bones. The Wise One showed the pearl as a metaphor for the Tathāgata.

He reveals the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha). However, the analogy of the jewel herein differs from that in the *Lotus Sūtra*; that sūtra refers to the planting of seeds through past connections, whereas this refers to what is inherently present—thus, their meanings are distinct.
△ Second, showing this concurrently to Ānanda (in two parts): First, Ānanda raises a question based on what preceded.
At that time, while Ānanda was among the great assembly... [until] "I only pray that you will, out of great compassion, reveal and clarify my confusion."

This is precisely the third instance where the interlocutor seizes upon the Buddha’s words to insist that causes and conditions are real. First, he insisted that the essence of seeing belongs to causes and conditions;
next, he insisted that all phenomena belong to causes and conditions; now, he insists that the realization of the fruit belongs to causes and conditions.
His intention is to say: "The Tathāgata has utterly rejected causes and conditions toward me; how can he now turn to me and speak of causes and conditions again? As for this...
The preceding text states: "By these causes and conditions, the world continues; by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue;
by these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue. Yet, when one investigates these causes and conditions to their root, it says:

"Awakened clarity and the dullness of emptiness interact to produce agitation," and so forth, as the causes and conditions for the world. This delusion of clarity is not from another source; the fault lies in awakened clarity itself.
...and so forth. Craving for sensual desire serves as the causal condition for sentient beings; craving for killing and craving for stealing serve as the causal conditions for the fruits of karma.

Now, it is further said: "If you simply allow the mind to rest and do not follow after discursive thought, then the threefold continuity of the world, sentient beings, and the fruits of karma will be suddenly severed.
Thus, the karmic causes of the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—"
They do not arise. When the enlightened mind comes to rest, delusions do not arise; when madness ceases, Bodhi manifests.
Thus, the explanations of causes and conditions are perfectly clear and evident. Why, then, would the Tathāgata first speak of causes and conditions and then suddenly discard them?
Furthermore, by means of these causes and conditions, our minds have attained awakening.

Indeed, as for the significance of these causes and conditions, how could they apply only to us young students who rely upon them to enter the Path? It is the same for those such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana within this assembly.

Although he initially practiced heterodox paths alongside the old brahmin, it was only because he encountered Upāli and others along the way and heard their exposition of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing and dependent origination that he was able to attain awakening. Only thereafter did he see the Buddha and achieve the fruit of sainthood.
Now you say, "The nature of madness subsides of its own accord; this subsiding is itself bodhi, requiring no dependence on causes and conditions. If this were so, then as for those outsiders—

The doctrine taught by those such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa—that after eighty thousand kalpas one spontaneously attains the Way, like a ball of thread that stops when it reaches its end, without depending on cultivation or realization—turns out to be the primary truth (paramārtha-satya).

Even if the Tathāgata does not fall into the realm of causes and conditions, he would still fall into the trap of spontaneity (svabhāva). This is precisely what we find bewildering and cannot understand.
I only hope that the Tathāgata will bestow great compassion, dispel my confusion and distress, and bring forth illumination for me.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s refutation of doubts and his exhortation (in two parts): First, the refutation of doubts; (in two parts) First, the refutation by means of the analogy itself.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Just as within the city... [up to] both 'causality' (*hetu-pratyaya*) and 'spontaneity' (*svabhāva*) are merely conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
This pair refutes both causality and spontaneity. The Buddha said: "Regarding what you have doubted—namely, causality and spontaneity..."
For now, let us temporarily employ the previous analogy to refute this. Suppose, for instance, that the causes and conditions for Yajñadatta’s madness were to be extinguished;

then his non-mad state would naturally emerge. Therefore, your insistence that this [non-madness] does not belong to causes and conditions, but rather belongs to spontaneity (*svabhāva*), is exhausted in these two paths alone. Thus, you remain unaware of the truth.
This is not yet the case. If you claim that Pūrṇa’s head is inherently natural (*prakṛti*), then it should be inherently eternal.

Yet, both his madness and his sanity are nothing other than natural; for what cause and what condition could there be such that, because of looking into a mirror, he suddenly became terrified at being headless and ran about in a frenzy?
There must certainly be a cause for this, and thus it is clear that the head is not inherently natural. If you say that the head...
This is its original nature. That one suddenly becomes startled upon the condition of looking into a mirror and runs about madly, thinking they have no head, is due to conditions that are not real.

Why is this so? If the causal conditions were truly existent, why would the head that was originally and naturally present be actually lost because of the condition of looking into a mirror? At the time of such madness, the head has never been lost at all.
When the madness ceases, the head is not something newly acquired; yet while the madness arises and ceases, the head itself has never undergone change.
Originally, there is neither gain nor loss, and it is clear that the head does not depend on the conditions of a mirror for its existence or non-existence.

If you claim that the root of delusion arises spontaneously, then one should have been constantly possessed by madness from the very beginning. One simply does not realize that prior to the onset of madness, this madness was already present.
Regarding the nature of fear: where could it hide so that it does not arise? Since there is no place for madness to hide, it is clear that madness is not spontaneous.
If one claims that the absence of madness is natural, then since the head was originally never lost, one should always remain free from the madness of running about;
why then would one run madly out of fear for the head? Therefore, there must be a cause.

It is not madness, nor is it spontaneous; this is clear. Thus, one should know that not only is the head neither dependent on causes and conditions nor spontaneous, but madness itself is likewise neither dependent on causes and conditions nor spontaneous.
Therefore, one knows that both wondrous enlightenment and ignorance are neither dependent on causes and conditions nor spontaneous.
