You have merely been consistently ignorant of the divine pearl within yourself, seeking food elsewhere while clinging to external conditions.

To cling to the self is something one cannot avoid. However, if you were to awaken to the fact that the original head is neither self nor condition, you would then recognize that this frantic running is likewise so.
Thus, what you grasp as "causes and conditions" or "spontaneity" are both merely the delirious chatter, idle laughter, and playful talk of a dream; they possess no real substance whatsoever.
△ Second, the illustration by means of a dharma analogy.
Therefore, when I say that "because the three conditions are severed" (up to this point), only at this phrase is it called the "dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
Here, the Buddha uses a dharma analogy to correctly reveal the essential purport that "resting is itself bodhi. The meaning is as follows: by...

The two aforementioned [views] are both conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). Therefore, I say that when one attains the three kinds of discernment and their conditions are severed, this very moment is the true mind of bodhi.
Nevertheless, one must by no means conceive of this as "producing" bodhi. Why?
Because if one thinks that the mind of bodhi is produced and the mind of birth-and-death is extinguished, this is merely birth-and-death.
This mind is still not the true mind of bodhi. It is only permitted that when conditions cease, it is bodhicitta;

it is not permitted that bodhicitta arises from the cessation of conditions. This precisely reveals that not only does the mind of arising and ceasing come to an end, but that which extinguishes arising and ceasing is also entirely exhausted.
Upon reaching the eighth stage, one abandons the ālayavijñāna, and the path of non-effort flows spontaneously.
One enters the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). However, it must not be grasped as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

Because the true mind can be so [grasped], if there were a spontaneous arising of the mind and a ceasing of the mind of birth-and-death, then this spontaneity itself would also be subject to birth and death;
it would not be something devoid of birth and death. Why is this so? For example, that which is without birth and death according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is designated as...
This is the natural state. That which arises and ceases within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is called "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya);

it is established through mutual opposition and is not truly without arising and ceasing. It is like worldly objects that, through the blending and combining of various characteristics, form a single entity;
this is called the nature of the harmony of causal conditions. Consequently, one points to that which is not such a harmony and designates it as the "Original."
Regarding the nature of spontaneity (*t'ien-jan*), this spontaneity and that dependent origination (*yin-yüan*) both belong to the realm of duality;

they are equally mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and neither constitutes the ultimate reality. This continues until one reaches the state where "being as-it-is" (*pen-jan*) is not "as-it-is," and "conjunction" (*ho-ho*) is not "conjunction.
One must distance oneself from both conjunction and being-as-it-is; yet even this distancing and this conjunction are both ultimately non-existent. Thus it is.
Only such phrases can be called "correct phrases" and "living phrases"; they are the Dharma that is truly free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

"Separation" (*li*) is neither conjunction nor spontaneity; it is a phrase that simultaneously negates both. "Union" (*he*) is precisely conjunction and precisely spontaneity; it is a phrase that simultaneously illuminates both.
"Neither" (*ju fei*) correctly clarifies that illumination is itself negation and negation is itself illumination; this is why there is negation.
It is not that negation is excluded; illumination is not that illumination. Therefore, it is said that both are negated.
△ Second, the exhortation (in two parts): First, the warning against hearing in vain and achieving no merit.
"Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far away" (up to) "...the river of craving shall dry up, bringing you liberation."
This admonition is not for those who hear it but achieve no merit. It means precisely this:

although the place where the frantic mind ceases is itself Bodhi, one must know that while the principle is realized suddenly (*tunwu*), its realization depends on the gradual removal of phenomena. Between the two paths of nature (*xing*) and cultivation (*xiu*), neither may be neglected.

If cultivation can arise from nature and thus cultivation returns to self-nature, such that nature and cultivation are perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*), only then is it truly real. Otherwise, it is not.
Even if you were able to achieve great penetration and great enlightenment, you would only have clarified the true mind of the causal stage;

as for the awakening of the resultant stage of Bodhi and Nirvana, it would still remain far off. It is not through your arduous toil and diligent practice over kalpas that this true cultivation is realized.
In the end, one will be unable to realize it. Not only will one fail to be able to remember the Dharma I have taught, but it will be in vain and without merit.

Even if one were to memorize and retain the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the scriptures—the nine small and three large [vehicles]—and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, if one does not practice them authentically, it will only increase frivolous proliferation and ultimately lead to nothing.

It has no real efficacy. For instance, although you are able to explain both causality and spontaneity with absolute clarity regarding principle and phenomena, without the slightest error, people thus call you the foremost among disciples in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
Yet, despite this extensive learning accumulated through熏習 (*vāsanā*) over many kalpas, you could not avoid the calamity of the Ḍākinī; from this, one knows that it is not truly existent.

It is clear that true cultivation consists in more than mere hearing; it is useless if there is no actual merit. If mere hearing were sufficient to produce merit, then one would naturally not be swayed by malevolent arts.

Why, then, would it have been necessary for me to preach this Great Buddha-Crown Secret Divine Mantra before Dāṅkā’s lustful fires could suddenly be extinguished, before she could turn from evil to the right, sever her worldly mind, and immediately ascend to the state of a sage?
"Your station within my Buddha-dharma has now become a grove of diligence.
Because that lustful mind has withered away and the river of craving has dried up, I have released you at this critical juncture of birth and death, so that you may wander freely in liberation.
Had it not been for the power of the Tathāgata’s true cultivation and actual realization of meditative concentration, how could I have delivered you from the peril of your Daṅkā? Thus it is known:"
Merely hearing [the teachings] is of no merit; it is not equal to the benefit of genuine cultivation.

Anāgāmin means "one who does not return," so called because they have been able to sever the nine grades of innate afflictions of the desire realm and are thus said to have emerged from the mire of desire.
Because they do not return to take birth in the desire realm, this is the name for the third fruit among the stages of holiness in the Hīnayāna.
△ Second, the exhortation that true cultivation is beneficial:
"Therefore, Ānanda, although you have passed through kalpas... (up to) "...how can you deceive yourself and still linger in viewing and listening?
This is the exhortation to practice. It directly follows the preceding text regarding how mere hearing is fruitless. For this reason, although you have passed through kalpas...

To memorize and recite the secret mantras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for an eon—mantras whose wondrous principles are subtle and rigorous—is not equal to resting the deluded mind for a single day, giving rise to no further discrimination, and suddenly severing the three conditions so that the three causes do not arise.
Only then can it be called true cultivation of untainted karma; thus one will not fall into the dust and toil of birth and death, remaining far removed from the mundane world.
Hating what is different and loving what is similar—these two types of ignorance cause one to undergo the suffering of birth.
This is just like the case of Dengga, who was formerly a courtesan; yet how profound and deep were her karmic obstructions!

Through the unfathomable power of my divine mantra, her lustful mind was extinguished and her craving severed, so that she entered the Buddha-dharma. She is now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlaguptā. Moreover,
Together with Yaśodharā, they simultaneously awakened to their karmic causes from past lives, realizing that all suffering stems from craving and attachment.
From this single thought, they cultivated and diligently practiced the pure, untainted dharmas of the Four Noble Truths regarding arising and ceasing.

For this reason, some attained the third fruit and emerged from the bonds of affliction, while others realized the fourth fruit and received the Buddha’s prediction. These were all women of frail constitution, yet they were still able to achieve such things.
It is thus. Why do you, a dignified man of stature, instead deceive yourself?

You remain attached to what you have seen and heard, stubbornly clinging to worldly causes and conditions, natural frivolous discourse, names, and forms, refusing to let them go. Truly, this is inferior to the understanding of women;
are you not ashamed? To observe the Tathāgata’s ultimate response to the needs of the occasion can be called the pinnacle of perfection.
It is finished. Such bitter words are truly like spears, lances, swords, and halberds; every phrase pierces the bones, and every character startles the heart.
Although the phrasing is one of reproach, the intent is actually one of exhortation. The Sanskrit term *maṇḍagā* means "original nature" (*prakṛti*) in this language.
Now, following her former name, she is called the Bhikṣuṇī Śrī (Nature). Rāhula means "obscuration," and Yaśodharā means "glorious color.
△ Third, the attainment of benefit and the opening of understanding.
When Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha’s instruction, their bodies and minds attained a lightness and tranquility such as they had never experienced before.
This passage describes how the great assembly benefited from hearing the Dharma and thereby achieved awakening and understanding.

For, as previously mentioned, the Buddha’s exposition on causes and conditions and spontaneity was clear and explicit; it inspired them to practice and his exhortations were most earnest and profound. Upon reaching this point—

At this very moment, having attained sudden enlightenment, the doubts regarding causes, conditions, and spontaneity are thereby dissolved; the delusions of frivolous discourse and conceptual names are removed from this point forward.
Only now do you know that where the wild mind ceases is precisely the Bodhi—the supreme, pure, and luminous mind—which is not obtained from another.
Thus, you have clearly realized the true mind and awakened to the reality-mark (*dharmatā*). For this reason:
Whether in body or mind, there was none who did not attain pliancy. Hearing what they had never heard before, they attained what they had never attained before.

This is the description by the sutra compiler of how the great assembly at that dharma-assembly gained benefit, achieved understanding, and experienced a sense of joy and relief pervading their entire beings.

The above serves as a general conclusion to the preceding text. Having discussed the essential nature of samādhi by means of refutation and revelation, the principle of clear understanding and realization is now complete.

△ Second, discussing the application of samādhi through cultivation and realization to clarify the matters of practice and attainment (in two parts): 1. Clarifying the primary and auxiliary practices to demonstrate the path (in two parts): 1.
Demonstrating the perfect and penetrating correct cultivation appropriate for the occasion (in two parts): 1. Ānanda’s summary and reception of the teaching.
"Please.
Once again, with tears of compassion, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet (until: "the assembly stood with single-minded devotion awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate instruction").
This passage describes how, having already understood the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, he requested the method for further cultivation. As previously mentioned...

Although his tears of sorrow were many, they had all been due to the pain of delusion and ignorance. Now, having clearly realized his own nature, his understanding was profound and his sense of grief became even more intense.
For this reason, he wept again and again, and with the three karmas most earnestly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
Most honored, supreme, and endowed with great kindness and great compassion; pure and untainted, clean and unstained;
the king of all jewels, like a wish-fulfilling gem that fulfills all desires according to one's heart so that none fail to obtain benefit.
You are skilled at manifesting and guiding us toward our own minds, being able to use such various causes and conditions as the mirror of Ādarśamukha to illuminate [the truth]. And...

In accordance with the natural course, through winding turns and indirect maneuvers, by means of skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*), he further clarifies that mere hearing is of no merit, while encouraging true practice is beneficial.
These are all methods to entice those submerged in the long night of saṃsāra to emerge from the ocean of the two sufferings of hatred and attachment.
How could this kindness and virtue ever be repaid? Thus, O World-Honored One, we—
Now, although you have received the preceding teaching on perfect interfusion— pointing out that it is "neither identical nor different, yet both identical and different"—
until the deluded mind naturally subsides, which is itself Bodhi, you have understood and realized through such Dharma-sounds the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha,
the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, which is pure and fundamental, pervading the ten directions. Therefore, as for its essence, it is non-...
It does not contain anything, yet its function is such that there is nothing it does not develop and bring forth.
Even the wondrous lands of the Tathāgata’s realm, adorned with jewels, are all contained within and developed by it. Having now attained this mind, I am truly fortunate;
I thought that once "the One" was known, all matters would be concluded and there would be nothing else remaining. I did not expect the Tathāgata to further reproach me for my mere erudition.
It is of no merit; it does not equal the benefit of true cultivation. Yet, if one wishes to practice, how can it be done?
The nature of the treasury is subtle and inconceivable; the paths of mind and speech are cut off, and there is no door through which to enter. What is to be done?
Today we are like homeless and jobless travelers, drifting in poverty and suffering, who have suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King.

They did not find its door and, in the end, were unable to enter. I only pray that the Tathāgata will show the path for entering the gate to those gathered here who are deluded, ignorant, dull-witted, and slow;
let them abandon the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna and ultimately personally attain the Tathāgata’s own realization of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
I earnestly beg for instruction. Regarding the Buddha’s past, when he was on the causal ground...

Having resolved to attain enlightenment, one follows the path of personal cultivation to cause those in training to gather and subdue their discursive thoughts and attachments from time immemorial through which Dharma-gates?
How may one suddenly attain single-minded total retention (*ekāgra-dhāraṇī*) so that the Three Piṭakas are perfectly integrated?

"Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one attains the Great Dharma-gate of universal characteristics. Within this, there is no ground of awakening for the fruit-stage of *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
rather, it concerns the path of initial aspiration and the mind of the causal stage. This is precisely to demonstrate the causal mind in order to approach the awakening of the fruit.

To dwell on land is called "lodging," and to dwell upon water is called "mooring. When the mind wanders beyond principle, it is metaphorically described as lodging or mooring. The Buddha possesses the Dharma.

“Realm” (dhātu) is like a heavenly king; “bestowing” is a metaphor for opening and revealing. “The flowered mansion” is a metaphor for the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha). Although one has “attained” it, this is a metaphor for faith and understanding;
yet one must enter through a gate, which is a metaphor for initiating practice based on that understanding. Through practice, one realizes the principle.

“Without remainder” means that the five stages of dwelling [in ignorance] are all exhausted and the two types of death have forever perished; thus, there are no remaining afflictions. “Ch’u-hsi” (疇昔) is equivalent to saying “of old. Dhāraṇī...
“Ni” means *dhāraṇī*. “Zhù” means to wait or await.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s proclamation of the essential Dharma (in two parts): First, the sūtra author’s introduction of the intent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those in the assembly... [proceeded] to proclaim it to Ānanda and the great multitude.

This is the sūtra-master’s narration of the Buddha’s intention: it is precisely for the sake of compassionate pity and mindfulness, so that [beings] might abandon the Small Vehicle and turn toward the Great;
and although they have realized the true mind of Bodhi, they have not yet entered the gate and thus lack mastery.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of those sentient beings in the future final age who are able to give rise to the Bodhicitta, opening for them the unsurpassed True Vehicle as a sublime practice.
This is the essential path; for this reason, it is proclaimed for those who are ready to receive the teaching and shown to the great assembly.
△ Second, the World-Honored One’s direct instruction (in two parts): First, the dual examination of the root (in two parts): First, the general inquiry.
"You all must resolutely resolve to generate the Bodhicitta" (up to) "how are the two meanings of the initial resolve determined?
This is a general inquiry into the two meanings of resolution. The Buddha said: "You all must certainly and definitively resolve to generate the unsurpassed Bodhicitta.
Regarding the Great Buddha-Usnīsa Śūraṅgama King, which all Tathāgatas of the ten directions..."
Cultivating and realizing the wondrous samādhi requires a sharp resolve and diligent practice, without giving rise to indolence, fatigue, or weariness;

one must never regress and must certainly be free from hesitation. This is truly difficult to attain. However, one must first clarify that the initial awakening arises from fundamental awareness (*mūla-bodhi*);
regarding this primordial mind, there are two aspects—true and false—which must be decisively discerned and clearly distinguished.
Only when concentration is true will it not be confused; through cultivation, one may then enter this wondrous samādhi.
Therefore, he asks in summary: "How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? This was prompted by Ānanda’s question regarding *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the path of the original arousal of the bodhicitta and the subduing of objective conditions to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the Buddha therefore spoke of the two definitive meanings.

The intent is that if one wishes to know the path of the original arousal of the bodhicitta, one must simply resolve to eliminate the deluded mind of arising and ceasing, and attain the non-arising and non-ceasing as the mind for the causal stage;
only then will one perfectly accomplish the fruit-virtue of nirvana, which is neither born nor extinguished.
This is the first definitive principle for the beginner. If one wishes to subdue and master discursive attachments, one must carefully examine where the root of afflictions resides.
Once the root is known, one should then definitively select the fundamental organ of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-mūla-indriya*).
By entering deeply through a single gateway, the six organs of cognition will simultaneously become pure. This is the second definitive principle for the beginner.
...Thus it is.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts): First, examining the mind of the causal ground (in two parts). First, a general exhortation to examine it:
"Ānanda, as for the primary truth (*paramārtha*), if you [disciples] desire [to attain it]... [up to] "...there is no such place where there is neither birth nor extinction."

This is a specific explanation of the two certainties: one must rely on the cause of the mind and the fruit of awakening, ensuring that the beginning and the end correspond, as this serves as the foundation for further cultivation. As Ānanda said:
"Regarding the first certainty of meaning—if you wish to resolve your will, renounce the Hīnayāna, advance toward the Mahāyāna, and desire to realize and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision..."

If this were so, one should examine and contemplate with meticulous scrutiny: Is the initial mind employed in the stages of the causal ground—the very same as the true mind of original enlightenment (*pratyagātman*) in the stage of the Buddha-fruit? Or are they different?
If they are the same, then it would be permissible to employ within the causal ground that which is characterized by the arising and ceasing of discriminative causes, conditions, and spontaneity.

To take this as the cause for spiritual cultivation while seeking the unsurpassed True Vehicle—the fruit of Buddhahood that is unborn, undying, and eternally abiding—is like steaming sand to make rice or seeking waves by discarding water; such a thing is absolutely impossible.
This is because the mind of birth and death belongs to the conditioned and impermanent, whereas the unborn and undying belongs to the unconditioned and true.
This is the constant principle: it is necessary that cause and effect correspond. Only then can Bodhi and Nirvana be hoped for;
this is what is meant by "the head being straight and the tail being straight."
△ Second, the correct demonstration of what should be examined (in two parts): First, the general establishment of the analogy:
"For this reason, you should illuminate [the truth]... because from beginning to end there is no destruction."

This clarifies that the space of the world— whether conditioned or unconditioned— is a general illustration for the relationship between the arising-and-ceasing mind and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing [nature].
The intent is that because the causal mind and the resultant awakening must be identical in nature, one should first examine this through reflection,
even if you have not yet understood it, given that the mind possesses both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing aspects.
Examine clearly the principles of permanence and impermanence regarding the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). However, whatever phenomena are subject to being produced are ultimately impermanent;
they all undergo transformation, and there is none that does not perish. Ānanda, you should further observe and scrutinize carefully:
among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which one is indestructible? Yet, one never hears of empty space (*ākāśa*) decaying or perishing. Why is this so?
For this reason, because empty space cannot be produced through effort, and since there is no such production, it likewise has neither beginning nor end, nor does it undergo destruction.
Therefore, one who seeks the fruit of non-arising and non-extinction must take as their cause that which is unconditioned and indestructible;
they must not further employ a mind characterized by arising and ceasing. Qingliang said: "Regarding 'the world' (*loka*), 'world' (*lo*) carries the meaning of concealment."

Because it conceals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and because it has the sense of being destructible, as it is transmuted by the three times (*trikāla*). "Interstice" (*antara*) means falling into the midst of the false and deceptive;
since its very nature of concealment is itself to fall into the false and deceptive, "world" (*loka*) is identical to "interstice. This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

△ Second, the specific exposition of the dharmas (in two parts): 1. Using the dharma of arising and ceasing as an analogy for what is conditioned (*kṛtaka*). 2. The general heading on the production of delusion:
"That which has the characteristic of solidity within your body is earth" (extending to) "from beginning to end, the five aggregates are turbid."
This is discussed with respect to a single body, wherein its falsity is exposed; it serves as a general indication that all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing can be so treated.
The underlying intent is this: if one must take a mind free from arising and ceasing as the causal ground, what then can be said of the fruit?
This is because the ocean of the mind is turbid with the five factors and is never pure; now, wishing to clarify it, one takes the Buddha-fruit as the goal—this is not non-arising.

To consider cessation as the cause of the mind is certainly impossible. Yet, the true mind—which is neither born nor extinguished and is eternally abiding—is fundamentally free from turbidity; how could it possibly arise [from such causes]?
Thus, within this body of yours, the solid characteristics of bone and flesh are termed "earth," the moist essence of fluids is termed "water," and the gaseous characteristic of warm touch—
That which is called fire is the throbbing of the pulse; that which is called wind is movement. All of these are conditioned phenomena subject to decay.
Because one grasps at these four great elements as a self, one becomes entangled and bound by them.
Thus, the eternally abiding true mind—which is fundamentally without birth or extinction—is instead turned into something turbid, subject to birth and extinction. From this, differentiation arises.
The opening of the profound, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment has, from this point on, separated it from the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind.
Thus, that which resides in the eye is merely called "seeing"; that which resides in the ear is designated as "hearing"; those which reside in the nose, tongue, and body are all termed "sensation";

and that which resides in the mind is simply called "discernment. One should know that the original source is but a single refined spirit, which through delusion becomes the six harmonies. When these unite—

Within that which is without division, delusion creates divisions. From the initial moment of straying from the one true reality until the final stage of the formation of the six sense bases, the phenomena of turbidity thus come to have five layers.
However, other sutras clarify the five turbidities by taking the five sharp afflictions as "views" and the five dull afflictions as "afflictions.
Sentient beings merely grasp the fruits of these views and conceit, thereby establishing this [distinction].

The provisional name "life" (jīva) takes as its essence the maintenance of a single period of form and mind; the eon (kalpa) has no separate essence, but is merely the time when the four turbidities (kaṣāya) are gathered together.
This scripture, however, is not so; it defines the five turbidities based on the deluded thoughts of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Since there are already the six faculties capable of perceiving and discerning, there must necessarily be the six objects that are perceived and discerned;
these together constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Through these six faculties, the reception of the six objects constitutes the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Taking the preceding sense-objects as conditions, that which gives rise to discrimination is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Once discrimination has arisen, it universally takes all objects as its conditions;
arising and ceasing from moment to moment in an uninterrupted succession, this is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Since the preceding seven [aggregates] exist as both seeds and manifestations, they perfume the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya-svabhāva*), transforming it into the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*); this is then called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Furthermore, with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as...
Beginning with the *vijñāna-skandha* and ending with it, there thus arise the five kinds of turbidity (*kaṣāya*). "Layered" (*dié*) means "repeated" or "heavy.
△ Second, the detailed explanation according to the meaning (in two parts): 1. A general clarification of the meaning of turbidity.
"What is meant by turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water [up to] 'your fivefold turbidity is likewise so.
This explains the meaning of turbidity. Why is it called turbidity? Ānanda, for example, clear water is pure by its very nature.
If there are things such as dust, soil, ash, or sand, their substance creates obstruction and..."

There are two distinct forms: a solid mass and clear water. Each of these possesses its own fixed nature, such that by their very essence they do not accord with one another. Suddenly, someone takes that dust and throws it into the pure water;
then that which was obstructive loses its obstruction, and that which was clean loses its clarity, as both are transformed together into a turbid mixture.
The appearance of the water and the features of the earth are turbid and difficult to discern; therefore, it is called "turbid.

Indeed, your turbidity consists of five layers, which is likewise the case here. Qingliang says: "In Sanskrit, *dharmatā* means 'the natural state of phenomena' (*fǎ'ěr*), also called 'the realm of phenomena' (*fǎjiè*), or 'the nature of phenomena' (*fǎxìng*).
To say "the natural state of phenomena" means that phenomena are fundamentally spontaneous and ought to be thus.
"Thus. 'Turbid' (gì) means confusion; it refers to the mixing of water and soil, such that they are intermingled and difficult to distinguish.
△ Second, specifically indicating the names of the turbidities:
"Ānanda, you see empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions... (up to)... this is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life."
This demonstrates the names of the turbidities. Ānanda, regarding the turbidity of the covering, there are five aspects in detail.
For instance, when you raise your eyes to see space, whether it be the space or the seeing, both pervade the ten directions.
Yet, for the moment, you do not know which is the boundary of space and which is the limit of seeing; thus, space and seeing are confused and indistinguishable.
Therefore, where there is space, there is no substance capable of seeing; where there is seeing, there is no space that can be perceived.
Thus, these two—space and seeing—are interwoven like warp and woof, inseparable from one another, falsely forming turbid appearances. As it is with seeing space, so it is with seeing form. The eye...
As it is with the sense organs (*indriya*), so it is with the others. This arises from falsely identifying the four great elements as the characteristics of the body;

thus, there is the mutual confrontation of sense organs and objects (*viṣaya*), which disturbs the true nature and turbidly muddies the wondrous clarity, eventually forming the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

This is the first layer, called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). This is because the five turbidities depend upon the five aggregates, and since both the sense organs and their objects are of the nature of form.
This belongs to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). To say that one sees space with the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) clarifies the meaning of "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*).

Since formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness are all termed *kalpa*, seeing space is thus designated as the turbidity of the *kalpa* (*kalpakaṣāya*). Once the faculties and their objects have already come into mutual correspondence...

Consciousness will inevitably arise, experiencing the external objects to form the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Therefore, it is said that your body originally lacks the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
It is only due to the present life—initially taking conception in the womb—that you gather semen and blood, causing the four great elements to increase and form a physical body.
Thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally one refined spirit; originally, they are without obstruction. Because of these four...
When there is great congestion that cannot be made to flow through, that which was without obstruction becomes obstructed.

Earth, water, fire, and wind are originally inert substances, fundamentally devoid of cognition; yet, being subjected to this cognitive awareness, they circulate and receive sensations, thereby constituting the body and its environment.
Thus, that which was without cognition comes to possess cognition, arising from this single circulation and single congestion.
The principle is like that of a single warp and a single woof: when the two are interwoven, they cannot be separated.
For this reason, although the four great elements are originally devoid of sentience, through the weaving of delusion, even the prick of a needle or a blade of grass is felt as pain.
Consequently, sentient beings give rise to the view of a self as a cause, and further produce views of annihilationism, eternalism, existence, and non-existence, culminating in the sixty-two views.
To turbidly disturb the true mind is the second layer, called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). As for views being the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*):
because seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are known as the six faculties of reception, the turbidity of views depends upon the aggregate of sensation.

Because the images reflected from the preceding sense objects fall away to give rise to the six consciousnesses, forming the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it is said: "Furthermore, within your own minds..."
One recollects the past, discriminates the present, and contemplates the future; yet these three are originally devoid of intrinsic nature.
It is because of the mental consciousness that cognition and views arise. This very mental consciousness is fundamentally without form or perception.
They are manifested by the six sense objects and appear to possess form and cognition;

therefore, when consciousness is separated from its objects, it lacks the self-characteristic of consciousness, and when objects are separated from conscious awareness, they likewise lack the intrinsic nature of objects. Thus, each object and each cognition [are mutually dependent].
It is like warp and woof threads interwoven with one another, such that they cannot be distinguished.

Thus, because thoughts conditioned by sensory objects involve insatiable craving and attachment, they form turbid characteristics that disturb the true nature; this is called the third heavy defilement, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).
Since the first six consciousnesses take the sense organs and their objects as conditions, the seventh consciousness then engages in deliberation and clings to a self.
Within true nature, it falsely gives rise to arising and ceasing, flowing and shifting from moment to moment, thereby forming the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Therefore it is said:

"Furthermore, within your mind, from morning until evening, there is arising, abiding, change, and cessation that does not pause for even a moment. If one relies upon this cognition and view that clings to a self..."
One always wishes for them to remain forever in this world, yet the workings of their good and evil karma repeatedly urge them to constantly migrate to other lands.
It is like a person with a private heart who, though longing for their hometown, must travel to another country due to official business.

Therefore, that which remains cannot remain forever, and that which migrates likewise cannot migrate all at once. One remaining and one migrating interweave with one another, inseparable from each other;
thus, delusion produces turbid appearances, overturning the nature of nirvana to become the cause of birth and death.

Rising and sinking within the three realms, wandering back and forth through the seven clusters [of existence], and turbidly disturbing the true nature—this is the fourth layer, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
Because the preceding triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness all possess both seeds and manifestations that perfume the *tathāgatagarbha*, it transforms into the *ālayavijñāna*.
This very state, which contains and maintains [all phenomena], constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Therefore, it is said: "That which you see and hear is originally one..."

The substance is fundamentally without distinct natures; it is only due to the separation by various sensory objects that individual gateways are opened, resulting in what appear to be disparate manifestations.
However, when discussed from the perspective of their inherent nature, they belong to the same family; their cognitive awareness is mutually pervasive, appearing as one rather than being different.
If we speak according to the functioning within the midst [of phenomena], there is not an absence of mutual contradiction between this and that; they appear different yet are not the same.
First, identity and difference both lose their standard; second, as the two interweave, they falsely form turbid appearances.

This turns the Tathāgatagarbha and, following the causes of defilement and purity, it deludes the True Mind, acting as the sovereign lord of the collective retribution. This is the fifth layer of existence for the sake of life.

This is turbidity. "Life" (*jīva*) refers to the eighth consciousness; that which is called the triad of warmth, breath, and consciousness, maintaining continuity without interruption, is termed "life.
Therefore, the turbidity of life depends upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). These five turbidities arise collectively from deluding the truth and pursuing the false.
Consequently, it becomes turbid and can no longer remain clear. Now the Buddha is about to bestow the method for clarifying this turbidity;
therefore, he first points out the cause by which the turbidity arises.
△ Second, using the absence of arising and ceasing as an analogy for empty space (in two parts): 1. Clarifying the turbid and returning it to clarity.
"Ānanda, you now wish to cause [the faculties] to see, hear, perceive, and know... (until) thereafter you shall perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the ground of fruition.
This clarifies that by purifying turbidity one returns to clarity, demonstrating the effort required in the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For, when speaking of the individual characteristics of the four great elements, the five aggregates, and the phenomena of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses, they are nothing other than turbid water. Yet, when discussed from the perspective of their fundamental nature (*dhātu*), they are all the Tathāgata.
The essence of water is nothing other than clarity within turbidity. Now, the Tathāgata intends to lead those whose faculties are suited to practice by means of the auditory faculty;
this is precisely because there is a nature of clarity within turbid water. Therefore, it is said:
"You now desire to manifest that which is presently possessed and used daily—this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing."
The four natures must necessarily correspond to the Tathāgata’s four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
If this is so, one should first clarify that the four entanglements are illusory transformations, all arising from false causes and conditions.
By discerning and removing these five layers, which are the very root of birth and death, one may subsequently rely upon and attain the unborn, undying, perfect, tranquil, and eternal state.
Abiding in true nature, one gives rise to cultivation from that nature and returns to cultivate that very self-nature. Only when nature and cultivation are non-dual can success be achieved.
Since one relies on the profound nature as the essence of concentration, one takes that profound nature as the function of concentration.

One turns back the false roots and objects and transforms them into the true self-nature, subduing and eliminating the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, thereby returning once more to the single truth.
One then attains the primordially existing, wondrously luminous, true awakening—unborn and undying, the eternally abiding true nature—and takes this as the mind of the causal ground.
Only upon reaching this point does one enter the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Thereafter, from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) through to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), one undergoes the true cultivation of the fruit-ground, culminating finally in the actualization of the fruit-ground of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

This constitutes the correspondence between the name and its referent: the cause is the mind, and the fruit is awakening. From the initial arousal of the mind to its ultimate fulfillment, they are non-dual and not different.
Within this, first one eliminates the turbidity of birth-and-death and the like; then, by subduing [the afflictions] and returning to original awakening, one returns to clarity.
This is the most essential point for progress and cultivation throughout this entire sutra. Those who wish to practice this samādhi should carefully savor these words.
△ Second, the application of the analogy to the Dharma.
"As when turbid water is settled and stored in a quiet vessel" (extending to) "...all accord with the pure and wondrous virtues of Nirvana.

This is an analogy for the aforementioned practice of turning back delusion within the perfect and profound stillness (*yuan-zhan*). The preceding [passage] uses the throwing of earth as an analogy for turbidity.
The sign: now, by settling the turbidity, it returns to becoming clear water; this serves as a metaphor for the signs of cultivation and realization.
"Turbid water" generally illustrates the five layers of turbidity. "A clean vessel" specifically symbolizes the nature of the perfect and penetrating faculties (*indriya*).

Just as one must store turbid water in a clean vessel, so too, to eliminate the turbidity, one must select a perfect faculty. Being still, deep, and unmoving is a metaphor for the firmness of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The sand and soil naturally settle; this is a metaphor for the fact that the preceding four levels of gravity do not interweave again.
The five abodes of afflictions (*pañca-vāsanā*) are completely subdued, and thus their coarse impurities fall away spontaneously. The clear water appears before one;

this is a metaphor for the True Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), wherein the profound, perfect fundamental substance—the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind—finally manifests. Reaching this point is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
It is like the sand and soil from before that have initially settled, yet the mud remains; this is a metaphor for the destruction of the four *skandhas*.

Although one has severed the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realms, the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the external realms—the root of the *vijñāna-skandha*—remains dormant and is not yet severed.

When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, it is a metaphor for the destruction of the *vijñāna-skandha*. When half of the arising-and-ceasing is eliminated and one enters the profound stillness to merge with that stillness, one is precisely severing the ignorance of the external realms.

It is clarified. From the first stage of the Perfect [Teaching] (*yuan chu-zhu*), it is severed partially, until at the ultimate stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), it is completely severed.
Therefore it is said: "This is called the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). All that precedes is a metaphor for the effort of clarifying turbidity;
from here below, the text clarifies the virtuous function of returning to clarity. Because the five turbidities have been exhausted, this mind-water becomes clear and...
It is luminous, pure, and unadulterated. It is precisely like the ocean-seal (sāgaramudrā), wherein all the myriad forms and states of the world are reflected without exception.
It is not confined by the afflictions of the four entanglements (catvāraḥ saṃyojanāni) and the five aggregates (pañca skandhāḥ).

Whatever actions are undertaken are entirely wondrous functions, all of which accord with the Tathāgata’s wondrous virtue of effortless (anabhisaṃskāra) and pure nirvāṇa—characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is like when the mud has been exhausted and the water is pure; it may be stirred and filtered as one pleases, yet it will never become turbid again.
△ Second, examining the root of afflictions (in two parts): First, a general exhortation to examine.
The second meaning is this: "If you all truly desire [to attain]... how shall you subdue [the afflictions] and take the rank of a Tathāgata?
This exhorts one to examine the root of the afflictions and the place where they arise and cease. As for what is called the second meaning:
if you, Ānanda and the others, among this great assembly, definitely desire to give rise to and realize the bodhicitta within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, then...

O Great Hero! You must resolutely subdue and definitively abandon all past objects of attachment, as well as the four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), the five turbidities (*kaṣāya*), and all conditioned phenomena that are characterized by falsehood.

If you are thus resolved, you should carefully and minutely examine the root of affliction (*kleśa*). Having investigated this root of affliction from the beginningless past until the present, how has it been?
This is called "initiating karma. How, then, is it termed "moistening rebirth"? Who is the head that initiates karma?

Who is the master who receives retribution? Generally speaking, afflictions are precisely the ignorance that initiates karma, for they can manifest the functional activity of formative karma (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, [afflictions] such as discrimination, grasping, and rejecting belong to the sixth consciousness. Fundamental [ignorance], however, is what moistens rebirth.

Ignorance moistens the seeds so that birth is received; thus, it is like one who gives rise to hatred and attachment, enters the womb, and receives a life-span—this belongs to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
However, regarding the activity of grasping objects (*ālambana*), the six consciousnesses are most predominant;

they are the "head" of karmic activity because they can produce the causes for both defiled and pure karma. Yet, as for that which receives retribution, it is solely this eighth consciousness, for it is the totality.
It is called the "retributive master" because it is able to contain, grasp, and maintain the seeds of both the defiled and the pure, ensuring they are not lost.
However, upon subtle investigation, one finds that the preceding seven consciousnesses all belong to the self-manifestation of the eighth consciousness;

this is what is meant by "one's own actions, one's own retribution. Therefore, Ānanda, if you wish to cultivate and realize unexcelled Bodhi, suppose you are unable to examine [the nature of] these...

When one clearly understands afflictions and minutely examines their root, one cannot know from where the false six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) arise, nor how this perversion exists.

This is because the seeds of the faculties, objects, and consciousness—namely, the subtle causes of arising and ceasing—are all contained within the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). Since one does not know this, one naturally cannot know the faculties.

Although the dharmas of sensory consciousness manifest, they are fundamentally illusory. It is merely due to the initial moment of non-awakening that one falsely differentiates between subject and object;
by pursuing delusion and losing sight of the truth, one consequently falls into perversion.
Thus, one knows that this perversion arises from within the eight consciousnesses. Since one cannot even recognize the locus of this perversion, how can one hope to...?
Having subdued the攀緣 (pān-yuan, *ālambana*, objective conditions), one attains the fruit-stage of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, those who wish to extinguish delusions must know the locus from which these delusions arise.
△ Second, the correct instruction on what should be examined (2): First, the general establishment of the analogy.
"Ānanda, you observe those in the world who untie knots... [until] ...because in emptiness there are no forms or characteristics, and thus there is neither knotting nor untying."
This establishes an analogy for the binding and the unbinding, by which to illustrate the true nature. Therefore it is said:

"Ānanda, if you do not know the state of inversion and the state of non-inversion, simply observe the world’s knots; from the knot itself and the person who unbinds the knot, the matter will become clear.
For the act of knotting illustrates the state of inversion, while the unbinding of the knot illustrates the state of non-inversion. Thus, [it concerns] the binding and the unbinding.
Although they differ, they are all this same person. Therefore, if one wishes to untie a knot, one must see the place where it is knotted.

If one does not see the place where it is knotted, how can one know the place to untie it? This is precisely analogous to the aforementioned inability to know where the delusions occur within the false faculties and objects.
If one does not even know the location [of the delusion], how can one subdue it and attain the state of a Tathāgata?
How much more so, then, must it be understood that there is both binding and liberation; yet these still belong to the mind of birth-and-death consciousness.
This is not like the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is fundamentally without binding or liberation, and is neither born nor extinguished.
Therefore, you have never heard of space in the world being destroyed or split asunder by you. Why is this? Because space is fundamentally...
It is because it has no form or characteristics, and is likewise without bondage or liberation. Thus one should know that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is also like this.
The meaning of "shattering" is equivalent to "untying."
△ Second, the detailed exposition of the Dharma (in two parts): First, concluding by way of analogy with inversion (in two parts). First, a general indication concluding on the roots [of perception]:
"Thus, your present eyes, ears, nose, and tongue... cannot transcend the vessel-world."
This demonstrates the root source of the fetters. The meaning is this: what is it that is called a "fetter"?
It is these very things before you—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

By means of these six organs, one gives rise to the six consciousnesses and draws in the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), thereby turbidizing the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya-vijñāna*). This is like a family member acting as a go-between for a thief.

They entice the internal thief and plunder their own family treasures. Due to these dharmas of sense organs, objects, and consciousness, since beginningless time, they have falsely identified the four elements and five aggregates as their body and mind; thus there exist the primary retribution of sentient beings and the world.
From this, false discrimination arises, naturally producing entanglements and bonds, which divide the profound, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Because they dwell within the vessel-world of the dependent retribution, their vision cannot transcend form, and their hearing cannot go beyond sound.
This is truly due to the mutual entanglement of the faculties, objects, and consciousness, which together form a knot.
Viewed from this perspective, these three are originally manifestations arising from the single, profound, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind.
Yet, by doing so, one instead destroys the treasures of merit and dharma within the Tathāgatagarbha.
How is this different from a thief from a foreign clan who plunders the family jewels? However, if one can untie those knots, then the faculties and their objects will no longer couple;
the wondrous function will manifest before one, and thus the very thief who destroyed the house becomes the master who guards it.

△ Second, the specific explanation of the characteristics of the assembly (in two parts): First, regarding the nature of sentient beings, it clarifies that there is no fixed number, whether more or less.
Ānanda asks: "What is meant by the world of sentient beings? ... [up to] "...each possessing twelve hundred merits."
This is explained with respect to the world of sentient beings, clarifying that their entanglements prevent them from transcending the vessel-world (bhājana-loka).
This is because the faculties possess knots, characteristics, quantities, and fixed limitations.

However, those who wish to cultivate meditative concentration must first untie the knots within their faculties before they can advance in their practice. Furthermore, these faculties are either complete or incomplete.
The effort of cultivation increases tenfold with each passing day; one must not fail to select [the appropriate faculty].

If one wishes to select those of perfect faculties (*paripūrṇendriya*), one must thoroughly understand the numerical categories of the six faculties. Were it otherwise, by what means could one untie the knots and make such a selection? Therefore, the Buddha inquired:
"Ānanda, what is meant by the world that constitutes the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of sentient beings? "World" refers to the present.
All that flows and shifts within the body is called the world (*loka*). That which constitutes the front, back, above, below, left, right, and middle of this very body is called the realm (*dhātu*).
You should now know that when the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below constitute the realms, there are ten spatial orientations.
When the past, future, and present constitute the worlds, there are three temporal sequences.
It is truly because all sentient beings originally lack the marks of bodily bondage;
it is only due to the mutual interweaving of the four great elements and the five aggregates that they falsely produce the marks of bodily bondage.

Once the marks of the body, roots, and sense objects exist, then the world and its realms are contained within a single body, where they trade with one another and flow into each other in succession; hence it is said: "The world and..."

"Directions" (*diś*) refers to their mutual interpenetration. Although directions comprise the ten quarters, within these ten quarters only the four cardinal points—east, west, south, and north—are taken as primary;
the zenith and nadir are not so taken, because the zenith and nadir are simply the vertical dimensions of those four cardinal points.

Because there is no fixed location, the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*) are not taken; for the intermediate directions are merely the junctions between the four cardinal directions and lack a fixed orientation.

Thus, by means of these fixed directions, one traverses those shifting three periods of time (*tri-kāla*). Since each of the four directions possesses three periods, they together constitute twelve. If one wishes to traverse the directions by means of the periods, then the three periods— *Note:
