Each [direction] has four sides, thus forming twelve. Therefore it is said: "Twelvefold in its winding turns, flowing and transforming.

As for the "three folds," this refers to how a single thought-moment, through its successive flow, transforms into the three folds of ten, hundred, and thousand. Now, let us first examine these folds by way of the directions and their engagement with the world, to clarify the three folds.
Regarding the first fold: based on the four directions, each is discussed in terms of the three periods of time; thus, four times three is—
Together they total twelve. In the second layer, within the three times of the eastern direction, each one transforms into ten, making thirty.
The same applies to the southern, western, and northern directions. Together, the four directions total one hundred and twenty. This is the third layer.

Taking thirty from the east and multiplying ten by ten to make one hundred, this results in three hundred. The same applies to the other three directions. Thus, the four directions together total one thousand two hundred.
What is now referred to as "one, ten, hundred, and thousand" merely cites the larger figures. If one wishes to apply worldly conventions to the directions, they may be inferred accordingly;
such is the fixed number for the interpenetration and formation of characteristics of this world-system. If one were to...

Regarding this body, if we discuss its numerical scope in a general sense: beginning from the first transformation into twelve and ending with the hundredth transformation into one thousand and twenty, it generally possesses one thousand two hundred [transformations] in its entirety.
This may be likened to the "One Great Ultimate" (Taiji) as a unified whole. Although this is a total number, within each of the six sense faculties, it likewise exists individually.
It is fully endowed with functional power and virtuous application. Regarding the "one thousand two hundred," this refers to each individual object being one *taiji* (Great Ultimate).
This is based on the numerical measure of the merit within a single thought-moment of the body; such is the case. If it were for a single moment or a single day, how could it ever be calculated?
"Power" (*gong*) refers to strength; "virtue" (*de*) refers to function. That is to say, within each of the six sense faculties, there are [these powers and functions].

This refers to the power and function of mutual interpenetration, transverse and longitudinal interweaving. This is because, with respect to the nature of discernment within the six sense faculties, they are identical;

hence it is said that each possesses twelve hundred merits. Below, with respect to the function of discerning the six sense objects, there are differences, and thus the merits are either complete or deficient and not equal.
This means that while they know one another within their nature, they manifest one another within their function.

This concludes the section on the "Back. △ Second, regarding the characteristics of the objects of perception, it clarifies that there are differences in the excellence or inferiority of their functions.
"Ānanda, you should further determine the excellence or inferiority among these [until] they are fully endowed with one thousand two hundred merits."

This clarifies that the functions of the six sense organs in relation to their objects are not without degrees of superiority and inferiority; therefore, it causes those who are ready to choose for themselves.

Above, we spoke of mutual correspondence within the nature, where there is no superiority or inferiority; here, we clarify mutual divergence within the functioning, and thus superiority and inferiority exist.
Ānanda, among these six sense organs, you should first determine for yourself which one is most suitable.
What is superior? What is inferior? For example, if the eye functions by means of seeing, it cannot see what is behind;
darkness alone can see what is in front. By combining the light of the front with the darkness of the back, as well as the lateral views to the left and right, these constitute the four directions.
According to the calculation of their merits, each of the four directions consists of two hundred [units], and the four intermediate corners likewise.
Each [side] has one hundred. Now, looking at the front, as well as the left and right, these constitute three sides, totaling six hundred.
Together with the two previous corners totaling two hundred, they form eight hundred. Only the single rear side of two hundred and the two rear corners of two hundred are not seen;
yet if one discusses them by dividing them into three parts across the three periods of time, one now obtains eight hundred. Thus, it is three.
This constitutes two parts. If one were to divide it according to the four directions, four parts would be distinct. Now, three sides are visible; this refers to three parts possessing merit.
One side is not seen; this is one part lacking virtue. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits and is not a perfect faculty (*paripūrṇendriya*).
As for the ear, which takes hearing as its function, its hearing is most all-pervasive.
It is all-pervasive; even regarding matters throughout the ten directions, there is nothing left unperceived.
Thus, when it moves and produces sound, one immediately knows whether it is near or far; when it is still and silent, one further perceives its boundlessness and limitlessness.
One should know that the faculty of hearing is complete in its twelve hundred functions, without any deficiency, and among all the faculties, it is the most excellent. As...
As for the nose, which functions through smelling: smelling involves the simultaneous passage of both exhalation and inhalation.
Nevertheless, although there is exhalation and inhalation, there is an absence of their intermediate junction. By this it is verified that among its three parts, one is missing;
thus, one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits and is not a perfect faculty, just as is the case with the tongue.
As for its function: it does not merely perceive flavors, but solely takes up the proclamation [of the Dharma]. It is able to discourse upon all mundane and supramundane wisdoms;
though its speech has its methods and its phrasing may be limited, its principle is inexhaustible and its meaning is comprehensive and pervasive.
One should know that the perfection of the tongue-faculty as twelve hundredfold is likewise the nature of the perfect faculty. As for the body, it takes the perception of touch as its function.
As for its function: when it encounters contact, there is both opposition and compliance; yet it can perceive when in conjunction, but does not know when separated.
Because it perceives when in conjunction—experiencing both opposition and compliance—it possesses two parts.

If one examines the body-faculty through these three parts, it lacks the one pertaining to separation; thus, one should know that the body-faculty has only eight hundred [subdivisions] and is not complete.

The faculty of mind (*manas*). Because it takes all phenomena as its object through universal cognition, it is able to silently encompass the ten directions and the three periods of time, including all worldly and world-transcending dharmas, whether sacred or mundane;
there is nothing it does not contain, reaching to the very limits of existence.

Thus, this faculty of mind is complete with twelve hundred [qualities], and is also called the "perfect faculty" (*paripūrṇendriya*). Among the merits of these six faculties, some are superior and some are inferior.
"Inferior! You should decisively determine and choose for yourself.
II. Explaining by way of the example of subduing (2): 1. Briefly showing the essential point of the mind.
"Ānanda, you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death... until those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified."
This briefly demonstrates that selecting the faculties (*indriya*) and unraveling the knots is the essential secret for cultivating the mind. The meaning is this:

having understood the root of these illusory knots and further recognized the six faculties—some perfect and some deficient—it is precisely appropriate to select the perfect faculty and untie the manifestations of the knots;
this is the most urgent requirement for cultivating the mind. Therefore, it is said: "Ānanda, you and the others now wish to go against..."

Regarding the two kinds of birth and death, one who does not follow the current of the five sensory desires must, for the time being, certainly trace back to the root from which the flow of desire arises and the fetters are produced, in order to reach the stage of neither-arising-nor-ceasing.

First, one should examine these six types of faculties capable of experiencing objects: which perceive their objects through contact (*saṃyukta-grāhaka*), which perceive their objects without contact (*asaṃyukta-grāhaka*), and which are deep?
It is difficult to fathom. Which is shallow and easy to know? Which functions as a complete and universal instrument?
Which is incomplete and lacks utility? If you can examine and verify these six faculties of sensory reception for yourself, you will realize which one it is.

To establish a faculty of perfect penetration, one must select this very faculty; only then can one reverse that knot of birth and death which, since beginningless time, has been woven by the four elements and six faculties into a state of delusion, where they flow outward and rush toward objects. Now, wishing to untie it, one must again rely on the six faculties.
However, among the functions of these six faculties, some are perfect and others are imperfect; one need only follow and accord with that which is perfect.
Only when one sense-faculty (*indriya*) is perfectly penetrating can it be considered supremely wondrous.
Even if one were to compare the efficacy of a faculty that is not detached, not profound, and not perfect, the difference would be as vast as the interval between a day and an eon.

I have now, in the preceding sections, fully revealed within the six faculties the nature of profound, perfect clarity and the quantity of merits originally possessed by them, both in their separation and their integration.
There are depths and shallows; there are wholes and fragments. All are distinct and clear—this is simply how it is.
You must examine them for yourself and discern among them that which you are capable of entering into the state of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Once I have revealed and pointed this out for you, I shall cause your power of concentration to increase and enable you to advance toward Bodhi. However, I have allowed you to choose for yourself, and not...

As for the selections made for you, these also exist inherently. This is because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions establish teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, resulting in myriad distinctions and a thousand variations.
Within the seven elements and eighteen realms, one may practice through each individual path; every door is accessible for entry.
All have attained the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi, and there is no distinction of superior or inferior by which they may be selected.

It is only because your faculties are dull and inferior that you have not yet attained universal penetration or the wisdom of mastery; thus, regarding the six sense-gates, you remain unacquainted with them.
Therefore, I shall proclaim for you, one by one, their separations and unions, their strengths and weaknesses, so that you may [attain realization] herein.
Among these six gates, choose but one and enter deeply from it. If you can enter deeply into one gate, you will attain a single faculty free from delusive knots;

this is "the understanding of one which is the understanding of all. Thereby, those six types of faculties capable of knowing will simultaneously and instantaneously attain purity—this is what was previously called the ten directions' Tathāgatas.
"This is the single gate that transcends the path of wondrous adornment. Who is it? This is a term used for inquiry.
The eyes and ears are detached; the nose, tongue, and body are conjoined. The mind is deep while the [other] five are shallow; the tongue and mind are complete, while the remaining three are not so.
The six faculties of enjoyment (*upabhoga-indriya*) are so called because the various objects, such as forms and so forth, are that which is enjoyed by the six faculties, beginning with the eye.
The six faculties are "profoundly clear and perfectly luminous" (*zhan yuan ming*) because all six faculties are formed through their adherence to the profound stillness (*zhan*).
△ II. An Extensive Demonstration of the Essential Points of the Mind (2) I.

Inquiry and Request. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does one flow against the current... [and so on] ...so as to enable the six sense faculties to become pure simultaneously?"
This doubt involves two points relevant to the occasion. The intention is to ask: how does one turn back to exhaust the flowing sense-faculties?
Furthermore, since there are six faculties, there are naturally six knots; how can one enter the state where the non-delusive is one, such that all six become pure?
This is because the understanding has not yet been fully clarified; thus, building upon the previous two points, he requests further instruction.
△ II. The Correct Demonstration (II) A. A General Demonstration Based on the Essence of Afflictions (II) 1. A Comprehensive Demonstration of the Flowing Roots. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"You have now attained [the realization]... up to... the enumeration of the portions of arising, abiding, change, and cessation."
This correctly and extensively demonstrates the essential point of the mind, while first indicating the stream that must be countered. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Although you have now entered from the state of an ordinary person into the state of a sage, having already attained the first fruit and joined the stream of the sages, you have already extinguished the eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned during the stage of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) for sentient beings within the three realms. This is the vision..."

The "outflow" (*āsrava*) refers to the arising of discriminative views when the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmas*). Because of this, one wanders through birth and death and is unable to achieve liberation;

hence it is called the "outflow of views. Although one may understand this, one still does not yet know that within the mental faculty, seeds give rise to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), and manifest activity gives rise to seeds, such that they have been mutually producing one another throughout accumulated kalpas since beginningless time—this is false and delusive.
Regarding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): those habitual tendencies must be severed through the cultivation of the path.

These consist of ninety-one grades of afflictions of thought (*cetanā-kleśa*), also known as the flow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the flow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the flow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). As for the flow of desire: it refers to the craving of the first five sense faculties for the five sensory objects;
this is termed the affliction of thought. Due to these afflictions of thought, one transmigrates within the desire realm and is unable to achieve liberation.
Therefore, it is called the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*). Regarding the "outflow of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*): because cause and effect are not false, it is termed "existence.

This refers to the afflictions of volition within the realms of form and formlessness. Because of these afflictions of volition, one transmigrates through the realms of form and formlessness and is unable to escape them;

therefore, it is called the "outflow of existence. Regarding the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*): this refers to a lack of clear comprehension, which constitutes one portion of the afflictions of volition within the three realms.

The characteristic of delusion (*moha*). Due to this ignorance (*avidyā*), one transmigrates through the three realms and is unable to achieve liberation; therefore, it is called the "flow of ignorance.

By severing these three flows, one realizes the four fruits. Because the paths toward the second, third, and fourth fruits all constitute the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are termed "attained through abandonment by cultivation.
Thus, the aforementioned four flows consist of both the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), which pertain to all realms.

This is abandoned internally; it is not something abandoned by those who have already transcended the realms (*dhātu*). This statement applies to those for whom even the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) has not yet been exhausted.

How much more so, then, regarding the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) outside the realms, as well as the subtle, innate delusions of self and phenomena within this *ālayavijñāna*—namely, the so-called "dust-like sands" of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
As for birth, abiding, change, and cessation (*jāti-sthiti-anyathātva-vināśa*), according to the *Utpatti-...* [text].

Regarding the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*: among the three subtle states, the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*) is the phase of arising (*utpādakṣaṇa*). The latter two of the three subtle states and the first two of the six coarse states constitute the phase of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).

The third and fourth of the six coarse states constitute the phase of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*). The fifth constitutes the phase of cessation (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*). The sixth does not participate in these phases.
Regarding the enumeration of the stages: from the first dwelling up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment, there are forty-two levels in total.
It is said that only a Buddha and a Buddha can reach the ultimate consummation of these; how then could you, who have attained but the small fruit of a Stream-enterer, know them?
This is because you have not yet realized the single mind and have been unable to enter deeply through a single gate, thereby failing to trace back to the source of the delusive flow.
Root. Thus, the six kinds of fetters are suddenly difficult to purify. Furthermore, regarding the divisions and enumerations of arising, abiding, change, and cessation:

ordinary beings perceive the characteristic of cessation; those of the Two Vehicles perceive the characteristic of change; Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Dharma-body perceive the characteristic of abiding;
and Bodhisattvas at the stage of fulfillment perceive the characteristic of arising. This refers to the divisions for severing delusions and their respective enumerations.

It concerns enumeration. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "One who cultivates dhyāna clearly knows within the mind the limits and the number of the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
However, this teaching differs from that [other] one. The meaning of this present text is intended to sever those [phases of] arising;
the discourse of that sūtra is intended to know these numbers. Thus, their meanings are simply different.
△ Second, the clarification of "one" and "six.
Now, you should observe the six faculties present before you... (up to) the six faculties of sensory experience are likewise so.
This answers the meaning of the "one entrance" and the "six purities," clarifying that fundamentally there is neither one nor six. The Buddha said: "Since you..."
It is because you do not understand that these six enter into oneness and purity. Now, observe for a moment these six faculties before you:
are they definitively one, or are they definitively six? If you say they are definitively one, then the ear could see, the eye could hear, the head could tread, and the feet could speak;
yet this is not the case. How, then, can they be definitively one? If you say they are definitively six, then...
The body, the mouth, and the ear each have their own distinct nature; they do not function as one another's instruments.
Now that I am preaching the Dharma, which of your six sense organs comes to receive it? Ānanda replied, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "Since you have already established these as six,"
If your ears hear by themselves, they would have no connection with your body or speech; how then could the mouth ask while the body bows? Thus, it can be seen that the six [senses] are not fixed.
Therefore, you should know that fundamentally they are not fixed as one, and ultimately they are not fixed as six. Why is this?
Because at the beginning, they mutually recognize one another within their nature, they are not fixed as six; and at the end, because they mutually manifest within their function...

Since they turn their backs [on one another], they are certainly not a single entity. How could it ever be otherwise? Do your six sense organs originally possess a fixed oneness, or do they originally possess a fixed sixfold nature?
Ānanda, you should know that since they are neither fixed as one nor fixed as six, why is it that sentient beings perceive them as either six or one?
This is truly due to the inversion of a single thought-moment from beginningless time.
The faculties and objects are falsely interwoven, mutually drowning one another and alternating in succession to form the root of bondage.
Thus, within the perfect, eternally abiding, and profoundly serene essence of nature, they falsely give rise to discrimination, functioning as seeing and hearing, as sensing and perceiving.
Thus, the meaning of "one" and "six" arises from this. Consequently, ordinary beings cling to the six, while those of the Lesser Vehicle cling to the one;

yet neither has ever known that the essence of the perfectly湛 (zhan) nature-body is fundamentally neither one nor six. Now that you have attained the stage of Srotāpanna, you do not enter the six sense-objects.
Although the six functions no longer operate, you have merely eliminated their active manifestations (*saṃmukhībhūta-vṛtti*); however, the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) remain latent.
It still remains within the *ālayavijñāna*; for this reason, it has not yet been able to eliminate even one [of the six].
Because both the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), along with their seeds, persist, it is natural that one does not understand why the "one" enters the purity of the "six.

Nevertheless, although the correct principle of "one and six" arises based on the essence of perfect clarity (*pariniṣpanna-vimala*), the essential nature of that perfect clarity is fundamentally neither "one" nor "six," just like the various forms within the great void.
It contains all vessels. Because the shapes of these vessels differ—being square, round, long, or short—one consequently names the great void as "differentiated space.
Is this not erroneous? Suppose one were to remove the differences of the vessels and observe the empty space itself;
one might then say that space is one. Yet even this is to speak of "one" in contrast to "difference"; how could there actually be oneness or difference in empty space? May it be hoped...
It is not known whether they are one or different. Space conforms to the shape of its vessel; because the shapes of the vessels differ, space is said to be diverse.
However, when the vessel is removed, space is said to be uniform; it depends solely on the presence or absence of the vessel.
That great void—how could it truly become either identical to or different from you based on your verbal expressions?
Since it does not become identical to or different from you, how much less can it be said that this great void is "one" or "not one"?
Thus, to speak of emptiness as being either distinct or identical is both true and false. If the great void is thus, then...

"You understand the six faculties of experience in this same way: it is not that the nature is spoken of as six because of the roots of fettering, nor that the nature is spoken of as one because the roots of fettering have been eliminated;
these are merely words. The essence of the perfect and湛 (zhan) nature— " (Note: *zhan* is a transliteration of the Sanskrit *ghana*, meaning "solid," "compact," or "undifferentiated.")
How could your verbal expressions truly establish a distinction between "one" and "six"?
Since these faculties and natures are fundamentally neither one nor six, when the one is understood, the six dissolve; thus, by entering into the one, the six are purified.
△ Second, a detailed exposition of the distinctions among the knots (in two parts): First, explaining how delusion regarding the Truth results in the formation of knots.

Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, [the mind] reaches a point where there is neither extinction nor arising, and thus it finds its secure resting place in clear comprehension.
This clarifies how delusion regarding the true essence gives rise to the roots of bondage. It directly follows from the preceding text which stated: "It is neither one nor six.
If that is so, by what cause do the six [roots] come to exist? Therefore, this passage identifies their root:

because the nature of the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and profound essence is fundamentally neither one nor six, yet through the adhesion to this profound clarity, delusion is generated, leading to such a state. Indeed, it is the perfectly湛 and profound...
The fundamental substance is like a mirror reflecting objects; it is inherently free from defilement or attachment.

It is merely through the mutual interweaving of the two types of sensory objects—light and darkness—that within this wondrous perfection, the profoundly still and perfect wondrous nature momentarily fails to awaken and consequently becomes adhered to.
This triggers the visual essence (*darśana-vidyā*), which reflects upon and grasps the sensory objects of form, coalescing them into a single mass as the "superior" [consciousness].

The sense-faculty of meaning (*arthendriya*). Although this faculty belongs to the category of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), it is nonetheless pure matter (*viśuddharūpa*) that has not yet been defiled by coarseness or turbidity; therefore, it is called the "root-source.
It is designated as the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*); its characteristics are so subtle that none but the divine eye of an *ārya* can discern them.
Because there is a supreme essence (*paramārtha*), it serves as the fundamental source of the floating root; based upon this, the name is established, and it constitutes the substance of the eye.
Like a cluster of grapes, once the floating root exists, it relies externally on form, fragrance, taste, and touch, and internally on earth, water, fire, and wind, thereby forming the two faculties.
Thus, the visual essence leans upon the faculty and flows outward, rushing toward forms; following the flow of forms, it revolves without returning.

At that time, this constitutes the knotting of the eye-faculty. Due to the mutual striking of the two kinds of sound-objects—movement and stillness—within the wondrously perfect [state], the profoundly still and perfectly wondrous nature fails to awaken for even a single thought-moment and is consequently defiled by attachment.
It triggers the essence of hearing and illuminates the sensory object of sound; it then rolls up the sensory object of sound and consolidates it into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Although this faculty belongs to the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), it is nonetheless pure form (*viśuddha-rūpa*) and has not yet been defiled by coarse touch; therefore, it is called the "root-source. It is designated as the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
its characteristics are subtle and difficult for the ignorant to discern. Because it possesses the ultimate truth, it serves as the root-source of the floating faculties, upon which they depend.
This designation constitutes the very substance of the ear. Like a newly curled leaf, there exists the floating root (*mūla*).

This has as its external support the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*) and as its internal support the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). These eight factors—four objects and four elements—combine to form the two faculties [of hearing and consciousness].

When the auditory essence (*śabda-tanmātra*) relies upon this faculty and flows outward, rushing toward sounds, it follows the stream of sound without end; this is what constitutes the knotting of the ear-faculty.

"Mutually striking" means they strike one another; there is no mutual accommodation. "Enveloping" means to wrap and encompass. From "due to opening and closing" downward, this clarifies the knotting of the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*).
"Mutually inciting" means they mutually provoke one another. "Ingesting" means to absorb and take in. The remainder is explained according to the above.
From "due to tranquility and change" downward, this clarifies the knotting of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*). "Tranquility" (*tián*) means to be tranquil and unmoving; it is without flavor.

This is the flavor [of all flavors]. "Transformation" (bian) is the totality of the five flavors; it is the flavor of having flavor. It constitutes two types through the contrast between having flavor and being without flavor.
"Interspersed" (canza) means blended. "Twisted and coiled" (jiaoxuan) refers to taking [the essence]. This proceeds from separation and union downward.
This clarifies the binding of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). "The two meeting" refers to *mā* (rubbing); "grasping" means seizing.

A waist-drum is colloquially called a staff-drum; its "skull" (*sàng*) refers to the drum-body. From the section on "birth and extinction" below, the binding of the mind-faculty (*manendriya*) is clarified.
"One who knows the essence" refers to the ultimate sense-faculty (*paramārthendriya*). "Mental intention" (*manas*) means that the mind has deliberation and discernment as its essential nature.
One who sees from within a dark room is like a person in a place of light who cannot see those inside the dark room, whereas the person within the dark room can see the person in the place of light.
This is because this faculty of the mind (manas) resides within the body and performs the functions of deliberation and evaluation for the first five faculties.
As stated below, the summary concludes: "Thus, these six faculties all arise from the perfectly clear and profound awareness (*bodhi*)."
The essence of luminosity, through a single moment of non-awakening, possesses a "luminous awareness" that is capable of illuminating.
This awareness, being a single delusion, consequently loses its subtle, true, and thorough cognition. From this, it becomes adhered to the sensory objects such as form and sound;
for this reason, it falsely emits the radiance of seeing, hearing, and so forth. This is precisely the origin by which the six sense-faculties were first bound together. Thus, these six...
The roots are fundamentally composed of the dust of form; therefore, at present, if you are separated from the dust of light, darkness, and color, there is no capacity for seeing.
The self-substance is separated from the dust of movement and stillness and sound; fundamentally, there is no essence of hearing.
If there is no dust of fragrance—whether unobstructed or obstructed—then the nature of smelling does not arise. If there is no dust of flavor—whether changing or bland—then there is no tasting.
The nature of these [faculties] has no source from which they emerge. If they do not involve separation or union, then the nature of perceiving touch is fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then one understands that the sense organs likewise have no place where they can be settled or lodged.
In this context, the three characters "flowing out," "rushing," and "chasing" precisely describe how the six sense organs cling to objects with such intensity, resulting in manifold deluded thoughts.
The flowing is like a raging torrent rushing into a ravine; the surging is like a wild fire consuming the mountains;
the rushing is like a spirited horse galloping down a slope. Such is the force of its natural momentum, impossible to obstruct.
If one wishes to dissolve the dust of delusion and untie the knots of affliction, how could this be achieved without a mechanism that cuts across the current? How else could it be controlled?
△ Second, explaining the reversal of delusion as liberation (in three parts): First, showing the perfect uprooting by reversing delusion.
"You need only not follow after movement and stillness, union and separation... [until] all other five adhesions should be uprooted for a complete liberation."
This clarifies that by returning from delusion, one enters the six purities, thereby demonstrating the method for untying the knots.

It is precisely because the essence of the perfectly湛 (zhan) nature originally lacks the six sense organs, yet they are specifically woven together by the appearances of delusory objects (*viṣaya*) to form these knots.

Now, if you wish to truly untie them, you must eliminate these delusory objects; therefore it says: "You need only turn back and revolve the six sense organs, rather than following along with them as they move."
The twelve kinds of conditioned activities, such as tranquility and so forth, are but illusory marks of sensory dust.
If one merely attains non-compliance with these sensory objects and allows them to flow spontaneously, then the knots within the faculties will be untied all at once;
this clearly demonstrates that the practice of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching is the most concise and easy. This refers precisely to the six sense-faculties present before one.
From among these, select any single root as the point of entry. Focus your mind with diligent effort, keeping your attention fixed right there.
Like a cat pouncing on a mouse, let there be no interval between moments of mind; concentrate all your strength on this one point and twist it out. Once you have gained a single foothold, [proceed].

When external attachments to sensory objects are shed and internal faculties are withdrawn and subdued, then the faculties and objects no longer meet; thus, the familiar places gradually become unfamiliar, and the unfamiliar places gradually become familiar.
Being able to subdue delusion, one will naturally return to the Truth. Thereby, the originally existing, eternally abiding true mind manifests itself.
One no longer pursues forms or seeks sounds, forever severing攀緣 (pānyuán—clinging and seeking) and false conceptualization. Thus, of itself—
The nature is fundamentally endowed with the Great Radiant Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsaraśmi-garbha*). From this point, it emits its brilliance;

from here, it illuminates heaven and reflects the earth, shining through antiquity and soaring into the present. Indeed, when the luminous nature is manifested from true clarity (*bhūta-prakāśa*), then the remaining five sense-faculties—their attachments, defilements, and fetters—are simultaneously uprooted, and one attains perfect liberation.
Reaching this state, one does not depend on external objects, nor does one follow internal [conceptions].
The faculties: the numinous light shines alone, utterly detached from the faculties and their objects; this is what is called the "white ox in the open field.
These two characters, "not following," constitute the reversal of delusion and the essential secret: they are the bridle and reins that restrain the rushing toward and fleeing after external dust.
△ Second, demonstrating that the true [nature] and its manifestations are mutually interchangeable (2): First, identifying those who can achieve this mutual interchangeability.
"Not relying on the cognitions and views arising from external objects" ... "should be contemplated as transforming into supreme enlightened awareness."
This clarifies the realization of the True. Specifically, six individuals are cited to testify to the mutual functioning of the six sense faculties.
The intent is that once one has realized the true nature, at this stage, one no longer depends on the twelve kinds of external objects;

therefore, the cognition that arises is truly knowing, and the vision that arises is truly seeing. Furthermore, internally, one does not follow the two faculties of the superior (the mind) or the floating (the five senses). Therefore...
The light of the mind is uniquely revealed, penetrating and illuminating without limit. It is provisionally entrusted to the two faculties, where its radiance spontaneously issues forth.

Regarding this "entrustment," as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The celestial eye born of retribution resides within the physical eye. This means that by relying upon the physical eye, one attains the celestial eye.
Likewise, the present awakened awareness and insight rely upon the various sensory organs (*indriyas*) so that their radiance may spontaneously issue forth. Thus...
Because these faculties and their objects are both liberated, the six faculties manifest before one another as mutually functioning;

thus, the ear may see forms and the eye may hear sounds. At times, a single faculty performs the functions of all the others, and at times, all the faculties together perform the function of a single one.
The six functions interpenetrate, and the six faculties attain mastery. This is precisely entering into the state of "one without delusion," wherein those six cognitions [are unified].
The faculties are simultaneously purified. Therefore, the scripture is cited as proof:
"Ānanda, do you not know that within this Saṃghāṭa Assembly at the Jetavana Grove, such as Aniruddha, who though eyeless is able to see;
and the Naga Baddhālaka, who though earless is able to hear; and the goddess of the Gaṅgā, who though lacking a nose is able to smell fragrances?"
Kauṇḍinya, one who lacks a tongue can still perceive flavors; Śūnyatā-deva, one who has no body can still sense touch;
Mahākāśyapa, one whose mental faculty has been extinguished can still achieve clear understanding.

These six individuals—whether their status was that of ordinary beings subject to karmic retribution or practitioners of the Lesser Vehicle who attained these through cultivation—were already not restricted by their sensory faculties; how much more so for one who has completely uprooted them?
Yet they do not function interchangeably. Ānanda, at present your faculties are impaired and have not been fully uprooted.

If you could fully uproot them, would it be merely that the six faculties function interchangeably? Rather, the light of the mind would blaze forth, and both the internal and external would become transparently clear.

When the internal and external are as one, then the sensory faculties—both the superficial and the ultimate—and the various changing phenomena of the physical world, such as light, darkness, form, and emptiness, will, like thin ice melting in boiling water, be transformed in a single thought-moment;
in an instant, they shall all be transmuted into supreme knowledge and supreme awakening. As Āniruddha said:
Aniruddha, because he slept excessively, was rebuked by the Buddha. For seven days he did not sleep, and consequently lost both his eyes.

The Buddha then instructed him to cultivate the *Ratnaprabhāsa-vajrasamādhi* (the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination), whereupon he immediately attained the "half-head" divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and beheld the trichiliocosm as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand. Thus it is said: "Though without eyes, he sees. [The commentary] notes: "Excellent! Nanda said: "Joyful!"
Joy! These two brothers, the nāgas, constantly protect the kingdom of Magadha; they send down rain in due season, so that the people never suffer from famine.
King Bimbisāra holds a great assembly once a year to repay the dragons' virtue, and because all the people rejoice at this, it is named accordingly.
Because the dragon’s sense of hearing was impaired, he used his horns to listen; thus it is said that "though without ears, he can hear. This is called the Gaṅgā.
"From Heaven. This is the name of a river. It flows out from the Silver Elephant's Mouth on the southern side of Lake Anavatapta and enters East India.
It sinks underground and emerges at Mount Jishi (Accumulated Stones), which is the source of the Yellow River of this land.
The deity is the presiding deity of the river; she is female in form. She was reborn as a lowly maidservant due to the influence of residual karmic habits.
It is so. Pārvati was called "the Cow-chewer" because he suffered from the ailment of ruminating like a cow;
his tongue resembled that of a cow and differed from that of ordinary people, as he could discern all flavors, hence it is said that his extraordinary tongue knows tastes.
Śūnyatābha refers to the deity who presides over space; although he has no body, he is able to perceive touch, for this deity has been without a body for many kalpas.

It is suffering. The Tathāgata emits the light that uproots suffering, causing it to manifest for a moment; because there is physical contact, the pleasure is beyond description. The substance of the manifested body has the characteristic of wind;
therefore, it is said that "there is no body, yet one perceives touch. As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), both the Great and Small Vehicles possess it;
however, their cultivation of the mind differs. In the Small Vehicle, this is the cessation of phenomena, wherein only the six [consciousnesses] are ceased.

The entirety of consciousness—specifically the defiled portion of the seven consciousnesses—is called "extinction. However, the pure portion is retained without interruption for the sake of maintaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

In the Mahāyāna, this is an extinction of principle (*li-mie*); it possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the eight consciousnesses, and all phenomena consisting of the subject-object duality (*dṛśya-darśana*) of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
The essence itself is quiescent extinction, exhausted without remainder. Thus, Qingliang said: "All dharmas are extinguished; through samādhi, wisdom penetrates [this].
Mahākāśyapa said: "The Great Kāśyapa is he who now wears the robe and enters meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda, awaiting the descent of Maitreya.
The two characters "emitting light" (fāguāng) correspond to the previous "adhering to delusion and emitting" (niánwàng fā).

The light and the text illuminate and correspond with one another. That which "adheres to and gives rise to delusion" refers to the light of the conditioned image; that which "shines forth from internal clarity" refers to the light of the true mind.
△ Second, citing examples of mutual correspondence.
"Ānanda, it is like those worldly people who gather their visual perceptions in the eye" (up to) "how could the awakened clarity fail to be perfectly wondrous?

This cites the analogy of the six faculties functioning interchangeably. Although the preceding section has elucidated the principle and facts of the six faculties' mutual functioning in detail, there is a fear that [practitioners] might merely seek after external traces or grasp at this as something achieved through cultivation, rather than awakening to its inherent nature. Therefore, [the text] cites...

Ordinary people take this as an illustration. My intention is to say, Ānanda: if you do not comprehend the principle that the six faculties are purified through a single entry and function interchangeably, then simply observe ordinary people who see without relying on light; from this example, the meaning can be known.

Just as those ordinary people have not yet awakened to the luminosity of their nature and do not know that the seeing-nature is perfectly integrated and unobstructed, they regard the seeing-nature merely as a collection [of sensory data].
Regarding the faculty of the eye: because one is separated from the faculty and separated from light, one simply says that one does not see.

Even if one were to force both eyes to close tightly, the appearance of darkness would manifest before one, and nothing at all would be seen. Although the six faculties are present, they are dark and indistinguishable;
this is no different from the case where the head and feet cannot see or hear. However, if that person were to use their hand...
Following the body, one touches and presses its exterior, moving up and down and all around it.
Although the person has closed their eyes and never actually seen it, they can distinguish every part from head to foot with perfect clarity and without confusion.
Thus, the perception in the dark is fundamentally no different from the perception in the light; it is evident that they are the same. Therefore, we know that [perception] relies upon conditions.
Seeing necessarily depends on light; were it to encounter darkness, seeing would cease to exist.

If this nature of seeing could manifest spontaneously without relying on the condition of light, only then could it be called true seeing. In that case, various forms of darkness could never obscure it.
Thus we know that true seeing is such that light cannot make it bright, nor can darkness make it dark.
This means that its intrinsic nature is luminously radiant and primordially complete.
If even ordinary people can see without depending on external light, how much more so for one whose sense organs and objects have already dissolved and whose inner clarity emits radiance?
How could the essence of true awakening lack wondrous luminosity such that it fails to achieve perfect, harmonious, and subtle function?
△ III. Revealing the Nature of True Permanence (II) A. Demonstrating the Perfectly Constant Nature (I) 1. Inquiry Arising from Doubt.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said... [omitted] ...I only pray that you will bestow great compassion and dispel my ignorance and delusion.”
This was due to the interlocutor’s erroneous interpretation of the Buddha’s words, giving rise to groundless doubts regarding annihilationism, which led him to pose this question.
Having heard that the sense faculties and their objects have already been dissolved, he wondered: "If the enlightened clarity does not become perfectly wondrous, how can it be so? He meant to ask:
since the simultaneous dissolution of both faculties and objects is what constitutes 'untying the knot,' why then do you instruct one to select a single perfect faculty from among the six?"

Furthermore, the six sense faculties all belong to the realm of arising and ceasing. If one continues to employ them, one seeks the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing by means of the causes of arising and ceasing; would this not result in a discrepancy between cause and effect?
Therefore, having consulted the definitive words of the Buddha, he addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha previously told me: 'If, at the stage of the causal ground...'"
To take a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the basis, while cultivating causes to seek the Buddha-vehicle, such that one attains the non-arising and non-ceasing—this is impossible.
Thus, those who wish to seek the eternally abiding must ensure that the awakened mind of the causal ground corresponds in name and substance with the awakening of the resultant ground;
only then will it be possible. World-Honored One, if, within the state of fruition, one were to sever the five abodes... [obtained]...
Bodhi; Nirvana realized by transcending the two deaths; True Suchness (Tathatā), which is unchanging yet follows conditions and follows conditions yet remains unchanging;
Buddha-nature (Buddhadhātu), whose intrinsic awareness is wondrously luminous and whose fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous;
the Āmalaka-consciousness, originally pure, stainless, and free from obstructions; Emptiness, fundamentally quiescent and pure, wherein not a single speck of dust can stand; the Tathāgata.
The great mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is the transformation of the evolving consciousnesses back into their fundamental nature, a comprehensive reflection that leaves nothing out.
Although these seven types [of wisdom] differ in name, they are all the virtues of self-realization on the stage of fruition; they are primordially pure and inherently perfect.
Therefore, its essential nature is firm and immovable, concentrated and non-flowing, never subject to change or extinction.
Like the vajra-king jewel, it can destroy all things while remaining itself indestructible by anything; it is ultimately solid, eternally abiding, and imperishable.
Once accomplished, it is forever accomplished; there is no further change or alteration. Thus, it is clear that if one wishes to obtain this fruit, an indestructible cause is indispensable.
Previously, I was graced by the Buddha’s full elucidation of the six kinds of stillness and his instruction to select a single faculty for me to clarify and develop further.
Now, however, you again state that apart from light and apart from darkness, there is no seeing and so forth. If...

Listen to this: if these sense faculties were ultimately devoid of any substance apart from such objects as light and darkness, motion and stillness, or penetration and obstruction, then how would they differ from the "discriminating consciousness" that the Tathāgata previously refuted in the "Seven Locations"—that which clings to conditions moment by moment, arising and ceasing in accordance with objects?
Since the Tathāgata has stated that birth and cessation are its cause, it cannot [be the true self].

Thus one attains the fruit of eternal abiding. How can you take this faculty of annihilation as the mind for the causal stage, desiring to attain the seven kinds of eternally abiding fruits of the Tathāgata?
World-Honored One, if vision is separated from light and darkness, it is ultimately empty;
if this faculty is separated from its objects, it has no substance. If it is separated from the external objects before it, the thought of its own nature ceases. This is...

If the mind is separated from objects, it likewise has no substance. I shall now advance to contemplate the nature of the mind and retreat to examine the faculties and their objects, investigating them minutely through repeated cycles. If separated from the faculties, my mind fundamentally does not exist;
if separated from objects, the mind has no location. Since both faculties and objects have dissolved, the mind is also extinguished. Furthermore, with what thing could one...

Do you establish the causal mind and thereby seek the awakening of the stage of the unsurpassed fruit? Furthermore, the Tathāgata previously taught that the six sense-bases are profound, perfect, constant, and eternal;
yet now you say they are detached from objects and non-existent, being of a nature of total annihilation.
This contradicts his sincere words and ultimately results in mere frivolous discourse. Why do the Tathāgata’s earlier and later statements contradict one another? Please explain.
Are these the words of one who speaks truth and speaks reality? Yet, my own mind is clouded by ignorance and burdened by the doubts of base stinginess;
such is my state. I pray only for your great compassion to reveal and instruct me.
△ Second, Dispelling Doubts and Providing Clarification (3): First, Reproaching Delusion and Granting Instruction.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You have studied much learning... [down to] ...mundane affairs; you should eliminate your doubts."
This rebukes the practitioner for mistaking the permanent for the annihilated, yet it permits his request for instruction. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because you merely delight in study and much hearing, you have not yet exhausted all three outflows (*āsrava*).
Therefore, I previously specifically pointed out the place where delusion arises, so that you might apply effort to eliminate its seeds and remove the habitual tendencies of names and words."
Qi! Who would have thought that within your mind you merely know how to engage in inversion, serving as the cause for all delusions, while your habitual tendencies remain intact?

You simply memorize words and phrases; yet when the two meanings—the perfect, true, and eternal, and the birth-and-death of inversion—appear before you, you are truly muddled and unable to discern them. Now, I wish to directly reveal the faculty-base.

The nature [of reality] is truly eternal. I only fear that your mind—sincere yet foolish, base, stingy, and deluded—still harbors hesitation and is unable to achieve faith and submission all at once. I shall now provisionally employ skillful means;
let me attempt to elucidate this by using matters from the mundane world that are easy to understand. You will surely dispel your doubts through these.
△ Second, resolving doubts regarding the actual facts (in two parts): First, determining the matter with respect to the object of sound.
At that time, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula... [up to] ...how is it that this is not called evasive speech?
This was to definitively ascertain the nature of hearing through the sound of a bell, thereby clarifying the distinction between permanence and impermanence.
At that moment, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We hear it.
Alas! At such a Dharma assembly as the *Śūraṅgama*, with so many people as Ānanda and the assembly present, [how could they fail to perceive?]
There was not a single clever young man among them. Had they been true connoisseurs, why would the Patriarch need to add salt and sauce?

It would have been unnecessary to exhaust his tongue and lips; had Rāhula received a single blow from the cold ground, the knot of doubt would have been instantly shattered, and he would have known his home immediately.
Why then would there have been the need for such repeated questioning? When the Tathāgata reached this point...

Seeing that these men lacked any backbone and were merely drifting with the wind like a ship’s rudder, [the Buddha] struck the bell again when it had ceased ringing and asked once more, "Do you hear it?
They all replied, "We do not. When he struck it again and asked once more, "Do you hear it? they then replied, "We both hear it.
At this moment, Ānanda and the great assembly had, of their own accord, provided themselves with a handle by which they could be seized. It was already there before them.
Bring it here! For this reason, he opens two paths simultaneously, seizing the thief and pursuing the stolen goods to examine them, asking:
"How do you hear? How do you not hear? He intends for all people to seek the ultimate source within the very capacity to hear.
Yet, unexpectedly, those present only know that pure tones are "sounds" and direct roars are "echoes. If both are utterly transcended, it is called "non-existence."
"I have heard that a venerable elder of great learning has been granted a view of annihilation, following the same path as the non-Buddhists.
The Tathāgata saw that his fundamental realization had not yet reached its limit; since our words did not meet, he could do nothing but change the terminology.
He then tested him once more at the very place where he had heard [the teaching], and for this reason, he again commanded Rāhu to strike the bell and asked:"
Ānanda said, "You sleepyheads! Do you perceive sound now? They both replied, "There is sound.

After a short while, when the sound of the bell had faded away, he questioned them again, saying, "Is there sound? They both replied, "There is no sound. A moment later, Rāhula came again to strike the bell.
He questioned them once more, "Is there sound? They both replied, "There is sound. When the Tathāgata reached this point [he said]:...
Seeing that all present were entirely unrelated [to the matter] and that there was absolutely no way in, he could do nothing but follow the error with the error.
He questioned them both, saying: "In what way is there sound? In what way is there no sound? Ānanda and the great assembly answered as they had before.
Not moving an inch from its spot—this is what is called "a donkey choosing a damp place to urinate; it cannot forget a familiar scene.

To the Tathāgata, every single thing manifests the truth, desiring to lead others to realization. To those who encounter this teaching, however, it is missed at every turn, as they remain heedless and unconcerned.
Truly, they are dull-witted creatures; what can be done for them? Thus, the Buddha has no choice but to directly rebuke their error. And...
He rebuked him, saying: "How is it that you now speak with such deceptive confusion? Ānanda and the great assembly do not yet know your fault; they all ask the Buddha together:
'Why do you speak with deceptive confusion? The Buddha said: 'When asked about hearing, you answer regarding hearing; when asked about sound, you answer regarding sound.
You follow along with people's delusions and inversions, failing to realize that hearing and sound each have their own distinctions—whether they exist or do not exist.'"

This pertains to the sense-object of sound. How can you answer so confusedly? By asserting that the nature which hears is likewise like the sound of the bell—as being either existent or non-existent—you thus respond with a muddled mixture of existence and non-existence, lacking any initial certainty. How is this not mere equivocation?
△ Second, the nature of hearing itself reveals its permanence:
"Ānanda, when sounds have ceased and there is no resonance, you say there is no hearing... (up to) how could this nature be extinguished for you?"
This explains the correct principle to clarify that while sounds arise and perish, the nature of hearing is eternally present.
This serves to eliminate doubts such as whether there is an original substance of hearing apart from movement and stillness.

Since the previous discourse using the bell as a teaching was perfectly clear, yet the audience remained unable to realize it, the Buddha, having reached this point, could do nothing but add further annotations and thus addressed them:
The Buddha said to him: "Ānanda, when the first tolling of the bell has ceased, there is simply no sound;

it is not that there is no hearing. Why do you say there is no hearing? If, in truth, there were no hearing, then your faculty of hearing would have perished along with the sound, and you would be like a withered tree devoid of sensation or consciousness. How then could [the subsequent] bell-sound..."
"It strikes you again. How can you know this and yet say that [the hearing] hears both?
If it continues to hear even when struck again, then it is clear that this nature of hearing is not the same as sound, for it exists when there is no sound.

Since your nature of hearing knows both the presence and absence of sound, it is evident that its being present or absent pertains to the object of sound itself; how could that nature of hearing be dependent upon sound?"
There is. Is it because there is sound that you establish its existence, or because there is no sound that you establish its non-existence?
Suppose the nature of hearing truly perished along with the sound; yet when you say "there is no [sound]," at the second instance, you again command Rāhula to strike the golden bell once more.
After a short while, when it has faded away, I ask if there is sound, and he replies, "There is no sound. Now, who is it that perceives this?
Do you understand that sound is non-existent? Therefore, Ānanda, the sound of the bell exists within the nature of hearing;

it arises and ceases of itself. It is not that your nature of hearing arises following the sound of the bell and thereby causes your nature of hearing to exist, nor that your nature of hearing ceases following the sound of the bell and thereby causes your nature of hearing to become non-existent. Thus, one knows that sound—
When sound arises, the nature of hearing does not arise; when sound ceases, the nature of hearing does not cease. Thus, it is neither arising nor ceasing—it is the quiescent, eternal, true nature.
If you do not recognize this, what else would you seek? Therefore, he concludes with a reprimand: "The nature of the faculty is subject to annihilation or permanence;
or one might find it difficult to determine whether the object of sound exists or not. It ought to be easy to know, yet even now you still..."
To mistake inverted and deceptive confusion for the nature of hearing due to delusion regarding sounds—how can this be surprising?

To have one’s head lost in a dark and gloomy world, mistaking a reflection for one’s own head, and to take the truly eternal faculty of the root-nature to be the annihilated dust of sound—is this not to be lamented?
Now that this has been clarified, you should not speak of it again for the rest of your life.

The hearing-nature of the ear-faculty is detached from the two objects of movement and stillness, as well as from obstruction and openness; whether one is listening or not listening, it cannot be said that the nature of hearing lacks permanence.
Furthermore, the true and constant nature of hearing exists not only during the movement of daily activities, but even—

It is like a person in the world who is in a deep sleep, slumbering without awakening, sleeping soundly without awareness, in a state of profound stupor and confusion amidst their bedding and pillows.
Yet, while they are there, people in the house are pounding silk and husking rice, and the sounds of mortars and pestles arise all at once.
Because that person is in a dream with heavy sleep and clouded consciousness, their perceptions are largely disordered; thus, they hear the sounds of pounding and husking.
It then produces the resonance of other objects; sometimes it is taken for the beating of drums, and sometimes for the striking of bells.
Furthermore, within the dream, one is startled and bewildered, saying to oneself: "This is clearly a bell or a drum;
why then does it produce the resonance of wood or stone? Because of this astonishment and bewilderment, one suddenly awakens and immediately realizes that it was merely sound.

It was merely the sound of a mortar and pestle. He then told his family members: "While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding grain and took it to be the resonance of bells and drums.
This is truly 'explaining a dream while one's eyes are wide open. Below this, he definitively establishes that the root-nature is permanent.
Therefore it is said: "Ānanda, when this person is fast asleep and in the midst of a dream, his entire body is forgotten;
how could he possibly remember the two objects of stillness and movement, or the opening and closing, the penetration and obstruction of the other sense organs?

Yet although his physical form is in slumber, the nature of hearing does not become darkened. This is the true verification that the nature of hearing is detached from objects and is an unextinguished, truly eternal clarity."

It is so. Not only does deep sleep not extinguish it, but even if your physical body were to perish, your life-force following the migration of karma and your radiance fading with the end of its retribution, this nature would still remain constant.

How could it be that because your physical form perishes, this faculty of hearing would also perish along with it? Since it does not perish, it naturally belongs to the true and eternal; why, then, do you harbor any doubt?

This is precisely how the Tathāgata, using the newly unrolled leaf, pointed out the single, eternally abiding true nature that is neither born nor extinguished, as the authentic causal mind for those who cultivate the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.

Thus, one takes the nature that is able to hear the sound of pounding and beating, rather than taking the deluded state of the bell or drum; for the delusion is the bell, while the drum is merely a solitary manifestation.
It is the consciousness [that is thus]. This is due to inverted deluded thoughts.
△ Third, the conclusion indicating the refutation of permanence and annihilation:
From the time sentient beings have been without beginning... (up to) ...why do they not achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

This concludes the explanation that delusion pursues the transient and abandons the eternal, thereby giving rise to saṃsāra; whereas by discarding the transient and upholding the eternal, one immediately achieves perfect enlightenment.
This is truly because sentient beings, from beginningless time until the present, have been deluded regarding the truth and have identified with the false.
Chasing after forms and following sounds, they pursue their delusive thoughts, transmigrating and flowing through the cycles of existence, never once awakening to the pure nature within the root.
The wondrous, true, and eternal is unstained and unbound; it neither perishes nor arises.

Yet, one casts it aside and disregards it, failing to follow the eternal nature inherent in the six sense faculties, and instead pursues the delusive objects of arising and ceasing, thereby creating all karma.
Consequently, from lifetime to lifetime, one wanders through the cycle of defiled saṃsāra, transmigrating through the various realms of existence; thus, there is birth and death.
If you can firmly plant your feet in stability, raise your eyebrows, and cast aside the twelve kinds of sensory dusts of arising and ceasing;

if you detach from external clinging and subdue the mind within, turning the six sense-faculties back upon themselves to guard your own nature—the originally existing true permanence—then that eternally abiding true mind and its originally existing radiance will manifest before you of their own accord. Once this constant light is revealed, then as for the eighteen realms...

If the faculties, the objects, and the conscious mind were to be dissolved and shed all at once, then what is called the "radiant nature" would manifest, and the remaining five adhesions would be uprooted and completely liberated;

only then could the two divisions of subject and object and their subtle seeds—the delusive dust of conceptual signs and the defilement of consciousness clinging to objects—be entirely eliminated. If one perceives...
If both characteristics are distanced from and purified until nothing remains, then your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.
This is precisely the state where arising and ceasing have been extinguished, and quiescent extinction is manifest before you; how could this not constitute unsurpassed awakening?

△ Second, showing that bondage and liberation are fundamentally one (in two parts): First, clarifying that bondage and liberation are non-dual (in two parts). First, the request out of doubt.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has spoken [as follows], I now stand waiting for the unsurpassed revelation of the Tathāgata."
This cord is the very source from which the innate attachments to self and dharmas arise and are resolved.
For the Buddha has already previously demonstrated the origins of the six sense faculties, as well as their manifest attachments and their fundamental source, analyzing them all in detail.

Although the recipient of the teaching knows that the six faculties constitute these attachments, he assumes they belong solely to the category of discriminative attachments to self and dharmas; yet he still does not yet understand the innate [attachments].
Subtle afflictions constitute the root of the knots; yet, in what location do they reside? This is the purpose of this inquiry.
Thus, he asks about the root of the knots formed by the co-nascent self and dharmas. Not realizing that it is none other than the six sense faculties, he refers back to the Buddha’s words, saying:
"Although the Tathāgata has previously explained the second gateway of meaning, providing a detailed demonstration of the root of the knots of the faculties."
Furthermore, the method for untying the knots is clearly and distinctly explained. Yet, because our delusions and hindrances are so profound, we have not yet attained full clarity.
Which, precisely, is the source from which the innate knots of self and dharmas arise and are untied? Now, observing what the Buddha has taught:
In this world, if one wishes to untie a knot, it is necessary to know the origin of that which is knotted;
only then can the knot be completely undone. If one does not know the origin of the knot, I am certain that such a person will ultimately be unable to untie it.
World-Honored One, we who are still in training are likewise so. This is truly because, from the beginningless past, [we have been bound] with...

All ignorance regarding the internal and external realms that arises simultaneously with the conceptualization of a self and phenomena ceases together when [that ignorance] ceases, and arises together when it arises.
It is because of these co-arising subtle afflictions that one wanders through birth and death.
Although I have attained this root of merit from extensive learning, it does not go beyond being merely called "leaving home. Why is this? When the Buddha revealed [this truth],...

For a time it seems as though there is understanding, but upon reaching the stage of cultivation, one remains as confused as before. This is what is meant by "seeming enlightened when speaking, yet returning to delusion when facing objects.
One is alternately deluded and awakened, like a tertian fever. Only when the afflictions of conceptual discrimination are eliminated will it be like a day of peace.
The innate [afflictions] still persist, like the rising sun. I pray that Your Great Compassion will take pity on those submerged in suffering.
Regarding my present state—whether body or mind—how is it that these are innate fetters? From what point must one practice to eliminate them?

Only then can it truly be called "liberation. If you would deign to grant us this instruction, not only will we benefit in the present, but all sentient beings of the future—subject to the eight sufferings and eight difficulties—will also avoid falling into the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Thus [he spoke]. Those who wait with uplifted hope are like birds spreading their wings while awaiting their food; for they are those whose capacity is ready to receive the teaching.
Regarding this doubt: although one takes the co-arising of self and dharmas to be the root of the fetters of birth and death, one still does not know where they reside.
How could one know that these are none other than the six sense faculties and nothing else?
△ 2. Pointing Out (in two parts): 1. The Sūtra Master Describes the Auspicious Omen.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda... [up to] ...this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.

This passage describes an auspicious omen to symbolize the Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those of the present and the future, desiring to bring about transcendence from the world and cultivate the true cause, universally manifested himself as the Eye of Men and Devas for all who would come after.
Therefore, with his hand—supreme gold and *tūla* cotton-soft—he stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head; this precisely symbolizes the conferring of the "Crown Dharma" (*mūrdha-dharma*) upon him. (6)

The various earth-tremors signify that the six knots are about to be removed. The light from all Buddhas pouring over the crown of the Tathāgata’s head signifies that this "Crown Dharma" (*mūrdha-dharma*) is what all Buddhas have collectively realized—namely, the single path to *nirvāṇa* taught by the Bhagavats of the ten directions.
Question: From the beginning until now, there have been four occasions of emitting light; why is it that on this particular occasion, all the Buddhas act in unison?
[The Master] said: "Release it. And how is this different? [The disciple] replied: "First, the mantra was taught to subdue the heterodox; next, by destroying the false, the true was revealed;

finally, the manifestation of seeing gave rise to faith. Now, for the purpose of cultivating meditative concentration to perfect practice, the former three stages relied on the teachings for faith and understanding."
One has not yet been able to shatter delusion; now, by practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one will certainly destroy ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, all Buddhas collectively emit [this light]. This precisely symbolizes that the essence of the knots being untied is non-dual. Furthermore, this chapter on "Untying the Knots" is the vital artery for the essential process of practice, attainment, and realization.
It is because of this teaching that the subsequent passage on the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ" arises; thus, it is manifested here.
"Shuai" (Auspicious Omen) means to prefigure and report [the truth].
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s direct instruction (in two parts): First, the common teaching of all Buddhas.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly... [up to] "...are also your six faculties and are nothing other than these things."
Regarding what all these Buddhas speak in concert: although those suited to this teaching have attained the dissolution of the six [sense faculties], they have not yet eliminated even one.

Therefore, within the sense faculties, they cannot fully comprehend the beginningless habitual tendencies of emptiness—the boundaries and enumerations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—nor the co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).
Consequently, they falsely assume that apart from these, there exists a separate source of bondage; for this reason, the Buddhas speak with one voice.
With one voice, they declared: "The root-source of birth and death is none other than your six sense organs;

there is no other thing. Supreme Bodhi, likewise, is also your six sense organs; it is not any other thing. They spoke with one voice because the Way of every Buddha is the same, and what they said was without difference.
"Roots of bondage" refers to that which is firm and does not open; it is called a "bond" (*grantha*) because it continues and does not [cease].

It is severed; thus it is called a "root. This refers to the six knots within the roots, which arise simultaneously with the roots; hence they are termed "co-arising ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*). They constitute the primary source of the knots.

The phrase "only the six roots, indeed the six roots" precisely reveals that the roots are the foundation for both bondage and liberation; they are the chief of transgressions and the foremost of merits.

Unsurpassed Bodhi is the realization of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). How could it be...? *Note: The final character "安" (ān) appears to be a fragment or an incomplete word, possibly part of a larger term such as "安住" (āśraya, dwelling in peace/stability).*
The "eternal, blissful, self, and pure" four virtues realized through bliss and the other [feelings].
△ Second, the personal proclamation by the Teacher (in two parts): First, the inquiry.
Although Ānanda had heard such sounds of the Dharma... [up to] "...these are likewise the six sense faculties and nothing else."
This expresses a doubt and inquiry. The meaning is as follows: The three—sense organs (*indriya*), sense objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—are called the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
It is certainly true that when one is deluded regarding them, they become the root of the bonds of birth and death; yet when awakened to, they are all the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Why is it that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions speak only of birth and death and peace and bliss in relation to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), while omitting the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*)?
Why is this so? △ Second, the actual demonstration (in two parts): First, the prose section.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share the same source... how could anything else be admitted within this?"
This Buddha’s elucidation also concerns only the reason for the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). Therefore, he said:
"The Buddhas speak of the organs and do not mention the objects (*viṣaya*) or consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); this is not because they neglect the objects and consciousnesses.

For while the triad of organ, object, and consciousness has its distinct characteristics when viewed from their own nature, when discussed according to their underlying principle, they do not transcend the 'seer' and the 'seen. Nevertheless, all of them depend upon..."
Arising from self-realization, one traces back against the current to exhaust the source; there is but a single essence.

Furthermore, although the faculties and their objects have distinctions of internal and external, or intimacy and distance, they are all but manifestations of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga). Thus, they share a common root and a single source; therefore, when bound, they are bound together.

When liberated, they are liberated together; though bound and liberated together, they fundamentally possess no dual substance. Therefore, by mentioning the faculty (the root), the object (the dust) is included therein.
The reason consciousness is not mentioned is that although it belongs to the faculty of sight, its nature has no source;
rather, it arises through the mutual triggering of the faculty and the object. What are called the false appearances and perceptions of external objects are like flowers in the sky.
They are utterly devoid of substantial reality. Since they are neither the root of bondage nor the basis of liberation, by grasping the roots, consciousness is also included therein.

Because these six sense-objects have no separate substance and the six consciousnesses have no separate source, all Buddhas unanimously declare that both bondage and liberation reside solely within the six sense-faculties; it is for this reason. Not so?
It is only the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness that is thus. Ānanda, even these two aspects—the seeing and the perceived—lack any substantial reality.
Why is this? Because the six faculties give rise to cognition and vision only by means of the six objects, and the six objects [manifest] because of the six faculties.

Thus, while the characteristic of dust exists, the characteristic is separated from seeing; the self-nature is without characteristics. If seeing is separated from characteristics, the self-nature is without seeing.
One then knows that characteristics and seeing are established in mutual dependence and both belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), fundamentally lacking any real nature.
This is like two reeds leaning against one another to support each other: if either is removed, they fall to the ground and cannot stand independently. For this reason:
