The Buddhas together proclaim that the cycle of birth and death, as well as peace, bliss, and wondrous permanence, are all equally the six sense faculties;
there are no other objects or consciousnesses apart from them. This is precisely what you fail to understand at present:

that the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing occurring at the gates of the six faculties originally depend upon others, yet you establish their nature as being truly existent. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—[their essence is empty and still].
One gives rise to pervasive conceptual grasping and pursues objects through clinging; thus, the six sense organs are themselves the root of ignorance, bondage, and the cycle of birth and death.

If, at the gateway of the six sense organs, one realizes that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are, in their very substance, dependently originated and empty, then pervasive conceptualization will not arise.
Consequently, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will subside into a state of profound stillness and quiescence.
The single, perfectly clear, and truly realized nature is such that these six sense-faculties are themselves the very foundation of blissful liberation, quiescent, wondrously eternal nirvāṇa.
Yet, regarding these six sense-faculties, sentient beings do not know them to be the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the nature arising from others).
Because one gives rise to the conceptualizing mind, that which is originally outflow-free (anāsrava) becomes illusorily outflow-filled (sāsrava);
within that which is originally true and pure, it illusorily becomes deluded defilement. Thus, when cognition and vision establish further cognition, this is the binding of birth and death;
this binding originates from the root, and there is no other thing that serves as its source of bondage. When cognition and vision are without seeing, this is liberation and nirvana. It is also...

"Understanding" means liberation from the roots. How could any other thing be permitted to serve as the primary element of liberation? For this reason, all Buddhas collectively state that there is no such other thing.
△ Second, the verse commentary (in two parts): first, the introductory verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Generally, there are four types of verse compositions: first, the *anuṣṭubh* verse;
regardless of whether it is in prose or metrical form, thirty-two syllables constitute four lines, which together form one verse. Second is the *gāthā*... [text continues]

*Geya* (translated here as "Chanting" or "Not a Verse"): This refers to that which is not a verse [in contrast to prose], or it is called "Direct Verse," meaning it directly expounds the Dharma in verse form.

Third is *Ge ya* (translated as "Responsive Verse"): this means it corresponds with the prose [of the preceding section], or it is called "Repetitive Verse," meaning it is a repetition of the prose; this is because the meaning of what was taught therein has not yet... [been fully realized].

Because they are exhaustive. The *catuḥ-skandhaka-dharmapada*—this is what is called a *dharmapada-gāthā* (verse of dharma-gift)—so called because it collects many meanings into few words and bestows them upon others for recitation and retention.
Furthermore, there are eight reasons why the Sūtras establish verses (*gāthā*): first, because few syllables encompass many meanings;
second, because those who offer praise mostly use verses; third, because they are spoken again for the sake of those with dull faculties; fourth...

It is for the sake of those who come later; secondly, because it accords with their inclinations; thirdly, because it is easy to uphold and receive; fourthly, because it further clarifies what was previously taught;
and fifthly, because it contains matters not yet explained in the prose (*gadya*). Within this present sutra, among the first four [purposes], it is subsumed under the second and third;
and among the eight intentions, it primarily consists of the third and seventh, while also encompassing the second, fifth, and eighth. However, regarding the prose and the verses (*śloka*):

Viewed from beginning to end, according to the *Qingliang* [commentary], there are still five pairs and ten instances, namely: existence and non-existence, expansion and brevity, separation and combination, priority and posteriority, and concealment and manifestation;
these can be understood from the text itself. From here on, the verse section consists of nine stanzas.

Among them, the *ying-song* (corresponding verses) and *feng-song* (recitative verses) are interwoven with one another throughout the preceding and following sections. For the most part, they elucidate the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

The knots are untied; the true and the false are swept away, merging back into the hidden nature (tathatā-garbha). This constitutes the secret cause for the cultivation and realization of this samādhi.
△ Second, the direct verses (in two parts): First, the geya verses recapitulating the preceding.
"The true nature is empty of the conditioned" (up to) "delusion and obscurity are ignorance; illumination and clarity are liberation.

This should have been in prose, yet it is rendered in verse. The meaning is as follows: the aforementioned three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—as well as the two parts of seeing and appearance.
If we discuss this based on the wondrous true suchness of the original Tathāgatagarbha, all are worldly conditioned phenomena whose very substance is entirely empty.
Because they are of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is nothing that does not arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions.
There is no entity possessing intrinsic nature; therefore, all things are illusory.

Not only are the phenomena of arising and ceasing within the three categories and two divisions of the mundane world like illusions—being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)—but even the supramundane principles of enlightenment (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa, which are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), non-arising, and non-ceasing, are likewise unreal because they are manifested through their opposition [to the mundane]. They are just like space.

"Flower. This verse correctly summarizes the preceding points: that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share a single source; that bondage and liberation are non-dual; and that the nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.

If one were to apply this to the *Pāṇilekhana-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Palm), the first half-verse should be formulated as a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "Ultimate reality (*tattva*) is the subject (*dharmin*)."

Taking the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*) is stated: "because it arises in dependence on conditions. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "like a magical illusion.
The latter half of the verse should also be formulated accordingly: taking true nature (*tathatā*) as the subject, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The reason is: "because it is without arising or ceasing. The concordant example is: "like a flower in the sky. Below, this is further explained: for what reason are both the conditioned and the unconditioned alike like [the examples given]?
Are illusory phenomena and empty flowers both unreal? This is because what is called "falsehood" is nothing other than that which reveals the truth;
it exists only as a relative concept. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent.
Now, since there is no dependence, there is likewise no phenomenon that is established. Therefore, since the false is false precisely because of its relativity, [it is not ultimately real].
If truth itself becomes false, would this not result in two kinds of falsity?

Therefore, that which I describe as the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā), is neither the "truth" of supramundane, unconditioned nirvāṇa, nor is it the "non-truth" of mundane, conditioned saṃsāra. Thus, this nature is neither true, nor is it non-true.
How could there be the sense-faculty and consciousness that perceive, as well as the objective marks of the perceived?
One must understand that the internal faculty, the external object, the intervening nature of consciousness, and the two divisions of seeing and appearance are all devoid of substantial reality.
For this reason, they are like intertwined reeds: if one side is removed, the other cannot stand. Therefore, their conjunction is identical [to their lack of independent existence].
When bound, they are bound together; when liberated, they are liberated together. They share a single cause: they are equally the six sense faculties, with nothing else besides them.
It is simply that through liberation one is a sage, and through bondage one is an ordinary person. This is why birth-and-death and nirvana have fundamentally no two separate paths.
Even if you do not yet penetrate the principle of true nature, observe for a moment this nature within the interlocking reeds, and it will become clear to you.
If one calls it "empty," the appearance of the reeds remains distinct; if one calls it "existent," there is no substantial entity within.
Thus, know that the faculties, objects, and perceptions are likewise so: if one calls them "empty," they still manifest functional activity. If one calls them...
It exists, yet it truly lacks self-nature. Therefore, know that this nature is neither the nirvana of true emptiness nor the birth-and-death of conditioned existence.
Whether as empty or as existent, both are incorrect. It is only because sentient beings are deluded and obscure this nature that it becomes ignorance, binding the six sense faculties.
If one can bring forth and illuminate this nature, it is the very liberation of the six faculties from their adhesions.
One is liberated from bondage. Therefore, know that in the true nature (*dharmatā*), there are fundamentally no ordinary beings or sages, nor birth-and-death or nirvana.

For those who are deluded and obscured, this very nature constitutes bondage and knots, becoming the state of an ordinary being and birth-and-death. For those who have attained illumination, it constitutes liberation and resolution, becoming the state of a sage and nirvana.
Such is the natural law; there is nothing else. It depends solely upon whether the person themselves attains illumination or not.
This clarifies the meaning. These three verses are a versification of the preceding section from "Knowledge arises from the objects" up to "How could anything else be contained therein?
△ Second, the *gāthā* opens what follows.
"Unraveling the knots follows a sequence" (up to) "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions share one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa.

This verse serves as a direct introduction to what follows. Its meaning is this: although it was previously stated that the binding and the unraveling share the same cause, in order to unravel the knots, one must rely on a sequential process.
However, once the knots of the six sense-faculties are unraveled, one must realize that even "one" cannot be established; they are all [empty].
"To perish together" precisely opens up the doubt regarding the subsequent "six dissolutions and one perishing. As for the sequence, it refers to what is said later:
"When this faculty first resolves, one first attains the emptiness of persons; when the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from phenomena;
having liberated from phenomena, both are empty and do not arise"—this is the sequence. Regarding "one also perishes," it refers to what is said later: "If..."

To untie them all: if the knots do not arise, then there is neither "this" nor "that," and they cannot even be called "one. How, then, could six be formed? This is the meaning of the disappearance of this "one.

However, in wishing to untie the knots, one must select the faculty (*indriya*). If one can choose and attain a single faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), one may then enter the stream and forget the object;
only then will quiescence manifest before one, and one shall achieve equal and right enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This further opens the way for the subsequent cultivation and realization of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). However, although the primary disciple heard that the faculties and their objects share a common source, he still did not know what that source was.
Although he heard of the nature within the intersection [of subject and object], he moreover did not comprehend which thing constitutes that nature.
Although he heard that the six are dissolved and the one is extinguished, he yet did not know by what means they constitute "the one. Therefore—

This is shown here. That which is the single source of all phenomena is precisely the eighth consciousness. In Sanskrit it is called *ālayavijñāna*; in Chinese, it is translated as "holding" (*zhíchí*).
It is so named because it is able to hold and maintain all seeds of defilement and purity, as well as the sense organs, the body, and the physical world, ensuring they do not disperse or perish.
This consciousness is none other than the Tathāgatagarbha; when it receives perfuming for even a single thought-moment, it undergoes transformation.
The ālayavijñāna thus contains all seeds and habitual tendencies within it; therefore, its essence is profound and unfathomable, subtle and difficult to know.
Those of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom its source, and even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment cannot perceive its limits.

However, since beginningless time, this consciousness has been subject to the mutual perfuming of delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), thereby giving rise to the perceived object (*nimitta*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana*).
The preceding seven evolving consciousnesses spontaneously engage with objects, flowing turbulently like a torrent that cannot be dammed.
If one claims it is real, how can it contain delusive habitual tendencies? If one claims it is not real, how can its essence be identical to *tathatā* (suchness)?
If I were to say that [this] is the truth, I fear people would mistake delusion for reality and end up taking bricks for jade.
If I were to say it is not the truth, I fear they would abandon the truth to pursue delusion, thereby discarding the water to seek the waves.

Therefore, as for both "truth" and "not truth," both are difficult to express. For this reason, in my usual provisional teachings for those of lesser capacity, I do not lightly open [the door] for them.

This refers to those who preach and expound [erroneously]. Because they do not realize that the three—sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—as well as the two aspects of seeing and appearance, are fundamentally one mind, they mistakenly take the capacity to see to be the mind and falsely grasp what is seen to be the object. Thus, they treat their own mind...

It nevertheless arises from one's own mind; that is, from within the fundamentally rootless and objectless non-illusory essence, one grasps at sensory objects and binds together the faculties, thereby illusorily forming the faculties and their objects.
This is thus the formation of ultimately illusory phenomena from within that which is ultimately non-illusory.

However, if one can revolve the six faculties so that they detach from their adhesions and turn inward to rest, and no longer grasp at the six sense-objects, then the world will forever cease to exist.
There are, in between, the illusory phenomena of birth and death, and the non-illusory phenomena of supramundane, unconditioned nirvāṇa.
Because of this false grasping, there exist the illusory and the non-illusory. If one does not grasp falsely, not only is there no illusion, but there is also no non-illusion;
for if even the non-illusory phenomenon does not arise, how much less so the conditioned, illusory phenomena?
How is it established? For this reason, this samādhi is named "The Wondrous Lotus, Vajra King, Jewel-Awakening, Illusion-like Samādhi.
Because the self-nature of this dharma-gate is inherently present: it exists within the conditioned yet is not existent;
it is absent within the unconditioned yet is not non-existent. It is unstained by purity and untainted by defilement; it is described as neither true nor untrue.
It is called "illusion" yet not "illusion," for it is like a wondrous lotus flower that dwells in the mud without being defiled; this reveals the virtue of the Dharmakāya.
When touched by the afflictions of the sense organs, objects, and karmic fetters, these are dissolved; when struck by beginningless ignorance, they shatter at once.
Therefore, it is called the "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening. This reveals the virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom).

Because this root-nature is both existence and emptiness, neither arising nor ceasing, there is cultivation without cultivation, yet it does not preclude illusory cultivation; there is realization without realization, yet it does not preclude illusory realization.
Therefore, it is called "like an illusion. This reveals the virtue of *vimukti* (liberation). These three inconceivable virtues are unified as one.
The three virtues of the mind serve to revolve the faculties away from their objects and cultivate right concentration; therefore, it is called *samādhi*.

This is precisely the Great Buddha-Crown *Śūraṅgama-rāja Samādhi* elucidated in this sutra, and it is also the True *Samādhi* of the Vajra-King, the Illusory, and the Inconceivable Mother of Buddhas. Although their names differ, [they are one].

Yet the essence of principle is one. If you can, in this regard, externally detach from worldly conditions and internally revolve the faculty of nature, in the space of a single snap of the fingers, you may transcend the stage of no-more-learning. As it is said: "Where the wild mind ceases, that is itself Bodhi.
You must know that this samādhi of the faculty of nature is an incomparable Dharma-gate; it is the very gate of Nirvana through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions enter.
It is also a great path. In Sanskrit it is *samādhi*; here it is translated as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*), because one does not receive any [defiled] sensations or desires.
It is also called "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*) to distinguish it from that which is partial or deviant. Therefore, the *Abhidharma* calls it the "Incomparable Dharma.
The Blessed One (*Bhagavān*) possesses six meanings: namely, sovereignty, brilliance, and physical majesty; renown, auspiciousness, and venerability.
"Venerable One: According to the *Mahā-śāstra*, 'Bhaga' means 'to destroy,' and 'Vān' means 'affliction' (*kleśa*). Thus, it signifies that which can destroy afflictions.
Here, the word 'gate' (*mukha*) should properly refer to the 'gate of the causal conditions' requested previously;
therefore, this indicates that the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi) serves as the primary entrance to the pavilion of flowers."
△ Second, clarifying that the six [consciousnesses] dissolve and the one [mind] perishes. (2) First, recounting the benefit and presenting the doubt:
At this, Ānanda and the great assembly... [up to] bestowed the sound of the Dharma to wash away their deep-seated defilements.

This passage records that [Aniruddha] has already realized that the binding and untying pertain solely to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). However, he alone does not yet know the sequence for untying the knots;
since even the principle that "when the six are untied, the one perishes" is not yet clear to him, he requests further instruction once more. "Kindly instruction" refers back to the preceding verse.
*Geya* (祇夜) means "corresponding verse" (*anugīti*) or "repeated verse"; it refers to verses that correspond to and repeat the prose (*gadya*). *Gāthā* (伽陀) means...
It is called *bùsòng* (non-verse), also known as *zhísòng* (direct verse), further named *gūqǐ* (isolated arising), and alternatively termed *fèngsòng* (recitative verse).

This refers to verses that do not follow a prose narrative (*chángxíng*), but instead arise independently, reciting with melodic praise. As for "intermingled" (*záyòu*), it means that the recitation and the response are presented in alternation, with preceding and succeeding parts reflecting one another;
its phrasing is like the loom weaving brocade, and its meaning is like the wondrous movement of a pearl on a platter. As for "polished and translucent" (*jīngyíng*), it means...

The expressive text is elegant and brilliant; its characters and phrases are polished and luminous. Thus, the principle expressed is subtle yet wondrous, clear and penetrating, and manifest enough to be known at once.
How could it fail to cause the mind to open and the intellect to resolve, while the eyes become clear and bright?
Thereupon, he sighed and said: "Were it not for the Tathāgata’s revelation and exposition of the *tathāgatagarbha*, how [could this be]?"
Having realized that the self-nature is fundamentally settled, this truth has never existed as such before.
For this reason, I join my palms and prostrate in homage, expressing gratitude for previous benefits while presenting subsequent doubts. Regarding "unrestricted great compassion":

it refers to the nature within these faculties which the Tathāgata has customarily withheld from teaching for fear that people might become deluded; now, however, he teaches it without restriction. Thus it is said.
It was through the Great Compassion that this was revealed and expounded. I have now realized the nature within the faculties:
it is originally pure, originally subtle and wondrous, and originally true and eternal.

Only now do I know that all that the Tathāgata has spoken in the past is true speech and actual speech—neither deceptive nor divergent—being the very words of the True Dharma as it truly is. Yet, my mind...
Within this, there is still that which has not been fully understood. The former Buddha already stated: "The faculties and their objects share the same source;

bondage and liberation are non-dual. Delusion and obscurity constitute ignorance; illumination and clarity constitute liberation. This implies that the knots have no before or after, and liberation has no sequence.

If the six faculties were liberated simultaneously, a single awakening should manifest at once. Why, then, do you speak of a sequential method for untying the knots, such that the six are liberated and then become one?

This is indeed a point that remains unexplained. I only hope you will once again clarify the sequence of the loose and the knotted, and provide the reason for their disappearance, so that from now on all sentient beings may cleanse the accumulated, empty habits within their faculties throughout successive lifetimes.
Profound defilements and the dust-like sands of ignorance have thereby attained purity.
△ Second, citing specific instances to provide a detailed response (in two parts): First, explaining the analogy of tying a cloth to illustrate delusion.
"Immediately, the Tathāgata, upon the lion throne... (up to) "...ultimately identical yet ultimately different.
This first answers the sequence of binding and untying, establishing the certainty of identity and difference to illustrate delusion through analogy. "Immediately," and so forth.

This clearly elucidates how the Tathāgata’s words and gestures manifest together, demonstrating his skillful intention in teaching the Dharma so that people may easily understand it. "To arrange" means to adjust or set in order.
*Nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* refers to the inner garment, which is the lower robe. *Saṃghāṭī* refers to the "variegated" or "patchwork" garment, which is the great outer robe (*mahāsaṃghāṭī*).
*Kālapara* refers to the "time-period," namely the Yāma Heaven. As for "tying a knot," it means to take hold of [the robe].
He took the flowered handkerchief and, crossing it over from left to right and interlacing them with one another, pulled them into a single knot and showed it to Ānanda, asking, "What is this called?
They all replied, "It is a knot. Next, the Tathāgata again tied another knot and asked the same question;
they likewise answered that it was a knot. Proceeding in this sequence, he tied up to six knots, holding each one up and questioning them, and they all gave the same answer.
This refers to the binding knots. This demonstrates that at the time the knots arise, there is originally a sequential order, which is clearly evident.

Since the six knots within the body are based upon the *ālayavijñāna*, they are inherently difficult for people to understand; therefore, a cloth is used as a metaphor to make them easy to comprehend.
However, the general meaning of this analogy must be clarified. The Buddha uses the example of a precious cloth and flowers to represent the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.

The weaving of these into a headcloth represents the *tathāgatagarbha* transforming according to conditions to become the *ādānavijñāna*, which is the eighth consciousness, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The headcloth is originally a single strip, yet it is tied into six knots; this represents the manifestation of the "seeing" and "seen" aspects (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) from within the storehouse consciousness.
There are two parts, yet these two parts are originally one substance, just like a single piece of cloth.

It is only because they appear as the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*) and the object perceived (*ālambana*) that the sense organ and its object couple together to give rise to the consciousness-mind; this is called "binding.
Even if the sense organ and its object do not couple, the consciousness-mind likewise does not exist; thus, when the binding mind is resolved, it immediately disperses. Thus spoke the Buddha.

Below, Ānanda, a single cloth is used as a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*. The cloth has two ends, which metaphorically represent the two divisions—the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*)—that manifest from the *ālayavijñāna*.
The tying of six knots metaphorically represents how the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are formed through the binding together of the perceived objects and the perceiving subjects.
The Master said: "A headcloth is truly a single strip of cord; it ought to form only one knot. When I first tied it, you all called it a 'knot. This is logically correct.
But why do you all likewise call the second, third, and even up to the sixth [tyings] 'knots'?
What does this mean? This was the Tathāgata using worldly sentiments to inquire about matters, establishing a method to test his disciples. He wished—
This causes him to confess without being prompted; for this reason, he interrogates him a second and a third time so that it shall not be called a formal binding.
The aim is to ensure the practitioner speaks for himself. The substance of the headcloth is originally one, yet through knots it becomes six.

Thus, "one" is designated in contrast to the six, while the "six" is named by relying upon the one. If one considers the substance of the headcloth, it is originally one; if one considers the knots...

Regarding the discourse on characteristics: although they manifest as six, and while the designations for "right view" may nominally be either one or six, in reality its fundamental essence is neither one nor six. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Since you know that this cloth was originally a single piece, it was only because of my tying six knots that it came to be called 'six knots. You should now examine it closely and carefully: before it was knotted..."
The substance of the cloth is no different; fundamentally, it is one and the same. Originally there was not even one. Once tied, because of the tying, there are six;
thus they become distinct, and for this reason they are called "six. What do you think?

If I were now to take the sixth knot and call it the first—just as if one were to use the faculty of the mind as the function of the faculty of the eye—would that actually be possible? This, O Buddha...
Because they are known to one another within their own nature, [the Buddha] questioned whether they could be interchanged.
The disciple replied, "No, World-Honored One. If the six knots still exist, this is called the sixth; it can never become the first.
Even with the most brilliant eloquence, one cannot cause the sixth knot to be inverted or confused so that it becomes the name of the first knot. This was the insight of the disciple.
Because they are mutually opposed in their functions, he answered that they cannot be used interchangeably. Therefore, the Buddha welcomed his words and granted him permission, saying:

"As for what you have said regarding these six knots—though they are indeed different—if one traces them back to their origin, they were originally but a single piece of cloth that was fashioned into six knots.
If you wish to have them rearranged in order from front to back and change their sequence, their names will become confused."
In the end, it cannot be established. Thus, your present six sense faculties are also like this. Prior to their formation, they were fundamentally the wondrous true suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha;
originally there was neither sameness nor difference, and fundamentally they were neither one nor six.

Once they had been formed, the objects of sight and appearance suddenly arose, each dividing its own boundaries; thus, there came to be sameness and difference, and they became one and six. Therefore, as for seeing...
Regarding the aspects (nimitta), faculties (indriya), and objects (viṣaya) in relation to the *ālayavijñāna*, they are identical and one;

yet, when discussed from the perspective of the *ālayavijñāna* in contrast to the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), the aspects, faculties, and objects, they are distinct and sixfold. This is precisely the delusion of the true and the pursuit of the false:
from within the ultimate absence of identity as one or six, there arises the ultimate distinction of one and six.
△ Second, the exposition of the metaphor of removing the head-wrap to illustrate awakening (3). First, the metaphor of the six being resolved and the one vanishing.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you must find this [world] detestable... all are but the deluded toil of inverted, flower-like appearances."
This further clarifies that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished; it is intended to enable those present to personally realize the method for untying the knots.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Although I have tied this cloth into knots, you surely do not find them pleasing; you loathe these six knots."
"I do not wish for them to become six; I only wish that you would joyfully restore them to being a single cloth.
"But even so, according to your own principle, by what method could this possibly be achieved? Ānanda said, "If the six knots exist, then each has its own distinct position and its own distinct name.
If one were to make the six into one, then 'that' would be right and 'this' would be wrong, and sharp disputes would arise."
It is absolutely impossible to obtain [a single entity]. This is because this knot is not that knot, and that knot is not this knot.
Suppose the Tathāgata were today to untie all six knots at once; since the knots would no longer exist, there would naturally be no "this" or "that.
If "this" and "that" do not exist, then even the name "one" cannot be obtained—how, then, could the meaning of "six" arise and be established?
Yes. The Buddha saw that Ānanda was on the verge of losing his way, so he guided him according to what he understood, saying:
"You must know that the dissolution of the six and the extinction of the one are likewise thus. It is because you have, from time immemorial, pursued delusion and been confused about the truth."
Thus, there is only "one-sixth. As for the "nature of the mind," this refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), in its entirety and its great functioning;

this corresponds to the aforementioned "folded jewel-cloth. "Madness and confusion" means that truth is taken as delusion, whereby the Tathāgatagarbha turns according to conditions to become the eighth consciousness, the Ālayavijñāna; this corresponds to the previous "weaving threads to form a cloth."
Furthermore, "the false arising of knowledge and vision, with this false arising never ceasing," refers to the manifestation of the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-portion) from the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

"The wearying of vision giving rise to objects" refers to the further formation of the *nimitta-bhāga* (object-portion) from the *darśana-bhāga*. Once the faculty of vision (*darśana-indriya*) is established, the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are complete;
combined with the previous single cloth, they form six knots. Below, a further analogy is provided to clarify the Dharma: the wearying of the eyes serves as the metaphor.

The "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*) is like the metaphor of mad flowers, which represent the "image-division" (*nimitta-bhāga*). Regarding the phrase "the profound clarity and brilliance arising without cause":

this refers to how, within the Tathāgatagarbha—which is profoundly clear, perfectly bright, pure, and primordial—a single thought-moment follows conditions and thus becomes the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Consequently, there arise the seeing-division and image-division, as well as the sense organs, objects, and all that is sentient and insentient in the world; thus, the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*) exists.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth; in the world of sentient beings there are birth, old age, sickness, and death, while in the world of perfect enlightenment there are bodhi and nirvana.
Yet if one observes with the correct eye, all these belong to the deluded agitation of the mind-nature, no different from what is seen by a weary eye.
Therefore, when the mind-nature is inverted, both the sentient and the insentient, as well as the sense organs and their objects, [are likewise deluded].
16. This is precisely like the inverted vision of one with fatigued eyes, who falsely perceives the appearance of flowers in the void.

If one can turn back from delusion to return to the Truth and abide within *samādhi*, then the seeing, the objects of seeing, and all perceived appearances will be seen as flowers in the void—fundamentally non-existent. When even "one" has no name, how could there be "six"?
△ Second, the analogy for understanding that the binding of knots is solely mind.
Ānanda said: "This affliction is like the knots; how can it be resolved? (up to: "When all delusions have been extinguished, what need is there for the unreal?"
This clarifies that the knots must be untied by means of the mind. Ānanda asked:
"These six sense faculties, which arise from the dust of the toiling vision, are indeed like the six knots tied from a single cloth. I only do not know what method can be used to untie them.
The Tathāgata pulled at the left side with a central pull; therefore he asked: "Is it untied like this? He replied: "No."
"No, World-Honored One. This analogy refers to those who grasp at the divisions of views as being substantially existent; they cannot attain the emptiness of mind, and thus it is not yet understood.
[The Master] then turned [the rope] toward the right side and asked again: "Is it understood in this way? He replied: "No, World-Honored One."

This analogy regarding those who grasp at the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as being substantially real shows that they cannot attain the stillness of the object; this remains difficult to understand.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, wishing for him to awaken to it himself, asked in return: "Now I pull from the left and tug from the right, yet in the end I cannot untie it.
You should devise a skillful means yourself; how would you calculate so that it can be successfully untied? Ānanda thought to himself:
"This is an easy matter. You need only apply your hand to the empty space at the center of the knot and untie it once;
it will immediately fall apart. What difficulty could there be? You must know that while the analogy for the present occasion is clear, the Dharma itself has not yet been realized.
Therefore, the Buddha briefly confirmed it, saying: 'If the analogy is thus, the Dharma is also thus. If you wish to untie the six sense-faculties..."
To form this bond, it is simply not possible unless one begins from the mind of resolution. This "mind of resolution" is a metaphor for the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).
If one can manifest before oneself the inward-turning of the faculties and the cessation of external sensory conditions, then active manifestations will not arise and seeds will naturally perish;
thus, the partial arising and ceasing within the *ādāna-vijñāna* will be dissolved through this process.
Thus, that which conceals and that which is concealed, as well as the self-grasping *ālayavijñāna*, are entirely transformed into the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

At that very moment, primordial ignorance (*avidyā*) becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Only in this way can it be said that one has successfully applied the moxa to the correct point to cure the illness.
"The untying of the knots must take place at the heart. However, one might reasonably suspect that the practitioner would wonder here:
"If it is because of the delusion of untying the knots that one realizes the truth, then cause and condition are clearly evident. Why, then, have you repeatedly rejected them previously?
For this reason, he explains: "Ānanda, when I speak of the Dharma for attaining Buddhahood as arising from causes and conditions, it does not refer to the grasping of the four [elements]."
The Great Harmonious Convergence elucidates the coarse causes and conditions for the various transformative phenomena of the world.

That which the Tathāgata has elucidated today—the defiled dharmas of the six classes of ordinary beings and the pure dharmas of the four types of noble ones—is known one by one to arise according to their respective conditions from their original causes.
Indeed, these are the causes of the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones.
Based upon the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it forms the ten dharma-realms according to conditions of defilement or purity;

that is to say, they manifest in accordance with the mind, respond to its capacity, and appear following one's karma. This is precisely the ignorance that brings about phenomenal existence as the nature of the *garbha* follows conditions.
Therefore, when I instructed you that the untying of the knots proceeds from the mind, it was precisely because the essence of ignorance is empty;
this is none other than the immovable *tathatā* (suchness). This clarifies the cause, which is fundamentally immovable, and the conditions, which are wondrously capable of producing phenomena.
How could this be the coarse appearance known by your ordinary understanding? It is not merely this. Thus, regarding all things—mundane and supramundane, sacred and profane—...
Regarding defilement and purity, as well as all mountains, rivers, and the great earth; light and darkness, obstructions and space;
even down to a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—I know their respective limits and numbers, as well as all present phenomena and appearances.
For instance, why the pine is straight, why the thorn is crooked, why the crane is white, and why the crow is black...
Why is it profound? I have fully realized and understood it; as for the reason why I know its fundamental source:

because whether it be the holy or the ordinary, the defiled or the pure, the sentient or the insentient, from the vastness of the world down to the finest motes of dust, there is nothing that does not take the *tathāgatagarbha*—the mind of suchness—as its essential substance.
Since I now, through the principle of neither ceasing nor arising, am in union with the *tathāgatagarbha*, and...
The Tathāgata-garbha perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm; therefore, all things are objects of one's own mind.
Thus, it perceives everything with absolute clarity and without the slightest error, precisely because it has penetrated to the very source of phenomena.
For this reason, Ānanda, following your own aspiration, let your heart rejoice and choose one of the six faculties as a "perfect faculty" (*yuan-gen*); you need only focus on a single gateway.

If one penetrates deeply, then the remaining five faculties should be uprooted for perfect liberation. Once the fetters of the faculties are removed, the seeds of the seeing-part are exhausted and the mind is empty.
When the characteristics of objects naturally cease, the seeds of the perceived-part are exhausted and the objective realm becomes tranquil.

If, indeed, the various delusions of subject and object are extinguished along with their seeds and habitual tendencies, then the knots of the sense faculties and their objects will both vanish into non-existence.
At this juncture, the mind is empty and the environment is tranquil, like the bright moon suspended in the sky; thus, the true samādhi of one's own nature is fully manifested before one.
Should it not be so, what else could one wait for?
△ Third, the analogy for resolving the knot illustrates the certainty [of the teaching].
Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth... (up to) ...attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from samādhi.
This clarifies that both the faculties (*indriya*) and the knots (*granthi*) are simultaneously liberated; it is the manifestation of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

Having above elucidated the wondrous true *tathatā* nature of the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*, and since no further aggregates (*skandha*) remain, this now clearly demonstrates the simultaneous liberation of the faculties and the knots.
This very moment is the true concentration of self-nature; it is the Great *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-śūraṅgama-rāja*, the illusory-like *samādhi*.
"Indeed. For this reason, the World-Honored One again used the analogy of untying knots to ask Ānanda:
'These six knots currently manifest before you; I shall untie their entanglements all at once. I wonder, can they be removed simultaneously without following a sequence?
He replied: 'No, World-Honored One. These knots originally arose one by one, from the first to the sixth.'"
The knots were tied in succession. Now, I wish to untie them; it would be appropriate to untie them one by one, from the first to the sixth, in successive order.
Although these six knots share the same substance as the single cloth, the Tathāgata tied the knots at different times.
Since there was a sequence when they were tied, there must likewise be a sequence when they are untied. How could they possibly be untied all at once?
Are they removed simultaneously? If one were to apply the sequence according to the dharmas, that would be a case of the mind-nature becoming deranged and false perceptions arising;

it would be a laborious seeing that gives rise to dust. This is not what is meant by first untangling the knot of the eye, next untangling the knot of the ear, and finally untangling the knot of the nose.
The reason the six knots cannot be untangled at once is that the mind of a beginner has no duality.

In applying effort, one must be single-minded. Even if one attempts to practice the "work" (gongfu) simultaneously across all six sense faculties, it is inevitable that the mind will be divided, resulting instead in distraction.
Therefore, one must select a single perfect faculty (*yuan-gen*) and begin the practice there.

Once one faculty is first liberated, the remaining five will spontaneously follow suit, attaining perfect liberation. This is because the practitioner already understands that the knots are tied according to a specific sequence.
They may be removed simultaneously. Therefore, the Buddha, seeing that there were sentient beings with the capacity for reception, guided them by saying:
"The liberation of the six sense organs is also like this. When one of these organs is first liberated, then all are liberated, because their nature has no dual essence.
Thus, when one organ returns to its source, the six organs are liberated. Since the organs no longer perceive objects, the dusts [of sensory data]..."
When there is nothing with which to pair, consciousness does not arise; thus, the two types of self-grasping—discriminative and co-emergent—are first severed from this point.

Consequently, one attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Having attained the emptiness of persons, one knows that the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the world do not exist and that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are fundamentally empty.
Looking back at birth and death, one sees they are entirely like flowers in the sky. Through this, one attains perfect awakening and clearly understands all phenomena (*dharma*).

When the nature [of phenomena] is realized as being entirely empty in its very essence, the two types of attachment to dharmas—conceptual and innate—are suddenly severed, and one achieves liberation through dharmas (*dharmavimukti*).
Having attained the emptiness of dharmas, one then knows that supramundane unconditioned states are not real and that bodhi is fundamentally non-existent.
Looking back at nirvāṇa, it too is seen to be a mere illusory phenomenon. Thus, with both person and dharmas being empty, after liberation has been attained—
One must not immediately form the thought that one has reached the destination; if one does so, one falls into the realm of dharmas.
One must empty both types of emptiness, and even the thought of "emptiness" itself must not arise. Only in this way is one called a Bodhisattva of Innate Cultivation (*xingxiu*).
From within the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King Samādhi, which is like an illusion, one truly attains the non-arising (*anutpāda*).
This is the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas. One must know that the essential meaning expounded by this sutra—the perfect penetration and correct cultivation—resides solely herein.
The accounts subsequently provided by each of the various sages are nothing more than the records of their personal progress as they emerged from this very state.
Therefore, the ancient interpretations failed to grasp this meaning; their forced citations and alignments were all like the superfluous appendages of a snake.

I shall not adopt them here at all, so that we may avoid failing to recognize that this very sutra possesses its own "one mind and three contemplations," only to obscure it further by resorting to speculative theories and generating needless complications.
How is this any different from abandoning one's domestic chicken to covet wild ducks? Indeed, the original...
The "single-mindedness" of the sutra refers to the aforementioned single essence with three names, the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
The "three contemplations" refer to the present single concentration with three names, wherein both person and phenomena are empty. With such a mind, one cultivates such contemplations.

By relying on such contemplation and realizing such a mind, one may then say that the cause is the mind and the fruit is awakening; this is what is meant by the correspondence of names and designations.
Thus, the subsequent passage states: "One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; as for those who contemplate otherwise, I do not know them.
This somewhat fulfills the request of Miaoshe, briefly clarifying that there is samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown.

This is the meaning [of the text]. Some say: "From the Tang and Song dynasties onwards, various commentaries and sub-commentaries on this sutra have appeared, as clear as the sun and stars, all of which remain in the world and need no further discussion.
Yet there are certain masters who, out of a fondness for such things, have forcibly correlated it with the Three Contemplations."
One forcibly elevates the six consciousnesses. However, the meaning of such terminology has been practiced as a prevailing custom for no fewer than a day;
now you brush this aside—how can you hope to prevent those who come after from disputing it? I replied: "It is not so.

For the commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* composed by various masters either describe their own realizations and proofs, or align themselves with their own specific schools; these are, in fact, the *Śūraṅgama* of those respective masters."
This is not the Śūraṅgama of Śākyamuni. What is now being described is solely the Śūraṅgama of Śākyamuni, which comprises the ten dharma realms.
This Śūraṅgama that is fully possessed is not the Śūraṅgama of my person alone; how could there be any dispute?
I know for certain that henceforth, those who possess a public mind and are endowed with the discerning eye of the Dharma will not dispute with me.
Even if this were not the case, should they know my faults or condemn me, what excuse could I possibly have?
△ II. Direct Instruction on the Single Door (5) 1. The Audience Seeks Instruction.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s opening instruction, [withdraw] until they conceal their secret capacities, hoping for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
This inquiry seeks to reveal the fundamental root of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*) as a skillful means for the practice of meditative concentration;

it is precisely what was previously called "entering the door of the flowered hall. Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, although they had attained the single mind and the three contemplations—which is termed "wisdom-awakening"—and achieved the dissolution of the six through a single understanding, which is "perfect penetration," they were still unable to attain liberation because they understood that the six dissolve while the one remains.
Because the body is empty, it is unimpeded. Having attained liberation from phenomena, both are empty and do not arise; therefore, the mind is unimpeded.
Yet, one has still not reached the point of discerning which among the six sense organs is the most perfect and penetrating (*yuan-tong*), so that one may select and cultivate that fundamental organ.
This is truly because we have drifted like water plants through the six realms, tossed about by birth and death, deluded regarding the Truth for accumulated kalpas, and left without refuge.
"Without reliance. The meaning is like that of an orphan: although he has obtained a magnificent mansion, he has not yet entered its door;

his situation remains as if dwelling in the open air. "With what heart or what concern? means that his joy exceeds all expectations. "Yu" (pre) means "still remaining. Regarding "heavenly relations" (*tiantun*):
because father, son, and brothers share the intimacy of their innate nature, their order is natural. The one present at the occasion was the Buddha’s younger brother, hence it is said thus.
It is like a child who has lost its mother’s milk suddenly encountering a compassionate mother; having long been deprived of the milk of the Dharma, one now fortunately obtains it.
If, by virtue of this fortunate encounter, one is able to attain the Way, would that not be most joyful? Even if it were otherwise, [it remains a blessing].

Thus, what I previously received through the Buddha’s instruction—my realization and attainment of the *dhātu* and *indriya*, the single awakening that extinguishes the six [consciousnesses], the wisdom of the three emptiness contemplations, and such esoteric words—all become useless. Why?
Since there is no place for effort to be applied, it remains exactly as it was before, when I had not yet awakened; fundamentally, it is the same as when I had not heard [the teaching].
Dāna, the three voids [of body, speech, and mind] are no different from the one void [of the Dharma-realm]. I pray that you will extend great compassion and take pity on our suffering;
may you certainly bestow upon us the secret dharma-gate. To which faculty does it belong, so that we may easily advance upon the path of wondrous adornment?
"This fully accomplishes our cultivation of perfect penetration; it clearly demonstrates the Tathāgata’s beginning-to-end guidance and serves as the final instruction on the nature of concentration.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and withdrew to stand to one side.
The secret mechanism is hidden within; I can only hope that the Tathāgata will transmit it to me in the profound stillness. As a former Buddha said:
"According to your own mind, choose one of the six faculties; whichever is most capable of entry, I shall illuminate for you so that you may advance.
Now that the opportunity has arrived, since I am unable to choose for myself and yet dare not request it again, I simply seek the Tathāgata’s subtle permeation and empowerment.
[This] provides shelter; perhaps one might find a single thread by which to approach it and transmit it.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s universal inquiry:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly... [down to] "by what skillful means does one enter samādhi?"
This Buddha inquired universally of all the sages, commanding them to describe their perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) in response to the secret request of those with karmic potential.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly at large, saying: "You all were born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma;
within my teaching, you have attained the rank of Bodhisattvas or the stage of no-more-learning among the four fruits. I now question you."

At the outset, by what dharma did you give rise to the bodhicitta? Among these eighteen realms—the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses—who was it that realized perfect penetration?
Starting from which dharma did you first apply the skillful means of practice, and how did you subsequently enter samādhi?
[The Buddha] questioned the twenty-five sages below regarding the object of their contemplation.
Regarding the Dharma, there are three categories and seven elements (*dhātu*). Why is it that the Buddha now mentions only the three categories and does not include the seven elements?

Answer: The three categories and the seven elements differ only in their expansion and contraction. The "element of consciousness" (*vijñāna-dhātu*) from the seven elements is combined with these six consciousnesses;

the "element of faculties" (*indriya-dhātu*) from the seven elements is combined with these six faculties; and the remaining five elements from the seven are collectively combined with the six objects (*viṣaya*). By means of these six objects...
This is because their substance does not transcend earth, water, fire, wind, or space. By merely mentioning the three categories (triskandha), the seven elements (mahābhūta) are subsumed;
thus it was said in the preceding text: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by practicing within each of the eighteen realms (aṣṭādaśadhātu), all attain the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi.
Furthermore, even if these three categories were combined, they would not open up [the distinction between] the sense objects (viṣaya) and consciousness (vijñāna).

It is solely these six sense organs. Therefore, the preceding text stated: "That which causes you to undergo birth and death, and that which is peace, bliss, and wondrous permanence—these are all equally the six sense organs and nothing else. This refers to that very point.
△ III. The Various Sages Each Speak (II) 1. The Sages Briefly Clarify (IV) 1. The Six Objects as Perfect Penetrations (VI) 1.
Cūdapanthaka Contemplates Sound.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats... [up to] "...as I have realized, sound is supreme.
This refers to entering perfect penetration through the sense-object of sound. Kauṇḍinya means "Fire-Vessel" (Agnīdhra);

he took this as his surname because in a previous life he was a fire-worshipping heretic. "Ajñāta" is his given name; it translates as "One Without Knowledge," yet it does not mean that he has nothing to know.
"Knowing" means knowing that there is no [object] to be known; this is true knowledge of non-knowing, which is to say, there is nothing that is not known.
Some call him Kauṇḍinya; this translates as "One Who Has Already Known," and it also translates as "The First Understanding.
As for the five bhikṣus: three were from his paternal clan, namely Aśvajit, Bhadrika, and Vāṣpa; two were from his maternal clan, namely Kauṇḍinya and Daśabalakāśyapa.
Furthermore, when the Buddha first entered the mountains, his father the King, out of longing for him, dispatched these five men as attendants.
Among them, three delighted in the five desires, while two delighted in asceticism. When the Buddha practiced austerities, the three abandoned him and departed;
when he accepted the milk-gruel, the two again abandoned him and left. They went together to the Deer Park, where they practiced heterodox paths until [the Buddha] attained the Way of the Buddha.
Afterwards, [the Buddha] reflected for three weeks and first sought out Dignāga to deliver the teaching of the Four Noble Truths. Dignāga was the first to attain awakening.
When the Buddha asked him three times whether he had understood and comprehended, he replied three times that he already knew and already understood.

This was because this Venerable One, before all the assembly of devas, humans, and arhats, was the very first to hear the Buddha-dharma, to understand it, and to attain the Way. As for "Kyi-yuan" (the Chicken Garden): *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the life of Dignāga (Cienana/Cenana). The term "Kyi-yuan" refers to the Kukkuṭārāma, the monastery located near Śrāvastī.*
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the past, when a wild fire consumed a forest, there was a pheasant within it that entered the water to soak its feathers in order to extinguish the blaze;
for this reason, the site was named [after it]. This is what the *Zuanyao* refers to as the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery.

Candrakīrti’s intention is that he saw the Tathāgata, at these two locations immediately following his initial attainment of enlightenment, turning the Wheel of Dharma by means of the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths. All of these were borrowed from...
"Sound and voice: we who have attained enlightenment likewise rely upon sound and voice. Because I first understood through them, the Buddha used that understanding to certify my name.
Since I first heard the subtle sounds of the Four Noble Truths, I did not follow after the sounds, but turned the hearing back toward my own nature;
thus, sense organs and objects were simultaneously liberated, and both subject and object became empty. By this, I entered into a secret resonance with the Four Noble Truths."
"I attained perfect penetration. I truly realized Arhatship through the threefold turning of the Buddha’s voice.
Since the Buddha now asks me about the perfect penetration I have realized, I should take sound to be supreme.

Thus, these twenty-five sages each described their own perfect penetration precisely because the Tathāgata had previously taught that the three categories and seven elements are fundamentally the wondrous Tathāgatagarbha.

This is the clear verification of the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Desiring to point out to the assembly of bodhisattvas who were present as the primary audience the Śūraṅgama-samādhi—the foremost of the myriad practices—the Buddha entrusted this task to various sages, commanding them to expound it so as to clarify the three categories and the seven elements.
There is none who does not enter the gate of the Flower-Garland House; there is none who does not ultimately reach the firm and solid; there is none that is not truly and perfectly penetrating.
Thus, the fact that this section begins with the sense-object of sound and concludes with the faculty of hearing is intended for Ānanda and for those of a similar disposition in this land.
For this reason, Mañjuśrī specifically distinguished it, saying: "The true teaching of this land..."
"The essence is pure within hearing; if one wishes to attain samādhi, it is truly through entering via hearing. This refers to that.
△ Second, Śrāvakas contemplating form.
Upānanda rose from his seat... [until] "...as I have realized, form is the primary cause.
This refers to entering perfect penetration through the sense-object of form. Upānanda said that the nature of form is empty;
it is also called "near" or "slight," because a subtle atom is a small portion close to emptiness. Because he was excessively prone to desire, the Buddha instructed him to practice this.
One employs the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as its antidote, causing the mind of desire to turn into a mind of revulsion.
Regarding the contemplation of impurity: prior to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), one first contemplates the notion of death and impurity.

This means contemplating the thirty-six impure substances within the body, as well as the constant flow of impurities from the nine external orifices; thus, from the very moment of taking birth, the seed is impure.
Upon entering the womb, the dwelling place is impure; when about to emerge from the womb, the place of birth is impure;
and at the time of death, it is ultimately impure. From this, one proceeds to practice the nine contemplations on the stages of decomposition: first, the bloated corpse.
2. The visualization of the livid corpse; 3. the visualization of the festering corpse; 4. the visualization of the blood-smeared corpse; 5. the visualization of the pus-filled corpse; 6.
the visualization of the worm-infested corpse; 7. the visualization of the dismembered corpse; 8. the visualization of the skeletal corpse; 9. the visualization of the cremated corpse.

By performing these contemplations, one firmly understands that from the beginning of birth until the end of death, this body possesses not a single atom of purity; even the white bones, when burned to fine dust, are likewise impure.
Thereby, one gives rise to great revulsion and awakens to the nature of all worlds:

that the beauty which could topple a kingdom or a city, with its temperament like clouds and rain, does not fail to decay and return to white bones, transforming into fine dust and ultimately becoming emptiness.

This is because, at the outset, one uses the nine meditations on repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as antidotes to the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*); thus, one regards form as a source of affliction.
Emptiness is the medicine. Once emptiness is known, the disease is cured and the medicine is discarded;

thus, both the emptiness that empties and the form that is emptied are neither established nor remain, being swept away together. Because both form and emptiness are non-existent, the fetters and afflictions are suddenly eliminated, and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is attained.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has certified my name as "The Nature of Form is Emptiness."
Knowing that the forms of the sensory objects of desire are impure and that their nature is fundamentally empty, I attained the form of supreme purity, wondrousness, and clarity.

Having secretly realized this meaning, I entered perfect penetration (*pariṣvaṅga*). From the coarse and turbid characteristics of sensory forms, I awakened to the characteristics of wondrous form, supreme purity, and thereby attained Arhatship. Now the Buddha asks me about the perfect penetration I have realized.
"I take the cultivation based on the cause of physical forms as supreme.
△ Third, the Contemplation of Fragrance by the Youth Fragrance-Adornment.
The Youth Fragrance-Adornment immediately rose from his seat... (until) "...as I have realized, the cultivation based on fragrance is supreme."
This is entry into perfect penetration through the sense-object of fragrance.

Formerly, the Tathāgata instructed me to examine and contemplate within all phenomena of the eighteen realms that all conditioned things are illusory in nature. At that time, I took my leave of the Buddha.
Sitting serenely and quietly, I concealed my traces and practiced in seclusion. Within my pure and clean chamber, I happened to see a bhikṣu burning aloeswood incense.
The fragrance of this incense was without sound or form; it was neither color nor smoke—silent and still as it entered my nostrils.
Indeed, such fragrant odors are but one manifestation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Thereupon, I contemplated this fragrance with close attention.
The fragrance does not belong to the wood. Why? Because if there were merely wood without fire, it would not produce fragrance;

therefore, we know it does not belong to the wood. It does not belong to space. Why? Because the nature of space is ever-present, and the fragrance should then be produced constantly. Yet, it exists only when burning.

If it does not burn, it does not exist; therefore, we know it is not empty [of fire]. Nor does it belong to smoke. Why? Because one perceives smoke and smells fragrance, one may say that smoke has arisen.
Now, without perceiving smoke, there is still a fragrance in stillness; therefore, we know it is not smoke. Nor does it belong to fire.

Why is this? If fire were capable of producing [fragrance], then everything it burns should be fragrant; yet when it burns other types of wood, there is no fragrance. Therefore, we know it is not fire.
If one carefully examines the place where it disperses, there is no abiding or attachment in the east, west, south, or north.
When observing its drifting arrival, it does not arise from the wood, nor from space, nor from smoke or fire. By examining it thus, one sees that it is not produced by the wood.
It does not arise from itself; it is neither empty nor causeless. It is not born from fire; it is not co-arisen with smoke.
There is no arising in any of the four conditions. Suddenly, I attained awakening. The dust of sensory objects and the deluded mind dissolved away. The wisdom of non-arising became manifest.

In that very moment, I realized the light of enlightenment and instantly attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the Tathāgata bestowed upon me the name "Fragrance-Veneration" (*Gandhabhūti*). By means of the fragrance of sensory objects, I...
Suddenly, [all sensory perceptions] were extinguished, and the wondrous fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body manifested before me.
Through this secret realization, I attained entry into perfect penetration; thus, I attained Arhatship through the "Venerable of Fragrance.

Now that the Buddha asks me about the perfect penetration I have realized, I hold that being adorned by wondrous fragrance and practicing cultivation thereby constitutes the highest [attainment]. Since you asked whether I was a youth, then from—
Regarding the title "Bodhisattva," how does one become an Arhat? The answer is: this describes what was realized in the past; it does not refer to the present.
It is just as with the youth Candraprabha, who first attained the lesser fruit [of Arhatship] and later, in the presence of the Buddha, received the name "Cūḍābhūta" (the Youth).
This is merely to introduce the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
△ Fourth, the Medicine King contemplates flavor.
The two Dharma Princes, Medicine King and Superior Medicine... (up to)... "As I have realized, the cause of flavor is supreme."

This refers to attaining the perfect penetration through the sense-object of taste. As for the "Dharma Prince," it means that these two Bodhisattvas are capable of succeeding to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it shall not be severed.
The five hundred Brahmā devas are their followers; they served as physicians who tasted the medicine.
This describes the distant causes. Although medicines are numerous, they do not exceed the categories of herbs, woods, minerals, and metals.

Yet, as for their flavors, I know them all: whether bitter, sour, salty, sweet, or pungent—these are all flavors of flavor—and even the "bland," which is the flavor of no-flavor according to the sutras.
These are combined together in harmony to form a single compound, which is then directly employed.

He fully understands their simultaneous arising, the transformations resulting from processing through refinement and roasting, and their inherent natures—whether they are cold or hot, toxic or non-toxic.
Although he now serves the Tathāgata, his past habitual tendencies are not forgotten;
thus, by means of the nature of taste, he observes and thoroughly knows the nature of all flavors.
The nature of flavor is intensely present upon the tongue; therefore, one knows it is not empty. Furthermore, because it lacks form or substance, one knows it is not existent.
The body is the tongue, and the mind is consciousness. Yet, when observing the nature of flavor, it is neither identical to the tongue nor to consciousness. Why?
Because when various flavors do not arrive, the tongue and consciousness remain perpetually tranquil and indifferent. Thus, one knows that the nature of flavor is not identical to the tongue.

It arises through consciousness. It does not exist apart from tongue-consciousness. Why? Because if the tongue-consciousness does not taste, then flavors such as sweet and bitter cannot manifest of themselves.
Thus, one knows that the nature of flavor does not exist apart from tongue-consciousness. To analyze each factor of the causes of the nature of flavor:
it is neither empty nor existent, neither identical nor separate. From this, one attains understanding and enters into realization.
"O Yuantong, at that time I was honored by the Buddha with the confirmation of the names of my two brothers, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
Now, within this assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I am humbled to be a son of the Dharma King. In the past, it was due to the cause of discriminating between the nature of flavors."
Only then does one attain the essence of the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Now, the Buddha asks me which *pariśuddha-āyatana* (perfect penetration) I have realized;
I have chosen the cause of discerning the nature of flavors as the foremost. According to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-sūtra*, there was a Buddha in the past.
The land was named Vaidūryanirbhāsa. There was a bhikṣu named Sūryagarbha who proclaimed the True Dharma.
There was an elder named Jyotirprabha who, having heard him preach the Dharma, took various medicines such as harītakī and offered them to Sūryagarbha and the great assembly, vowing:

"May I, in the future, be able to heal the two types of illness—those of body and mind—for all sentient beings. The entire world rejoiced and bestowed upon him the name Bhaiṣajyarāja. His younger brother...

He was named Dian Guangming (Lightning Radiance). Furthermore, because he provided the supreme medicinal elixir of *sarpis* (clarified butter) to the great assembly of Rìzàng (Sun-Treasury), he was named Yàoshàng (Medicine Superior).
Viewed in this light, these names of the bodhisattva were actually seals bestowed by the Buddha at that time; they were not acquired now.
△ Fifth, Bhadrapāla contemplates touch.
Bhadrapāla and his companions [attained realization] up to the point where they said, "The cause of touch as I have realized it is supreme.
This is entry into perfect penetration through the sense-object of touch. Bhadrapāla is also called Bhadrapāla; he is also called Bhadra-pālita (Worthy Protector).

This means that he personally maintains noble virtue and further protects sentient beings. Alternatively, he is called "Worthy Head" (Xian-shou), because his rank is at the head of the multitude of worthy ones on the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
"K'ai-shih" (開士) is an alternative designation for a Bodhisattva; it refers to a Great Being (Mahāsattva) who can awaken himself and further awaken sentient beings.
The phrase "previously, during the time of Wei-yin" and so forth describes his past lives.
It was by following the cause of water that he suddenly awakened to perfect penetration (*pariṣvaṅga*). This precisely clarifies the bathing of the body in water:
when the sensations of cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness are all simultaneously contacted, one should arouse right mindfulness and investigate thoroughly why these contacts exist.
If one were to say that these contacts exist because they arise from washing away dust, then since dust is inherently insentient, how could it produce contact?
It is clear, then, that this touch does not exist because of the washing away of dust.

If one were to claim that this touch exists because of the washing of the body, then since the four great elements are fundamentally empty, how could there be any touch? It is therefore clear that it does not exist because of the washing of the body.
Investigating from this perspective, since the sense objects do not arise, the sense organs likewise do not exist; the mind that perceives contact in the interval remains tranquil and unmoving.
By means of this, one attains entry into perfect penetration and realizes that both the external objects and the internal essence—the washer and the washed—are equally non-existent.
Because he had practiced this contemplation in previous lives, even though many kalpas have passed, his original [nature]...
I have never forgotten this, even until now, when I have gone forth from the household life under the Buddha. It was also through this contemplation that I attained the state of *aśaikṣa*.
At that time, the Buddha King of Majestic Sound named me Bhadrapāla.

By means of my wondrous awakening to the sense objects, I proclaimed and fully clarified the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and became a son of the Buddha, established in his dwelling. Now, the Buddha...
Question: "I ask about the perfect penetration I have realized. For me, the sense-object of touch is the foremost.
6. Kāśyapa’s Contemplation of Dharmas:
From "Mahākāśyapa and the Bhikṣuṇī Jambūnada-prabhāsā" (up to) "As I have realized, the dharmas as cause are the foremost."

This refers to attaining perfect penetration through the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Mahākāśyapa—also called Mahākūrma, meaning "Great Tortoise," or Pīṭhara, meaning "Drinker of Light"—is his clan name.
His personal name was Pipphala, because his mother obtained him by praying to a tree. His wife's name was Bhadrā; she was his spouse during their lay life.
He recounts two superior causes for his practice: offering lamps and anointing the Buddha with fragrant paste. Consequently, he attained a body of purple-gold throughout successive kalpas.

The "radiant body" (guāngshēn) refers to baring the torso to swallow the sun. As for the "six objects" (liùchén): because the dharma-object (fǎchén) is the shadow left behind by the cessation of the five objects, they are called "six.
Regarding "transformation and decay" (biànhuài): since the dharma-object relies upon the mental consciousness (yìshí), it appears momentarily and then vanishes;

arising and ceasing in every thought-moment within a single kṣaṇa. One should weary of this transformation and decay, and through emptiness and stillness alone, cultivate the extinction of the six [objects] until they are exhausted.
The seventh concentration. This concentration can extinguish the six consciousnesses and empty the dharma-object.
Because it exhausts seven-eighths of the defiled *manas*, it still retains one-eighth of the pure *manas* to sustain the concentration.

For one who enters this concentration, whether in body or mind, they forget both place and time, and can pass through many kalpas as if it were the snap of a finger. Thus, in the present day, in the land of India...
This is the one who entered this meditative concentration on Mount Kukkutapāda to await the appearance of Maitreya.

By means of the contemplation of emptiness, I have eliminated the dust of dharmas and severed all fetters to become an Arhat; for this reason, the World-Honored One has always declared me the foremost among those who practice *dhūta*.
This is because I am able to shake off the dust of dharmas. Due to the nature of arising and ceasing...

Once the dust has been extinguished, the subtle and wondrous *dharmatā* manifests before one; thus, one attains awakening and clearly realizes the *tathāgatagarbha*, entering suddenly into perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
Therefore, all worldly outflows (*āsrava*) are eliminated. The Buddha now asks me about the means by which I realized perfect penetration;
I have taken the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as my primary cause. *Dhūta* is newly translated as *duṭo*. [End of section.]
Regarding "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*): in terms of principle, it refers to shaking off the dust of the dharmas; as the karmic dust naturally exhausts itself, it is called "shaking off.
In terms of practice, there are twelve types of conduct: first, dwelling in an *āraṇyaka*; second, always begging for food; third, begging in successive order.
1. Eating only one meal a day; 2. Moderating the amount of food consumed; 3. Not drinking liquids after midday; 4. Wearing rag-robes; 5. Possessing only the three robes;
6. Dwelling among burial mounds; 7. Dwelling at the foot of a tree; 8. Dwelling in the open air; 9. Sitting only and not lying down.
△ II. The Five Perfect Penetrations of the Five Faculties (5) 1. Aniruddha’s Contemplation of the Eye.
Aniruddha rose from his seat... [up to] ...turning the vision back to its source; this is the foremost.
This refers to entering the perfect penetration through the faculty of the eye. Aniruddha means "Without Poverty" and is also called "As He Wishes.

He was the son of King Śuklodana and was the Buddha’s younger cousin. Because in a past life he increased his offering by one meal and gave it to a Pratyekabuddha, he was moved by this merit to experience no suffering of poverty for ninety-one kalpas and to enjoy the bliss of "as he wishes. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*...
[The *Sūtra of Containing the Essentials*: The Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, preaching the Dharma for the assembly. Nanda (Naluo) fell asleep. The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Alas! Why do you sleep?
You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster; having slept for a thousand years, you shall not hear the name of the Buddha.

Thereupon, Nanda resolved with vigor never to sleep again, and consequently lost both his eyes. The World-Honored One then revealed to him the "Illumination of Delightful Vision" (*Sudarśana-prabhāsa*).
As for the Vajra Samādhi: it causes the mind to be gathered and focused so that, within the nature of seeing, one delights in seeing with single-mindedness and desires exclusively to illuminate.
