With only this one thought and no other thoughts, through right mindfulness remaining unmoving, it is like a vajra.
Therefore, this samādhi can destroy all things, yet nothing can destroy it.
Because the power of mindfulness is firm, the adamantine eye appears, half-emerging from the head. Thus, one does not perceive the ten directions by means of the visual faculty;
hence, one knows that this essence of seeing is not mixed with sensory dust. To realize the truth is not to be the same as delusion.
I have seen it. It is because within the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamental luminosity has been manifested;
thus, I am able to penetrate and discern the great trichiliocosm as clearly as if it were close at hand—just like looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
For this reason, the Tathāgata certified me as an Arhat. Now that the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration I have realized, I know that externally I do not follow after sensory dust.
Therefore, it is able to turn back its vision; because it does not internally rely on the sense organs, it is able to follow the source.
By this means, one exchanges the grape-like [eyes] for the vajra-eye and enters perfect penetration. Thus, one should take this vision that follows the source as the foremost.
The "Origin" (*yuan*) is the true vision inherently possessed by us; it is precisely that vision which previously gazed into the darkness and the vision that circled externally.
As stated previously, because that vision was the "true essence" (*zhenjing*), it was not called "vision.
This is why one speaks of "following the Origin" rather than "following vision"—it is for this very reason.
△ Second, Cūḍapanthaka contemplates the nose.
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat... (up to) "...reversing the breath and following it into emptiness; this is the foremost.
This is entry through the faculty of the nose into perfect penetration. "Cūḍapanthaka" refers to the two brothers by their respective names. "Cūḍa" means... [text continues]
Upāli is also called Cūḍapanthaka; this means "born by the side of the great road. Puṇṇa is also called Śagata;
this means "born by the side of the small road," and is also named "Successor of the Road. His mother was the daughter of a householder who followed her husband to another country.
As she was about to give birth and was returning home, she gave birth to her son midway along the journey. This happened twice in succession. Both...
By the side of the road, he gave birth to two sons; thus they were named according to their seniority.
As for Jidao (Continuing the Road), it was because his brothers were born one after another along the road. His younger brother was the bhikṣu Sūcīlaṭṭha (Sweeping-Broom);

in a past life, he had been a great Dharma master who was secretive and stingy regarding the Buddha-dharma, refusing to instruct others, and consequently received the retribution of being dull-witted.
Due to the power of past roots of goodness, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life. Five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single verse together, which said:
"Do not commit evil through the actions of body, speech, or mind; Do not afflict any sentient beings in the world. With right mindfulness, contemplate that the realm of desire is empty."
"Suffering that is without benefit should be avoided. Thus he instructed him for three years, teaching him day after day, yet [Panthaka] could not achieve mastery.
Seeing his younger brother unable to recite what he had been taught, the elder brother said to him, "If you cannot recite it, why do you not remain a layman?
Upon hearing this, Panthaka took a rope and went weeping to the foot of a tree in the rear garden, intending to take his own life.

[The tree spirit] was exhausted [with grief]. The Buddha transformed himself into a tree spirit and rebuked him, saying: "During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were a Tripitaka master with five hundred disciples;
because you were stingy with the Dharma and did not instruct them, you have received this retribution. You should merely reproach yourself; why do you injure yourself?
He then manifested his own Buddha-body and said to him: "Do not fear. The attainment of unsurpassed awakening does not depend on your elder brother. Thereupon, the Buddha...

He took him by the hand and led him to a quiet room, instructing him to recite a single verse concerning a broom. After a hundred days had passed, he could remember the first word, "broom," but had forgotten the last, "sweep";
he could hold onto the last word, "sweep," but had forgotten the first, "broom. Thus, as the days went on, his memory became increasingly fragmented.
Gradually becoming tamed and proficient, the Buddha took the broom and renamed it "Remover of Impurities. Pūrṇa reflected:
"Just as ash and dust are cleared away to achieve purity, my present fetters are the impurities and wisdom is the remover. If by means of wisdom..."

"Is it not also fitting to sweep away these fetters? The Buddha, knowing his disposition and pitying his ignorance, instructed him to observe the ninety-day rains retreat and bestowed upon him the concentration of *ānāpāna*, the regulation of the breath—meaning the adjustment of the exhalation and inhalation through the nostrils.
At that time, I focused my observation solely on the faculty of the nose as I regulated the incoming and outgoing breaths; gradually, my practice became proficient.
The mind gradually becomes subtle. First, one merely regulates its inhalation and exhalation; subsequently, one investigates its arising and ceasing.
These four characteristics—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—are what constitute "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*). Within a single breath, all these characteristics are fully present.
Within a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there are ninety-nine moments (*kṣaṇa*). Within a single moment, there are further ninety-nine instances of arising and ceasing.
Such is the nature of the single dharma of the characteristic of arising; the same applies to the three characteristics of abiding, change, and cessation.

By observing in this way that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to momentary arising and ceasing, one realizes that it is not only the exhalation and inhalation themselves that are empty, but also [the internal...].
Because all sense organs and external objects are entirely empty, his mind attained a sudden and vast awakening.
He entered into perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), attained great wisdom, and became free and unimpeded.

Eventually, all outflows (*āsrava*) were completely exhausted, and he became an Arhat dwelling beneath the Buddha’s seat, specifically receiving the Buddha’s seal of approval and attaining the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Now the Buddha asks you about that which you have realized.
"O Won-t'ong, I have entered into perfect penetration by tracing back to the cessation of birth and death and following the unconditioned, true emptiness;
therefore, you should likewise trace back and follow the faculty of the nose as the primary means."
△ Third, Kātyāyanagupta contemplates the tongue.
Kātyāyanagupta then rose from his seat... [until] "...returning the flavor to the faculty of cognition; this is the foremost.
This is entry through the faculty of the nose into perfect penetration. Kātyāyanagupta is called "the Cow-Chewer" because he does not eat at times.
This is also a case of vain chewing; such is his affliction. Long ago, seeing an old monk who had no teeth yet continued to eat, [the Bodhisattva] laughed at him for resembling an ox.

Consequently, he experienced the retribution of being born with an ox’s tongue in successive lifetimes. To prevent such slander, the Buddha bestowed upon him a rosary and instructed him to constantly recollect the Buddha.
Furthermore, he taught him to turn back and observe the very nature of the tongue-root that perceives taste, specifically at the moment it perceives blandness.
Knowing that it is not bland, and even knowing when it is bitter, one knows that it is not bitter and so forth. Through this, one realizes that flavor is flavorless;
therefore, it is called "one flavor" (*ekarasa*). Unmixed with other conditions and purely singular and pure, this is the Dharma-gate of the original ground of one's own mind.
Thus, I am now able to extinguish the mind that perceives flavor and enter right concentration. Because...
The cognition that observes and knows taste does not arise from the substance of the tongue-faculty, nor does it emerge from sweet or bitter objects.
Because both faculty and object are thus detached, one should, through mindfulness, transcend all taints of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

Because one realizes that [the self] has no substantial essence, one is inwardly liberated from body and mind; because one realizes that [external things] are not objective entities, one casts away the world externally.

Having transcended all outflows (*āsrava*), one remains far removed from the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). Having been liberated from the sense organs and their objects, one is like a bird escaping from a cage.
That which is called "perceptual images as dust" and "consciousness-affections as defilement" are, upon reaching this state, entirely distanced and extinguished. Therefore—

I attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, entered perfect penetration, and became an Arhat. Furthermore, I was personally authorized by the Tathāgata’s own mouth to ascend the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Now that the Buddha inquires as to which perfect penetration I have realized, I shall describe how I entered perfect penetration by returning the flavors to detach from sensory objects and turning back the cognition to subdue it within; thus, I take this returning and turning back of the tongue-faculty as my primary [method].
First. △ Fourth, Piṅgala contemplates the body.
Piṅgalavatsa immediately rose from his seat... (until)... "Pure awareness leaves the body behind; this is the foremost."

This refers to entering the perfect penetration through the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Pūrṇa (Pilengjiabochuo) spoke of "residual habits" when he addressed the goddess of the Ganges as a "little slave girl.
This was not due to a deliberate intention; rather, it was because of residual habits of pride (*māna*) from his past life as a Brahmin.
At the very beginning of his entry into the Path, he heard what the Buddha taught regarding suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and impurity. The world...
At that time, I reflected that all phenomena are not to be delighted in. While practicing alms-gathering, I contemplated entering this meditative observation;

unaware, a thorn pierced my foot on the road. Because I was contemplating things that are not to be delighted in, I encountered an object that was not to be delighted in—this too was a karmic occasion for awakening and realization.
At that moment, the poison spread through my body, and I experienced intense, agonizing pain throughout. I then thought: "This body possesses..."
Only through knowing can one understand this profound suffering. At the very moment of profound suffering, one must establish the foundation of one's footing so as not to be swayed by the pain.
One should then immediately investigate: "Ultimately, who is it that knows this pain?
Through this, one comes to know that although the body possesses sensation and perceives profound suffering, my fundamentally awakened, pure mind is truly without [such sensation].
There is pain. This mind that perceives pain—I further reflect:
in such a single body, how could there be both the sensation of pain and a perception that does not reach it? Could this single body possess two distinct perceptions?
If there were two simultaneous awakenings, it would follow that there must be two Buddhas—is such a principle possible?

Thereupon, he secured the firm gate, gathered his mental conceptions, and returned to the pure awakened mind. Before long, the painful false body and the perceiving false mind were suddenly forgotten both at once;
with the mind empty, he attained the "first place" and entered perfect penetration in no more than twenty-one days.

Within this, all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted completely without remainder. It is the pure, singular, original enlightenment, the true mind of clarity, forever free from false and delusive cognitions.
Having attained the state of an Arhat, I received the personal seal of approval from the Tathāgata.

I have realized the true mind and perfected the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Now that the Buddha asks about the means by which I attained perfect penetration, I shall speak of my singular...
Fundamental enlightenment (benjue) involves casting off the deluded body and mind to enter perfect penetration; thus, one should take this body-faculty of pure enlightenment as the foremost.
△ Fifth, the contemplative intent of Ākāśagarbha.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to the source of the Dharma; this is the foremost [attainment].
This is entry into perfect penetration through the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). Subhūti is called "Born of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-ja*) and also "Well-Appeared" (*Sujāta*), among other names.
Because at the time of birth he manifested emptiness, his mind attained emptiness, and he constantly practiced the conduct of emptiness, he was thus named.
It is said that since kalpas past, due to the emptiness of his own mind, all phenomena have been empty; therefore, he has attained everything without obstruction.
He recalls his own deaths and rebirths as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, yet he has never experienced the confusion of the intermediate state between lives.

Regarding the delusion of dwelling in the womb: at the very beginning of this life, while still in the mother’s womb, one immediately knows that all dharmas are empty and quiescent in their essential nature.
Although one undergoes birth according to worldly conditions, the principle of emptiness remains unobscured, such that the five aggregates, body, and mind are fully understood.
Each and every one is ultimately ungraspable. Not only is the primary retribution (the physical body) empty, but the secondary retribution (the external environment) is likewise so.
Beyond the mother’s own body, extending throughout the ten directions, all becomes empty and quiescent.

Upon emerging from the womb, she extensively transforms sentient beings, causing each and every one to realize the nature of emptiness and quiescence—what is known as the emptiness of both person and phenomena, and the quiescence of both self and other. Yet, even so...

Not yet having attained the wondrous existence within true emptiness, I further received from the Tathāgata the revelation of the true emptiness of the nature of awakening and the true awakening of the nature of emptiness.
Thereupon, I attained fundamental right wisdom and realized the true emptiness of self-nature;
moreover, there was neither the wisdom that realizes nor the emptiness that is realized. Thus, through the identity of wisdom and principle, the nature of emptiness is finally perfected.
He attained Arhatship and immediately realized the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, the wondrous nature of precious luminosity, the oceanic treasury of true emptiness.
Thereupon, he came to know as the Buddha knows and see as the Buddha sees. Having received the Buddha’s seal of approval, he perfected the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Although he realized that his own nature is fundamentally empty, he did not remain stagnant in emptiness; thus, he was able to liberate himself from the nature of emptiness and enter [the ultimate state].
This is perfect penetration (*yuantong*). The Buddha now asks about the perfect penetration realized by each; I have entered all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) into the markless.
Both the subject that negates and the object that is negated are completely eliminated. Internally, the method of turning back the faculties returns to original non-being (*mūla-abhāva*).
Thus, I take this method of liberating through the turning back of the faculties as the foremost. These aforementioned characters—*fei* (non-), *wu* (no-), and *jin* (exhausted)—are used here.
This is merely a variation of the term "emptiness. First, by means of single emptiness, one empties all marks; hence it is said, "all marks enter into non-being.

Next, by means of double emptiness, one further empties that non-being of marks; hence it is said, "that which is non-being is exhausted. This is precisely the simultaneous emptiness of persons and dharmas.
△ III. The Six Consciousnesses Attaining Perfect Penetration (6) 1. Śāriputra’s Eye-Consciousness.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet... [until] "...this supreme knowledge and vision is the foremost."
This refers to entering the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*) through eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Śāriputra is called "The Son of the Śāri Bird.
When the mind perceives, it is precisely eye-consciousness; because it does not give rise to delusive defilements regarding the objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), it is called "pure.

Regarding both the mundane and supramundane—namely, all phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)—it is due to defiled causes and conditions that there arise the various transformations of the mundane world.
Through the purification of causes and conditions, there arise various supramundane transformations. These are perceived solely by the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*);

upon a single glance, they are penetrated, clearly understood, and attained without obstruction. There is no need for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to exert effort through conceptualization and investigation before one comes to know them.
This precisely demonstrates that the visual consciousness has been so sharp and lucid throughout many eons. However, in this present life, it was not previously...
"Venerable One, on the road I happened to encounter Kāśyapa, who was traveling together with his brothers.
For my sake, he proclaimed the Dharma of dependent origination: 'What I teach is emptiness; it is also called a provisional designation.'"
This is also called the meaning of the Middle Way. Upon hearing this verse but once, he immediately attained awakening to all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds:
that they take form through the mind; that dharmas are fundamentally unarisen; and that the mind is empty across the three periods of time. As it is said:

"If one seeks the mind throughout the three periods, the mind is not found. Where the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent. Where delusion is fundamentally non-existent, that is itself Bodhi. Thus, birth [is extinguished].
Death and nirvana are fundamentally equal; it was upon this realization that he resolved his mind and left the household life under the Buddha.

Although his discernment previously was capable of thorough penetration, it had not yet attained perfect clarity; now, with delusions exhausted and reality fully realized, he has attained true and correct discernment.
When consciousness is refined, lucid, and perfect, one enters through universal penetration (*samyak-prativedha*). Consequently, regarding both principle and phenomena, nothing remains obscure;
one attains great mastery and is endowed with the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*). It is precisely because of this authentic insight and discernment that what is spoken is fearless.
By this means, he severed the fetters and became an Arhat. Among the assembly, he was foremost in wisdom;
by virtue of his wisdom, he held the preeminent position as the Buddha’s eldest son. Having attained the Dharma-body through hearing the Buddha’s teachings, he was "born from the mouth of the Buddha.
Having been refined and gradually imbued within the dispensation, nurturing the holy embryo, he was "born through transformation from the Dharma."
Now, as the Buddha asks me about the perfect penetration I have realized, I shall manifest the light of wisdom through my visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
When this light of wisdom reaches its ultimate limit, it penetrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, by means of this mind-vision that emits light, I am ranked first.
Here, the "seeing-awareness" and "mind-seeing" mentioned above refer to the visual consciousness.
△ Second, Samantabhadra’s Ear-Consciousness.
"The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra immediately rose from his seat" (extending to) "...this mastery of discernment is foremost.

This entry into perfect penetration is through the ear-consciousness. Regarding Samantabhadra: his practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm, hence he is called "Universal" (*Samanta*); his rank is adjacent to [Buddhahood].
The ultimate sage is called "Worthy. The faculties of a Bodhisattva refer to the faculties of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
The "Practices of Samantabhadra" refers precisely to the Ten Great Vows; it is these that cause every single color and fragrance to pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
That all are designated by the name "Practices of Samantabhadra" clearly demonstrates the vastness of the established model. "Mental hearing" means not relying on the ears.
The sense organs [are distinct], yet when the ear-consciousness is produced by means of the mind-organ (*manas-indriya*), one knows that a single organ can produce all six consciousnesses;

this clarifies the sovereign freedom of their mutual functioning. "That which is manifested within the mind" means that since it does not issue forth from the mouth, if it were not heard by the mind, who could possibly know it?
This is precisely the subtlety of resonance and response. "If, below... clarifies the manifestation of the stimulus and the manifestation of the response, even though...

The former refers to the profound depth; the latter clarifies that the faculty is profound and the response is profound. This, moreover, is the subtle wonder of the faculty and its response coinciding like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a chick and its mother.

The meaning is this: when the Buddha now inquires about the perfect penetration realized, my statement regarding the original cause for cultivation and realization—that "mental hearing" refers precisely to the ear-consciousness—is because by contemplating the ear-consciousness, one reveals the nature of the storehouse (ālaya-vijñāna) and attains entry into perfect penetration. Therefore, it is obtained.
The divine transformations are unfathomable, and the wondrous responses are without fixed direction; yet, they are characterized by sovereign discernment.
Thus, one should take this mind as the primary faculty for hearing and auditory consciousness. Question: Why not take this [consciousness] instead, but rather take the sense organ?

Answer: Without the sense object, the organ cannot perform discernment; without the sense organ, consciousness does not arise. The organ is proximate to consciousness, whereas the object is remote; therefore—
It is not taken up. Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "the mind hears": although this is indeed the true cause, it is nonetheless severed from the initial mind.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī distinguished it. If one were to discuss the similarities and differences regarding Avalokiteśvara, the single cause is different; it is the skillful means of the initial mind.

Second, the objects are different; this constitutes the perfect penetration of the ear faculty. Third, the hearing is different; since that [method] prioritizes the extraction from suffering, it is not the same as this.
△ Third, Nanda’s nose-consciousness.
Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...until he attained the perfection of clarity and extinguished all outflows;

this was ranked as the foremost. This [attainment] entered the perfect penetration through nose-consciousness. "Sundara" means "lovely" or "beloved," which is the name of his wife. "Nanda" means "joy," which is his own name.
In the Ci'en tradition, these two names are translated together as "Glorious Joy. This was done to distinguish him from Gopā.
Nanda, for this reason, his wife was specifically mentioned; he was the biological younger brother of the Tathāgata.
Because his worldly attachments did not cease upon his initial renunciation, the Buddha ordered him to observe the tip of the nose with Kauṣṭhila to remedy his mental distraction.
For the first three weeks, he observed the incoming and outgoing breaths, which appeared like smoke; this is because the inhalation and exhalation of the nasal breath arise from wind and fire.
The turbidity of afflictions agitates [the mind], and thus its manifestation is like smoke and flames. This clarifies the initial stage of practice:
one begins by observing at the coarse level because those who are distracted possess coarse and turbid vital energy (*kāya-vāyu*).
From this point, one gradually observes until the root-body and the vessel-world both become smoke and flames. As one enters deeper and deeper, pure contemplation manifests before them.
As the afflictions are thinned and diminished, the body and mind internally emit a brilliant light that is perfect and penetrating.
Both the primary and secondary realms become universally empty and luminous, becoming pure all at once. At this time, the internal and external reflect one another with clarity, like lapis lazuli.
This is because the contemplating mind is purely clean and about to give rise to the wisdom of emptiness; therefore, one sees the appearance of smoke gradually dissipate.
It ceased, and the breath entering and exiting through his nostrils turned white. In an instant, his mind opened and his understanding was resolved;
he realized and entered perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). All outflows (*āsrava*) were forever exhausted from this point on.
What had previously been exhalations and inhalations—appearing as smoke and flames—now all transformed into light and radiance. Not only did they become perfectly round...
My body pervades the worlds of the ten directions; through this body and these worlds, I illuminate everything without exception and have thus attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Therefore, the World-Honored One prophesied that I am able to turn back afflictions and shall attain Bodhi. Now, as the Buddha asks me about the perfect penetration I have realized, I rely on my olfactory consciousness:
I know the exhalation and the inhalation, dissolving and transforming turbid breath into pure breath. For a long time...
Thus, illumination is revealed; the light becomes perfect and full, whereby all outflows (*āsrava*) are extinguished and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) is realized.
One should therefore take this cessation of the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna*) as the foremost method. Question: What is the difference between this and the case of Pāṇḍaka? Answer:

The former concerned the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), instructing him to regulate his breath and collect his mind to give rise to wisdom. The present one concerns the nose-consciousness, instructing him...
He focuses his mind on the white [object] to eliminate distraction. Since the faculties and the teachings differ, they are naturally distinct from one another.
△ Fourth, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s tongue-consciousness:
[from] "Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra" [to] "he is foremost in the extinction of all outflows."
This refers to his entry into perfect penetration through the consciousness of the tongue. His father’s name was Pūrṇa, meaning "Full," and his mother’s name was Maitrāyaṇī, meaning "Compassionate.
This Venerable One was named after his parents; thus he is called the Son of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. "I, throughout kalpas of antiquity" describes the distant causes.
There are four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*): first, unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), which knows the general characteristics of all dharmas.

1. Unimpededness regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pratisaṃvid*): knowing the specific characteristics of all phenomena. 2. Unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): because there is no exhaustion or end [to the meanings]. 3.

Unimpededness regarding language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): because there is no weariness or fatigue [in teaching]. Suffering (*duḥkha*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are the provisional meanings of the Three Vehicles; true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is the ultimate meaning of the One Vehicle.
One who penetrates deeply realizes that worldly birth-and-death is impure, impermanent, suffering, and empty, and perceives its very substance as such.
This is precisely the supramundane *nirvāṇa*—eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is the non-duality of the provisional and the real.

Whether it be one Buddha, two Buddhas, or even as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, regarding these profound and secret, hidden and subtle Dharma-gates, I am able to reveal each one among the great assembly through subtle and refined principles and skillful expressions.
All of this is possible because he has attained the four kinds of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*). Indeed, the Buddha possesses three wheels (*cakra*):
the wheel of the body, which manifests supernatural powers; the wheel of speech, which expounds the Dharma; and the wheel of the mind, which discerns the capacities of sentient beings.

He is named Ajita, which means "Invincible. Because he was born endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence and his noble virtue is unsurpassed, he is now addressed by his clan name as Maitreya. Furthermore, there are three reasons for this: first, due to his original vow;

Because of his samādhi. Thirdly, because while his mother was carrying him in her womb, he already possessed a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*). Furthermore, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* states:

"Any sentient being who sees him immediately attains the samādhi of loving-kindness. From the passage beginning with "I recall in the past" down to "entering into samādhi," he recounts the events from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) entering the state of a sage (*ārya*), which occurred during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
At the time he was still an ordinary person, he had not yet realized that all phenomena are mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
Therefore, my back was turned to the Way as I pursued external objects; though my body had left the household life, my mind was not stained by the Path.
I valued only worldly fame, reputation, profit, and sustenance, and delighted only in associating with the noble and the great clans.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught me to practice the samādhi of "the three realms are mind-only" and "all phenomena are consciousness-only," so that I might enter into *samādhi*. This was...

This is the medicine for those who have realized the truth. For those who, out of attachment to worldly fame and lineage, give rise to vain pursuits because they perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind and cling to names and forms, one bestows the concentration of Mind-Only Consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti*). This "only" (*mātra*) serves to negate the existence of external objects.
Consciousness is distinguished from the mind and is empty. If one attains this samādhi, then objects are subsumed within the mind;
looking back upon all fame, profit, gain, and noble lineage, they are all like illusions and transformations—not merely like worn-out shoes. What is there to crave or seek?
From that time forth, throughout successive kalpas, one has served [the Buddhas] by means of this very Samādhi of Consciousness-Only.
After all the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, had practiced for a long time, their power of meditative concentration became profound.
They realized that all phenomena are nothing but one's own fundamental mind; thus, they cultivated only internal contemplation and no longer sought externally.

Consequently, the mind that seeks worldly fame was finally able to cease abruptly, being extinguished until it no longer existed. Progressing in this manner, I reached the era of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, whereupon I attained [Buddhahood].

The supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the mind-consciousness suddenly awakens to the nature of consciousness, clearly knowing that the luminous clarity of awareness is the true consciousness—the wondrous true suchness-nature of the fundamental Tathāgata-garbha.

Not only can it empty all worldly fame and noble lineages, but it can even exhaustively empty all supramundane realms of self-realization by all Tathāgatas, including the land of eternal quiescent light. By means of this—
Whether it be the purity of the supramundane, the defilement of the mundane, the conditioned existence of the six realms, or the unconditioned state of the four types of noble ones—
all are nothing other than manifestations of my own conscious mind. World-Honored One, since I have realized that all such phenomena of the mundane and supramundane,
the holy and the ordinary, the defiled and the pure, are manifested solely by the mind and consciousness, there is nothing further [to be grasped].
It is not another thing. For this reason, from this very nature of consciousness, there already flow forth immeasurable realms of quiescence and immeasurable Buddhas;
how much more so would the nine realms of existence, including both the environment and its inhabitants, not flow forth? This clarifies that one’s own mind creates the Buddha.
One’s own mind is itself the Buddha; one’s own mind is the Buddha. All things—both the environment and its inhabitants—are but consciousness and but mind;
there is no other dharma whatsoever. Having clarified this principle, I have now received the Bodhisattva prediction that I shall succeed my Buddha in his place.
When the Buddha questioned me regarding the perfect penetration I have realized, I replied that through the Great Element of Consciousness, I have observed all things with true discernment.
Mind-only and the ten directions are but consciousness-only. To realize that consciousness and mind are non-dual is to attain the single essence of perfect luminosity;

thus, one is able to fully accomplish the nature of reality. By means of this true nature, while the emotional [subjective] aspect is non-existent, the principle [objective] aspect exists; while appearances are non-existent, the nature exists.

Therefore, one is able to remain far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which has appearance yet lacks intrinsic existence; and from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which exists in the mind but not in reality.

For indeed, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the truth, while the imagined nature is delusion. The pure portion of the dependent nature accords with the truth, while its defiled portion accords with delusion.

By remaining far removed from these two types of emotional attachments—the dependent and the imagined—one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enters into perfect penetration. This is precisely what it means.

To contemplate consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) through this truth is the foremost [method]. Regarding consciousness-only, it says: first is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The verse states:
"By means of various pervasive conceptualizations, One conceptualizes various things; This nature of pervasive conceptualization Is non-existent in its own-being. The commentary says:
Because it universally and exhaustively calculates and deliberates, it is called "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*). Its categories are numerous; thus it is said:

Those various [entities]—namely, the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness—which, throughout all defiled and pure phenomena, falsely conceptualize them as real self and dharmas, are called the "thoroughly imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It is like a snake [imagined] upon a rope. Second is the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The verse says:

"The dependent nature is that which arises from conditions through discrimination. The commentary states: "It refers to the essence and the characteristics of the mind and mental factors produced by a multitude of conditions."

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) arises entirely in dependence upon other conditions; because it arises through the mutual conjunction of dependent conditions, it is like a magical illusion or a rope on a heap of sesame seeds.
Regarding the third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the verse says: "The perfected nature is that which, in relation to the former, is eternally devoid of its nature.
The commentary states: This refers to that very [dependent nature]; it is eternally devoid... of the former nature upon that dependent-arising (*paratantra*).
It is of the nature of true suchness (tathatā) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, which is free from the previously mentioned parikalpita-parikalpita (imagined nature).
However, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is the essence of consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātratā). From the conceptualization of the dependent nature, it is the imagined;

from the realization of reality within the dependent nature, it is the perfected (pariniṣpanna). This is the single, true, empty, perfect, and fully realized nature of suchness. Therefore, it is said:

This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). In this regard, it is like the hemp remaining alone. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like a snake;

the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is like a rope; the perfected nature is like the hemp. Even the production of a rope from hemp is still false, let alone the further production of a snake upon the rope."

The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta and his peers [attained] samādhi; this is the foremost.

This proceeds from the greatness of the roots (*indriya*) to enter perfect penetration. Regarding the sequence of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), the roots are presented first and consciousness last; now, first—

It serves as a bridge for the Dharma in the final age, and much depends upon it. Furthermore, this samādhi is also called the "King of Samādhis," because it is able to encompass and govern all other samādhis.
According to the *Amitābha Sūtra*, it uses the light of wisdom to universally illumine all things, causing them to...
He has departed from the three miserable realms and attained supreme power; thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"In the past, during the causal stage, when Amitābha was a universal monarch (cakravartin), Avalokiteśvara was his eldest son and Mahāsthāmaprāpta was his second son.

Now, in Sukhāvatī, they dwell at the Buddha’s left and right, serving as assistants in his transformation of beings. "Of the same class" means of equal category. [This refers to] the twelve Tathāgatas.

The final Buddha among them was named Surpassing the Light of the Sun and Moon. That Buddha taught me the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).
Samādhi. Furthermore, there are three types of this samādhi that must be distinguished. First, mindfulness solely of one’s own Buddha; second, mindfulness solely of another Buddha;

third, mindfulness of both oneself and another. If one achieves the realization that one's own mind is the Buddha through mindfulness solely of one's own Buddha, then one is identical to those who attained the twenty-four kinds of perfect penetration. This, then, encompasses all of them.
All teachings and all Chan school methods of direct pointing are fully and exhaustively contained herein.
If one contemplates only another Buddha, this differs from the twenty-four kinds of perfect penetration;

for there, the six sense organs act as the subject of contemplation and Amitābha as the object of contemplation, seeking rebirth through the continuous succession of pure mindfulness. This, however, encompasses both the Amitābha and Bhaiṣajyaguru traditions.
The *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Pure Land* and other such scriptures, as well as the methods for contemplating the affairs of the Lotus Society, are all set forth here exhaustively.
If one contemplates both oneself and others together, then among the twenty-four kinds of perfect penetration (*pūrṇa-abhijñā*), they are both identical and yet distinct.

First, one must open up the understanding of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*samyak-sadyas-naya*), realizing that the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without difference. One's own mind and the Buddhas of others are fundamentally and originally non-dual.
This involves relying upon another Buddha to manifest one's own mind; this is the point where one opens the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), which is the same as that of all the sages.

However, the point of relying upon another Buddha is what distinguishes [this teaching] from other sages; thus, it is what the *Amitābha Sūtra* refers to as the "superior and extraordinary skillful means" (*viśiṣṭopāya*).
Those who today attain the opening of their minds without depending on such skillful means do so because these skillful means are the most superior and extraordinary. Furthermore...
No other expedient means are required. Now, regarding this mindfulness of the Dharma, it is like these two people existing at present:

one person is exclusively mindful, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings; the other person is exclusively forgetful, which is a metaphor for sentient beings’ mindfulness of the Buddha.
Because the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings never ceases for even a moment, it is said that "whether encountering or seeing them. As for what can be done...

Sentient beings lack the mind to recollect the Buddha; therefore, it is said that they do not encounter him and do not see him. Suppose two people were to remember one another, even to the point of never being at odds;
this is analogous to the Buddhas of the ten directions arising with a shared mindfulness, like a form and its shadow, never separated by even a single step.
How could this be merely a matter of encountering and seeing? It is because the Buddhas of the ten directions take pity [on sentient beings].
"Mindfulness of sentient beings is like a mother’s remembrance of her child. This corresponds to the previous analogy of one person who remembers exclusively.
"If the child has fled and wandered away, though she remembers him, what can she do? This corresponds to the previous analogy of one person who forgets exclusively.

"If the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, and mother and child do not become estranged throughout successive lifetimes," this corresponds to the previous analogy of two people remembering each other. Thus...
It reaches the point where form and shadow are inseparable. If sentient beings truly concentrate their minds to recollect the Buddha and chant his name, they will see the Buddha before them.
Having seen him in the present, they know that they will certainly see the Buddha in the future, free from all doubt.
Although they have not yet immediately attained Buddhahood, they are nonetheless not far from it, for they know that their own mind is itself the Buddha.
Because of the Buddha, one does not rely on the skillful means of other Buddhas, yet spontaneously attains the opening of the mind and beholds all Buddhas.

This is like a person who has been anointed with incense; their body carries a fragrance. It is a metaphor for how those who recollect and mindfulness of the Buddha naturally possess the potential for Buddhahood.
"Adorned with Fragrant Light" is a metaphor for how those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha constantly [rely upon] the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.

Fragrance is the light of wisdom; it adorns oneself as well. In my original stage of practice, through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, I entered the patience of non-arising and thereby attained perfect penetration. For this reason, I am now present here in this Sahā world.
I gather in those with the karmic affinity to practice Buddha-recollection, leading them to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss to be born there by transformation from a lotus flower.
Now, when the Buddha asks me about the perfect penetration I have realized, I have made no selection; I have instead fully gathered my six sense faculties.
Thus, whatever is seen by the eyes is nothing other than the form of the Buddha; whatever is heard by the ears is nothing other than the voice of the Buddha; and as for what is smelled by the nose...

There is nothing that is not the fragrance of the Buddha; whatever the tongue proclaims is none other than the name of the Buddha. Whatever this body touches is none other than the realm of the Buddha;
whatever the mind contemplates is none other than the Dharma of the Buddha. One need only ensure that no other conditions interfere, maintaining a single-minded, pure recollection.

In this way, with each thought succeeding the next without interruption, one will naturally be able to see the Buddha, realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), attain *samādhi*, and achieve perfect penetration.
One should then, by means of this, thoroughly gather the six sense faculties and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
This is the foremost [method]. Indeed, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and pure karma—these two gates are the essential paths for transcending birth and death and entering Bodhi.

Thus, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta each opened their own doors: one through the practice of Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*) to benefit sentient beings, and the other through meditative concentration to instruct the assembly.
These were all expedient means (*upāya*) applied according to the capacities of beings, leading them back to the Supreme Vehicle (*Ekayāna*).
In this degenerate age, the mountains of self and others are high, and people compete with one another;

consequently, those who practice *dhyāna* do not understand the profound meaning of reciting the Buddha’s name, while those who cultivate Pure Land practices have no means to grasp the subtle secret of investigating *chan*.
If one does not investigate *chan* through the principle of "single-mindedness without distraction," then *chan* will certainly not be realized; if it is not like a cat pouncing upon a mouse...
If one merely recites the Buddha’s name according to a fixed formula, the Buddha will certainly not be realized. Do not say that reciting the Buddha’s name is easy while Zen meditation is difficult;
you must know that if it is difficult, it is difficult for all, and if it is easy, it is easy for all.

It depends solely on the depth of one’s own power of faith and whether one’s seeds have ripened or not. Nevertheless, these twenty-five gates, which are the ordinary six sense-objects, all begin with...

Regarding form (*rūpa*), we have now begun with sound (*śabda*). Furthermore, the reason the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is specifically reserved as the final element is precisely to manifest that the true essence of the teaching in this land is "purity resides in the hearing of sounds.
Therefore, it begins with sound and concludes with hearing; thus, it serves as the governing principle of the essence of the teaching, uniquely adapted to the capacities of those in this land.
This corresponds to the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*), where the element of earth (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) should come first; here, however, it begins with the element of fire (*tejas-mahābhūta*).

Regarding the "priority": it is because excessive lust summons fire that this sutra specifically clarifies its descent through lustful arousal, serving as a warning to the learned to eliminate the outflow of desire (*kāśrava*).

Furthermore, while the seven great elements should conclude with the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*), here the conclusion of the element of the faculties (*indriya-mahābhūta*) is reached by means of the mutual correspondence between the mindfulness of Amitābha (Śrī-megha) and the meditative concentration of Avalokiteśvara; both serve as the main gate to the jeweled mansion.
Thus, it is shown to us that if one does not practice Chan meditation, one should instead recite the Buddha’s name;

this is what is meant by "many doors of skillful means, yet no second path. This is indeed the profound intent behind the fact that the sutra text does not conclude with the Great Understanding (識大), but rather concludes with the Great Root (根大).

Composed by the Śramaṇa Pǔwěn of Gānglíng, who was granted the title "Dharma-Jie Temple Preacher" by Imperial Decree during the Great Qing Dynasty.
△ II. Extensive Exposition of Avalokiteśvara (II) 1. General Account of the Origins (III) 1. Explaining the Bestowal of Samādhi by Ancient Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat... [until] ...entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This entry into perfect penetration is through the faculty of hearing. If we were to discuss the three categories [of faculties, elements, and aggregates], it should follow the faculty of sight;

however, the perfect penetrations realized by the various sages previously mentioned are neither suitable expedients for the beginner’s mind nor a teaching-essence that can be practiced equally by those at shallow or deep stages.
Now, because of the meaning of this Bodhisattva’s perfect penetration, he extensively illustrates it as a method easy to practice for beginners.

Furthermore, wishing to minutely analyze the essential nature of the meditative realization that is like an illusion, and to fully manifest the inconceivable meditative function of compassionate yearning, I shall set this forth in detail once the accounts of the various sages have been completed.
In the Sanskrit language, he is called *Avalokiteśvara*; here it is translated as "Contemplator of the World’s Sounds.
This is because when this Great Being first resolved his mind, he heard the Perfectly Awakened One, the Buddha of the World...

The "teaching" refers to the sound of the voice; because it enters the mind and forms contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), this contemplation is the wisdom that contemplates, while the "World-Sound" is the object of that contemplation.
This is precisely the meaning of what is now called: "beginning from within hearing... until quiescence manifests before one."
That the Buddha whom we take as our teacher is also named Avalokiteśvara clearly demonstrates that the ancient and the modern are non-dual, and that cause and effect correspond.

From the sages of the past to the sages of the future, their Way is one and the same. One who arouses the bodhicitta—meaning that having already opened up right knowledge and right awakening—must necessarily seek the fruit of Buddhahood above and transform sentient beings below; for if one does not arouse this mind, one cannot achieve Bodhi.
If one fails to arouse the mind [of enlightenment], then all practices cultivated will be entirely subsumed by Māra.
Therefore, if one wishes to cultivate the Great Samādhi that leads to Buddhahood, one must first give rise to this great Bodhicitta.

This is just as the audience, having gained deep faith in the *tathāgatagarbha*, spoke verses of praise and gratitude, and gave rise to great vows. Those who enter *samādhi* through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation do so by means of this very method.
The substance of the teaching belongs to sound and hearing. "Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

It means turning the hearing back toward itself, not following the arising and ceasing of the auditory objects (*śabda-viṣaya*) with discursive discrimination, but flowing upstream in a single flavor to turn the hearing back toward one's own nature. This is what is called the true hearing that hears neither hearing nor non-hearing.

"Contemplation" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). It means externally not contemplating in accordance with sensory objects, internally not contemplating by following the sense faculties, and [in the middle...]

Without conceptualizing or discriminating, when not a single thought arises, the whole body manifests. This is precisely "thinking without thinking," the correct thinking that is free from all thought.

Cultivation refers to the cultivation of wisdom; it means refining and polishing the accumulated empty habits of past lives, washing away the seeds of names and words, transforming delusion into awakening, and turning the false into the true. This is cultivation without cultivation—the cultivation of the nature of illusion.
If one can indeed be fully endowed with the three types of wisdom and possess a pure single mind, then one will immediately enter the Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama;
what difficulty could there be? This is also like the present Buddha’s secret instruction for the appropriate recipient:

taking the nature of the faculty of hearing as the observing wisdom (*prajñā*), and taking the two objects of motion and stillness as the observed realm. From this point on, through the illusory perfuming of hearing...
Through illusory contemplation and cultivation, one enters the illusion-like samādhi.
△ Second, clarifying the cultivation of concentration according to the teachings:
First, within hearing, one enters the stream and causes the objects of perception to vanish (up to: sharing the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings).
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva cultivates correct concentration based on the ancient teachings of the Buddha.
Indeed, when a Mahāsattva first practices the wondrous concentration, it fundamentally does not depart from the two—the faculty of hearing and the auditory object of sound.

It is simply because all of us possess this nature of being able to hear. If one can merely go against the current of the flow of birth and death, turn the light back upon oneself, and use hearing to realize one's own nature, then one has entered the stream; at that point, one is no different from the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas).

Yet, although we possess this nature, it is as if it is stuck by the two defilements of movement and stillness, causing the profound clarity to give rise to listening, which then flows away into distraction.

The "running sound" refers to the outward movement following the flow of sensory objects. If one can rotate the hearing that hears sounds and turn it back to hear one's own nature, this is called "internal entry and returning the flow.
This is what is meant by "returning to exhaust the root of the flow until reaching the state of non-arising and non-ceasing.
If one can do so, then the two sensory objects of movement and stillness, which are ordinarily heard, will no longer interact with one another.

Since the faculties no longer take objects as conditions, the sense-objects have nothing with which to pair. Without waiting for their destruction, the delusory objects of perception vanish of their own accord.
Reaching this point, the faculties that enter the stream have already entered it; thus, these faculties are stilled.
The objects that are entered have already vanished; thus, these objects are stilled. When both faculties and objects are stilled, the consciousness-mind does not arise.
It is not only when there is movement and the characteristic of sound is clearly manifest that the discriminating mind does not arise;
even when it is still and the characteristic of sound is absent, the discriminating mind likewise does not arise.

In this way, the two sensory objects of movement and stillness gradually dissolve away, and through this, one’s practice of right concentration advances. Not only do the objects of perception vanish, but furthermore—
There is no further capacity [to act]. One is then able to hear that which is heard; whether it be the sense faculties (*indriya*) or their objects (*viṣaya*), both are extinguished.

By this, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*)—both its conceptualized (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) forms—are eliminated. Through this, they are severed forever. This is the ultimate achievement of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).
This refers precisely to what was previously called "this faculty first attains liberation," whereby one first realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

If one were to abide in this state where both subject and object are exhausted, it would again become an obstacle to the principle (*dharma-āvaraṇa*). Therefore, although one has exhausted both the capacity to hear and that which is heard, one must not dwell in attachment;

rather, one should further give rise to contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to illuminate and perceive the obstacle to the principle. One must strive to penetrate through all principles of truth (*satya*). Nevertheless, although...

If one were to maintain that there is a truly existent wisdom capable of awakening and that the principle of emptiness which is awakened to is likewise subject and object, one would again fall into attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
It is necessary that both the wisdom capable of awakening and the principle of emptiness which is awakened to are not established as separate entities.

Thus, the principle of emptiness and the wisdom that awakens to it are of one suchness and non-dual; they are perfectly interfused. Therefore, the wisdom that awakens to emptiness and that which is emptied [are identical].

Regarding the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): only when both [the afflictive and cognitive hindrances] are simultaneously stilled can the cognitive hindrance be removed. The conceptual and innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is also severed without remainder;

this represents the ultimate perfection of the power of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*). This is what is meant by the "perfectly luminous nature of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-prakṛti-prabhāsvarā*) resulting in the liberation through the Dharma (*dharma-vimukti*).

Nevertheless, although the subject—the awakening wisdom that realizes emptiness—and the object—the cognitive hindrance that is emptied—are both perfectly extinguished, if one were to regard them as having been fully accomplished...
Then one falls into the trap of the "body of dharmas" (dharmakāya). Unable to turn back from this path to enter the wondrous, even this very word "extinction" (nirodha) becomes a great illness.
This is why it was said previously that while the bodhicitta arises and the mind of arising-and-extinction ceases, this [bodhicitta] itself is also subject to arising and extinction.
One must know that while arising should indeed be extinguished, extinction itself must also be extinguished; only then can both medicine and illness vanish together. This—
Thus, the perfect and wondrous is accomplished. Therefore, one knows that worldly phenomena are birthless even as they arise, and supramundane phenomena are non-extinguished even as they cease.
Understanding that arising is illusory arising, one does not hinder extinction by means of illusory extinction.

Through this, one awakens to the fact that the self-nature is fundamentally quiescent—the Tathāgatagarbha mind, whose essence is inherently true and eternal, and whose nature is inherently tranquil and extinguished. For this reason, all...
The subtle ignorance as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is entirely severed; this is the ultimate perfection of the merit of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
What is called "the dharma of liberation having already become empty and non-arising" refers precisely to this: the Bodhisattva entering the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*) from samādhi.

However, since the essence of the contemplation of the three emptinesses has already been fully realized and the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is complete, [the path is perfected].

Thus, the wondrous function is fully prepared. Therefore, at the moment of sudden realization when all things are simultaneously empty within right concentration, in an instant, one transcends the sentient beings of the six realms of the mundane world and is no longer bound by the two types of objective obstacles of self-clinging within the realm;
one also transcends the worthy and sage practitioners of the three vehicles of the supramundane and is no longer bound by the two types of clinging to phenomena outside the realm.

Bound by the obstacles of principle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one transcends both self and dharmas; thus, not being fettered by the dust-like and sand-like ignorance (*avidyā*), one attains the pure and original nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
It pervades the ten directions and perfectly illuminates the *dharmadhātu*, constituting the single Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*).
Therein, one immediately acquires two kinds of extraordinary merit: first, it harmonizes upward with the ten...

Regarding "firstly, with the Buddhas": this means that these Great Beings, having perfected the causes and fulfilled the fruits, unite their *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (beginning-awakening) causal mind with the resultant virtues of *mūlajñāna* (original-awakening).
Thus, they are identical with the entirety of the great function realized by all Buddhas; there is no duality and no distinction, for they are entirely in accord.
Second, regarding "below, with the sentient beings of the six realms": this means that Buddhas and sentient beings share the same entirety.
The essence is the great function; that which the Great Being (Mahāsattva) realizes is precisely the complete essence and great function inherently shared with the Buddha.

Therefore, upon attaining this samādhi and clarifying this mind, one is immediately able to harmonize both the upper and lower realms without omission—this is what is meant by the non-differentiation of the three:
mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. This is because it transcends the mundane world.
Because it accords with the Dharma, it can harmonize upward with the Buddhas’ identical mind of benevolence and compassion— the power of roots of goodness that bestows happiness.
Because it transcends worldly dharmas, it can harmonize downward with sentient beings’ identical mind of sorrow and suffering— their longing, aspiration, and yearning for joy.
△ III. The Manifestation and Functioning of the Three Clarities through Samādhi (2): 1. A Brief Account of the Power of Self-Realized Samādhi. From the passage:
"The World-Honored One, by virtue of my making offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara... [up to] the thirty-two manifestations entering all lands."
This describes the primary excellence of self-realization in its fundamental state. It harmonizes upward with the compassionate power shared by all Buddhas.

The phrase "by me making offerings" indicates that virtue has a basis; "receiving transmission from them" reveals that the lineage of teachers has a foundation and the attainment of the Dharma has a source.
This is because the pure awakened mind is fundamentally devoid of a single thing, yet it follows along with the flow.

When one pursues delusion, there arise the sense faculties and their objects. Once one knows that the faculties and objects are not real and that the nature of hearing is truly eternal, then within this true eternity, one seeks for internal faculties and external objects; yet all dharmas are utterly unobtainable, being entirely like illusory phenomena.

Therefore, it is said to be "like an illusion. Initially, the fundamental awakening (benjue) of the nature of hearing permeates the initial awakening (shijue), whereby initial awakening is generated within the nature of hearing;
one continues to cultivate fundamental awakening. This is precisely the arising of cultivation from the entirety of the nature, such that the entirety of cultivation is the nature itself.

Thus, from within the absence of seeing and hearing, there is illusorily formed the capacity to hear and the object heard; yet this illusory hearing does not obstruct [the reality of] the illusory [nature].

It is perfumed. Since it arises from the state of hearing, reflection, and cultivation that are fundamentally non-existent, yet is illusorily formed within the state of existence, there is no hindrance to illusory reflection and illusory cultivation.
Therefore, it is said: "illusory perfuming through hearing and illusory cultivation through hearing.

Because the essence of this samādhi is precisely the true mind of original enlightenment, the *tathāgatagarbha*, which remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanged, it is able to sever [the afflictions] from time immemorial.
Ignorance can shatter all fetters and karmic actions, yet its essential nature remains indestructible; thus it is called "Vajra.
This is the attainment of the Buddha's essence (*tathatā*). That which accords with the power of compassion is the attainment of the Buddha's function (*karman*).
Because both essence and function are fully possessed, my body manifests thirty-two transformations, entering into all realms of true recompense, skillful means, and the shared dwelling.
The various manifestations are all due to the power of the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi).

Indeed, the thirty-two responses, in sum, do not exceed the bodies of the ten dharma-realms—the four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings—because the responsive capacities of those who perceive them do not go beyond these categories.

It is not that the responses of the Great Being are limited to these alone. If one follows the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*): first, the... [text fragment ends] ...three.

First, the mind-made body produced from the delight in subtle concentration (*sukhāsvādābhinirvṛtta-manomaya-kāya*); its stage corresponds to the eighth bhūmi. Second, the mind-made body produced from the awakening to the self-nature of dharmas (*dharmasvabhāvābhisambodhi-manomaya-kāya*);

its stage corresponds to the ninth bhūmi up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Third, the mind-made body produced from the simultaneous arising of various types and being effortless (*nānāprakāra-jāti-sahaja-anābhoga-manomaya-kāya*);

this corresponds to the stage of entering Sublime Enlightenment (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) from Equal Enlightenment. Because the bodies of the noble lineage manifest simultaneously, the Great Being’s sublime response is manifested.
It is the body born of mental formation (*manomaya-kāya*) that arises simultaneously with the correct category [of concentration] and without volitional effort (*anabhisamskāra*).
△ Second, the detailed exposition of the application of the concentration for the benefit of others (three parts): First, the exposition of the thirty-two modes of response (two parts):
First, the explicit clarification of the wondrous application according to circumstances (two parts): First, according to the four types of noble disciples.

World-Honored One, if various bodhisattvas enter samādhi (up to) the Buddha preaching the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation—this is the manifestation of the body (nirmāṇakāya) preaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of the four types of noble beings. These bodhisattvas are not restricted to any particular teaching or stage.

As for those who advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), by means of a "similar stage," they advance in the cultivation of the Middle Way and the untainted; thus, [the stages] are divided.

One realizes the perfection of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Furthermore, if one cultivates the diamond-like untainted state (*anāsrava*), then one ultimately realizes the perfection of resolute conviction.
This is because the understanding of the Mahāyāna is vastly different from that of the two vehicles; thus it is called "resolute conviction.

Because each [practitioner] cultivates their respective dharma-gates, and the wisdom and principle of their own vehicle are about to manifest and achieve full perfection, it is called "manifestation" (*mian*).

[The character] "yuan" (round/perfect). All subsequent instances follow this pattern. As for those who manifest the body of a Buddha, each manifests the body of the ultimate fruit (*phala*) of their respective teaching, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate for them, causing them to partially realize the two ultimate liberations (*vimukti*).

Generally, the term "one in training" (*śaikṣa*) refers to the time when one has reached the culmination of practice and is about to realize the state of "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). [Those who] appear in worlds where no Buddha exists observe all things...
They transform and transcend, realizing for themselves that there is no arising; thus they are called *Pratyekabuddhas* (Solitary Realizers). Like a rhinoceros horn, they awaken alone.

Because they delight in solitary tranquility, they are called "quiescent. Because they seek spontaneous wisdom, they are called "wondrously luminous. All those below this are included within the same category of activity.
Those who uphold the Buddha's teaching and realize the Way by contemplating conditions are called *Pratyayabuddhas* (Conditioned Realizers). This is because...
One knows the supreme nature of delusion. Through the twelve links of dependent origination, one cuts this [delusion] off at its source.

From the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, the nature of the severed conditions is revealed; hence it is called the "supreme nature of severed conditions.

By awakening to the emptiness of the nature of causes and conditions, the wondrous nature of non-arising manifests perfectly before one. This refers to the stages of the worthy (*śaikṣa*) and the noble (*ārya*) prior to the three fruits.

Both belong to the stage of those still in training (*śaikṣa*). Through the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one eliminates the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions of the four truths, thereby attaining the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

hence it is said that one "attains the emptiness of the four truths. Following the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one proceeds to eliminate the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions (*vāsana-anuśaya*) of the three realms;
for each grade, one realizes a portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*); hence it is said:
They enter extinction through the path of cultivation. It is not said that they manifest as bodhisattvas because the Great Being (Mahāsattva) demonstrates abiding in the rank of a bodhisattva.
△ Second, responding to the capacities of the six classes of ordinary beings (in two parts): first, responding to their hearts of aspiration.
If there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds to clarity, [up to] one should preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve realization.
This refers to the case where one should aspire to manifest in the form of a celestial or human being to preach the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who feel weary of the lower realms' suffering, coarseness, and obscurations, and who rejoice in the higher realms' purity, subtlety, and renunciation, and one wishes to cause their minds to become clear, bright, awakened, and liberated—[this is the case where one should not manifest as such].

If there are those who are willing to abandon the defilements of the dust of sensual desire, seeking to make their bodies luminous and pure so as to be born in the fourth dhyāna and no longer undergo the suffering,
coarseness, and obstructions of the desire realm, I shall manifest before them in the form of a Brahmā King, the sovereign of the form realm.

For them, he expounds the superior ten roots of goodness, fundamental dhyāna-concentration, and the methods for the cultivation and realization of the factors of entering and emerging from dhyāna, so that they may become free from desire, attain liberation, and be born in the Brahma-world. If there are sentient beings who love to preside over the various heavens, [he likewise provides the means for their attainment].

I then manifest the physical form of Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and for their sake expound the five precepts and ten wholesome actions of the highest grade, causing their roots of virtue to be purified.
Thus they are born at the summit of the earth, dwelling in the Sudarśana Palace, presiding over the thirty-two heavens as their sovereign.
If there are sentient beings who wish to attain such a body, roaming with ease and self-mastery, [they should practice these].

Without obstruction throughout the ten directions, I manifest at the summit of the heavens in the desire realm—known in full as Devavati, which here means "Paranirmita-vaśavartin" (Mastery over Others' Emanations).
This refers to those who, by relying on the emanations of others, attain mastery for themselves.
For them, I preach the ten superior wholesome deeds and the concentration of the "not-yet-reached stage. By means of such teachings, I cause them to achieve rebirth in the sixth heaven.
Furthermore, some say that on the sixth heaven there is a separate palace of the Māra King, which is likewise included within the realm of Īśvara.

If sentient beings desire for this very body to attain great mastery (mahā-vaśitā), to fly with great speed, and to travel back and forth through space at will for their own amusement, I then manifest as Maheśvara, the Great Lord, at the summit of Akaniṣṭha; this is what is discussed in the treatise.
He is said to have three eyes and eight arms, riding a white ox and holding a white fly-whisk, capable of flying through the void to reach other realms.
For his sake, the four dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds were taught, causing him to achieve the status of Mahādeva.
As for the Celestial General, he is the great general commanded by the Four Heavenly Kings, stationed in separate divisions.
The thirty-two heavens each lead ghosts and spirits to pacify and protect the four directions.
Just as the Great General Vaiśravaṇa commands twenty-eight divisions to patrol the world, rewarding the good and punishing the evil, subduing demons and protecting living beings.
According to the *Gantong zhuan*, the celestial being Mr. Fei stated that beneath each king there are eight generals; thus, the four kings together [command] thirty-two.
The thirty-two generals traverse the four worlds below, going back and forth to protect and assist all practitioners.
Like the celestial general Weituo, who is one of the eight generals of the Heavenly King of the South, he is the leader of these thirty-two generals.
Whenever there are sons or daughters of Māra who treat bhikṣus with contempt or mockery, the General rushes to the scene and eradicates them instantly. Even if [the demons] reach...

At the king’s residence, the king saw them and rose from his seat for all of them. This was because General Wei had cultivated the practice of *kumārabhūta* (the youthful truth) and had received the Buddha’s final charge to protect the True Dharma. As for the Four Heavenly Kings:

in the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, translated as "Holder of the Nation," who dwells upon a golden terrace and leads the two classes of *gandharva* and *piśāca*. In the south is Virūḍhaka, translated as "Increase."
He dwells upon a lapis lazuli terrace and presides over the two classes of *kumbhāṇḍas* and *pīśācas*.
In the west is Vaiśravaṇa, known as "Broad Eyes," who dwells upon a white silver terrace and presides over the two classes of *piśācas* and *mahoragas*.
In the north is Vaiśravaṇa, known as "Much Hearing," who dwells upon a crystal terrace and presides over the two classes of *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*. Thus it is said in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
[The Buddha] clarified the sutras. Then the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We four kings, along with our retinues of eight classes and hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, constantly manifest our protection over this Jambudvīpa with our pure divine eyes.
For this reason, we are called the World-Protecting Kings. These four heavens are the foremost of those ascending upward and the first heaven of the lower realms, situated upon Mount Sumeru."
The mountains each occupy one terrace. The ministers serve under Śakra, with each governing four continents. The generals and assistants they lead each consist of two divisions;
together there are eight classes of divine generals who protect the world. As for the princes of these kingdoms, they are of the same lineage as Nārāyaṇa.
According to the Mahālaṅkāra-sūtra (Daji-yi jing), each of the Four World-Protecting Kings has ninety-one [sons].
Their sons were handsome in appearance and possessed great power; all were named "Emperors" (Ti).

Based on these four kings, there were three hundred and sixty-four sons in total, each capable of governing spirits and deities, assisting in governance, and protecting the world—just as a crown prince in the human world remains at court to oversee the state and goes forth to lead the military. All of the above are due to the five precepts and ten wholesome actions.
It is through the method of destroying the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox that [this goal] is accomplished. This clarifies how the Great Being responds to the requests of the various devas.
"King" (wang) means "to go toward," signifying that all people beneath heaven turn toward him in submission. Furthermore, there are five kinds [of kings].
1. A Golden Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) rules over the four continents. 2. A Silver Wheel-Turning King rules over three continents, excluding the northern continent. 3.

A Copper Wheel-Turning King rules over two continents, excluding the northwestern and northeastern continents. 4. An Iron Wheel-Turning King rules over one continent, governing only the southern continent.
5. A Fragmentary King (Kṣudra-rāja), such as those of the five heavens and sixteen kingdoms in this land.
It is the kings of the various feudal states. They likewise bring others to fulfillment through the method of transforming them by means of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "When a king protects the Dharma, he increases three kinds of vital essence (*ojas*): first, the vital essence of the land, which refers to the abundant ripening of the five grains;
second, the vital essence of sentient beings, which refers to their having handsome and dignified appearances and being free from all epidemics; third..."
The vital essence of wholesome dharmas refers to the cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, faith, and so forth. Question:
There are those in the world who harbor deluded ambitions for kingship; does the Mahāsattva likewise manifest his body before them to teach them the methods for fulfilling their desires? Answer: No.
