It is because such a person must possess benevolence and virtue, and out of compassion for the chaos and separation of the world, they have made a vow desiring to become a ruler of the Way.

When you govern the state according to principle, the Great Being manifests his form for you to preach the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions as the causes for rebirth into noble status, thereby perfuming the seeds of future lives.
How could this possibly be teaching the artifice of treacherous plots like those of Wang Mang, Cao Cao, or Wen Yi?

Now, as for the term "elder" (gṛhapati), it refers to those who are honored as seniors in the world. In India, one who possesses billions in accumulated wealth and is characterized by benevolence and charitable giving is called an elder;
if one were merely wealthy but lacked benevolence, they would not be worthy of this title.
Therefore, Master Han said: "One who dwells in gravity and sincerity is called a 'Venerable One' (Chang-zhe).

Formerly, when the High Ancestor of Han enfeoffed his nephew as the Marquis of Gaigeng, he remarked, 'It is only because his mother is not a Venerable One. When Wang Ling’s mother addressed the imperial envoy, she said, 'The King of Han is a Venerable One;
you should serve him well. Verifying this through such examples, one sees that the rank of Marquis or King can be attained by force, yet—"

The title of "Elder" (sthavira) is difficult to attain by mere fortune. For while those who are kings or nobles may be granted this name and served in outward appearance, those who are true elders are granted it in reality and are honored with heartfelt respect.
Thus, they become the masters of their clans and are esteemed by the world. According to the textual passages, one should possess ten virtues. First, noble lineage; that is to say:
They are descendants of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors; they belong to families where the left [cap] is adorned with sable fur and the right is inserted [with feathers].

First is high rank, referring to those who serve as counselors and prime ministers, like the salt-and-vinegar stewers or the Minister of State (Aheng). Second is great wealth, referring to those possessing copper hills and golden valleys, who are abundant and extravagant.

Third is awe-inspiring majesty, referring to those whose sternness is so profound that order is achieved without the need for rigorous enforcement, like the heavy frost. Fourth is deep wisdom, referring to those whose chests are like armories, possessing strategic power.
1. Extraordinary Eminence: At sixty years of age, he was so venerable and dignified that all beings naturally bowed before him.

2. Purity of Conduct: Like a flawless white jade, his actions perfectly matched his words. 3. Perfection of Rites: His decorum and measured bearing were such that the world looked up to him as a model.
4. Praise from Above: He was highly extolled by the sovereign, the sole person above. 5. Reverence from Below: As for those below... [text fragment]

The four seas all turn toward him with virtue. Possessing these ten meanings, he is called a "longer" (elders). As for the "householder" (*jushi*), this refers to a gentleman who dwells in rectitude and possesses the Way.
As for "illustrious words," these are elegant expressions that have become famous throughout the world. Such a person does not seek fame or advancement;
rather, they maintain a pure and upright will, dwelling in the Way as their own abode. A "state" (*guo*) is a territory; the larger of these is called a "kingdom" (*bang*).
This is the principle of conferring enfeoffments. It is precisely because one has performed meritorious service that one is enfeoffed. A "district" (*yì*) is equivalent to a "county" (*xiàn*).

Those who govern them—such as the Three Dukes and Ministers who rectify the fundamental principles, establish the regulations, transform customs, change social habits, promote benefit, and eliminate harm—are these very individuals.

As for "decisive judgment": it refers to those such as provincial governors and county magistrates who settle lawsuits with a few words, resulting in simplified litigation and clear administration of justice;
this is an example. Now, although the offices of the Three Dukes and high ministers differ from those of provincial governors and county magistrates, they are all termed "officials" (*zhíguān*).

This is because "to govern" (*zhǎi*) signifies the principle of righteousness, while "office" (*guān*) signifies the function of capability. The Three Dukes assist the King in governance through their functional capabilities; therefore, it is said:
A *zài guān* (official) refers to governors, prefects, and magistrates who, by virtue of their administrative capacity, govern the people below; they are also called *zài guān*.

"Numbers" (*shù*) refers to the art of calculation; "techniques" (*shù*) refers to the skills of incantation and prohibition, such as astronomy, geography, divining good and bad fortune, writing spells, drawing talismans, and commanding spirits or subjugating ghosts. "Regulating and protecting" (*shè wèi*) means to harmonize and maintain the body.

The mind preserves the fundamental principles of hygiene, much like compounding medicines or refining elixirs in pursuit of longevity and increased life span. *Brahmaṇa* means "pure conduct" (*śuddhacaryā*);
it is one of the four castes of the Western Regions (India) and a lineage from the beginning of the kalpa. Because they dwell in seclusion among mountains and wilds, they are called "Pure Conduct.
*Śīla* means "precepts" (*śīla*), and *Vinaya* means "discipline" (*vinaya*). It is by relying on these laws of discipline that one guards against what is non-virtuous.
To cease evil is therefore called "precept" (*śīla*). This ranges from the ten precepts up to the full ordination of two hundred and fifty precepts.
*Nī* means "woman. Regarding "prohibitory precepts," this refers to the eight prohibitory rules (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*) for *nīs*.
*Upāsaka* means "male lay follower," and *upāsikā* means "female lay follower"; both maintain themselves by means of the five precepts and are thus capable [of practicing the Dharma].
This refers to those who draw near to and serve the Triple Gem. As for the five precepts, they are:

not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol or eating meat. The *Upāsaka-sūtra* states: "If one violates these five, in heaven one will offend the five stars;
on earth one will offend the five sacred peaks; in the cardinal directions one will offend the five emperors; and within the body one will offend the five viscera. If...
Regarding the supramundane, it would destroy the fivefold Dharma-body and all Buddha-dharmas, for the five precepts are the root of both the Great and Small Vehicle *śīla*.
As for "internal governance": women hold the correct position within the home; hence it is called "internal governance.

To be noble yet capable of diligence, and wealthy yet capable of frugality—this is called "establishing one's person. Regarding "cultivating the family and the state," the inner quarters are the foundation.
It is the source of the myriad transformations. Therefore, the practice of the Way of Women is related to the order or disorder of the state and the family;
it must not fail to be cultivated. The consort of the Son of Heaven is called the "Mistress of the Realm" (*zhǔ*). The wife of a lord of a state is called a "Lady of the State" (*guó fūrén*).

A wife attains the honor of her husband and becomes a "Lady by Decree" (*mìngfù*). *Jiā* (家) is pronounced as *gū* (姑). For example, Cao Shetou of Fufeng during the Later Han dynasty married Ban [Zhuo] of the same commandery.
The daughter of Biao was named Zhao, with the courtesy name Huíjī. Emperor Hè summoned her to the palace several times and commanded the Empress and the noble ladies to serve her as their teacher;
she was addressed as "Dàjiā" (the Great Lady), among other such titles. She did not damage the male organ [of men];

that is, she was one who resolved to never violate sexual desire for the rest of her life. A "chǔnǚ" (virgin) is also called a "chǔzǐ" (maiden); this refers to a woman who has not yet married. [She was] beloved.
Regarding "delighting in dwelling in the body": this is the vow to always remain a maiden and never marry for the rest of one's life. Regarding "not seeking":

this means wishing to constantly maintain firm integrity and refusing to allow members of other clans to seek her hand. Even if there were others who, belonging to different clans, forcibly committed acts of aggression and violence.
This is also something he vowed never to follow. This is precisely how a Great Being responds to the needs of those in the human realm.

It is evident that through the Samādhi of Illusion-like Nature, he sports with supernormal powers; he adapts to harmonize and meets others by chance. Carrying his staff wherever he goes, he performs his play upon whatever stage he encounters.
This is the subtle art of gathering and transforming beings through the method of "identical activity" (samānārthatā).
△ Second, the mind of revulsion and detachment.
If there are devas who desire to leave their celestial status (up to the point where he) preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it.
This manifestation of a body in the various realms of existence is intended to inspire revulsion and detachment. Below this are the eight classes of beings, with the garuḍas being fewest in number.

This is merely an abbreviation by the translator. However, these seven classes, though they possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), merit, and authority, all belong to *saṃsāra* and are equally subject to suffering and affliction.
Consequently, many wish to escape these realms and hope to attain human birth, so as to aspire toward further cultivation.
Even for the various devas, despite their pleasures, they cannot avoid the suffering of the five signs of decline (*pañca-vyasanāni*); thus, there are those who seek to emerge from them.
As for "classes" (*lun*): dragons suffer from hot sands and the various afflictions of the *garuḍas*. Therefore, there are those who wish to escape their class.
*Yakṣa* means "light and agile," because they fly through the air with the greatest swiftness; in the language of Qin, it means "noble person. They are the deities of mountains and rivers.
There are three types: first, those beneath the earth; second, those in the air; and third, those in heaven.
Because the terrestrial yakṣas give only material gifts, they are unable to fly. The two types of celestial yakṣas, however, give gifts of chariots and horses, and therefore they are able to fly.
Thus, when the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, the terrestrial yakṣas proclaim it and the celestial yakṣas hear it;
the celestial yakṣas proclaim it and the Four Great Kings hear it; in this manner it is transmitted successively until it reaches the Brahma world.
Furthermore, *gandharva* means "fragrance-body" (*gandha-āśraya*). This deity does not consume wine or meat, but sustains its five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) by eating various fragrances.

It is also called "one who travels seeking fragrance" (*gandha-anveṣin*), because when it is time to perform music in the palace of Śakra within the Vajra Cave to the south of Mount Sumeru, this deity immediately seeks out the scent as the aloeswood incense is burned.
The former is the celestial deity known as the *gandharva*. The *asura* is said to be "not upright," because their women are beautiful while their men are ugly;
in new translations, they are called "non-gods" (*amara*), because they are deceitful and lack the conduct of gods.

Nevertheless, the karmic retribution of these deities is most excellent and resembles that of the various heavens, yet in reality they are not among the gods. The *kiṃnara* is called the "doubtful deity."
They are also called *amanuṣya* (non-humans), because they resemble humans yet have horns upon their heads; those who see them all doubt, asking, "Is this a human?
Or is it a non-human? It is from this that their name was established. They are also deities of the celestial lord’s stringed and wind instruments and songs.
*Mahoraga* means "earth-dragon," also called "great python" or "belly-crawlers. These are the deities of worldly shrines.
The spirit received the wine and meat offered by the man, which all entered the belly of a python.

Because he had violated the precepts, been deceitful and sycophantic, harbored much anger and gave little in alms, and was greedily addicted to wine and meat, he fell into the realm of ghosts and spirits. There, many wrathful insects entered his body and devoured him.

Thus, in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), there is the account of a fellow student of An Shigao who, due to his excessive anger, fell into the body of a giant python and became the deity of Quting Lake;
he was subsequently saved by this very circumstance. This is precisely such a case. The retributions experienced by these beings consist of a mixture of suffering and pleasure;
however, their physical forms are utterly hideous, and thus they long to escape their lot and aspire to become human.
It is the human body. Since all Buddhas attain the Way among human beings, Master Pei said: "To rectify the mind and incline toward Bodhi, only the human path is capable of this.

Those who delight in being human and cultivate humanity are those who, while currently in the human realm, seek to obtain a human body again after casting off this present one; for it is the human path that is easy to regain.
Hearing the Dharma and practicing it easily is not like the gods who are addicted to pleasure, nor like those in other realms who sink into suffering.
Therefore, one seeks to never lose the human body from life to life and birth to birth, so as to facilitate progress in cultivation.

Regarding the following passage, according to Changshui, "having form" refers to possessing the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), such as the "spirits of auspicious and inauspicious omens" mentioned below; "lacking form" refers to lacking the aggregate of form, such as [the spirits] mentioned below.
Those who are empty, scattered, or dissolved, etc., possess perception and the four aggregates, such as the spirits, ghosts, and numinous beings mentioned below.
Those without perception lack the four aggregates, such as when the spirit or consciousness transforms into earth, wood, metal, or stone; these are all not human.
This explanation is indeed correct; yet it does not compare to the broad scope encompassed by Zhuchuan. He states: "Excluding the human realm, the remaining five destinies are all termed 'non-humans.
Those with form collectively subsume the desire and form realms; those without form are specifically assigned to the formless realm.

These include the two heavens of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness, as well as the Heaven of No-Thought, the Heaven of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. This...
Thus, the Great Being of Right View manifests his body and preaches the Dharma to all classes of beings, from the celestial palaces above down to the hells below—
including the various evil destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals— without a single category to which he does not manifest his form and teach the Dharma.
△ Second, the general conclusion regarding the efficacy derived from the power of meditative concentration:
This is called the "Wondrously Pure Thirty-two Manifestations" (up to) "the spontaneous accomplishment of wondrous, effortless sovereign power.
This generally concludes the merit of the preceding thirty-two manifestations entering various lands to manifest bodies and preach the Dharma; all [of these]...

This is due to the power of the Vajra-samādhi cultivated through hearing and practicing what is heard, which is like an illusion. Because it manifests skillfully according to the various types [of beings], it is called "wondrous" (miao).

Because it is untainted by faults and afflictions, it is called "pure" (jing). Because it uproots suffering in accordance with its true nature, it is called "unconditioned wondrous power" (wu zuo miao li).
Because it spontaneously bestows bliss, it is called "spontaneous accomplishment" (zizai chengjiu).
△ Second, the exposition of the fourteen kinds of fearlessness (3): First, the initial indication of the power of self-realization through meditative concentration.
"World-Honored One, by means of this further cultivation of hearing and practice of what has been heard... [I] shall obtain the merit of fourteen kinds of fearlessness."
This indicates the power of self-realization through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] below shares the same compassion and longing as sentient beings.

For the Great Being has turned the hearing back toward his own nature and thereby awakened to the compassion of the same essence (*samatā-karuṇā*), realizing that the living being and the Buddha are non-dual.
Thus, he is able to harmonize with those above and accord with those below. Therefore, the mind of sentient beings’ sorrowful longing is itself within the mind of the Great Being.
The compassionate mind of the Great Being resides within the hearts of sentient beings; for ordinary beings and sages share the same essence, they respond to one another through mutual resonance.
Thus it is said that all sentient beings shall obtain fourteen kinds of fearless merit within the body and mind of this Great Being.
Although "fearlessness" refers to sentient beings, it is because those who encounter calamity are precisely [those who seek it].
Amongst fears and terrors, one who is protected and delivered from them becomes fearless.

Although "merit" (*guṇa*) here refers specifically to the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), because he saves living beings and delivers them from fear, it constitutes the causal merit and fruit of the realization of Bodhi.
This is one way of explaining it; however, according to the correct explanation, the fearlessness of sentient beings is itself the fearlessness of the Great Being. Great...
The virtues of the Bodhisattva are, in fact, the virtues of sentient beings; this is because one perceives that the Great Being’s compassion is of the same essence as theirs.
△ Second, the explicit explanation of the function of bestowing fearlessness (four parts): First, fearlessness regarding the eight difficulties.

First, from "Because I do not observe sounds" up to "passing through dangerous paths where thieves cannot plunder," this causes sentient beings to attain fearlessness regarding the eight difficulties by means of the Great Being’s mind.
First, because I do not follow the cognitions and views arising from the dust of sound, but rather turn back the inverted hearing-faculty to hear one's own nature; it is not like...
Worldly people perceive sounds through the faculty of hearing, its objects, and their consciousness;

I, however, observe them solely with the wisdom of contemplative insight, and thereby attain mastery. Furthermore, even if all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions were to inflict physical suffering upon me and disturb my mind, if they should but once call my name, I shall then contemplate them.
By chanting and reciting my name, they shall immediately attain great mastery within my mind and be liberated from suffering and affliction;

thus, they will have no fear regarding the hardships of suffering. Second, because my single faculty returns to its source and the six faculties are liberated, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing all turn back to their origin, achieving perfect liberation from all sensory objects.
Then the fires of the four great elements, the five desires, and the six sense objects will all vanish from this point on.
What other fire could there be to act as a burner? Thus, it enables all sentient beings who call upon my name to obtain these merits within my heart, such that fire cannot burn them;
consequently, they have no fear of the calamity of fire. Thirdly, it is because my six sense organs function interchangeably through contemplation.
By listening, one does not follow after the flow of sounds and objects; thus, the nature of hearing is turned back toward its source.
When this occurs, the flow of desire, the flow of existence, and the flow of ignorance will instantly dry up. What further water could then drown or submerge you?
Therefore, all sentient beings who maintain this recitation shall, within my heart, obtain this merit: they cannot be drowned by water, and thus the hardship of water is overcome.

One is fearless. Fourth, because externally I do not follow after sensory objects, internally I do not pursue the sense organs, and in between I sever and extinguish the deluded mind of consciousness so that it does not arise—since this mind of consciousness, from time immemorial, has plundered the Dharma-body and injured the life of wisdom like a ghost or a water-demon, it is deeply to be feared;
now that it has been severed and extinguished, this [fear] no longer exists.
What further thing could there be within the deluded mind that can cause harm? Therefore, it enables all sentient beings who recite my name to obtain this merit within my heart;
ghosts cannot harm them, and thus they have no fear of demonic calamities.

Fifth, because I attained the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, I first, within the process of hearing, cultivated and refined through hearing until I realized the true nature of hearing.
Thus, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are melted away and the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are restored to their source.

Looking back at the phenomena of the faculties, objects, and consciousness (*indriya-viṣaya-vijñāna*), they are like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent—and identical to echoes; they can merely be heard but cannot be grasped.
Indeed, the faculties, objects, and consciousness are interwoven with one another and mutually destructive, like swords and weapons against one another. Now...

Then that which is heard is exhausted in hearing, and that which is perceived is empty of perception. The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses dissolve, leaving only the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Like a vajra banner, it is unshakable; what further sword or spear could possibly harm it?
Thus, it enables all sentient beings who recite my name to obtain this merit within my heart, even if they should be harmed.
A blade will break into pieces, for the nature of dust is empty. Even if one were to forcibly apply weapons, it would be like cutting water or blowing upon light;
there would be no damage at all, for the nature of the faculties is quiescent. Indeed, although this body exists, it is just like an echo or the reflection of light in water.
Thus, sound can be heard but cannot be grasped; water can be cut but cannot be split.
Light can be seen but cannot be grasped; thus one may know that this nature cannot be shaken by swords, staves, weapons, or spears.
Therefore, there will be no fear of the calamities of war. Sixth, through my cultivation of hearing and practice of what I have heard, the contemplative practice is perfected;
consequently, the essence of mind leaves behind hearing. Externally it does not attach to objects, and internally luminosity issues forth as light. Thereafter, the radiance continues...

When [the light] is perfected and pervades the entire dharma-realm, then all ghosts and spirits—who dwell in obscurity and darkness and whose very nature is to cling to material objects—will be unable to preserve themselves.
Why is this? Because that which ghosts and spirits approach and cling to is exclusively the dark and the obscure;
now, since his mind no longer clings to objects and his light illuminates the dharma-realm, they will all be subjected to that gloomy atmosphere. How could they endure it?
They are able to draw near and gaze upward. Thus, they enable those sentient beings who hold my name to obtain these merits within my heart:
namely, the yakṣas—the swift-moving spirits; the rākṣasas—the terrifying spirits; the kumbhāṇḍas—the spirits that cause nightmares;
the piśācas—the spirits that devour vital energy; and the pūtanas—the spirits of feverish disease.

As for ghosts: because light can destroy darkness, these various ghosts, though wishing to draw near to a person’s side, are not only unable to cause harm, but cannot even look up at them with their own eyes.

This is like the owl that is blind by day, the rākṣasa who turns his back to the sun, the local deity who does not see Dongshan, or the ghost messenger who does not see the monks of the host monastery.
Thus, ghosts and spirits will find it difficult to cause fear. The preceding passage concerned the difficulty of entering the realm of ghosts;

this section concerns the difficulty of ghosts coming to harass people. Seventh, when one turns the hearing back toward itself, both movement and stillness, as well as sound and its nature, are simultaneously and completely dissolved.
As seeing and hearing turn back to listen, one enters the One and loses the six [senses]. Thereby, both the sense organs and their objects are liberated.
Thus, internally there are no fetters of the six sense organs, and externally the shackles of the six sense objects are severed.

Having already departed from all deluded roots and objects, what further thing could serve as a fetter or lock? Therefore, it enables all sentient beings who maintain this recitation to obtain these merits within my heart;
such that fetters and shackles cannot take hold of them—thus, the shackles are difficult [to bind].
Fearless! Eighth, because at the time of entering the stream, I extinguished sound and attained liberation from the sensory object of sound;

through perfect hearing, I realized the ultimate nature of the faculties. When the sensory objects are extinguished, one does not invite the host of thieves; when the nature is perfected, all return to the single mind.
Therefore, at all times and in all places, there universally arises the power of the roots of goodness of impartial kindness and compassion, and no longer any perilous evil.
As for the characteristics of the mind, what further dangers or bandits could possibly plunder it?
Therefore, sentient beings who uphold my name shall obtain these merits within my heart; even when passing through perilous paths, though there may be powerful bandits, [they shall remain unharmed].
Furthermore, if one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), even a robber cannot plunder them; thus, one has no fear regarding the calamity of being robbed by thieves. Question:

How does the "revolving" (*pratyāvartana*) of what is seen and heard concern sentient beings? How can it cause them to be liberated from hardships such as water and fire simply by calling upon [the Bodhisattva’s] name?
Answer: In the past, when Cai Shun’s mother bit her finger, Shun felt pain in his heart. Is this not proof that the bond between mother and son is shared?

They are of one essence and mutually interpenetrate. If this is so even for ordinary people, how much more so for those who have realized the Great Compassion of the same essence—how could one doubt that they cannot act in such a way?
△ Second and third: Fearlessness regarding the three poisons.
Ninth, through the cultivation of hearing, one is freed from the dust of sensory objects and cannot be plundered by them (up to: all *icchantikas* are forever freed from the darkness of delusion).
This enables sentient beings, from the mind of a Great Being, to attain fearlessness regarding the three poisons. This refers specifically to greed, anger, and delusion.
This clarifies the elimination of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Ninth, through the cultivation of hearing by means of the self, one becomes authentic.
One becomes detached from all phenomena such as forms and sounds associated with the sense organs and their objects.

Because these organs and objects have been dissolved, the phenomena that serve as objects—such as beautiful forms and lustful sounds—can no longer plunder the family treasure. Since these organs and objects are already empty, [even] greed...
How could there be any desire in the mind? Therefore, it enables all sentient beings who hold my name to obtain these merits within my heart;
it transforms many lustful minds into the flames of wisdom, causing them to distance themselves from the suffering and hardships of greed and desire.
Thus, the peril of the poison of greed is no longer to be feared. Tenth, by virtue of my pure and singular nature of hearing sounds, I distinguish...

There are no objects of perception to oppose it. Therefore, whether it be the sense faculties or their respective objects, all are perfectly interfused and mutually functional, without distinction between self and other.
Since hatred arises from opposition, when there is no longer a division between "that" and "this," and neither a subject that opposes nor an object that is opposed, then hatred has no basis to arise.
Thus, it can cause those sentient beings who maintain this recitation to [perceive] my mind...
By attaining this merit, one remains far removed from resentment and malice; thus, the peril of the poison of anger is no longer to be feared.

Eleventh, because I have eliminated the darkness of the sense bases and their objects and restored the true luminosity of the self-nature, the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind are transparently and clearly illuminated, just like...
Lapis lazuli is the singular nature of the treasury; it shines forth with brilliant penetration and is without obstruction. Thus, the nature of deluded darkness has no basis from which to arise.

Consequently, it enables all sentient beings who maintain this recitation to obtain these merits within my heart, forever departing from the gloom of all view-delusions, the dullness of thought-delusions, and the obstructive nature of ignorance. And...
Ānantarya [karma] refers to that which is said to lack a virtuous mind; this is the most extreme form of deluded darkness.
If one causes all such beings to be forever separated from it and gives rise to wisdom, then the peril of the poison of delusion will no longer be worth fearing.
△ Third, the two [sections] on seeking fearlessness.
Twelfth: The fusion of forms; furthermore, hearing of the immovable site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) (up to): a woman with auspicious marks who is loved and respected by the multitude.
This enables sentient beings, from the mind of a Great Being, to obtain the fearlessness of fulfilling the two kinds of seeking. Twelfth:
because I have integrated the forms and substances of the sense organs and their objects, I have returned to the true hearing of self-nature.

Thus, without moving from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I enter into the mundane world. Since the obstructions of form have been dissolved, although I enter [the world], I do not destroy the realms.
The marks do not obstruct the fact that the world itself is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Therefore, one is able to reach everywhere throughout the ten directions, making offerings to the Buddhas to fulfill the perfection of merit, and hearing the Dharma to fulfill the perfection of wisdom. With both merit and wisdom combined, one succeeds to and flourishes the Dharma-activity at the side of each Buddha.
Thus, my own mind has already become a true son of the Dharma King; what cause for concern is there in seeking it?

It is not so. Therefore, for all sentient beings throughout the dharma realms who have no offspring, if they single-mindedly recite my name and seek a son, they shall obtain this merit within my heart and be able to give birth to a male child endowed with both fortune and wisdom.
Thus, those who seek a son need have no fear that they will not obtain one. Thirteenth, by...

Once one faculty has been uprooted, the six faculties become perfectly penetrating; compassionate light shines universally, impartial and non-dual, nurturing all within the ten directions as the single Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the empty nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Thus, one is able to reverently uphold and accord with the secret Dharma-gate.
Because of this illuminating clarity, it is established as Mirror Wisdom, manifesting that there is no form whatsoever that does not appear.
Because she encompasses and nurtures all, she is established as the "Empty Treasury" (*śūnyagarbha*), clarifying that there is nothing that this emptiness cannot contain.

Because she encompasses all, she is able to accord with and follow the Dharma-gates; because she is empty, she is able to receive and accept them without loss. Thus, this encompassing and nurturing, this acceding and following, and this receiving and accepting—all are my own mind.
As for the virtues of a woman, why worry about not finding them when one seeks them? Therefore, she is able to...

Within that Dharma-realm, there are no women. If any sentient being single-mindedly invokes my name, desiring to give birth to a daughter, and attains this merit within my heart, they shall be able to give birth to one who is handsome and upright in appearance, possessed of fortune and virtue, and gentle and compliant in temperament.
Among all sentient beings who see her, there will be none who do not love and revere her, because of this.
This is because the girl possesses the marks of merit and virtue; thus, those who seek her have no fear that they will not obtain her.
Now, those who seek sons or daughters only fear that they will not obtain a great being (mahāsattva). Since their request has now been fulfilled, they have no further fear of failure.
△ Fourth, the fearlessness of upholding the name.
Fourteenth: "In this trichiliocosm... (up to)... by my cultivation, I have attained true and perfect penetration.
This enables sentient beings, from the mind of a Great Being, to obtain the fearlessness of upholding the name. Regarding those who uphold the name, there is...

What is it that is feared, such that one speaks of "fearlessness"? It is because one who holds the name of a single Great Being might, upon encountering one who holds the names of many Bodhisattvas, doubt whether their own merit is superior and fear falling short of them.
Now, by demonstrating that they are equal and no different, this fear is eliminated. Furthermore, within these three thousand great chiliocosms...
The Sun and Moon currently abide in the world. The number of these sons of the Dharma is as great as sixty-two billion Ganges sands.
Some cultivate the methods for attaining Buddhahood for their own benefit, while others act for the benefit of others.
They extensively provide models for future students; they are none other than guides who accord with and teach all sentient beings.
Among them, there are those who employ skillful means and provisional wisdom, and those who employ wisdom and ultimate reality;
although their respective functions differ, none transcend my perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. By means of this faculty of hearing—
This wondrous gate is universally capable of containing all bodies and minds;
it is the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Thus, what bodhisattva is there who is not encompassed within it?
For this reason, a sentient being who upholds my single name and a sentient being who upholds the names of many bodhisattvas—these two individuals... [are equal].
The merit obtained is exactly equal; there is no difference whatsoever. Thus, one who holds even a single name shall have nothing to fear.
World-Honored One, how is it that holding my single name is equal and no different from holding many names?
Why is this? It is because I have cultivated and mastered the single gateway of the ear-organ, which is truly perfect and penetrating.
Thus, although the various sages are many, they can together match only my one person. How, then, could those who hold the Name have anything to fear?
△ Third, the conclusion on the function of bestowing fearlessness.
This is called "the fourteen powers of bestowing fearlessness that provide blessings for sentient beings";
this is the name of this concluding section. As described above in various ways, these are the fourteen [powers] which cause all sentient beings to [rely] upon my mind.
Within this, one attains fearlessness. It is not merely that one is liberated from dread;
it also causes one to be endowed with merit and virtue, for my own merit is entirely present within sentient beings, and the merit of sentient beings is likewise taken up and present within me.
This sufficiently demonstrates that the Great Being possesses the great compassion of the single essence (*ekatva*), in which the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated.
△ III. The Threefold Exposition of the Four Inconceivables (II) 1. General Summary:
"World-Honored One, I have further attained this perfect penetration... [up to] ...the four inconceivable, effortless, and wondrous virtues."

This is a general indication of the four inconceivables. Although what preceded—both ascending in accord with the Buddhas and descending to harmonize with sentient beings—was all according to capacity and thus still possessed limitations, it remained within the realm of mental reflection and verbal discussion. Therefore, what preceded was based on the *śrotra-indriya-samādhi* (the samādhi of the ear-organ), which pertains to the cause.
Here, however, it is stated directly that one "realizes the Unsurpassed Way," which involves the awakening of the fruit; therefore, [it is inconceivable].

This is something that can indeed be conceived and deliberated upon. Therefore, it is said: "I have further attained this heart of the non-differentiation among the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind—this subtle, wondrous, and perfect penetration.

Because I cultivate and realize the Unsurpassed Way through this perfect penetration, I am furthermore well-able, within the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), to manifest the four kinds of ultimate, divine, and most wondrous states that are inconceivable by the mind."
This refers to the subtle, pure virtue of effortless spontaneity, which is beyond conceptualization, unconditioned, and non-active.
One must understand that from this point forward, manifesting forms, reciting mantras, receiving offerings, and performing worship are all not the result of deliberate, conditioned intention;
rather, they are the spontaneous accomplishment of the sublime virtue of non-action and non-conditioning by the Great Being.
△ II. Detailed Enumeration (Four): 1. The Inconceivable Manifestation of Images. First:
From the moment I first attained the wondrous and sublime mind of hearing [the Dharma]... until attaining great mastery in rescuing and protecting sentient beings.
This clarifies how one manifests many bodies from within a single body, thereby demonstrating the inconceivable nature of the one and the many.
It precisely reveals that the faculty of hearing possesses three kinds of reality and is wondrously preeminent among all other faculties.

Because I first obtained wondrous hearing through this faculty of hearing, I thereby awakened to the storehouse-nature (ālaya-vijñāna), which is the wondrous mind. This describes the foundation of his virtues. As it is said:
The mind is fundamentally true; it is neither coarse nor subtle. Because it is beyond all relative distinctions, it is the most sublime among the sublime.
Because it is not mixed with delusive thoughts, it is called "the essence of mind. Because it is not confined by the sense organs or their objects, it is called "transcending hearing.
Once a single faculty is uprooted, the five faculties are liberated in their entirety; thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing cannot be separated, and all become one.
The substance [of these mantras] is the perfectly interfused and mutually functional treasury of the Tathāgata’s nature—the pure, inherently luminous, and precious true mind of awakened awareness.

Therefore, from within this inherently compassionate and immeasurable mind, it spontaneously accords with conditions to manifest myriad wondrous forms and proclaim various secret mantras, thereby accomplishing inconceivable and sublime virtues. *Śakara* means "firm."
"Solidly. *Mudrā* means "seal. "Pure jewel-eyes" refers to the perfect clarity of the five eyes. The head represents the Dharmakāya transcending the two extremes;
the arms represent liberation uprooting all sufferings; and the eyes represent Prajñā illuminating and discerning the myriad objects.
Furthermore, that these qualities all extend to eighty-four thousand represents the essence and function of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It universally responds to worldly toil. Whether compassionate or majestic, it concludes with the head. Whether in meditative concentration or wisdom, it concludes with the arms and eyes.
Since the human head is but one, it increases from the odd numbers; since the arms are two, they are distinguished by the even numbers.
Human eyes are only two, while celestial eyes may be three; thus, both odd and even are employed to clarify the meaning. Therefore:
The Great Being may manifest an image of compassion and joy to gather the hearts of virtuous people;
or he may manifest an image of majestic severity and wrath to break the courage of malevolent spirits.

Or he may display an image of meditative concentration with hands and eyes calmly withdrawn to block the mind from distraction; or he may display an image of wisdom with hands and eyes wide open and illuminating.
This is for the purpose of destroying the cave of ignorance; there is nothing that does not rescue and deliver sentient beings, enabling them to forever attain great sovereignty.
Thus, whether it be through compassion or majesty, or through meditative concentration or wisdom, all these are beyond the reach of thought or calculation.
△ Second, the inconceivability of the power of mantras.
Second, from "By means of my hearing and contemplation, I have escaped the six sense-objects" (up to) "all call me the Bestower of Fearlessness."
This clarifies that each form and each mantra possesses an inconceivable power individually.
Second, because I have entered samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, my six sense faculties have been completely uprooted; thus, I have transcended the six objects of perception.
Consequently, the objects cannot obstruct the faculties, just as sound passes through a wall while the wall cannot obstruct the sound.
It is an obstruction. Therefore, I am able here to liberate myself from the six sense objects.
Furthermore, with immeasurable compassion, I manifest various forms and recite various mantras according to conditions as they arise; yet these forms and mantras can grant all beings fearlessness.

He universally bestows [fearlessness] upon all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm. For this reason, in the worlds of the ten directions, within lands as numerous as motes of dust, all address him by my name as "the one who is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings. Question: How does this differ from the previous fourteen?
What is the difference? The answer is that the previous fourteen [methods] involve sentient beings being liberated through the mere recitation of names;

their capacity to evoke [the response] is limited, restricted to those fourteen types. Now, however, regardless of whether the response is evoked or not, or whether the name is recited or not, the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) all manifest clouds of bodies and, together with the recitation of the secret mantras, cause all to be freed from suffering and liberated from all fears. This is why...
They are not the same. It is precisely like the bright sun suspended in the sky, illuminating everything without exception; how could it be subject to conceptual thought?
△ Third, the inconceivability of receiving offerings.
Third, "By my cultivation of the fundamentally wondrous and perfect penetration" (up to) "...abandoning their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.
This clarifies the inconceivable power of transformation and guidance throughout the places traversed. Third, "by my cultivation":
it is fundamentally and originally wondrous—the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. By means of this faculty-nature, it is the pure *tathāgatagarbha*.

This is the fundamental nature: a root-nature entirely free from defilement and attachment. Within this state, one gives rise to the immeasurable mind of joy (*muditā*), sporting spontaneously and guiding others according to conditions.

Consequently, throughout all the worlds one traverses, wherever one transforms others or preserves the divine spirit, one causes sentient beings to turn their thoughts of stinginess and greed into a heart of joyful relinquishment, sometimes even giving away internal wealth such as body and life.
Or, when sentient beings seek my compassion by offering precious treasures or external objects, I accept them to perform the Buddha-work of giving.
Since the stinginess of these sentient beings is most firm and extremely difficult to break, if I can now cause them to break their stinginess and joyfully practice relinquishment,
how could the ritual of this transformation and the method of this transformation be conceivable?
△ Fourth, the inconceivable offering of service.
Fourth: "I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate" (up to) "seeking great nirvāṇa and attaining great nirvāṇa."
This clarifies the inconceivability of the mind that makes offerings to the Buddha and brings forth [the Tathāgata].
Fourth, because that which I have attained is precisely the birth of the Buddha, we share the same *tathāgatagarbha* mind;

therefore, one is able to realize the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost samādhi of ultimate firmness regarding all phenomena. Once this mind is attained, then all things of both the mundane and supramundane realms...

The Dharma is entirely a thing within my own treasury. Thus, one can give rise to the immeasurable mind of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*), and by means of this, produce various kinds of rare treasures to make offerings to the Buddhas above and extend them to sentient beings below.

This precisely reveals how the Great Being (Mahāsattva) regards sentient beings and Buddhas as non-dual through a mind of equality, thereby performing such offerings. Therefore, for sentient beings in the world, there is...

It is not that one seeks external material gifts of wealth; rather, it is like one who, having no wife, seeks a wife and then obtains a wife, or one who, having no son, seeks a son and then obtains a son—such are the external riches obtained according to one's requests.
Furthermore, those who seek longevity, freedom from aging, and increased years of life shall obtain longevity, freedom from aging, and increased years of life.
This internal wealth is available for whatever one seeks. It is not merely the giving of material goods;

rather, all sentient beings, whether mundane or supramundane, who desire to seek samādhi shall immediately attain it—be it the four dhyānas, the eight concentrations, or even the samādhis of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the three stages of worthiness, and the ten stages of sagehood. In this manner, even those who seek great nirvāṇa...

One who attains Buddhahood immediately realizes great ultimate *nirvāṇa* and thereby achieves enlightenment. This constitutes the gift of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, fulfilling whatever is sought.

For the Great Being has already realized the equality of True Suchness within the single true Dharma-realm, and has thoroughly understood all things—mundane and supramundane—including wife, children, life-span, and *samādhi-nirvāṇa*.
The trays are all the various goods stored within the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, they respond according to whatever is requested.

As for the fact that living beings and Buddhas equally partake of offerings, and that the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are without distinction, how could the mind that gives rise to such offerings ever be fathomed by thought?
△ Second, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration.

From "The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration; I [attained it] through the gateway of the ear" (up to) "therefore the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions," this is the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration.
The meaning is that now the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration realized; I have only, from...
This ear-faculty is a single gateway; by means of the perfect illumination of the three types of wisdom, one awakens to the One Mind and attains samādhi, thereby entering perfect penetration.
Thus, one is able to manifest the thirty-two transformations and the fourteen fearlessnesses, responding to conditions to display emanations, all of which proceed from the mind.
Whether manifesting forms, reciting mantras, receiving offerings, or performing acts of worship, these spontaneous activities are entirely free and sovereign. However...

If one investigates its cause, it all arises from entering the stream [of the Dharma], whereby the characteristics of subject and object are extinguished, and one subsequently attains the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King, the illusory-like samādhi.
Thus, one achieves the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi by entering perfect penetration;
therefore, one should take this entry into the stream via the faculty of hearing as the foremost expedient means. This...

This is precisely what is clarified in this single sutra: the most essential and pivotal point, the very first expedient means requested by the assembly, and the one gate through which the Tathāgata permits transcendence throughout the ten directions. It is also the main entrance to the jeweled hall sought in the four fascicles.
This is why Mañjuśrī, having received his command, specifically selected these faculties; it is where all Buddhas converge.

Guang (Guangju) likewise attests to this teaching. All those hereafter who wish to give rise to the bodhicitta, vow to transcend the afflictions of birth and death, and realize bodhi and nirvana, should read these words three times over; do not let them pass by in haste.
Below this, the Great Being recounts the reason for his own attainment of the name. At that time, the World-Honored One was an ancient Buddha...

The Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara praised me because I had skillfully attained the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, which serves as the gateway for entering the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
For this reason, amidst the great assembly, he specifically conferred upon me the title of Avalokiteśvara.
Because I listen through contemplation rather than following after the sense organs and their objects, I have attained the perfect fusion of the ten directions and radiant clarity.
He is unimpeded; like sound passing through a wall, or like the moon reflected in water, all who seek him find their response, and no wish goes unfulfilled.
Thus, the name "Avalokiteśvara" has spread throughout the worlds of the ten directions. This demonstrates that the name must have a corresponding reality;
it is established by means of observing the locus from which sounds are heard, and by observing the nature of that hearing itself. It is from this that the name is derived.
△ Section Four: The Seal of the Auspicious Omens Manifested by the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, upon the lion throne... [up to] "the chanting of *brahma* hymns and songs was spontaneously performed.
This clarifies that our Buddha and the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously manifested auspicious omens, thereby providing a seal of certification for the perfection of the Great Being.

This is the penetration. As for the five limbs emitting light, it symbolizes that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the seven great elements are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
As for the Buddha and the various Buddhas mutually exchanging light and pouring it over one another at their crowns, this precisely reveals that the Way of all Buddhas is identical;
the Dharma of the crown is non-dual, being solely the one treasury-mind (*ekagarbha-citta*). All Buddhas take this as their secret.

The "cause" refers to that upon which the Bodhisattvas rely to cultivate the myriad practices. The "forest and pond emitting sounds" symbolizes the non-separation between the sense faculties and their objects.
The "treasure lights mutually reflecting" reveals the mutual integration of seeing and hearing.

Thus, the great assembly beheld these auspicious signs with their eyes, heard the perfect concentration with their ears, dwelt within the Dharma assembly with their bodies, and touched the light of wisdom with their crowns; all were able to see and hear.
Since time immemorial, there has never been, nor have we ever heard of, even a single instance to the contrary.

Therefore, at every assembly of all dharmas, whether among the noble ones or the ordinary, those with eyes see it and those with ears hear it together; there is none who does not realize the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
Therefore, they universally attain the Vajra Samādhi—the ultimate solidity of all matters realized by the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas).

This reveals that they have equally awakened to the fact that the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), as well as the seven bases, are fundamentally the wondrous True Suchness (Tathatā) of the Tathāgata-garbha;
that while it follows conditions, it does not change, and while it changes according to conditions, its essence is like a vajra, indestructible.
As for the lotus flower made of a hundred jewels, it symbolizes that this samādhi is fully endowed with the myriad practices (*sādhana*).
As for its blue, yellow, red, and white colors, they symbolize the forty subtle causes of the stages of abiding, practice, and advancement (*vihāra-caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*).

As for their intermingling and blending, they symbolize that at each stage all merits are perfectly complete. As for the jewel-colored light of space, it symbolizes the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It forms...
This is liberation through the Dharma. That the Sahā world and the great earth both do not appear signifies that the dharmas of liberation are already simultaneously empty and non-arising.
That the ten directions become a single realm signifies that all phenomena are empty and the one true reality alone is manifest;
as it is said, "When all delusions have vanished, what need is there for the non-true? The performance of *brahmā-gāthā* chants precisely symbolizes the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
The Ear-faculty’s Perfect Penetration (*karṇendriya-pariśuddhi-samantabheda*) is what is meant by the statement that "the true essence of the teaching in this land is purity within sound-hearing.
*Brahma* (in full, *brahman*) is translated here as "purity"; it refers to the celestial sounds.

When the various devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) come to pay homage to the Buddha, they all offer hymns of praise, and worldly people practice them by imitating those sounds; thus, the sound is called *brahma*. In full, it is called *bhāṣa* (chanting).

*Ani*. This is translated as "praise" (*stotra*). It is also a celestial sound. Thus, the existence of *bhāṣya* (chanting) in the West is like the existence of "praise" (*zàn*) in the Eastern Land of Thunder.
While "praise" forms chapters according to prose, *bhāṣya* consists of short verses set to flowing hymns.
In brief, these are the sounds of the Brahma-heaven; through song, praise, and the unfolding of rhythmic cadences, they celebrate the Great Being.
This is the Perfect Penetration.
△ Fifth, Mañjuśrī’s Selection (in three parts): 1. The Buddha’s Command to Select.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī: [up to] "By which door of expedient means can [enlightenment] be easily accomplished?"
This passage has Mañjuśrī select the faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-indriya*).

Previously, it was stated in general terms that those who can follow a perfect faculty and those with an imperfect faculty differ by factors of ten million eons; however, it had not yet been definitively determined which faculty is perfect. Therefore, this selection is made.
Furthermore, there is a profound significance in the Buddha not selecting it himself but instead having Mañjuśrī select it: because, during the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in the past...
Samantabhadra is the supreme minister of the myriad practices; Avalokiteśvara is the supreme general of great compassion;

Mañjuśrī is the head of those awakening from ignorance and the teacher who receives the faithful. Thus, it is his business that at the beginning he proclaims the names and the Four Noble Truths to open the gate of perfect faith, and at the end he points toward Sudhana’s universal pilgrimage to spiritual friends. The present selection of faculties is fundamentally intended for beginners. If...
It would not be possible unless one were the foremost of those who awaken the unenlightened and a teacher who receives the faith of others.
This is why the Tathāgata specifically addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī in this manner: "Now you observe these twenty-five ranks of Bodhisattvas and Arhats;
each has already spoken of their initial generation of the mind, up until their attainment of the Way—there is nothing that is not [so]."
The three categories and seven elements serve as the initial point of entry.

These skillful and expedient means all state that by practicing in reliance upon them, one will ultimately attain the true, perfect penetration. Thus, regarding their cultivation and realization, they are all equally real;
fundamentally, there is no superiority or inferiority, nor any distinction of priority or sequence. Therefore, it is improper to make a selection among them.
It is so. However, I now wish to cause Ānanda to awaken to the treasury of the mind.
I do not yet know which of those twenty-five kinds of cultivation practices would suit Ānanda’s faculties;
furthermore, I require that they be easily accomplished by a beginner. For this reason, I cannot help but discern and select among them. It is unavoidable.

This teaching is addressed solely to Ānanda for the present, yet it also extends to all sentient beings in this Sahā world after my parinirvāṇa who wish to enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path.
What method from among the great categories should they employ at the outset as a gate of skillful means, so that they may easily practice and achieve success?
Regarding his entry into right concentration: this arises from the initial expedient means previously requested and the gateway to the jeweled house.

Therefore, he now commands the selection of that initial expedient as the door for entering the house; this is intended so that those who are currently responsive to the teaching, as well as all sentient beings of the present and future, may equally receive the true gift.
△ II. Mañjuśrī’s Verses in Response (2). 1. The Sūtra Master’s Account of the Ritual:
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command... [omitted] ...relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke verses in response to the Buddha.
This is the scribe’s account of Mañjuśrī’s ritual proceedings. "To receive the command" means to honor the teacher's instruction.

"Rising to prostrate" means to extend one’s own respect. "Responding with verses received from the Buddha" implies that what one has selected was done through the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual protection, and not out of one’s own arbitrary choice.
△ II. Mañjuśrī’s Proper Selection (5) A. The Source from Which One Should Select (3) 1. The Source of Reality and Delusion. The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect;

its limpid perfection makes awakening fundamentally subtle and wondrous. Fundamental luminosity shines forth, giving rise to the "object" (*viṣaya*); once the object is established, the nature of the shining light perishes.
This correctly elucidates how the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind follows along with defiled and pure conditions to become the two sources of the real and the false.

The first half-verse first clarifies the essence of the unchanging *tathatā*. This is like the preceding passage, where, before explaining "illumination" and "non-illumination," one first designates the two types of awakening—innate and acquired;
and where, before refuting the conditioned and the unconditioned, one first designates the two aspects of true nature.
This is a name. That which is called "Awakening" (jue) is the nature of the original awakening of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Because this nature is inherently numinous and luminous, and because from the beginning it is devoid of even a single thing—being pure and fundamental by its very nature—it cannot be designated by any name;
yet it is forcibly termed "Awakening. The "ocean" is a metaphor, for this nature of the fundamental awakening-garbha is vast and boundless, profound and unfathomable.
There is nothing with which it can be compared; for the sake of illustration, we shall use the depth and vastness of the ocean as a metaphor.
Thus, its essence is fundamentally clear and pure, never turbid from the beginning; it is fundamentally complete, never deficient from the beginning.
This is what is called the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening, which is quiescent yet constantly illuminating. It is inherently complete, inherently clear and pure, and fundamentally...

Self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*) is the fundamentally primordial and wondrous true essence. It is what is called "original awakening, luminous and wondrous," which is eternally quiescent despite its illumination.
Yet this true essence, although it accords with conditions, has never changed from the beginning. It is inherently possessed by every person and is lacking in none;
it is what is called the "eternally abiding true mind, the nature of purity and luminosity. This refers to the ocean of awakening.
The term "substance" (*ti*) reveals the greatness of substance; "clarity and perfection" (*chengyuan*), discussed in terms of characteristics (*xiang*), reveals the greatness of characteristics;

"primordial subtlety" (*yuanyao*), spoken in relation to function (*yong*), is the greatness of function. These three great aspects of the one mind are what all people universally possess—the true source that is no different from that of the Buddhas.
If one can merely awaken to this nature, it immediately becomes the secret treasury of the three virtues (*sande*). And as for the second half [of the verse]...
The verse clarifies that delusion has indeed occurred; this very nature thus becomes the false source of the threefold continuity.
This is because this nature is fundamentally and originally luminous, requiring no contrived effort and transcending all subject and object.

Yet, it is like that first moment of non-awakening, when, upon the body of original, wondrous, and original luminosity—the fundamental awakening—a false mind of "subjective illumination" suddenly arises.
Consequently, the delusory objects illuminated [by consciousness] arise. Once these delusory objects have been established, the true nature—which is neither subject nor object—is lost.

It then transforms into the delusory mind that performs the illumination; thus, from the fundamental storehouse of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-ālaya*), it becomes the storehouse consciousness of ignorance (*avidyā-ālayavijñāna*).
The preceding phrase refers to the aforementioned principle that "the enlightened nature of awareness must be luminous," yet through delusion...

This refers to luminous awareness. The subsequent phrase means that based on the previously established cause of luminosity, an object is posited; once the object is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.
△ Second, the source of the arising and ceasing of phenomena.
"From delusion comes empty space... when the bubble is extinguished, the space was originally non-existent; how much more so for the three realms of existence.
This further elucidates that by being deluded regarding the truth and pursuing the false, one creates the source of birth and death.

Since one has already become ignorant (avidyā) regarding the store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) through being deluded about the nature of original enlightenment (prakṛti-ālaya), one becomes deluded regarding the emptiness of nature and treats it as inert, materialistic space. Therefore, it is said:
Delusion gives rise to space. Within this dark obscurity of emptiness, darkness coagulates into form, thereby establishing the two kinds of worlds:
those of sentient beings and those of insentient things. Thus it is said that the world is established based upon space.
By grasping a portion of ignorant delusive thought and allowing it to congeal, the realm of insentient matter is formed; by grasping a portion of conscious delusive thought...

Through the discrimination of perceptions, one becomes a sentient being. This occurs by relying on the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) of ignorance, whereby the two retributions—the environment and the body—arise, resulting in the two divisions of the perceived object (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving subject (darśana-bhāga).
However, since this text speaks of both the world and sentient beings, it is evident that their karmic fruits are also implied; thus, the three types of continuity arise in mutual interaction.

This is truly because sentient beings recognize delusion within awakening. Confined by the sense organs and their objects, they perceive empty space as vast and boundless, eternally abiding and indestructible.

Yet how could they know that this immense empty space arises within the heart of Great Awakening, appearing no more than a single bubble on the ocean? Its minuteness is such as this; its lack of substantiality is likewise.
This is also the case here; how much more so for the contaminated realms (*sāsrava-dhātu*)?
Within them, all sentient beings—whether of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and all their karmic fruits—are even more clearly understood to be insubstantial.

If one knows that the nature of foam is unreal and that its cessation still returns to the sea, then one will know that the nature of emptiness is fundamentally without cessation and still returns to Suchness (*tathatā*).

This is the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*. These eight preceding lines correspond to the previous [passage]: "giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), giving rise to the world, and in stillness forming empty space.
The following two lines correspond to the previous: "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise;
the deluded mind naturally rests; this resting is itself *bodhi*. Question: The Buddha’s command to select [the successor] was of great urgency. Why did Mañjuśrī...

This is not direct. You have selected the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*) as your intent, yet you pull here and drag there, discussing the real and the false, speaking of birth and extinction, and expounding upon these non-urgent matters. Why is this? Answer: This is precisely the urgent task.

It is because sentient beings wander in saṃsāra solely due to their failure to understand the nature of reality and unreality, and of birth and extinction. Therefore, they remain perpetually within the realm of birth and death.

"Do not enter the cave of ignorance; rather, enter the Tathāgatagarbha. Now that the faculties have been selected and cultivation is enjoined, this is intended to lead all people toward the Tathāgatagarbha, to reach the path of wondrous adornment, and to enter the gate of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is necessary to fully manifest the distinction between the real and the false, so that one may resolve upon what to adopt and what to reject.
By minutely analyzing the falsity of its arising, one is made to know the manner of its extinction and removal.

This is indeed the *Yi* (Change/Transformation). The reason for citing this to initiate the discourse is that it addresses the immediate and essential needs of the present assembly, as well as all those of the past and future, so that they may return home along the very path they are on.
This is the compassionate heart of Mañjuśrī, acting for the sake of both the Dharma and sentient beings.
△ Third, the explicit instruction on what should be selected:
"The nature of returning to the source is non-dual... the speed with which the initial mind enters samādhi differs from one to another.
This clarifies the intent behind the necessity of selecting [a specific method] for perfect penetration. Following the preceding text, the meaning is that if one can simply...
Once the realms of deluded consciousness have been extinguished, one may return to the original, primordial *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
Having returned to this single nature, the principle is non-dual. Should one wish to enter this *tathāgatagarbha*, as for the skillful means:
There are naturally many gateways, just as the capital district has a single entry point yet many diverging paths.
If one were to discuss how the Buddhas and the twenty-five sages realized this nature, there would be no element among the three aggregates or the seven elements that was not perfectly penetrating.
Cultivating both in forward and reverse order are all skillful means; there is no practice that does not serve as a gateway for entering the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus, Dignāga entered the Way through sound—this is cultivation in the forward order—while Śraddhākaravarman became weary of and detached from the impure.
This is the practice of "reversal" (*viparyaya*). The divine eye of Aniruddha achieves the "conformity" (*anuloma*) by means of reversal.

The breath-regulation of Revata achieves the "reversal" by means of conformity. The mental vision of Śāriputra is the practice of conformity. The nose-contemplation of Ānanda is the treatment through reversal.
Up to the mindfulness of Amitābha by Mahāsthāmaprāpta, which is the practice of conformity; the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara is the treatment through reversal. If one examines this in detail...
To discuss this: there are twenty-five gates, and within each gate there are two kinds of skillful means—namely, the direct and the inverse.
Thus, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all able to realize [enlightenment] within the eighteen realms; why then should one make selections?
However, for a person who has first resolved their mind and wishes to enter samādhi, whether they possess complete faculties or incomplete faculties, days and kalpas are as equal as...
Twofold. Because one who attains the perfect faculties (*paripūrṇendriya*) proceeds with ease and speed, a single day may equal many eons (*kalpa*).
One who does not attain the perfect faculties proceeds with difficulty and slowness; thus, even if they practice for many eons, it cannot match a single day [of the former].

Therefore, because of these differences in slowness versus speed and difficulty versus ease, they cannot be treated as equivalent or categorized in the same manner. Hence, it is not permitted [to do so].
There is no need for further selection.
△ Second, the specific selection of various gates (four). First, the selection of the six sense objects:
"The perception of form binds one to the sense-object" (extending to) "subject and object do not pervade everywhere; how then can one attain perfect penetration?"
This distinguishes the six sense objects as the perfect penetration; it is not swift but slow, difficult rather than easy.

What the Buddha previously stated—that their respective practices are truly without superiority or inferiority—was said in reference to the realization of the *tathāgatagarbha* by those various sages.
Now, for those who wish to cultivate and realize the samādhi of the initial mind, there are distinctions between being slow or swift, and difficult or easy;

therefore, one cannot fail to exercise discernment. This is because, as in the case of Upānanda, those who enter through contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of form do so because this nature of form is originally but a false thought that has coagulated into material obstruction.
Dust. If one attempts to understand and clarify it with the essence of the mind, it still does not penetrate through.
How can one, regarding these things that are neither clear nor penetrating, obstructed and impassable, desire for a beginner to rely upon them to swiftly attain perfect penetration?
Is this not difficult? Although Dharmatrāta attained realization through the sound of the Dharma, that very sound—

Sound is a single phenomenon (*dharma*), yet it cannot avoid being mixed with language and written characters; it consists merely of the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*).
A single character directly designates a thing as a "name," which expresses its own essential nature (*svabhāva*);

for example, the word "fire" expresses only fire and does not include earth, water, and so forth, nor does it indicate what kind of fire it is. Multiple characters combined express distinctions as a "phrase," which expresses specific differences (*viśeṣa*).
It is as stated in passages concerning incense, lamps, and so forth; that is, the *vyañjana* (phoneme/letter) serves as the basis for both [the *pada* and the *nāman*] to manifest their meaning.
Therefore, the ancients regarded the *vyañjana* as the "flavor" (*rasa*), because the phoneme can manifest these two, just as flavor manifests the saltiness or blandness within food.
Furthermore, a single *nāman* (name/word) cannot contain a single *pada* (phrase), nor can a single *pada* contain a single *nāman*.

This refers to one who has thoroughly mastered all principles and meanings. Since these two [aspects] do not mutually penetrate, how can one who is at the initial stage of practice wish to rely upon this to swiftly attain perfect penetration?
Is this not difficult? Regarding the character "yi" (依) here, Changshui interprets it as "shi" (是), while Wenling interprets it as "wei" (惟).
The ancient text reads "yi" (依); since sound merely relies upon the three—name, phrase, and flavor—it seems that "relying upon" (*yi*) is the correct reading. This is because...

The character "yi" (伊) is merely a phonetic corruption of "wei" (偽). Although Xiangyan attained awakening through the sensory object of fragrance, he could only perceive that fragrance when the fragrance and his nose were in mutual contact; were they separated from the faculty of the nose, there would fundamentally be no fragrance.
Furthermore, the faculty capable of perception can never be in constant union with the fragrance being perceived.
When conditions coincide, there is the capacity for cognition; when conditions separate, there is nothing cognized. Yet, the subject and object cannot remain in constant conjunction.
How can you wish for the initial mind to rely upon such impermanent things to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of the true and eternal?
Is this not difficult? Although Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata attained awakening through the sense-object of taste, [it was not by relying on that impermanence].

As for "entering": although this nature of taste is not inherently and spontaneously aware of its own existence as taste, it must wait for the time when the faculty of the tongue tastes it for the flavor to manifest; only then does one know the natures of sour, salty, bitter, bland, cold, or hot.
Furthermore, the faculty that is capable of perceiving does not constantly merge into a single unity with the perceived object, the dust of taste. Because of the taste—
When they meet, there is the nature of the perceiving consciousness; when the flavor ceases, there is no object to be perceived.
Since these two do not constantly unite as one, how can the initial mind rely upon this impermanent flavor while seeking to swiftly attain the eternally abiding, perfect penetration?
Is this not difficult? Although Bhadrapāla attained awakening through the sense-object of touch, touch has no self-nature.
The nature [of contact] must manifest the object that touches only through the body that is touched.
If there were no body to be touched, then even if the object that touches existed, it would not be clearly manifested;

nor could the nature of contact itself be established, for contact does not touch itself—it is only through the object being touched that it is revealed. Thus, the subject and object must both conjoin. Then...
The sense-object of touch has a nature; yet when subject and object are separated, the sense-object of touch lacks a nature.
Whether in conjunction or separation, one knows that its nature is not fixed or permanently abiding.

How can you, at the initial stage of practice, rely upon this impermanent thing to swiftly attain the permanent and all-pervading penetration? Is this not difficult? Although Kāśyapa relied upon the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),...

As for "entering through awakening": the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) is the shadow or residue left by the cessation of the preceding five sensory objects. Since it is perceived exclusively by the mind alone, it is called the "internal object.
If one relies upon this internal object and practices based upon it, one must necessarily differentiate between the subject (the capacity to perceive) and the object (that which is perceived).

Thus, the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) becomes the perceiving subject, and the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) becomes the perceived object. Once the characteristics of subject and object have been so differentiated, then...

This is not a nature that is universally pervasive. How can you wish for a beginner to rely upon such a thing—which is neither universal nor penetrating—to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of universal pervasiveness? Is this not difficult? [The word "pin yi" (憑依) means "to rely upon.

Each of these [six sense-objects] leads to the realization of perfect penetration through its respective dust; yet they are all now set aside because, while they were holy for those [practitioners], [they are not so for others].
In their essential nature, there is nothing they do not penetrate; yet here, their speed and slowness differ in kind.

Therefore, among the six sense organs, consciousness, and the seven great elements that follow, all those which are not selected are considered slow rather than swift and are thus unsuitable for beginners.
Only the ear organ is selected because it is swift rather than slow, and is uniquely suitable for beginners.
△ Second, the exclusion of the five sense organs.
Although the nature of seeing is transparently clear... [up to] "...the conceptual thoughts cannot be shed; how could one attain perfect penetration?
