This excludes the perfect penetration of the five sense organs, which is slow rather than swift, and difficult rather than easy. If Ānanda...

Ratna, although one may enter into awakening by means of seeing its nature, the nature of this faculty of sight, though it may be thoroughly penetrating and clear, when discussing the four directions, only the first three are clarified, while the last one is not. If one discusses the four intermediate directions...
The first two dimensions are clear, yet one sees only half; the latter two dimensions are deficient, and one does not see half.
How can you wish for a beginner to rely upon such a defective and incomplete faculty to swiftly attain perfect, all-encompassing penetration?
Is this not difficult? Although Baṇḍin attained awakening through the breath of the nose-faculty, nevertheless—
Regarding the breath of the nose: although its inhalation and exhalation pass through, when the exhalation is finished, it cannot immediately enter;
and when the inhalation is finished, it cannot immediately exit. Thus, even in this present inhalation and exhalation, there is no intermediate connecting breath.

Furthermore, as the parts are separated and dispersed during inhalation and exhalation, each occurs independently—there being only exhalation without inhalation, or only inhalation without exhalation.
Furthermore, these are not yet the perfect faculties that mutually intersect and interpenetrate.
How can you, at this initial stage, wish to rely upon these imperfect and intermittent faculties to swiftly attain this perfect, eternal, and universal penetration?

Is this not difficult? It is not that they are not so; they do indeed involve mutual intersection and interpenetration. Although Āṭavī was led by his awareness of flavors, [he eventually attained it].
As for those who awaken and enter [into this truth]: this cognition of the tongue-faculty does not arise without cause;
it must depend upon the objects of various flavors to give rise to the cognition of awareness. If the objects of flavor were to perish, then the cognition of awareness would likewise cease to exist.
Since it is not permanent, how can you wish for the initial mind to rely upon this impermanence?
As for the sense-faculties: is it not difficult for one to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of the eternally abiding?
Although Pilindavatsa attained awakening through the body-faculty, this body-faculty is identical in meaning to the previously mentioned object of touch.
It is only by means of the touching object (*viṣaya*) that the touched body is manifested; thus, the subject and object manifest each other, both being equally devoid of self-nature. Both...
This is not the perfect contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Furthermore, the body-faculty and the object of touch differ in their capacity for cognition;
each has its own boundaries and each has its own limitations. They do not merge with one another and cannot be brought into harmonious union through perfect penetration.
How can you wish for a beginner to rely on such a faculty that lacks perfect penetration in order to swiftly attain perfect penetration? Is this not difficult?
Yes. Although Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kongsheng) attained awakening by means of the faculty of mind (*manas*), this faculty of mental cognition is actually the seventh consciousness.

Because the six [consciousnesses] take the seventh as their root, it is called the "faculty of mental cognition. Since this faculty of mental cognition and the sixth consciousness are intermingled, constantly and critically deliberating, it is termed "distracted thought.
However, when one returns from delusion to the truth, one enters into profound stillness and merges with that profound stillness.
At the moment of awakening, one ultimately finds that there is no such thing as the faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, the mind and cognition are mutually dependent, and it is through their mutual manifestation that they are designated as "faculties.

Since the discursive thoughts of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the conceptual reflections of the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*) cannot both be suddenly and simultaneously liberated, even those who have long practiced the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are still unable to escape them.
The faculty of seeing is transcendent and uniquely prominent, manifesting as the faculty of consciousness.

How could you wish for the initial mind to rely upon this faculty, which is chaotic and lacks detachment, in order to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of total detachment? Is this not difficult?
Herein, the faculties of seeing and smelling are distinguished as being imperfect; the faculties of the tongue and body are distinguished as being impermanent. They are imperfect.
Taken together, these are known as "shallow. The intention behind this knowledge is to distinguish that which is not purely free [from defilement]. Question:

Regarding the five sense-faculties (*indriya*), since they are all equally termed "nature" (*prakṛti*), why are they also distinguished? Answer: Although the faculties are indeed nature, they are superior to their respective objects and consciousnesses.

Nevertheless, because their direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is uneven—being either complete or incomplete—the preceding text stated: "The complete and the incomplete differ by factors of ten million eons. It is precisely for this reason that they are now being distinguished.
Those that are not constant, not pervasive, or not integrated are shallow and incomplete.
△ Third, the exclusion of the six consciousnesses:
"The consciousness-seeing is a mixture of the three harmonies" (up to) "conditioned by thought and not apart from objects; how can one attain perfect penetration?"
This selection of the six consciousnesses as the perfect penetration is not swift but slow; it is not easy but difficult.

As for the son of the Vulture Peak (Śāriputra), although he attained awakening through the visual consciousness, this consciousness of seeing must involve the intermingling of the faculty and the object;
only when these three conditions harmonize does false birth arise. If one investigates its root, the four modes of being are without birth. It is not...
It possesses a substantial characteristic: it exists when the sense organ and its object meet, and does not exist when they are separated.
Furthermore, its own substance is not originally fixed or permanent. How then can the initial mind, relying upon this impermanent consciousness, seek to swiftly attain perfect penetration?

Is this not difficult? Although Samantabhadra attained awakening through the faculty of auditory consciousness, this "hearing with the mind" that penetrates the ten directions is produced by the power of great vows resulting from long-term cultivation of causal practices.
If one is a beginner or a latecomer in their studies, one cannot enter [this state]. How, then, can a beginner rely upon this which has been so long-established?
As for the cause by which one swiftly attains perfect penetration—is this not difficult?

Although Yanxi attained awakening through the nose-consciousness, this visualization of the white [spot] at the tip of the nose was merely a provisional device established to respond to his specific capacity.

It was intended only to cause his scattered mind to be withdrawn and to abide temporarily. Furthermore, once the mind has achieved the ability to abide, then the appearance of the white [spot] at the tip of the nose—
This constitutes abiding in what has been accomplished. Yet, the true mind is without abiding;
how can you wish for the initial mind to rely upon this mind that has abiding in order to swiftly attain perfect penetration? Is this not difficult?

Although Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra attained awakening through the tongue-consciousness while preaching the Dharma, this preaching was merely the manipulation of sounds and characters. It was through this that he achieved enlightenment.
This is entirely because the roots of merit from previous lives have matured, whereby one attains awakening through fearless eloquence;

it is not something that can be achieved by the faculty of the tongue in a single moment. How much less so could it be accomplished by sounds or written characters, both of which belong to the conditioned and the outflowing realm?
It is not something unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) or untainted (*anāsrava*).
How can you wish for the initial mind to rely upon these conditioned and tainted phenomena to swiftly attain perfect penetration? Is this not difficult?

Although Upāli attained awakening through the body-consciousness by upholding the precepts, within these precepts—both the observance of prohibitions and the performance of duties—it merely restrains the body-consciousness. Even if...
It is not body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). If one were to rely on it, there would be neither restraint nor transgression, and nothing to bind one.

Furthermore, body-consciousness is limited solely to the body and cannot universally penetrate all phenomena. How can you expect a beginner to rely on this non-penetrating consciousness to swiftly attain perfect penetration?
Would this not be difficult? Although Maudgalyāyana attained enlightenment through mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), [he did so by means of the faculty of hearing].

As for "entering": the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is by nature the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). Spiritual powers are rooted in causes from past lives; they do not intersect with one another.
How, then, could it have anything to do with the discrimination of mental objects? Furthermore, the mental consciousness clings to objects moment after moment;
it is not capable of being detached from things. How can you wish for a beginner to rely upon this clinging?
To rely on deluded consciousness and thereby swiftly attain perfect penetration—is this not difficult?
△ Fourth, the examination of the seven elements:
"If one contemplates the nature of earth" (up to) "the cause and effect are now distinct; how can one attain perfect penetration?"
This distinguishes [the preceding methods] as all being slow rather than swift, and difficult rather than easy.
Although Kṣitigarbha attained realization through leveling the earth and thus entered the element of earth, if one were to observe the nature of the earth-element itself:
However, this is merely a state of firm solidity, obstruction, and lack of penetration; it is not a thing of unimpeded penetration.
Furthermore, the labor of leveling and filling the main thoroughfares belongs to the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Were it not for encountering the Buddha’s instruction, how could one attain the sagely nature that is everywhere unobstructed? How, then, can a beginner rely upon such an obstructed thing?

Is it not difficult, then, to swiftly attain perfect penetration? Although Candraprabha attained realization through the water element, if one were to observe the nature of that water element, it would all arise from mental conceptions, thereby constituting his contemplative practice.
This is not the true principle of suchness (*tathatā*). To accord with the principle of suchness as immovable, one must possess the wisdom that is suchness as immovable;
only then will it be possible. It cannot be realized by the mind of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) involving applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
How then can a beginner, relying on this mind of applied and sustained thought, desire to quickly attain [it]?

"Perfect penetration"—is this not indeed difficult? Although Aśvajit attained entry through the nature of the fire element, if one were to observe by means of the nature of the fire element, he did so because he grew weary of the fires of desire and sought liberation from them;
it was not a severance of the nature itself, nor was there any true reality to be abandoned. Furthermore, he practiced because of his many desires."
Regarding this contemplation, how could it be that all beginners are exactly like this? There are also those who have few desires and have severed desire;
how then should they proceed? One must know for certain that this method is not a universal expedient.
How then can one expect a beginner to rely on this non-universal method to swiftly attain perfect penetration—is this not difficult? Although Vairocana... [text ends]... because of this...

Regarding those who attain awakening through the wind-element: if one observes with the nature of the wind-element, although one may observe extensively both internally and externally, all are merely transformations driven by the power of delusive conditions. Yet, the wind has movement and stillness;
it is not without its relative counterparts. Since there are such counterparts, it cannot be the unsurpassed, peerless, and eternally abiding awakened mind. How then [could it be]?

If those who desire to rely on this dharma of movement and stillness— which is neither permanent nor constant— in order to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of the true and eternal, is this not indeed difficult?
Although K'ong-tsang (Gaganagañja) attained entry through the greatness of space, if one were to observe with the nature of the greatness of space itself,
then although he was able to observe that the four great elements have no basis and thus perfectly realize the nature of emptiness, nevertheless—
This empty space is formed by the dark obscurity of ignorance. As for its essential nature, it is originally turbid and lacking clarity;
it is dull and lacks sentience. It is not something characterized by spiritual luminosity, correct knowledge, or correct awakening.
Since it is an insentient and unawakened, obstinate thing, it is fundamentally different from the Bodhi of correct knowledge and correct awakening.
It is so. How can you wish for the initial mind to rely upon this insentient object in order to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of Buddhahood?

Is this not difficult? Although Maitreya attained entry through the great element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*), if one were to observe the nature of this great consciousness, one would find that the nature of this consciousness arises and ceases from moment to moment; it is indeed...
It is not permanent. To merely preserve the mind that contemplates while wishing to contemplate the great element of consciousness is like placing a head upon one's own head;
it is already a delusion. How much more so would the great element of consciousness being contemplated fail to be a delusion?
How can one desire to rely upon this initial, deluded, and impermanent mind to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of the eternally abiding?

Is this not difficult? Although Śrī-Ābhāsvara entered awakening through the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha by universally gathering the six sense faculties, one must know that there are contemplative methods for all six elements; it is only this single door that does not require [external aids].
This is a skillful means; therefore, it does not say that "contemplation" refers to the contemplative method of recollecting the Buddha by means of pure mindfulness alone.
Nevertheless, whenever the mind is raised or a thought is stirred, it belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and is thus a phenomenon of impermanence.
Even if pure mindfulness continues uninterrupted and all six sense faculties are fully gathered, it fundamentally does not escape the nature of successive arising in a prior-and-subsequent sequence.
This is the extinction of the mind. Since one has taken arising and ceasing as the cause, one will only induce the fruit of arising and ceasing.
Now, if you seek the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is utterly incompatible with what has been induced.

How can you wish for a beginner to rely on this mind of arising and ceasing thoughts to swiftly attain the perfect penetration of non-arising and non-ceasing? Is this not difficult? Thus, because of...

If the fruit is not of a similar nature, it will be difficult to attain. Nevertheless, among all the Dharma-gates, this alone is the one that can produce the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing by means of the causes of arising and ceasing.
Students must not fail to know this; do not, out of negligence, cast away your own life-preserving raft. Why is this?
Because this is the most expedient among all the expedients of the Buddhas; it is a Dharma-gate of Other-Power. Therefore...
This includes both the wise and the ignorant, and embraces both those of sharp and dull faculties, so that all may obtain benefit.
It is merely distinguished because there is a difference in how the causal mind and the resultant awakening interact as subject and object;
it is not that the Buddha-remembrance practice (*nienfo*) cannot transcend birth and death, and thus it is distinguished. Let the wise examine this in detail.
△ 3. Correctly Selecting the Ear-Faculty (5): 1. Clarifying the Sublimity of the Dharma.
I now address the World-Honored One: [omitted] I wish to attain samādhi; in truth, I shall enter through hearing.
This correct selection of the Ear-faculty Perfect Penetration is swift rather than slow, easy rather than difficult;
it alone accords with the essential body of the teachings for this region. It is truly the most wondrous Dharma-gate for cultivation by those at the initial stage.
My current address to the World-Honored One consists of words reporting back in accordance with the imperial decree. "Saha" here means "Endurance. The trichiliocosm...
This is their collective name. Indeed, when the Buddhas appear in the world, the essential substance (*śarīra*) of their teachings varies according to the region;

thus, there are those for whom light constitutes the teaching-substance, those for whom the Bodhi tree serves as the teaching-substance, or those for whom it is a garden, a pavilion, the open sky, or celestial robes;
or even those for whom it is non-speaking and non-demonstrating, up to the Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*).
In this world, there are those who do not employ written words but perform the Buddha-work solely through various fragrances;

from this, one knows that all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) may serve as the substance of the teaching. Nevertheless, in this region, three sense objects are predominantly employed, such as the yellow scrolls and blue silk [of books].

Thus, when the sense-object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) serves as the substance of the teaching, one gains benefit by hearing the Dharma; when sound (*śabda*) serves as the substance of the teaching, one gains benefit by hearing the Dharma;

and when the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharma-viṣaya*) serves as the substance of the teaching, one gains benefit by contemplating the dharmas through observation. Now, considering the era of the Buddha, those who gained benefit by hearing his voice were numerous;
furthermore, even in the degenerate age, there are many who attain awakening through the guidance of sound. Therefore, it is said that in this land, the true teaching consists of sound.
The gate of practice for the essence of purity consists solely in hearing through sound.
Although the substance of the teaching resides in sound and hearing, if one wishes to cultivate right concentration and seek its actual efficacy, one must rely upon the faculty of the ear;

only from within the nature of hearing can one enter *samādhi*. For although the teachings of sound can express and represent [the truth], were it not for the nature of hearing, they would be incapable of doing so.
This is a wondrous accord. Thus, while the hearing of the Way relies upon sounds, its realization and verification depend solely upon the nature of hearing.
Consequently, from the time of the selection of faculties for instruction, this land has definitively pointed to the faculty of the ear;
it is the most wondrous dharma-gate for beginners to practice easily, leading to perfection and penetration.
△ Second, explaining the excellence of the person.
"Leaving suffering to attain liberation... saving the world so that all are at peace, transcending the world to obtain the eternal abode.

This clarifies the superiority of the Great Being’s two benefits [for self and others]. The intent is that [he overcomes] the suffering of birth and death, bound by the fetters of the sense faculties and their objects.
That which people find difficult to abandon, the Great Being has abandoned; with one faculty returning to its source, all six faculties are liberated.

That which people find difficult to attain, the Great Being has attained. If one compares him to other sages who have achieved perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), then Avalokiteśvara is truly most excellent;
he is seen as the sole individual among kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This clarifies [the matter].
"Transforming and guiding" means that temporally, one exhausts the three periods of time. "Entering lands as numerous as motes of dust" clarifies the places where one manifests the body;
"extensively" means that spatially, one pervades the ten directions. This precisely refers to the meaning of the thirty-two manifestations preaching the Dharma according to conditions.
"Attaining the power of mastery" means attaining the four inconceivable masteries and accomplishing great spiritual powers.
Furthermore, regarding the "bestower of fearlessness": he is able to universally bestow the fourteen kinds of fearlessness upon all sentient beings.

Because this Great Being’s preaching of the Dharma is unhindered, he is called "Wondrous Sound" (Miaoyin). Because he seeks out sounds to rescue beings from suffering, he is named "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanyin).

Because the nature of his sound is undefiled, it is called the "Brahma-sound. Because his responses do not miss the proper time, they constitute the "Sound of the Ocean Tide. For these reasons, he is so named.
Because it is real, it is able to rescue the world from suffering and bring all beings to peace and security— just as one who seeks a wife or children obtains a wife or children,

and even one who seeks long life obtains long life. To rescue them from the suffering of the supramundane and cause them to attain the eternal abode is like one who seeks samādhi and obtains samādhi, and even one who seeks great nirvāṇa and obtains great nirvāṇa.
"Pan" means "is. △ Third, clarifying the reality of meditative concentration:
I now address the Tathāgata... [up to] awakening and contemplation transcend discursive thought; body and mind cannot reach them.

This clarifies that the ear-faculty cultivated by this Great Being is easy rather than difficult, swift rather than slow, and possesses the three kinds of true reality—perfection, pervasiveness, and constancy.
It is the genuine cultivation of the sincere and upright concentration of a beginner. The meaning is:
why is it that I have now set aside all other faculties and selected the ear-faculty alone to address the Tathāgata?

Indeed. Regarding the Dharma-gate of the ear-faculty as taught by Avalokiteśvara, there are three kinds of truly wondrous meanings that distinguish it from the other faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and the seven elements.
First, for example, when a person is dwelling in stillness, even if drums were struck simultaneously in all ten directions, this ear-faculty would [perceive] those ten locations at once.
Both hear simultaneously; there has never been a time when they were divided. Where was it heard first? Where was it heard later? Where is there hearing?
Where is there no hearing? Thus one knows that the nature of hearing within our faculty of the ear is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through immediate contact, not requiring inference (*anumāna*).
It is fundamentally perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions;

this is what is called "perfect fusion and universal pervasion," the wondrous meaning of being true rather than false, and real rather than empty. Second, if one compares the faculty of hearing with the other five faculties:
Its functional supremacy must be examined. For instance, although the eyes are capable of seeing, they cannot perceive what lies beyond obstructions.
It is just as when one looks through window paper and does not see external objects, or when one looks through the skin and does not see the internal organs.
Thus, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) necessarily requires contact with an object (*viṣaya*) before it can be known to exist.
The same applies to the tongue and nose faculties and their objects, taste and fragrance; if one moves even a few inches away, they are no longer perceived.
Although the mind-faculty is all-pervasive, it is further entangled with consciousness, thought, and mental formations, which are so chaotic and disordered as to have no coherent beginning or end.
As for the ear-faculty, while in active use, it can hear through a wall, unlike the eye-faculty.
It does not fail to perceive what lies beyond obstructions; it hears both from afar and nearby, unlike the three physical organs which cannot perceive when separated from their objects.
When in a state of quietude, these organs hear all sounds simultaneously and together, unlike the mental organ (*manas*), which is disordered and lacks coherence.
Viewed from this perspective, the functions of the other five sense organs cannot equal those of the ear organ.
Thus, this faculty is pervasive and unimpeded; it is what is called the wondrous principle that is true and real, neither empty nor false.
Although the nature of sound may at times be moving and at times still, in all cases...
Within the essence of the nature of hearing, which is profoundly still, there is spontaneous arising and spontaneous ceasing, and spontaneous existence and non-existence.
Thus, at the time of movement, it arises as existence; at the limit of stillness and silence, it dissolves as non-existence—and this is what constitutes delusion.
Failing to realize this principle, one labels the moments when no sound exists as "the absence of hearing.
Yet one does not know that it is merely the sounds themselves that are non-existent and unreal; the nature of hearing is likewise non-existent.

Thus, when sounds are naturally absent, this nature of hearing does not perish by following the sounds into non-existence; and when sounds are naturally present, this nature of hearing— [does not arise by following them].
Nor does it arise following the sound. For when the sound arises, the nature of hearing knows its arising;

when the sound ceases, the nature of hearing knows its cessation. This sufficiently demonstrates that the nature of hearing is perfectly complete and pervasive throughout both modes of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, even when the sound arises, the nature of hearing has never arisen; and even when the sound ceases, [the nature of hearing remains].
Yet the nature of hearing has never known extinction; thus, existence and non-existence, as well as arising and ceasing—these two paths—are both perfect and both transcended.
This means that while the sensory object of sound arises and ceases of its own accord, this nature of hearing remains profoundly still and eternally present.
Is this not the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure clarity, the ultimate reality that is not illusory?

Is this not the wondrous meaning of non-delusion? This very nature of hearing, even when one is in a state of neither dreaming nor conceptualizing, does not cease to exist simply because it is not being thought of or conceived.

Therefore, the essence and function of this nature of hearing transcend the path of sensory perception and mental observation, and stand far above the realm of discursive thought. For this reason, as for the remaining five sense organs and six sense objects...
From this body up to the consciousness-mind, as well as the seven elements such as earth and water—none of these can reach it.
Nevertheless, these three kinds of reality are all present within our daily, ordinary lives.
As for those who manifest [this] fully, it does not depend upon cultivation before coming into being.

If one can apply oneself to this and reflect back upon one's own nature, it is like setting sail with the current or fanning a fire with the wind; one will naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
He then took the Great Being by the hand and walked together with him, resolving that they would never be mistaken for one another. May all who possess aspiration exert themselves!
△ Fourth, clarifying what should be practiced.
"Now, in this Sahā world... is it not that by following the whirlpool of immersion, one attains non-delusion?
This clarifies that the practice of the ear-faculty gate is precisely suited for the beginner, being swift and easy to cultivate.
The meaning is that in this Sahā world, the faculty of hearing is sharp and keen; if we discuss the essence of the teaching, it must be through the guidance and pointing of the Tathāgata.
Various discursive measurements of sounds, voices, and languages are displayed; only then can the underlying principles be fully articulated and the nature of the mind be clearly realized.
Yet sentient beings are deluded and fail to awaken; they cannot realize the Way through words, nor do they contemplate the mind upon hearing the teachings.
Instead, they merely follow after sounds and pursue echoes, and thus they cannot avoid being caught once again by the very sounds and teachings they seek.
This cycle of transmigration arises entirely from savoring the inherently existing nature of hearing; it is for this reason alone.

It is just like Ānanda, who, even if he were able to memorize the subtle principles elucidated in the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—would still be subject to such conditions.
Yet they still cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts and becoming submerged in the chamber of lust, unable to attain freedom.
Is this not precisely because they have lost their fundamental faculty of hearing and have been swept away by following after sounds and teachings?

If one can, like the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, turn back the mechanism of inverted hearing, enter the stream so that the object of perception vanishes, and return to hear one's own nature, then one will be able to realize perfect penetration and attain the Truth.
It is eternally thus, and therefore free from falsehood. One should know that for those who wish to transcend birth and death and realize wondrous permanence, this alone is the way.
It requires nothing more than, at all times and in all places, focusing solely on the faculty of hearing to turn the hearing back toward one's own nature;
there is no other matter involved. Is this not swift and easy to practice?
△ Five Sciences to be Cultivated (2) 1. Entrusting the Instruction to Listen and Practice.
Ānanda, listen attentively... [until] "How can one who hears and upholds not hear what is heard by the Buddha?"

This clarifies that the Ear-faculty Perfect Penetration (*karṇendriya-pariśuddha-avavāda*) should be cultivated; thus, he entrusts [the disciples] to listen to the teaching so that they may clearly understand its merits and faults.
"Ānanda, you must listen attentively" is spoken to propagate the Buddha’s command and proclaim it.
"As I do now," refers to nothing other than relying on the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority (*prabhāva*), whereby I proclaim the Golden [Vajra-samādhi] realized by Avalokiteśvara.
The *Vajra-rāja-asādhya-acintya-buddha-mātṛ-samādhi* is so named because it can destroy all delusions;
thus, it is called the virtue of the *Vajraprajñā*. Because it establishes all dharmas, it is called the virtue of liberation as an illusion (*māyā-vimokṣa*).
Because destruction and establishment occur simultaneously, it is called the virtue of the inconceivable *Dharmakāya*. All Buddhas arise from this...
Because it emerges from this, it is called the "Mother of Buddhas. Indeed, this samādhi is the foremost among all samādhis—truly eternal, perfect, and penetrating.

Yet, although you have been able to hear all the secret dharma-gates spoken by as many Buddhas as there are atoms of dust, if you do not practice them with genuine cultivation, but instead reverse the faculty of hearing and use that hearing to realize your own nature, none of these will avail you.

This is for the sake of benefit. Because the faculty of hearing cannot turn back its own hearing, it instead flows outward and chases after sounds, thereby further increasing the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and words.

Consequently, one cannot escape the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*). If you wish to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), even if you do not first eliminate the seeds and habits of names and words, you must still take the faculty of hearing as that which can store; yet sound has nothing to store. If this is so, then—
When subject and object become mutually entangled, one remains bound; not only can one fail to achieve right concentration, but one instead incurs great error and is ultimately deceived by it.
Since you are using this faculty of hearing to uphold the Buddha-dharma of all Buddhas, you cannot avoid such errors.
Why, then, do you not employ this faculty of hearing throughout the twenty-four hours of the day—while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down?

Is it not rather to turn back and investigate one’s own nature of hearing? If this is so, then practicing without practice is identical to the true cultivation of Avalokiteśvara, which is like an illusion.
△ Second, a detailed explanation of the practice (three parts): First, the teaching by means of Dharma.
"Sound is not born spontaneously" (up to) "Mātanga was but a dream; who could have retained your form?
This initial explanation of the Dharma provides a detailed clarification of the matter of cultivation. The meaning is that this faculty of hearing is not produced without cause or spontaneously;
rather, it arises because of the impact of the two kinds of objective sounds—the moving and the still—at the very beginning.
Within the wondrous perfection, the cause of attachment to stillness gives rise to hearing; subsequently, sound is withdrawn to form the faculty.
Thus, there is the designation "ear-faculty. This is precisely the mediator for the household thief; one must not fail to recognize it.
If one can rotate the faculty of hearing to hear back into one's own nature and become detached from the object of sound, this is the master who guards the house; [one must not...]
I do not understand. Since one has already been able to detach from that perceived object, the sound-dust, whom else could one designate as the "ear-faculty" that acts as the perceiver?
Once this single ear-faculty has returned to its source, then the remaining five faculties are simultaneously purified, all attaining liberation.
Consequently, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are all like illusions, obscuring the dusty appearances of the three realms.
In total, it is like flowers in the sky. Once the nature of hearing is restored, the cataract of the sense organ is naturally removed, and the appearances of sensory objects vanish.
Then, the essence of the wondrous enlightenment—the originally existing *tathāgatagarbha*—is spontaneously perfect and spontaneously pure.

If one can purify it further and further until reaching the ultimate purity, then the light of the mind will burst forth, illuminating heaven and reflecting the earth, shining through antiquity and soaring into the present, such that there is nowhere it does not reach.

It is pervasive, reaching everywhere without obstruction. Because it is eternally illuminating while remaining quiescent, and eternally quiescent while remaining illuminating, its quiescence and illumination are mutually fused.

Thus, its essence encompasses the Dharma-realm and it contains and exhales the void. When one turns back to observe from this state, all that is established in dependence upon the void—the sentient and the insentient, and all worldly phenomena and their continuous karmic fruits—is like everything experienced within a dream.
Viewed from this perspective, even Mātaṅgī is within a dream. How could she use the arts of a dream to detain your physical form?
It is simply because your mind is deluded that you cannot cast off the dust of the senses, turn the faculties inward, and return to hear your own true nature;
instead, you mistake illusory cataracts for the true mind and grasp at empty flowers as having substantial reality, failing to awaken.
All things are identical to dream-events; therefore, they are constrained by them. Who, then, is this?
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy:
"Just as in the world a skillful illusionist... (up to) "...ceasing his artifice and returning to stillness, all illusions become devoid of intrinsic nature."
This analogy clarifies the matter of cultivation. The "skillful illusionist" refers to the person who performs the act; it is a metaphor for True Suchness (tathatā) being able to follow conditions.
"Illusory creation" refers to that which is produced; the "illusionist's art" is a metaphor for the ignorance of accomplishing phenomena (nirmāṇa-avidyā).

The "various men and women" are those created by the illusion; they are a metaphor for the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya). "When a single trigger is pulled" refers to pulling all [the strings] at once.
The "mechanisms" of male and female are metaphors for the single, luminous *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).

This is because this consciousness is fundamentally a single luminosity that manifests as the sixfold combination; thus, when it is in the eye, it functions as seeing; when in the ear, it functions as hearing;
and when in the nose, tongue, body, and mind, it is called smelling, tasting, sensing, and cognizing—just like a single mechanism that is pulled. Therefore, it is said to "pull."
By moving the mechanism, the mouths and eyes of the illusory man and woman move accordingly.
If one ceases this activity and does not pull the mechanism, then the mouths and eyes of the illusory man and woman all return to stillness; they are inherently quiescent.
Thus, all these men and women realize their original nature, which is neither movement nor stillness. This precisely illustrates the aforementioned faculty of hearing.
The nature is fundamentally without movement or stillness, nor birth or extinction. It is only by relying on the *ālaya-vijñāna* that there arises movement and birth.
If one can transform the *ālaya-vijñāna* back into the nature of the *ālaya*, then the functioning of the mind will cease and quiescence will be achieved;

only then will one perceive for the first time one's own original true nature, which is neither moving nor still, and neither born nor extinguished. Formerly, when King Mu of Zhou was hunting in the west, someone presented [him with...]

A master artisan named Yan Shi said, "What I have created is capable of performing as a singer. King Mu looked at it in astonishment; its gait, steps, bowing, and rising were indistinguishable from those of a real person.
When the craftsman tilted its chin, the singing harmonized with the musical scales; when he stroked its hand, the dancing responded to the rhythm.
The King took it for an actual human being and had it perform together with Lady Sheng and his inner attendants. Thus did the performance proceed.
As the performer was about to die, he blinked his eyes and beckoned the King’s attendants and inner women. The King was greatly incensed and intended to execute Yan Shi on the spot.

Yan Shi was utterly terrified; he immediately dismembered the performer to show him to the King, revealing that it was merely a fabrication of leather, wood, glue, lacquer, white, black, cinnabar, and azure pigments.
Internally, it consisted of liver, gallbladder, heart, lungs, spleen, and so forth.
The kidneys, intestines, stomach, as well as the external tendons, bones, limbs, joints, skin, hair, teeth, and scalp—all are merely borrowed things, yet they are all fully present.
When they are assembled, it is as if one has seen them for the first time. Your Majesty, try removing the heart, and the mouth will be unable to speak;
remove the liver, and the eyes will be unable to see; remove the kidneys, and the feet will be unable to walk. Your Majesty, at the very beginning...
He spoke and sighed, saying, "The ingenuity of man can indeed rival the Creator in its efficacy. Zhang Zan said, "All these things operate by means of mechanical contrivances;
yet as for the master of those contrivances, they cannot be controlled by one another.
Observing this, we know that all sentient beings fundamentally have no 'self,' nor do they possess anything belonging to a self. It is merely due to..."
The four great elements and the five aggregates combine to form the characteristics of male, female, and so forth.
Although there is movement, stillness, and activity, none of it is anything other than this single point of deluded mind that does not cease.

If one can simply allow it to cease, then all will immediately become tranquil, and the true nature—which is fundamentally neither moving nor still, neither ceasing nor arising—will manifest of itself before one. Therefore, it is said:
The place where the狂心 (mad mind) ceases is itself Bodhi.
△ Third, the correspondence of dharmas:
The six sense organs are also like this... up to ... when the remaining objects are further clarified and the illumination reaches its ultimate limit, that is the Tathāgata.
This combines with the preceding metaphor. The meaning is that the six sense organs are precisely like the man and woman created by a magician.
This "one refined clarity" is the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness; the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is like the magician’s single mechanism.
For the six sense organs originally depend upon this one refined clarity to separately grasp the six objects of perception, each forming a distinct faculty.
Appearance. Thus, when it is in the eye, it is called "seeing"; when in the ear, it is called "hearing," and so forth.
Because it is formed by the conjunction of these three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—it is termed the "sixfold conjunction. It is like a man or woman created by illusion.

Although the six functions differ from one another, they are all merely transformations of a single, pure luminosity. This is like how, although one perceives the movement of various sense organs, it must ultimately depend on that One.

This is the pivot. If you can revolve the faculties and turn back the hearing, so that this single locus—the faculty of hearing—attains rest and returns to the original truth, then the remaining five attachments will be uprooted and you will achieve perfect liberation; thus, the functions of the six [senses] will [be restored].
None of these can be accomplished. This is like the cessation of mental activity returning to stillness. It is precisely what the Buddha meant by "this faculty first being understood;
one first attains the emptiness of persons. If this is so, then conceptual appearances become dust and cognitive attachments become defilement;
the innate seeds and habitual tendencies will dissolve upon reflection. When the *ālayavijñāna* is overturned to become the *tathāgatagarbha*, its essence is fundamentally— [The text ends here.]

It is spontaneously perfect and luminous, primordially pure and wondrous, and fundamentally devoid of even a single dharma. This is illustrated by the various illusions within the parable, which demonstrate the absence of intrinsic nature.
This is what the Buddha called the "perfectly luminous emptiness-nature," which constitutes liberation through the dharmas.

If there remains even the slightest trace of defilement or residual habituation that has not been fully exhausted, one still dwells in the stage of training and is not termed "ultimate. If, however, it is truly non-existent...
The clarity is suddenly exhausted; one realizes the ultimate fundamental luminosity. Such a person is identical to the *tathāgatagarbha* realized by the Tathāgata—non-dual and without distinction.
This is what the Buddha calls the dharma of liberation: already co-extensive with emptiness and non-arising.
This is precisely what is meant by a Bodhisattva entering the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through samādhi. By practicing this dharma-gate, one may...
It is easy; there is no difficulty in attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, I have specifically selected this for you, Ānanda, as a skillful means for the beginner’s mind.
Listen attentively to it. The meaning of its cultivation is simply this. This concludes the formal selection.
△ Fourth, the universal exhortation to practice.

From "The great assembly and Ānanda" (up to) "I also realized it through this, not only Avalokiteśvara," this is the universal exhortation to practice by means of the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. The intent is that the merit of "returning the hearing" is easy [to accomplish].
Furthermore, it is swift; its actual efficacy is such as this. Now, let this great assembly not be deluded regarding their original hearing, and you, Ānanda, do not rely on forced memory.
This was Mañjuśrī’s response to the command, having completed his selection, to announce to the Dharma assembly and to exhort them toward cultivation and progress.
Through true and perfect penetration, there is no other method; it simply requires that you turn [the mind] back. You all should follow...

Sentient beings with inverted faculties hear falsely through sound; if they reverse this false hearing to hear their own self-nature (*svabhāva*), then upon attaining this nature, they will achieve Buddhahood on the spot.
This is, in that very moment, the unsurpassed path of enlightenment—what difficulty could there be?
Although there are many types of gateways to perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-dvāra*), if one determines the true reality, it is easy rather than difficult for a beginner.

That which is swift and not slow is this one gate alone; it is the single, direct, and wondrously adorned path by which the dust-mote-like Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time reach the home of Bodhi and enter the gate of Nirvana.
Thus, the Tathāgatas of the past attained accomplishment through this gate, and the Bodhisattvas of the present likewise do so through it.
One enters perfect luminosity. For this reason, all persons who practice and study in the future must certainly rely upon this method of the ear-faculty’s "return-hearing" as their gateway.
Not only do all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enter through this, even I, Mañjuśrī, do not go outside of it; we all cultivate within this return-hearing of the ear-faculty.

This is the realization. It is not only for Avalokiteśvara alone that this is so; thus, it is clear that one knows this Dharma to be the path universally cultivated by both sentient beings and Buddhas, and the gateway through which they universally enter. You all should likewise practice in accordance with this.
△ Fifth: The Conclusion and Request for Truth.
Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One [has taught], that which is perfectly penetrating and surpasses all others is the true mind.
This is the formal response to the imperial decree, concluding the answer regarding perfect penetration. I request that you grant me your protection, thereby clarifying the faculty of the ear.
This is indeed true. The first two phrases concern the previous text’s twenty-five sages:
which one corresponds to Ānanda’s faculties, and by what door of skillful means can he attain the mandate of easy accomplishment?
The next phrase further extends to the mandate of sentient beings in this realm after my parinirvāṇa. The two phrases beginning with “seeking to emerge” refer to entering the stage of a bodhisattva.

"Vehicle" refers to the life-force of seeking the Unsurpassed Way. This means that previously, when the Buddha questioned me regarding such skillful means (*upāya*), he commanded me to select among them.
However, if one seeks that which is most perfect and excellent, there is only the single gateway of Avalokiteśvara’s ear-faculty;
among all skillful means, it is the most sublime. As for the remaining twenty-four sages, they enter [the path] through other means.
Regarding these skillful means of the Way, as I observe them, they are all protected by the Buddha’s power and majestic spiritual authority;
thus, one attains awakening and entry. They cause one to abandon worldly toil through the very phenomena at hand.

These are not methods for beginning practitioners of this land to cultivate over a long period, nor are they intended for those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties, or for those of shallow or deep capacities.
These are matters that can be discussed in the same way. For instance, there was Nanda’s loss of sight and Pindola’s being pricked by thorns;
yet not everyone is like this—how could one apply such ordinary cases as a universal rule?

Consider the great causal conditions of Samantabhadra, the innate eloquence of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti’s realization of emptiness, and Śāriputra’s pure vision—all these belong to the realm of the profound mind. How could...
Can those of shallow wisdom and initial resolve enter [this path]? Consider the case of Ucchuṣma, who was overcome by lust, and Cūḍapanthaka, who was deficient in his recitation;
these were merely people of limited understanding. How could those with profound intent not likewise enter by means of such [methods]?
Since each has its own particular bias, it is necessarily restricted; how could this be a path for long-term, universal cultivation? Nor is it for those of shallow [capacity].

Profound. This Dharma that can be explained in common—such as the Dharma-gate of Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of hearing—is one wherein both the shallow and the profound can be discussed together, and where long-term cultivation can be shared. As for the skillful means for entering the gate at the very beginning, nothing is more excellent than this.
This concludes the formal response. Following the command already issued below, [the text] now formally requests protection and grace.
This is to clarify the ultimate reality. By means of this single gateway of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), one cultivates and realizes the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is precisely the principle-essence of the self-nature purity of the three *tathāgatagarbhas* as taught by the former Buddhas.

The functional application of the realized concentration belongs to the inconceivable phenomenal function of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is the Tathāgata’s true *tathatā*-dharma-body in its entirety.
The essence is great and its function is vast; therefore, I prostrate and pray for your protection. May future students have no further doubts regarding this single gateway.
This is the correct expedient for beginners, which is swift rather than slow and easily accomplished.
It is fit to be used to instruct Ānanda as well as all those sinking in the mire during the final age; it only requires—
By cultivating and advancing through this single faculty, the merit of perfect penetration will naturally surpass that of the other twenty-four sages.
That is to say, if one wishes to cultivate the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, one must first turn the hearing back toward the ear-faculty to seek its true reality;
the essential secret for cultivating the mind does not exceed this.
△ Third, the benefits obtained by the great assembly.
Thus, Ānanda and the great assembly [attained] the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This passage describes how Ānanda and the great assembly attained benefit and realized awakening. The meaning is that after Mañjuśrī had finished speaking...
At this, Ānanda and the great assembly all attained a clear and lucid awakening regarding the knots of the three categories, the seven elements, and the root-body.
Previously, they did not know what the body and mind were, nor how these knots could be untied, or from what they were to be called "untying."

Although you heard the voices of as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust throughout the ten directions, all speaking with one voice that birth-and-death and wondrous permanence are both the six sense organs and nothing else, you were not yet fully clear about it.
Even when the Tathāgata demonstrated by tying his headcloth in various ways within his prose and verse teachings, you were still not entirely clear;
therefore, you hoped for a hidden transmission. Now you hear that the twenty-five sages are all Mañjuśrī.

The Master Mañjuśrī has explained both the extensive and the concise versions with clear discernment; only then can one recognize the Tathāgata’s indirect prodding and direct striking, his oral transmissions and spoken words, and his single-minded compassionate heart.
Only then does one come to know the signs of binding and liberation within the single gateway of the auditory faculty, as well as the methods of cultivation and realization.
Consequently, the binding and liberation of all other faculties—of the body and the mental faculty—are also understood with perfect clarity.
Thus one attains clarity. From this point on, one surveys universally the supreme fruit of Bodhi and Great Nirvana of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas as if returning to one's own home.
Yet, because the mind arises in pursuit of external objects, one flows away and forgets the source, like a person who travels far away for the sake of some business.
Consequently, one abandons birth only to pursue further birth, accumulating delusion upon delusion, and ascends and descends through the seven realms of existence.
Wandering back and forth through the three realms is like not yet having returned home to one’s native land.

Indeed, from beginningless time until the present, throughout vast kalpas, as days and years have deepened, not only has one failed to return, but even the path to that hometown has been forgotten and no longer recognized.
Now, one has heard this teaching on the faculty of hearing turning back to hear itself.
Entering deeply through the gate, although one has not yet set out on the journey to practice, one is just like a traveler who has left home;
though they have not yet packed their bags, they will surely return in splendor. Yet, they already clearly understand the path by which that home is reached.
Therefore, the entire assembly has all recognized the inherently existing true mind. If one takes this very mind as the causal ground for cultivation...
Nevertheless, one may reach the original home of Bodhi. For this reason, the dust of conceptual marks and the defilement of cognitive afflictions are both distanced;
one suddenly attains the Dharma-eye, becoming pure all at once, and universally realizes the Path of True Seeing.
The Bhikṣuṇī Xiàng had previously realized the third fruit; now she has further progressed, becoming an Arhat and realizing the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
Even all those present at the Dharma assembly shall give rise to the great mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A-sama" is translated here as "unequaled.

Because the fruit of Buddhahood, Bodhi, is unsurpassed and also characterized by the absence of marks (*animitta*), one who is now able to give rise to the mind for attaining Buddhahood is equal to a Buddha. This is what is meant:
There is nothing with which it can be equaled; now, having attained such equality, it is called "unequaled" (asama-sama).

One must understand that from the beginning of this assembly, what the practitioners sought was merely referred to as a "path" or a "gate," even when the house was granted—this was because they had not yet known there was a "home.
Now, after hearing of the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty, the Sūtra author directly states: "The home is..."

This clearly reveals that the assembly present, having fully understood their own minds, did not obtain this realization from another; the meaning is as explained in the "Original House" chapter, which is not comparable to being granted a house.
Nevertheless, it is precisely through this faculty of hearing, by turning the hearing back upon itself, that one takes the path to return to the land of Nirvana and to go home to the house of Bodhi.
Thus concludes the first demonstration: the Perfect Penetration and Right Practice for those present.
△ Second, showing the auxiliary practices for the future site of enlightenment (3): 1. The request.
Ānanda adjusted his robes amidst the great assembly... until [he said]: "In the mind of bodhi, one attains freedom from retreat or dejection."

The intent of this request is as follows: seeing that those who are currently suited to the teaching would use this Dharma to deliver future generations, and fearing that the false words of the final age might disturb the truth, he requested the rules for stabilizing the mind to distance oneself from demons and for establishing the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
For this reason, he adjusted his robes, emerged from the assembly, and prostrated; it was at this moment that he realized his original nature.

The Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrous nature of True Suchness; hence it is said that the mind is perfectly round and luminous. To attain the "return-hearing" through the faculty of the ear is precisely the path home;
hence it is said that the trace is perfectly round and luminous. "Compassion" refers to the suffering of being mired in delusion for many kalpas;
"rejoicing" refers to the joy of a sudden awakening in an instant. It is like a person who has lost their way and remained long stranded in a foreign land, only to suddenly find...
On the way back, I was thus filled with both sorrow and joy. Although my own understanding was already perfected, I felt compassion for those who had not yet awakened;
for this reason, I addressed the Buddha: "O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, as for me now, although I have already attained awakening to the Dharma-door of the Buddhas..."
From this, by relying on the practice of turning the hearing back toward the faculty of hearing itself, one shall attain freedom from delusion.
Now, as for the common words spoken by the Tathāgata: "To seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the initial resolve of a Bodhisattva;
to awaken oneself fully and thereby be able to awaken others is the manifestation of a Tathāgata in the world. Although I have not yet—
"O World-Honored One, I vow to learn as a Bodhisattva. First, by means of this Dharma, I shall deliver all sentient beings who have newly resolved to practice during the final kalpa.

World-Honored One, it is my good fortune to have encountered the Buddha and attained knowledge of the faculty of hearing that turns back to hear its own nature, thereby returning to the true and correct path.
However, as for the sentient beings of this degenerate age, their eyes do not behold the mark of the jade-white brow-hair, and their ears do not..."
We have already heard the voice from the Golden Mouth; how much more so now that we are increasingly distant from the Buddha?
Yet false teachers preach the Dharma to delude and mislead beginners, and such instances are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Moreover, since the false inevitably confuses the correct, how difficult it must be for those of us who are beginners and late learners to collect and stabilize our minds, entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation! How could this not be a great challenge?

I venture to ask: how, ultimately, does the Tathāgata enable those who have newly begun their practice and are still beginners to securely establish a field for entering the Way, such that all demonic activities are naturally kept at a distance and cannot delude or disturb their bodhicitta?
Only then will one be free from regret and remorse, enabling one to enter directly with a single blade, without being confused by devious and winding paths.

This is precisely because compassion for those suited to the teaching has reached the final age (*kalpa*), when the orthodox is scarce and the heterodox is abundant; if one does not discern this in advance, there is fear of being led astray.
Thus, the *Zhi guan tong lei* states: "Since the Sage departed long ago, no more sages have appeared; the masses are now dull and ignorant."
Thus it has come to pass that heterodox demons and delusive factions have flourished both in the realms of emptiness and existence (as described at length).
Some fall into pits and traps; some cling to the literal words and dare not move; some drift upon vast, surging waves and cannot find a place to rest;
some find the goal too distant and resign themselves to never reaching it; and some find it too near, realizing that their very own bodies are it.
There are those who call withered wood "meditative concentration" (samādhi); those who call hollow sounds "wisdom" (prajñā); those who call running about on non-paths "expedient means" (upāya);
those who rely on ghosts and spirits to claim "penetration"; those who let their minds wander to claim "vastness"; those who speak rarely to claim "secrecy";
and those who transmit things through the teeth and tongue in secret to call them "oral instructions. All of these—

Those of this ilk establish themselves as patriarchs and their descendants as lineages; they subvert the scriptures and disparage the sages, violently distorting the Way and throwing order into chaos.
Thus, when we speak of "evil teachers" who concern themselves with the immediate situation, it refers precisely to these individuals.
△ Second, the praise and permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly... Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and respectfully received the instruction.
This [passage] praises the appropriateness of his inquiry and grants permission for the teaching. The repetition of "Excellent! (Sādhu) is as follows: [The text continues below].
Out of compassion for those capable of practicing the Way during the final age, and in order to accord with the Tathāgata’s intention to preach, he praises it again and again.

His meaning is this: regarding what you have asked, I fear that false teachers and demonic doctrines may disturb the concentrated mind, inevitably leading to regression and instruction [in error], thereby entering upon devious paths; therefore, one must first establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) before [proceeding].
"Distance yourself from this! This is truly the means to rescue all sentient beings of the final age, the most essential matter for avoiding drowning in suffering.
Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and explain it for you. Then Ānanda and the great assembly all responded with "So be it," accepting the command and the teaching, and listened attentively.
△ III. The Correct Exposition (2) 1. Explaining that Precepts are the Foundation (1) a. General Indication of the Foundation of the Three Trainings.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You have often heard me [say]... this is what is called the three trainings in the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)."
This is the Buddha’s exposition of the auxiliary practices for the site of enlightenment. Observing the precepts and reciting mantras constitute the auxiliary cultivation.

This is because the preceding Buddha, in response to the specific capacity of the practitioner, had primarily elucidated the Tathāgatagarbha-mind through the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

Those who awaken to the principle and enter directly constitute "correct cultivation. Now, for the sake of those currently responsive to the teaching and out of compassion for those in the final age—fearing they will encounter many obstacles and difficulties—I have requested that you distinguish [the practice] from distant demons and establish the *dharmapūjā* site (*dharmamaṇḍala*).
Thus, the Tathāgata has this discourse on "auxiliary practices," which refers to practices that assist correct cultivation. Now, as for these auxiliaries...

There are two [types of practitioners]. First, those for whom afflictions are heavy: they first maintain the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*) to restrain and sever the ignorance that gives rise to karma.
Second, those for whom habitual tendencies are heavy: they additionally maintain secret mantras (*dhāraṇī*) to permeate and sever innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).

Therefore, one should know that in the final age, those who practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) will not avoid being deluded by false teachers and becoming possessed by demons if they do not employ these auxiliary practices.
Therefore, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "Do you wish to know the rules for establishing the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) and remaining far removed from the works of Māra?

This is also easy to do. Yet, have you not heard in the ordinary course of things what I have proclaimed in the Vinaya—that there are three kinds of definitive meanings of practice? Namely, the definitive gathering..."
The mind is the precept. It is certain that concentration arises from the precept; it is certain that wisdom is produced from concentration.
These are called the three kinds of certainty. This is the untainted study by which one becomes a Buddha or a Patriarch. The *Vinaya* states briefly:

*Vinaya*. This is translated as "skillful governance" (*shan-zhi*). It means governing oneself regarding lust, anger, and ignorance, while also being able to govern the lust, anger, and ignorance of others.

It is also called "subjugation" (*tiaofu*), meaning to refine the three karmas and to restrain transgressions and faults; it is the general name for the *Vinaya-piṭaka* of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Regarding the phrase "taking the gathering of the mind as the purpose of the precepts," the character "by" (*you*) may also be used as a substitute, meaning "desiring to gather."

That mind must necessarily be governed by the observance of precepts. If one does not use the precepts to restrain the mind, by what means could one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox?

Furthermore, it is only through the restraint of the mind that one truly observes the precepts; this clearly demonstrates that upholding or violating the precepts is not merely a matter of constraining the body.
Thus, by means of the precepts, one restrains the mind, and only thereafter do concentration arise and wisdom develop. These three trainings are—
This is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava). If this is not the case, then even if wisdom and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) manifest before one, one will inevitably fall into the realm of demons;

all such states become "with-outflow" (sāsrava). Alas! There are in this world base creatures whose very nature is that of demons, who slander and revile the precepts, claiming them to be the "Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*), while falsely styling themselves as practitioners of the "Supreme One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*). Are these not indeed of the lineage of Māra? Such are the false teachers.
...the likes of them?
△ Second, the specific exposition of the fourfold precepts (four parts): First, the precept against sexual misconduct.
Ānanda, how does one restrain the mind? That which I call the precept... [up to] ...if it is not explained in this way, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This clarifies that the precepts are the foremost of the three trainings. From the first fascicle to the middle of the fourth fascicle, all clarify the generation of faith and the opening of understanding;

this constitutes the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). From the point where the analogy of the magnificent mansion is raised according to the capacity of the audience until this point, it constitutes the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).

For this reason, what follows below correctly elucidates the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*). Thus, one should know that this sutra expounds all three trainings and serves as the comprehensive summary of the Tripitaka.
However, it specifically teaches only the four grave prohibitions because these constitute the fundamental precepts common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Furthermore, most other sutras place the precept against killing at the beginning, as the Buddha’s transformative teaching is based on compassion (*karuṇā*).
In this sutra, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first. This indicates that true cultivation takes the renunciation of desire as its essential requirement;

therefore, the precept against sexual misconduct is clarified at the outset. Because the energy of desire is coarse and turbid, it defiles the wondrously luminous nature of the mind, and such wild delusion easily precedes the attainment of right concentration.
Consequently, in terms of losing one's fundamental nature and undergoing the cycle of samsara, nothing is more severe than this; thus, it must be the foremost precept.
Ānanda asked: "In what sense do you mean that withdrawing and gathering the body and mind is what I have called 'right precepts'?
This [question] generally indicates the following section, which specifically demonstrates [the answer].

It is because all sentient beings of the six realms within the world sustain their very life and nature through lustful desire. If lustful desire is not severed, then birth and death cannot be eliminated. Therefore, those who wish to transcend...
Regarding birth and death, one must first sever the mind of lust. If the mind is truly free from lust, then the tree will fall and its roots be severed;
branches and leaves will not grow, and one will naturally no longer follow the cycle of coming and going in birth and death, nor continue through successive rebirths.
This is just as when you practice right concentration: you ought by nature to transcend the defilements of views and thoughts. If...
If this lustful mind cannot be eliminated, then the defilements of view and thought will certainly not be transcended.
Even if one possesses many abilities and skills, or worldly wisdom and eloquence, one will merely attain mundane, out-flowing meditative concentrations that manifest before one.

If one does not sever lust, one will inevitably join the ranks of Māra. Even if one lacks mundane wisdom (*loka-jñāna*), if one possesses meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one will fall directly [into the realms of form].

Generally, mundane wisdom and meditative concentration—such as the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis—are like "changing the womb and replacing the cauldron," or the process of "selecting the former and refining the latter.
Therefore, those whose practice is profound constitute the superior grade; those next in order constitute the middling grade; and those following them constitute the inferior grade.
This is classified as the lowest grade. Nevertheless, those of this kind are truly numerous.

Each of them claims that by means of the methods of sexual desire, through the sequence of extraction and refinement, one achieves the Unsurpassed Way. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such types flourished in the world;
they instead used sexual methods to instruct the ignorant, kept many seductive women, greedily sought their nourishing benefits, and practiced [these ways] everywhere.
Regarding the arts of lust, they consider practicing sexual intercourse to be the most excellent deed.

They believe themselves to be skilled in the practice of lust and well-acquainted with its principles, claiming it can ensure the proliferation of descendants, restore youthfulness, enable ascension to heaven by day, and grant longevity and eternal vision. Thus, they transmit the methods of lustful desire to one another, commanding—
It is never severed. Because of this, foolish men and women—deluded and insentient beings—fail to recognize good from evil and cannot distinguish between the upright and the virtuous.
Consequently, men crave and women love, both falling into the pit of desire and together becoming entangled in birth and death;
such is the affliction of delusive thought. Furthermore, they mistakenly claim that sexual desire is the method for true cultivation, thereby giving rise to various false views. Thus...
Falling into the pit of views means that once one dwells within this deep pit of craving and views, one will forever lose the correct path to Bodhi.
Therefore, if you wish to teach and transform those of initial resolve in the final age who seek to cultivate right concentration, you must first sever these dharmas;
not only must the body refrain from sexual misconduct, but the mind must likewise be free of lustful thoughts. Only then can one be considered [a true practitioner].
This is acceptable. This is precisely the admonition to prevent the sprouting of evil at its inception and to stem it before it becomes manifest—the warning regarding the first signs of frost.

If one can truly act in this manner, only then may it be called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, and ultimate instruction for the pure cultivation and study that decisively eliminates lustful desire.
For the mind of lust is the very root of birth and death; it is fundamentally incompatible with the fruit of Buddhahood.
It is like sand and stones, which can never be the source of rice; yet the cultivation of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) is likened to steaming it.

Taking the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause of cultivation, one subsequently achieves the perfect realization of the stage of fruition—this is likened to steaming rice until it becomes cooked.
If one cultivates concentration with a lustful mind and thereby produces demonic blessings, this is likened to being unable to produce rice, for one is merely steaming sand.

It is merely stone with hot vapors. Even if one attains wondrous enlightenment, if it is all rooted in lust, then even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it shall be called nothing but "hot sand.
The five phrases from the root text below correspond to the statement in the preceding scripture that "this is not rice," because it is fundamentally composed of sand and stones.
"The mechanism" refers to the mechanism by which the aforementioned illusory person was pulled; it points specifically to the seed of the lustful root.
This means that as long as the seeds are not eliminated, contact with objects will immediately trigger them; once this mechanism is activated, body and mind follow in motion.
Therefore, one must sever these seeds, whereby the two paths of body and mind will naturally cease their sexual activity. To speak from the ultimate perspective:
Even if both body and mind are severed, if the nature that performs the severing persists, then the residual shadows of the objects thus severed will still remain;
they will ultimately not be completely eliminated, and these too belong to the root of birth and death and must be severed.

This nature of severing must also be rendered non-existent, which is called the simultaneous removal of both medicine and disease, only then attaining complete recovery. It is just like the cessation of mental activity and the return to quiescence. Thus, all...
Illusion is established as being without intrinsic nature. It is precisely this nature of non-illusion that can be conjoined with the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit.
Thus, the great matter of attaining Buddhahood—the true cause and true fruit—can be hoped for. For it is the body that is severed by the *prātimokṣa* (individual liberation) precepts;

the mind that is severed by the *dhyāna-samvara* (meditative concentration) precepts; and even the nature [of the mind] that is severed by the *mārga-samvara* (path) precepts. This concludes the formal summary.

To distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and to provide deep protection against future demonic and heterodox delusions, one must correctly seek out the means of discernment and examine the differences with fixed rules.

Therefore, the Buddha taught these four fundamental precepts to serve as a means of verification, so that those who practice and study in the final age may forever take them as a guiding mirror. Thus it is said: "As I have spoken this..."

This is called the Buddha’s correct teaching. If one were to teach otherwise—either claiming that practicing sexual misconduct does not obstruct cultivation, or claiming that practicing sexual misconduct is itself true cultivation—such views belong to Māra Pāpīyas.
"Pāpīyas" is a corruption; it is correctly called *Pāpīya*, which means "the Evil One. There are three kinds of evil [associated with him].
The first is called "Evil" (Āpāyika); the second is called "Great Evil" (Mahāpāyika); the third is called "Evil among Evils" (Aghāpāyika).

It is also called "The Killer," because he is able to harm the Dharma-body and is a thief who slays the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*). This is the name of the Māra-king at the time of Śākyamuni’s appearance in the world.

The character for "Māra" (魔) is written with the "stone" radical; Emperor Liang Wudi said that because it signifies "afflicting and harming people," he changed it to the character for "ghost" (鬼). Now, [it is] followed as such.

This is the "I Ching" of Liang [Zhiyi]. Observe these words of the Buddha: "Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them," and further, "Even if one attains wondrous enlightenment, it is all rooted in lust.
How painful are these words! If even wondrous enlightenment is thus, how much more so for that which is not yet enlightened?
If even great wisdom and meditative concentration are thus, how much more so for those who have not attained even a small portion of concentration and wisdom?
△ Second, the precept against killing.
From "Ānanda, furthermore, the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds" (up to) "if one does not speak thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
This clarifies that not only must one refrain from committing killing with the body, but one must also ensure that the mind is free of murderous intent; only then is one truly upholding the precepts.
This means that one may cultivate *samādhi*. The five subsequent sentences of Ānanda clarify the benefits of non-killing.
The intent is that if one’s mind is free from the thought of killing, then birth and death will be forever severed and will no longer continue in succession.
Why is it said that bearing the debt of life constitutes the cause of birth and death? Since one has now ceased killing, the cycle does not continue. You should cultivate...
The following clarifies the harm of taking life. For the cultivation of samādhi is fundamentally intended for transcendence from the mundane world;
yet, if the mind of killing is not eliminated, one cannot escape the afflictions of the world. This remains true even if one possesses great versatility, worldly wisdom, eloquence, and intelligence.
