However, one may bring forth mundane meditative concentrations that are still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*). For example, if one does not cease killing, one will certainly fall into the realm of ghosts and spirits (*preta*);
for although ghosts and spirits vary in their relative superiority or inferiority, they are all equally part of the evil destinies (*durgati*).
Thus, to go from the human realm into that state constitutes a fall. If a person can cultivate superior-grade practice, they may merely become a powerful being [within those realms].
The ghosts are like humans; they revere and address one another as "Emperor" or "Heavenly One.
If they belong to the middle grade, they are flying ghosts, acting as commanders for categories such as those of the mountain deities, river spirits, and local village officials.
If they belong to the lower grade, they are earth-walking ghosts that devour humans, such as the rākṣasa ghost kingdoms along the shores of the great ocean. Those various ghosts and spirits also...
These followers each recognize themselves as right while failing to realize their own errors; they all falsely claim to have attained the unsurpassed Way.
Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, many of the demonic hordes and evil factions prevalent in the world will be of this sort, proclaiming that one may attain bodhi by eating meat.
This is not the path of true practice. Thus, Ānanda, in the past I heard various...

"Monks, as for these five kinds of pure meat—meat that is not seen, not heard, and not suspected [to have been killed for one's sake], and meat from animals that died naturally or was left over by birds—is it not because there is no such thing?
Indeed, all this pure meat is merely manifested through my supernatural power; it possesses no life-force.
This is because the lands where you Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas dwell are hot and humid."
It is low-lying and damp, further infested with sand and gravel; moreover, it is composed of stone.
Not only does it fail to produce the five grains, but even grasses and vegetables cannot grow there. If there were no meat to eat, by what means could you sustain yourselves?
Therefore, out of my great compassionate power, I take pity on your hunger and emptiness, and have thereby transformed it into five kinds of pure meat, so that you may obtain sustenance for a time.

As for its flavor, it is merely used to sustain the body; for this reason, it is provisionally called "meat," yet it is not the true meat of the life-force and sense-faculties of sentient beings with consciousness. Even that which you all eat is nothing more than transformed meat.
How can it be that after my parinirvāṇa, there will be those who truly eat the flesh of living beings by taking their lives, and yet still wish to call it [my teaching]?
Are you a disciple of the Śākya lineage? Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Good son, from this day forward, I do not permit the eating of meat.
You should regard such food as being like the flesh of your own child. Indeed, those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion" (and so forth), up until:
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there will always be bhikṣus whose appearance..."
He upheld the Vinaya but had read few scriptures; he was greedy for food and drink, nourishing his body until his head hair, beard, nails, and hair were all long and thick.
Although he wore the kāṣāya robe, he resembled a hunter; he peered closely and walked slowly, like a cat stalking a mouse.

Their wrong views will flourish, and they will slander the True Dharma. They will destroy the precepts, right practice, and dignified conduct taught by the Tathāgata, acting according to their own whims.
Inverting the sūtras and the Vinaya, they will say, "The Tathāgata permits us all to eat meat.
Having themselves fabricated this doctrine, they claim it is the word of the Buddha, engaging in mutual disputes and each asserting their own position as correct. These śramaṇas—
O disciples of the Buddha, you should know this: even if those who eat meat should happen to attain mundane meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), it will last but a short while.
Should their minds open up such that it appears similar to right concentration, it is ultimately not the true, authentic *samādhi*.
However, those who eat meat are all powerful ghost generals and members of the rākṣasa class; it is because of this that they manifest such retributions in their present lives.

Nevertheless, their ultimate karmic retribution will not last long, for they are certain to sink forever into the hells and the three miserable realms, flowing into the ocean of suffering of birth and death. These are all the followers of ghosts; they are not [human beings].
The disciples of the Buddha are indeed considered true disciples of the Buddha because they seek to escape the three realms.
Yet, such people as these continue to kill, devour, and consume one another without end; their calamities and enmities are intertwined, never ceasing.
How can such persons escape the three realms and resolve the debt of their lives through liberation? Thus, you [are teaching] future generations—

A person who cultivates *samādhi* must first sever the mind of killing. This is the second definitive, pure instruction for training to its ultimate conclusion, given by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddha of former ages.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one were to say that one can cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without severing the mind of killing, it would be like someone who plugs their ears and raises a loud voice, seeking to hear themselves.

"I do not hear. This is precisely the desire to remain hidden while becoming all the more exposed. It is like covering one's own ears while claiming that there is no retribution for killing living beings and eating their flesh;
it is like shouting at the top of one's voice while those who harm creatures and violate compassion eat them at will.
To seek someone who can remain unheard and yet be without fault is impossible. And so, as for cultivation...

Seeking liberation from birth and death through meditation is called *yuyin* (the concealment of desire). Furthermore, killing living beings and perpetuating cycles of vengeance and calamity is called *milu* (exposing the full extent of evil).
One must know that even pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not intentionally tread upon or pull up the grass growing by the roadside;
their benevolent compassion extends even to plants and trees. How much more so for one who possesses the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
How could one endure taking the flesh and blood of sentient beings to fill one's belly and satisfy one's cravings, eating them at will?
There are two kinds of "clothing" (*vastra*): first, clothing for the body, such as silk, cotton, brocade, leather boots, furs, and wool;
second, clothing for consumption, such as milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Although both categories are here prohibited without distinction, if we follow the sūtras and vinaya...

In the Abhidharma-piṭaka, there is no lack of distinction between what is light and what is heavy. Regarding silk, cotton, and fine fabrics, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna equally prohibit them, because they cause the death of many living beings.
As for boots, leather shoes, furs, and wool, the Hīnayāna permits them entirely, and the Mahāyāna does not completely forbid them;
this is because these items are not specifically produced for the purpose of killing living beings. Regarding milk, curd, and clarified butter (ghṛta)...

This is permitted for minor [offenses]. Therefore, the original scripture states: "When you regularly hold your alms bowl among the assembly during the two times of the day, if you should encounter milk, curd, or clarified butter (ghṛta) in the meantime, these are called superior flavors.
Subsequently, in the ritual procedures for the altar site, these same substances are also employed.

One makes offerings to the Triple Gem. Because one merely consumes what remains after sharing and does not harm living beings, the current prohibition against eating meat is intended to carry this principle to its ultimate conclusion.
Since abstaining from meat is thus possible, it is all the better to do so. If one can act in this manner, it is excellent.
Thus, this bhikṣu has truly attained liberation from all worlds; he owes no karmic debt that must be repaid, nor will he return again to wander through the three realms.

For his clothing, food, body, and even his very faculties are all conditioned by those [past] causes, just as the people at the beginning of the kalpa were able to fly because they consumed the "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) and naturally grown non-glutinous rice.

Thus, his feet do not leave the ground. This serves as a metaphor for subduing the constituent parts of those sentient beings; it indicates the difficulty of escaping from the category of sentient beings.
Regarding the "hundred grains," the *Wuli lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Things) states: "Millet (*liang*) is the general name for *shu* and *ji*;
rice (*dao*) is the general name for *ging* and *nuo*; beans (*shu*) are the general name for various legumes. There are twenty varieties of each of these three grains, totaling sixty.
There are sixty kinds of fruits and vegetables, twenty varieties each, which constitute the hundred grains.
As for the body, it belongs to the category of flesh and blood; as for the bodily parts, they belong to the category of skin, hair, milk, and curd.
Now, since this body does not wear its own parts and the mouth does not eat its own parts, and furthermore, this mind has no craving or desire to consume them.
When one realizes that body and mind are two distinct paths, there is true liberation.
Being no longer entangled by the debt of life, one can emerge from the three realms. Whatever pertains to future lives that accords with my teaching is called the Buddha’s teaching;
that which does not accord with this—such as the claim that eating meat does not obstruct Bodhi—is the work of the demon Pāpīyān.
This is what has been taught.
△ Third, the precept against stealing.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms in the world... (up to)... if it is not spoken thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
This clarifies that it is not merely the body that must be free from stealing;

rather, one must also be free from the mental intention to steal to be a true upholder of the precepts, thereby able to cultivate samādhi. The five subsequent lines beginning with "Ānanda" clarify the benefits of non-stealing.
The meaning is this: if one’s mind is free from theft, then birth and death can be transcended and will no longer continue in succession.
Why then say that the debts incurred by theft are all causes for birth and death? Now, since you do not steal or plunder, they shall not continue.
You have cultivated the lower illumination regarding the harm of theft; indeed, the original purpose of cultivating samādhi is to transcend the mundane world. Yet, as for...
If the thieving mind is not eliminated, then the afflictions (*kleśa*) likewise cannot be transcended.
Even if one possesses extensive worldly cleverness and wisdom, it will merely result in the attainment of mundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) that are still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
If one does not sever this thieving heart, one will inevitably fall into the paths of demons and heterodoxy; those of superior grade are termed "spirits" (*piśāca*), which refers to stealing...

Those that are the essence of the sun and moon, having become numinous over the long course of years—such as mountain sprites and tree monsters who resemble immortals yet are not immortals, and resemble deities yet are not deities—are of the category of those who first gather [essence] and later refine it. Those of middle grade are called *yāo-mèi* (sprites and phantoms);
this refers to those capable of transformations to bewitch and enthrall people, such as foxes and other such creatures, which steal away the vital energy (*jingqi*) of humans.
They are of this kind. Those of the lower grade are called "wicked persons. This means their mental resolve is not upright;
they are devious and crooked, possessed by various ghosts, specters, and malevolent spirits who delude and confuse people's minds in order to seize their wealth and property, and so forth.
However, these cases all refer to those who cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom; yet even they receive such retribution for failing to eliminate their thieving minds.

Were one not to practice at all, but instead merely engage in theft, the resulting retribution would not stop at this. Furthermore, those packs of foxes and other depraved types also have their own followers;
with their false knowledge and false views, they do not perceive their own wrongdoing, each believing themselves to be right.

That is to say: by means of the arts of skillful theft, they accomplish the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, many such demonic and heterodox practitioners will flourish, deluding the masses and prevailing throughout the world;
they will conceal their tracks in secrecy, hiding their deceptions and harboring wickedness, deceiving the age and stealing its reputation.
They were called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) because they were thought to be well-acquainted with the affairs of theft and well-versed in the principles of theft.
Each of them claimed to have realized the stages of the Three Worthies and Ten Sages, as well as the dharmas of gods, immortals, and superior men.
Some manifested demonic supernatural powers to deceive the eyes of others, while others made demonic pronouncements to delude and confuse them.
It causes those who are ignorant and lacking in discernment to be startled, suspicious, and terrified, leading them to revere [the practitioner] as if they were a divine being.
They alter their conduct and change their resolve, causing them to lose their original mind. Consequently, wherever these demonic and heterodox practitioners pass, people are all deluded;
they even come to disregard their own lives and exhaust their wealth to serve them. Thus, the family’s resources are depleted, and there is no...

As for others, they have been scattered and lost almost entirely. Thus, the harm wrought by demons and malevolent spirits can cause fools to ruin their families and squander their fortunes, even leading to the loss of body and life to such an extent. Should those who read this sutra not discern this?
Question: Is it not the case that the Buddha permitted his disciples to be "mendicants" (*bhikṣu*), which is the same as this practice? Answer:
When I instruct my bhikṣus to beg for food according to the methods of all Buddhas, it is because I wish to cause them to abandon stinginess and greed and to accomplish the path to Bodhi.
How could this be the same as those who manifest heterodox wonders to delude the masses, who crave the offerings of others, and who create the cycle of birth and death?
Regarding the practice of alms-seeking (*piṇḍapāta*): in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is termed "begging for sustenance" (*fenwei*).
This means distributing [alms] to sentient beings and thereby protecting and attaining the power of the Path; it is a method that involves no hoarding of possessions and no lingering attachment.

Briefly, there are four intentions behind this: first, to bring benefit and merit to sentient beings; second, to subdue arrogance; third, to realize that the body is illusory; and fourth, [to maintain purity].
The fourth is to eliminate attachment; all these follow the principle of the Dharma.

Now, the reason I do not instruct the bhikṣus to establish their own hearths for cooking and preparing meals is to cause them to know that the body is an illusion and to realize that the world is not solid.
They merely dwell in the world as temporary sojourners, seeking only to bring an end to this remaining life. It is just like a traveler staying overnight on a journey.
It is said: "Journey. Lodging by water is called "mooring. There is nothing that does not borrow these three realms as an inn or a passenger ship, to demonstrate this single passage back and forth.

From this point onward, there shall be no returning again. How could one possibly remain attached to the mundane world, accumulating and amassing deeply and extensively to make plans for the long term?
Only through practicing in this manner is one truly a child of the Buddha. Why is this so?
In the degenerate age, there are demonic thieves and heterodox persons who harbor personal gain within while outwardly assuming the deportment of the Sangha.

They falsely borrow the robes of the Tathāgata to peddle the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata; this refers precisely to those of today who sell garments and fly-whisks, claiming to transmit the lineage of the source.
Thus, they practice trade under the guise of the Buddha-dharma, using these various objects as their means of livelihood.
Regarding these rare treasures, they delude the ignorant and blind, seeking gain and sustenance to nourish their four elements.
They create all manner of karma while still wearing a forced smile, claiming that what they practice is the supreme vehicle and the true Dharma of the Buddha.
Furthermore, they disparage others, instead pointing the finger at those who are truly ordained bhikṣus with precepts and genuine practitioners as [the objects of their contempt].

Regarding the path of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), they falsely claim for themselves, "I am of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Displaying an air of superiority through unconventional conduct, they delude and mislead the ignorant.
For this reason, like one blind man leading a multitude, they drag them into a pit. Because of their doubt, they do not believe in the Threefold Training of the Taintless (anāsrava-śikṣā);
because of their error, they mistakenly place their faith in the teachings of demons and heretics. Thus, immeasurable sentient beings are all... [afflicted] by them.
Those who are deluded shall all fall into the five kinds of Avīci hells; how, then, can the harm caused by such demonic and heterodox influences be fully described?
Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, should there be those who wish to cultivate samādhi, even if they do not possess [the aforementioned] qualities in this present life...
This aforementioned mind of theft and pilfering may still be feared to have been unavoidable due to past lives; therefore, one is instructed to repent.
If one can, before an image of the Buddha, offer the sincere devotion of lighting lamps or burning a finger, then the karmic debt incurred from past stealing and deception will be repaid.
Only then may one bid a long farewell to the world and forever escape all outflows (*āsrava*). If one is truly able to practice this—
Although such a person has not yet suddenly awakened to the path of supreme enlightenment, they already possess a resolute mind capable of believing in the True Dharma.
If they do not repay their debts by sacrificing their own bodies for this purpose, they must seek repentance through such a subtle cause.
Even if one attains the fruit of Buddhahood and achieves the untainted and unconditioned state, one will inevitably return to be born among humans to repay past debts;
this is exactly equal and no different from my own retribution for eating horse-grams in the city of Verañjā.
The *Udānavarga* states: "In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was a brahmin..."
The king, named Ajātaśatru, invited the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus for a three-month summer retreat.

At that time, a celestial Māra deluded the king’s mind, causing him to return to his palace and become addicted to the five desires. After providing offerings for six days, he then forbade the bhikṣus from begging for alms;
for three days they returned empty-handed. A horse trainer from the country of Pāṭaliputra informed the bhikṣus [of this].
"There is only horse-barley here. Are you able to eat it? Five hundred horses each consume two *sheng* daily;
half of this shall be provided for the *bhikṣus*. One excellent horse consumes four *sheng* daily; half of this shall be offered to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, I was a brahmin named Indragiri, who was extensively learned in the four Vedas."
At that time, the king hosted a great assembly and invited the Buddha and his retinue for a meal. There was one bhikṣu who was ill and unable to travel.
After the Buddha and the great assembly had finished eating, he requested food on behalf of the sick bhikṣu.

As they passed Mount Brahmin, a brahmin smelled the fragrance of the exquisite food and, filled with jealousy, reviled them, saying: "These shaven-headed śramaṇas ought to eat horse fodder; they should not [eat such as this]."
"Eat this. The young boys replied, "These teachers should also eat horse fodder. At that time, the brahmin was my own self;
the five hundred boys were the five hundred arhats; and the sick bhikṣu was Maitreya.
It was due to these causes and conditions that he underwent [suffering] in hell for countless thousands of years.
Although he has now attained the Way, the residual karmic conditions from that time resulted in his eating horse fodder for ninety days in the village of Verañjā.

Observing this, one knows that even a casual evil word still requires repayment as an oral debt; how much more so for those who, in past lives, committed theft or plundered the property of others—how could they possibly [escape retribution]?
Is this not so? Therefore, for you who teach the cultivation of *samādhi*, after one has severed lust and killing, one must still sever the mind of stealing.
This is called the Tathāgata’s third definitive instruction on pure training.
Thus, Ānanda, if those who cultivate meditative concentration do not sever the mind of stealing, even if...
Even after passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one cannot increase wisdom or bring bodhi to fulfillment.
It is like pouring the water of meditative concentration and wisdom into a leaking chalice made of stolen goods; how could it ever be filled? This is because my disciples who have become bhikṣus...
Apart from the three robes and one alms bowl, whatever surplus remains—even if it is but a single thread or an inch of cloth—is not permitted to be hoarded;
this is for the purpose of severing the mind of greed. Even when begging for food, if there is a slight remainder, one must immediately divide it into four parts:
one part to offer to fellow practitioners of the holy life, one part to give to the destitute beggars, one part to give to the various ghosts and spirits, and one part [for oneself].

"Eating by oneself. This statement regarding "giving to hungry sentient beings" encompasses the three categories of those practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the destitute, and the ghosts and spirits;
this is to sever the mind of stinginess. "Worshiping the assembly at a great gathering" is to sever the mind of pride. "Receiving beatings or insults as if they were praise" is to...
To sever the mind of anger. To relinquish both body and mind is to sever the two attachments to self and phenomena, thereby eliminating the mind of delusion.
To share one's own flesh with the multitude is to transform greed, anger, delusion, and egoism into the great compassion of the same essence (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*).
The above concerns the severance of the thieving mind regarding the two retributions—the primary and the secondary. The following four lines are essential for...

In the Buddha-dharma, one must likewise eliminate the mind of theft. Regarding teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), the *Āgama Sūtras* state that one may possess items to support the body and advance on the Path;
as permitted in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, one may possess one of each of a hundred types of objects.

It is simply that the other two [vehicles] are prohibited. If, based on this principle, one reverses the Mahāyāna and instead clings to the Hīnayāna as one’s own understanding, then one misleads beginners; for such a person is unable to practice the Mahāyāna themselves.

To instead perversely cite and draw upon the provisional and incomplete teachings of the Lesser Vehicle—thereby misleading oneself and others—is entirely due to the failure to extinguish the thieving mind.
If one can truly act in this way so that the thieving mind is completely severed, then such a person is certified as having attained the true samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
What I have spoken thus is called the Buddha’s correct teaching; if it were otherwise...

Thus it was said. Others have remarked: "To take what is not given, though it be a thieving mind, does not obstruct one who practices the Right Path"—this is the teaching of Māra Pāpīyān; you must examine this. Regarding the term *bìfàn* (peddler):

Zhang Heng’s *Xijing Fu* (Rhapsody on the Western Capital) states, "The peddling husband and wife sell the good mixed with the bitter. The commentary notes that *bì* means "to augment" or "to benefit."
"Dealing" refers to buying low and selling high for one's own profit. "Prostrating with a long bow" (chángyì) is equivalent to a permanent farewell. [The interlocutor] asks:
If the Buddha possesses supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and can thus manifest the five kinds of pure meat, why does he not simply manifest the five grains, grasses, and vegetables?
[The Master] answers: Because the Buddha accords with the requirements of the times and does not establish what is extraordinary. Since these lands originally do not produce the five grains, and—

Now, if grass and vegetables were to suddenly sprout where there was none before, people would consider it strange. Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, should one encounter a place where the five grains and even grass and vegetables do not grow, what then?

For this reason, when the Buddha and the bhikṣus once encountered a famine, Maudgalyāyana wished to employ his supernatural powers to summon the "earth-essence" (pṛthivī-rasa) and to fetch the naturally growing non-glutinous rice from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
The Buddha did not permit any of these. He further said, "In future generations, when there is no Maudgalyāyana, what will you do?
One should know that the Dharma of the Buddha can be transmitted and inherited in this very manner.
△ Fourth, false speech.
"Ānanda, such beings of the six realms in this world" (up to) "if one does not speak thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
This clarifies non-false speech; it is not merely that one’s mouth does not utter falsehoods, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, or harsh abuse. One must...
When the mind likewise harbors no such thoughts, it is only then called upholding the precepts; one may then cultivate samādhi.

Therefore it is said: "Ānanda, although these sentient beings mentioned above have attained purity of both body and mind, and are already free from the thoughts of killing, stealing, and sexual desire—thus having perfected these three courses of conduct—if they nevertheless disregard their speech..."

In the Buddha-dharma, what is at stake is no small matter. To speak of those who, within the ordinary conventional truth, mistake right for wrong and take the crooked for straight—those who seek fame and reputation through minor falsehoods—need not be discussed for now.

However, if one is within the Buddha-dharma and has not yet attained realization of the Way, yet falsely claims to have realized it; or has not yet attained the fruit of realization, yet falsely claims to have attained it...
To falsely claim to have realized the fruits of the path is to deceive the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, to deceive others and one's own mind, and to deceive the world.
No thief of reputation exceeds this; it is truly what is called "great false speech. Such a person possesses a mind that is perverted and defiled;
even if they wish to cultivate what is called *samādhi*, it will likewise become perverted and defiled, and they shall not attain purity.

This is impure. Not only can such a person not achieve the true fruit of Buddhahood, but upon examining their mental disposition, they can achieve nothing more than becoming a demon of craving and views.
This is because such a person utters these false words out of greed for fame and renown, and out of love for gain and offerings.
One thus breaks the pure precepts and becomes possessed by demonic influences. To explain this in detail, there are two meanings.

First, as when a person clearly believes in cause and effect and maintains right view within their heart, yet for the sake of seeking their own superiority and coveting the offerings of others, they eventually break the precepts;
this is called the "demon of craving. Second, it is when one’s views are incorrect, leading them to repudiate cause and effect.

They give rise to various false views. Having originally not awakened to the Way, they falsely claim to have awakened to the Way; having originally not realized the fruit, they falsely claim to have realized the fruit.
This is called the demon of views. Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha mind inherently exists as the seed for attaining Buddhahood.
Now, being plundered by the two Māras, it is said that "the lineage of the Tathāgata has been lost. The following is the formal explanation.

Why is this called a great falsehood? It refers to claiming to have attained awakening when the Way has not yet been realized, and claiming to have realized the fruit when it has not yet been attained.
To take what is non-existent as existent and to speak such false words offhandedly—this may be because one seeks transcendence from the world.

"In this world, I am the most honored; my Dharma is the most supreme. Regarding both myself and my Dharma as the foremost, he addresses those present before him, saying: "I have now attained the first fruit, that of the *srotāpanna*;
or perhaps the second fruit, that of the *sakṛdāgāmin*; or perhaps the third fruit, that of the *anāgāmin*."

Some say that the four fruits of Arhatship constitute the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Others say that Pratyekabuddhas belong to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) of the dependent and solitary [realizers].

This extends even to those who speak with reckless abandon regarding the three stages of worthiness (*triyāna-piṭaka*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), as well as the stages prior to them—faith, abiding, practice, and direction.
Why is this? It is nothing other than seeking out people present before them to pay homage and prostrate to. All...
As for those who commit offenses, they request others to perform repentance solely out of greed for offerings. Such persons are truly icchantikas;
they destroy within themselves the seed of Buddhahood, for they have committed a great falsehood in their pursuit of gain and sustenance.
One who has eternally destroyed their roots of goodness is just like a *tāla* tree severed with a sword; it will never grow again, and there is no difference between them.
The Buddha prophesied that such a person not only severs their roots of goodness forever, but will also never again possess right knowledge and right view.
They shall sink eternally into the ocean of suffering of the three miserable realms—hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—and will be unable to achieve the realization of the Right Path.

This is ignorance. Even after my parinirvāṇa, I shall command all the holy ones to manifest forms in accordance with the needs of beings, appearing in that age of the final dharma (*mofa*) to assume various guises and deliver all sentient beings wandering through the cycle of saṃsāra.
At times they may appear in conformity with the world, such as śramaṇas, lay devotees, kings, officials, or even children; at other times they may appear in opposition, such as courtesans.
Widows, the depraved and treacherous, corrupt officials, great thieves, and petty robbers— even down to butchers, wine-sellers, and peddlers—
whether pure or defiled, rebellious or compliant— who mingle their light with the world and blend in with these sentient beings, are [the objects] for whom the Bodhisattva benefits living beings.
There are four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*): first, giving (*dāna*), by which one causes others to feel affinity for oneself through the two kinds of gifts—material wealth and the Dharma;

second, kind speech (*priyavāditā*), by which one consoles those being transformed with gentle and compliant words; third, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), by which one benefits others through the three types of action (*trikarma*) so that they may give rise to reverence;
fourth, cooperation (*samānārthatā*), by which one manifests various forms to engage in common activities with them. As the Sūtra says: "One works together with them."
This is one of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely *samānārthatā* (common purpose).

It consists entirely of extolling and praising the subtle and wondrous Buddha-dharma of the Supreme Vehicle (*ekayāna*), so that both body and mind may attain purity and enter the state of true *samādhi*, the locus of correct practice. Yet, they never say of themselves: "I am a bodhisattva" or "I am an arhat."
This would be to leak the secret causes of the Buddha’s intent and to recklessly utter false words regarding those who have not yet studied.

With the sole exception of such a person, who at the time of death might privately leave behind instructions to entrust the Buddha-dharma so as to inspire reverence and faith—yet even this is never certain—it does nothing more than delude the masses;
it is merely shown in private to those who have entered one's gate, as in the words of Nanyue.
The Iron Wheel: Du Shun’s manifestation as Mañjuśrī, Fenggan’s pointing toward Han and Shi, and Han and Shi’s speaking of Fenggan—all belong to this category.
Therefore, when one abides, there is no leakage; when there is leakage, one does not abide. This is the fixed and certain rule.
Why then do such people of craving and views use such talk to delude and confuse future generations?
Is it not a great falsehood to claim that unlearned sentient beings have already realized the four fruits and the ten stages?

Therefore, for those beginners of later generations who wish to cultivate samādhi according to your teaching, even if they are first able to sever lust, killing, and theft, they must subsequently further sever such great falsehoods as these; this is called the fourth [precept].
This is the clear instruction for training in the purity of the precept that definitively abandons false speech.

Ānanda, if one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without having eliminated great falsehoods, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood and hoping to find its fragrance—how could it ever be obtained?
This is because the mental activity of false speech is likened to human excrement, whereas meditative concentration is the truth.

Cultivation is likened to sandalwood. This means that if one seeks the fragrance of the dharma-body of meditative concentration with a mind defiled by the filth of false speech, how could the fragrance of the dharma-body ever abide within such a foul and stinking mind?
Therefore, I teach the bhikṣus that relying solely upon a straightforward and upright mind is itself the site of attaining the Way. Thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or...
Even in the four postures of lying down, and indeed in all activities—whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still—one must maintain uprightness and never resort to falsehood.

How could one be possessed by demons and delusions, falsely claiming superiority and asserting that one has attained the various vehicles, whether great or small, as well as the dharmas of the superior person?
This is like a destitute man who falsely calls himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution by the state for the extermination of his clan.
This is a calamity that brings about the extinction of one's lineage. Furthermore, even the ruler of a single nation will not tolerate someone’s reckless usurpation of a noble title;
how much more so for the Compassionate Father of the Three Realms, the Dharma King who has appeared in the world?

To wish to recklessly usurp his name and position—would this not lead to eternal fall into the three miserable realms and sever one’s own connection to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? With such causes, one invites such results. Thus it is said:

This is the fixed law of the Way. For such a person who speaks falsely, since the mind at the stage of the cause is not upright, the affairs at the stage of the fruit will naturally be circuitous and crooked.
If one wishes to seek the Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit, it cannot be accomplished by oneself.
It is like a person trying to bite their own navel; they can never reach it. Because one has uttered such false speech oneself, the seed of the Buddha is destroyed.
Whom else, then, could one hope to achieve success through? If, O bhikṣus, you are truly able to act according to my teaching, [you shall succeed].
The mind is free from flattery and crookedness, as straight as a bowstring.

In all actions—whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still—all is authentic and entirely devoid of falsehood; thus, one can enter directly into samādhi, where demonic obstacles will never arise.
I have personally verified this: such a person shall attain unsurpassed enlightenment; this is truly not false. If...
To speak in this manner is called the Buddha’s correct teaching. If one does not speak in this way, it may be considered false speech;
however, for those who practice authentically, there is no hindrance. This is precisely what was spoken by Māra Pāpīyas, and one should discern it accordingly.
In full, it is called *Atinika*, which means "extremely evil. In full, it is called *Pātala*, which means "bank-shaped. By means of this—
Its shape is like that of a palmyra palm; it stands upright and majestic, tall and straight, reaching eighty to ninety feet in height.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that it originates from the country of Kāñcipurī in South India.

To the north lies a forest of tārā trees extending for more than thirty li; their leaves are long, broad, lustrous, and smooth, such that no country for writing employs them without adopting them. Even if...
If one’s head is severed by a sword, one cannot be restored to life. Regarding the phrase "biting one's navel," the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu zhuan) states:

"If you do not plan ahead, later the ruler will bite his own navel. Du Yu’s commentary explains that this refers to gnawing at one’s own belly-navel, serving as a metaphor for reaching a point where it is too late to act.
This refers to Liu Youqiu, the District Magistrate of Tang, who said to Huan Yanfan and Xu Jinghui: "While Wu Sansi still remains, you gentlemen..."

In the end, there will be no place for burial. If you do not plan ahead, it will be too late to bite your own navel. Furthermore, Zhuangzi said: "When a musk deer is pursued by men, it bites its own navel;
in the end, it cannot escape its peril. These three meanings all serve as metaphors for the pointlessness of regret once the moment has passed.
In this context, the meaning of "regret" is not intended; rather, it is taken as a metaphor for great falsehood. If one seeks Bodhi, one will be unable to attain it.
The current edition of the sutra says, "If the ground is not true," whereas the ancient edition says, "not straightforward. Here, I follow the interpretation of the ancient version.
