△ Second, explaining the recitation of mantras to eliminate habitual tendencies (in two parts): First, a general summary connecting to the preceding text:
"Ānanda, regarding your question on concentrating the mind, I shall now first explain... [up to] how all demonic activities arise."

This passage serves as a general conclusion to the preceding sections concerning the proper cultivation of the ear-faculty and the use of mental concentration as an auxiliary practice for the precepts.
Its meaning is this: Ānanda, you previously asked me how to concentrate the mind when establishing a place of practice (*maṇḍala*).
I have already explained that, regarding the skillful and subtle methods for initial training in entering *samādhi*, there is only this single gateway of the ear-faculty.

And that is all. However, if one wishes to seek the Great Path to Buddhahood through the One Vehicle of the Bodhisattva, it is essential to first maintain these four types of restraint—against lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood—so that they are pure and pristine, like ice and frost.
Only when the fundamental precepts are thus purified can one avoid the spontaneous growth of branches and leaves; for these "branches and leaves" are simply all other [lesser] matters.
Subtle rules of discipline (*sūkṣma-śīla-dharma*). For example, among the ten unwholesome paths of action, the three mental factors of greed, anger, and delusion constitute the third category.
The four verbal actions—false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech—constitute the fourth.

These include the last six of the ten precepts for bhikṣus, the remaining two hundred and forty-six rules, the last six of the eight grave offenses for bodhisattvas, the forty-eight light offenses, and so forth; all of these are branches.

These are the leaves. All depend upon the preceding four as their root. Therefore, once the root is severed, even if its branches and leaves should wish to sprout falsely, they will certainly lack the cause for doing so.
Ānanda, if you can thus remain diligent in every thought-moment, rigorous at every instant, without forgetfulness, and maintain these four kinds of disciplinary restraints without loss, then this—
If the human mind does not even take the six sense-objects, such as form and so forth, as its conditions, how could there be any demonic affairs?
Since demons must rely upon sense-objects to manifest, if one does not condition oneself upon these objects, then all demonic affairs will naturally fail to arise.
Therefore, for those who practice concentration and wisdom in equal measure, they must take the precepts as the foundation.

The preceding section, concerning the breaking of the precepts, used the metaphor of a *tāla* tree severed by a blade that can never grow again to illustrate how one's roots of goodness are destroyed.

The present section, concerning the upholding of the precepts, states that when the source of evil is extinguished, the branches and leaves will not sprout. This is the subtle way in which the preceding and subsequent scriptural passages correspond to one another.
△ Second, the formal opening of the subsequent exposition (II). First, a brief description of receiving and upholding (I). First, exhorting to uphold to manifest the benefits (II).
First, the exhortation to uphold:
"If there are those with past habitual tendencies that cannot be extinguished... [down to] the heart-mantra spoken while seated upon the precious lotus flower."

This is a formal exhortation to maintain the recitation of mantras in order to eliminate past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Previously, it was taught that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) destroy the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the study of ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) was further clarified to destroy the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Now, by exhorting the maintenance of mantra recitation, one further eliminates past habitual tendencies and simultaneously destroys the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
If these three obstacles are indeed destroyed, the single mind becomes pure; thus, one can naturally distance oneself from demons and enter the Path. This is the intended meaning.

This means that if a practitioner who has newly begun their training possesses the seeds of afflictions, karma, and habitual tendencies from many past lives which they are unable to eliminate, they will consequently prefer the correct yet remain firmly attached to the deviant;
desire to be pure yet remain biased toward defilement; find that matters do not proceed according to their wishes;
and experience a state of hidden subtlety and mental vagueness as if driven by some external force—all of which are brought about by their former habitual tendencies.
At such a time, if one wishes to enter right concentration, would it not be difficult?
Nevertheless, you should teach only such persons as this, commanding them to single-mindedly recite what I have spoken:
the Mahā-pratisarā, the Great White Parasol of Fearless Radiance from the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa. Because the essence of this mantra-heart has no counterpart, it is said:

"Great" signifies that its characteristics are utterly severed from worldly defilement. "White" signifies that it covers all things; thus, it is called the "parasol-canopy," which is none other than the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*.
Now, this single mind is the mantra of the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*, the treasury of the three great secrets, supreme and unfathomable in its divine power.
This is the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown of the head, manifesting as the Buddha of the Unconditioned Mind.
Furthermore, this Buddha of the Mind emits a hundred jewel-lights from his crown, radiating brilliance that illuminates worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers.
This is what is expounded by the Buddha of the True Mind seated upon a precious lotus flower; it is the unsurpassed Heart Mantra. Thus, one should know that this mantra is...
It is the most honored among the honored and the most secret among the secrets; thus, it is able to eliminate all delusive habits and keep one far removed from the works of Māra.
△ Second, the manifestation of benefits.
Furthermore, regarding your past lives with Mātanga (up to the phrase) "sailing with the wind," what difficulty or peril could there be?

This reveals the beneficial power of the mantra. The meaning is that as for your past lives with Mātanga—if one considers the causes and conditions of your coiled hair over kalpas, the affectionate attachment and the habitual tendencies of craving are like fish and water.
This has not been for a single morning or evening, nor for a single lifetime or a single kalpa; its origins are remote. It is therefore fitting that it is difficult to eradicate suddenly.
According to the *Dengqie jing* (Devadatta Sūtra), once Ānanda had returned to his female form, his weeping did not cease and his obsessive thoughts continued.
Ānanda followed her to the Jetavana Monastery. The Buddha sent someone to call her back and asked her, "Why do you follow Ānanda? What do you seek?
The woman replied, "I have heard that Ānanda has no wife, and I myself have no husband. The Buddha said, "Ānanda has no hair; can you shave his head?
The woman returned home and told her mother that she had already consented to shave her head. The Buddha then asked, "Do you love..."
“Ānanda, what do you love? He replied, “I love Ānanda’s eyes, ears, mouth, nose, and even his physical form.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda, there is only tears in the eyes; there is only wax in the ears; there is only saliva in the mouth.”
Within the nose there is only mucus; within the body there is only excrement and urine. Where there are husband and wife, there is impurity;
where there is impurity, one gives birth to children; where there are children, there is death. Since there is death and loss, there is weeping and wailing.
"What benefit is there in this body? What is it that you cherish? Upon hearing these words, the woman straightened her mind and immediately attained entry into the Path.

The Buddha said: "For five hundred lifetimes, this woman was Ānanda’s wife. Because they held one another in mutual respect and were bound by mutual desire, even now, when they meet, they are like an elder brother and a younger brother, difficult to part from one another. Only those who have forever severed the heart of attachment [can transcend this]."

"Refers to attaining the three fruits upon first hearing the mantra. "Arhat" refers to the aforementioned Mañjuśrī’s selection of the perfect penetration and his subsequent realization of the fourth fruit.
This is truly because he first received the power of the mantra to eliminate his past habitual tendencies, and subsequently relied upon the sound of the Dharma.

He realized and clarified the holy fruit. Had it not been for the power of the mantra, how could he have eliminated these karmic habits from past lives and attained a mind of lustlessness that accords with the unconditioned Dharma?

Therefore, the merit is still attributed to the power of the mantra. Furthermore, although Kāmandakī’s habits were deep-rooted and she was but a courtesan without any intention to practice, she nonetheless swiftly attained realization through the inconceivable power of the divine mantra and its hidden support.
This applies even to those at the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning, let alone you śrāvakas gathered here whose afflictions and habitual tendencies are shallow and thin.
Furthermore, is it not the case that what you seek is the path of the Supreme Vehicle, which brings about the firm self-confidence of attaining Buddhahood?

You must understand that past habitual tendencies are like dust, while the power of the mantra is like a favorable wind; thus, the removal of these tendencies through the recitation of mantras is like riding upon a great wind.
The wind raises light dust; what difficulty or obstacle could there be?
△ Second, the response through diligent cultivation:
"If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment... (up to) "...he will stroke their heads in comfort, causing them to attain awakening."
This clarifies that if one diligently cultivates the restraints (*vinaya*), recites secret mantras, and practices according to the teachings, the Buddha will certainly respond.

The intent is this: if, in the final age, there should be one who cultivates the perfect penetration of the ear organ (*śrotra-āyatana*) and resolves to sit in the field of practice, they must first maintain the purity of the four fundamental *bhikṣu* restraints and prohibitions. However...
At the time of receiving the precepts, one must carefully select a preceptor. This teacher must be pure, for the preceptor is the model for the student.
If the model is deviant or crooked, it is rare that one who relies upon them can become a vessel for perfection.
Therefore, those who desire to obtain the precepts must choose as their teacher one whose root of morality (*śīla-mūla*) is foremost in purity. (In the Sanskrit language...)
"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "diligent cessation. This means to diligently cultivate precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and to cease and extinguish greed, anger, and ignorance.
By realizing the mind and penetrating its source, one is thus called a śramaṇa; this is the general designation for the great saṃgha.

If one does not encounter such a truly pure and authentic member of the great saṃgha, then even if one receives the precepts, it will be nothing more than a hollow name; in reality, there will be no [attainment].
If one’s precept-body (*śīla-skandha*) is defiled by outflows (*āsrava*), it will certainly not be accomplished. Only upon encountering a true monk (*bhikṣu*) will the precepts finally be fulfilled.
From this point forward, according to the family’s abundance or scarcity and in accordance with one’s own capacity, those who have new robes shall wear new robes;
those without new robes shall wash and dye them until they are pure, and then wear these pure robes. [One should] burn aloeswood incense and remain at leisure...
Dwelling in solitude, this signifies that both the internal and external are pure, and both the inner and outer are cleansed.

As for reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, it is for the purpose of eliminating the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the precepts rectify present karma and the mantra eliminates past habitual tendencies, demonic obstacles will not arise.
Only then may one follow the various Secret Sections (*Guhyatantra*) to select an auspicious day, demarcate the boundary, and establish the ritual altar (*maṇḍala*).

Once the ritual platform has been established, one may then practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Yet, fearing that past obstacles have not yet been eliminated and thus wisdom cannot be awakened, it is necessary to look upward and pray for the Buddhas to emit light and bestow empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), so as to assist in the awakening of wisdom.
Ānanda, although these two groups of renunciants in the Dharma-ending age and the two groups of laypeople at home share the same ritual platform, nevertheless...

Each must belong to its own category; they must not be intermingled. For example, laymen (*upāsaka*) follow behind the great assembly of monks, and laywomen (*upāsikā*) follow behind the assembly of nuns.

This is the fixed order. Although it is permitted for them to be on the same altar, they must have extinguished within their minds thoughts of greed, delusion, and lustful desire, and must be those who uphold the pure precepts of the Buddhas. Only then—
This is acceptable. However, should it not be so, do not permit indiscriminate following [of worldly ways], lest it hinder your spiritual practice (*mārga-karman*).

Within the site of cultivation (*bhāvanā-maṇḍala*), you must resolve upon the Four Great Vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) of a Bodhisattva. Whenever entering or exiting the latrine, you must bathe to purify your body.
During these six periods—three times by day and three times by night—you must apply yourself with diligent effort without interruption.
Constantly practicing the Way in this manner, remaining sleepless, dispelling dullness and distraction, and inwardly gathering the mind for twenty-one days— three times seven days—
I shall certainly personally manifest my body before the practitioner, touching their crown to receive them,
comforting and guiding them so that the practitioner may spontaneously attain awakening and clearly perceive the hidden heart-mind. This is because...
As for the Buddha manifesting to touch one’s crown with his hand: this is precisely what was sought; it is the meeting of the Way through resonance, like the moon appearing when the water is clear.
Although such a state is attained, the practitioner must remain mindful that it is "mind-only" and not grasp at it as existing outside the mind.
To become attached to external phenomena leads to the occurrence of demonic obstacles. Be careful, be careful!
△ II. Extensive Exposition of the Ritual for Manifesting the Meaning (2) A. Direct Presentation of the Ritual (2) 1.

Inquiry. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, having received [instruction] from the Tathāgata... [until] I shall accord with the pure ritual rules of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.”
This is the ritual procedure for establishing boundaries and constructing altars for practice in the Dharma-ending age. The practitioner may say:

"I have already received the Buddha’s unsurpassed great compassion. Since the opening of this assembly, I have been guided in manifold ways and instructed through various teachings, culminating in the four kinds of purity.
Having clearly received these instructions, my clouds have now dispersed into the vast sky, and my mind..."

Like the bright moon, I have already attained understanding and realization. I know for myself that by relying on this perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), and through the cultivation of hearing based on the illusory perfuming of hearing, I shall enter the illusory *samādhi*.
Thus, my path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) will certainly be accomplished; there is no further doubt. However, regarding the practice of beginners in the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*):

One must necessarily establish a site for the cultivation of the path. I do not yet understand how one should demarcate the boundaries so as to accord with the Buddha’s regulations and not contradict the pure rules of conduct taught by the World-Honored One.
△ Second, showing the answer (in two parts). First, the specific explanation (in two parts). First, the ritual for establishing the altar (in two parts). First, the method for establishing the altar.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If in the world at the end of the age... [omitted] ...one should construct an octagonal altar measuring one zhang and six chi in both length and width."
This demonstrates the ritual procedures for the maṇḍala site. Generally, in the arrangements established by the Sage, every matter must have its underlying principle.
Although one manifests matters based on principles, it is truly by means of matters that principles are revealed. How could this be merely establishing the rituals of the maṇḍala to dazzle the eyes?

While the matters are indeed as they appear in the text and can be understood accordingly, the principles are not manifest without symbolic representation. As for "the Snowy Mountains," it symbolizes...

Suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are the unchanging principle and essence. The powerful white ox symbolizes the fundamental right wisdom of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
On the Snowy Mountains there is grass called "Patience" (*kṣānti*); if the ox eats it, he immediately obtains the *sarpis-maṇḍa* (ghee).

The grass is a metaphor for the three types of wisdom, while the *sarpis-maṇḍa* is a metaphor for the [Buddha-]nature; this signifies that one attains the *tathāgatagarbha*-nature through the three types of wisdom.

The clear water represents the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* (the foremost heroic concentration). The ox that chews its cud with water and grass represents the practitioner who cultivates both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in equal measure.
The fineness of its dung represents how concentration arises from precepts (*śīla*), and wisdom is brought forth by concentration.
The dung mixed with sandalwood to plaster the ground represents how the three untainted trainings (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi*) can perfume the *dharmakāya*.
This refers to the mind that serves as the cause for realizing the truth. If it were not for the snow mountain, its oxen would be foul-smelling and unfit for smearing upon the ground;
this symbolizes that if the mind of birth-and-death is taken as the fundamental cause of cultivation, one cannot perfectly realize the fruit-ground of cultivation and realization.
Furthermore, the absence of the snow mountain and white oxen symbolizes the lack of the most supreme capacity. Its distinction from the plains symbolizes the deficiency of the superior [capacity].

Regarding the faculties, we take the medium faculty as the standard. Piercing through the surface soil symbolizes the elimination of external affairs to cultivate the practice of "returning to hearing" (śravaṇa).
The depth of five feet or less symbolizes following the unraveling of the knots to break through the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). The yellow earth symbolizes that yellow is the central color;
it represents the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way at the gateway of the six sense faculties. Mixing ten kinds of incense symbolizes being endowed with the ten [virtues].
"Excellent. What is meant is that the body is free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the mouth is free from false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh abuse;

and the mind is free from greed, anger, and delusion. That the fine hemp is ground into powder represents the ten wholesome acts being integrated and expanded into the myriad practices (*sahasra-saṃskāra*).
That the earth is mixed with it to form mud represents that the myriad practices are but the mind. That this is used to smear the ground represents the realization [of the Dharma-realm]."
It is the true cause. The square and round dimensions of one zhang and six chi symbolize that the Eightfold Noble Path subsumes the eight forms of wrong practice.
The eight corners signify that which is square yet round, and round yet square; this represents the non-duality of essence and function, and the ultimate convergence of phenomena and principle.

The white ox atop the canopy precisely represents the person of the highest capacity, who, by not following after discursive thought, immediately severs the three conditions and does not give rise to the three causes.
Thus, the nature of madness naturally subsides; this subsiding is itself Bodhi. It is likened to the fact that only cow dung can be used to blend with sandalwood.
Should one be unable to suddenly bring this madness to rest, one must know that there are two paths of cultivation.

Regarding the definitive meaning: at the gateway of the six sense organs, one demolishes the five aggregates and attains the fundamental, luminous awareness whose nature is without birth or extinction;

this serves as the mind for the causal stage. Only when further augmented by the four kinds of restraint and the divine mantras of the five assemblies does one become a practitioner of wondrous cultivation.
This is analogous to adding nine fragrances to the yellow earth outside of the sandalwood. *Candana* in Sanskrit is translated here as [sandalwood].
“Yule” (With Joy) refers to white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*). Zhu Fanzhen stated that it originates from foreign lands; on Mount Luo, there are white sandalwood trees.
This sutra uses it to smear the ground, which is not the same as the six *zhu* of *candana* from the seashore mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*, whose value equals that of the Sahā world.
Regarding “scented agallochum” (*kālāguru*), the *Yiwuzhi* states that it originates from Jinnan (Junnanshi). Whenever one wishes to harvest it, one cuts down the tree and applies [the resin].
The earth [substance] becomes rotten and decayed after a long time. That which is most solid in its core sinks when placed in water. Regarding *suhar* (sūhē):
the *Continued History of the Han* states that it comes from the kingdom of Daqin (大秦). Various incenses are combined and their juices are boiled down; this is called *suhar*. Some say it is *suhar*.
The people of the country collect the sap of the flowers, boil it to produce an ointment, and sell it to passing travelers.

Regarding *kunkuma* (turmeric), the *Nanfang Caomu Zhang* states that it comes from large trees growing on the seashore of the Da Qin kingdom; it grows in the sand, and its resin exudes during the height of summer.
It flows across the sands and is naturally effective at relieving pain; it is gathered and sold as such. Regarding *uraga* (turmeric):

the *Shuowen* states that *uranchang* is the flower of all hundred grasses, a tribute presented by distant peoples. The *uran* official pounds and boils it to mix with wine for the descent of spirits.
Regarding *baijiao* (bdellium): the *Bencao* states that there are many trees resembling the white poplar (*baifang*) in the region between Shang and Luo, which bear fruit...
It is as large as a bird’s egg and can eliminate noxious vapors and remove skin sores; it is the resin of the *fengxiang* tree.

Regarding *qingmu*, the *Nanzhou yiwuzhi* states that it is a root capable of awakening those suffering from sleep paralysis (*yanmei*); it resembles licorice in appearance and originates from Jiaozhou.
*Zhiling* (Zeroing). The *Nanyue zhi* states that it is also called *yancǎo* (Yan grass) and further named *xūncǎo* (incense grass). It grows among the mountain valleys of Zhiling Commandery.
Its leaves resemble those of *luòlè* (rue). It can arrest seminal emission and clarify the eyes. *Gānsōng* (Gansong). It grows on the various mountains of Liangzhou.
It can harmonize various fragrances, relieve abdominal distension, and also facilitate the downward movement of qi. *Jīshè* (Cherry tree). From the *Yiwuzhi*.
It is said that it originates from Java. It is said that this is a withered herb. It was the *shangshu lang* (Court Gentleman for the Secretariat) Han Zhi who reported on this during the Han dynasty.
If one takes it for a long time, it can cause both body and mouth to be fragrant; it is the clove (*jīngxiāng*). As for the term "field site" (*chǎngdì*), it refers to... [text ends].

This is what is meant in the Secret Section (Guhyatantra) by "drawing lines on the ground to form a site. However, when one wishes to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is essential to select an auspicious day, delimit the boundaries (*sīmābandha*), construct an altar (*maṇḍala*), and perform the practice.

Once it is completed, one must immediately dissolve the boundaries and dismantle the altar; one must not leave them standing until the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*). This is the established rule. As the ancients said:
"To enclose soil is called a *tán* (altar); to clear the ground is called a *shàn* (plain). 'Clearing' means to sweep away. [End of] National [Standard].
The text states: "The ground cleared for the altar is called the *cháng* (enclosure); 'sealing the earth' (*fēngtǔ*) refers to the act of raising the soil.
The area of this site may be like a leveled clearing (*shàn*). Now that it is designated as an *altár* (*tán*), it must necessarily have raised earth;

therefore, one first clears the ground to form the enclosure, and subsequently takes yellow earth mixed with incense to plaster over the enclosure, thereby creating the physical appearance of the altar. It continues: "In..."
In the center of the hall. This demonstrates the ritual protocol for the *Lengyan* altar site.
△ Second, the method of making offerings (in two parts): First, the articles for offering within the altar.
Place a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or wood at the center of the altar (up to the point where it is burned until the smoke has vanished) to offer to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This clarifies the items to be offered within the altar. Regarding "gold, silver, copper, or wood," this means one should act according to one's capacity;
there is no need for rigid adherence. However, the "center of the altar" represents the Middle Way, the causal mind, and the *tathatā* (suchness).
This is the essence. The lotus flower symbolizes the simultaneity of cause and effect and the non-duality of defilement and purity.

"That which is created" symbolizes that within the state of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is originally no distinction between cause and effect, nor between defilement and purity; yet, because it can follow conditions (*pratyaya*), it manifests as the causes and effects of defilement and purity.

The bowl is called the "appropriate vessel" (*saṃbhoga-pātra*); it symbolizes the perfect integration of phenomena and principle within the Tathāgatagarbha, responding to the minds of sentient beings.
The eight vases represent the measure of all that is known (*jñeya-pramāṇa*). The dew on the eighth month represents the pure and true *śūraṅgama* samādhi of the Middle Way.
The lotus petals placed accordingly represent the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way through hearing and cultivation, which is like an illusion.

The eight mirrors placed in their positions represent that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of the eight consciousnesses, inherently possessed by sentient beings, does not depart from its own place. They surround [the central mirror].
The flower bowl symbolizes that sublime wisdom constantly relies upon the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness).
The lotus flowers and incense burner established outside the mirror symbolize that, based on wisdom, one initiates practice, arising from the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) to cultivate.

The requirement for sixteen of each symbolizes that the flowers of wisdom and the fragrance of precepts represent the eightfold path for self-cultivation and the eightfold path for transforming others. The interspersed flowers and the arrangement adorning the incense burner signify this integration.
This signifies that precepts and wisdom mutually adorn one another, returning to cultivate their own nature.
"Purely burning aloeswood so as not to let the fire be seen" signifies the wondrous precept of formlessness, which dwells amidst delusions and karma yet is not defiled by them.

"The white ox-milk cake and the other seven items" signify the joy of dharma and the delight of meditation arising in accordance with the true nature; these are what are known as the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is flavor (*rasa*). That each [petal] is surrounded by sixteen outside the flower signifies that each and every right path possesses the two kinds of Eightfold Path:

that for one's own practice and that for transforming others. That they are offered to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas signifies that the flavor of the right path—the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna already realized—is turned back from the causal mind toward the fruit-virtue. At every [stage],...

If one makes offerings at the time of the midday meal or during the midnight hour, it is because the fifth watch (wu) represents the center of the day and the eleventh watch (zi) represents the center of the night;
this signifies that the various stages of sainthood must flow through the very center of the center.
Honey is the essence of flowers, and ghee is the essence of milk; both are the supreme flavors among all flavors. This signifies the wondrous, wondrous hearing of the faculty of the ear.

This refers to the mind. The number three, formed by counting within half a *sheng*, represents the Middle Way; it signifies that the concentrated mind (*samādhi-citta*) can harmonize the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and realize the three voids (*trīṇi śūnyatā*).
As for the small fire-brazier placed separately before the altar, it precisely symbolizes that one enters deeply through this single gate of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).
Regarding *dūrva* incense, the *Yiwuzhi* (Records of Strange Things) states: "It comes from a country by the sea; it resembles *duliang* [incense]."

*Gandha*. It is also translated as "produced in the land of ghosts and spirits. Since this substance does not exist in this region, it is not translated [into Chinese]. Alternatively, it is translated as "fragrant herb.

The old tradition states that *bai-mao-xiang* (white mugwort) is used to boil water for bathing the charcoal; this symbolizes the purity of the root of precepts (*śīla-mūla*) and how the power of the mantra (*dhāraṇī-bala*) eliminates habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Thus, both the primary and auxiliary practices are complete, giving rise to the true cultivation of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). It is cast into the butter-lamp (*ghṛta-sthālī*).

This signifies cultivating the ear-root samādhi from within the wondrous mind. "Burning it until the smoke is exhausted" precisely symbolizes that, beginning from the midst of hearing, one reaches the ultimate perfection of the realization of emptiness, whereby both the emptiness and that which was emptied are extinguished. "Offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" refers to...
This indicates that once birth and extinction have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests. The preceding section revealed the two kinds of excellence: "superior conformity" and "inferior union.
△ Second, the external adornments of the altar.
"Have banners and flowers hung everywhere on its four outer sides" (up to) "so that their forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in layers.

This clarifies the Buddhas, sages, and ornaments offered outside the maṇḍala. "On its four outer sides" symbolizes that beyond the four kinds of clear instructions (*vidyā-mantra*), various practices may mutually adorn one another without hindrance.
Indeed, the banners symbolize secret mantras possessing the power to destroy [obstacles].
The power of the heterodox supports the orthodox; the lotus symbolizes the secret cause as the essence of the six perfections and the myriad practices.
As for the arrangement upon the four walls within the altar chamber, it symbolizes that the single true dharma-realm (ekadharmadhātu) encompasses the four dharma-realms.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions symbolize the fruition-awakening (phala-bodhi). The images of the Bodhisattvas symbolize the causal mind. In Sanskrit, this is called Vairocana.
This is called "Illumination," meaning that his radiance shines everywhere. He is the true sovereign of the tranquil site of the One True Dharma-realm;
this is the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya*. In Sanskrit he is Śākyamuni, which means "Capable Sage" (Able Benevolent One) and "Silent Tranquility.
He is the teacher of the Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousand-fold worlds; this is the compassion of the *nirmāṇakāya*. In Sanskrit he is Maitreya.
This one is called Maitreya; he is the future Teacher. In Sanskrit, his name is Akṣobhya, which means "Immovable.
He dwells at the head of all movement in the eastern quarter, signifying the wisdom of immovability within movement. In Sanskrit, his name is Amitābha, which means "Immeasurable Life.
He dwells in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the western quarter, signifying the bestowing of bliss; this is the unconditioned [compassion].

This is Maitreya. As for the various great transformation forms of Avalokiteśvara—such as those with many heads, arms, and eyes as clarified in the preceding text—these are the masters of perfect penetration in the Exoteric Teaching (*kengyō*).
As for Vajragarbha, he constantly leads the vajra-holders to protect those who recite mantras, subduing demons and removing obstacles;
he is thus the master of perfect penetration in the Esoteric Teaching (*mikkyō*). Those positioned at his left and right are [as follows].
This signifies that both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are equally manifest. Śakra is called "The Able-Maker" (Kartṛ) and is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Brahmā does not transgress the dust of desire and is the lord of the First Dhyāna. Ucchuṣma is the Vajra of Fire-Head.
Nīladaṇḍa is the Blue-Faced Vajra. Cundā is also a name for a Vajra. Bhṛkuṭī is the miraculous manifestation of Vairocana.
The Sūtra states: "On the right side is Bhṛkuṭī, her hand holding a rosary garland; she has three eyes and wears her hair in a topknot.
Her form is like a brilliant white full moon, her color incomparable. This refers to her.
As for the Four Heavenly Kings, they are those of the southeast, east, north, and west, namely Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa. Piṇāka is the Boar-headed Messenger.
Yakṣas are the elephant-nosed messengers who descend from Śakra; these outer protectors collectively manifest the function of destroying the heterodox and revealing the orthodox.

As for the eight mirrors suspended in space: they symbolize the transformation of the eight consciousnesses at the stage of Buddhahood into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which, arising from the empty Tathāgatagarbha, universally illumines the lands and atoms throughout the ten directions.
That which faces the mirror on the altar represents that the mind of the ordinary being is itself the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind is not different from the mind of the ordinary being.

That their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in layers represents the mutual fusion of the ordinary being and the Buddha, such that there is no difference between the holy and the profane.
This is indeed an inconceivable realm. That the human mirror within the space reflects downward upon the altar mirror symbolizes that the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause.
That the eight mirrors on the altar reflect upward toward the mirror in the space symbolizes that the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit.
If a practitioner, during the twelve periods of the day and night, should cast even a single glance upon this ritual arrangement of the altar, they will clearly understand it.

By this principle, one knows that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind are non-differentiated in these three; thus, the entire body is pervasively present within the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
△ Second, the cultivation of practice. (3) First, showing the conduct of cultivation. (2) First, the auxiliary practices during the seven days.

During the first seven days, one should perform wholehearted prostrations until reaching the place where the mirrors reflect each other’s light, thereby receiving the Buddha’s empowerment by stroking the crown of the head.
This demonstrates the ritual procedure for worship, recitation, and auxiliary cultivation during the three periods of seven days.

Whatever one seeks to attain, one must first take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem as the primary expedient; therefore, during the first seven days, one should perform wholehearted prostrations.

Regarding the veneration of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats by reciting their names: this is done to rely upon the inconceivable power of the Buddha-saints to provide protection and assistance on the path.

Furthermore, one must constantly, throughout the six periods of day and night, maintain the recitation of the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-hṛdaya-mantra* while circumambulating the altar, practicing the Buddha-way with a heart of utmost sincerity. At each [period]...
At that time, one should circumambulate the altar, constantly performing one hundred and eight rounds. This is the practice for the first seven days.

During the second seven days, it is necessary to remain single-mindedly without mixing in other thoughts; with exclusive concentration, one should give rise to the bodhisattva vows, striving to ensure that the mind continues from moment to moment, thought after thought, without interruption or cessation. Within the Vinaya, there are previously established instructions regarding these vows.
This refers to the Ten Great Vow-Kings from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* as well as the Four Great Vows;

these constitute the second seven-day period. During the third seven-day period, one must be diligent and courageous day and night, for twelve hours, without slackening for even a moment, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s *Pāṭala* mantra until the end of the seventh [period].
At the end of the day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear at the place where the various mirrors within the space of the altar reflect one another’s light.
Such a practitioner will surely be graced by all the Buddhas, who personally touch the crown of their head. This is precisely like the moon appearing when the water is clear.
The mutual resonance between the Way and the practitioner has been established; this is the time when the ordinary mind is transformed into the Buddha-mind.
△ Second, the formal cultivation after the twenty-one days:
one immediately cultivates *samādhi* within the practice hall (until) body and mind are clear and pure, like lapis lazuli.

This clarifies that after the three-week period, once the ritual procedures for the altar have ceased but the site remains, one should practice right concentration within the walking path inside the chamber.
This enables sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who train after the seven days to attain great awakening;
their bodies and minds become clear and pure, like lapis lazuli, transparent both within and without.
When the faculties and their objects are unimpeded, this primary cause causes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to give rise to wisdom.

Thus, one should know that there is no difference between the perfect penetration attained through the manifest practice of cultivation and the secret practice of recitation. Herein, "samādhi" refers precisely to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, the King of Śūraṅgama.
One must understand that the two types of auxiliary practices mentioned above—observing the precepts and chanting mantras—are solely intended to assist this [primary practice].

If the principles of the primary practice (*samyak-samādhi*) and its true cultivation, or the intent of the primary and auxiliary practices, are not clearly understood, then the descriptions of the boundary fields and altar configurations will all be nothing more than empty words.
Therefore, those who are resolved to practice *samyak-samādhi* should carefully savor these teachings.
△ Second, distinguishing those who do not achieve success:
"Ānanda, if this bhikṣu’s original preceptor... [down to] ...such a place of practice (maṇḍala), success will generally not be achieved.

This clarifies that although the ritual procedures for the altar have been established, if the master or fellow practitioners are impure, it will likewise be difficult to achieve success. (10th Comparison)
Regarding the term "group" (*qiu*): according to the *Vaipulya Dhāraṇī*, when practicing this rite, ten people are the maximum limit;
it does not exceed this number. The sutras provide clear instructions, and those who wish to practice must not contravene them.
Even if there are no like-minded companions, one may rather practice alone; one need not force the number of participants to be complete at the risk of causing impurity. Thus it is said:
What has been cultivated will not be accomplished. Within this context, there are two types of deficiencies: first, receiving the precepts in an improper manner;
second, practicing the path in an improper manner. Among these two, if even one is impure, one will be unable to attain realization within a fixed period.
Thus, it is known that one must also exercise careful discernment regarding one's teachers and companions.
△ Third, clarifying the benefits obtained.
From the end of the three weeks [of practice], sitting in meditative seclusion during the summer retreat (until) he definitively knew for himself that his attainment of Buddhahood was not in error.
This clarifies that even if one does not achieve success within the *bodhimaṇḍa*, if one can remain in meditative seclusion for a hundred days, one will likewise obtain benefit. This is because...
Although the methods for cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) differ from one another, there are four types of practice that encompass all *samādhis*.
The first is "constant sitting" (*nitya-prahāṇa*), as described by Mañjuśrī: it involves opening the body to remain constantly seated while prohibiting walking, standing, or lying down;

this is the "one-practice *samādhi*" (*ekavyūha-samādhi*). The second is "constant walking," which appears in the *Pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra* (*Banzhou jing*): it consists exclusively of focused circumambulation, without sitting or lying down.
These are the Buddha-standing samādhi and the [Buddha-sitting] samādhi; both last for ninety days, constituting one session.

The third is called "half-walking and half-sitting," as stated in the Vaipulya sūtras: "Having circumambulated two hundred and one times, he then sat down and entered into contemplation. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:

Whether walking or standing, one recites this sutra; or while sitting, one contemplates this sutra. The fourth is "according to one's own inclination," such as in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* and other Mahāyāna scriptures.
These are neither specifically walking nor sitting, yet they effectively encompass both walking and sitting.
These two do not establish a fixed time limit. As for the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* mentioned in the present sutra, if one follows what was previously stated, it involves three weeks.
"Sleeping" refers to practicing while walking; "sitting" now refers to practicing while seated for one hundred days. Thus, we know that this method is the samādhi of half-walking and half-sitting.
Those of keen faculties are those whose afflictive obstructions are both light and whose merit and wisdom are pure and profound.
*Srotāpanna* means "entering the stream," which is the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), corresponding to the first stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching. As it says:
Ānanda has attained perfect realization of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature and has suddenly acquired the *dharmakāya*.

Although his body and mind may still harbor subtle afflictions that cannot be severed all at once, and the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*) has not yet been fully realized, he knows with certainty that the matter of attaining Buddhahood is not false or erroneous.
This is what is meant by "once believed, forever believed": having gained faith in one's own mind as being the Buddha.
As for the self-nature, the Buddha no longer has any further doubts.
△ Second, the summary:
You have asked how the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is established; it is thus.
This is the summary response. Its meaning is as follows: regarding your inquiry concerning the rules for purifying the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), I have already explained them;
both the method for its establishment and the method for its cultivation and study are none other than those described above.
It is so. △ Second, the repeated proclamation of the divine mantra (in three parts): First, the request made by the one who is the primary recipient.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha: [omitted] "...I await to hear the secret verses and phrases of the Tathāgata."
This is a request for the mantra to be recited again. The intention is as follows:

Since I abandoned worldly life and left home to become a monk, I have habitually relied upon the Buddha’s compassion and affection, seeking only extensive learning and attaining merely the first fruit of the path.

Thus, my power of the Way became weak and I was captured by Māra; this was because I had not yet attained true cultivation, actual realization, or the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is so.

Because I encountered that Śvākarā and was constrained by the prohibitions of his former Brahma-mantras and heterodox arts, although my mind remained clear at that time, it was as if the power of the Path were too slight; I could not free myself from his caresses.
Fortunately, I met Mañjuśrī, who took those mantras away and enabled me to be liberated from the peril of lust at that moment, so that I was finally able to return.
Although we have received this divine mantra, Mañjuśrī has been reciting it in secret to destroy heterodoxy and eliminate lust, while we have only obtained its power invisibly;
we have not yet personally heard it clearly. We pray that the World-Honored One, in your great kindness and compassion, will proclaim it once more for us.
This would be sufficient to manifest your compassion from beginning to end and save us.

May the grace be extended so that those currently present at this assembly, as well as those who will be within the cycle of saṃsāra in the future, may all equally partake in the benefits of the Dharma.
For one who is able to reverently receive the sound of the secret mantra, they shall distance themselves from demons and leave behind hardships, attaining liberation of the body;
they shall shatter delusions and realize the truth, attaining liberation of the mind. Having made this request, the entire great assembly...
They all paid homage to the Buddha, wishing to hear the subtle and wondrous phrases of the Tathāgata’s secret divine incantations.
△ Second, the World-Honored One’s formal proclamation (in two parts): 1. The manifested Buddha speaks the incantation; 2. Manifesting transformation to reveal [the truth].
At that time, the World-Honored One [emerged] from the *uṣṇīṣa* (the crown protuberance)... the Tathāgata Emitting Light proclaimed a divine mantra (*vidyā*).
This indicates that before the mantra was to be repeated, he first manifested a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*) to make it manifest.

Regarding the *uṣṇīṣa*, according to the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (The Sutra on the Supreme Basis), it is the bone of the crown of the head that rises upward, naturally forming a topknot; this is the Great Buddha-Crown (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*).
The appearance of this [lotus] symbolizes the immovable fundamental essence.
That light is emitted from it symbolizes the Dharma of the Honored Victorious Crown, which is produced by supreme, wondrous wisdom. The "hundred jewels" symbolize the hundred realms.

That lotuses surge forth within the light symbolizes that the sublime cause is generated based upon wondrous wisdom. The "thousand petals" symbolize the thousand suchnesses. Therein are transformations...

The Buddha sitting amidst the flowers symbolizes that cause and effect are one, and that the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses are none other than the wondrous true *tathāgatagarbha* nature of suchness.
From the Buddha’s crown to his crown, he radiates jewel-light from jewel-light.
This represents the most honored among the honored and the most secret among the secret. As for the single topknot emitting ten rays of light endowed with the colors of a hundred jewels:
it symbolizes that from the one mind of the *tathāgatagarbha*, ten kinds of dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) flow forth;
each realm possesses ten, thus forming a hundred dharma-realms. Each individual ray of light pervading ten rivers of sand: this symbolizes each individual dharma...

All realms are fully endowed with the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which perfectly encompasses the ten realms. Therefore, as its essence, it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
"The Vajra pervades the realm" symbolizes the wondrous function of responding to conditions—manifesting according to karma to give rise to goodness and extinguish evil.
Furthermore, this *garbha*-mind, in its entirety and great function, is like a vajra; nothing can [destroy it].
It is that which destroys and demolishes. Thus, it shatters the birth-and-death of the ten realms and reveals the nirvana of the ten realms.
Because it possesses the majesty of subjugation, it causes people to look up in awe; yet, because it possesses the compassion of gathering-in, it causes people to look down in reflection with love.
This precisely means that its majestic spiritual power is to be feared, while its compassionate countenance is to be cherished—the two qualities being present together.
Although they differ, both equally cause one to be unable to let them go from one's heart.

As for the Buddha’s recitation of the mantra at the crown of the head, it precisely symbolizes the unconditioned Mind-Buddha and the unsurpassed Heart-Mantra, thereby manifesting the subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable nature of the hidden mind.

"Mantra" (zhòu) means "to invoke blessings. By means of this mantra, the Buddha invokes blessings upon sentient beings, causing them to transform from the mundane into the sacred without even realizing it themselves.
It is like the *gongling* wasp that blesses the *mínglíng* caterpillar, saying, "Be like me! Be like me! After a long time, the latter comes to resemble it;
yet they call it "divine" because the mantra can suppress the heterodox and assist the orthodox, shatter delusion and realize the Truth, and possesses all such [powers].
This measures his majestic spiritual power. In Sanskrit he is called *Guhyaka*; here it is translated as "Lord of Secrets.
Because he knows the merits of the Buddha’s three secrets and serves as the master who attains the Dharma, he manifests as a deity; thus he is called "Secret Trace" (*Miji*).
△ Second, the actual recitation of the divine mantra:
*Namo satvathā samyaksambuddhāya* (1–37). *Ime tathāgatāya namo 'stu*.
(When the reciter reaches this point, they should say: "I, disciple [name], receive and uphold it.")
Oṃ [a-hu] (38–40) *iṇtu namo mā vā (78). (Up to this point, follow the previous procedure for reciting the name;
if a layperson, say "disciple so-and-so"). Rājaparyāya (79–81) *iṇtu namo mā vā (72). (Up to this point, recite the disciple’s name as before).
Bhagavan (73–75) *mā *iṇtu namo mā vā (32). (Up to this point, recite the disciple’s name as before).
*Tusṭa-citta svāhā* (33–27). The above divine mantra consists of five assemblies, totaling four hundred twenty-seven phrases and two thousand six hundred twenty characters.
It is the secret exposition of the *dharmakāya* of the Great Buddha, the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the heart-mind (*cittamaya*). Compared to the preceding exoteric [teachings]...

It is said that their benefit is no different. This is because there are sentient beings who will derive benefit from explicit teachings, and there are also sentient beings who will derive benefit from esoteric teachings.
Although these explicit and esoteric modes are presented alternately, they all elucidate the inconceivable essence and function of the Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgatagarbha.
This is consistent with the general principle of divine mantras found in various sūtras.

None of these are translated [into Chinese]. Since ancient times, masters of the human path have held many differing views. The virtuous ones of old synthesized them, finding that they do not go beyond the four *siddhāntas*.
First, it is said: A mantra is the name of a ghost-king. By invoking the name of this king, his tribes respect their lord and dare not commit wrongs.
This is the *loka-siddhānta*, in the sense of bringing about joy. Second, it is said: A mantra is like a secret password within an army.
Chanting the name in resonance, there is nothing to be censured or questioned; those who do not resonate with it are immediately restrained and governed.
This is the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the standpoint of the person), which has the meaning of generating wholesome states. Third, as for "mantra": it is a secret and silent warding off of evil.
Others who lack such knowledge are like lowly commoners who flee to a foreign land and falsely claim to be princes; that country then marries them to its princess.
There was much anger and difficulty. A wise man came from that country, and the princess went to him to complain.
The man said to her: "When you feel angry, you should recite this verse: 'Having no kin, I have gone to another land; I have deceived all people.'"
"Coarse food is one's regular sustenance; why trouble yourself by becoming angry again? When this verse was spoken, his anger subsided in silence.
This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment), which serves to destroy evil. Fourth, as for "mantra," these are the secret words of the Buddhas, known only to the Sages.
It is like a king who requests "Saindhava"—a single name that actually possesses four realities, namely: salt, water, a vessel, and a horse.
The subordinates could not understand it; only the wise minister comprehended it. A mantra is also like this:

though it is but a single teaching, it possesses manifold powers—namely, to engender joy and wholesome states, to extinguish evil, and to lead one into the principle. This is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established truth).
Because they possess four specific meanings, their original sounds are retained rather than being translated.
Generally, according to the principles of translating scriptures, there are four rules and five instances for non-translation; those who engage in this work must know them. As for the four rules:

first, translating the characters but not the sound, which refers to various mantras; second, translating the sound but not the characters, such as the *svastika* (卍) and so forth. These are from the West...
Regarding transliteration: in this region, "wan" (萬) and "yi" (伊) are used; these are not Western sounds. Translating all three phonemes refers to the texts of various sūtras.
Translating all four phonemes refers to the Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts (*vrajapustaka*).
As for the five reasons for not translating: first, secrecy, which refers to various mantras; second, multiple meanings, such as the three meanings of *bhikṣu* or the six meanings of *bhagavat*.

Regarding the five reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms]: first, those whose meaning is equivalent to existing Chinese terms; second, those that are non-existent in this land and thus cannot be translated, such as the *Jambū* tree;
third, those that follow ancient precedent and are not translated, such as *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

fourth, those treated with reverence and not translated, such as *Prajñā*, which is revered while "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*) is considered light and thin; and fifth, [the category of] mantras, which fall within these four cases—namely, the characters are translated but the sounds are not.
Among the five reasons for not translating, this is the case of "not translating due to secrecy. However, these secret mantras are not merely Sanskrit;
they are the heart-seals (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas and the secret Dharma. As for the Sanskrit language, the people of this land [China]—
Although some may not understand it, the people of India have never been unaware of it.
As for secret mantras, not only do ordinary people in India not know them, but even those of lower rank among the sages and worthies do not comprehend the mantras of those of higher rank.
Therefore, apart from the Exoteric Section (Vidyādhara-piṭaka), there is the separate Esoteric Section (Guhyaka-piṭaka).

Now, within the Secret Section in the Western Regions, it is divided into East, West, South, North, and Center, making five sections in total. This mantra precisely belongs to the Central Vairocana Consecration Section.
Nevertheless, in the edification established by all Buddhas, both Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are present; they are like the body and its shadow.
These two are mutually supportive and complementary, such that neither is neglected. It is like a skilled physician of the world treating a person's illness, which generally follows two approaches.
The first is to provide a prescription, wherein he explicitly explains the origin of the disease, as well as the nature of the medicine and the methods for its preparation;
this is analogous to the explicit teachings (*vyakta-dharma*) of the Buddhas. The second is to provide only pills, powders, or decoctions.

The medicinal compound is not formulated with specific names, nor is its composition explained; it is called a "soup-head" (tāngtóu). It is intended solely for the patient to take so that their illness may be cured;
there is no necessity to know which specific drugs or treatments were used. This is analogous to the esoteric teachings of the Buddhas.

Therefore, these secret mantras are exactly like being given medicine: one need not seek an explanation, but by merely reciting and upholding them, one will surely remain far removed from demonic influences.
To escape calamities, sever delusions, realize the truth, transcend birth and death, and enter nirvana; it is to transform afflictions and realize bodhi.
△ Second, describing the merit and exhorting to uphold (in two parts): First, describing the merit of the realized person’s self-benefit and benefit for others.
"Ānanda, this 'Gathering of Light from the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa' (up to) is also called the 'Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa.
This describes how, for one at the stage of fruition, both self-benefit and benefit for others are the functional power of this mantra-heart.
Because the essence of this mantra is the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, it is called the 'mantra-heart. Furthermore, it flows forth from the Tathāgatagarbha-mind."

This mantra is recited; it is also called the "Heart Mantra. This refers to the entire mantra as the heart, rather than indicating that the six syllables *siddhārthahṛdaya* alone constitute the heart, for those are merely the title of the mantra.
One should know that this mantra is designated as a verse (*gāthā*) from the Secret Initiation Section (*Abhiṣeka-guhya-kula*), and is thus subtle, profound, and wondrous.
It is inconceivable and cannot be explained. Nevertheless, its five assemblies are divided into four hundred and twenty-seven chapters;
every phrase is a secret exposition of the *cittagarbha* (storehouse mind), no different from the explicit teachings. Yet, this single mind possesses three meanings.
Its essence is without counterpart, and thus it is called "Great. It is the wondrously luminous mind of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is fundamentally and truly empty.

The meaning of non-emptiness (*aśūnya*) is that its characteristics are severed from all worldly defilements; thus it is called "white. This refers to the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha’s fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and true mind as emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Its function of covering all things is called the "parasol" (*chattra*); this refers to the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha’s primordial luminosity, the wondrous and true mind as non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*).
Because it possesses these three qualities, it is able to generate heaven and earth and nourish both the sages and the ordinary. Therefore...
All Buddhas of the ten directions have not failed to emerge through this; they are born from it.
Thus, one knows that the path by which the Buddhas manifest their bodies and the virtue of their generation and growth are all the efficacy of this secret mantra-heart.
It is not merely for the sake of birth; rather, it is because of this secret mantra-heart that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain unexcelled Bodhi and are called Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Without taking this non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause of cultivation and as the secret cause, they could not subsequently perfect the path of awakening at the stage of fruition. Thus, one should know that all...
The Buddha is the cause and the awakened mind is the fruit; from beginning to end they are non-dual, both being that which is elucidated by this secret mantra: the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
It is not merely cause and fruit; it is the very essence of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, capable of subduing all demons of the five aggregates.

Those non-Buddhists who hold to views of eternalism and nihilism have none who do not grasp this secret mantra-heart, the Vajra King Sword, as the supreme instrument for subduing Māras and overcoming outsiders.
Thus, one knows that the Buddhas subdue Māras and overcome outsiders by means of this.

All of this is the efficacy of this mantra-heart. Not only is it so; these are the universal clouds of manifestations of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, sitting upon precious lotus flowers and responding everywhere to all lands as numerous as motes of dust.

Is it not because they ride upon this Great White Ox Cart of the secret mantra-heart that they are able to travel through lands as numerous as motes of dust, manifesting in accordance with the various types of beings?
When one manifests a physical body, it is known that the Buddhas' ability to respond universally throughout the mundane world is entirely due to the efficacy of this mantra-heart.
Not only does it manifest bodies, but even the ten directions of Tathāgatas, with their eightfold voices and four kinds of eloquence,
preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings and turning the Great Wheel of Dharma within lands as numerous as motes of dust— all of these are contained within this secret mantra-heart.
Taking the treasury of the Dharma-eye as the wood of virtue, one may then reveal it to others.

Thus, we know that the Buddhas' ability to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings is entirely the functional power of this mantra-heart. Not only does it enable them to preach the Dharma;
it is also that which allows the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, after attaining the Way, to compassionately embrace and transform sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

Upon the crown of his head, he bestows predictions upon others. Even if one has not yet fully realized the fruit for oneself while still dwelling on the stage of the causal ground, one is likewise able to receive the protection and the stroking of the head by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, who bestow the prediction of Bodhi.
There are none who do not hold this secret mantra-heart as their talisman; thus, they are able to act as teacher and disciple, with the transmission of the teaching clearly defined.
Thus, one knows that whether in cause or fruit, from the stage of ordinary beings to the state of sainthood, all Buddhas rely solely upon this secret mantra.
With single-minded devotion, it serves as the true seal for attaining Buddhahood and the essential key for delivering sentient beings. It is not merely a matter of transmission;

it is that which enables the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to rescue and deliver all from manifold calamities, sudden misfortunes, the eight sufferings, and the eight difficulties throughout the ten directions.

Regarding the "difficulties" (*durgati*): this is also the heart-essence of this mantra. As for the commentary on this section, according to the ancient interpretation, the eight sufferings and eight difficulties (*aṣṭau durgatayaḥ*) are all distinct from the conventional understanding.
Ordinarily, one takes birth, old age, sickness, and death, together with the four [sufferings] such as enmity and hatred, to constitute the eight;
however, these are further augmented by various great and small calamities to exhaust all remaining forms of suffering. The eight difficulties are also distinct from those [conventional ones].
The sutras differ. Now, eight calamities are enumerated: the king as a thief, imprisonment, wind, fire, water, famine, and hunger;

△ Seven: Fulfilling Wishes According to Requests.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women... [as far as] ...the lowly and base classes of the borderlands, let alone those of mixed forms.

This clarifies the fulfillment of wishes through the *Parṇaśavarī* [dhāraṇī]. Since all that preceded was explained with reference to male practitioners, this section is primarily elucidated in relation to women.
Although the section on "seeking long life" and below includes men as well, it predominantly concerns the female perspective.
Those who seek to have their karmic fruits and rewards swiftly perfected are seeking immediate efficacy; this refers to the fruits and rewards of merit and benefit. For example, as for the body...
"To likewise obtain robust health, longevity, upright physical appearance, and strong vitality" refers to the aforementioned swift attainment of perfection.
This describes those of inferior faculties and weak capacities who do not realize that the retribution for upholding mantras serves as the cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future,
but instead seek only the benefits for their present physical bodies and desire [perfection] quickly.

One attains it; thus, one’s wishes are also fulfilled. As for those of diverse forms—such as ghosts, spirits, birds, and beasts—one takes them with this incantation as freely as with a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi);
there is no restriction in taking them, and they are inexhaustible in use. Therefore, in the present time...

One shall obtain all that is sought, and at the time of death, one will be reborn according to one's vows. Thus, it is known that there is nothing that does not accord with the mind and no wish that is not fulfilled.
△ Eight: Protecting the Nation and Pacifying the People.
"Ānanda, if [this spell is recited] in all kingdoms, prefectures, counties, and villages... (up to) no evil omens or calamities will ever be able to enter.

This clearly demonstrates that this dhāraṇī can protect the state, bring peace to the people, and transform misfortune into good fortune. "Malignant pestilence" (*li*) refers to the vapors of disharmony during the four seasons;
when humans contract them, they result in epidemics. "Other calamities and hardships" include, for example, insect plagues, droughts, and so forth.
"Liáo" (floods, etc. refers to this. "Dì" (ground) refers to the locations of kingdoms, prefectures, counties, and villages.
The Sanskrit term *caitya* translates here as "place worthy of offerings"; it is a general designation for a pure *kṣetra* (buddha-field).
The Sanskrit term *dhvaja* means "banner. Furthermore, *ja* is glossed as "summit" (*du*). Thus, *dhvadu* refers to a city tower—that is, a high and prominent place. (1)
Regarding mental offerings: one must concentrate the mind and pay respectful homage before efficacy can be attained.
As for the "five grains," these refer to hemp, millet, sorghum, wheat, and beans. Ten billion is called a *zhào*; a *zhào* is also a *jīngzhào*, referring to the vast population of a great state.

Since the stars each have their own directions, they are said to be "according to direction. That which is on the hand is called a *niǔ* (cuff); that which is on the foot is called a *xiè* (shackle); that which is on the neck—
They are called *jiā* (shackles) and *suǒ* (fetters); these consist of three types of wood and one type of iron. Furthermore, there are eight kinds of calamities and anomalies:
namely, famine, pestilence, warfare, the threat of bandits, strife, wind and rain [out of season], punishments, and the portents of malevolent stars.
When the sun and moon lose their proper courses, eclipses become portents; when wind and rain do not occur at their proper times, they likewise bring misfortune.
Thus, their destruction brings calamity. When the five planets lose their proper courses, the state of Zhou suffers misfortune.

These aberrations that contravene natural order are caused by human beings; Heaven responds to them with portents and transformations. This does not mean that the stars themselves possess malevolence.
All such things arise because the human heart is not good, and thus the celestial phenomena also manifest their evil. Therefore...
The execution of the violent brings many whirlwinds; the perversion of the law brings many locusts and moths. Thus, when Zou Yan was imprisoned, frost flew even in the sixth month;
when a Qi woman harbored a grievance, it did not rain for three years—this is the same principle.
As for the mention of eighty-four thousand, this is the total number of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) arrayed across the heavens. The twenty-eight [mansions] constitute the four directions.
The eight great stars are the woof that follows the warp of this scripture; they are the five planets along with Rāhu, Ketu, and Śani.

When their movements accord with the proper order, they bring blessings; when they move contrary to it, they bring calamity. This is what is meant by "following the auspicious brings good fortune, while following the perverse brings misfortune.
Therefore, speaking in terms of their portents of disaster, they are called "malevolent stars" (*pāpagraha*). When they manifest in various forms appearing in the world, as for example...
It manifests as small children singing songs or as old women uttering prophecies concerning "red" and "white"—all of which are of this nature.
For this reason, it can give rise to all manner of calamities, afflictions, transformations, and extraordinary, unpredictable events among all sentient beings in the world.
However, in a place where this secret mantra exists, one can turn misfortune into good fortune. So it is said.
As for the statement that "all calamitous omens are completely extinguished": through the power of the divine mantra, all things accord with a hundredfold auspiciousness;
thus, all malevolent transformations are utterly extinguished, and celestial portents of disaster do not enter its borders. Regarding the *yojana*, it is correctly called *yojanana*;
this is translated as "joining" (*he*) and is comparable to a postal station in this region. It is the place where a Wheel-Turning King halts during his tour of inspection.
[The term] *śa* [is used here]. However, those *yojana*s vary in size; they may be forty *li* or sixty *li*.
This is what is meant in our own region by "an auspicious journey" (*ji-xing*) of thirty *li*. As for "auspicious" (*xiang*), it refers to a precursor to good or bad fortune.
△ Third, the exhortation to uphold the reality.

Therefore, from "the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra" up to "the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods," this is a summary exhortation to maintain [the practice], clarifying that its merit is real. The meaning is that by upholding the mantra, one can obtain [such results].
Because of the various benefits manifested above, this mantra is proclaimed and preserved for the sake of future generations, so as to provide protection.

It is intended to bring peace and security to those who, having first begun their practice and study, enter right concentration through the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, ensuring they are free from all afflictions and harms.
Furthermore, those who wish to practice it in the present or the future must know this:
There are four matters through which one can obtain benefit; otherwise, there will be no success. First, one must rely upon my maṇḍala.

Second, one should observe my precepts and rules. Third, one’s teacher must be free from impurity. Fourth, one must have no doubts regarding the mantra. If one is able to act in this way, [success will follow].

It is entirely without deficiency. Good son, even if one were to give rise to this physical body composed of the four elements and five aggregates through the union of paternal seed and maternal blood,
if one cannot attain the realization of the *amala-vijñāna* (the heart-mind of the treasury of clarity) and thereby achieve perfect penetration,
then the teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would not be called true speech, real speech, or suchness-speech.
To not deceive would be to speak words that are false; this conversely clarifies that what is spoken is true and will certainly not lead one astray.
△ Third, the vow for protection by the assembly of sages (2): First, the vow of the celestial deities to obtain [the teaching].
Having spoken these words, immeasurable [beings] within the assembly attained the realization of Bodhi, forever free from demonic interference.
This clarifies that the external hosts—the Vajrapāṇis, as well as the heavenly deities and terrestrial spirits—made vows and obtained the dhāraṇī.
As for the "Vajras," they are the Vajrapāṇi deities; they constitute the host of Mallas (wrestlers). Because they obtained the dhāraṇī, therefore...
The "protector" (hu ren) is likely a member of the King of the Treasury's retinue; he is not the Bodhisattva mentioned in the subsequent text.
One who "cultivates Bodhi" refers to one who cultivates the perfect penetration of the ear faculty, thereby attaining the true samādhi of Bodhi.
The character "one" (zhe) specifically identifies that person. That is to say, if one seeks true samādhi, one must first maintain the heart-mantra to assist those who practice.
The subsequent sections are all explained according to this principle. "At that time" refers to the assembly of the various devas below. "Shen" (審) means indeed or as a result.
"Fulfilling one's wishes in a single lifetime" means that throughout the present life, whatever one undertakes will be entirely able to accord with one's aspirations.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable yakṣas; these belong to the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭa-nikāya*).
"Leaders" (*śūrai*) refers to generals, that is, the chiefs among the spirits. Furthermore, there are immeasurable celestial hosts of the sun and moon;
those listed here include wind, clouds, rain, thunder, the sun, the moon, the stars and constellations, as well as lightning and its like. Regarding lightning: it is the union of yin and yang.
They interact with one another; when thin, they become lightning. Lightning is the light of thunder. According to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), there are four types of lightning:

that of the East is called Shēnwèi (Body Flavor); that of the South is named Bózhǔ (Lord of the Hundred); that of the West is titled Ājiéluó (Ajagara); and that of the North is termed Āzhùlán (Aśvalāna).

Now, the titles "Shī" (Master) and "Bó" (Hundred/Lord) used for these are honorific designations for those who exercise sovereign authority and leadership. As for the "Official Who Patrols the Years":
This refers to the annual inspector who surveys all the good and evil among humanity throughout the year.
This person vows to provide protection at the time the ritual site (*dōjō*) is established; this differs from the aforementioned text.
While the former vow was to protect [the practitioner] for a lifetime, this refers to ensuring that no calamities such as wind or rain shall afflict the site when it is established. Thus it is said.
Therefore, what was stated previously—that "the devas and nāgas rejoice, and wind and rain follow their proper seasons"—precisely clarifies the intent of these protectors of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable numbers of mountain deities and other spirits; the "mountain deities" refers specifically to the presiding deities of mountains.
Examples include Yangyuan and the Five Sacred Peaks. The Sea Deity is the presiding deity of the sea, such as the Water Palace and the Four Great Rivers.
The Land Deity is the presiding deity of the earth, such as the Earth-Sustaining Deity (Dṛḍhā). These deities traverse the water, land, and air.

These three abodes are cited here to encompass all deities. "The spirits of all things" refers to such entities as the presiding deities of trees, flowers, fruits, vegetables, and crops; these belong to the category of those with form.
The following clarifies the multitude of those without form. Indeed, what has been cited above already exhausts the two realms of desire and form. Within this context, it says:
The Wind Deity King is the presiding deity of wind. The gods of the Formless Realm are a class of celestial beings who possess no physical form resulting from karmic fruit;
this refers generally to the four heavens of the Formless Realm in the higher realms.

Viewed in this light, among the heavenly deities and terrestrial spirits—indeed, all the numinous and venerable entities within the myriad things of the three realms—there are none who have not resolved their minds to receive and uphold this divine mantra.
One can fully understand that this mantra is a secret exposition of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Although the myriad phenomena of the three realms do not transcend it, it is the Way universally held and inherently possessed by all sentient beings. Therefore, "to uphold" means to uphold this mind;
"to protect" means to protect this mind. Whether upholding or protecting, neither lies outside of this very mind.
△ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ vow for attainment.
At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas... (up to) "may this person’s undertakings always be fulfilled according to their wishes.
This clarifies that the inner sage Vajragarbha-rāja makes a vow to protect the mantra. As for Vajragarbha-rāja, he is...
The name is established based on the total manifestation of the ultimate, firm *tathāgatagarbha*-mind.
