Indeed, the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* is also called the *vajra-samādhi*; it is by means of this that Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) shatter ignorance.
All [this] employs the correct wisdom of the vajra. Because fundamental ignorance is most subtle and extremely firm, it cannot be destroyed unless by the correct wisdom of the vajra.
Therefore, this heart-mantra is also called "vajra," for it flows forth from within the Tathāgata’s vajra-mind.
Thus, it is able to eliminate past obstructions, shatter ignorance, and overturn [delusion].
From within the dust and toil [of saṃsāra], one becomes a protector of the Dharma; thus there are eighty-four thousand Vajra-Right Wisdoms that constantly follow and guard [the practitioner].

"Not taking nirvāṇa, but following the mantra to obtain the person" means that by manifesting the fruit while practicing the cause, one fulfills the fundamental vow to protect and sustain living beings.
"Constantly following whether in concentration or distraction" clearly reveals the profound resolve to serve both the Dharma and sentient beings.

As for Maheśvara, he is the Māra-deva of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). That his head was shattered by the jewel-topped vajra was the Great Sage’s teaching of beings through both subduing and gathering, employing the skillful means of expedient power (*upāya-kauśalya*). "That which is done shall be as wished" means:
Thus, whatever actions one undertakes, the Bodhisattva provides protection so that all may be fulfilled according to one's wishes;

this is the accomplishment of the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming, which is like an illusion. Therefore, one should know that in the final age, those who are able to maintain mantras and enter right concentration do so entirely through the power of this Bodhisattva’s protection. Furthermore, in this practice, there is both the primary method and its auxiliary support.

One must not fail to understand this. If one possesses sharp faculties, they should immediately turn their hearing back toward the self-nature through the faculty of the ear; this is called "correct cultivation.

Even if one's faculties are somewhat inferior, it does not hinder the establishment of boundaries, the setting up of altars, the observance of precepts, or the recitation of mantras—all of which serve as auxiliary practices.
These are termed the practices that assist correct cultivation. The above constitutes the first section, clarifying correct and auxiliary practices to demonstrate the conduct.
△ 2. Distinguishing Delusion and Enlightenment to Clarify Realization (2) 1. The Stage of Requesting Instruction on Awakening and Cultivation for the Appropriate Audience.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, [and so forth], awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate voice while gazing up with a dazed and longing look.

This clarifies that the practitioners present have already awakened to the cultivation of both the primary and auxiliary practices, and further request confirmation regarding the stages of the fruition.
As for the reason they wish to inquire about these stages, they first express gratitude for the instruction, saying: "As for those such as ourselves, we are ignorant and dull-witted.
That we do not understand the principle of right concentration is our ignorance; that we have not severed the delusions from time immemorial is our dullness. And...

How much more so for those who are addicted to the pleasures of sensory objects and attached to the habitual tendencies of names and words; they may delight in extensive learning, yet it merely serves to increase their erudition.
Consequently, they have not been able to transcend or distance themselves from all outflows (*āsrava*) pertaining to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Now, having received the compassionate instruction of the Buddha, I have finally attained the primary and auxiliary practices for cultivating the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Therefore, if...
If my body were like my mind, there would be nothing that did not bring me joy. Truly, today I have obtained the most magnificent abundance and benefit.
Thus, World-Honored One, if one practices according to these primary and auxiliary methods of cultivation, one will certainly be able to realize the fruit.
Being identical with all Buddhas and abiding within samādhi, there should be no difference. I venture to ask the World-Honored One:
from the initial stage until the final limit, prior to ultimate nirvāṇa, how is it that the very first arousal of the mind is called the stage of "dry wisdom"?
Regarding the forty-four minds, by what means does this gradual progression occur?
"Next, is it possible to attain the designation of 'one who has accomplished practice'? From this point forward, where must one go before it can be called 'entering the ten stages' (*daśabhūmi*)?
How does one cultivate [the path] so as to be named a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*)?
Having spoken these words, he gazed fixedly at the Buddha with wide-open eyes, looking up in hope for guidance. Indeed, these four questions—[from the *Nirvāṇa*...]"
"Pan" (pari) refers to the final, perfectly consummate fruit. "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-vijñāna) refers to the initial cause of awakening. Between these two lie the forty-four minds:
namely, the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, as well as the four stages of application—Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Worldly First Dharma.
By gradually progressing through these forty-four minds, one reaches the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).

This marks the initial attainment of the designation "seeing the Way" (*darśanamārga*). From the stage of "leaving defilement" (*vimalā*) onward, it is called the practice within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
When the Way is perfected and virtues are complete, one is equal to a Buddha; this is termed "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*).

All stages above these belong to the position of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If one reaches *nirvāṇa*, it is termed "Wondrous Enlightenment" (*pratyakṣabodhi*), which belongs to the realization of the fruit (*phala*).

This constitutes the stages of the path. Herein, the beginning and end of both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are comprehensively integrated, resulting in fifty-five stages that constitute the sublime path of practice.
However, this is not like the provisional, minor practices of ordinary cultivation; rather, it is established within the true principle of illusory perfuming (*māyopama-vāsanā*).
It is established from the perspective of the primordial absence of stages for cultivation, yet it is nonetheless established through the process of cultivation.
Regarding the stages and positions: they are like gaining entry through a gate into a house; one must recognize the varying depths of the main hall and inner chambers.
For *nirvāṇa* is like the inner sanctum of one's own home, the various *bhūmis* are the varying depths of that inner sanctum, and spiritual cultivation is the movement of the master within it.
△ II. The Tathāgata’s Commendation and Instruction (II) 1. Commendation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: [up to] “With palms joined and hearts opened, they silently received the instruction.”
This praise is granted for the sake of discourse. Indeed, the Buddha deeply commends those who are ready to receive the teaching;

it is not for the sake of a single person or a single lifetime, but is intended universally for the great assembly present here, as well as for those of the future, all of whom cultivate the Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama* and seek the Mahāyāna Dharma—from ordinary beings at the outset, proceeding through the three gradual stages, until finally reaching the ocean of Great Nirvāṇa of Wondrous Enlightenment.
Regarding all the stages experienced therein, I pray that you may first provide a prophetic indication of the fifty-five positions on the path of correct practice for supreme enlightenment,
so that those currently or in the future practicing right concentration may enter by the most direct course,
without falling into side-branches and without any further detours. Thus he requested.
This may be called "good and yet good. "To carve" (kū) means to pare away.

It is like what the *I Ching* refers to as "carving wood to make a boat," which involves stripping away its solid core to leave the interior hollow. In all cases, when a disciple receives the Dharma from a teacher...
If one wishes to draw water from a jar, one must first empty its interior; only then can anything be obtained.
△ Second, the opening instruction (in two parts): First, a general indication of the source of the true and the deluded.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that from 'the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous' up to 'the two designations of the twofold transformation of the basis' refers to the Great Nirvāṇa.
This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is the source of both the true and the delusive. As for its essence, it is beyond names and transcends all marks."
Fundamentally, there is not a single thing. If one speaks of its function, it manifests according to karma, resulting in a thousand differences.

Because it can follow those two conditions of defilement and purity, there arise the names and characteristics of delusion and enlightenment, and of sentient beings and Buddhas. My meaning is this, Ānanda:
you should know that the "wondrous nature" is precisely the wondrous *tathatā*-nature, the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is perfectly luminous.
This is precisely the functioning of the Tathāgatagarbha, the perfectly luminous and wondrous mind.

Taken together, the phrase "the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous" refers to the complete essence and great functioning of the Tathāgatagarbha. Indeed, this nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is pure and fundamental;
it is free from all names such as "sentient being" or "Buddha," and from all appearances of "delusion" or "enlightenment. Because it is, from the very beginning...

In ultimate purity, there is not a single thing; even the single word "Buddha" cannot be found, let alone the existence of the worlds of the supported and the supporting, or sentient beings with their thoughts and perceptions.

Nevertheless, the reason why the names of "sentient being" and "Buddha," and the appearances of "delusion" and "awakening," arise is truly because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains immutable in its essence, yet its function is able to accord with conditions.
Following along with defiled and pure karma, there arise the names and characteristics of birth and buddhahood, delusion and awakening.

Because of that initial single thought, non-awakening arises from the True [Suchness] to produce delusion, thereby forming ignorance (*avidyā*). Consequently, the world and sentient beings suddenly come into being.
Since they arise through delusion due to ignorance, then because of this deluded arising, there is also deluded cessation. What...
Because that which arises and that which ceases are both termed delusions, there are thus two kinds of inversion, extending even to the twelve classes of beings;
this establishes the names and characteristics of the world of sentient beings based on defiled conditions.
Since that which can extinguish delusion is termed "True," there are therefore three stages of gradual progression and fifty-five positions of true cultivation.
Regarding the path: this establishes the names and characteristics of bodhi and nirvāṇa based on the pure object-condition (*viśuddha-pratyaya*).

Thus we know that although it is commonly said that the Tathāgata has attained supreme right wisdom and realized great nirvāṇa, this is nothing other than the transformation of afflictions into bodhi and the transformation of birth-and-death into nirvāṇa.
This sufficiently demonstrates the identity of afflictions, birth-and-death, and bodhi.
Nirvana and samsara are both the Buddha of birth; through delusion and awakening, they depend upon one another in turn.
They are merely two designations and possess no substantial reality. One must know that the twelve classes of beings below do not transcend arising and ceasing.
"Name" refers to delusion. The fifty-five stages do not transcend the extinction of delusion; "name" here refers to truth. These are the two phrases.

△ Second, specifically demonstrating the principles of delusion and awakening (in two parts): First, showing that deluding the truth and pursuing delusion constitutes the various classes of sentient beings;
second, generally clarifying the two inversions.
"Ānanda, you now wish to cultivate the true *samādhi*... this is the Tathāgata’s true *samādhi*.
This passage clarifies that one must recognize two kinds of causes for delusion. The meaning is:
Ānanda, if you now wish to reach the fifty-five stages and require the true cultivation of the *Śūraṅgama-rāja* illusion-like *samādhi*, [you must first understand these causes]."
Those who would go to the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa should first recognize the two causes for the arising of the two kinds of inversion—
namely, that of sentient beings and that of the world— and clearly and fully awaken to them without any doubt.

Only then may one advance in cultivation. If one can indeed attain this state where inverted emotions and calculations do not arise falsely, this is the true samādhi of the "single-gate transcendence" of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
This is what is meant by the statement: "The nature of madness ceases of itself; when it ceases, that is bodhi.
As for "true," it means that cultivation arises entirely from the nature, and cultivation is entirely within the nature; therefore, it is so called.

This is indeed so. "Directly proceeding" means going straight ahead. It refers to the state where, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the ultimate realization, one maintains a direct mind and right mindfulness throughout the interval, forever free from any form of deviousness. Question: This was previously mentioned within the chapter on Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
If it is said that there are three continuities (*saṃtati*), why is it that only two inversions (*viparyāsa*) are mentioned here? The answer is:

by citing the inversions of sentient beings, the continuity of karma and its fruit is thereby subsumed. Because the former Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra sought the source from which birth arises, the Buddha told him this.

Third, the continuity of karmic cause and effect serves as the cause for non-interruption. Here, however, because the practitioners seek the stage of cultivation and abandonment (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*), the Buddha spoke only of the two inversions and did not clarify karmic cause and effect;
he merely demonstrated the principle of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

This is the Tathāgata’s true responsiveness to people, revealing the subtlety of teaching the Dharma according to specific circumstances. How could this be something that those who "fix the peg" (i.e., dogmatists) could understand?

How true it is! Thus, regarding these two causes for universal illumination: when one's nature is inverted, one transforms Bodhi into afflictions, thereby becoming the nature of the twelve classes of beings;
when one's nature is not inverted, one transforms birth-and-death into Nirvana, thereby traversing the fifty-five stages up to the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
One can thus know that the single word "cause" [is of such profound significance].
This is the very source of the defilement and purification of both the holy and the ordinary.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the two inversions (2-1). First, explaining the inversion of sentient beings:
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of sentient beings? ... [omitted] ... for this reason there is the inversion of sentient beings.
This explains the perversion of sentient beings. The phrase "How so? is a term of inquiry.
The meaning is that Ānanda, all [this] arises because the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure luminosity—does not maintain its own nature but manifests in accordance with karma.
Therefore, within this luminous nature, the entire body and great function follow defiled or pure conditions to manifest as the ten realms. Because it follows purity...
Through perfuming, one attains the stages of sagehood; through perfuming that follows defilement, one becomes a being of the [deluded] categories.

That which can be true and can be false is because within the essence of the luminous nature, the ten realms are perfectly complete. However, due to a single thought-moment, a deluded "capable of luminosity" is established, thereby becoming deluded luminosity.
Consequently, because of this deluded luminosity, a deluded nature is subsequently aroused, forming the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*). Because of this...
This delusive nature further gives rise to delusive seeing, which constitutes the "evolving aspect.

Thus, from within the essence of True Suchness—which is ultimately devoid of the marks of birth-and-death and nirvana—there subsequently arises, through delusion, the appearance of the mark of sentient beings.

There is the delusive appearance of the characteristics of worlds; this is what is meant by "manifesting appearances. All arise from a single moment of deluded movement within the luminous essence of nature, whereby delusive clarity emerges.
Due to delusive clarity, delusive karma is formed; due to delusive karma, there is the process of transformation and manifestation;
and due to transformation and manifestation, there are worlds and sentient beings. This refers to that which blazes forth within the state where neither identity nor difference exists.
This refers to the "formation of diversity. However, these three subtle states all arise from the fundamental absence of intrinsic substance;
they exist solely through the false delusion of a single thought-moment of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, the ignorance that is capable of producing them and the world and sentient beings that are produced by it have no prior cause, nor do they have a cause for their arising, nor do they have a place of abiding. For their...
They abide by depending upon it, like flowers in the sky or dreams during sleep; when interrogated, they have no root at all, and when sought, they have no basis at all.

Thus, one returns to this very basis of non-abiding: from within a world where there are originally no sentient beings, and through ignorance, the delusive and false construction of worlds and sentient beings occurs—namely, arising from that which is ultimately non-existent.
This refers to the establishment of ultimate existence. Thus, one should know that the world of sentient beings does not transcend the single mind;
it is established entirely through ignorance (*avidyā*). Because ignorance and [afflictions of] views and thoughts arise in mutual dependence, there is the delusion of sentient beings.
Because ignorance and the faculties and objects interact, there is the delusion of the world. All these faults arise from being deluded regarding this.
The essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) is primordially perfect and luminous. From this, beginningless ignorance and delusion arise, establishing the two kinds of inversion:
sentient beings and the world. Consequently, this mind is entirely composed of delusion.
However, these two kinds of inverted, false natures arise from ignorance and are themselves also delusory; they have no substantial reality and are not [ultimately real].
There is that which depends and that upon which it depends. Since ignorance is fundamentally empty, there is nothing that depends;
how much less so can the world and sentient beings established by means of ignorance be considered the basis? How could they possibly exist in reality?
Thus, one may see that while the True is unchanging, the delusive is fundamentally empty. Since the delusive is fundamentally empty, there is nothing to be extinguished. As for the True, since it...

Once transformed, there is nothing further to restore. Now, if you wish to extinguish ignorance and return to the true nature, you must simply realize that delusion is fundamentally empty and know that truth is fundamentally present.
Then the frantic mind will naturally cease; this cessation is itself Bodhi. Thus, the supremely pure and luminous mind is not obtained from another.
If it were otherwise, and you wished to extinguish delusion by seeking truth outside of this, [you would fail].
This would already constitute a delusion; it would not be the fundamentally existent, unchanging True Suchness, the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity.
For one seeks to forcibly extinguish that which cannot be extinguished, and to restore that which cannot be restored.
Yet, wishing to forcibly restore it is like "riding a donkey while searching for a donkey" or creating trouble where none exists.

Since one does not know that this is not the true [nature], one erroneously clings to it as being true; thus, one rushes outward in pursuit, desiring to forcibly restore it again and again without ceasing.
This is like the tracks of a sacred tortoise: the more one brushes them away, the more they multiply. How could such efforts ever recover what is originally possessed?
As for true nature (*tathatā*): when one merely perceives the world and its sentient beings, with afflictions filling the eye, it appears as a manifest state of unreality.
How, then, can the truly authentic nature of True Suchness (*bhūtatathatā*) be attained?
It is because this mind is fundamentally devoid of the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, yet falsely manifests these four marks; in truth, they do not exist.

Regarding the four inversions of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena: it is the false existence of these four inversions of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—this is what is meant by "completely forming non-characteristics.

Nevertheless, due to these false appearances and false inversions, they circulate and revolve, inciting and giving rise to karma, up to the point of moistening rebirth. This is because the power of ignorance and karma that moistens rebirth is predominant.
As for the statement that "the manifestation of bright forms and the emission of perfuming constitute the formation of karma," this refers to the completion of the perception of clarity and vision.
Because the parents and oneself—these three—possess identical karma, they mutually influence one another; through their sexual union, they act as the catalyst for conception.

Karmic consciousness acts as the condition for sensation, whereby it seizes the two drops of red and white; thus, the marks of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) cease and the marks of the subsequent state arise.
From this point, one enters the womb until emerging from it; hence, sentient beings possess these inverted characteristics.
Question: Since this chapter explains the delusions of sentient beings, why does it contain a discourse on the establishment of the world?
Answer: Sentient beings and the world are fundamentally one mind, inseparable from one another.
This is because sentient beings must dwell within a world, and a world must be established by means of sentient beings. Indeed, the world is like the great earth.

Sentient beings are like grass and trees. To say that "sentient beings" does not preclude including a discussion of the world is like saying "grass and trees" does not preclude including a discussion of the great earth.

Moreover, since the subsequent section on the "inversions of the world" also speaks of transformed sentient beings constituting the twelve categories, one can clearly understand this by observing both passages together across the two chapters.
...Thus. △ Second, explaining the inversion of the world (in three parts): First, a general explanation of the names of the causes.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world"? ...up to... "neither with perception nor without perception."
This is a general explanation of the cause of the world’s inversion. Although this section explains the world, it also encompasses sentient beings;
thus, one knows that the world of sentient beings and the world itself are nothing other than the single deluded mind, fundamentally inseparable from one another.

Here, as in the preceding passage, it should be stated: "Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the nature of the mind is perfectly bright, through this luminosity, [delusion] arises."
"Nature. This nature arises from deluded vision; from ultimate non-existence, it becomes ultimate existence. Only by connecting this with the present text can the meaning be fully penetrated;
it is merely that the translator omitted this point. "How so? and so forth are words of inquiry.
That the world is inverted is due to this capacity for beginningless ignorance (*anādikāla-avidyā*); thus there exists the world and its multitudes.
Thus, sentient beings have the segmentation of the root-body, and the world has the segmentation of spatial directions;
all of these arise from a single thought-moment of ignorance within the mind of True Suchness (tathatā). Because of this segmentation, [sentient beings and the world are differentiated].
Thus, the realms (*dhātu*) are established by this. If one seeks the reason for this, fundamentally there is no cause; that which serves as the cause for their arising likewise has no abiding.
That which serves as the place where they abide is entirely due to the constant flux of every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*), wherein each new moment fails to remain.
Therefore, there are the past, present, and future. Because of this non-abiding, the worlds (*loka*) are thereby formed. Thus, of itself—
In terms of time, there are three periods; in terms of realms, there are four directions.
By applying the three to the four and the four to the three, these three and four harmonize and interpenetrate one another, revolving until they all form the number twelve.
Therefore, the transformation of sentient beings also corresponds to this number, resulting in twelve categories. Thus, as for the world...
All realms arise because, within the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*), a single thought of non-awakening causes the deluded movement of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Thus, externally, a wind-circle is induced, and sound consequently manifests. Because of space, there arises vibration; because of the establishment of firm clarity, there is obstruction, and thus form is established.
When the metal and the wind rub against each other, fire-light arises; from fire comes vapor, and from vapor comes fragrance. From the luster of the jewels, moisture is produced.
The fire’s light rises and steams upward, from which flowing water arises. Because this water possesses both cold and warmth, it constitutes the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).

Touch is divided into the rough and the smooth; when it encounters the tongue, taste (*rasa*) arises. When these five objects of the senses harmonize with the mind, they are termed "phenomena" (*dharma*).

These six sensory objects defile and attach themselves to the six sense organs, interweaving and entangling one another so that they are difficult to distinguish; thus, they are called the "six confusions. By means of these...
This deluded thought gives rise to various afflictions and attachments, and through its creative activity, it constitutes the nature of karma.
Karma inevitably entails retribution, which is differentiated according to twelve categories. It is by means of these that one revolves in saṃsāra.

Therefore, among the six sense organs and six sense objects of the world, if even a single phenomenon is mentioned, all twelve phenomena manifest simultaneously. Thus, it is said that the sense organs and sense objects exhaustively encompass the ten [realms].

The second transformation refers to the manifestation of sentient beings through transformation, forming the twelve categories of birth. This constitutes one complete cycle of circulation and recurrence.
Because the faculties and objects give rise to karma, and since these twelve factors are fully present, beings ride upon this karmic power to revolve through the various realms of existence;
thus, the inverted characteristics of the world also constitute the twelve categories of birth. For this reason:
Thus there are those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation, up to those who are neither with perception nor without perception.
Yet when one mentions any single category of these beings, all twelve categories appear simultaneously; they exhaust the twelve transformations.
Because it revolves, circulates, and recurs in a single cycle, it constitutes a world of inversion.
Nevertheless, when the twelve classes of living beings are condensed, they do not transcend the two dharmas of emotion (*qing*) and thought (*xiang*). Each gives rise to four modes of manifestation.

From emotion arise: first, those with form; second, those without form; third, those who are neither with nor without form; and fourth, those who are neither without nor with form. From thought arise: [the same four].
First, those with perception; second, those without perception; third, those with neither perception nor non-perception; and fourth, those with neither perception nor non-perception.

Womb-birth arises from emotion; egg-birth arises solely from perception. The union of emotion and perception constitutes moisture-birth; the separation of emotion and perception constitutes transformation-birth. When emotion is predominant and perception is absent, it is apparitional birth.
Thus, emptiness, scattering, and sinking, as well as the perception of the "above" and the "non-perception," result in being like earth, wood, metal, or stone.
Although these two belong to the insentient and the non-perceiving, they both arise from the transformations of the marks of consciousness and views.

Therefore, the inversion of sentient beings is their individual karma (*pratyeka-karma*), because it is seen by them alone; the inversion of the world is the collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*) of sentient beings.

Because they are shared by all, if one shatters the attachment to the self (*ātman-grāha*), one realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), eliminates birth-and-death through segmentation (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), and attains *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;

thus, the delusions of sentient beings begin to cease. If one shatters the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), one realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), eliminates birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*), and attains *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; thus, the delusions of the world begin to become empty. Therefore, it is said: "Delusion..."
That which does not arise through inversion is precisely what is called the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the characteristics of the fruit (twelve): first, the characteristic of birth from an egg.
"Ānanda, because of the world’s delusory saṃsāra... [down to] fish, birds, turtles, and snakes, their kinds fill it.

This section below provides a detailed explanation of the twelve types of birth. All arise from the Tathāgatagarbha mind; through non-awakening, delusions are stirred up, and one undergoes retribution according to karma.
This clarifies the principle of "responding to conditions according to the mind. Here, we shall first explain the first type: birth from an egg.

This describes the characteristics of how delusions arise, karma is created, and retribution is received. However, while the subsequent sections all clarify the twelve classes of beings, why does each begin by stating, "due to the world as cause"?
This is because the preceding text, within the section on the inversion of the world, states:
"The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and harmonize, transforming sentient beings into the twelve classes. This refers precisely to that.
All of these arise from the world's perversion, serving to clarify that birth exists only through delusion. Therefore it is said:
"Ānanda, because the worlds interact with one another, there are those who are born from a protective shell; this is called birth from an egg.
For an egg is produced solely through thought (*saṃjñā*); delusion is itself thought. From such false conceptualization, the cycle continues without ceasing.

Therefore, it is called saṃsāra. This occurs because True Suchness (tathatā) does not maintain its own nature; being without [intrinsic reality], it falsely moves. Is this not the delusion of inversion?
From this false movement, the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) is induced, and thus sound and breath arise.
Consequently, deluded thought immediately forms a combination with sound and breath. As for those born from eggs, they mostly rely on sound and breath for their union.
Therefore, it is said that "qi is formed. This is as in the saying: "The male bird cries from upwind; the female cries from downwind. Through emptiness, qi is generated;
through qi, form is constituted," and so forth. However, this is a delusion born of empty conceptualization.
Since one follows the karma of sound and qi, and as for the nature of qi itself, if it is too rigid, it will be excessively flighty and restless; yet if it is too supple...
This refers to the fault of being mired in dull stagnation. From this, there arise eighty-four thousand [afflictions], which correspond to the number of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Thus, excessive rigidity leads to the deluded thoughts of flightiness and cleverness;
excessive softness leads to the deluded thoughts of being mired in dull stagnation. The above clarifies the arising of delusions and the creation of karma; as for what follows:

This clearly explains the characteristics of receiving retribution; that is to say, such a cause brings about such a retribution. "Existence" (bhava) refers to the fact that cause and effect do not perish.
*Kalala* is translated as "coagulated mucus," which is the initial stage of entering the womb, the state where the embryo and the eggshell have not yet separated.
From this point, one emerges from the shell and undergoes a continuous flow of transmigrations through all lands; therefore—
The birds fly high, while the other three sink low; this is the retribution induced by the karma of these two perceptions of flying and sinking. Question:
It is commonly said that there are four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation. Why is it that here the egg-born is placed before the womb-born? Answer:

This section clarifies how the nature of the storehouse (ālayavijñāna) follows conditions; it specifically concerns the process of arising from the fundamental source down to its final manifestations.
This is indeed how the sequence of arising ought to be. To take ignorance as the "egg" refers to the deluded, hidden mind;

it is the state where the characteristics of the perceived and the perceiver have not yet been distinguished during the time of non-awakening. This is precisely what worldly people refer to when they speak of the "egg of chaos" (*hundun*).
It is so. Therefore, the *Yao Shi* (Medicine Master) says: "That which breaks the eggshell of ignorance is this. We know for certain that this is the primary fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Since it is the root, it is explained first. Relying upon this ignorance, one is able to initiate karma;

as it resides within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), there is the category of being contained within a womb. Moistened by the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is the category of being joined with warmth and moisture.

Arising from non-existence to existence, they thus constitute the category of transformational manifestations (*nirmāṇa*). Because these characteristics arise in a sequence based on their original presence, eighty-four thousand are specifically cited at the outset.
This is discussed in terms of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), categorized as sharp or dull, arranged in three tiers, based on the full complement of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since the single dharma-entity of ignorance inherently possesses both sharp and dull aspects, there are ten; and each of these ten possesses all others in mutual combination.
Thus, one hundred is formed. Within these one hundred, each further possesses ten; thus, one thousand is formed.

When this is assigned to the seven branches of body and speech, with each branch having one thousand, seven thousand are formed. Furthermore, when divided according to the three periods of time, twenty-one thousand are formed.
Based on the four types of mental states equally distributed among the three poisons, each possesses twenty-one thousand. Combined together, they total...
This totals eighty-four thousand. Subsequent categories explained in the text should all be understood according to this principle.
△ Second, the characteristics of birth from wombs:
From the world’s causes of defiled saṃsāra (up to) humans, beasts, dragons, and immortals, their various types fill the realm.
This clarifies the characteristics of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, and receiving retribution within the womb-born mode of birth.
Because the worlds interact with one another due to causal conditions, there are those who emerge from a concealed state; this is called "womb-birth" (*jarāyu-ja*).

Essentially, the womb exists because of emotional attachment (*sneha*), and defilement is precisely that attachment. Thus, through these emotional objects, beings greedily desire and affectionately love one another, revolving without ceasing; hence it is called "saṃsāra."

This is precisely the activation of karma and the moistening of rebirth. When the habitual tendencies of delusion increase and become predominant, one falsely perceives agreeable objects where none exist, thereby giving rise to thoughts of aversion and attachment.
Is this not the delusion of inverted craving? Due to this aversion and attachment, defilement ensues.
Thus, through the harmonious conjunction of the three conditions—the parents and oneself—birth occurs spontaneously; hence, the womb.
Those who are born mostly create karma through sensual desire, engaging with semen and blood; therefore, it is called "nourishing" (*tzu*).
This refers to the union of yin and yang, such as the meeting of the vital essences between men and women.

However, these defiled thoughts of sensual desire follow the karma of sexual intercourse, and as for the nature of emotion itself, there is that which is correct and that which is incorrect, just as in the case of a husband... [text continues].
The way of a wife is the rectitude of emotion. Should she happen to contravene principle or harm the social order, then her emotion is not rectitudinous.
From this, there arise transverse and vertical disordered thoughts; thus, when emotion is not rectitudinous, it results in transgressive conduct and disordered thoughts.

As for those whose emotions are correct, they instead form upright and orderly thoughts. One must understand that while horizontal and upright are indeed different, disordered thought is one and the same.
Thus, the distinction between humans and animals lies solely in whether their emotions are correct or incorrect.
The above concerns delusions and karma; the following clarifies the reception of retribution. That is to say, by means of such karma, such retributive existence is induced;
this refers to the fact that the causes and effects of both deviant and correct states do not perish.

"Aṭaḥpuṭa" (遏蒲曇) is translated as "blister," which refers to the stage where the embryo or egg gradually begins to differentiate. Following this, one emerges from the womb and grows to maturity, propagating the species and continuing the lineage.
It continues to grow and spreads throughout all lands. Thus, those who are humans or immortals walk upright with their heads held high, because they have attained the correctness of their emotions.
Those who are animals or dragons travel on their bellies with their hands placed before their feet, because they have attained the incorrectness of their emotions.
This is brought about by the karma of these two types of emotion—either deviant or correct.
Because there are two kinds of retribution— horizontal and vertical— beings of this class exist everywhere,
pervading the lands and filling the worlds.
△ Third, the characteristics of moisture-born beings.
"From the cause of the world’s attachment to saṃsāra... down to being filled with crawling insects and wriggling creatures.
This clarifies the characteristics of moisture-born beings as they give rise to delusion, create karma, and undergo retribution.
Because the worlds interact with one another, there arise those produced by moist warmth; these are called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*). Indeed, moisture is felt through conjunction and attachment.
To "attach" means to conjoin. Due to such deluded thoughts and attachments, one pursues the times and aligns with others, revolving without ceasing; hence it is called *saṃsāra*.

This is precisely because one fails to realize that the pure *tathāgatagarbha* mind is fundamentally free from defiled attachment, yet instead seeks out fragrance and pursues stench, esteeming heat and despising cold—is this not the delusion of inverted pursuit and alignment? Because of this, the fluctuations of warmth and chill easily...
Aspiration means that attachment remains in the mind; for this reason, upon smelling a fragrance, one proceeds toward it. Encountering moisture, it immediately coalesces.

Thus, through the harmonious conjunction of these three conditions—moisture, warmth, and the self—one eventually achieves rebirth. Therefore, those born from moisture mostly rely on vital energy (*yángqì*) and delight in intense heat;
hence they are called "warm. This is precisely like those among humanity who rush toward the heat and seek to attach themselves to those warming their hands.
However, this inclination toward sycophancy follows the karma of burning heat; thus, its destination is likewise without fixed standard.
It is characterized by violating the heart and betraying trust, seeking only personal gain. One moment it becomes clouds with the flip of a hand, and the next it becomes rain with the turn of a palm.
Therefore, it is said that there are "reversing and overturning disordered thoughts. The above explains delusions and karma; the following clarifies the reception of retribution.
This refers to the principle that such karma produces such retribution, which is to say that cause and effect do not perish. *Bhṛśa* (蔽尸) refers to soft flesh.
This is precisely the initial sign of moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*). Since they do not enter a womb, they lack the first two stages [of birth].

Following this, they were transmitted and circulated in succession throughout all lands; some became crawling creatures, others became wriggling insects, such as the *kṣudraka* (vinegar flies) and *makṣikā* (gnats).
Thus, these kinds of beings exist everywhere, filling the lands and crowding them to the point of obstruction.

In this world, those who throughout their lives do not follow the path of righteousness, but instead chase after the times and cling to power, using flattery and sycophancy while utterly lacking any upright spirit, shall receive the retribution of being dull and devoid of consciousness; how can one not lament this?
△ Fourth, the characteristics of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).
From "due to the world’s cycle of change and transmigration" (extending to) "their species fill the air as they molt and fly.
This clarifies the characteristics of how those born by transformation give rise to delusion, create karma, and undergo retribution. Due to the mutual [interactions] of the world...
Through these negotiations, there are those who are born with altered countenances and changed forms; this is called "transformational birth" (*upapāduka*).

Transformation implies detachment from response, and change implies detachment from the former state. Thus, through further alteration and modification, one detaches from this and entrusts oneself to that, circulating without end.
Therefore, it is called "saṃsāra. This is precisely because one fails to realize the unchanging *tathatā* (true suchness), and instead undergoes constant change according to time;
being provisional, it is easily renewed. Is this not the delusion of inverted and false appearances? Because of these changes, there is no stability;

because of this lack of constancy in one's conduct, one delights in the new and loathes the old, shifting one's affections as one encounters various objects. Thus, one relies on this and entrusts oneself to that.

It changes according to whatever it encounters; therefore, it is called "contact" (*sparśa*). This is like those among humans who possess no integrity or faithfulness, shifting their allegiance from Qin in the morning to Chu in the evening—those who are fair-faced in front but treacherous behind, feigning intimacy with others.

Yet this delusion of feigned intimacy follows the karma of constant change, and the substance upon which it relies is likewise not permanent. It is what is called acting according to one's whims and desires, driven by attachment.
This forgets that; at the time of its formation, it relies on conditions and takes advantage of circumstances. Being weary of the old, it delights in the new;

hence it is said that "new and old thoughts are in turmoil. The above clarifies delusion and karma; the following clarifies the retribution received—meaning that by means of such karma, one invites such retribution, which is what is meant by the phrase "cause and effect do not perish.
*Kalala* refers to hard flesh, for as soon as it sloughs off, it becomes solid substance; therefore, there is no softness.
Regarding the term "xiàng" (form/characteristic): from this point downward, all that is called *kalala* serves as a general designation for these various classes.
If one refers to the fifth stage, *praśākhā*, as the "position of form," then it refers specifically to particular physical appearances and is not a general designation.
Following this, [the tradition] was transmitted and circulated through successive generations throughout various lands; some even shed their skins and fly, such as silkworms shedding their cocoons.

They become moths; insects transform into butterflies. Or they shed their skins and fly away as wanderers, such as the quail turning into a frog or the blue fly changing into a maggot—all belong to this category of transformation.
Therefore, these kinds of beings exist everywhere, pervading the lands and filling the world, because throughout their lives they have possessed no integrity whatsoever.
Failing to follow correct principle, one encounters objects and undergoes transformation; as the mind shifts in pursuit of external things, this retribution is experienced.

Herein, the explanation follows the text to clarify only the transformation that occurs within the substance itself. If one wishes to encompass the subject more broadly, one should clarify the four types of transformation.

What is called "sentient beings transforming sentient beings," "insentient things transforming insentient things," "insentient things transforming sentient beings," "sentient beings transforming insentient things," as well as transformation from non-existence to sudden existence— such as the various heavens, hells, and so forth—
exhausts the categories of birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
△ Five: The Characteristics of Those with Form.
From the world of causes, due to the cycle of obstruction and hindrance... (up to) "the spirits of good and ill fortune fill the realm.
This clarifies the characteristics of one class of beings with form who give rise to delusion, create karma, and undergo retribution. Due to the world of causes...
As they interact with one another, there arise those who seek out the characteristics of luminous form; these are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*).
For "form" (*rūpa*) refers to material substance, whose nature is not pervasive or penetrating.

Because it is an obstructive thing that blocks and retains, one forcibly seeks clarity and seeks penetration within it without ceasing; thus it is called "saṃsāra. This is precisely the failure to awaken to oneself.
The nature is the perfectly pervasive Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*), yet one instead follows after sensory objects and pursues forms.

Because of this lingering obstruction, one then seeks light through the sun, moon, water, and fire; yet one fails to realize that seeking obstruction through obstruction is surely a delusion of inverted self-obscuration.
Since it is concealed and withheld, it cannot be manifested; because it is obstructed, it is difficult to penetrate. For this reason, one desires—
Seeking a manifest brilliance, they then give rise to thoughts of union with a place of penetrating clarity;

they may swallow its essence or inhale its flowers, their intent being to invoke a response and, by borrowing that refined vitality, achieve their own manifestation. Therefore, this is called "attachment.
All of these are practices of those who have failed to attain the correct path. Since they possess the karma of seeking illumination, [they... themselves...
One obtains the retribution of radiance; thus, the perception of refined, brilliant light is formed. All of these are delusions and karma.
Below, one then undergoes retribution—what is called "such karma inviting such retribution," which means that cause and effect do not perish.
As for "form-phenomena" (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), it means that those false thoughts have already become refined and radiant, consisting solely of form-phenomena.
From that time onward, these influences were transmitted and circulated, pervading all lands as either auspicious or calamitous. Sometimes they became the refined essence of the sun and moon;

sometimes they manifested as the brilliant radiance of the stars and constellations. Thus, among the sun, moon, and stars, those that are favorable are called "auspicious" (*xiū*), while those that are unfavorable are called "calamitous" (*jiù*).
Consequently, from the nine celestial bodies above, including water and fire, down to the rhinoceros horn and the glowworm, [all are encompassed].
All such phenomena as these are subsumed within this category. Therefore, there is nowhere this category does not exist; it pervades the lands and fills the worlds.
△ Sixth: Formless Appearances.
"From the cause of the world’s dissolution and the cycle of rebirth... (until)... emptiness disperses and sinks, filling all such categories.
This clarifies the characteristics of how one class of formless beings gives rise to delusion, creates karma, and undergoes retribution.
Because worlds interact with one another through causes, there is aversion and pursuit; as emptiness extinguishes and form returns, that which arises from nothingness is called [the formless realm].
"Formless. Now, "formless" means the absence of form and color. Because the physical body acts as an obstruction, it is the root of great affliction.

One desires to dissolve this obstruction and enter into non-existence, dispersing form back into emptiness. Pushing this to its extreme, one exhausts emptiness until nothing remains, yet returns to a state of ceaseless grinding away;
hence, it is called saṃsāra. This is precisely because one does not realize that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature [of emptiness is true form].

Space is the true form, yet one instead turns outward to erode and grind away obstructions, analyzing form to return to space in a quest for non-obstruction—is this not the height of perverse delusion?
For by doing so, one seeks to eliminate hindrances while wishing to attain non-obstruction.
Therefore, within this stubborn emptiness, they subsequently give rise to the notion of conjunction. Thereupon, they congeal darkness into form; thus it is named "darkness.
This results in the perception of gloom, obscurity, and seclusion. All of these are instances of taking the tainted heavens (*sāsrava-dhātu*) as an understanding of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having engaged in the karma of seeking that which is unobstructed, they naturally receive the retribution of stubborn emptiness; hence, they become shrouded in gloom and darkness.
These thoughts of hidden seclusion are all delusions and karma; they lead downward to receive retribution.
This is what is meant by "such karma inducing such retribution," which signifies that cause and effect do not perish.

As for the "formless" (ārūpya), it refers to those who possess only the mind of perception but lack physical form. Following this, [the teaching] was transmitted and spread successively throughout all lands.

"To be empty, to be dispersed; to be dissolved, to be submerged. This corresponds to the four *ākāśas* (voids). "Empty" refers to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), for by escaping the cage of form, one becomes empty.

"Dispersed" refers to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); because concentration arises by taking consciousness as its object, one cannot yet avoid dispersion. "Dissolved" refers to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), for it dissolves the preceding consciousness.
"Submerged" refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), for it reaches the very bottom of emptiness. Thus, it is said: "until [one reaches] Śūnyatā."
Deities, whirlwinds, and *pūtana* ghosts are all subsumed within this category; thus, there is no place where they do not exist, pervading the lands and filling the world. Question:

Since it is said that they are "formless" (*arūpin*), why are they called *kalala*? Answer: This refers to the "form that is the fruit of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) to designate this category;
it does not refer to the "form that is the fruit of karma" (*karma-phala-rūpa*). Therefore, this *kalala* is precisely the fruit of meditative concentration.
Although form lacks the characteristic of karma, it does not preclude its being designated based on the fruits of meditative concentration.
△ Seventh, the characteristic of having perception:
From the world’s delusive cycles of rebirth (until) gods, ghosts, and spirits fill every corner.
This clarifies the characteristics of a class of beings with perception who give rise to delusions, create karma, and undergo retribution.

Because the worlds interact with one another due to causes, there arises falsehood; losing touch with reality and relying perversely on reflected images, those who take birth are called "those with perception.
This means they lack substantial form and possess only the mind of perception. Indeed, those with perception rely solely upon—
Reflections are dim and indistinct, vague and unreal; they possess no substantial trace whatsoever. Thus, delusion does not cease and mental projections continue without end;
hence, it is called *saṃsāra*. This is precisely because one fails to realize the true nature of one's own essence, instead erroneously grasping at external reflections.
Is this not the inverted delusion of mistaking one’s head for its reflection? For this reason...

It is false and illusory; one grasps at shadows while losing the true reality. For this reason, from dawn until dusk, one gathers the mind and suspends it in a single place, blending it with illusory images.

Through affectionate longing, yearning, and spontaneous recollection, one becomes habituated to such patterns over time. Thus, sentient beings with conceptual thought rely largely upon these mental conceptions before they take on a physical form;
hence they are called "those who remember. This is like humans in the world who flatter gods and curry favor with ghosts.
Their aspirations are directed toward those who possess spiritual penetration. Yet, this delusion of recollective thought follows the karmic traces of the formless and the intangible;

consequently, within the hidden and profound depths, they falsely forge the causes for rebirth. Thus it is said: "In secret they bind up disordered thoughts," referring to the aforementioned delusions and karma.
The following clarifies the receiving of retribution. That is to say, by means of such karma, one invites such retribution;
this refers to the principle that cause and effect do not perish. Regarding those with "perception" (*saṃjñā*): they possess no manifest form, but have only latent, interconnected perceptions.
From this point onward, [this state] is transmitted and circulated, spreading throughout all lands; thus, there are those who exist within the realm of heaven and earth.

Those who become gods or ghosts exist within the myriad things; those who become spirits or numina, though their forms and colors cannot be seen, nevertheless possess a hidden and spiritual penetration that is not non-existent.
These are all retributions obtained by mistaking the shadow for the reality and neglecting the true essence. Thus, such beings exist everywhere, filling the lands and saturating the world.
"Entanglement" (*wangxiang*) is what is meant by "vague semblance"; it is a shadow within a shadow, a manifestation of unreality.
This is because ghosts, spirits, and numinous beings possess only images and shadows, having no actual substance whatsoever. This is what Zhuangzi meant when he said that water has "entanglement."
△ Eighth, the characteristic of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñin*).
From the cause of the world’s dullness and cyclic existence... (down to) "earth, wood, stone, and metal, their kinds filling [the realm].
This clarifies the characteristic of how one class of non-conceptual beings gives rise to delusion, creates karma, and undergoes retribution. Due to the cause of the world...
Through their mutual interaction, there arises a class of beings who do not clearly understand the principles of reality (*tattva*), being stubbornly devoid of knowledge and consciousness;
these are called "Non-conceptualizers" (*asaṃjñin*). This means that while they possess physical form (*rūpa*), they lack ideation (*saṃjñā*).

Indeed, these Non-conceptualizers rely solely upon ignorance, stupidity, and dullness; they reject intelligence and sever all knowledge and consciousness. Thus, through such persistent delusion, they— [do not...]

It rests; hence it is called "saṃsāra. This is precisely because one fails to realize that the *dharmakāya* of one's own nature is eternally abiding and indestructible, yet instead erroneously calculates that insentient things possess life and that metals and stones are solid and durable. Is this not the delusion of ignorance and perversion?
Due to this stubborn ignorance, one consequently gives rise to conceptualizations, all of which are like ashes congealing; for this reason, one takes the lack of consciousness as [the ultimate].
True cultivation takes the stubborn and ignorant as the ultimate Way. Within a state of non-cognition, one falsely gives rise to thoughts of conjunction;

by indulging in spontaneous deep reflection, one immediately becomes a member of the stubborn class. Thus, those sentient beings without thought mostly extinguish their conceptual minds before entering a womb;
for this reason, they are called "stubborn. This is like people in the human world who, not understanding the holy teachings, mistakenly claim that there is no mind. This is so.

This belongs to the category of the Path. However, these delusions of the ignorant and dull, having followed the karma of stubborn folly, result in a mind like withered wood and thoughts like cold ashes;
hence it is said, "withered and parched chaotic thoughts. The above explains delusions and karma; the following clarifies the reception of retribution.
This is what is meant by the saying that such karma invites such retribution, wherein cause and effect do not perish.
Furthermore, as for "non-conceptualization" (wúxiǎng), it refers merely to a state of dull, inert appearance, devoid of any thought or conception.
From that time onward, this tradition was transmitted and circulated, spreading throughout all lands;

thus there arose the anomalies of wood and earth, and the specters of metal and stone, such as the *huábǎo* pillar becoming a spirit and the "Yellow Head" (*huángtóu*) turning into stone. Consequently, these possess only a dull, inert appearance, yet...
These are beings without thought or mind; they are all dull and devoid of consciousness. They are the retribution experienced by those who take the absence of mind to be the Way.
Therefore, these types of beings exist everywhere, filling the lands and crowding the world.
One must know that these are merely states where the deluded mind has coagulated and is temporarily suppressed from functioning, like withered plants whose root-nature remains intact.
It still remains. Therefore, although their spirits may transform into wood or stone, it is because of stubborn thoughts that they become stubborn objects;

once the power of those stubborn thoughts is exhausted, they continue to transmigrate. Just as grass and trees sprout forth when they encounter spring, the same principle applies to those in the Heaven of No-Thought whose retributions come to an end and enter the cycle of rebirth.
△ Ninth, the non-material forms.

From "Due to the world of causes revolving through mutual dependence" (up to) "using shrimp as eyes, their kind fills the [oceans]," this clarifies the characteristics of a class of non-material beings who give rise to delusion, create karma, and undergo retribution. Due to the world...

The elements interact with one another; thus, they depend upon and require each other. Relying on material objects as guides and depending on impurity to form a body, that which undergoes birth is called "non-existent form" (*arūpin*).
This means that it is fundamentally non-existent in terms of form and color, yet it borrows material objects to constitute form and color.
Indeed, that which is "non-existent form" exists solely through the mutual relationship between this and that, being a provisional construct that lacks independent utility.
Things depend on one another to fulfill their functions, borrowing from each other without ceasing; hence it is called "saṃsāra.

This is precisely because one fails to understand that the treasury of the true Dharma eye is the purity of one's own nature, yet instead borrows the light of external objects to form one's own views.
Is this not the delusion of falsehood and inversion? Because of this falsehood, one becomes confused about oneself.
It is inherently true. To falsely rely on the floating and deceptive is to give rise to deluded notions of conjunction within the realm of mutual dependence.
To indulge in this spontaneously results in the category of defilement; therefore, it is not a form of matter. There is a class of sentient beings who do not take birth from their own kind.
It relies extensively upon impure substances before entrusting itself to a womb; therefore, it is called "defilement" (rajas).

This is like those in the human world who borrow the tiger's prestige or rely on shifting power structures to sustain themselves and nourish their lives—a class of beings whose tracks are marked by such [base] conduct. Such, however, is the delusion of mutual dependence.
Having followed the karma of false defilement, they thus borrow from one another and rely upon each other; hence it is called "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*).
Relying on this basis, they give rise to chaotic thoughts; with these superior delusions and karmas as the cause, they receive retribution here below. That is to say, by means of such karma.
They receive such retribution; this refers to the principle that cause and effect do not perish.
They are not "possessors of form" because they do not receive bodies from their own kind, but rather they are originally formless entities that acquire form through association with other things.
From that point onward, as they were transmitted and circulated throughout various lands, there came to be creatures such as the *siphonophore* (water-mother), which uses shrimp as its eyes.

Such are their kinds. The *shuǐmǔ* (water-jelly), commonly called the *xiāzhái* (sea-slug), possesses consciousness but lacks an abdomen; it forms its body from water froth, and its shape resembles a sheep’s stomach.
However, it has no eyes of its own and uses the shrimp as its eyes; thus, the *shuǐmǔ* moves by means of the shrimp, while the shrimp obtains food by relying on the *shuǐmǔ*.
This is like the *qióngxū* carrying the *huì*, or the *huíqiáo* worms dwelling within humans—all belong to this same category.
All of these rely on sound and depend upon power, mutually supporting one another;
thus, the retribution they evoke is such that there is nowhere this kind does not exist, filling the lands and saturating the world—how can it be described in words?
△ Ten: The Non-existence of Formless Phenomena.
Due to the world’s phenomena inducing one another in saṃsāra... (up to) ...curses and incantations arise, and their species fill the realm.
This clarifies that it is not the case that there is no single class of beings who give rise to delusion, create karma, and undergo retribution. Due to the world...
The realms interact with one another; thus, there is a type [of being] that, due to being summoned by sound, triggers the consciousness and is born.
This is called "not non-material" (fei wuse), meaning that while it was originally not material, it manifests spiritual anomalies through such summoning and is therefore not non-material.
Indeed, this "not non-material" exists solely by relying on the heterodox incantations and arts of worldly people.
They call out to one another and summon one another, pulling and leading each other into birth, revolving without end; thus it is called "saṃsāra.
This is precisely because they do not realize that their own nature is fundamentally without movement, yet instead follow the pull of heterodox arts.

Is this not the delusion of the mind-nature losing its true essence and falling into perversion? Because of this pulling and leading, they confuse their own nature, and at the place of calling and summoning, they falsely—
The thought of harmonious union arises; they submit to being dispatched and obey commands. Thus, they become a class of mantras. Therefore, they are not formless.
A certain class of sentient beings mostly arise after relying upon heterodox arts and heterodox mantras; hence, they are called "mantras" (*dhāraṇī*).
This is like people in the human world who, failing to understand correct principles, entice and seduce one another, leading each other along with heterodox speech.
False speech is that which is formed through the habitual cultivation of its nature. Yet these delusions, being mutually induced, follow from the karma of invocation;
thus, they enter into mutual covenants with one another. Some say they arrive according to their tokens, while others say they come upon hearing the mantra.
Hence it is called "harmonious union" (*saṃnipāta*). From this point, once the mantra is perfected, there arise ghosts who can be summoned and spirits who can be invoked.
The spirit thereby succeeds in forming this chaotic thought. The above clarifies the delusions and karma; the following clarifies the retribution received.
That is to say, by means of such karma, one invites such retribution; this is what is meant by the phrase "cause and effect do not perish.
It is not that they are formless, for although they were originally without form, because they are produced through incantations, they are not formless. From this point on...

Thereafter, as it was transmitted and circulated throughout various lands, there arose those who manifested supernatural powers through incantations and curses, being called "gods" or "immortals," and those who brought about calamities through malevolent prayers, being regarded as "monsters" or "calamities.

These are all malevolent entities that listen to human commands and employ them to report on good or bad fortune, such as the *zhāngguǐ* (cinnabar ghosts) and *jīxiān* (spirit-medium immortals). This arises from...
Those who frequently summon [spirits] with raucous cries and improper enticements receive a retribution for what they have obtained.
As for true deities, if one lacks utmost sincerity and supreme virtue, one cannot move them; how could they heed the summons of a deluded person?
Therefore, such types exist everywhere, pervading the lands and filling the world, beyond counting and impossible to exhaust.
The Way! △ Eleven:
The Characteristic of Non-Existence of Perception.
From the world’s conjunction with delusion leading to saṃsāra... (up to) ...different substances forming one another, their kinds filling all space.
This clarifies the characteristics of those who give rise to delusions, create karma, and undergo retribution while not possessing the perception of existence.

Because the worlds interact with one another due to causes, there is a class of beings who falsely claim others' property as their own; these are called "those with the perception of non-existence" (*asat-saṃjñin*).
This means they do not possess the perception of existence found in those who transmit life-force within the womb or egg, as is the case with the perception of existence. Indeed, it is not...
Regarding those who possess perception: they merely rely on two entities that together are deluded, jointly forming a false construct. They grasp at one another in a continuous cycle without ceasing;

hence it is called "saṃsāra. This is precisely because these men of wisdom and women of concentration fail to realize their own inherent nature—which is fundamentally without interruption—and instead adopt the children of others to claim as their own. Is this not a mutual deception that constitutes a perversion?
Is this not a delusion? Because of such falsehoods, they take what is different to be the same and turn what belongs to another into their own.

Amidst things of different categories, they falsely conceive of a harmonious union; through spontaneous delusion, they cause the different to become identical with themselves. Therefore, this is not "having thought.
A class of sentient beings mostly relies upon things of different categories before they can be born; thus it is called "different. This is like the human realm.
They turn their backs on their kin and turn toward righteousness; they abandon their own roots to follow others. They erroneously continue a separate lineage and falsely inherit the clan of another.
Thus, these delusions of conflation arise because they follow the karma of a different species;

consequently, they deceive one another, like those who originally have no son yet falsely claim to have one, or those who are not the father yet falsely claim to be him. For this reason, both self and other...
There is nothing else so difficult to distinguish as identity and difference; this is solely because they arise from mutual confusion and reciprocal entanglement within delusion.
Thus it is said: "reciprocal entanglement and disordered thoughts. Having explained the afflictions and karma above, the following clarifies the retribution received, namely: by means of such karma.
This invites such retribution; it is what is meant by saying that cause and effect do not perish.
"Not having the mark of thought, yet forming a thought" means that the subject and object are of different natures and originally lack the mark of thought;

yet, desiring to produce this mark, one merely joins with delusion and eventually brings about that very thought. From that time forward, it has been transmitted and circulated, spreading throughout all lands like a parasitic wasp.
This refers to what is commonly called the *xiēwēng* (wasp), also known as the *guǒluó*. It takes the offspring of the *mínglíng* (cicada larvae) of a different substance to form its own offspring.
As the *Fǎyán* says: "The offspring of the *mínglíng*, having been killed, encounter the *guǒluó*, which chants over them, saying:
'Be like me! Be like me! After a long time, they resemble it. How fast! All such claims are merely attempts to deceive by taking the property of others.
This is the retribution for claiming [beings] as one's own. Therefore, these kinds of beings exist everywhere;
they fill the lands and pervade the world—how could they have any limit?
△ Twelfth: The Characteristic of Not Being Without Perception.

This refers to how, due to the world’s causes of enmity and cyclic existence (extending to) all being devoured by one another until their kind fills the realm, this clarifies the characteristic of a class of beings who are not without perception, yet give rise to delusions, create karma, and undergo retribution. Due to the causes of the world...

The realms interact with one another; thus, there is a class of beings who harbor resentment and plot revenge, whose mode of existence is strange and perverse, called "not non-percipient" (*na-asaṃjñin*).

This refers to sentient beings such as fathers and sons who are "not non-percipient. Indeed, those who are "not non-percipient" rely solely upon unresolved hatred and resentment, plotting harm against one another in a continuous succession that knows no end;
therefore, it is called *saṃsāra*. This is precisely [the case of]— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available content.)

Having realized the equality of enemies and kin, to instead rely upon one's own closest relatives—father and son—and incite the most grievous act of killing against them—is this not the ultimate marvel, the most preposterous, and a perverse delusion? It is because of this that thoughts of harboring resentment and plotting harm arise.

Consequently, they engage in union that destroys moral boundaries and disrupts the constant order of nature; within these strange and anomalous circumstances, they rely upon them to lodge their *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, it is not the case that there are no sentient beings of this class who, for the most part, rely on strange thoughts to find a physical basis for rebirth, and are thus called "anomalous.
This is like those in the world who commit patricide, matricide, or acts that wound Heaven and violate principle. Yet, once this delusion of resentment and malice has arisen—
Following the karma of killing, they consequently give rise to the thought that even parents—those of one's own kin—may be eaten; hence it is said, "the thought of eating one's parents.

The above explains the delusions and karma; the following clarifies the retribution received, meaning that such karma invites such retribution, which is what is meant by the phrase "cause and effect do not perish.
It is not that there is no perception or characteristic; rather, "no-perception" refers to this state.
This means that at the very beginning of their conception, there is mutual affection and longing; therefore, it is said they are not without the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Later, when they have fully developed and the parents encounter them as food, they no longer have such affection and longing; therefore, they are said to be without perception (*asaṃjñā*).

From that point onward, they propagate and multiply, spreading throughout various lands, such as the species of earth-owls who attach themselves to clods of earth to produce offspring, as well as the *pāriplava* (the "broken-mirror" insect) and others.
Taking the fruit of a poisonous tree and embracing it as their own child, once that child has grown large, both its parents will meet their end by being devoured by it.
According to the *Shiji*, "Basic Record of Emperor Wu of the Xia Dynasty," in the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one uses a *xiao* and a *pojing*. Meng Kang’s commentary states:
"The *xiao* is the name of a bird that eats its mother; the *pojing* is the name of a beast that eats its father. The Yellow Emperor wished to exterminate these [monsters]."
It is said that these [beasts] were used for all the hundred sacrifices. The *Shuyiji* states: "The form of the *pojing* is like that of a tiger or leopard, yet small;

when it is first born, it returns to eat its mother. The current mention of a "bird" (*niao*) is likely an error by the translator, or perhaps the character "bird" should have been "equal" (*deng*), which was mistakenly transcribed as such. These [interpretations] are all unfaithful to the original.
As for the retribution experienced by those who are unfilial, rebellious, and evil, such as these exist everywhere, filling the lands and crowding the world; how can one even bear to speak of it?
△ Third, the general conclusion of their names:
"These are called the twelve kinds of sentient beings.

This is the general conclusion regarding the twelve categories. Indeed, at the beginning of the text concerning the categories of birth, it always says "the world," and this is the point of conclusion.
As for the term "sentient beings" (zhòngshēng), it is so called because of the mutual interpenetration of their characteristics; therefore, it is named the world (*lokadhātu*).

If discussed in terms of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), they are called sentient beings. Thus, the preceding text states: "The three periods of time and the four directions harmoniously interpenetrate and transform sentient beings, forming the twelve categories. This refers to that very point.

△ Second, showing that returning from delusion to the truth immediately constitutes the stage of sainthood (III). First, a general clarification of the three stages of gradual progression (I).
1. Concluding the preceding and opening the subsequent.
Ānanda, it is thus that within each and every class of sentient beings, after washing and purifying their vessels, one stores the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).

This correctly concludes the preceding section on how True Suchness (*tathatā*), being perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), gives rise to defiled functions, thereby forming the twelve classes of inverted beings.
Furthermore, it opens the subsequent section on how True Suchness, perfuming ignorance, gives rise to pure functions.
The twelve categories, both singular and plural, refer to the twelve stages of the sages. The meaning is this:

Ānanda, you should know that among all these aforementioned classes of sentient beings, within each and every class, there are likewise found, respectively, the twelve types of inverted and confused thoughts.
Take, for example, the single category of those born from the womb; even considering only those among human beings, there may be—
Is one who acts in rebellion against the natural order, murdering father and harming mother, not a case of the perverted delusion of a *chao* or a *jing* bird?
Or is there one who abandons their own ancestral sacrifices to inherit the rites of another lineage; is this not a case of the perverted delusion and deception of a *puluo* (wasp)?
Or is there one who writes talismans, fashions secret gestures, and employs incantations to summon spirits; is this not...?
