For the principle of *nirvāṇa* realized in the First Stage is like empty space; it arises loftily through the transformation of the Ten Transferences.

It transforms the mountain of birth-and-death. Now, because there is a slight obstruction below, it is called "having a basis" (*yī*); because the body enters into empty space, it is called "without a basis" (*fēiyī*).
This clarifies that within the stage of the Ten Transferences (*shíxiàng*), one portion of *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death) is about to be relinquished but not yet relinquished;
and within the first stage (*dì*), one portion of *tathatā-nirvāṇa* (true-suchness nirvana) is about to be realized but not yet realized. However, as for the effort...
Having reached this point, one has attained the ultimate; therefore, it is called the "Stage of the Summit" (*mūrdhan-bhūmi*).

First, one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind; thus, the Buddha and the mind are identical. Next, one takes one's own mind as that which the Buddha treads upon; thus, the mind and the Buddha are identical.
Because the mind and the Buddha are both identical, one has successfully grasped the ultimate principle of the Middle Way, and it is clearly illuminated within the breast.
There is no further doubt; yet, one knows it only within oneself and finds it difficult to disclose. This is like a person who practices forbearance:
if they wish to harbor it in their heart, they find it impossible to harbor; if they wish to express it with their mouth, it cannot be conveyed through speech.
Therefore, regarding the matter for which one endures, neither harboring nor expressing it is called the "ground of forbearance" (kṣānti-bhūmi).

Furthermore, regarding the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma): in the initial stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind, yet still retains the numerical quantity of one's own mind.
In the second stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan), although one takes what the Buddha has traversed as one's own mind, one still retains the numerical quantity of the Buddha’s traversal.
These two stages both involve the numerical quantification of the Middle Way within delusion. In the third stage of "Patience" (kṣānti), [the duality of] mind and Buddha...
The same applies here. There still remain two identical quantities, which are precisely the quantities of awakening within the Middle Way.
Now, there is not only no delusion, but also no awakening. Below, there is no self-mind; above, there is no Buddha-awakening.

Thus, when both mind and Buddha are found to have nothing by which they can be designated, then quantity and number are both dissolved, and delusion and awakening are both extinguished. Therefore, one transcends loftily.
It transcends the world; therefore, it is called the "Supreme Worldly Stage" (laukikāgra-dharma).

Although this cultivation of its nature is extremely perfect and sudden—such that in a single thought-moment it can encompass the cause and penetrate to the fruit—within that single thought-moment, it naturally possesses these four stages of preparatory application (prayoga).
Although these four practices are described as sequential, their actual practice occurs simultaneously; for this reason, it is termed "sublime" (miao).
[This concludes] the section on the perfection [of the stages]. △ Seventh, the Attainment of the Grounds:
"Ānanda, this good man, regarding Great Bodhi... [up to] ...the ocean of Nirvāṇa, is named the Dharma-Cloud Ground (Dharmameghā-bhūmi)."
This clarifies the sequence for ascending the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the meaning of "stage" (*bhūmi*), there are generally two types:
first, "fulfillment" (*pariniṣpanna*), which means being able to accomplish all phenomena, taking solidity as its essence;
second, "generation" (*utpāda*), which means being able to develop all things, taking growth as its cause. This is because... [text fragment ends]

Faith alone cannot establish virtue; it is through abiding that virtue can be perfected. Yet, although the roots of virtue may be established, if they are not put into practice, one cannot benefit oneself or others.
Once both forms of benefit are complete, if there is no dedication of merit, [the roots will not lead to enlightenment].

Furthermore, one cannot properly harmonize with the Middle Way. Once the Middle Way is attained, even if it is not through deliberate application (*prayoga*), one must sweep away the two extremes and brush aside the Middle Way itself, so that conceptual measures (*citta-pramāṇa*) may vanish in secret and the mind and the Buddha may mutually dissolve.

Otherwise, it will be difficult to ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, Wénlǐng said: "The preceding dharmas accumulate until they reach the state of perfected reality; all Buddha-dharmas depend [upon this]."

Because this [wisdom] arises, it is called the "ground" (*bhūmi*). Ānanda, once these sons of good family have successfully accomplished this from the stage of application (*prayoga*) up to the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), they suddenly and completely shatter a portion of the ignorance that obstructs the first ground.
Therefore, within the stage of the fruit of sainthood, one thoroughly attains penetration into the nature of Great Bodhi.
Because the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) that awakens to bodhi is entirely identical to that of a Buddha, he is named "Tathāgata Whose Awakening Penetrates" (*Juetong*).

Because the nirvāṇa of cessation-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) which is awakened to is entirely identical to that of a Buddha, he is named "Exhausting the Realm of the Buddha. This is as it should be attained by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"I have already attained that which all sentient beings inherently possess; I have already realized it. Therefore, I rejoice for myself and rejoice for others;
this is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi). Although those in the preceding stages had severed ignorance,"
This is still merely being "wise and holy" (賢聖), not yet being "holy and wise" (聖賢); this is termed the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Now, having ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*), one truly perceives the noble path (*āryamārga*) and directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness), becoming of one essence with the Buddhas; this is termed the nature of being born together (*sahaja-tva*). Nevertheless, it is called "sameness" in contrast to "difference."

Difference is indeed a defilement, and identity is likewise a defilement. Now, both identity and difference are simultaneously extinguished; therefore, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Being able to leave behind defilement constitutes purity, and when purity reaches its ultimate limit, radiant light breaks forth;

therefore, it is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). When radiant light reaches its ultimate limit, the wisdom of awakening becomes perfect and complete; therefore, it is called...

This is the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). Possessing blazing wisdom, one is able to thoroughly illuminate the inconceivable principle and also able to thoroughly illuminate inconceivable phenomena.
By illuminating the principle and further illuminating phenomena, one accomplishes the supramundane wisdom of the single nature of all things, which cannot be reached by others.
Because one illuminates phenomena and further illuminates the principle, [one attains] the mundane [wisdom] of the diverse natures of all things.

The wisdom of the intermediate stages cannot reach it; "to reach" means to arrive at. Because the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*) can only eliminate the distinction between identity and difference, whereas this ground [the Ground Difficult to Conquer] synthesizes and harmonizes identity and difference, it cannot be attained by either mundane or supramundane wisdom.

Therefore, it is named the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*). Whether as phenomena or as principle, their very substance is entirely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally pure.
It is pure; now it has been illuminated and made manifest, and is therefore called the Ground of Manifestation (Abhimukhī-bhūmi).
Having realized that all phenomena are entirely *tathatā* (thusness), one has thoroughly investigated the profound and reached the furthest limits of the very essence of *tathatā*;

therefore, it is called the Ground of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi). Since the practice is now deep and far-reaching, it vertically exhausts and horizontally pervades all things as the single nature of *tathatā*.
The pure and luminous mind cannot be shaken by anything other than arising and ceasing; therefore, it is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Having realized the entire, immovable substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one necessarily manifests the great function of True Suchness responding to conditions; therefore, it is called the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
This means that this Bodhisattva skillfully employs both provisional and ultimate wisdom.

Indeed, from the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and transference up to this point, although all have arisen from the nature through cultivation and do not constitute the same as the phenomenal aspect, nevertheless, the merit of cultivation arising in accordance with the nature is certainly not absent.
Upon reaching this stage, the merit of practicing in accordance with the nature is also completed.
Since all the merits of great wisdom and great compassion have already been perfected, this ninth stage is also designated as the "stage of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Upon reaching the tenth stage, however, one engages in effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), spontaneously benefiting sentient beings.
Therefore, the cloud-like manifestation of the sublime body universally covers the ocean of the originally existent *nirvāṇa*-nature through a heart of compassion;
thus, the path of the two benefits becomes fully perfected from this point onward. Furthermore, the preaching of the Dharma is like rain and the manifestation of the body is like clouds;
for this reason, the tenth stage is named the "Dharma Cloud" (*dharmameghā*) stage.
△ Eighth, the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksaṃbodhi*).
As the Tathāgata flows against the current, so does this Bodhisattva proceed with the flow until the boundary of enlightenment is reached and the two intersect; this is called Equal Enlightenment.

This clarifies the stage of Equal Enlightenment, wherein initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇabodha*) is equalized with wondrous awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). For the Tathāgata has already realized the Dharma.
The true nature flows onward; yet from within this dharma-nature, it flows back upstream and emerges, flowing together with the nine realms to deliver sentient beings.
Thus, the bodhisattva flows against the current of birth and death and follows the current of dharma-nature, proceeding until they reach the source of the dharma-flow of original enlightenment.
On one hand, they return to the essence from its function; on the other hand, they give rise to function from the essence. It is like two people: one [flows downstream], and one [flows upstream].
On one side they enter, and on the other side they exit; it is appropriate at this juncture that their entry and exit intersect.
With one foot inside and one foot outside, although their entry and exit differ, the phenomena are equal; therefore, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi).
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom responds downward to the resonance of capacities and is called "quiescent illumination" (寂照).

The Bodhisattva’s ultimate wisdom accords upward with the awakened mind and is called "illuminating quiescence" (照寂). From the perspective of a Buddha, even this is still termed "Bodhisattva"; yet from the perspective of one's own arising observation...

Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, they are therefore called "Equal-Enlightened Bodhisattvas" (Samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva). Nevertheless, from the stage of self-confidence up to this point, all belong to the category of partial enlightenment (anupūrva-bodhi).
△ Ninth, the Stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miao-jue-wei).
"Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one finally exhausts the Subtle Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.

This clarifies the ultimate stage of Subtle Enlightenment. The meaning is that Ānanda, from the initial mind of Dry Wisdom until the final mind of Equal Enlightenment, has followed the sequence of the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and direction, as well as the four levels of application and the ten grounds, from beginning to end."

It is merely for this reason. Through these [stages], within the heart of the Perfectly Awakened Vajra, one is finally able to attain the "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) mind—that initial resolve first generated to sever birth-and-death and eternally destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*). However, that which was first called "mind" (*citta*) is subsequently termed "ground" (*bhūmi*);
this means that when this mind reaches this point, it finally finds firm footing on the ground. This is what is meant by the saying: "When the head is upright, the tail follows."
It is correct that the initial arousal of the mind and its ultimate fulfillment are not distinct.

Regarding the names "Dry Wisdom" (*kandhī*) at the beginning and end of this sutra, the various commentaries of antiquity have offered conflicting interpretations, entirely lacking a definitive standard; consequently, later students likewise have no reliable basis for understanding.
This is truly because they have not fully grasped the precise intent of this fundamental scripture. For it is because all sentient beings of the nine realms are driven by the three types of karma...
There are five abodes of affliction (*kleśa*) that give rise to two kinds of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The five abodes are:

the abode of desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), the abode of form-attachment (*rūparāga*), the abode of formless-attachment (*ārūpyarāga*), the abode of all views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the abode of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The three floods (*ogha*) are: the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*), the flood of existence (*bhavaugha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyaugha*). The first four abodes constitute the floods of desire and existence.
The flow [of outflows] (*āsrava*) gives rise to birth-and-death with distinct segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*). This has already been severed at the first stage of faith (*prathama-śraddhā*).

The subsequent ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is the flow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), which gives rise to birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*); this is severed only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood.

Judging by this, the aforementioned stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is the initial mind of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), wherein one first severs the two flows of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and emerges from birth-and-death with distinct segments.
For this reason, the Sūtra says: "When the thirst of desire is dried up and the faculties no longer encounter their objects, the remaining physical form before one no longer continues to be reborn.
It is like settling turbid water: the sand and silt sink of their own accord, and clear water appears; this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
From the stage of the first faith (*prathama-śraddhā*) onward, one resolves to sever ignorance (*avidyā*), yet its accumulated habits are deep."

Thick. Thus, passing through fifty-four stages until reaching the final mind of the Vajra-like Samādhi of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), the nascent aspect of ignorance (*avidyā*) is just about to dry up.

It is only within this state of meditative concentration that this ignorance is permanently severed. Therefore, it is said: "This awakening first attains the stage of Initial Dry Wisdom (*ādi-śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) within the Vajra-like Mind.
This signifies that the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) are completely exhausted and the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*) are forever extinguished.

One thus enters wondrous enlightenment and emerges from the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). This is what is meant by "removing the mud to reveal pure water," which is termed the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
This is the essential purport of this sutra. Although the stages of sagehood inherently possess a beginning and an end, the mind of the Vajra-samādhi is fundamentally without priority or sequence;
therefore, from beginning to end, there is only the single mind of Vajra-dry-wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).
By relying upon such a vajra-wisdom mind that is without difference from beginning to end, one is able to establish the single sevenfold, the repeated fivefold, and the twelvefold noble stages.

Only then can one completely sever the ignorance of the characteristic of arising and enter the stage of subtle, pure, ultimate awakening, thereby accomplishing the path to the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. As for the "single sevenfold":

This means that "single" refers to one name and one stage, such as the seven stages of Dry Wisdom (*kandha*), Warmth (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Worldly First Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), along with the Wonderful (*sūkṣma*).
"Double" refers to one name and multiple stages, such as the five stages of Faith (*śraddhā*), Abiding (*sthiti*), Practice (*caryā*), Direction (*abhimukha*), and Ground (*bhūmi*).
Because there are seven layers of the single and five layers of the double, it is called "layer upon layer. Furthermore, the single...
There is a sequence of the single and the double, mutually interlaced: first, the single stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā*); next, the double stages of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Direction;
then again, the single stage of Preparatory Application (*prayoga*); followed by the double stages of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*);
and finally, the single stages of Equality and Subtlety (*samatā* and *sūkṣmatā*). This process of being single and then double, double and then single, is also called...
Layer upon layer.
△ Third, the conclusion of the stages of practice and realization:
These various stages are all [attained] by means of the vajra... (up to) ...if one views them otherwise, it is called a false view.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s comprehensive conclusion regarding the stages previously discussed;
all are established according to the beginning and end of the Great Samādhi of Subtle and Secret Contemplation. The intent is this:

as for what has been briefly discussed above, from the three gradual steps up to the Equal and Wondrous [Enlightenment], there are the stages traversed in between—the faith, abiding, practice, and direction, the four aids, and the ten sages. These are the seeds...
The cultivation of all the stages is established by means of the adamantine treasury-mind (*vajragarbha-citta*) and the observation of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).

This is because "adamantine observation" denotes the simultaneous elevation of both essence and function: the "adamantine" is the essence of the treasury-nature (*garbhadhātu-svabhāva*), while "observation" is the function of the treasury-nature.
This is precisely the total essence and great function of the treasury-nature, which is also the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
This is the essence and function [of all practice]. It is this which serves as the general dharma-gate for śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.

Thus, the Tathāgata universally extols the concentration of intrinsic nature (xingding) for the sake of the assembly of practitioners suited to the teaching, manifesting from beginning to end the wondrous wisdom of the Vajra, thereby clarifying that the universal cultivation of all stages does not transcend this. As it says:

Regarding "illusion": for instance, within the three gradual stages, when one observes that the faculties and their objects are like illusions, one enters the stage of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-jñāna), which is a semblance of awakening.
If one can further observe that this dry wisdom itself is like an illusion, one then enters the stage of the ten faiths, which is a partial awakening.
Continuing thus, one contemplates that even perfect enlightenment is like an illusion, and thereby enters into the ultimate awakening of wondrous enlightenment.
This refers to the method of gradual, deep entry into the pure cultivation and realization that is entirely free from obstruction.

This is precisely what Avalokiteśvara himself described as the Vajra Samādhi of hearing-permeation and hearing-cultivation which is like an illusion; it is also what Mañjuśrī referred to when he proclaimed: [The passage continues with the proclamation: "All dharmas are like illusions... and so forth.
This is the True Samādhi of the Vajra King, the Inconceivable Mother of Buddhas who is like an illusion.
Therefore, the Tathāgata summarizes it by saying: "These various stages are all attained through the Vajra-contemplation Samādhi that perceives all things as illusions.
Thus, one knows that throughout the fifty-five positions from beginning to end, there is only the single Vajragarbha-mind, which is the contemplation of all things as being like an illusion.
It is simply a matter of observation. As for the ten similes: first, a magical illusion; second, a mirage; third, the moon reflected in water; fourth, flowers in the sky; fifth, an echo;
sixth, a city of the gandharvas; seventh, a dream; eighth, a shadow; ninth, a reflection; and tenth, a transformation.
Regarding what is called "profound," it does not merely involve observing that conditioned phenomena are like illusions and transformations; it is the observation of the unconditioned as well.
The Dharma is also like an illusion or a magical transformation; for this reason, it is called "profound. An ancient master said:

"To cultivate the myriad practices of empty flowers, to sit peacefully in the water-moon meditation hall, to subdue the mirror-image celestial Māras, and to realize the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream"—this refers to that very state.
Śamatha is translated as "stopping" (zhi), and vipaśyanā is translated as "contemplation" (guan). Now, regarding this dhyāna of stopping and contemplation:

All of these belong to the specific manifestations of the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi. If one examines them according to their essential substance, they are collectively nothing other than the single Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

This serves as a general conclusion to what the Buddha previously permitted, stating that there is a samādhi named "The Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King," which is fully endowed with the myriad practices and through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend [all states] in a single gate.
This is the public case concerning the Path of Sublime Adornment. Therefore, the conclusion below states:
"Ānanda, all these various stages mentioned above are none other than the cultivation of the three gradual sequences through both primary and auxiliary practices.

For this reason, from beginning to end, one is well able to accomplish these ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, [ten transferences, ten grounds, five ranks, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment]."
This refers to the fifty-five stages, consisting of the four stages of application (*prayoga*) plus the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the "True Path to Bodhi": this is the actual path by which the aforementioned stages return to the household of Bodhi.

Since the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) belongs to a semblance of awakening and true faith has not yet arisen—being like one who has not yet set out on the journey—it is not considered a path and is therefore excluded. This is excellent.
Awakening belongs to ultimate awakening; it is like having already reached one's destination—it is no longer the path, and thus it too is excluded.

Therefore, one should know that the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi are precisely the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.
For this reason, if a practitioner can truly rely upon this mind of non-arising and non-extinction, they will subsequently achieve perfection.
The cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition begins from the ear-faculty and culminates in entry into the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.

Throughout the fifty-five stages in between, one cultivates without cultivation and yet does not hinder "illusory" cultivation; one realizes without realization and yet does not hinder "illusory" realization.
Within this process of profound penetration that is fundamentally devoid of gradual progression, one may nonetheless establish illusory gradations.
Delve deeply into this. Only those who can truly investigate in such a manner are said to possess right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

If it is otherwise—if one speculates at will, recklessly assigning names and categories, claiming that there is no arising or ceasing in the mind, or that there are no stages of cultivation—and if one takes the six consciousnesses to be the true cause and regards mere ritualistic practice as true cultivation—all such views belong to others.
Contemplation that is not the Great Samādhi of one’s own mind is called "erroneous contemplation" (邪觀); it is not the Great Samādhi of intrinsic nature (自性).

Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) states: "If one says that Buddhahood is achieved by transcending this, then it is the same as the teaching of Māra. This is precisely what is meant here.
The above concludes the first section, which discusses the beginning and end of the Great Samādhi in its correct sense.
△ II. General Presentation of the Titles of the Entire Scripture (3). 1. Mañjuśrī’s Request for the Title and Its Upholding.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince... [down to] ...how shall I and all sentient beings uphold it?

This is the request for the name of the sutra, intended for its reverent reception and upholding. For when the text reaches this point, faith is born, understanding is opened, practice is initiated, and realization is attained;
thus, the entire cycle is brought to completion. This dharma-gate shall now flow down to future generations.
A title for this sutra must be established; even if it were not yet known, how could one invoke its essence to revere, uphold, and disseminate it?
Now, the fact that this single sutra begins with Ānanda initiating [the discourse] signifies that no one but expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) can inaugurate the teaching.
That it concludes with Mañjuśrī requesting the title signifies that nothing but ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) is capable of entering into the principle. This reveals—
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi has been transmitted to this degenerate age; yet, beginners must employ both provisional and ultimate wisdom, as well as primary and auxiliary practices, in their cultivation.
Only then can they achieve the perfect integration of phenomena and principle, and fully realize the meaning of the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of inherent purity and luminosity.
△ Second, the Tathāgata reveals the name and instructs on its upholding.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This sūtra is named [The Śūraṅgama Samādhi], the Foremost of Myriad Practices; you should uphold it."
This establishes the title of the sutra as the method for reverently upholding it. Regarding the five names that follow, the first is explained first:
"The Great Uṣṇīṣa" refers to what was spoken by the Tathāgata from his mark of the invisible crown, emitting the light of great wisdom.
*Sitātapatra* means "White Parasol. It is a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, which is originally unstained and universally covers all things.

It is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma King, which definitively establishes all sages; therefore, it is named "Jewel Seal" (*ratnamudrā*). Its pure and wondrous essence possesses boundless illumination and function;
therefore, it is named "Ocean Eye" (*sāgaralocana*). These names are established based on its wisdom and principle (*jñāna* and *tattva*). First...
"Second, the causes for rescuing and protecting one's kin" is the general heading. "Delivering and liberating... and so forth is the specific explanation.
Regarding "causes for one's kin": this refers to those who are actual kin, as well as those who are like kin, such as Ānanda’s father and the nun Śīlavatī.
This demonstrates that whether they are kin or [spiritual] causes, there are none whom he does not rescue, protect, and deliver. Having attained the bodhicitta, he gives rise to the Great...
It is the vehicle of the mind. It enters the ocean of universal knowledge and realizes the principle of perfect permanence; this name is established based on its functional efficacy.
Third, as for the "secret cause": the realized beings of the three periods of time enter the secret treasury, all taking the nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*) as their secret cause.
Furthermore, this Great Samādhi encompasses all practices, yet it is not something accessible to those of the provisional or Lesser Vehicles.
It can be known; for this reason, it is called the "Secret Cause. The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have taught this Dharma-gate as the ultimate teaching;

therefore, it is called "Definitive Meaning" (*nītārtha*). This name is established based on both the person and the dharma. Fourth, because it is vast and encompasses the boundless, it is called "Great" (*mahā*);
because the True Dharma maintains itself, it is called "Square" (*catura*); and because it pervades universally in accordance with its essence, it is called "Broad" (*vipula*).

This refers to the meaning of the three great aspects. "Wondrous" means inconceivable. "Lotus" is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb of the Tathāgata), which encompasses all phenomena of cause and effect.
Furthermore, because it can serve as the essence of the great principle and unify all *samādhis*, it is called the "King.
Because it can give birth to all Buddhas, it is called the "Mother. It upholds the good and wards off the evil. In total...
The gathering of meritorious qualities is called *dhāraṇī*. "Mantra" (*zhòu*) signifies "vow. These names are established according to both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions.
Fifth, this sutra flows forth from the *Abhiṣeka* (Consecration) section of India; thus, according to the esoteric terminology, it is named the "Chapter of Consecration Phrases.
For those who can recite and uphold it, the water of the Tathāgata’s wisdom shall be poured upon their crowns and hearts, just as [in the ritual of consecration].
Regarding the reception of office in every buddha-field, the myriad practices of a bodhisattva take the Śūraṅgama as their foundation.
Furthermore, one who cultivates this samādhi possesses all myriad practices within a single mind. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śūraṅga" means that all matters are completed;
"Vigour" (or "Majesty") signifies firmness. Because all matters are definitively settled, one attains ultimate firmness.
This is merely establishing the name based on the teaching and practice. The above establishes the names, answering the first question.
"You should uphold this" answers the second question; its meaning is that you should simply rely on the preceding five categories and contemplate the meaning according to the name.

To practice according to what has been taught and transmit it to future generations so that all beings may attain awakening is precisely what it means to uphold the teachings in accordance with the instructions.
Question: Since this sutra already possesses five titles, for what reason do you select only these nineteen characters? Answer:

This is because the general encompasses the particular, and the concise subsumes the extensive. For example, "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa*) refers to the Great Vaipulya, the Wondrous Lotus King.
The rest is easily understood and therefore not listed separately.
△ Third, Ānanda hears the sutra and attains benefit.
After these words were spoken, immediately Ānanda... [up to] the six grades of subtle afflictions in his cultivation of the mind.
This clarifies that benefit is obtained through hearing the sutra and its title. However, the origins of this attainment of benefit extend very far back.
First, one receives the revelation of the meaning of *paṇḍara*; this refers to the preceding passage where the divine mantra was proclaimed again, describing its efficacy and exhorting its upholding.
Second, it provides a forward-looking exposition of the fifty-five stages of spiritual progress. Third, it includes the hearing of the fundamental sutra itself.
This is a designation. *Dhyāna* (禪那) is translated as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), which is a general term for both stillness and insight.
It is one of the three names for the single essence of the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi. This corresponds to what was previously stated:

"within *śamatha*, employing the pure cultivation and realization of the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas. Because this contemplation (*dhyāna*) is free from stagnation, it is empty; because this stillness is free from... [text truncated]
"Because of distraction, [the mind] becomes turbid. This clarifies that the power of hearing the sutras serves as the support for the characteristics of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Generally, there are eighty-one grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the cultivation of the mind within the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Now, regarding the mention of "six grades," if one follows the perspective of the Hīnayāna, within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are nine grounds (*bhūmi*) across the three realms, each divided into nine grades. However, concerning the four...

Since the fruits are attained through the successive abandonment of each stage, one realizes the second fruit within the body of the first fruit by abandoning the first six grades of the nine grades of afflictions belonging to the first stage of the desire realm;
and within the body of the second fruit, one realizes the third fruit by abandoning the remaining three lower grades.
Within the body of the third fruit, one abandons seventy-two grades of the two upper realms to realize the fruit of Arhatship;
now, realizing the second fruit, one abandons six grades. Because these are afflictions of thought, they are called "subtle defilements.

One must know that from the opening of the assembly until this point, the stages of faith, understanding, practice, and realization have proceeded from cause to fruit, traversing the positions of the sages.
The names, phenomena, principles, essence, and function are all fully and completely provided. At this point, there should be a concluding passage for bowing and withdrawing;
however, none is concluded because the audience has important further requests. Although the times may differ, the intent appears continuous;
thus, the compilers of the sutra have categorized them by meaning to form a single volume. This is why no conclusion is made here. Above.
The formal request and the formal exposition are concluded. What follows is the second assembly, consisting of a renewed request and a renewed exposition.

As for Ānanda’s questions, they concern matters immediately present; the details regarding the time and age differences have already been explained in the "Account of the Transmission of the Teachings" (*Jiaozhi zhong shuo*) and will not be repeated here.
Those who require them should consult that source.
△ II. Double Request and Double Explanation (2) A. The Immediate Audience Re-requests Based on the Present Matter (1) 1. Describing the Benefits and Thanking the Previous [Teaching].
Rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet... until: "his body and mind were refreshed, and he attained great benefit."
This desire to request further instruction will be addressed later; for now, he first expresses gratitude for previous benefits.

"Of great majestic power" means that the Buddha possesses the majesty to subdue and the virtue to sustain others; thus, he is able to reprove and admonish, causing people to look up to him with joy and accept his teachings.
"Compassionate voice without partiality" means that his teaching makes no distinction between kin and stranger, nor does it discriminate among those with the capacity to receive it. Good.

"Opening" refers to skillful exposition. Because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), which are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), are difficult to discern, they are called "subtle.
Because they have co-arisen since beginningless time, they are called "deep-seated delusions. Because the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) are eliminated, one attains "relief.
Because one advances toward the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), it is called "beneficial. All of these express gratitude for the benefits previously obtained.
△ Second, the request following the double doubt (3): First, the doubt as to how the false could exist within the real.
"World-Honored One, if this wondrously bright, truly pure, and sublime mind... is it produced by the deluded habits of sentient beings?"
If this doubt should arise as to how there can be the delusion of the seven destinies when the Buddha-body is already true:
World-Honored One, if the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature) of these sentient beings—its very essence—is fundamentally and spontaneously wondrous and self-luminous, fundamentally real and pure;
that is to say, the subtle and sublime true mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect.

Since this is so, then the four great elements and the five aggregates, the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, even down to empty space, the great earth, grasses, trees, and insects—none are not originally and fundamentally the one true *tathatā* nature.
Thus, this nature is the true body of the Buddhas of the ten directions; it is non-dual and without distinction. Since it is itself the Buddha-body...
It should be true and without falsehood. How then can there be the falsehood of the seven destinies within the essence of the Buddha?

World-Honored One, from what cause do these various paths arise? Do they exist inherently within the essence of True Suchness from the very beginning, or do they arise spontaneously from the false habitual tendencies within the minds of sentient beings?
...is it not so? Question: What difference is there between this doubt and that of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? Answer: The former doubt concerns the fact that the fundamental principle is originally pure;
why, then, do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? This takes the "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*) as its primary focus.

The present doubt concerns the fact that the nature is fundamentally real; why, then, are there further paths such as those of humans and devas? This takes the "retributive body" (*pratigraha-vipāka*) as its primary focus. Thus we know that the former...
Doubt serves to reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); here, doubt serves to clarify the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

It is precisely because one wishes for the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional that one returns to the Middle Way, the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*). There is a commentary which judges that from the point where Mañjuśrī asks about the name [of the sutra], it enters the section on circulation (*parivarta*).
This is likely due to not having fully examined the intent of this sutra; for the Buddha himself opened the assembly and immediately spoke of "two kinds."
There are two fundamental bases: first, the fundamental basis of nirvāṇa; second, the fundamental basis of saṃsāra.

Therefore, from the first fascicle up to this point, although both the true and the deluded have been elucidated in turn, the primary intent lies solely in the fundamentally pure essence that is the fundamental basis of nirvāṇa.
The nature of non-arising and non-extinction serves as the fundamental cause for realizing the fruit of unsurpassed *bodhi*, which is itself neither arising nor extinguishing.
What follows clarifies the root of birth and death: namely, those who take the攀緣心 (*pān-yuán-xīn*, the攀缘心, or "clinging mind") as their own self-nature use arising and extinction as their cause;
therefore, they experience the fruit of arising and extinction within the seven realms of existence. This refers to what was first...

This means that practitioners who are unable to achieve unexcelled Bodhi, and instead become Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths—including various devas, Māras, and their retinues—are the subject of the detailed discussion on the manifestations of Māra that follows.
Thus, it should be understood that the subsequent passages still belong to the orthodox main body of the teaching; they are not [a separate or secondary section].
The Circulation Section (Pravartana-bhāga). Regarding "those on the same path": this means being equal to the path of the sages (ṛṣi-mārga).
△ Second, the doubt concerning whether the hells are common or distinct:
"World-Honored One, as with the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā... (up to)... each gives rise to karma and receives its retribution individually."
This cites a present case to inquire about the retribution of hell. The intent is this:
as in the case of Baolianxiang, who had already upheld the Bodhisattva precepts yet privately engaged in sexual misconduct;

having thus violated the precepts, she furthermore slandered them with false speech, claiming that practicing sexual desire does no harm and is not comparable to killing living beings or stealing and plundering.
"Yet there are those who harbor enmity and suffer the retribution for their sins. This [act of] lust, however, is merely mutual pleasure between two parties;
there is no enmity involved. For this reason, one knows that there is no karmic retribution. Having spoken these words, he first produced fire from his female organ.

Later, his bones and joints will burn with fire, and he shall fall into the Avīci Hell. For private sexual misconduct is the breaking of the precepts (*śīla*), and to say there is no retribution is the breaking of right view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Once both precept and view are broken, one falls directly [into hell]; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, there are two kinds of retribution:

first, retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), meaning the body is consumed by its own flames; second, retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), meaning falling into hell to undergo suffering. As for King Virūḍhaka, who deposed his father and [seized the throne]...
He rose up and executed the Gautama clan to avenge the insult of a single word. This was neither because he had violated any precepts nor because he denied the law of cause and effect;
rather, it was because his hatred had intensified to such an extent that he committed excessive slaughter and consequently fell into hell.
Thus, the *Vaiśālī-pradeśa-sūtra* states: "Formerly, in the kingdom of Kālapura, there were five hundred members of the noble Śākya clan..."
The Elder built a hall for the Buddha and made a vow, saying: "No śramaṇa, brahmin, or even commoner shall ascend this hall before the Buddha.
The Prince of Śrāvastī, Virūḍhaka, having become engaged to the daughter of a brahmin named Bhadra-karman, saw that the hall was lofty and vast, so he stayed upon it.
A man of noble lineage cursed him, saying: "This is the offspring of a slave woman!"
He dared to sit among them, and they drove him out. The Prince spoke with great bitterness, saying, "The Śākyas have insulted me.
When I succeed to the throne, you must inform me. Later, he established himself as king;
when he was informed, he gathered an army to avenge his disgrace and killed more than three hundred million people of the Śākya clan. The Buddha prophesied that seven days hence, he would enter hell.
The king, fearing for his life, boarded a boat and entered the sea waters; naturally, fire emerged and consumed it. The Buddha said:
"In the past, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a pond full of fish. Many people from the city went to the pond to catch fish. In that pond, there were two fish."
One was named *Pūti* (the Putrid) and the other was named *Bahujihva* (Many-Tongued); each harbored a grudge for revenge.
There was a young boy who, seeing those fish leap, struck them on the head with a staff. The fisherman at that time was none other than the Śākya clan; the *Pūti* fish was King Virūḍhaka.
The "Many-Tongued Fish" refers to this very person. "One who delights in suffering" refers to myself when I was a child. Regarding the "proponent of emptiness, Sūrya," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The bhikṣu Sūrya, although he had studied the various sūtras, destroyed the fetters of the desire realm, and attained the four dhyānas."
Not understanding the meaning of even a single verse or a single phrase, he associated with evil friends and consequently lost his meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Thereupon, he gave rise to false views and falsely proclaimed: "There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no Nirvāṇa.
Although the Tathāgata had preached the Dharma for me, I truly maintained that there is neither cause nor effect. While at the Nairañjanā River, he saw the Buddha from afar.
He came here, but because he gave rise to evil thoughts, his living body fell into hell.
According to the translation, his Sanskrit name is Sukīrtara (Sūgītara), which means "Good Star" (Śunakṣatra). He was the illegitimate son of the Buddha’s younger cousin.
Thus, these three individuals—due to their acts of lust, killing, and lying—all entered hell with their very bodies alive. I venture to ask the World-Honored One: regarding this...

Regarding the various hells: are they fundamentally and inherently fixed such that, despite differences in the karma created, all beings must return to these places and undergo retribution collectively?

Or do they each exist as such, with distinct variations, where the specific karmic actions initiated differ so that each receives their own individual retribution according to their private deeds? This refers to the retribution of the hells; it is not known whether this is...
"Distinct karma shared by all" refers to distinct karma that is experienced collectively; this is why it is not explicitly clarified and thus gives rise to doubt.
△ Third, earnestly beseeching compassionate instruction:
"May you, out of great compassion, grant an exposition for the sake of the ignorant" (up to) "...receiving with joy upon our heads, maintaining purity and avoiding transgression."
This is a request for instruction. "Child" (*tóng*) refers to one who is young; "ignorant" (*méng*) refers to one whose mind is clouded.
This is the practitioner’s self-deprecation, expressing that he lacks great wisdom and earnestly seeks to have his understanding opened and developed. His intention is this:

if those who uphold the precepts were to hear that cause and effect are as false as flowers in the sky, they would wonder, "What benefit is there in upholding them? What harm is there in not upholding them?"
One cannot help but fall into indolence and retreat. If, however, one is shown the gateway of definitive meaning, the mind will rejoice and the body will receive it with reverence upon its crown.
If both body and mind are thus cautious and diligent, the essence of the precepts will remain pure and white, and naturally no transgressions will occur.
Observing this profound doubt, the intention behind the subsequent request lies precisely in supporting the Vinaya while discussing the eternal truth.
△ 2. The Tathāgata’s Re-explanation in Response to a Request (2) 1. A Detailed Re-examination of the Seven Destinations to Encourage Diligent Cultivation (1) 1.1.
Granting Permission. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Excellent indeed is this question! ... You should now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."
The Buddha praised this and permitted its exposition because the question posed perfectly accorded with his own intent; thus he said, "Excellent!
As for the aforementioned [views on] lust, anger, killing, and the false teaching that phenomena are empty—all these are wrong views and none are the true cause.
Now, through this inquiry, they have been clarified so as to cause all sentient beings universally to return to the Right Path and not enter into wrong views.
"How joyful this is! Thus he granted his request, saying: "Listen attentively now;
I shall analyze and explain for you the meaning of the distinction between the true and the false, and between the common and the specific hells."
△ Second, the detailed exposition (three parts): First, a general clarification; second, a specific analysis (four parts). First, a general clarification of the true and the deluded:
"Ānanda, all sentient beings are in reality fundamentally true and pure" (up to) "...thereby distinguishing between the internal division and the external division."
This passage clarifies that *tathatā* (suchness) is obscured by deluded habit-energies;
once these are removed, how could there remain any doubt regarding the reality of the Buddha-body for those who are the intended audience?

"Truly fundamentally pure" means that the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) possessed by sentient beings of the seven destinies is, in reality, the originally and primordially endowed *tathatā*-Buddha-nature—the wondrously pure mind free from all defilements.

Because of that single moment of losing sight of the true nature, deluded views were consequently formed. Due to the existence of these deluded views, there arose deluded habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Thus, the seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*) emerged from this. Indeed, deluded views are the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), while deluded habitual tendencies are the seeds of defilement (*saṃkleśa-bīja*).
With the seeds and habitual tendencies of ignorance as their cause, there arise false emotional perceptions and conceptualizations.

"Indeed, you may wonder why there is delusion within what is ultimately real; it is precisely because of this. What follows is intended to provide a detailed explanation of delusion and to clarify the nature of mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*).

For this reason, it is divided into two parts: internal and external. Although these mental conceptions differ in their ascent or descent, and in their superiority or inferiority, they all collectively do not transcend the mere habitual energy (*vāsanā*) of delusion."
△ Second, the dual demonstration of the internal and external (2). First, the internal portion.
Ānanda, the internal portion is precisely the portion of sentient beings; [from] "within" (to) "spontaneously fall," this is called the internal portion.
This explains the internal division (*antarbhāga*). Ānanda, what is meant by the "internal division"?

It refers to that which sentient beings engage in daily and habitually, following their own inclinations and indulging their attachments, remaining settled within their own kind and seeking no further progress;
rather, they take emotional desire and craving as their internal affairs. It is because of these minds of attachment and defilement that this [suffering] truly arises.
The seeds of the fundamental consciousness of death, through contact with objects, give rise to grasping and manifest activity;
clinging to them without relinquishing is called "deluded sentiment. Because this deluded sentiment accumulates over time without ceasing, it can produce the water of craving and defilement.
For this reason, when sentient beings think of delicious flavors, their mouths—
Water flows forth. When the mind recollects a person from the past, tears fill the eyes; when the mind loves wealth and treasures, the entire body becomes lustrous and moist;
when the mind is attached to sensual desire, fluids flow from the orifices. All of these are brought about by emotional attachment.
Therefore, Ānanda, although the objects loved in these various instances differ from one another, that which is capable of loving them remains the same.
The mind is firmly bound and cannot be untied; its wandering and dissipation are one and the same.
Now, since delusive emotions can give rise to the waters of craving and attachment, the harm wrought by water begins with soaking, proceeds to moistening, and finally results in sinking.
It cannot ascend; this is the natural law—that it falls downward and does not ascend.
This is what is called the internal constituent of sentient beings. Thus we know that those who fall from their own fundamental kind do so due to the cause of emotional attachment.
II. The External Constituent.
Ānanda, the external constituent (*bāhya-bhāga*) refers to that which extends beyond the various directions (up to) naturally transcending them;
this is called the external constituent. This explains the external constituent. Ānanda, what is meant by the external constituent?
It refers to the daily, ordinary activities of sentient beings, wherein they harbor deluded and false thoughts, failing to abide in their own true nature, and instead aspiring for liberation. And...
To take superior realms as objects of craving and regard them as external matters is precisely this.
Due to the yearning mind of such cravings, the fundamental seed-consciousness of the primary karma is activated;

consequently, through longing for objects, active manifestations arise, which are falsely recorded and deliberated upon—this is called "vain conceptualization" (*vithapana*). When this vain conceptualization accumulates over a long period without ceasing, then...

One is able to give rise to a sublime mind and a vast, expansive spirit (*hao-ran zhi qi*). For this reason, when sentient beings maintain the prohibitive precepts in their minds, their bodies become light and pure;
when they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their gaze becomes heroic and resolute; when they desire to be born in the heavens in their minds, they dream of levitating;
when they fix their minds on the Buddha-lands, sacred realms manifest in the darkness; and when they direct their minds toward spiritual mentors...
That one regards one’s own body and life as light is entirely due to the influence of the conceptualizing mind.
Therefore, Ānanda, although these various matters—the objects of thought—differ from one another, the mind that conceives them remains clear and unturbid;
its buoyancy and elevation are the same. If such false conceptions can give rise to a vast and majestic vital energy (*hao-ran zhi qi*), then...
The manifestation of *qi* consists of flying, ascending, and moving; it is supremely firm and vast, filling heaven and earth.
By its very nature, it belongs to the upward-moving and does not sink downward; this is the natural principle by which it must transcend its own kind and never fall into decline.
This is what is called the "external division" of sentient beings. Thus, one knows that it transcends from its own fundamental category.
These are all causes of empty conceptualization. Although the aforementioned two categories differ in their ascent or descent, neither transcends the mind of emotional conceptualization.
△ Third, a general demonstration of ascent and descent.
From "Ānanda, all the worlds of birth and death continue in succession" (up to) "further reborn in the Avīci Hell of the ten directions.

This generally demonstrates the fruits summoned by the various degrees of emotional attachment (*qing*) and conceptual thought (*xiang*). The meaning is that although the various realms of existence differ, they do not transcend emotional attachment.
One should contemplate two causes; it is solely due to the internal and external, and the light and heavy, that there are distinctions between ascending and sinking.

Ānanda, as for all sentient beings who, within the world of their primary retribution, continue in an uninterrupted succession from birth to death, this is because there is none among them who does not crave life and loathe death.
Therefore, in taking birth, they follow what they desire and fulfill their own inclinations.
This is because matters of greedy attachment and longing all follow one's habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Therefore, at death, one does not obtain what was desired;
it runs contrary to one's will and intention, for the matter of changing form and undergoing retribution alters one's entire category of existence.
Thus, when life is about to end, although the breath has ceased, warmth remains within the sense-faculty of the body.

The characteristics of contact have not yet been entirely relinquished; at this very moment, the present aggregate (skandha) is about to cease and the intermediate state (antarābhava) has not yet arisen.
At this juncture, whatever one has done throughout a lifetime—whether wholesome or unwholesome—all manifests simultaneously before one.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "For example, when a person is about to die, they see the signs of the retribution they will receive according to their accumulated karma."
For those who have performed evil deeds, there immediately appear all the realms of suffering belonging to the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
For those who have performed virtuous deeds, there immediately appear the palaces of the devas, with hosts of celestial maidens and various garments, all fully adorned and exquisitely beautiful.
Although their bodies have not yet died, they see these things through the power of karma.
Therefore, one knows that hell and heaven originally have no fixed location; though the body has not yet departed, they already manifest within one’s own mind.

Before the objective realm appears before one, it is merely a delusive vision of the mind. For this reason, at this present moment of the final stage of the *āśraya-skandha* (the aggregate of the dying) and the initial emergence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are these two tendencies:
the contrary habit-energy of death and the conforming habit-energy of birth. These two tendencies are new...
Therefore, in the interval between their successive transitions, they rely solely upon their thoughts and conceptions; whether these are light or heavy determines whether they ascend or fall.
Thus, those whose thoughts are purely virtuous and devoid of worldly attachment immediately ascend and will certainly not fall, but will be born in the heavens.
It can be seen that all the various heavens within the triple world are the result of the wholesome karma produced by the mind of such conceptualization. Even if one’s heart is set on ascending...
Among these, there are those who, during their ordinary lives, have concurrently cultivated merit and wisdom, extensively practiced the six perfections, and made the four great vows;
those who desire to behold the Buddhas and personally receive their prediction of enlightenment;

as well as those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land, single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, and aspire to the Western Paradise. For such individuals who wish to see the Buddha, they will naturally understand this clearly for themselves.
The mind-ground becomes opened and clear, and one penetrates the vision [of reality].

If those who wish to be reborn among all the Buddhas of the ten directions do so, they will be reborn according to their vows in all the pure lands existing in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
One should see that these cases also belong to the category of "pure thought," yet because they are combined with merit, wisdom, and the power of aspiration, they surpass all the heavens.
"Ear. Next, as for those whose emotion is slight and thought is abundant: this refers to those whose superior thoughts are not pure, being slightly intermingled with subtle emotion.
"Lightly ascending but not far-reaching" means that although they ascend lightly, they do not go far;
for vertically they do not transcend the Four Heavens, and horizontally they do not go beyond the Cakravāḍa mountains. This is how these types are categorized.
If one possesses one emotion and nine thoughts, one becomes a flying immortal (*fei-xian*). With two emotions and eight thoughts, one becomes a powerful ghost king (*da-li gui-wang*).
With three emotions and seven thoughts, one becomes a flying yakṣa (*fei-hang ye-chao*). With four emotions and six thoughts, one becomes a terrestrial rākṣasa (*di-xing luo-che*).
All of these are able to soar through the air and roam throughout the four continents of a world-system (*yi-si tian-xia*). Their coming and going are entirely without obstruction.
This refers to being unimpeded by rivers, lakes, streams, and seas, and unhindered by mountains, valleys, walls, and barriers.
Nevertheless, among these four classes of beings, if there are those who can give rise to virtuous vows and maintain a virtuous mind, wishing to protect my Dharma and safeguard the Triple Gem;
or those who protect the precepts and follow those who uphold the precepts—[such individuals shall be protected].

Some protect dharanis and follow those who uphold them; others protect meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and provide guardianship and care for those who cultivate the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Such individuals are able to dwell eternally beneath the Dharma-seat of the Tathāgata.
This clarifies that even those who harbor deviant sentiments may possess virtuous aspirations. Therefore, among the eight classes of beings, all are [classified as] ghosts (*preta*).
This is how one’s spirit-body attains proximity to the Buddha and receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

As for "the passions and perceptions being equal," this refers to the five passions and the five perceptions. Regarding "neither flying nor falling": it does not ascend to the ranks of celestial immortals, *devas*, or spirits;

hence it is said they do not fly. It does not descend into the hells or the three miserable realms; hence it is said they do not fall. For this reason, they participate in the Way of Heaven and Earth.

Among these, those who are able to be born into the human realm do so because they possess the five *saṃjñās* (perceptions). Since perception belongs to the realm of clarity (*prakāśa*), it results in acuity;
since feeling (*vedanā*) belongs to the realm of obscurity (*tamas*), it results in dullness.

One must understand that on the path of humanity, from the highest wisdom to the lowest folly, all are distinguished by feeling and perception. Thus, for those whose perception is clear and who progress ever further day by day, they become acute.

The more intelligent one becomes, eventually attaining superior wisdom. If, however, one’s disposition remains obscure and obscurely dark while they advance day by day, then they are duller than the dull, becoming naturally the lowest of the ignorant.
Yet, this wisdom and folly have no fixed nature from the beginning; both can be transformed.
If those who are obscure practice clarity, they will turn from stubborn ignorance into sagely wisdom. If those who are clear practice obscurity, they will change their sagacity [into ignorance].
Wisdom becomes stubborn ignorance; thus, superior wisdom and inferior folly depend solely upon what each individual takes for themselves.
Therefore, those whose passions and attachments are many while their noble thoughts are few sink into the three miserable realms.
Consequently, when the six sense-faculties and four perceptions give rise to transmigration, those in whom the passions are somewhat heavy become the fur-bearing beasts of the wild.
...and so forth. Thus, their feet do not leave the earth. Those whose emotions are somewhat lighter become the feathered species of flying birds;

thus, their bodies still soar through the air. Those with seven emotions and three thoughts sink beneath the water wheel and are born at the edge of the fire wheel, in the place where water and fire intersect, undergoing these two [conditions].
The *qi* (vital energy) forms their bodies as beings of the preta realm. Because they receive fiery *qi*, their karmic nature is intensely burning, and they are constantly scorched and roasted.
Because they receive watery *qi*, the power of karma obstructs it so that when they drink, it turns into fire, which can harm their own bodies.
Regarding those who have neither food nor drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this refers briefly to the preta realm.
There are three kinds [of obstacles]. First, due to external obstructions, they are unable to obtain food or drink.
That is to say, those sentient beings, having practiced extreme stinginess, are born into this realm of rebirth. Their skin, bones, blood, and veins are all withered and parched, like burning coals.
Their hair is disheveled and matted; their faces are dark and sunken; their lips and mouths are dry and scorched. They constantly lick their mouths and faces with their tongues out of hunger.

Driven by thirst and filled with terror, they run hither and thither. To every spring and pool they reach, other sentient beings—holding swords, staves, and nooses—stand in rows to guard them, preventing them from approaching.

Or, even if they force their way toward them, the springs are seen to have turned into pus and blood, which they do not wish to drink themselves. This is called being prevented from obtaining food and drink due to external obstacles. Second:

Due to internal obstacles, they are unable to obtain food and drink; that is to say, the mouths of those sentient beings may be like needles, or like flaming torches, or they may have goiters on their necks while their bellies are vast and large. Even if they obtain food and drink, they are naturally incapable of either eating or drinking.
This is called being unable to obtain food and drink due to internal obstacles. Third, there are no obstacles regarding food and drink; that is to say, those...
There is a class of hungry ghosts named *Tīkṣṇajvālāmālin* (Fierce Flame Garland). Whatever they drink or eat is entirely consumed by fire; this is called "unimpeded eating and drinking.

When the original sutra states that there are "neither food nor drink," it refers to the aforementioned two types [of hells]. Those with eight parts of passion and two parts of thought are born in the *Antarābhava* (Intermediate) hell;
those with nine parts of passion and one part of thought are born in the *Avīci* (Uninterrupted) hell. As for the phrase "the ground where the two intersect":
This is precisely the place where the two wheels of wind and fire intersect. Since one’s body dwells therein, its suffering can be known of itself.
Here, the lighter [degrees of suffering] are designated as the eight cold hells; thus there is an interval between them, namely the seven hot hells.
Those whose offenses are grave constitute the nine states of emotion; consequently, they are born into the eight hells of uninterrupted suffering (*avīci*).

However, these "uninterrupted" hells are designated by that name in contrast to the preceding questions, and are not the same as the *Avīci* hell mentioned later in the text. Thus, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"Outside these four continents, there are eight thousand continents surrounding them, which in turn are encircled by a great ocean."
Beyond the eight thousand worlds, there is a Great Vajra Mountain that encircles the waters of the great ocean.
Outside this Vajra Mountain, there is a second Great Vajra Mountain, also known as the Second Iron Ring Mountain (*Dvitīya-Cakravāḍa*).
Between these two mountains, it is profound and dark, such that even the majestic radiance of the sun and moon cannot illuminate it. Therein lie eight great hells; each hell...
There are sixteen hells that serve as its retinue. The first great hell is named Sañjīva (Reviving); the second is Kālasūtra (Black Rope);
the third is Saṃghāta (Crushing); the fourth is Raurava (Crying Out); the fifth is Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out);

the sixth is Tapana (Burning); the seventh is Pratāpana (Great Burning); and the eighth is Avīci (Uninterrupted). Regarding the terms "with interval" and "without interval," these refer to the seventh and [eighth]...
There are eight types of hells. If one’s mind is purely perverse and entirely devoid of right thought, one immediately sinks into the Avīci Hell.
In the Sanskrit language, *Avīci* means "Without Interval. Because one has committed such karma, one receives its retribution immediately;
there is no other karma or other birth capable of intervening. Furthermore, there are five meanings of "without interval."
First, the physical stature; second, the number of kalpas; third, the lifespan; fourth, the instruments of suffering;

and fifth, the experience of retribution—since these all occur without interruption, they are places where those who are purely emotional and devoid of correct understanding fall. They remain there until the end of the kalpa, at which point an opportunity for escape finally arises.
If one sinks even deeper into the mind, it is because they still harbor slander against the Mahāyāna, such as the great arrogance of a Brahmin.
Those who violate the prohibitions and precepts, such as Ratnapadmagandha; those who preach deceptive and false doctrines, such as Sunakṣatra;

and even those who lack true practice yet greedily covet the resources of the faithful's offerings, or who lack true virtue yet unworthily receive the reverence of the fourfold assembly—down to those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses, leaving no evil deed uncommitted—such as these...
If one belongs to this category, there will be no end to their time there. Even when a kalpa is destroyed, they sink into this hell only to be reborn again.
Regarding the Avīci hells throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it should be understood that those consisting purely of sentient beings have two types.
The first consists of those who do not slander the Mahāyāna and so forth; when the kalpa is destroyed, they are able to escape—this refers to the "exhaustible" Avīci.
Second, those who slander the Mahāyāna and so forth cannot escape even when the kalpa is destroyed;

they are reborn again in the Avīci hell of the ten directions. This is the inexhaustible *ānantarya* (immediate retribution). Regarding the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"In terms of location, excluding only the northern continent; in terms of person, excluding the *ṣaṇḍha*. Four are bodily actions and one is vocal action: three are killings and one is false speech."

It is so. Regarding the ten grave offenses, according to the *Guhyagarbha-tantra* (*Dense Treasury Sūtra*), Kāśyapa asked the Buddha: "Among the ten non-virtuous actions, which is the most grave? The Buddha replied:

"If a son kills his father who has attained the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, this is called the gravest among the ten types of killing. To seize the property of the Triple Gem is called the gravest among the ten types of stealing.
To engage in sexual misconduct with one's mother or with an Arhat is called the gravest among the ten types of sexual misconduct. To speak words that are untrue..."

To slander and revile the Buddhas is the gravest among forms of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). To use words to cause a harmonious Saṃgha to split is the gravest among forms of divisive speech (*paiśunya*).

To insult and abuse the Noble Ones (*ārya*) is the gravest among forms of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). To use language that disrupts and confuses those seeking the Dharma is the gravest among forms of frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
If one commits the first act of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), this is the gravest among forms of malice (*vyāpāda*). To plunder those who uphold the precepts...

Among the various types of persons, greed is the most serious among the mental afflictions; false views regarding the self and one's surroundings are the most serious among the ten non-virtuous actions.
All of these constitute crimes for which there is no end within the five realms of the Avīci Hell.
△ Fourth, the conclusion regarding the commonality and individuality [of the hells].
Although one invites [rebirth] through the performance of evil karma, within the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) thus obtained, there is also the inclusion of the original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*).
This is the formal conclusion answering the previous question: namely, whether the various hells have fixed locations or whether they are experienced individually. Therefore...
The answer states: All sentient beings, each following their own nature, create evil karma that invites the suffering of the *sabhāga-naraka* (the common-retribution hell).
Although these are evil karmas created by individuals, they are nonetheless experienced collectively by all within the *sabhāga-naraka*.
As for the degree of severity, each person possesses both their own original [karma] and [that of others].
Because the original causes differ, the karma they create is not without variations in depth; thus, the retributions they receive naturally possess distinctions.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that there are both "distinctive commonality" (*sabhāgatā*) and "non-distinctive commonality.

When many beings collectively experience numerous instruments of suffering through the same karma and undergo this suffering together, it is called non-distinctive commonality. If, however, one receives [retribution] according to the lightness or gravity [of the karma], [it is called distinctive commonality].
The retributions differ; this is what is meant by the "distinction of homogeneous realms" (*sabhāgatā*). Now, "original ground" refers to the fundamental stage of the causal ground;

it carries the meaning of "differentiation. This directly concludes the response regarding "distinct karma with a common retribution," clarifying that the experiences of retribution vary according to their respective degrees of lightness or gravity.
△ Second, a detailed explanation of the seven destinies (7). First, the destiny of hell (3). First, a general statement on the causes of habituation and the mutual retribution thereof.
Ānanda, all these [beings]—from "these are all those sentient beings" up to—"they create ten causes of habituation and undergo six types of mutual retribution."

This summarizes what preceded in order to introduce what follows. Previously, it was shown that emotional attachments and perceptions serve as the cause, thereby eliciting the fruits of ascent and descent across the seven realms of existence.
Here, it is clarified that the ten habitual practices serve as the cause, resulting in the retribution of sinful karma within the three miserable paths.
The intent is to convey that the heavens and hells contained within these aforementioned seven realms are not created by a celestial deity.
The establishment of the realms is neither bestowed by others nor brought about without cause; rather, it is the result of what is summoned and experienced through one's own karma.
As for the "ten habitual tendencies," they refer to lust, greed, arrogance, anger, deceit, guile, resentment, false views, vindictiveness, and litigation.
As for the "six mutual interactions," they refer to the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; that is, when a single faculty creates karma, the others act as its assistants.
When the time comes for them to receive retribution, although they may be distinguished as leaders and followers, they nonetheless experience it together with one another and cannot escape it.
△ Second, specifically showing the mutual retribution of the habitual causes (in two parts): First, explaining the ten habitual causes (in ten sections). First, the habit of lust.
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, the first is the habit-energy of lust (*kāma-vāsanā*)—[continuing] until: "The Bodhisattva views desire as if avoiding a pit of fire.
This clarifies the karmic retribution of the habit-energy of lust. Indeed, lust is a thicket of all evils and the source of greedy attachment and emotional delusion;
it is the very root of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). For this reason, it is explained at the forefront both before and after [the other causes]. The intention is to say: "How..."
"What are these so-called ten causes of habitual practice? This is a general inquiry; the specific explanations follow below.
Ānanda, first, all sentient beings in the world establish their very nature and life through sexual desire. Now, this habit of lust is the cause for creating karma;
it must involve the internal sense-faculties and external objects coming together in mutual union, with one meeting the other, before [karma can be produced].
Karma is thus accomplished through the conjunction of defiled minds, which incite one another to mutual friction in the pursuit of tactile pleasure.
Thus, that greed and this craving are like water and fish; they grind against each other without end and rub against each other without ceasing.
Consequently, one's vital essence and blood are thereby dissipated, leading to the exhaustion of water and the arising of fire; this is the natural law.
For this reason, a great and fierce flame blazes forth within the two organs even while one is still alive, manifesting as ailments such as consumption and internal heat.
Thus, at the time of death, it can be understood that the fires of karma are summoned.
Knowing this, the following analogy is established to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution.
It is like a person who, for no reason, rubs their two hands together; because of this, a sensation of warmth manifests—this is what it means.
The above explains the habituation to karma; the following clarifies the habituation to retribution.

Due to these two types of habituation—habituation to karma and habituation to retribution—and specifically the habituation to sexual misconduct, they mutually incite one another like dry firewood meeting fire. Consequently, there arises the retribution of experiencing such things as the iron bed and the copper pillar.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-samādhi Sūtra*, regarding the Copper Pillar Hell: there is a copper pillar whose appearance...
It is like a volcano, six hundred *yojanas* in height. Beneath it is a fierce fire; atop the fire is an iron bed, and above that are wheels of blades.

Between them dwell iron-beaked insects and birds. Those who violate the moral code and destroy the transformative teachings, or who engage in impure conduct at improper times and places, will at the end of their lives be born upon the summit of a copper pillar.
