There, the fierce flames blaze intensely, incinerating their bodies, causing them to tremble with terror.
Looking down in terror, he saw upon an iron bed a beautiful woman. If it were a woman, seeing a handsome man, she would conceive a mind of passionate attachment.
From the copper pillar down to the iron bed, the fires of both male and female organs blazed up simultaneously.
Iron-beaked insects entered through the eyes of the man and woman and emerged from their respective organs, day and night.
Nine hundred billion births and nine hundred billion deaths—this is it. By observing this, one knows the bitterness of the retribution for sexual misconduct;
how can it be described too strongly? For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions give this single act of committing sexual misconduct the name "the fire of desire.
This means that the harm of desire exceeds that of a fierce fire; therefore, there are none who encounter it who are not scorched.
One’s head may fester and one’s forehead be scorched. Yet when a Bodhisattva encounters these realms of lust, they distance themselves further and further away, as if avoiding a pit of fire.
It is said that if one does not fall, it is well; but if one falls, one will surely lose one's body and life. For this reason, all Buddhas alike rebuke it;
one should examine this and engrave it into one's very bones. Bodhisattvas avoid it together; how could they not feel cold at heart? Alas! Lust is a fire.
The poison is such as this. I pray that wise men and women will not, by their own doing, imitate the moth that flies into a lamp.
△ Second, the habit of greed.
Second, the habit of greed involves mutual calculation, arising from mutual attraction... (up to) the Bodhisattva views greed as one would avoid a sea of miasma.
This clarifies the karmic retribution resulting from the habituation of greed. For greed is precisely craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it is a root affliction (*mūlakleśa*), one of the six primary afflictions.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, its nature is that of defiled attachment toward existence and the means of existence; its function is to obstruct non-greed and to produce suffering.
This is because the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) arise through the power of craving. Thus, sentient beings, by virtue of this habitual tendency, [experience such results].
They consult with one another and calculate their mutual schemes; only then do they complete their undertakings.
Driven by insatiable greed, they pursue their goals from one another, impelled by the power of craving. Thus, they mutually extract from each other to satisfy their private interests.
This is precisely what is meant by taking the property of others as one’s own and seizing others to make them one’s own. Consequently, this mutual extraction continues without ceasing.
As they continue to grasp at one another without ceasing, their saliva of craving flows forth more and more. Thus, the act of greedily inhaling belongs to the element of water;
as water accumulates, cold arises—such is the natural law. Consequently, there occurs the phenomenon of accumulated cold, solid ice, and freezing chill, which already exists within one's own mind.
Therefore, the following analogy is established to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution: it is like a person who, with their mouth...
It is empty and stretched out; without cause or reason, it inhales wind and contracts its breath. It is from this that the sensation of cold arises.
The above explains the habitual karma (*vāsanā-karma*); below, the habitual retribution (*vāsanā-vipāka*) is clarified.

Because these two types of habitual tendencies—karmic habituation and retributive habituation—mutually oppress one another, there arises the perceived sound of *ṭhakka-pala* and the cold ice of blue, red, and white colors.
Such are the retributions for these deeds. This "Ṭhapala" is the sound of those enduring the pain of cold within the hells.
The blue, red, and white lotuses are the forms and colors of the freezing cold within the hells. For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions name and designate them as such.
To greedily inhale and seek much is collectively termed "greed-water"; this refers to how the harm of greed exceeds [all other harms].
Poisonous water; therefore, those who drink it have none whose intestines do not rot and whose bellies do not burst.

Thus, when the Bodhisattva encounters this realm of craving, he distances himself from it and distances himself further, as if avoiding a miasmic sea. It is said that if one does not inhale [the vapor], there is no harm;

but if one inhales it, it will inevitably trigger malaria and destroy one's life. "Miasma" refers to pestilential vapors; they are found wherever there are hot regions by mountains and seas. Suppose a person...
Unaware, he inhaled its breath by mistake and immediately contracted a malarial fever, which ultimately led to his death.
This illustrates that the poison of greed for inhalation is likewise like this.
△ Third, the habit of pride.
Third, the habitual tendencies of pride intermingle and assail one another, arising from mutual reliance... (up to)... "The Bodhisattva views pride as he would avoid a great abyss.
This clarifies the karmic retribution of the habitual tendencies of pride. Generally, pride consists of relying on oneself to overstep others;

its nature is loftiness and arrogance, and its function is to obstruct non-pride and to produce suffering. This means that one who possesses pride does not have a humble mind toward those with virtue or those who possess virtue.
Because of this, the cycle of birth and death revolves without end, as one undergoes all manner of suffering. Arrogance serves as its habitual practice;
by looking down upon others and treating things with haughtiness, exalting oneself and degrading others, people fail to submit to one another and compete for superiority.
Yet there must be something upon which they rely, such as fame, status, power, wealth, learning, or literary talent. Therefore, it is said that [arrogance] arises from mutual reliance.
Relying on this, they inevitably oppress others; their nature is haughty and elevated, like water surging into waves.
Rushing and flowing away, each refuses to yield to the other, thereby forming their karma. Because of this, they surge forward without ceasing and flow in turbulent currents without rest;
thus, the waves of their delusion and pride accumulate more and more. As they continue to accumulate without end, they eventually become a great flood—this is the natural law.
The principle is thus. Therefore, there are surging waves that rise upward and wild billows that rush forward;
within one's own mind, these have already become waters of accumulated waves. Hence, the following analogy is established to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution.
This is like a person who, with the tongue in the mouth, presses it against the upper palate and repeatedly contracts the throat, becoming so attached to the resulting taste that saliva is produced.
The above explains the habituation of karma; the following clarifies the habituation of retribution.
Through these two habituations—karmic habituation and retributive habituation—they mutually stimulate one another, like wind blowing upon objects, causing them only to rise upward.
Yet they do not fall downward. For this reason, there is the retribution of such things as the river of blood that is experienced.
As for the "river of blood," it refers to the Saṃghāta Hell. Sentient beings undergoing punishment therein, terrified by their hundreds of thousands of wardens, flee into the mountains;
immediately, two great mountains arise before and behind them, closing together like a millstone, so that the flowing blood forms a river and the bones [form another].
Regarding "the internal organs rot away" and "the River of Ashes," the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinayas) states:

The River of Ashes Hell is five hundred *yojana*s in length, breadth, and depth. Ashy hot water surges and boils, emitting foul vapors and crackling flames. The swirling currents clash together, producing a terrifying roar.
From the bottom to the surface, iron thorns point in every direction. Upon the banks of this river stands a forest of sword-trees (*asipattravana*).

The branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all swords and blades. When the sinners enter the river, they are carried up and down by the waves, swirling and sinking as iron thorns pierce their bodies through from both inside and out.
Pus and blood flow forth, and though they endure myriad forms of agony, they are not allowed to die.
They then emerge from the Ash River and reach its bank, where there are jackals who seek to bite the sinners alive.
They eat their flesh and run toward the Sword Trees (*asipattravana*). When they ascend the trees, the sword-blades point downward; when they descend the trees, the sword-blades point upward.
As they climb, their hands are severed by grasping; as they tread, their feet are cut off. Their skin and flesh fall away, leaving only white bones held together by tendons and sinews.
At that time, iron-beaked birds on the Sword Trees peck at their heads and devour their brains. They wail in bitter agony, and thus—
They do not die; they return to enter the Ash River (*kṣāranadī*). Iron spikes pierce their bodies, causing the skin and flesh to rot and decay until only white bones remain, floating on the surface.
A cold wind blows upon them, and they immediately stand up. Driven by the牵引 (attraction) of their past karma, they are unaware as they suddenly arrive at the Black Sand Hell (*kālasūtra-naraka*).
A hot wind suddenly arises, blowing hot black sand that falls upon their bodies, burning the skin and penetrating through.

Bones appear, and flames burst forth from within the body, swirling and encircling it until the entire frame is scorched and rotted away. Because their retribution is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die.
Emerging from the Black Sands Hell, they arrive at the Boiling Excrement Hell, which is the Sea of Poison.
This is the most agonizing place within the realm of hungry ghosts; as it is said, when hungry they devour glowing iron balls, and when thirsty they drink molten copper. Thus, they are drenched.
These are the various matters concerning copper swallowing iron. Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this single matter of pride with the name "drinking the water of delusion.
This is because the harm caused by pride exceeds that of the water of delusion; thus, those who drink it [are so named].

There is none who does not become dazed and lose their true nature. Yet the Bodhisattva, seeing this realm of delusion and arrogance, keeps it at a distance, far, far away, as if avoiding a great drowning.
For "drowning" refers to the deep waters of the mud; one may say that not drowning is best, for once one has drowned, it is easy to fall in but difficult to emerge.
As for the "water of delusion," in the Western Land there is water which, if drunk, causes one to become deluded, just like...
These are like the "Greedy Spring" (Tan-quan) of Linghai and the "Dumb Spring" (Ya-quan) of Dian-Qian.
△ Fourth, the habit-energy of anger:
"Fourth, the habit-energy of anger, clashing and surging forth from mutual antagonism... [until] the Bodhisattva views anger as he would avoid execution."
This clarifies the karmic retribution for the habitual practice of hatred (*dveṣa*). For hatred is characterized by an intensification of resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering;
its nature is to obstruct non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and to be a state of lack of peace. Its function is to serve as the basis for unwholesome conduct.

This means that one who possesses hatred necessarily causes heat and affliction to body and mind, giving rise to various evil karmas because it is of an unwholesome nature. Since hatred is practiced habitually, it must necessarily arise from...
They strike one another and mutually oppress each other; thus it is said that they arise from mutual antagonism.

Because this antagonism inevitably involves collision and impact, their nature is one of feverish affliction, like fire smelting gold. Consequently, they become like knives, spears, swords, and halberds, engaging in mutual combat.
Thus they complete their karma. Consequently, their deception and provocation cease not, and their binding resentment does not subside;
thus the fire of their hatred grows ever more intense, and the metal of their fury becomes ever more rigid as it is moved. This is because the mind gives rise to the vital energy (prāṇa).
If one reverses the mind and subjects it to violent impact, the fire of the mind increases further, and the metal of the vital energy (prāṇa) becomes even more rigid.
Thus it is said: "The heat of the mind gives rise to fire; it casts the vital energy into metal. Such is the natural principle.
Therefore, matters such as the mountain of knives already exist within one's own mind; hence, the following analogy is established to verify the retribution of karma.

This is like a person who harbors resentment in their heart and bears a grievance that cannot be avenged; suddenly, the intent to kill the enemy arises, and their vital energy surges and vibrates—this is it.
The above explains the habituation of karma (*karmābhyāsa*); below, it clarifies the habituation of retribution (*vipākābhyāsa*).

From this, the two habituations—the habituation of karma and the habituation of retribution—strike one another. "Striking" is like the thrusting and stabbing of swords and halberds. It is for this reason.

There are various punishments for offenses such as those involving the palace. "Palace" refers to castration; "excision" means cutting off the nose—these two being among the five penal codes of the Qin dynasty.
"Decapitation" means severing the head; "hewing" refers to cutting off the arms; and "crushing" involves pulverizing the bones—all of which were capital punishments of the recent era.
"Piercing" was the ancient punishment of branding; today it is applied to those who have fled or committed theft and are sent into exile.
"Beating" refers to whipping and flogging; it corresponds to what are now known as the canes and staves of punishment.
For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this single matter of anger with the name "sharp sword. This means that if one touches it, one dies immediately;
if one strikes it, one is wounded. When a Bodhisattva encounters such an object of anger, they do not even have time to avoid it, much like fleeing from a falling thunderbolt.
They shall be executed with great slaughter. If one does not avoid this, then life and limb cannot be preserved, and it will be difficult to keep one's head and body intact.
△ Fifth, the habit of deceit:
Fifth, the habit of deceit involves mutual inducement arising from reciprocal provocation... (up to) "The Bodhisattva views deceit as he would fear the face of a jackal."

This clarifies the karmic retribution for the habitual practice of deceit. Deceit (*māyā*) is indeed the flattery (*śāṭhya*) among the minor derivative afflictions. For the purpose of deluding others, one feigns extraordinary conduct;
its intrinsic nature is crooked flattery, and its function is to obstruct non-flattery and instruction. That is to say, as for those who are crookedly flattering:
In order to deceive others, they perversely conform to the demands of the times, contriving expedient means to win over others' favor, or to conceal their own faults;
thus, they fail to submit to the correct instruction and admonition of teachers and friends. It is for this reason that sentient beings develop the habit of flattery and deceit through these actions.
They deceive one another and entice each other to complete their karma.

Due to flattery, guile, and unreality, they cheat one another, arising from mutual coaxing and inducement, and acting as mutual jesters. Consequently, they cannot refrain from inciting and drawing one another in.

As they create karma without ceasing, their arts of flattery and deception become increasingly ingenious, enabling them to lead others on without the latter’s awareness or knowledge, as if ensnaring them within a trap.
Like those bound by ropes, restrained by wooden stocks, or shackled and fettered, they cannot escape.
Because their mental application is such, the instruments of rope-torment and wooden stocks are already fully present within their own minds; thus it is said below.

An analogy is established to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution. This artifice of flattery and deception, which causes people to remain unaware, is just like water infiltrating a field, enabling grasses and trees to grow of their own accord without being conscious of it or knowing how it happens.

The above explains the cultivation of karma; below, it clarifies the cultivation of retribution. Thus, there are these two types of deceptive cultivation: the cultivation of karma and the cultivation of retribution.
Successively extending and drawing one another along, there arise the retributions of shackles upon the hands, fetters upon the feet, stocks upon the neck, and chains upon the throat;
thus the body undergoes the punishments of whips, staves, clubs, and maces.

For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate such individuals by name and title as "the treacherous, the sycophantic, the hypocritical," and "the slanderers and thieves"—meaning those who employ slanderous speech.
It is seductive; because it is even more treacherous than a thief, those who encounter it will none fail to ruin their households and exhaust their wealth.

When a Bodhisattva encounters such a realm of deceit and falsehood, they flee from it as quickly as possible, as if fearing a jackal. This is because the jackal is a beast of fierce and evil nature that must be avoided;
furthermore, it can divine future events, and one who follows it is certain to gain a reward. This is like [the danger of] flattery and deception.
A mere man who uses his craft to entice others succeeds a hundred times out of a hundred; it is just like this. "Jiāo" refers to shackles. The *Yì* says:
"Shoes with shackles destroy the feet; a yoke on the neck destroys the ears. This refers to these very objects.
△ Sixth, the habit-energy of deception (*māyā*).
"Sixth" refers to the habit-energy of deception, which arises from mutual cheating and mutual delusion... (up to) when a Bodhisattva sees deception, it is like treading upon a serpent or a viper.
This is called the karmic retribution of the habit-energy of deception. Now, as for deception: for the sake of profit and reputation, one feigns the possession of virtue through guile.
Deceit (*māyā*) has fraudulence as its intrinsic nature. Its function is to obstruct non-deception, and its activity is to constitute a wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This refers to those who are hypocritical and deceptive; harboring ulterior motives in their minds, they frequently manifest unreal and fraudulent acts for the sake of a wrong livelihood.

Thus, through this habit of hypocrisy and deception, sentient beings delude one another and mutually confuse each other, thereby completing their karma. Due to such hypocrisy and falsehood, [they deceive] one another...
Deception arises from mutual delusion and mutual slander; thus one falsely represents the unreal as real and deludes the non-existent into existence.
One deceives others regarding what they do not know or see, mocking them with falsehoods. Consequently, this false accusation continues without end, and this delusion persists without ceasing.
Consequently, they fly about with their minds, devising wicked schemes that appear and vanish like spirits and ghosts, causing people to fall into their traps without even realizing it.
Because they employ their minds in this manner, there arises dust, excrement, urine, and all manner of foul, impure filth.
Having already accumulated [karma] within one's own mind, the following analogy is provided to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution. This deceptive scheme causes people to become deluded;
those who do not know or see it are just like dust and sand swept up by the wind—the dust follows the force of the wind.
It is that which churns up empty space, darkening heaven and earth, so that people cannot see one another even when facing each other.
The above explains the habitual karma; the following clarifies the retribution for such habits.

Because these two types of deceptive habits—karmic habituation and retributive habituation—intermingle with one another, there arises the retribution they evoke. It is like using deceitful speech to entrap someone in unrighteousness.

Therefore, those who cause others to sink and drown experience the retribution of being submerged and swept away; those who seize and wrong others experience the retribution of being lifted up, tossed, and hurled;
and those who cause others to fall into pits or be seized experience the retributions of flying, falling, drifting, or drowning.

For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate these acts of mutual deception and mutual cheating with the name "Plundering Murder" (*jiesha*), as they are like a cosmic cataclysm (*kalpa*).
In the age of the final dharma, people kill one another; thus, those who encounter such circumstances invariably lose their lives.

When the Bodhisattva beholds this scene of deception and fraud, he does not dare set foot there, treating it as if treading upon a viper. For whoever treads upon them will surely suffer injury to their body.
A *huǐfú* (viper) is a species of snake three inches in width with a head like a split finger; it is the most venomous of all snakes.
△ Seven Habits of Enmity.
The seventh is the habit of enmity, which arises from mutual resentment and the harboring of hatred (extending to: "the Bodhisattva views an enemy as if drinking poisoned wine").
This clarifies the karmic retribution of the habit of enmity. Essentially, enmity is identical to hatred; it is preceded by anger and consists of harboring malice.
Enmity (*upanāha*) has resentment as its essential nature; it functions as an obstacle to non-resentment (*avyāpāda*). Its activity consists of causing burning affliction (*paridāha*);
that is to say, one who harbors enmity cannot exercise forbearance, because they are constantly afflicted by burning distress.

Thus, through this habituation to resentment, sentient beings mutually dislike and hate one another, harboring grudges against each other to complete their karma. Because they do not relinquish these grudges, they harbor mutual hatred and aversion.

It originates from harboring resentment. "Harboring" means to contain and conceal; this refers to what is called "concealing a malevolent heart," secretly administering poison so that the other party remains unaware.
Because their mental state is such, they harbor evil within their breast; hence there are chests for storage and carriage-cages.

To inflict a cruel and poisonous injury upon another is like hurling a flying stone or a heavy rock; it is like placing someone in a jar and roasting them over a fire, as in the expression "inviting you to enter the jar.
To "sack and strike" means to place a person inside a sack and beat them to death, such as when the *Shiji* records that the First Emperor of Qin "sacked and struck his two younger brothers.
These are all instances of harboring resentment and inflicting harm in secret, not allowing [the victim] to...
Because people understand this, the following analogy is established to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution.
It is like a person of hidden malice who harbors treacherous schemes, conceives great evil in their heart, and secretly plots to harm others; such is the nature of the aforementioned habitual karma.

One does not understand the retribution of habitual tendencies. Because of these two types of enmity—the habituation of karma and the habituation of retribution—they mutually combine and devour one another, as if saying, "While alive I did not eat meat;
now in life I shall pursue the souls [of others]. Thus, there is a retribution that is evoked.
For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate such resentful enemies by the name and title of "Harmful Ghosts" (*viheṭhaka-piśāca*). It is because of this violation...
They act contrary to correct principle and harm others in secret; they are most wicked ghosts.

Yet when the Bodhisattva encounters such a state of resentment and hatred, he does not dare to be tainted by it even slightly, just as one would avoid drinking poisoned wine. "Poisoned wine" refers to the wine of the *zhèn* bird (the *hārita* or "poisonous-winged" bird).

When its wing feathers are dipped into the wine, drinking it will injure the person, causing their intestines to break into pieces. This illustrates that the poison of resentment and hatred is likewise like this.
△ Eighth, the habit-energy of views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*).

"Eighth" refers to the mutual illumination of the habit-energy of views, which is like the *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity), up to its pervasive grasping at what is false, like entering a ravine of poison.
This clarifies the karmic retribution of the habit-energy of views. For "view" here refers to evil views; regarding the principles of the various truths, one speculates erroneously.
[The view of] seeking (*parāmarśa*) has defiled wisdom as its nature; its function is to obstruct right vision and to bring about suffering, for those with wrong views undergo much suffering.

There are five distinct types of this view in terms of its modes of activity: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which is translated here as "view of the body" (*shen-jian*); it consists of clinging to a self and what belongs to a self.

Second, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), which consists of clinging to either annihilationism or eternalism. Third, wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), which denies cause and effect. Fourth, [the view of]... [text fragment ends].
Grasping at what is not a fruit as being a fruit, such as regarding the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as *nirvāṇa*, and so forth;

and grasping at what is not a cause as being a cause, such as observing the precepts of cattle or dogs as a cause for rebirth in heaven, and so forth. These five types are collectively termed "wrong views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Thus, by means of these views, sentient beings habituate themselves to them, each clinging to their own understanding and mutually claiming their own views to be the truth.
If one clings exclusively to one [of these], then it is not the other four that can accomplish its function.
Because they hold mutually conflicting attachments, it is said that they give rise to opposition; because they judge each other as right and wrong, it is said that they produce contradictions.
This is not only a matter of opposing the correct [view], but even within their own category, they oppose one another; it is not only a matter of contradicting the views put forth by others.
This is also largely inconsistent with their own innate views, such as contradicting their own words or contradicting their own scriptures.

Furthermore, they are unwilling to follow others toward the truth. For this reason, there are royal messengers and chief clerks who hold official documents to bear witness, compelling them to confess their guilt so that they have no defense. Therefore, the following analogy is provided.
This serves to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution. It is like people traveling on a narrow path, coming and going from opposite directions;
they see one another and cannot avoid each other. The above explains the cultivation of karma; the following clarifies the cultivation of retribution.
Due to this cultivation of karma and retribution, two kinds of views are cultivated which mutually confront one another to distinguish right from wrong; thus [these phenomena] exist.
In the thorough investigation of what has been received through retribution, the deceptive enticements of falsehoods were examined with meticulous questioning;
through interrogation, the facts were verified, and the hidden intentions were scrutinized while the manifest matters were exposed and investigated.
It was as clear as a candle illuminating its surroundings, leaving nothing concealed. Furthermore, the boys of Goodness and Evil held their ledgers in hand and spoke.
The refutations and distinctions have been recorded in great detail and proven with extreme certainty.
Regarding such matters, how could one allow for baseless views, empty rhetoric, or fallacious arguments?

For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate these five kinds of evil views by the name "Pit of Views," because once one falls into them, one loses the Dharma-body. And as for the Bodhisattvas seeing all...
Deluded, evil views and pervasive false imaginings are like entering a valley of poison; once one falls into them, the life-force of wisdom is wounded.
△ Ninth, the habit of injustice.

Ninth, the habit-energy of resentment (*vañcanā*) intermingles and manifests as false accusation and slander; (up to: when a Bodhisattva encounters such resentment, it is like being struck by a thunderbolt.
This clarifies the karmic retribution for the habit-energy of resentment. As for "resentment," it refers to the wrongful harming of the innocent and the oppression of the virtuous.
To cause harm and affliction to others without a mind of compassion is what is subsumed under "harming" (*vihiṃsā*). What constitutes harming?
It refers to one who harms because they oppress and afflict others. Thus, due to the habit of wrongful harming, sentient beings inflict injury upon one another.
This refers to those who wish to inflict further guilt upon others; what need have they for fear of lacking pretexts?

Thus, they forcibly attribute guilt to one who is innocent, and they insistently claim that one whose principle is fundamentally upright is crooked. This is how those with power and influence suppress others.

Therefore, it is said that such actions arise from slander: to falsely implicate another with matters that are absolutely non-existent, and to malign them by claiming they possess what they do not. Purely.
It is used for forging [the body] to bring about its punishment. It is for this reason that there are objects such as the "Closing Mountains" (*saṃghāta-parvata*).
As stated in the *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* (Heterodoxies of the Sūtras and Vinaya): "The Closing Mountains" refers to two large rocky mountains facing each other.

When the sinner enters between them, the mountains close naturally, grinding his bones and flesh to dust; then the mountains return to their original positions. "Closing Rocks" refers to... lying down.
The sinners are placed upon large boulders, which are then closed over them like grapes being squeezed or oil being pressed.
They are crushed by great, glowing-hot iron wheels that trample the sinners, causing their bodies to shatter. "Milling" refers to small grinding stones;
"plowing" refers to tilling with a plow, which tears their tongues apart. "Grinding" refers to the Stone Mill Hell, where the sinners are seized and dashed against hot rocks.
[The victim] lies supine, with hands and feet extended, while large, scorching stones are placed upon his body and rotated to grind him down.
These are all the retributions for having unjustly oppressed the virtuous and good. Therefore, an analogy is provided below to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution;
it is like those in the world who, as slanderous and malicious thieves, oppress the innocent and unjustly harm the virtuous and good. By means of this—

The upper part explains the habituation of karma; the lower part clarifies the habituation of retribution. Due to these two types of habitual tendencies—karmic habituation and retributive habituation—they mutually oppress and exclude one another, such that wrongful harm does not cease.
Therefore, there is what is experienced as being forcibly pressed down and constrained to submission.
"Forcibly beaten" means to strike and press down in a chaotic manner. "Squeezing and filtering" refers to pressing out blood by means of a press. "Measuring across" (衡度).
This refers to weighing the lightness or heaviness [of offenses] and measuring the length or shortness [of transgressions] with a ruler in order to administer punishment.
For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this act of enmity, harm, and slander by the name "Slanderous Tiger" (*chánhù*), referring to the mouth of a treacherous slanderer.
Evil exceeds even that of a tiger; those who encounter it are inevitably harmed. Yet when a Bodhisattva beholds such a scene of wrongful injury, they regard it as if it were a delayed thunderclap.
A thunderbolt that strikes an object is called a *pīlì* (thunderclap); for those who encounter it—

It is for this reason that none fail to have their souls flee in terror. Nevertheless, I wish that those who possess power and status, as well as those who occupy positions of authority, would take heaven and earth and their parents as their heart’s concern.
If they were to encounter such genuine sincerity, they ought to feel compassion and pity rather than joy.
Should they not do so, they must simply consider the destination of these people: whom will they leave behind to take their place?
△ Ten Habits of Litigation.

"Ten" refers to the habit of litigation, which arises from mutual clamor and the concealment [of faults] (extending to) being like one wearing a high mountain upon their head while treading upon a vast ocean.
This clarifies the karmic retribution for the habit of litigation. Generally, litigation arises from concealment. As for what is called "concealment," regarding...
Its nature is to conceal one's own committed transgressions out of fear of losing profit and reputation; its function is to obstruct non-concealment and to produce remorse and distress.
This means that one who conceals a transgression will inevitably experience remorse and distress later on, as it leads to a lack of peace and stability.

Having committed a fault oneself, one is unable to confess it openly, and consequently invites litigation from others; this is one of the factors of affliction (*nīvaraṇa*). Preceded by anger and resentment, it pursues and provokes violent agitation.
It is hot and has a nature of cruelty. It functions as an obstacle to non-affliction, and its activity is that of stinging with maggots.
This means that when one pursues past evils and the mind encounters present adverse conditions, a cruel disposition arises profusely, leading to clamorous violence and wicked, coarse speech.
Because it stings others like maggots, it is called "contention" (*sarga*). Habituated to this contention, one frequently resorts to concealment; thus, mutual clamor ensues. That—

These signs attack one another to bring their karma to fruition. Because [the transgressions] are private, secret, obscure, and difficult to clarify, it is said they "arise from concealment"—that is to say, covering over one's faults and hiding one's secrets.
For this reason, there is the mirror of karma to reflect them, and the illuminating fire-jewel to shine upon them, so that one may not succeed in concealing them. Therefore...
Below is presented a metaphor to verify the characteristics of karmic retribution. This is like a person standing in the midday sun who cannot conceal their shadow.
The above explains the habituation of karma; the below clarifies the habituation of retribution.

Through these two types of habituation—karmic habituation and retributive habituation—they mutually attack and provoke one another, manifesting and revealing themselves spontaneously. Thus, there is that which is evoked and witnessed.
Evil friends are the "karmic mirror that reflects the gallbladder" and the "fire-jewel that discerns and verifies.
They cause one to disclose past karma and confront various circumstances; thus, everything will be clearly revealed, with not even a hair's breadth hidden.
For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions give the name "hidden thief" (*chāyā-caura*) to this single matter of concealment, meaning that one’s own offenses are secretly covered over.

This is truly to harm oneself. When a bodhisattva perceives this state of being shrouded by the aggregates (*skandhas*), it is as if one were carrying a high mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean;
thus, the burden becomes ever heavier and the drowning ever deeper. This serves as a metaphor for how transgressions become increasingly concealed and the resulting offenses grow ever more grave.
Therefore, the Preface to the Precepts states: "To repent brings peace and joy; to fail to repent causes sin to deepen further. And:

Those who uphold the precepts, please reflect deeply upon this. Question: Among the twenty-six root and secondary afflictions (*kleśa*), why are these ten alone designated as the causes for habitual practice?
Answer: When sentient beings give rise to delusion, create karma, and undergo retribution, it does not transcend these ten.

For instance, within the root afflictions, the two types—delusion (*moha*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—as well as the two intermediate [afflictions] and the eight great [secondary afflictions], correspond to these.

These ten causes all arise in mutual correspondence. Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the three—anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), and envy (*īrṣyā*)—are all subsumed under hatred (*dveṣa*).

Arrogance (*mada*) is subsumed under pride (*māna*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*) is subsumed under greed (*lobha*). For this reason, by citing these [three], the primary afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are encompassed without omission.
△ Second, explaining the six mutual retributions (2). First, the general inquiry:
"What are the six retributions, Ānanda... [down to] ...the evil retributions they attract emerge from the six sense faculties?"
This is a general inquiry regarding the six types of retributive interactions. It is because the aforementioned twelve classes of beings are said to possess all causes within a single cause;
this means that all effects are fully present within a single effect. As previously stated: "When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are simultaneously liberated.
This clarifies that while karma may be created by a single faculty, the resulting retribution is experienced interactively across all six faculties. (6)
Regarding consciousness as the creator of karma: because consciousness possesses the faculty of discernment, it is able to create karma;
thus, the six consciousnesses are the agents that summon [retribution], while the evil retribution is what is summoned. Furthermore, these karmic retributions all emerge from the six sense organs.
These six sense organs serve as the original intermediaries for thieves; they are the very passages through which thieves enter and exit.
When one creates karma, it proceeds through these eight [faculties]; thus, when one undergoes retribution, it likewise emerges from them.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in six parts). First, the retribution of views.
How does the retribution of evil emerge from the six sense faculties? (Extending to: Like sparks flying and scattering, fanning and filling the expanse of space.
This clarifies that while the visual consciousness creates karma, the other faculties collectively receive its retribution. The meaning is as follows:
how is it that the retribution for evil karma arises from all six faculties? First is the retribution of seeing:

this refers to the eye seeing forms, giving rise to delusion and creating karma, which leads to the acquisition of the visual faculty and the subsequent mutual reception of retribution by the other five faculties. For example, [in the case of] greed...

This refers to the karma created through beautiful forms. Because seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, this karmic retribution for perceiving form manifests at the juncture where birth and death intersect, specifically at the moment when life is about to end.
At that time, one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions; the deceased’s consciousness, whether flying upward or falling downward, is then obstructed by these smoky flames.
"O Deva, they enter directly into the Avīci Hell. One must know that for those who have committed extreme good or extreme evil, there is no intermediate state (antarābhava);
therefore, they enter directly. Once they have entered the hell, two signs first manifest: first, clear vision.
Because during their lifetime they were bold and reckless, committing various evil deeds without any sense of restraint, within this state—"
They see all manner of evil things, such as iron snakes, bronze dogs, sword-trees, knife-mountains, and the ox-headed *āpāṇakas*, which cause these sinners to give rise to immeasurable fear;
they perceive these realms through the lens of their own dread. Second is "dark vision":
because during their lifetime they deceived others' eyes and acted with hypocrisy in dark rooms, committing various evil deeds, they [perceive this] within this state.
The heavens grew dark and the earth was shrouded in gloom; all was silent and nothing could be seen. This caused the sinner to give rise to immeasurable fear, and his mind was seized by terror.
Furthermore, as he beheld the fires of retribution in this manner, they scorched his faculty of hearing, manifesting as the sounds of boiling cauldrons and molten copper;
they scorched his faculty of smell, manifesting as the fumes of black smoke and purple flames; they scorched his tongue...
One can experience the taste of molten pellets and iron porridge; the faculty of the body-root (kāyendriya) can experience the touch of burning embers and glowing coals;

and the cognition of the mind-root (manendriya) can experience the sensation of being burned. Thus, it can give rise to a fire like a shooting star, scattering and flaring up to produce thoughts that pervade all space and all realms.
This is because the eye-root (cakṣurindriya) exerts influence upon the other faculties. Because it acts...
At the time when karma ripens, although visual consciousness is primary, the other consciousnesses necessarily act as its assistants;

therefore, when receiving retribution now, they are also mutually implicated. This principle is indeed appropriate, for all of this is the retribution for the mind’s flight toward and pursuit of forms.
△ Second, the retribution of hearing.
Second, the retribution of hearing that invites evil fruits (extending to): "becoming lightning and hail that shatters the heart and soul.

This clarifies that while the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) creates the karma, the other sense-faculties collectively receive its retribution. Second, the retribution of hearing refers to the ear.
The evil karma created by hearing sounds draws forth the ear-faculty as well as the other five faculties, causing them to collectively undergo the retribution of suffering.
This is the case for those who create karma through the desire for licentious sounds.
Since the faculty of hearing belongs to the element of water, at the moment when birth and death intersect—that is, when life is about to end—the following vision first appears:
The waves and tides submerge and drown heaven and earth; thus, one's spirit-consciousness descends and flows along with the current, falling into hell.
Once having entered hell, it first gives rise to two aspects of perception: hearing and reporting. The first is "opening the hearing," which is the hearing of movement.
One merely hears various clamorous and chaotic sounds, causing the spirit to become agitated and disordered, leaving it without a master.
Second is "listening by closing [the ears]," which is hearing stillness; then there is silence where nothing is heard, causing the dark soul to sink into oblivion with no refuge.
Furthermore, such is the water of retribution for hearing; this hearing that pours into the ears can bring about retribution.

It is like a reprimand; it is like words of reproach for one’s transgressions. The sound of interrogation, the sight of a fixed gaze, can act as thunder and a roar, like the appearance of striking an object, or the manifestation of a malignant poison. It is the application of the faculty of the nose.

Thus, it can become rain or mist; just as a venomous insect has a foul odor pervading its entire body, when tasted by the tongue, it can become pus or blood, and various kinds of foul and impure flavors.

When applied to the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*), it can become the touch of animals or ghosts, or the sensation of excrement and urine. When known by the attention of the mind (*manas*), then...
They can manifest as lightning and hail, thereby shattering one's heart and soul; these are all retributions for the dissipation of the mind toward sounds.
△ Third, the retribution of smelling.
Third, the retribution for smelling that invites and draws forth evil fruits (extending to) having one’s body smashed by flying sand and gravel.
This clarifies that while the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna*) creates karma, the other faculties (*indriya*) collectively receive its retribution. Third, the retribution for smelling:
this refers to the evil karma created by the nose smelling fragrances, which invites and draws forth the olfactory faculty as well as the other faculties to collectively receive the evil fruit.
The nose belongs to the element of earth and possesses inhalation and exhalation. When inhaling, [the breath] enters from below; when exhaling, it exits from above.

Therefore, as a karmic retribution for this act of smelling fragrances, at the juncture where birth and death intersect—specifically at the moment when life is about to end—one first perceives poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings, and one's consciousness surges upward from the earth.
Furthermore, those who fall from above into hell are these very people. Once they have entered hell, two signs first manifest as retribution for their olfactory karma:
first, when it is pervasive and all-encompassing, they are overwhelmed by the extreme fuming of various foul vapors, and their minds become greatly disturbed;
second, when it is obstructed and not perceived, the vapors press down so that they cannot pass, leaving them in such agonizing distress that they feel as if they would perish.
They fall prostrate upon the ground. Furthermore, when the scent thus smelled strikes the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), it can either cause obstruction or allow for penetration;
for one creates karma through the olfactory faculty without departing from these scents of obstruction and penetration.
When it strikes the faculty of sight, it can manifest as the appearance of fire or a torch; when it strikes the faculty of hearing, it can manifest as the sound of drowning or boiling water;
when it strikes the faculty of taste, it can manifest as the putrid stench of rotten fish or the off-taste of spoiled broth;
and when it strikes the faculty of the body, it can manifest as a mountain of rotting flesh being gnawed by small insects.
When these tactile sensations strike the faculty of the mind, they can give rise to thoughts that reduce the body to ashes, miasma, sand, and rubble;
all of these are the retributions for the mind’s outward wandering in pursuit of fragrances.
△ Fourth, the retribution for flavors.
"Fourth" refers to the retribution for flavors that draws forth evil results, [extending] until flying red-hot iron rains down from the sky.

This clarifies that while the tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*) creates the karma, the other faculties collectively receive its retribution. "Fourth, the retribution for flavors" refers to the tongue.
The evil karma created through craving for flavors draws forth the tongue faculty and causes the other faculties as well to collectively undergo bitter retribution.

For the tongue belongs to the element of fire; during one's lifetime, for the sake of this tongue faculty, one set fires to mountains and cast nets across both land and water to satisfy the mouth and belly.
Thus, the karma of such greedy ignorance is repaid at the juncture where birth and death intersect.
At the moment when life is about to end, one first perceives an iron net completely covering the world.
One’s consciousness then penetrates downward through this net, hanging head-downward as it enters hell; this is what occurs. Once inside hell, two initial signs of retributive sensation manifest:
the first is the inhalation of breath. Because of this inhalation, the mouth necessarily becomes cold, and thus the sensation of cold is formed.
Ice. It freezes and chills the flesh of the body; this is precisely the state of gnawing the bones and sucking the marrow while alive.
Second is exhaling breath. Because those who exhale breath necessarily have heat in their mouths, fierce fires fly forth and scorch the marrow and bones to ruin.
This is precisely the state of blowing on a hot broth while it is being consumed.

Furthermore, regarding such tasted flavors, when they pass over the tongue and are experienced, they give rise to the mental states of acceptance and endurance; this is because one previously gave rise to craving for flavors.

They devour living beings, forcing them to endure and accept their fate; having no one to whom they can appeal their grievances, they must therefore undergo retribution after death, compelled to accept and endure it with silent acquiescence to their punishment.
When seen with the eyes, it appears as the color of molten gold and scorching stone; when heard with the ears, it sounds like the whizzing of sharp weapons and keen blades.
When sound passes through the breath of the nose, it can become the air of a vast iron cage that covers the entire land;
when it passes through the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it can become the touch of arrows, bows, and crossbows;

when it passes through the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), it can become the thought of flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky. All of these are the retributions for the wandering and rushing after sensory flavors.
△ Five kinds of retribution for contact.
The five [types of] retribution for contact attract and lead to evil fruits—[ranging from] falling, to flying, to being boiled, to being roasted.

This clarifies that while the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) creates karma, the other faculties collectively receive its retribution. These five are the retributions for contact; that is, the body.
The unwholesome karma created through craving for touch brings about the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) as well as the other faculties to experience its bitter fruit.
This is because that which the body-faculty encounters is exclusively the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).

Since a person in this world possesses this body-faculty, there is not a single instance of contact between men and women in lofty halls or spacious mansions that they do not crave; thus, the retribution for this karma of craving for touch [is as follows].
At the juncture where birth and death intersect, when life is about to end, one first sees great mountains closing in from all four sides with no way out.

Then the consciousness perceives a great iron city, further filled with fire-snakes and fire-dogs, as well as ox-headed and horse-faced beings who drive one into the city toward the Avīci Hell. Once having entered the hell:

Thus it is. First, the two characteristics of the retribution of touch are revealed: the first is the touch that joins with the body, whereby mountains press against one's person, causing the flesh and bones to follow along as they are completely shattered by the blood flowing through them; the second is the touch that separates from the body.
Then there are swords and blades that strike the body, causing the heart and liver to be completely butchered, torn apart, and shattered.
Furthermore, when such sensations of separation and union pass through the sense organ of the body, they can become the Way; yet they are also the path leading to hell.
"Observation" (*guan*) refers to the two watchtowers at the gate of the King of Hell. "Listening" (*ting*) and "the case" (*an*) both refer to the administration of punishment.
It is also the basis for bodily contact. When encountered by the eye’s vision, it manifests as the horrific sight of being burned and scorched;
when encountered by the ear’s hearing, it manifests as the evil sounds of clashing blows and piercing arrows—*zhi* meaning to thrust a blade into the flesh;
when encountered by the breath of the nose, it manifests as the stifling air of being gagged, bagged, interrogated, and bound; when encountered by the tongue...
Just as one who has tasted [the flavor] can perform the plowing of a plow, the shearing of scissors, the cutting of a sword,
or the slicing of a blade— such being the significance of this, when experienced through the cognition of the mind, it can produce the turbulent thoughts of falling,
flying, frying, roasting, and unstable heat-affliction; all of these are the retributions for the wandering and rushing toward sensory contact.
△ Sixth, the retribution of volition (*cetanā*).
"Sixth" refers to the retribution of volition that draws forth evil fruits, leading to ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths, whether prostrate or upright.
This clarifies that while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) creates karma, the other faculties collectively receive its retribution. "Sixth, the retribution of volition" refers to the mind.
Evil karma created through perverse thoughts draws forth the mental faculty (*manas*) as well as the other faculties, causing them to collectively experience bitter fruits.
For the mind belongs to the earth element; yet, that which the faculties encounter is solely the object-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Since people in this world allow their hearts and wills to run wild, there is no evil they will not commit. Therefore, the retribution for such karma of perverse thought occurs at the intersection of birth and death.
At the moment when life is about to end, one first perceives an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land; this is what it refers to.
One’s consciousness is blown upward into the air, and after circling there, it falls from the sky, carried by the wind into the Avīci Hell.
Once having entered the hell, the two initial manifestations of thought—the retributive and the conceptual—arise; the first is non-awakening, which immediately ceases.
Regarding the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*): when one is unaware of it, this constitutes the ultimate delusion; thus, one runs about in frantic agitation without ceasing.
When one is not deluded, the mental object arises; because one is not deluded, there is awareness and cognition, whereby one is tormented by suffering and pain that is difficult to endure.
Furthermore, when such delusive awareness and perverse thoughts become bound within the faculty of the mind (*manas*), they are able to act as...
When one forms thoughts that lead to the commission of offenses and sins, they become bound to the faculty of the eye, whereby it serves as a mirror and a witness, producing a vision of illumination.
When they are bound to the faculty of the ear, there arise the harsh sounds of clashing stones, frost, ice, earth, and mist.
The binding of the nose-faculty results in the foul breath of the fire-chariots and boat-cages; the binding of the tongue’s tasting results in wailing, lamentation, and weeping;
the binding of the body’s touch results in contortions and writhings—both great and small. These are all the retributions for the mind’s flight and indulgence in sensory phenomena.
△ Third: The Concluding Summary on the Causes of Habitual Tendencies and Reciprocal Retribution.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six fruits of the hells (extending to: "arising from false imagination, not existing from the beginning").

This concludes the summary of cause and effect to answer the preceding question. Ānanda, as has been explained above, these are called the ten kinds of habitual causes and the sixfold intersecting effects of the hells;
they all arise because sentient beings have themselves deluded their true mind.

These are produced by following after deluded sentiments. Nevertheless, although hell has been mentioned in a general sense, its specific number, the gravity of its retributive suffering, and the length of time it spans across kalpas have not yet been elucidated; therefore, I shall now analyze them. My intention is as follows:
If sentient beings, through their six sense faculties and ten causes, at all times commit such evil karma without exception,
this constitutes an extremely grave offense for which they enter the Avīci Great Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable eons.
Next, there are those who create the ten causes through each of the six sense faculties, where the preceding and succeeding actions are not equal.
It is not the case that they all commit them at one time. Even if they take up the causes created by those [others], they do not fully possess all ten.
For example, regarding the karma created, it may involve only several of the ten objects or only several of the six sense faculties;
in such cases, the person's transgression is somewhat lighter than the former, yet they still enter the eighth Avīci Hell. This applies whether through body, speech, or mind.
Third: If one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, then among the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), three are diminished; within the ten causes, seven are excluded.
The offenses of such a person are lighter than those mentioned previously, and thus they enter the eighteen hells.

According to the *Niraya Sūtra*, there are eight hot hells and ten cold hells; this refers to that. If one does not engage in all three types of unwholesome action (*trividha-karma-patha*) together, [the retribution is further reduced].
This means that if one lacks even one or two of the [three]— body, speech, or mind— and does not possess them all together,
yet in the interim commits one act of killing or one act of stealing— that is, if one lacks one or two of the [four], such as lust, killing, or stealing, and does not possess them all completely—
the person’s transgression is lighter than the former, and they enter the thirty-six hells where the suffering experienced is somewhat less severe for a certain number of kalpas.

It is somewhat shorter. If one perceives only a single faculty—that is, among the six faculties currently manifesting, there is only one—then within the ten causes, regarding what is created and what is done, one has committed only a single offense. The transgression of such a person is lighter than the former;
thus, upon entering the one hundred and eight hells, the suffering endured is even lighter and the duration of kalpas is even shorter. Therefore, it is so composed.
Karmic actions differ, and thus the retributions they receive are also distinct.
Although sentient beings each create their own evil karma, they all enter the various specific categories of hells within this world to undergo that retribution.
This is because, in response to the previous question as to whether these various hells have fixed locations or arise spontaneously, it is explained that each individual generates their own karma.
Is each [being] receiving it privately? Therefore, the present answer says: "Entering the stage of homogeneity within the world is clearly not a private reception.
Previously, there was another inquiry: "Does this Way exist inherently from the beginning, or does it arise from the deluded habitual practices of sentient beings?
Therefore, the present answer says: "It is produced by false conceptualization; it does not exist inherently from the beginning. Thus...
It is clear that this is a false arising.
△ Second, the various realms of hungry ghosts (three parts): First, the general indication.
Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings... [until] later, when their retribution for offenses is exhausted, they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts.
This serves as a general indication that those whose karmic retributions in the hells have been exhausted enter the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Now, "ghost" (*preta*) means "fearful";
because they are characterized by timidity and great dread, they are called ghosts. Furthermore, there are many types; to summarize, they are distinguished into four categories.
First, the ten evil deeds of the inferior grade directly summon their retribution. Second, the power of past ripening karma suddenly drags forth their retribution.
Third, when about to enter hell, one first undergoes the "flower-retribution" (the preliminary manifestation). Fourth, emerging from hell.
They receive these remaining retributions. Therefore, within the final aggregates (*paścima-skandha*) of the seven destinies (*gati*), each possesses this destiny;

yet, as there are degrees of excellence or inferiority in their reception of retribution, they are divided into three categories—those with wealth, those with little wealth, and those without wealth—each further distinguished by nine grades.
For now, let us briefly summarize and explain in detail the remaining retributions of the hells.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those sentient beings who undergo punishment in these various hells are not those who have violated the four or eight precepts of the śrāvaka discipline.
This does not refer to those who have transgressed the ten grave precepts of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, nor to those who have slandered the Buddha or reviled the Dharma of Nirvāṇa;
such individuals, by committing these acts, will fall forever into hell with no prospect of release.
Even if it is not such an act, but rather some other miscellaneous karma—such as the ten habitual tendencies—even though one must undergo punishment for them, [the situation is different].
They burn for kalpas on end; yet thereafter, there will still come a day when their retribution is exhausted and a time of liberation, whereby they may receive the form of a hungry ghost.
Question: Since this passage discusses all seven realms of existence, one should include the full category of hungry ghosts.

Why then do you restrict it only to those who have emerged from hell? Answer: It is because the Tathāgata, in his urgency, wished to cause people to hear of the suffering of the hells so that they might arouse the aspiration for Bodhi.
This is to focus the mind; therefore, the discussion proceeds from the hells in successive order.
As for the subsequent sections on animals, ghosts, humans, and animals again, these are treated specifically to demonstrate that cause and effect do not deviate by even a hair’s breadth.
Although this is not explicitly stated regarding the complete set of destinies, the underlying intent encompasses them all.
△ Second, the detailed explanation.

If one commits an offense due to greed for objects based on their original cause (up to) meeting a person and being named a *preta* who transmits [messages], this is the detailed explanation of the destinies of the various *pretas*.
This is because, as mentioned previously, the retributions received differ according to each of the ten causes.
It is the same. Therefore, this realm of hungry ghosts also consists of ten categories. The meaning is this:
regarding which objects were craved within the original ten habitual causes, one becomes a ghost of that corresponding type.

As for those who, in the past, incurred retribution by habitually craving material things, once such persons have completed their punishment and emerged from hell, they encounter objects and give rise to craving.
They attach themselves to form physical bodies; this is caused by the habituation of greed.
Thus, there are those who become spirits and manifest as monsters by attaching to grass or wood; for this reason, they are called "strange ghosts" (*guǐ*).
As for those of old who suffered retribution because they were habituated to lustful desire—once such persons have finished their punishment and emerged from hell, they then encounter...
Wind gives rise to desire; relying upon it, form is established. Wind, in this context, refers to the *fu* (passion/impulse).
As the commentary states: "Wind means to let loose. When a male and female animal entice one another, it is called 'wind.

Now, when [beings] encounter [conditions] and form is produced, it is likewise due to the 'wind' of horses and oxen letting loose and enticing one another until they encounter conditions and form is produced. This is brought about by the habit of lust. Therefore, there is..."
Tornadoes, drought-demons (*bà*), and their like—the *bà* is a female ghost, also called a female demon (*nǚyāo*).
Therefore, women who are excessively lustful are called *bàfù*. The modern term *pō* is a corruption of this. For this reason, they are named wind-*bà* ghosts.
As for those from the past who, having habituated themselves to greed, deceit, and delusion, have come to suffer retribution—such persons receive [this fate].

When their retribution is exhausted, they emerge from hell; yet, having falsely taken what was non-existent as existent, they rely upon the state of animals and depend on it to form a ghostly essence.

This is caused by the habituation to such falsehoods. Thus there are foxes, jackals, and other such species that transform their appearances to manifest seductive allurements, deluding the hearts of men;
for this reason, they are called *mei-gui* (seductive ghosts). As for those who were formerly greedy—

Those who have habituated themselves to hatred and thereby incurred retribution, once their punishment is complete and they emerge from hell, encounter venomous insects that take form by borrowing their physical shape;
this is caused by the habitual tendencies of their hatred. Thus, there are the poisons of snake and rat vermin, as well as frogs and other such creatures;
all these are presided over by these ghosts to repay past grudges, employing the vermin to administer poison.

Therefore, they are called *gudu* (contagious poison) ghosts. As for those who, in the past, habitually harbored resentment toward their enemies and suffered punishment because they did not let go of their hatred, once such individuals have finished their retribution and emerged from hell, they encounter times of human misfortune and attach themselves to form physical bodies;
this is caused by the persistence of that vengeful habit. Consequently, there arise toxic epidemics and contagious fevers.
Headaches, bone-fever, malaria, pestilence, and the like—all these are presided over by this ghost as retribution for past fears;

therefore, it is named the "Leprosy Ghost" (*lìguǐ*). As for those of the past who were habituated to greed, arrogance, and pride, and who fell into transgression by excessively pursuing empty vapors—when such persons have finished their punishment and emerged from hell, they encounter only this...
Qi (vital energy) then becomes physical form. This is what the preceding text refers to when it says: "Those who received qi from a fierce fire for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
It is caused by the habit of arrogance. Because they lack genuine virtue within, their bellies are empty yet their hearts are haughty;
they are like those who have no food or drink and possess only the "qi of hunger. For this reason, they are called *preta* (hungry ghosts). As for those who were formerly greedy—

Deception is their habitual practice. Those who incur retribution by taking what does not exist to be existent, once they have finished suffering their retribution and emerge from hell, encounter profound darkness and immediately assume a physical form; this is caused by the habituation to deception.
Those who deceive by tricking the ignorant and hoodwinking them—this is the meaning.
Such ghosts cause people to suffer from nightmares and bewitchment while they are in a state of昏寐 (deep sleep or stupor); therefore, they are called "yānmèi" (nightmare-bewitching) ghosts.

As for those of the past who, out of greed, were attached to evil views and the practices of heterodox illumination and thus underwent retribution—when such persons have finished their period of suffering...
Emerging from hell, whenever they encounter objects of refined spirit, they immediately manifest forms by taking them as their basis; this is caused by the habituation of their perceptions.
Thus, there are those such as the spirits of wood and stone, the numinous beings of mountains and marshes, and so forth; for this reason, they are called *wangliang* ghosts.
Although these are transformations of wood and stone, they are nonetheless the most refined and intelligent among the realms of ghosts. As for...

In the past, those who habituated themselves to greed and injustice, falsely harming the innocent and thereby incurring retribution—such persons, once their period of punishment has ended, will manifest forms whenever they encounter a place of spiritual clarity; this is caused by the persistence of that habit of wrongful conduct.

"Numinous brightness" refers to the deities of spirit temples. Because they wronged others in the past to perfect themselves, they now rely upon the deities of spirit temples to likewise wrong themselves to perfect others; they are subject to being driven and employed as servants.
Thus, there are those who carry sand and shoulder stones to fill rivers and block seas. For this reason, they are called "ghosts employed as laborers. As for instances such as...

In the past, those who were greedy for litigation, formed factions, and committed villainy thereby incurred retribution—such persons, once their punishment in hell has been completed and they have emerged from it, will assume a physical form whenever they encounter wicked people. This is caused by the habit of litigation.
Since litigation inevitably involves factions, these individuals testify to right and wrong and expose people's hidden secrets; therefore, when they become ghosts, [they manifest this tendency].
They also align themselves with others, claiming to be sages or immortals, speaking of gods or ghosts, and reporting omens of good or ill fortune.

Those who transmit words and deliver messages do so because their past habitual tendencies have not been forgotten. Thus, there are spirit mediums, *ge*, *jiān* spirits, female shamans, Daoist priests, and invocators;
these are simply the people they encounter, all of whom are termed "transmitting ghosts."
△ Third, the summary and indication.
"Ānanda, these beings all fall due to their pure passions" (extending to) "...then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous [nature] originally has nothing at all.
This is the cause and effect of the realm of hungry ghosts. Ānanda, these beings of the hells all [fall] due to the eight passions and two...
With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of form, up to the state of pure passion and no thought, they fall into the hells.
There, by various fires of karma, the water produced by their passionate attachments is burned for kalpas until it finally dries up.
Emerging from there, they become beings of the hungry ghost realm. Yet all of these are merely one's own deluded imaginings.
Through inversion, one creates the causal karma of the ten habitual actions; this is why one invites and undergoes the retributive suffering of the six modes of intersection.
These following three phrases answer the previous question regarding the Buddha-body’s true reality: "How can there still be realms such as the hells?
Therefore, the response says: if one can awaken to the Bodhi of one's own nature, then it is the single, wondrous, and perfect [reality].

The enlightened mind is fundamentally devoid of such realms of existence as these; they exist only because one has not awakened to bodhi, due to deluded thoughts and inversions. Thus, they are said to exist.
△ III. The Realm of Animals (3). 1. General Statement.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of the hungry ghosts has been exhausted, [the being] takes the body of an animal to repay its past debts.
This is a general designation for the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). In Sanskrit it is called *tiryañc*, which here means "animal" (*pāngxing*);
so called because those in this path mostly move horizontally with their bodies covered. It is also called "livestock" (*chuxing*), because their inherent nature is dull and ignorant.
They are unable to stand on their own and depend largely upon others for nourishment and sustenance. Nevertheless, this single realm (gati) actually comprises many types;
to summarize, there are four distinct categories: first, those who directly incur the fruit as a result of the ten unwholesome actions of middling intensity;
second, those whose past ripening karmic forces suddenly draw forth the fruit; third, those from the earth... [text truncated]
Upon emerging from hell, they immediately undergo retribution for their deeds. Fourth, those who come from the realm of hungry ghosts likewise undergo retribution for their deeds.

Thus, within the subsequent *pañcaskandhas* (aggregates) of all seven destinies, there are such types; furthermore, their experience of retribution varies in degree, being either superior or inferior.

Consequently, they are divided into three distinct categories—superior, middling, and inferior—each with its own differences. The present discussion, however, concerns exclusively those whose karmic debts as hungry ghosts have been fully exhausted.

This is explained in detail as follows: When the karma of the ghosts is exhausted, the pure emotion of Avīci Hell, the nine emotions and one thought of the Uninterrupted (Avīci) Hells, the eight emotions and two thoughts of the Interrupted Hells, and the seven emotions and three thoughts of the Hungry Ghosts are all scorched dry by the fires of karma.
Therefore, it is said that "emotion and thought become empty. Only then do they return to the human realm.

In the interim, they encounter those with whom they originally had debts or grievances; as these enemies and creditors meet one another, they still possess the six sense-faculties and four types of perception, which serve as the karma for moistening their rebirth and receiving a body.
Thus, they are born among the beasts of hair and the flocks of feathers to repay their past debts.
△ Second, the detailed explanation.
Regarding "strange ghostly objects": when the retribution for these objects is exhausted, they are mostly reborn in this world as members of their own kind.
This is a detailed explanation distinguishing the realm of animals. In the past, due to the habituation of greed, they became strange ghosts; thus, they are possessed [by them].
When the physical matter dissolves, the retribution of the ghost is also exhausted. Now, having been born into this world, they mostly become owls;

for the owl is an unfilial bird that eats its own parents. Because these strange ghosts were reborn through such causes, those who attach themselves to clods of earth and are subsequently devoured are all remnants of their former habits of extreme greed and utter strangeness.
In the past, due to their lustful habits, they took form by attaching to the wind. The wind—
Once their power has been neutralized, the retribution of the ghosts is also exhausted. In this present life, they frequently manifest as omens of calamity among all manner of anomalous creatures.
These "omens of calamity" (*jǒuzhēng*) are the precursors to misfortune; these "anomalous creatures" (*yìlèi*) refer to strange and extraordinary beings.
For instance, flocks of sparrows and swarms of rats serve as premonitions of famine and scarcity, while the *jiangtún* porpoise and the *shāngyáng* bird portend wind and rain.
The previous inquiry held that when the *pó* (drought-demon) appears, it portends drought; now that it has transformed into an animal, it still portends calamity.
This is the lingering habit of the wind-*pó*. Formerly, due to its deceptive habits, it relied upon animals to become a malevolent ghost (*mèiguǐ*).
Now that the animal has died and the retribution for the ghost has ended, it is born into this world mostly as a species of fox. Indeed, the fox is a demonic beast.
The *Xuánzhōng jì* states: "A fox of a thousand years becomes a wanton woman; a fox of a hundred years becomes a beautiful maiden. This is because the fox is capable of seducing people;
it is also a lingering habit from its power to bewitch. In the past, due to the habituation of resentment, it relied upon *gǔ* insects to become a poisonous ghost.
Now that the insects have perished, the retribution of the ghost has also ended. In this present life, it mostly becomes...
Regarding the category of poisons: as for this category of poisons, it refers to vipers, snakes, vipers, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes, which cause injury upon contact;
these are also the residual habits of resentment and poison. In the past, due to the habit of anger, they seized upon the vulnerabilities of others to become pestilent ghosts.
When their decline has reached its limit, the retribution of the ghosts is also exhausted. Now they are mostly born in this world as a class of worms;

for worms are parasites that digest food. Because they were pestilential when they entered the bodies of people, causing calamities and misfortunes, they have now been reborn as animals, again taking refuge within the body as roundworms or threadworms. They digest the food of humans, causing them to suffer from rapid hunger. This, too, is...
This is the residual habituation of past decline. Formerly, due to the habit of pride, they received the fiery breath of karma and became hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Once that breath had long since dissipated and the retribution of their ghosthood was exhausted, they were now born into this world mostly as types of food. As for these "types of food":
This refers to the category of edible things; that is to say, what the common world calls the "six domestic animals"—horses, oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, and pigs—which are those consumed by humans.
However, these few words have spread their poison through the human world, causing no small harm.

Those who are driven by the palate have taken them as a pretext to become arrogant, exalting themselves and looking down upon others, and on this basis, they have falsely claimed that [these animals] were created by Heaven.
All things are fundamentally intended for the nourishment of humanity; what harm is there in indulging one's own desires, eating heartily and to one's fill?

What does it matter whether sentient beings suffer pain or endure agony? Such a person not only lacks faith in the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and the Bodhisattvas, but furthermore disbelieves the bequeathed words of Confucius and Mencius.
