Regarding "perceiving the body as an obstruction" and so forth: this means one feels aversion toward the physical resistance and solidity of the body, diligently cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and causes the body to cease and return to non-existence.

Because one relies on emptiness through aversion to form (*rūpa*), it is called the "concentration of the sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*); thus, one is reborn in the sphere of infinite space as a result. There are two ways of relinquishing the mind:
if, at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one employs the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to sever delusions and enter emptiness, that is the bliss of concentration.

This is what is meant by "containing. If one employs the outflow-tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) within the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven to suppress delusions and enter emptiness, one is then a worldling or a non-Buddhist.

When all obstacles have dissolved and ceased to exist, one does not rely on form (*rūpa*). When even the non-obstructive state of non-existence is extinguished, one does not rely on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To retain the entire *ālayavijñāna* along with half of the *manas* is to loathe emptiness and rely upon consciousness (*vijñāna*).

In Sanskrit, it is called *ālaya*; here it is translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*). It possesses the meanings of being that which stores, that which is stored within, and that which is grasped.
*Manas* is translated here as "defiled"; it refers to the seventh consciousness, which serves as the support for the six consciousnesses.
What is now described as "half-subtle" refers to the sixth consciousness, half of which has already been suppressed through discernment and no longer functions as an object-condition.
Although external objects have ceased, there still remains a portion of internal conditions that arises simultaneously;

yet, the characteristics of this consciousness are so profound, subtle, and hidden that they are neither material form nor mere emptiness. Therefore, this is designated as the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).

When the perception of form has vanished from emptiness, one treads upon the preceding heaven. "The consciousness-mind is entirely extinguished" means that by relying on meditative power (*samādhi*), even the internal objects of the sixth consciousness are completely suppressed.
"Tranquil and without destination" means that because the objects of cognition no longer exist, the subject that cognizes does not arise;
through this aversion to consciousness, there is no further marginal consciousness, and thus the mind is dispersed and dissolved.

Having attained concentration, one then relinquishes the object-condition of consciousness; because there is no dharma whatsoever, it is called the "Concentration of the Sphere of Nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

Regarding "the mind of consciousness is unmoving": this is because the active functioning (*pravṛtti*) of the sixth consciousness has been entirely suppressed; thus it is said to be unmoving. As for "exhausting investigation through cessation":

this means that when the practitioner reaches this stage, their wisdom is exhausted and their strength is spent, such that they no longer investigate the truth or sever delusions. Therefore, at this point—

Within this nature that is fundamentally inexhaustible, one forcibly assumes mastery and delusively proclaims, "I am able to profoundly fathom the subtle principle and have exhausted the nature of both humans and things.
Yet they do not realize that this is merely due to the pressure of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
thus, although the nature of consciousness remains, it does not arise. Therefore it is said: "As if existing, yet not existing. Although consciousness is seen...

The nature [of this state] is exhausted, yet in reality it is not exhausted; therefore, it is said that "if exhausted, it is not exhausted. Because the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the six consciousnesses have been suppressed, it is not characterized by perception (*saṃjñā*);

yet because the seeds (*bīja*) still remain, it is not without perception. For this reason, it is named the "concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
Now, the lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Space is twenty thousand great eons (*mahākalpa*), and the lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is...

The life span in the Sphere of Infinite Space is forty thousand great eons; in the Sphere of Nothingness, it is sixty thousand great eons; and in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, it is eighty thousand great eons.
Regarding these four heavens above, they are all called "formless" because they lack the form that is the fruit of karma (*karmaphala-rūpa*).

Nevertheless, there exists the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*); this applies to both the environment and the inhabitants. Thus, they are entirely devoid of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). However, in these four heavens, the body is extinguished.
They return to nothingness; they all rely upon dull emptiness (*tūṣṇīka-śūnyatā*) for their practice. For this reason, first they loathe form and rely on emptiness;
next they loathe emptiness and rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*); thirdly, when form, emptiness, and consciousness are all extinguished, they rely on the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*).

Fourthly, relying on the nature of consciousness, they exhaustively investigate its extinction; yet none of them attain true extinction, as it is nothing other than a superior state of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-adhipati*).
These are those who possess good fruits but have not yet escaped saṃsāra and have not realized the path of the sages.

If we discuss the four heavens, where form reaches its limit and emptiness begins, then ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are the primary residents; the śrāvakas of fixed nature are temporary residents; and the heterodox practitioners of divergent views are those who dwell there intermingled.
△ Third, distinguishing the differences between the noble ones and ordinary beings.

These [ordinary beings] exhaustively investigate emptiness yet do not fully penetrate the principle of emptiness (up to: being deluded and leaking, they lack learning and thus enter the cycle of rebirth).

This is a general discussion of how the noble ones and ordinary beings differ in their emergence from and falling into [samsara]. The intent is that these ordinary beings and outsiders, as well as those [who are... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a Buddhist treatise, likely discussing the distinction between the *ārya* (noble ones) and the *pṛthagjana* (ordinary beings), specifically regarding their realization of emptiness and their karmic trajectories.)
[The Buddha] said: "Although each [dhyāna] exhausts emptiness, none of them can fully penetrate the ultimate principle of emptiness.

Why is this? For instance, when the first dhyāna exhausts emptiness by extinguishing form; the second dhyāna exhausts consciousness by extinguishing emptiness; the third dhyāna exhausts non-existence by extinguishing consciousness;

and the fourth dhyāna exhausts extinction by returning to the ultimate end—then regarding the realm of emptiness, one may indeed be said to have exerted all one's strength to exhaust it. Yet they remain unaware of this."
The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form. Now that you have grown weary of form and seek emptiness, it is just like seeking water by leaving the waves behind;
you will go further and further away. How could you ever exhaustively realize the principle of true emptiness?

If, from the five heavens of non-returning, you observe the five aggregates with the eight noble contemplations—viewing them as a disease, an abscess, a sore, and a thorn—then [you will truly understand].

Constantly contemplating suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity, those who exhaust themselves through this untainted path must wait until the eighty thousand great kalpas of celestial lifespan in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception are complete before they finally emerge from the three realms and are born in the Impure Land of Skillful Means.
They are called "non-retrogressive" dull-witted arhats; because of that, they cannot be like those at the Peak of Existence who retrogress their minds [to seek further progress].

Therefore, they are called "dull-witted. If those who come from among the non-Buddhist heavens of the Non-conceptualizers (*asaṃjñin*) or from the ordinary beings of the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*), and who exhaust themselves through the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) by means of the six practices—namely, rejoicing in what is above and loathing what is below—then they will single-mindedly incline toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
They do not know how to turn back their course to enter the wondrous, nor do they reflect upon the principle of the true emptiness of one's own nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). This...
Their names reach outward until they exhaust emptiness; thus, in the end, they can never find a place of ultimate refuge.
Because they are deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (*sāsrava*) and mistake them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), after eighty thousand kalpas their retributions are fully exhausted.

Having nothing left to rely upon, they enter the various realms of existence (*gati*), where they continue to revolve according to their past karma, remaining as they were before. Thus, for ordinary beings who look outward—

The path relies upon the first dhyāna to abandon the desires of the lower stages. In this manner, proceeding successively, it even relies upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to abandon the sphere of nothingness.
Beyond this, there is no further basis for reliance; thus, one cannot abandon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself.
Because there is no further place of reliance, one fears losing the self and dreads falling into the state of non-attainment. For this reason...
They are unable to transcend the triple world and instead continue to revolve in saṃsāra. This is like a caterpillar: it draws back its hind legs for stability before advancing its front legs.
When it reaches the end of its range and there is no further place to proceed, it simply returns to its starting point.
△ Fourth, it clarifies that kings and subjects differ.
Ānanda is a celestial being among each of the various heavens... (up to) ...dedicating [merit] toward the path of practice of the assembly of sages.
This clarifies that the various heavenly kings of the three realms differ from their subjects.

These "various heavens" refer collectively to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the thirteen of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), excluding only the five heavens of the non-returners (*anāgāmin*), as these are not places where ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) undergo retribution for their karma. "Heavenly beings" refers specifically to the inhabitants of each respective heaven.
Regarding these subjects and citizens, it is said that while in the causal stage as gods and humans, they cultivated only impure (*sāsrava*) wholesome karma;
thus, they were recompensed with such fruits as the six desire realms, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Consequently, once this retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) once more; this is an established principle. As for those gods and humans—

O King, this is precisely the Bodhisattva’s cultivation and advancement through provisional stations; there is nothing that does not utilize these celestial positions as the path for practicing toward the realization of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
Thus, one does not fall into saṃsāra. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In the third stage, one mostly becomes Śakra, the Heavenly King;
in the fourth stage, one mostly becomes Suyāma, the Heavenly King," and so on, up to the eighth stage.
They frequently act as Brahmā kings of a small chiliocosm; those on the tenth stage frequently act as Mahābrahmā kings of a great trichiliocosm, and so forth.
Regarding "roaming in samādhi": because Bodhisattvas skillfully enter, emerge from, and abide in hundreds of thousands of samādhis, they treat them as a form of play;
thus, abiding in these concentrations, they become celestial kings. The nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) are termed "skillful."
Entering is named "Lion’s Vigorous Stride" (Simhavijṛmbhita); emerging well is named "Surpassing Samādhi" (Vikrānta-samādhi); and abiding well is named "Stable Abiding.
There is nothing that does not rely on these stages of gradual progress to turn toward principle from phenomena and enter the ranks of the sages.
Yet that which is cultivated is the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama; it is precisely what is called "the path of wondrous cultivation."
△ The Names of the Five Devas of the Sphere of Emptiness.
Ānanda, from the point where the body and mind of these four devas of the sphere of emptiness are extinguished (until) the end of this section, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is the formal conclusion regarding the names of the four *ārūpya* heavens. Ānanda, in the first two of these four *ārūpya* heavens, there is a complete absence of the body and its objects;
thus, the body is extinguished. In the latter two heavens, the active manifestations of consciousness (*vijñāna*) are suppressed; thus, the mind is extinguished.

Because both body and mind are extinguished, the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) manifests. Consequently, during the time one is in concentration, there exists the "matter born of the fruit of concentration" (*samādhiphala-rūpa*), which follows [the practitioner].

The transformation [bodies] rely upon and freely enjoy the primary and secondary environments, yet they lack the physical forms of the faculties and the receptacle world produced by the karmic retribution of the Desire and Form Realms. "From this until the end" means that beyond this there are no other heavens;
thus, the illusory appearances of the three realms reach their conclusion here. Therefore, starting from the Sphere of Infinite Space...
Finally reaching the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, these are collectively termed the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
△ Second, concluding that these are all illusory:
"All these fail to understand the wondrous enlightened mind of clarity... down to the *pudgalas*, each following their own kind."

This is a summary stating that all three realms are entirely illusory. That is to say, from the six heavens of the desire realm up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, it is all because one fails to realize that one’s own fundamentally wondrous enlightened nature—the originally luminous true mind—is primordially devoid of such phenomena as birth and death or karmic retribution.
Consequently, by accumulating delusion upon delusion, the three realms are produced through delusion; this is why the various devas...
When the retribution is exhausted, one again follows deluded karma within those realms, sinking into the seven destinies to undergo their respective retributions.
*Pudgala* is translated here as "sentient being" (*yǒuqíng*) and also as "one who repeatedly takes rebirth" (*shùqǔqù*).

This refers to how sentient beings give rise to afflictions and create karma, repeatedly taking birth and repeatedly proceeding toward death within the three realms. As for why they take birth and proceed toward death: [it is due to the aforementioned causes].
That each and every being revolves through the classes of the seven realms according to their respective karmas of good and evil,
without a day of rest, is none other than due to the cause of false and deluded mental conceptions.
△ 7. The Realm of Asuras.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms (up to) those born from moisture, which are subsumed under the realm of animals—this clarifies the four types of asura realms.
In Sanskrit, they are called *asura*; here [in Chinese], they are translated as "Non-Gods" (*fei tian*). This is because...
There are those with much anger who possess celestial merit, yet because they lack celestial conduct, they are also said to be "not upright.
This is because while the husband is ugly, the wife is beautiful. They are also called "those without wine," for since their anger lacks harmonious energy, wine cannot be brewed.

Regarding the phrase "the power of the ghost-path's protective dharma," this refers to its prior causes; these individuals ascend by the power of virtue, though they subsequently descend from the heavens.
Virtue is likewise a prior cause; these beings fall [into their states] by the power of karma.

Those who uphold the world can also command spirits and deities, bringing calamity or fortune to human beings; however, their authority does not reach that of the heavens, and thus they are often angry and contend with them.
Originally, they contended for power with Śakra, yet the Four Kings constantly serve as Śakra’s vanguard. Or perhaps it was Śakra...
Śakra was not victorious; he likewise sought the assistance of Brahmā and others.
This is the king among the asuras, whose residence is beneath Mount Sumeru, in the midst of the great ocean, like Vemacitrin, who dwells within the waters of the Jambū River.
"Hand-attackers" (*shougong*) are of the same class as those who dwell in *Shanjian* (Good View). Those who are "lowly" are merely the subjects over whom they rule.
As for the "Aperture-mouthed" (*xuekou*), this refers to those born and raised at the mouths of oceanic apertures that discharge water; they reside directly at these openings.
This is what Zhuangzi meant by "the Tail-gate (*weilu*) discharging [the waters]"; for the Tail-gate is located to the east of the Azure Sea.
In that place there is a rock forty thousand *li* wide, situated at the bottom of a hundred rivers. Its tail forms the *lǚ* (village) and *zú* (clan), hence it is called "Tail-Gate" (*Wěilǚ*).

It is the cavern of the ocean and the mouth through which water is discharged. If classified according to the relative superiority of the seven destinies (*saptagati*), the asuras rank below the human realm;
however, because their affiliation is currently indeterminate, they are placed hereafter. Thus, regarding the six realms...
Each category has its own fixed place of inclusion; that which is subsumed under the asuras belongs to the four destinies (*gati*).

This not only reveals that there are four types of karmic retribution, but also shows that within each type, all four causes are present in combination. One simply observes which cause is predominant to determine into which destiny one falls.
For example, the medium-grade ten unwholesome actions serve as the cause for the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), while the lower-grade ten [unwholesome actions]...

Evil is the cause for rebirth as an animal; the intermediate grade of the ten wholesome actions is the cause for rebirth as a human; and the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions is the cause for rebirth as a deva.
If one’s wholesome or unwholesome karma is pure, one will accordingly receive the retribution of a hungry ghost, an animal, a human, or a deva.
Should one suddenly perform good and then suddenly perform evil, or suddenly fall to a lower state and then suddenly rise to a higher one, it may be that good and evil are intermingled.

In battle, throughout a single lifetime, the upper and lower realms may attack one another; because of this, at the very moment of a single thought, it causes one to receive retribution as death approaches.
The stronger force first drags one away: one may be born by way of the ghost realm through egg-birth;

or by way of the human realm through womb-birth; or by way of the heavenly realm through transformation-birth; or by way of the animal realm through moisture-birth. Yet, even if one is in the ghost realm, one can still...

Riding upon supernatural powers, they enter the void; though they belong to the realm of animals, they are able to roam the empty sky at dawn. Is this not a combination of the blessings of humans and devas?

As for those encompassed by the two destinies of humans and devas, although they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon and their power penetrates all things without fear, there are still three periods of suffering during day and night, such as rain falling like swords and blades, and food transforming into green mud. This is not...

Does this not also include the sin of treating spirits as mere cattle? Therefore, when the various heavens wage war against the asuras, they always divined victory or defeat based on the relative amount of good and evil among human beings.
If good deeds predominate, the heavens prevail; if unwholesome deeds predominate, the asuras prevail.
When the Heavenly Emperor and his forces fought one day, alternating between victory and defeat, it was because there was yet another factor at play in the world.
When a person intends to do good, a sudden evil thought may intervene; when they intend to do evil, a good thought may intervene.
Because they harbor such doubts and fail to reach a decision, it causes the Lord of Heaven to act in this manner.

Thus, for the practitioner, right and wrong, beauty and ugliness become intermingled within the divine mind, allowing suspicions and jealous thoughts to persist, and the desire for victory cannot be avoided.
One should likewise take this as a precept. This concludes the detailed explanation of the seven destinies above.
△ Third, concluding the discussion on delusion and exhorting to practice (in two parts): 1. Concluding the discussion on delusion.
Ānanda, it is thus that the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—up to the realms where existence and non-existence mutually oppose one another—give rise to the nature of saṃsāra.
This passage generally concludes the discussion on the causes and effects of the deluded mental conceptions of the seven destinies.

It means that when one minutely investigates the reasons for the ascent and descent, the coming and going, within these seven destinies, they all stem from the turbidity of emotional and conceptual thought, as well as ignorance, afflictions, and karma.

Because these serve as its causes, one experiences the various realms of rebirth—the phenomena of conditioned existence within the three worlds, rising and sinking—none of which fail to arise through birth in accordance with deluded thoughts and the reaping of rewards in accordance with deluded karma.

If, however, one realizes the inherently wondrous and originally perfect, luminous, unconditioned, and effortless True Mind that has existed from the beginning, then these seven realms of rebirth are all like flowers in the sky; they are merely appearances.
In the great void, there is fundamentally no place of attachment; it is nothing but a single illusion, devoid of any root or foundation, and likewise, no beginning can be found.

Ānanda, as for these seven realms of existence, all sentient beings have undergone this cycle of rebirth for many lifetimes precisely because they do not recognize their inherently existing true mind. Even throughout immeasurable kalpas, they will be unable to attain liberation.
True purity does not exist. Thus, while the four unwholesome acts are certainly all false defilements, even the three wholesome acts are not truly pure.
If one examines the reason for this, it cannot be without cause; they all arise from following along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, thereby forming the four unwholesome acts.
Even if one can turn away from these three types of actions, one may still give rise to [the notion of] "no killing," "no stealing," and "no..."
Sexual misconduct. Furthermore, these constitute the three unwholesome paths. If these three things exist, they are called the evil realms;
thus there are the classes of asuras, hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. If these three things do not exist, they are called the good realms;

thus there are the destinies of humans, seers, and the various devas. Because of the mutual displacement and subversion caused by the presence or absence of such good and evil, it is for this reason that—
The arising of the wheel of transmigration through the seven realms, which is of a conditioned nature consisting of false conceptualizations and emotions,

and the reason why it has not been obstructed or severed throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is entirely due to the causes and effects of these false conceptualizations and emotions.
△ Second, the exhortation to practice:
"If one attains the wondrous arising of samādhi... (up to) "...if another speaks, it is the speaking of Māra.
This is an admonition and encouragement for true cultivation, serving as a response to the previous question. The intent is that if one truly awakens to the wondrous [nature] inherently possessed...
As for the mind that gives rise to the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, it is able to realize the originally inherent, subtle, quiescent, and eternal true nature.
Therefore, because it is "subtle," there is no bondage within the seven destinies; because it is "eternal," there is no birth and death within the seven destinies;
because it is "quiescent," there is no wandering through the seven destinies. One need only reverse the hearing to return to such a nature.
Thus, there are four evils regarding existence and three virtues regarding non-existence; since both are absent, it is said that "existence and non-existence are both non-existent.

This marks a complete transcendence of the segmented birth-and-death (pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa) of both mundane and supramundane realms. One first attains the emptiness of persons and realizes *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Thus one exits the triple world. If one can further cause even this non-dual nature to be extinguished as well—precisely because it is said that "even the nature of cessation is non-existent," hence "non-duality is also extinguished"—then one transcends the provisional and Hinayana modes of birth-and-death involving transformation.

This is the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness, achieving the liberation of dharmas, until reaching the state where both are empty and no further arising occurs, thereby realizing the nirvana without remainder.

They abide in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and have attained *nirvāṇa*. At such a time, they do not even engage in the practices of the provisional vehicles or lesser sages—such as the precepts against killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct—let alone follow the conduct of ordinary people or externalists by committing acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
Such a state is the true, virtuous, and noble path; it is something they would not deign to practice, much less the wicked ways of Māra.
"Does the Way follow it? This section below provides the direct answer to the preceding question. The meaning is that Ānanda previously asked:
"Is there a fixed location, or does it arise spontaneously? As various karmas are initiated, do the three types of sensation each arise individually? Therefore, he answers:
"Because one cannot sever these three kinds of evil karma—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—for this reason, each [of them] exists individually."
Regarding their individual creation: because each [being] individually creates [their own karma], within the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of the multitude, there is no lack of a fixed location.
This means that although the creation of karma is private to each, the experience of its retribution must occur within that same commonality;
this is what is meant by "distinct karmas with a common retribution. Furthermore, from what do these hells of commonality arise? They are all...
The karma of one's own deluded imaginings is what causes this to arise. Since birth belongs to the realm of delusion, it has no cause;
therefore, there is no root or source that can be traced back or investigated to its ultimate limit.

Nevertheless, though no cause can be found through investigation, it must ultimately stem from the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as their fundamental basis. You must exert yourself with sincerity.
Regarding practice: if one truly desires to attain unsurpassed bodhi, one must necessarily sever these three kinds of delusion.
Since both the four evils and the three virtues are nothing other than delusions, it is essential to eliminate all three types of delusion completely.

If one does not fully eliminate these three delusions—for instance, if one merely eliminates the existence of the three while failing to eliminate the non-existence of the three—[one will not attain liberation].
Thus, one remains stagnant among the mundane outsiders and still dwells within birth and death.

Even if one attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as those of the celestial seers (*ṛṣi*), these are all worldly functions produced through conditioned effort; they are not supramundane, unconditioned functions.

Because they merely suppress active manifestations (*samudācāra*) without eliminating the seeds (*bīja*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) cannot be extinguished; when encountering conditions, they arise again. Even...
They may ascend, but in the end they will inevitably fall into the paths of celestial Māras and externalists.
Once fallen into these demonic paths, even if one wishes at this juncture to practice and eliminate delusion, one uses delusion to eliminate delusion, thereby doubling one's falsehoods. Why is this?
Because ordinary people among the devas and humans do not understand true cultivation; seeking it outwardly is already false, let alone [the further delusions that follow].
The non-Buddhists and celestial Māras are entirely devoid of right mindfulness;
yet, in their desire to eliminate delusion, they are truly substituting violence for violence and adding delusion upon delusion—thus increasing the falsehood within falsehood by another fold.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has taught that those in these seven realms of existence are truly pitiable and worthy of compassion. Furthermore, as to your previous question regarding the Buddha...
The essence is true reality. Why, then, are there those on the paths of humans, devas, and so forth?
Therefore, he replies: "It is your own deluded self-creation; it is not the fault of Bodhi. This clarifies that the various delusions appearing before you are all created by yourself;
they are not the fault or defect of the Buddha-fruit Bodhi. For this reason, the two types of affliction must be completely severed.

[These] are to be completely eliminated. If, in the final age, someone were to speak thus, exhorting others to completely eliminate these three delusions, that person would be propagating on behalf of the Buddha;

this is called the correct teaching. If, however, one praises these three types [of delusion] as being unimpeded, that person is merely repeating the heterodox teachings of the Mara-king. You must discern between them.

Thus, one knows that from beginning to end, this sutra uses the precepts to assist in the accomplishment of concentration and wisdom. Therefore, at the conclusion of the section on the seven destinies, it is revealed:
"All [beings] arise from following along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. This precisely clarifies the source of the afflictions experienced in the various destinies.
Hence, an ancient master said: "To practice meditation without maintaining the precepts is the work of Māra; this is false cultivation."
Regarding delusion, it is clear that the Buddha’s intention—to uphold the Vinaya and discourse on the eternal—is truly worthy of compassion. "Ming" (明) means to clarify;
"xu" (勗) means to exhort and admonish. II.
A second analysis of the five māras and their obstructive confusion (2): 1. A formal and detailed determination of the objects and activities of the māras (3).
First, a general announcement regarding matters concerning Māra that must be known.
At that time, the Tathāgata was about to conclude his discourse on the Dharma seat (up to the point where he says): "I shall now analyze this for you in detail.

This is an unasked self-exposition (*anāpṛṣṭa-svavādita*), intended to clarify the matters concerning Māra that must be known. This is truly because those present [the *adhikārika*] knew only how to request [instruction].
He was settled in meditative concentration, yet he did not recognize the demonic activities within that concentration. Furthermore, lacking the power of wisdom, he was unable to inquire about them.

However, the Buddha deeply understood the realms of dhyāna-concentration and the affairs of the demonic armies, knowing that they were crucial to the formation and destruction of the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.
The matters at stake are no small ones; therefore, having been about to cease, he remained and pointed them out one by one.

Now, those in the final age who cultivate right concentration should discern and distinguish between demons and outsiders so as not to be deluded by them. For this reason, out of his profound compassion, he spoke of his own accord without waiting for a request.
"At that time" and "below" are the narrator's descriptions; "about to cease from the Dharma-seat" clarifies [the context].
This is the final teaching. As for "turning the body to return," it manifests the inexhaustible nature of profound compassion.

When speaking solely of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), it is because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have already shattered the four aggregates; they need only eliminate the final fifth aggregate, the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).

For them, coarse external and heterodox objects—such as devas, ghosts, and spirits—no longer arrive. Herein, the discourse concerns exclusively the demons of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*).
As for the "objective realm," this is intended specifically for those in training (śaikṣa); therefore, it is singled out for mention.

The meaning is that although you all today possess the resolve to turn away from the Small Vehicle toward the Great, abandoning the teachings of the Small Vehicle to advance toward Great Bodhi, and casting aside the nirvāṇa with remainder to seek unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment—you may truly be said to have emerged from a dark valley and moved to a lofty tree.
Therefore, I have now revealed and expounded for you the true cultivation and actual practice of the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama.

Although I have taught such a Dharma, I fear that you may still not recognize all the subtle and hidden demonic activities within the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā in the practice of the Buddha-peak Śūraṅgama Samādhi. If [you do not recognize them] beforehand...

Know this: should a demonic realm suddenly appear before you, if you cannot recognize and shatter it to cleanse your own mind, but instead merely maintain right mindfulness, you will be deluded by even the slightest deviation and fall into false views; how can you not discern this?
For as for demonic affairs, they may be your own "hidden demons" (āntarāyika-māra), which are both general and specific. Generally, there are fifty...
These heavy objects are all termed the "demon of the aggregates" (*skandha-māra*), for they all arise based upon the five aggregates.

Specifically, the ten types within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are merely manifestations from within the aggregates themselves; they are called simply the substance of the aggregates and are not external intruders.

The ten types within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) involve external demons entering the mind, as well as encounters with malevolent spirits (*chi-mei*). The ten types within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) further involve the celestial demon (*deva-māra*).
And they become attached to ghosts and spirits. These two aforementioned obscurations both arise from gradually losing right mindfulness, which leads one into the influence of external māras.
Should a māra appear, if one cannot clearly discern and identify it within the mind, one may either consider oneself a sage or mistake the māra for a sage.
Both of these are cases of recognizing a thief as one's own child; then, before long, [disaster will follow].
Thus, one establishes the family treasure for the time of mourning. Furthermore, within these two categories of the mental and cognitive aggregates (*nāma-rūpa*), there are twenty types in total.
These do not exist as external objects; rather, they are the fault of the deluded mind giving rise to false views and being satisfied with a mere fraction of attainment.
Therefore, the text below immediately cites examples of those who hold such false views and are satisfied with little, using them to clarify this point. This...
Just as one who lacks learning, a bhikṣu merely cultivates the state of non-perception and takes no pleasure in hearing the Dharma.
Having obtained the four dhyānas as a karmic retribution, he escapes the calamities of the lower realms and then falsely claims to have realized the fruit of a Lesser Sage, the stage of Arhatship.

When his heavenly retribution is about to end, the mind of conceptualization arises again and the signs of decline appear before him; yet, not knowing that he had never actually realized the fruit from the beginning, he instead gives rise to [doubt].
With a mind of slander, he thought to himself: "I have already attained the fruit of Arhatship, yet today my body still undergoes further existence.
Therefore, I know that all that the Tathāgata has commonly taught is nothing but false speech. Because of this slanderous mind, he fell into the Avīci Hell.
Thus, for one with wrong views who considers a little attainment to be sufficient, the harm is such as this; how can one not stand in awe? Since—
However, since you wish to cultivate right concentration and proceed toward great enlightenment, you should recognize these various works of Māra.
I shall now, for your sake, distinguish them in detail and explain them clearly.
△ Second, the assembly rejoices and listens to the instruction.
Ānanda rose, as did those among the assembly who were fellow students; they joyfully prostrated themselves and listened humbly to the compassionate teaching.
This clarifies that he listened to the instruction with joy upon their meeting. Indeed, these are demonic occurrences within meditative concentration;
none but one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajña*) can discern them. At that time, the practitioner knew only that he was in a state of concentration, unaware that such things existed.
Thus, when he suddenly heard of these demonic matters, he involuntarily stood up in alarm. Not only did he prostrate with joy, but he also submitted.

That they listened to the compassionate instructions clearly demonstrates the great joy in their hearts, their sincere submission, and the utmost reverence of the great assembly for the Buddha and the Honored Dharma.
△ Third, the dual clarification of demonic activities, general and specific (three parts). First, the general clarification of the causes that stir up demons (two parts). First, the explanation.
Regarding the causes for the movement [of Māra], the Buddha told Ānanda and the great assembly: “[When you enter] samādhi, they will all come to harass you.
This clarifies the causes for the movement of Māra. Indeed, we ourselves inherently possess the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, which is primordial.
Because it is self-awakened, its function is subtle yet luminous; because it is awakened, its essence is profoundly perfect.
This is what is called the "ever-abiding true mind," the "essence of the nature that is utterly luminous.
Furthermore, this mind and this nature—in their entirety and great function—are fundamentally no different and not distinct from all the Buddhas of the ten directions. This is truly because...
In a single thought-moment, you failed to awaken; thus, ignorance and deluded conceptualization suddenly arose.
Consequently, you became deluded regarding the truth that is inherently present, resulting in the fault of unreality.

Thereupon, the fundamental ignorance of greed, anger, delusion, and craving emerged, followed by the activation of karma and the moistening of rebirth, all arising in an instant. From this, through false production and false manifestation, one will—
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which pervades the Dharma-realm, is deluded and thus becomes the boundless void.
For this reason, there exists the nature of emptiness; this is the delusion of the garbha-nature resulting in the nature of emptiness.

By obscuring true emptiness, one produces stubborn emptiness—this is what is meant by "the darkening of ignorance becoming emptiness. Thereupon, delusion further transforms into delusion without ceasing.
When it ceases, worlds arise once more from within that dull void; this is what is meant by "within the darkness of the void, the accumulation of darkness forms matter.

Viewed from this perspective, all the lands of even the finest atoms throughout these ten directions—whatever belongs to the outflows (*āsrava*) and is not free from them—are entirely due to sentient beings' failure to realize the fundamental source.

Awakened, one perceives that what was taken for the "vacuous void" is actually a "stolid void," and that by deluding oneself regarding the hidden nature, one gives rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
It is upon this false conceptualization that the world is established; this is precisely what is meant by "establishing the world based on the void.
You should know that the boundless, immovable void exists within your own true mind, like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky.
The interior is already so minute as to be insubstantial; it is a phantom creation and not real. How much more so, then, are all worlds that arise within the void?
Thus, their minuteness and insubstantiality, being phantom creations, can be known even more clearly.
This uses the arising of the void within your mind to illustrate how all worlds arise within the void. Suppose...
"Among you, were there even a single person whose mind was opened and whose understanding awakened, who illuminated the true nature, cultivated right concentration, and returned to the source;
who could cause the heart-light alone to be revealed—then this dark, dull emptiness of the ten directions would not fail to be extinguished and brought to its end.
How then could the knots of darkness within that dull emptiness constitute form?"

...of this land. How can it be preserved in its integrity without being shattered? This clarifies that the world of empty space is nothing other than the True Mind, which, through its obscured dullness, has coagulated into darkness.
For this reason, there are no suns, moons, or lamps; it is entirely shrouded in gloom.
This is precisely the phenomenal aspect of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, having cultivated right concentration, the mind-ground has awakened.
Because of this, the obscured and darkened are dissolved, and the knots of darkness are rent asunder. This is indeed the inevitable principle that when light arrives, darkness departs.

Nevertheless, you practitioners of śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna do so none other than to adorn the wondrous samādhi of the Śūraṅgama King, which naturally enables one to be with the sages and worthies of the ten directions.
Their vital energies harmonize, and their mental essences merge in perfect union. At this moment, they abide in profound stillness;
fundamentally, there is no fluctuation. As for all those heterodox practitioners, māras, and malevolent spirits or devils—
This is not the case for ordinary beings, the devas, and humans of the three realms.
They see their dwellings—whether palaces or halls—suddenly collapse and split apart without cause, causing the entire great earth to tremble and crack asunder.

Consequently, the sentient spirits of the rivers and seas that dwell in the water, the ghosts and monsters of the mountains and rivers that dwell on land, and the yakṣas who soar through the air [are all likewise affected].
Among the rākṣasas, there were none who were not struck with terror and cowed into submission. Yet, as for the human realm, all ordinary beings have minds clouded and consciousness obscured;
they fail to perceive at all this shifting transformation and deviation, remaining as they were before.

They all attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), with the sole exception of the one power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Since they still cling to worldly toil and yet know [the truth],...
Therefore, how could they bear it with equanimity? How could they willingly allow you all to crush, shatter, and tear apart their dwelling places?
This clarifies the reason why the celestial Māras, non-Buddhist heretics, malevolent spirits, evil ghosts, mountain sprites, and water monsters must cause such affliction:

for that upon which they rely is nothing other than a realm of perversion and darkness; yet when a practitioner cultivates meditative concentration and the light of the mind flashes forth, [they are inevitably destroyed].
It is able to illuminate and shatter the dark obscurity of ignorance and heterodoxy.

For this reason, when you are in stillness practicing samādhi, ghosts, spirits, heavenly Māras, and malevolent demons will conspire together, each exerting their full strength, baring their arms and vying for precedence, all coming to harass and disturb you, desiring to destroy your meditative concentration. "Qian" (僉) means "all."
△ Second, showing the gain and loss of delusion and awakening.
"Now, although those various māras may be greatly enraged" (up to) "they will roll about and fall away, with no one to pity or save them.

This demonstrates the gain and loss of awakening and delusion. The meaning is that although they may be greatly enraged and wish to come and disturb [the practitioner], [if they do not encounter the power of the Bodhisattva’s compassion, they will fail].
This will disturb your meditative concentration. However, he does not consider his own actions;

his are the perverse practices within the realm of worldly afflictions, whereas what you cultivate is the right concentration of wondrous enlightenment. Therefore, although the perverse may rage against the correct, it can ultimately do no harm.
When a person of the perverse seeks to harm the correct, it is like attempting to blow away the sun with the wind.
The light of the moon is like holding a blade to sever a long-flowing stream of water; yet it can never damage or cut that light-water.
Not only is it unable to inflict harm upon it, but it can instead transform it.
Therefore, you who practice meditative concentration are like boiling water, while those who cause you disturbance are like solid ice.
If one brings solid ice near boiling water, the warmth will gradually approach it, and before long, that solid ice [will melt].
It will naturally perish and vanish. Although they may vainly rely on the supernatural powers of the five *abhijñās* to cause turmoil from without, they can do no more than act as violent marauders.
Although you have not yet attained all such supernatural powers, if you can but give rise to not a single thought for even a moment, [the mind will be at peace].
If you remain steadfast within, you are ultimately the master. Furthermore, if you maintain your own defenses firmly, then even these violent guests will be unable to do anything.
However, that which brings about ruin and disorder does not depend on the violent guests;
it arises entirely from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within your own minds, which are the masters. Therefore, the violent guests merely wait for their masters to act. If this is so...
If the master loses right mindfulness and mistakes the thief for his own son, then that violent guest will be able to find an opportunity;
he will enter your house and plunder your precious treasures. Suppose your mind were the master of the five aggregates—at such a time as this...
Abiding in the samādhi of true dhyāna, not a single thought arises; there is no leakage whatsoever.
Furthermore, using the wondrous wisdom of the vajra, one observes and discerns, awakening to the state free from delusion.

Even if the power of those māras is violent and overbearing, they find no opening through which to enter and can do nothing to you. Once the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have been eliminated, one enters the Great [Vehicle].
The Treasury of Radiance: then those various māras, heterodox spirits, and monsters will naturally all be enveloped by the vapors of gloom and darkness.
From this time forth, they will dare to be angry but not dare to approach.
Because the radiance of your wisdom can destroy their darkness of ignorance, it is better that they do not approach; if they do approach, they will bring about their own destruction.
This is a calamity. It is like an owl entering the daylight or a rākṣasa facing the sun; naturally, it cannot move about lightly or recklessly.
How could it dare to remain here to disturb your meditative concentration?
If you, as the master of the five aggregates, cannot clearly awaken to those illusory phenomena—the various demons, both strong and weak—then fear may arise.

Attachment. Or, if you give rise to grasping and clinging, and slightly lose your alertness and illumination, even for the brief movement of a single thought, you will then be deluded by the various demons of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Since you, Ānanda, have already encountered such delusion and lost your right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), after the end of your life, you will surely become a child of the demonic family and achieve the nature of a demon. For instance:
The Mātangī girl was exceedingly young and lowly, yet she was still able to subdue you; how much more so, then, could a celestial Māra who is superior to her?
Moreover, that person’s initial intention was merely to cast a spell upon you to violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code in order to satisfy their own desires;
therefore, among the three thousand rules of majestic deportment and eighty thousand subtle practices of the Vinaya, [they failed to find a single transgression].
It can only destroy you by violating a single precept: that which forbids physical contact with a woman's body.
Because your mind is pure and fundamentally free from defilement, you do not commit a root offense;
thus, you have not yet destroyed the essence of your precepts and have not fallen into ruin. The mind of this demon, however, is not like this—it seeks rather to cause [your downfall].
You, whose entire body is composed of precious awakening, will surely cause you to lose the Dharma-body and directly sever your life-force of wisdom;
you shall remain forever a child of Māra until the end. Should you encounter such delusive confusion, it will be like a high minister’s family incurring the wrath of the Heavenly King.

Suddenly encountering his wrath, one’s family property will be confiscated and one’s kin will be seized; not only will one lose office and be demoted, but one shall also not escape the executioner’s axe and sword.
If you were indeed to destroy the entire body of the precious awakening, it would not merely mean that the fruit of the Way could not be attained;
you would also wander through the seven realms of existence and drown in the three miserable paths—what is called drifting aimlessly and being tossed about by the wind.

Dust falls and scatters; there is nothing upon which one can rely. At such a time, although the Buddhas possess great compassion and vast salvation, it is difficult to rescue those whose deviant minds have penetrated deep into their very vitals.

△ Second, a detailed explanation of the various realms of Māra (five sections). First, the realm of the Māra of the aggregate of form (three sections). First, a general clarification of the realm of the aggregates:
"Ānanda, you should know that from your sitting at the site of enlightenment... up to 'taking solid false imagination as its root.'"
This clarifies the boundaries of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) from its beginning to its end. As for the "site of practice" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is the field where the Way is cultivated.
According to the era of the Buddha or the final age, those of sharp faculties need only take a place suitable for peaceful dwelling as their site of practice.
However, if one intends to cultivate both phenomena and principle and seek realization within a fixed period, then following the ritual of the twenty-one-day altar, one should immediately do so here.
He dwells there and cultivates *samādhi*, even sitting upright in retreat for a period of one hundred days; this is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
"Dissolving all thoughts" means that, upon first sitting at the site of enlightenment, he screens out all deluded thoughts and mental activities.
This refers to the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, as described in the passage: "First, within the midst of hearing, entering the stream and losing the object. As for those thoughts...

"Exhausted" means that what was previously entered has already become quiescent. Because deluded thoughts have thus been completely eliminated, the various states free from thought—the eternally abiding true mind—naturally manifest.
Therefore, at all times and in all places, one should remain refined and unmixed.
It is luminous and not obscure; whether in motion or stillness, it cannot be shifted; whether remembering or forgetting, it remains the same in waking and sleep.
This means that the two prior characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise.

One who enters samādhi while abiding in this state is said to dwell securely in a mind where motion and stillness do not shift and where recollection and forgetfulness are as one. Thus, at that point—
In this state, through the cultivation of hearing and the refinement of what has been heard, one enters the Śūraṅgama Vajra Samādhi.
Nevertheless, as the power of concentration is not yet deep and the realm of principle has only just entered, one is still shrouded by the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

Thus, it is like a person with clear vision situated within a vast, pitch-black room. This is because, although the wondrously pure and luminous mind—the essential nature of the consciousness-essence—has been awakened, [it remains obscured].
As for its substance, it cannot yet be employed; because it has not yet emitted light, wherever it is perceived, there is only darkness and a total absence of radiance.
This is what is called the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). Regarding the term "domain" (qūyǔ):

this true mind is restricted and confined by the aggregate of form, hence it is called a "district" (qū); it is covered and concealed by the aggregate of form, hence it is called a "dwelling" (yǔ). This—
This is the sign that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) has not yet been shattered.

If the power of meditative concentration (samādhi) increases, the light of the mind will shine forth, transforming the preceding darkness entirely into radiance. Like the clarity of the eyes, one perceives all things clearly;
although one may not yet be able to reflect the great trichiliocosm in its entirety, one can see through all places within the ten directions before one without obstruction. Part I.
When both [sides] are opened up simultaneously, there is no longer any appearance of hidden, dark, or obscure phenomena;

this is what is called the "aggregate of form" (*rūpa-skandha*), which signifies its state of being completely shattered and eliminated. Now that the aggregate of form has been exhausted, such a person is able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
This is because emptiness is the root of form; it is by relying on emptiness that the realms (*dhātu*) are established, and by relying on the realms that time (*kāla*) is established. Thus...
Therefore, as soon as the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, one is able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

This is truly because we ourselves obscure and darken [our nature] into emptiness, thereby entering the turbidity of the eon; for immeasurable eons, we have long slumbered within the darkness of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Now, having shattered the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and departed from that profound darkness, it is said that one has "transcended.

Yet, when observing the origin from which this aggregate of form arises, there is nothing other than the very first moment of consciousness: through the establishment of obstruction by firm clarity, it becomes solidified and formed; thus, it is due to these deluded thoughts.
Therefore, there exist space, the four great elements, the five faculties, and the six sense objects, which interweave with one another to serve as their fundamental basis.

The infants they gave birth to all felt such compassion that they unconsciously shed tears.
However, this compassionate mind was not the same as the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) shared by all Buddhas; it arose merely because their internal effort at self-restraint was too intense.
For this reason, compassion arises. If one can quickly turn back and realize that this is not the correct path, then there will be no fault;

by not claiming it as a realization of a sage, it will naturally dissipate over time. However, if one claims for oneself that this is the same as the Great Compassion of the Buddha, then there is indeed compassion, yet it is the Mara who seizes the opportunity to enter the mind.
Seeing people, one weeps incessantly, thereby losing right concentration (*samādhi*) and falling into a perverted state of absorption. This is not [the true path].
Alas, one cannot advance by means of this, yet will surely fall away from it; how tragic! For there are five sensations:
namely, first, suffering; second, pleasure; third, sorrow; fourth, joy; and fifth, equanimity.
The present mind of compassion arises precisely because sentient beings undergo suffering.
△ Second, excessive emotion gives rise to vigor.
Ānanda, furthermore, those sons of good family within that samādhi (until) lose their correct reception and shall fall into ruin.
This clarifies that vigor arises from excessive emotion. As for "the skandha of sensation becoming clear and bright," it is because form is what receives [objects].
It was previously formed by darkness. Now that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been dismantled, the objects of perception and reception become clearly and vividly manifest.
"Superior characteristics" refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), meaning it surpasses the characteristics of the aforementioned aggregate of form.
"Manifest before one" means that as form has ceased, sensation manifests itself. "Excessive stimulation" refers to...
Because this removes one kind of material obstruction—the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)—it reveals a realm of empty luminosity;
thus, being moved by it, one gives rise to a mind of encouragement and inspiration. Although this belongs to wholesome thoughts, it is nonetheless excessive.
The reason one suddenly gives rise to such courage is the desire to swiftly attain Buddhahood. For this reason, the mind becomes fierce and sharp;
one resolves that in this very life, one must surely equal all Buddhas. One thinks: "While all Buddhas must cultivate for three incalculable eons, how dull they are!
If it were up to me, I would need only a single thought-moment to transcend them. Thus it is said.

How difficult this is! This is called "excessive application of effort. Because wisdom is frantic and meditative concentration is weak, one overreaches with negligence and transgresses the bounds of reason;
thus, such an interpretation is formed. If one were to realize this and turn back from it, there would be no fault.
If one persists in this attachment and does not turn back, then a mad demon will seize the opportunity to enter the mind, giving rise to great arrogance (*māna*).
Consequently, one will not wish to see the Buddha above, nor desire to see other people below; being self-important and conceited, one thus loses right concentration (*samādhi*).
And thus they fall into ruin. This is because they become deranged due to the pleasant sensations arising from their own minds.
△ Third, the decline of wisdom leads to the formation of memories.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (up to) lose their right absorption and shall consequently fall into ruin.

This clarifies that when concentration (*samādhi*) flourishes while wisdom (*prajñā*) declines, one becomes subject to recollection (*smṛti*). "There is no new realization" means the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered.

"Returning to lose one's former dwelling" means the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been exhausted. At this juncture, one should maintain both concentration and wisdom in equal measure; only then can there be no loss.
Now, however, the power of concentration is dominant while the power of wisdom is weak; therefore, one must advance [in wisdom].

In the interval between retreating, neither can be illuminated. Thus, having entered the middle space between form and sensation, although one wishes to move forward, there is no new realization to rely upon;
yet if one considers retreating, one loses the former dwelling place. Consequently, between these two states, there is no ground for advancing or retreating;
both thoughts collapse together, and both are simultaneously abandoned. Since there is neither illumination nor function, [the mind remains stuck].
As for the merit [of this], regarding the boundary of advancing and retreating, it is from this point on that they become utterly distinct and separate, such that nothing at all is perceived.
Consequently, within this state of concentrated mind, because there is no wisdom to provide mutual support, a great parching thirst suddenly arises.
Because this cause involves vacuous detachment from before and after, one’s thoughts sink into stillness and the mind dares not move.

Yet, by taking this very state of profound reflection and mindful recollection—wherein one dares not move—to be the mark of *vīrya* (diligence), one seeks to achieve the merit of breaking through the *skandhas*.
Is this not a grave error? This is called "cultivating the mind" while being biased toward concentration (*samādhi*) and devoid of wisdom (*prajñā*); thus, one loses oneself.
Regarding skillful means (*upāya*): if one can awaken to this and return once more to meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), then there will be no fault.

However, if one uses sunken recollection to wither and parch their meditative concentration, claiming to have realized the state of a sage, then the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*) will enter their mind.

The following section correctly clarifies the simultaneous loss of both progress and retreat: having neither the desire to move forward nor the desire to return, one employs deep reflection and recollective mindfulness.

This constitutes their primary activity. Therefore, day and night they constrain their minds, hanging them in anxious anticipation and calculation. They bind them to a single point, not daring to move.

This is precisely the state of withered dhyāna and deluded concentration—the mark of one who lacks wisdom to save themselves. Having already lost right reception (*samyaksamādhi*), [they remain thus].
Since falling into this state, this condition arises from the mind’s own equanimity (*upekṣā*), giving rise to parched thirst.
△ Fourth, the failure of superior wisdom to overcome inferiority:
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (up to) lose their right absorption (*samādhi*) and shall fall away.
This clarifies that when wisdom is strong and meditative concentration is weak, one becomes inferior. Regarding "the power of wisdom exceeding concentration and thus losing its intensity":
this means the power of wisdom surpasses that of concentration, yet it merely results in an excessive loss of vigor and sharpness.

Regarding "those who harbor the view of a superior nature": they falsely claim that one's own nature is inherently the Buddha and does not depend on cultivation for its realization; yet, in their seeking...
One constantly regards one's own mind and perpetually suspects that one’s very self is Vairocana Buddha, thinking there is no need for further cultivation.

Unaware that as soon as the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is broken through, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) remains entirely intact, such a person takes what is meager to be sufficient. Why is this?

It is because their application of the mind is biased, their power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is weak and prone to loss, while their power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) is excessively strong. They fail to maintain constant, careful scrutiny and awareness.
This is precisely because one is submerged in views and intellectual speculation. If one can awaken, there will be no fault.

However, if one stubbornly persists in this state of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and remains deluded without knowing how to return, then there arises the "inferior, easily-satisfied" demon who seizes the opportunity to enter the mind.
When such a person sees others, they claim, "I have already realized the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Consequently...
One loses right concentration and falls into ruin; this arises from the feeling of joy and the resulting complacency, because one harbors a sense of superiority.
△ Fifth, experiencing sorrow through traversing perilous paths.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) "will lose their right concentration and fall into ruin.

This clarifies that when both concentration and wisdom are deficient, one encounters hardships and gives rise to anxiety. "New realization has not yet been attained" means that the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) still remains.
"The mind has already perished" clarifies that the *rūpa-skandha* (form aggregate) has already been eliminated. Having surveyed...
Regarding "the two extremes naturally giving rise to hardship and peril": this refers to traversing the preceding and succeeding stages and surveying the midst between these two extremes;
unable to resolve what to adopt or reject, and having no direction to follow, one thus naturally gives rise to fear, apprehending the loss of what one guards.
Thus, whether advancing or retreating, there is difficulty at every turn, as if facing a profound abyss.

At that moment, an inexhaustible sorrow suddenly arises within one’s own mind, such that it feels as though one were sitting upon an iron bed. This leads to the thought of seeking someone to end one's life in order to attain liberation early;
this is what is called "cultivation. When fear in the heart becomes excessive and no further skillful means remain, one may merely resort to [this] for oneself.
It is for this reason that I have come to this state. If one were to reform their errors and forget their sorrows, they would naturally restore right mindfulness.
If one were to take such sorrow as proof of saintliness (*ārya*), then the demon of grief (*śoka-māra*) would seize the opportunity to enter the mind;

moreover, one might take up a blade to cut oneself, doing everything possible until one ultimately loses right concentration (*samādhi*) and falls into ruin. This is because, conditioned by the sensation of sorrow, one seeks self-harm.

...Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those sons of good family (up to) shall lose their right absorption and fall into ruin. △ Six: Realizing Peace Gives Rise to Joy. Also, within that concentration, those sons of good family (up to) shall lose their right absorption and fall into ruin.
This clarifies that joy arises from the lightness and ease born of concentration surpassing wisdom.
Because this is free from the obstruction of form due to the exhaustion of matter, one experiences clarity and attains purity. Abiding in this state, one is at peace and happy;

thus, great joy arises to such an extent that it reaches its ultimate peak and cannot be restrained. This is called the profound penetration of the power of concentration, and therefore it is attained.
That pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) arises as joy is entirely the fault of failing to restrain oneself with wisdom. If one can turn back and repent, there will be no blame.
If one were to claim that the mind of a sage delights in the Way and ought to be thus, then the demon of joy (*prīti-māra*) would seize the opportunity to enter the mind;
from this point on, one would indulge one's passions and follow one's whims, dancing, singing, and laughing, falsely believing that one has attained self-mastery.

There is no obstruction; all are liberated. Yet, they consequently lose right concentration (*samāpatti*) and fall into ruin. This is because the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*) arises from pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
△ Seven: Seeing superiority and forming pride.

Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right absorption and fall away from it—this clarifies how one who sees excellence but lacks wisdom gives rise to pride.

Thinking themselves sufficient, because they see the exhaustion of form and the clarity of sensation, they claim that the great task is already accomplished and their practice is complete, believing they have attained Buddhahood with something remaining; thus...
Thus, one falsely exalts oneself and looks down upon all noble ones (*ārya*). For this reason, there are the seven types of pride (*māna*) that arise without cause.
That which is born simultaneously with great pride (*mahāmāna*) refers to relying on oneself to oppress others; its essential nature is haughtiness, and it is the foremost among the seven prides.

This continues up to *māna* (pride), which means weighing oneself against others and comparing one’s own virtues with those of others; this is simply termed *māna*. Regarding others who are one's equals...
To consider oneself superior when one is not is called *abhimāna* (conceit). To consider oneself superior to those who are actually superior is called *mānātimāna* (excessive conceit).

To claim attainment of what has not been attained is called *adhimāna* (overweening conceit). To look back with self-congratulation despite knowing one's own inferiority is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority conceit).
To revile and destroy the scriptures and images is itself *mithyāmāna* (false conceit). If these seven types of conceit arise simultaneously within the mind, then in that state of mind—
One might think that one has already transcended the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, yet even so, one still holds all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time in low esteem;
how much more so for those of the Lesser Vehicle, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of inferior rank!
This is called seeing only one's own spirit as uniquely sublime and supreme, while lacking the wisdom to remedy this failing. If one employs contemplative observation, [one will realize the truth].
When contemplating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one does not even perceive the existence of sentient beings toward whom one might feel pride;
how much less so when the aggregates (*skandhas*) have not yet been shattered and one's practice remains weak and inferior—how could one dare to be arrogant toward the noble sages?

If one persists in delusion to the end without repentance or reform, then the demon of arrogance (*māna-māra*) will seize the opportunity to enter the mind, causing one’s madness to intensify until one goes so far as to destroy images of the Buddha, reducing them to mere bronze, copper, or clay.
He calls himself a living Buddha, eternal and true; he reviles the sacred scriptures as mere words and letters;
and he claims his own pronouncements to be the supreme, authentic teaching. He speaks with great arrogance without shame, misleading all and leading them into the Avīci Hell.
Consequently, he loses right concentration and falls into ruin. This is because, seeing only superiority, he lacks wisdom; it arises from the two feelings of joy and pleasure.
And thus various forms of conceit arise.
△ Eighth, being self-sufficient through light ease:
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) lose their right absorption and shall fall away from it.
This clarifies that through concentration one surpasses wisdom to attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and therein finds self-sufficiency.

"Entering the midst of refined clarity" means that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has already dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) is about to be exhausted. Having distanced oneself from the internal darkness of defilement, one enters into the midst of pure radiance;
furthermore, one perfectly awakens to the principle of such refined clarity within the aggregate of sensation, which is fundamentally thus.
The *ālayavijñāna* is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Once this principle is realized, the body and mind attain great mastery;
there is nothing that does not follow the mind, and nothing that does not accord with one's intent.

This is because the body and mind have become free from the defilements of all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), and an immeasurable bliss of lightness and tranquility spontaneously arises within them. Consequently, one may think, "I have now attained the fruit of sainthood."
One attains great mastery, becoming identical to all Buddhas—without duality or distinction—and need no longer practice further. This is called "causative concentration" (*hetu-samādhi*).
It slightly opens the nature of wisdom and temporarily brings about lightness and purity. If one realizes this is not yet realization, there is no fault;
however, if one remains settled within the realm of lightness and purity, then the "transcendent" demon (*atikrānta-māra*) will take advantage of the opening to enter the mind, leading one to say:
Their meritorious practices are already complete; their blessings and wisdom are already sufficient; they no longer seek further advancement.
Yet, such people delimit themselves by drawing boundaries, for the most part acting as ignorant bhikṣus. They bring ruin upon themselves and others, falling into the Avīci Hell.
As they are about to give rise to doubt and regret, they will inevitably slander the Buddha, lose right concentration, and sink into ruin. This is the causal condition.
Experiencing the two feelings of joy and pleasure, one obtains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and gives rise to a sense of self-satisfaction; consequently, the fault of lacking learning (*aśruta*) arises.
In short, this is because one has not realized the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
△ Ninth, attachment to emptiness and the destruction of precepts.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right absorption and shall fall away from it.
This clarifies that by clinging to the emptiness of annihilation, one thereby destroys the precepts. "Within clear awakening" refers to within the essence of cultivation.
Regarding "clarity": Yuanwu’s "clarity" refers to the principle. One who attains the nature of empty clarity perceives that the nature of empty-clarity delusion is fundamentally not truly existent;
yet, because they sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness, a thought of turning toward eternal extinction suddenly arises within their mind.
Consequently, they negate cause and effect, and thus cling to everything as being entirely... [non-existent].

This belongs to emptiness. Because the mind harbors such perverse seeds, if one persists in this for a long time without ceasing, the mind that clings to "annihilation-emptiness" will become fully realized before one.
Eventually, within the mind, false conceptions will arise and persist as a state of long-term annihilation.

Regarding such an understanding, if one awakens to the fact that this emptiness was originally a perverse calculation and not the realization of true emptiness (*tathatā*), there is no fault. However, were one to remain stubbornly attached to it...
To take the severance of stubborn emptiness as proof of saintliness is for the demon of emptiness to seize the opportunity and enter the mind;
consequently, one slanders the precepts, regarding them as the path of the Hīnayāna, while falsely assuming the status of a Bodhisattva. One delusively claims:

"If one merely attains the realization of emptiness, what need is there to uphold the precepts? Even drinking alcohol and eating meat are nothing other than fields of liberation. Thus, one becomes deceitful and greedy.
Lust is, in its entirety, the path to Bodhi; what further observance or transgression could there possibly be?

Because of the power of illusion, people are led to feel intimacy and trust, such that they consume food without distinguishing between the pure and the impure, considering it all to be equally empty.
They do this solely to subvert the Buddha’s Vinaya, to slander those who uphold the precepts, and to mislead many people into falling into [the abyss].

They undergo punishment in the intermediate hells and consequently lose their correct meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), falling into ruin. This occurs because they abandon feeling (*vedanā*) and achieve a conceptual understanding of emptiness;
it is the fault of having an excess of wisdom and a deficiency of concentration (*samādhi*).
△ Ten: Attachment with lustful desire.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (up to) lose their right absorption and shall fall away.
This clarifies attachment through lustful desire. Regarding "savoring its empty clarity," etc., it is because of the essence of empty clarity.
By nature, one develops a deep attachment and is unable to relinquish it; thus, a heart of craving arises.
Because the natural, sublime bliss within meditative concentration is beyond worldly comparison, its light and pure enjoyment is entirely to one's liking.

If one gives rise to greedy attachment toward this, one will consequently become deranged and fall into sensual desire. This occurs because the state of concentration is peaceful and harmonious as it enters the mind, yet lacks the power of wisdom.

Because they grasp at things as their own, they mistakenly enter into various desires. If one employs the power of wisdom to observe minutely and does not accept anything, returning instead to right reception (*samyak-samādāna*), then no fault will arise.
