If, however, one remains deluded and does not turn back, the Mara of desire (*kāma-māra*) will seize the opportunity to enter the mind;
such a person will claim that the pursuit of desire is the path to Bodhi and will even convert their followers to this view.
Reaching an incalculable number [of lifetimes], one day the mind of Māra gave rise to weariness and ceased to inhabit his body;
consequently, he was ensnared by royal law while alive and fell into the Avīci Hell after death. Thus, having now lost right concentration (*samādhi*), he has undergone this downfall.

This occurs because craving arises from the two sensations of joy and pleasure, and it also carries the fault of having meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without wisdom (*prajñā*). These ten cases above all speak of loss.

Regarding "right reception" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*): since receptions may be either deviant or correct, right reception belongs to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while deviant reception belongs to Māra.

Therefore, if one loses this right reception, one will follow deviant spirits and fall into ruin. However, while the preceding aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) all arises in dependence upon external objects, these subsequent four aggregates all depend upon the mind.
Thus, in this first [aggregate], when internal suppression is excessive, it gives rise to... [no-mind].
1. Excessive sorrow leads to exhaustion; 2. Excessive emotional arousal gives rise to boundless agitation; 3.

When intellectual power declines, one falls into deep-seated recollection; 4. When wisdom is strong but concentration weak, it conversely results in inferiority; 5. Because of having traversed both extremes.

Thus, they give rise to anxiety. Sixth, through the awakening of lightness and ease, they give rise to limitless joy. Seventh, by perceiving their own superiority, they give rise to great conceit (*māna*).
Eighth, because of their lightness and purity, they become self-satisfied. Ninth, by clinging to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they consequently destroy the precepts.

Tenth, by clinging to existence (*bhava*), they fall into greed and lust. Therefore, none of these escape the suffering, pleasure, anxiety, joy, and equanimity within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
These are the five characteristics.
△ Third, the conclusion, the warning against harm, and the exhortation to practice:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* (up to) maintaining and protecting [the mind] so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way."
I have recorded these hindrances and further encouraged their circulation to demonstrate them for the sake of future generations.
My intention is to show that the ten kinds of demonic activities mentioned above are all objective manifestations appearing within the mind of *dhyāna*.

However, these all arise because the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) has not yet been shattered and the application of the mind has not yet reached proficiency; thus, there is a mutual conflict between principle and desire, each seeking victory over the other.
Regarding these matters: from attaining radiant clarity up to attaining the nature of empty luminosity, all are instances where the power of contemplation overcomes delusive thought (*vikalpa*).
From the arousal of inexhaustible compassion up to the arising of limitless love, all are instances where delusive thought overcomes the power of contemplation.
This also carries the sense of the two engaging in combat, each having its victories and defeats. "Being deluded and unable to recognize oneself" means not knowing the light.

As for the radiance of the luminous void-nature, from what does it arise? To claim that one has attained sainthood when one has not yet attained it is called "great false speech," which results in falling into the Avīci Hell.

For this reason, you must transmit the words of the Tathāgata to the age of the Dharma-ending period, so that those who practice meditative concentration may awaken to this meaning and not be disturbed by demons. Thus shall it be.

One attains and maintains meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without being deluded or obscured; one guards right mindfulness so that it does not become disordered, thereby gradually practicing and realizing the Unsurpassed Way.
△ III. The Demon Realm of the Aggregate of Perception (3) — A General Clarification of the Realm of the Aggregates.
Ānanda, that good son who cultivates samādhi [up to] takes the delusion of fusion as its fundamental basis.

This is the stage of the final beginning and end of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) within the supernormal knowledges. Since form and sensation have already been exhausted, the first five sense organs and their objects no longer encounter one another;

the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) have been suppressed, and the conceptual grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) has likewise been suppressed. However, the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) remain entirely present.

Because innate self-clinging has not yet been eliminated, it is said that although the outflows (āsrava) have not been exhausted, since form and sensation have already ceased, one does not cling to the characteristics of the body;
thus the mind can depart from the physical form like a bird escaping from a cage, moving without obstruction wherever it goes. Regarding the sixty stages of the sages:
the three gradual steps serve as the means of advancement, while the fifty-seven stages constitute the objects of advancement. This is the relationship between the agent and the object.
Taken together, they total sixty. They are now collectively termed "Sages" (*ārya*) because they have entered the state of sainthood from the level of ordinary beings;
thus, the principles of cause and effect are identical. This precisely reveals perfect awakening and perfect realization—ascending from an ordinary body through the successive stages of the sages.

As for the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), it is so named by analogy with the mind’s movement, which is swift and unimpeded; it is derived from this metaphor. Furthermore, there are three [types].
There are three types: first, the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi; second, the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas;

and third, the mind-made body that is spontaneously born in accordance with its kind. These are spoken of in terms of partial realization; if one reaches the stage of ultimate awakening, [the classification differs].
Thus, with a single body, one manifests infinite bodies—namely, the pure *dharmakāya*, the source of both the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*.
It is like the single moon in the sky, which universally reflects in all waters; at that point, it is no longer called the "mind-born body" (*manomayakāya*).

Nevertheless, although the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) have been exhausted and the mind-born body attained, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered. It is just as if there were someone who is dazed and confused.

Deeply asleep, they are unaware and unconscious, yet they speak to themselves. Although these words may seem like long discourses or short treatises, in reality, they possess no understanding whatsoever.
Nevertheless, their somnolent speech and sleep-talk form distinct phonemes and follow a sequence without confusion, such that those who are not asleep can all comprehend their meaning.
This is analogous to when the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) has not yet [ceased].

Regarding "breaking": although one does not personally know the stages of cultivation, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fully know that this person, from this ordinary body, has passed through the sixty holy stages of a Bodhisattva;
within this interval, there have already been progressive advancements with their respective levels of depth and sequence.
This is precisely the sign that the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) has not yet been broken. If the sixth...

Consciousness conditions sensory objects and discriminates; perception and mind stir thoughts. If these can be exhausted, then floating, empty, and false imaginings will be eliminated from this point on.
This is like removing light dust and heavy grime from the pure, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind.

This awakened mind is like the substance of a mirror; the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is like dust and grime. When the dust and grime are cleansed, the light of the awakened mind shines forth.

Once the aggregate of perception is shattered and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is revealed, the cycle of birth and death for all classes of sentient beings within the triple world comes to an end.
They are all able to know from where birth comes and toward where death goes; thus, from beginning to end, they investigate with perfect clarity and penetration, such that nothing remains obscure.
This clarifies the sign that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted. For the essence of this aggregate of perception is the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*);
because the six consciousnesses take mental objects (*dharma-ālambana*) as their conditions, they give rise to afflictions, which turbidly cloud the True [Mind].
By this means, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted and one transcends the afflictions. Reaching this point, one looks back at the origin of the aggregate of perception:

it originally arises from pervasive delusive conceptualization (*yǒngtōng wàngxiǎng*), which, through mutual entanglement, forms delusion. This is because the aggregate of perception is capable of fusing together that which is substantial and obstructive.
This refers to such things as the mind imagining a sour plum and saliva flowing from the mouth. "Lun" (倫) means "category" or "type.
△ Second, specifically indicating demonic activities (ten points): 1. Craving for skillfulness.
"Ānanda, that good man, while the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, [will experience various states] up to being deluded and unaware, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell.
The ten types [of experiences] below all clarify the phenomena manifested within the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).

Here, first, it clarifies how through skillful attachment to perceptions one encounters demonic realms. The meaning is this, Ānanda: that good man has already broken through the aggregate of sensation."

One attains the subtle, wondrous, and vital function within the essence of the fundamentally enlightened true mind. This is precisely what was previously described as "turning back to observe apart from the body" and thereby attaining mastery;
it is not like the previous state where one had not yet attained such function. Thus, one does not encounter perverse thoughts.
This means that one no longer undergoes the perverse deliberations of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

"The perfect concentration brings forth illumination" means that once the first two aggregates have been shattered, one does not follow the distinctions arising from external objects; it is like clearing turbid water so that clear water appears before one.

All subsequent cases should be understood in this way. "The mind cherishes the perfect brightness," and so forth, refers to being within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), where one first attains perfection.

In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the light of enlightenment suddenly arises. With a heart of love, there is a yearning for attainment; with a mind of perfect clarity, there is nothing that is not perfectly known and perfectly illuminated.
Nothing is not skillful and successfully accomplished. Thus, one arouses indignation and fierce resolve, refining one’s thoughts and yearning for skillfulness.
The mind intends to employ great expedient means (*upāya*) to widely carry out transformation and instruction. It is from this single thought-moment...
If one harbors such greed, then the celestial Māras will find an opportunity. From this, they will fly like stars and dispatch their spirits to attach themselves.

Those who already possess a predisposition for evil and can be possessed are easily overcome; however, those whose aggregates (*skandhas*) have been exhausted and whose meditative concentration and wisdom are perfect and luminous cannot be shaken even by the preaching of sutras and dharmas, nor can they be deluded or disturbed by inferior demons and māras. Even if the celestial Māras...

Furthermore, it is difficult for [the truth] to enter the mind; therefore, he dispatches a malevolent spirit (*piśāca*) to attach itself to a person and delude them, causing them to destroy their own right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Thus, the Māra’s stratagem may indeed be called skillful.

If that person does not realize they are possessed by a Māra, then the person being possessed by the Māra likewise does not know themselves to be possessed by a Māra; consequently, even when they speak the scriptures and the Dharma...
Claiming for themselves that they had attained the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, bodhi, and nirvana, they came to the places of those skilled in arts, doing as they pleased.
At times they preached the Dharma, and at times they manifested transformations, extensively employing skillful means to stir their hearts.

Those seeking such skills, being deluded into thinking these were bodhisattvas, would naturally incline their hearts and place their trust in their teachings. Therefore, taking what [they had received]...
The mind practicing meditative concentration is entirely shaken and agitated; the precepts one upholds are all brought to ruin.

Generally, when a practitioner is possessed by a māra and lustful desires arise, it is first because the māras possess much greed and desire, and secondly because of the latent seeds within one's own mind.
Thus, whenever one is seized by a māra, greed destroys the precepts, and one is unable to attain liberation—this is precisely what occurs. However,
Those whose pure conduct is profound and whose wisdom is strong may exercise their skillful means beyond measure;

yet, if one observes that they incite lust and destroy the precepts, one immediately knows this is Mara and certainly not the Buddha. How could one allow the mind to be dissipated and the discipline broken, thereby becoming a child of Mara?
As for those who delight in speaking of portents such as calamities and blessings, these refer to people possessed by Mara, whose speech is strange and eccentric.
It is indeed strange and different from common talk; thus, it is able to incite and delude the minds of people.

To speak of the auspicious signs of a Buddha’s appearance in the world, and to speak of the calamities of the kalpa-ending fires and weapons—this is what is called "naming and designating to manifest harm.

These are the strange ghosts and the ghosts of the strange and absurd, those so-called spirits that take form by attaching to objects. It is only upon reaching old age that they begin to be employed by the celestial Māras to harm the Right Dharma.

This refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding "becoming weary and departing from the body": this means that after having been attached for a long time, the demon’s mind naturally becomes weary;

for this reason, it departs from the person upon whom it has attached itself. As for the disciple immediately seeking a skillful practitioner as a teacher: this refers to one who uses the Dharma to delude people.

A "foremost awakened one" (*pūrvajña*) is one who, by observing facial features and discerning complexions, immediately knows whether it is a demon; or by listening to their words and examining their principles [one gains such knowledge].
One then knows their falsehood. All such instances are perceived in advance; one is not deluded by them and thus does not enter saṃsāra.
If one were to be misled by them and fail to recognize their error, one would fall into the Avīci Hell.
△ Second, the experience of craving.
"Ānanda, furthermore, if a good man [perceives] the aggregate of sensation as empty and subtle... (up to) "...being deluded and unaware, he falls into the Avīci Hell.

This clarifies how the experience of craving leads to the influence of Māra. The passage beginning with "the aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle" follows the previous pattern. This is because...
Having already detached from the two aggregates of form and sensation, one is no longer constrained by physical substance.

Consequently, a heart of love arises, desiring to emulate the various sages by sporting with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Without leaving one’s current location, one pervades all dust-like lands (*rajas-kṣetra*) to perform Buddha-works;
hence it is called "loving the mind" (*xin'ai*), sporting and roaming freely in pursuit of self-mastery. Thereby, the spirit and soul desire to fly upward, exhausting [all worldly attachments].
Regarding his vital energy, he contemplated it morning and night. Because of this single thought, the celestial Māra found an opportunity and immediately flew like a shooting star.
He dispatched a spirit to possess a person and go forward to delude him. As for the one possessed by the Māra, he did not transform himself, but rather transformed into another form.
As for those who appeared before him as Buddhas, they were due to the seeker’s greed and his experiences; such was the state of mind established by that practitioner.
As for his ambition: wishing to be equal to the various sages, he causes his body to sit upon a precious lotus and his form to become a mass of gold.

Since he is already able to do this, what concern could there be that his wandering ambitions will not be fulfilled? This is precisely to cast a hook where his preferences lie. "This person" refers to one who seeks to experience [the supernatural];
since they have been possessed by a demon and are deluded into thinking they are a Bodhisattva, they will naturally offer their sincere devotion. And...

I take refuge [in this]. Those whose minds are licentious and dissolute rely on their own self-assumed realization of sainthood; they act with unrestrained indulgence and playfulness, having no sense of awe or avoidance.

Consequently, the mind that was intent on perfecting meditative concentration is transformed into a mind of unrestrained desire, and the body that maintained the precepts is turned, instead, into a body that violates them.
All that is spoken from the mouths of Māras takes the present moment to be the Buddha-land.
Because those practitioners intend not to leave their current location while simultaneously pervading all dust-motes and lands, these [teachings] are spoken to accommodate their inclinations.
Once their inclinations are accommodated, they will direct their hearts toward yearning and aspiration, thereby turning back from the heterodox to return to the orthodox.
This is called "pointing downward to the demons to reveal their harm. The *pó-guǐ* (魃鬼) refers to the drought-demon (*hàn-pó*), which is formed upon encountering the wind.
Form. Since his years have grown old, he serves at the beck and call of the celestial Māras. The remainder is explained according to the previous interpretation.
△ Third, the convergence of craving.
Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle... [up to] ...being deluded and ignorant, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
This clarifies that through the convergence of greedy thoughts, one brings about demonic interference. "Mian" (綿) means distant and subtle. "Hun" (淴) means convergence.
This means that they desire to reach far toward the subtle principle and secretly accord with the Buddha-mind.

Thus, they clarify their spirit and still their thoughts in order to greedily seek such a resonance. In short, their intention is to achieve spontaneous awakening without relying on physical forms or sounds.
Because they greedily crave this secret resonance, Māra seizes the opportunity to dispatch spectral spirits to attach themselves to those of heterodox ways. Consequently—
This is to entice them by manifesting the matters of secret realization. Regarding the phrase "the mind awakens of its own accord" and so forth: this refers to those who have attained awakening;
within their own minds, from moment to moment, they undergo further shifts and transformations, gradually entering deeper and deeper.

Consequently, there are those who attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-jñāna*) and thus know events prior to their birth, or those who attain the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). And...
They discern the beginnings of people’s thoughts and intentions, even down to their recitation of verses and sutras;

there is nothing that does not manifest as a state of opening the mind and attaining secret resonance, all for the purpose of deluding and ensnaring practitioners. Such a person is one who greedily seeks such a resonance.
"Those whose hearts are deeply attached" refers to those who, being deluded by Māra, also give rise to persistent attachment, desiring only to fulfill what their minds seek.
Once the practitioner has fallen into the realm of Māra, Māra further utters demonic words, gradually leading them deeper and deeper.
Therefore, because there is the matter of a secret initiation, they come to believe these extraordinary demonic words, and consequently...

Having intended to follow the original resolve previously made to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one instead washes it away until it is exhausted, thereby entering into false knowledge and false views.
This is called "inferior" (*adhas*); here, the name is cited to demonstrate the harm. "Malignant ghosts" (*māyā-pretas*) refers specifically to demonic and specter-like spirits.
This is what occurs when one encounters an animal that has taken form.
△ Fourth, the obsession with analytical disputation:
Furthermore, good son, if the *skandha* of sensation becomes empty and subtle (up to) being deluded and ignorant, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
This clarifies that the principle of analyzing the transformation of things through the conceptualization of craving leads to the arising of Māra.

"The root of mental attachment" refers to the love that exhaustively seeks the root of all phenomena. This serves as a general heading for the following four lines, which explain the exhaustive examination of the beginning and end of the nature of the transformation of things;
this is just as the Buddha taught: one must know the origin of both mundane and supramundane dharmas.

For this reason, all the various things appearing before one—such as pines being straight and thorns being crooked, cranes being white and crows being black—all have their fundamental causes fully understood.
Even down to a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, their total number is known.

This is what is meant by exhausting the beginning and end of the nature of things and thoroughly comprehending their fundamental source. One who refines and clarifies the mind is able to do so universally.
To know the beginning and end of all phenomena, penetrating them one by one, causes the spirit within the mind to become clear and bright, and thus expansive.
Those who seek through greed for analytical discrimination desire to distinguish and dissect the myriad phenomena before them, so as to be distinct and free from delusion.
However, all of this is the transformation of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas; it is the perfection.
The realm of the mirror’s universal illumination—how could it be something to be sought through the false greed of a beginner’s cultivation?

It is by this single thought that one invites a thief into the house; thus, the māras take advantage of the opportunity to cause disturbance and confusion. As for "subduing them through majestic spiritual power": [it refers to the power of the Tathāgata].
This means that the power of Māra is well able to crush and subdue the minds of people; therefore, those who hear the Dharma believe they have been subdued by it.
"The various people" refers to those individuals who receive Māra’s teachings and transmit them from one to another.
Because those people seek the source with their hearts, Māra—who has taken possession of them—speaks only of the phenomena of present arising and ceasing.
The physical body is the root of the three virtues; the manifestation of the fingers and hands is the source of permanence.
This pure method is precisely this very form of impure objects and marks; it is entirely my own body, for it accords with the desire for the fundamental source.
Yet practitioners are deluded by this, and thus lose their initial resolve for meditative concentration from this point on, believing only in what is before their eyes.
Father and son succeed one another in birth; thus, they take the two organs of male and female to be the fundamental source of all transformations.
They believe that the three fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding are entirely contained therein. Consequently, practitioners draw closer and closer to this view day by day.
Gradually entering and gradually deepening, they ultimately become children of Māra without even realizing it.

For that celestial Māra first employs his demonic power to crush and subdue them, and subsequently utters foul words to bewitch and delude them; thus, those of initial resolve and shallow practice [fall prey to him].

There are few who are not deluded by these and thus break their precepts and ruin their meditative concentration. The phrase "these are called" (下) refers to naming them specifically to indicate their harm.
*Gǔ* (蛊) refers to the *gǔ-dú* ghost; it takes form when encountering insects. *Yàn* (魘) refers to sleep paralysis (*yàn-mèi*); it takes form when encountering the dark or hidden spirits.
In the world, there are arts of suppression used to subdue such phenomena, which are also termed "overcoming sleep paralysis" (*yàn-shèng*).
△ Fifth, the dark resonance of greed.

Furthermore, when a son of good family experiences the emptiness and subtlety of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and ignorant and falls into the Avīci Hell—this clarifies that the dark resonance of greedy thoughts leads to a silent seeking that elicits a remote response, thereby bringing about the arrival of Māra. Regarding "the love for a remote response," it is remote...
"Remote" means that through one's own practice, one seeks to evoke the response of the Buddhas of the distant past.
This is the general heading; the following two phrases provide the explanation. "Pervasive circulation" means to survey everywhere and seek without ceasing.
"Meticulous investigation" means to contemplate with refined thought and to seek with ultimate sincerity. [This constitutes] profound resonance.
This means that one intends to take this sincere thought toward the profound darkness to move the Buddhas.
Because of this single thought’s false movement, heavenly demons and flying spirits immediately possess people, even to the point of preaching the Dharma, responding to that resonance.
As for "a hundred thousand years," it refers to the demon manifesting the appearance of extreme old age. Those sitting below, upon seeing this—

Because one is advanced in years, attachment arises and it is difficult to relinquish; furthermore, one is deluded into thinking [the teacher] was a master from a previous life or a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) from a former birth.
Thereupon, a distinct "Dharma-attachment" arises, as sticky as glue or lacquer, such that one cannot bear to part.
These are all people possessed by Māra, who permit the manifestation of signs of response. Once the practitioner is thus deluded by them, they draw near to the [teacher].
For a long time, they have inwardly believed in these appearances and abandoned the correct for the deviant, eventually becoming the children of Māra without even realizing it.
Furthermore, the devils first manifest matters of dark resonance within their bodies, and then proclaim words of dark resonance with their mouths.

How could a beginner practitioner not be deluded by such things? The "pestilence ghost" (*nairṛti*) refers specifically to the malarial pestilence ghost that manifests when one encounters a state of decline.
△ Sixth: Craving for Quietude.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle emptiness of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and unaware and falls into the Avīci Hell—this clarifies that through the desire for the tranquility of conceptualization, he seeks to penetrate deeply and thereby invites the Māra. This refers to one whose mind craves deep penetration.

This refers to the state where one intends to thoroughly investigate the objects of meditative concentration and enters them to the utmost depth. This phrase indicates the concentration itself, while the subsequent explanation establishes its nature.
"Exerting oneself with diligent toil" means that through the effort of self-discipline, one disregards all hardship and seeks only to enter deeply.
The reason one delights in dwelling in secluded, dark, and solitary places is solely the desire to seek and cultivate tranquility, in order to achieve the merit of deep penetration.
Yet this very single thought is the very beginning of inviting demons.
For this reason, when the celestial Māra sends those possessed by evil spirits to come and preach the Dharma to them, it is to entice them. Furthermore, the Māra is also capable of...

"Announcing one's own karma" refers to the supernormal power of knowing past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). "Becoming an animal before dying" refers to the supernormal powers of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the miraculous powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), and the knowledge of past lives.
"Arising the mind to know the beginning" refers to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*).

"Exerting extreme asceticism beyond the Buddha’s discipline" refers to practices such as abstaining from the five flavors, going naked, plucking out one's hair, and so forth. "Slandering and exposing [others]" and...

Regarding the statement that "misfortunes and blessings are all verified as they arise," this refers to depicting demonic, heterodox, and eccentric phenomena to demonstrate the ability to know the past, future, and present.

Although these aforementioned supernormal powers manifest through deceitful and heterodox means, there are few who are not deluded by them, especially those whose mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) has not yet been clarified. As for the "powerful ghosts," these possess superior supernormal powers.
It is a great ghost. Some say that this passage marks a chapter heading and should be transposed to the following section;
by moving this text [concerning] "tranquility" down and moving the text [concerning] "past lives" up, it would correspond perfectly.
While this argument certainly has its logic, the translation was established long ago; who would dare to claim for himself the title of primary translator?
△ Seventh is craving for past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).
Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, one may become deluded and fail to realize that one is falling into the Avīci Hell.
This clarifies that by craving thoughts of past lives and desiring to seek knowledge and vision, one invites Māra. This refers to those whose hearts cherish such knowledge and vision.
The underlying intention is the desire to seek that which the world does not know but oneself alone knows, and that which the world does not see but oneself alone sees.

This establishes the premise, which the following section explains in detail. It is because of attachment to knowledge and vision that one does not shrink from toil and suffering, but instead engages in research and reflection;
this is nothing other than the pursuit of past lives (*pūrvajñāna*). Due to this pursuit, Māra—
They then attach themselves to people and manifest strange phenomena of appearing and disappearing to delude them. "These people" refers to those who are greedy and seeking;
"obtaining a pearl without cause" means acquiring the pearl at the place where the Dharma is being heard.

That māra may transform into an animal and first carry a rare and precious object in its mouth to bestow upon such a person, or it may entice listeners, causing them all to conceal [the object] within.
"Below the earth-cave, there is moreover the 'bright moon pearl' (candraprabhā-maṇi) which illuminates that place;
this is like the practices of recent times such as closing one's door to transmit the Way, or descending to the earth to ascend to heaven.

Or, by eating medicinal herbs, even down to hemp and wheat, one is able to remain full and robust—all these are matters of falsely manifesting hidden wonders that are difficult to fathom, employed to cater to their desires."—Māra.
They are able to manifest strange and miraculous events that strike terror into people's hearts, and they further utter strange and miraculous words that bewitch the wills of the masses;
there are few who are not deluded and confused by them. These are all [the works of] such beings as those dwelling in mountains, forests, rivers, and peaks.

As he grew old, he became an agent of Māra. When asked about the deities of the local soil, the city wall, and the rivers and mountains—whom the world universally regards as orthodox deities—why it was that they had now become agents of Māra, the answer was:

"Although these deities are fundamentally upright, because they did not cease from lust and killing, and furthermore propagated lust and violated the precepts, they have ultimately become [agents of Māra] in their old age."
They are the retinues of Māra, driven and enslaved by him. "To proclaim licentiousness" means to speak of lewd matters;
it refers to instances such as those in the *Zuozhuan*, where Duke Ling of Chen practiced promiscuity in the court and the ruler and his ministers engaged in lewd jesting.
Some [versions] have "or even lower," all of which clarify that the factions of Māra are flourishing and not merely one or two; furthermore, their specific actions also differ from one another.
△ Eighth, the power of greed for supernatural abilities (*ṛddhi*).

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, [the practitioner] may fall into delusion and ignorance, thereby descending into the Avīci Hell.
This clarifies that the power of supernatural transformations born of greedy thoughts leads one to become possessed by Māra. The mind craves supernatural powers; this is the seed.
Regarding "various transformations": this refers to seeking supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that manifest in a thousand ways and ten thousand changes without obstruction.

This heading establishes the premise, which is then explained below: it means to investigate and exhaustively research the fundamental source of all transformations with the intent of riding upon them to manifest supernatural powers and transformations.
Because of this craving, Māra immediately attaches himself to the person and falsely manifests miraculous feats. By means of these...

This is delusion. Such a person is one possessed by a demon. Whether they grasp firelight or pass through windows and walls without obstruction, all these are false displays of supernatural powers intended to pander to what is liked.
Only when one is unable to wield weapons at will does one realize that these are illusions produced by heterodox arts and are not real; thus, they differ from the sages and worthies.

This is their true supernatural power (*abhijñā*). As for the statement that they "constantly speak of supernatural powers and the like from their mouths," it means that these demonic spirits not only fraudulently manifest illusory displays of miraculous transformations, but also deceitfully preach perverted teachings on supernatural powers, intending to pander to the preferences of practitioners.
To "vulgarity and obscenity in the transmission of the Dharma" refers, for example, to the practice of modern times known as "measuring the breath at the navel."
"Of a similar kind" means that which does not destroy [the mind], namely, praise. This refers to praising coarse and evil conduct;
thus, one's perverse thoughts become even more evident. The phrase "below this" indicates the naming and demonstration of harm. Regarding "the great power of Heaven and Earth," etc.:

It is clear that as the variety of types increases, the harm becomes more intense; thus, as the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) increases, the demonic afflictions become more widespread.
This is precisely what is meant by the worldly saying: "When the Way is one chi high, the demons are ten chi high."
△ Ninth: Greed for the Profound Emptiness.
Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes void and subtle, [the practitioner] falls into delusion and ignorance, descending into the Avīci Hell.
This clarifies that greed for the profound emptiness of ideation leads to demonic interference. Regarding "the mind loving entry into extinction," it is because he does not know [this].
The characteristics of all phenomena are inherently quiescent from the beginning; they do not depend on further extinction to become non-existent.

Therefore, one seeks to extinguish phenomena that possess characteristics in order to enter the emptiness that is without characteristics. This [passage] sets forth the thesis, which will be established through the subsequent explanation.

"Investigation" (*yanjiu*) means to examine with precision and exhaustively investigate. "The nature of transformation" (*huaxing*) refers to the essential nature of the myriad transformations. Thus, one investigates the nature of transformation.
This person merely desires to extinguish appearances and return to non-existence, seeking to enter deeply into emptiness and stillness.
Because of this single thought, Māra immediately possesses a person to disturb and confuse him. Amidst the great assembly, he follows his greed to enter extinction and pursue emptiness;
therefore, he manifests various signs of emptiness to cater to what that person favors. That his hands and feet were fragrant and like rock honey was entirely due to...

They manifest extraordinary phenomena to dazzle the world and alarm the common people. The two phrases regarding "slander" refer to slandering the Dharma and the Sangha based on the characteristics of emptiness.
Regarding the phrase "constantly speaking such things with their mouths," it means they speak only of nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*) to clarify that there are neither causes nor effects.
The phrase "though having attained empty stillness, they secretly practice lustful desires" reveals that these are demonic spirits and not the realization of a sage. [The text ends with] "receiving."

As for those who desire [such things], they likewise attain a "void mind" (*kōng-xīn*). Those who repudiate cause and effect are held under the sway of this demonic power, for they follow its transformations.
The phrase "below this" refers to naming and manifesting the harm, so that people may recognize it in advance and verify it for themselves.

Regarding the "dimming of the vital essence" (*jīng-qì*): the *Jingfáng Yìchuán* states that when the sun and moon appear red or yellow, it is called a "dimming" (*bó*). Furthermore, even when there is no conjunction...
An eclipse is called a "thinning" (bó). This refers to the malevolent vapors of the seven luminaries, which act as the spirits of eclipses.
Furthermore, although gold, jade, and numinous fungi are insentient objects, when they are possessed by spirits and monsters, they too are designated by these same terms.
△ Ten: Greed for Longevity.

Furthermore, when a son of good family experiences the subtle and wondrous nature of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and unaware that he has fallen into the Avīci Hell—this clarifies that the thought of greed for longevity leads to the influence of Māra. "Ji" (幾) means "subtle. This arises from craving for longevity.
Therefore, disregarding hardship and toil, they study the subtle principles of longevity, greedily seeking the path to eternal life.
According to the traditional explanation, the stage of Arhatship sought herein would be realized naturally after the discernment of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Now, desiring to realize it urgently, they seek it with restless haste; thus, they invite demonic harm. This is because [they have not yet transcended] the death and rebirth of the limited realm (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).
Only when the delusions of the three realms are exhausted can one transcend the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles;

only when a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*) has severed both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and entered the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) does he undergo the transformation of birth and death (*pariṇāmika-jāti-maraṇa*).

Now, as you have not yet left the three realms, yet wish to suddenly transform this coarse body into a subtle substance and change this short lifespan into a long one within the retribution of the segmented existence (*prādeśika-vidha*), it is therefore said: "to discard."

Those who seek to transcend birth through gradual stages and suddenly aspire to the transformation of the body, desiring to attain subtle characteristics and eternal abiding, may find themselves traveling ten thousand *li* in an instant;
such a phenomenon among the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) appears to belong to the power of psychic travel (*ṛddhivisaya*), yet it is merely a magical display manifested by a demon.
Thus, that which is extremely distant is made extremely near; and that which is but a few paces away may not be reached for many years.
This demon causes people to personally experience this, whereby the near becomes far.
Indeed, that the earth can contract or expand, and time can be prolonged or shortened, are all deceptive manifestations of the demon intended to delude and confuse the human mind. Because of this—
Regarding this mind that doubts whether the Buddha has appeared before it: this refers to those whose wisdom is slight and whose practice is inferior;

seeing little and suspecting much, they give rise to their own astonishment and fall into the midst of his arts. They constantly say with their own mouths that the Buddhas and their lands—the primary and secondary realms—arise entirely from him.
This clearly reveals that he is the primordial Buddha from beginningless time; thus, his long life and eternal longevity are indeed possible.
One knows this through reflection. Yet, those demonic spirits first manifest matters of long duration and further utter words concerning longevity;
how could those who greedily seek eternal years not believe them? The phrase "named below" refers to identifying the specific names of those who cause harm.
As for Maheśvara, he dwells in a separate abode of the Māra King atop the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). He is also another...
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven governs its retinue; this refers to the Demon King (Māra) not manifesting his own body, but rather dispatching his essence like a shooting star.
Cāmuṇḍā is called a "slave deity," which refers to a servant ghost.

She is also called the "jealous woman" or the "Vijñā-gaṇaka" (Vijñā-kumāra), which refers to the Piśāca ghost who consumes vital essence (*ojas*). All of these are subordinate to the Four [Great Kings].
As for the heavenly kings (*deva-rāja*): if [the practitioner] has already resolved his mind [on awakening], they protect him; if he has not yet resolved his mind, they harm him.
Because the practitioner’s concentrated mind is fixed, empty, and luminous, it becomes a benefit to them; thus, they consume his vital essence to harm him.
"Or not due to a teacher" means that it does not occur because of a teacher possessed by a māra;
rather, the practitioner personally sees the body of a māra, which may manifest as a Vajradhara or appear as a beautiful woman to harm them, while simultaneously speaking to themselves alone.
This refers to a practitioner speaking face-to-face with a māra; bystanders, not understanding this, think he is merely talking to himself.
Yet if one listens closely, it is as if with a malevolent spirit. The "former person" and "that person" are precisely those who have been deluded by the practitioner.
Those who do not investigate thoroughly cannot discern whether it is a māra or a sage, and thus they are deluded by him and even engage in sexual desire with him.
They frequently fall into royal calamities; before they even encounter execution, their vital energy has already been exhausted, and they die of parching thirst.
This arises from being deluded by demonic influences, whereby they meet with the king’s law in life and enter hell after death.
These ten types [of practitioners] all stem from the fact that, within the mind of perfect concentration, they falsely give rise to thoughts of greedy seeking. For this reason—

Indeed it is so. If one practices such Dharma-conforming diligence, such that not a single thought arises and one cultivates and realizes through the illusory nature of phenomena, then what skillful means would remain unattained?
What realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) would remain untraversed? What principle of capacity would remain unharmonized? What fundamental [nature] would remain unanalyzed?
What resonance and response would fail to be realized? What state of profound stillness would remain unentered? What of past lives...?

I do not know what spiritual powers they lack, what profound emptiness they have not realized, or what eternal abiding they have not attained, that they should suddenly give rise to a heart of attachment and fix their minds on greedy pursuit.

It is like thinking of soaring and leaping before scales and horns have formed, or attempting to ride the whirlwind before feathers are sufficient; it is as the saying goes: "Seeking office before one's learning is yet refined," or [the cinnabar]...

To swallow [the food] before it has been fully digested—is this permissible? Therefore, one should know that those who summon demons and fall into transgression do so entirely through the fault of their own deluded thoughts.
△ Third, the conclusion on the harm and the exhortation.
Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras [will] maintain and protect [the practitioner] until they achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
This concludes the section on the harms of the ten kinds of māra-realms; it is intended to exhort those who are currently practicing and to be transmitted to future generations.
Regarding those who cultivate the path within the Dharma, some may associate with bhikṣus, while others may manifest themselves in the form of bhikṣus. Formerly, when the Buddha dwelt in the world...
Māra desired to destroy the Dharma, but because the Buddha possessed supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he was unable to do so. Māra made a vow, saying: "I shall wait until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
then, having left the household life according to the teachings, I will destroy the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha then shed tears and said: "There is nothing that can be done against you.
It is like a worm within the body of a lion that eats the lion’s own flesh. The present sutra says: "Or those who manifest their own forms."

This refers to those who manifest themselves in the form of renunciants. All those who claim to have already attained perfect, universal enlightenment are merely using the false names and appearances of renunciants;
they are in fact the sons of Māra who destroy the Dharma. According to the ten types mentioned previously, only the tenth type manifests itself;
the others all attach themselves to human beings as Māra-teachers and Māra-sons. Regarding the phrase "passing it down through successive generations of lustful transmission," it means that by—
Lustful conduct spreads to others, its harm extending to future generations and widely destroying those with right faith.
"In the near term, nine lifetimes" means one hundred years constitute one lifetime; this refers to nine hundred years from now, when the True Dharma is about to perish.
"For many more than a hundred eons" means thirty years constitute one eon; this refers to three thousand years from now, when the [True Dharma]... [will be extinguished].
This refers to the period of the Final Dharma (*mappō*). Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"In the final age, the followers of Māra will manifest in the forms of bhikṣus, arhats, and so forth, to corrupt and destroy the True Dharma and revile the precepts. This is also the same case here.

From the words "You now," below, is the formal exhortation for those who are ready to receive the teaching, urging them to save and deliver beings in the final age. As for the phrase "one need not first seek nirvana," it means that while one has not yet [attained it oneself]...

"To cross over oneself and then cross over others" refers to the initial resolve of a Bodhisattva. Even those who have attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) yet remain out of their vows to save sentient beings are included among those previously mentioned who respond to the teaching;
that is, they vow, "May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King (*ratnarāja*), and then return to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.
"Rectifying the mind" refers to a person who possesses the intention to cultivate right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). "Deep faith" refers to...

Those who wish to cultivate and rectify samādhi deeply must believe in their own minds. "Right knowledge and vision" means correctly understanding one's own mind and penetratingly seeing the Buddha-nature.
"I now deliver you so that you may repay the Buddha’s kindness" refers likewise to those of appropriate capacity;
it is as said: "To offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. This...
In all cases, the teacher and disciple were in accord, sharing a single heart, solely for the purpose of propagating the teachings and benefiting sentient beings.
Thus, the ten kinds of demonic realms mentioned above are all covered by the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception).

Consequently, as the power of contemplation and discursive thought contend with one another—each gaining the upper hand and the other yielding—these ten types of phenomena arise. This is what is meant by "ascending."
"O Noble Ones," refers not only to those who have transcended delusion and demons as sages, but also to those who style themselves as belonging to the noble stream.

"You all" and below are the earnest instructions and entrustments. It is for this reason that, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma-treasury was compiled by those suited to the occasion, circulated in the heavens, and disseminated throughout the human realm, the palaces of the nāgas, and the oceanic repositories.

This is not merely for universal dissemination; from this day forward, all practitioners shall rely upon it for cultivation, maintaining the true mind and safeguarding meditative concentration, thereby attaining the path of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
All of this is due to the power of the Tathāgata’s entrustment, as well as his compassionate heart to save sentient beings according to their capacities.
The Jewel Mirror Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Nine;
The Jewel Mirror Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Ten.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Puyan of Guangling, who was granted the title of "Lecturer on the Sūtras at Fayue Monastery in Yunnan" by Imperial Decree during the Great Qing Dynasty.
△ Section Four: The Realm of the Aggregate-Demon (3). First, a general clarification of the realm of the aggregates:
"Ānanda, that good man who cultivates *samādhi*... [up to] takes subtle and hidden delusive thoughts as its basis."
This clarifies the beginning and end of the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. For the five illusory aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*) all take deluded thought (*vikalpa*) as their root.
Therefore, when the *saṃjñā-skandha* is completely subdued, even the ordinary dreams one experiences will be extinguished.
This is because as long as the *saṃjñā-skandha* remains, what occurs during waking is deluded thought, and what occurs during sleep is chaotic dreaming; thus it continues day and night.
At every moment, arising and ceasing are tumultuous, disturbing the true nature so that it cannot attain tranquility;

furthermore, there is no constant or fixed thought, which thereby disturbs the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment, such that not for a single moment can one attain purity, emptiness, and stillness.
Now that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, whether waking or sleeping, in ordinary circumstances, it is always as one and the same. There is no...
Because all disturbances have ceased, one attains the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind of original enlightenment;

from this point on, it becomes clear, empty, and tranquil, like a cloudless sky where nothing exists. Since the two aggregates of form and sensation (*rūpa* and *vedanā*) are absent, the coarse and heavy characteristics have already been extinguished.
Furthermore, by removing the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā*), even the shadow-like phenomena of discriminating based on external objects are eliminated.

Emptiness. For this reason, when one contemplates the great earth, mountains, and rivers of all worlds, they are like a precious mirror, its radiance penetratingly clear, manifesting in response to objects without any analytical discrimination.
Thus, as an object approaches, it appears; yet there is no clinging attachment. As the object passes, it ceases;
yet there is no trace left behind. It is exactly like that mirror: it merely receives through emptiness, reflects through emptiness, and responds through emptiness.
This being so, because within his mind there is no longer any trace of past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), only the true essence of the single consciousness-essence remains, serene and solitary.
This is the sign that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted.

The root-source of arising and ceasing refers precisely to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), for all shifting fluxes begin from this point. What is called "arising after arising" and "ceasing after ceasing" is indeed arising.
This is the fundamental cause for the cessation of that which does not abide. Because the previous three *skandhas* were not yet exhausted, this root-source was obscure and difficult to perceive;

now that the three *skandhas* have been exhausted, all roots of birth and death within the triple world are revealed through this very process of unraveling. Thus, one perceives the twelve [links] of the ten directions.
Regarding the categories of birth, the causes and effects of transgressions and blessings, and their fundamental origins and lineages—one is ultimately able to fully comprehend all such categories.

This is the reason why there is birth and extinction. Although one has not yet attained mastery over the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) and thus certainly does not know the fundamental origins and lineages by which each category receives its life-force, when observing the *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate), one sees that these various categories share in common...
The basis for rebirth has already been seen in its initial manifestation. "Wild horses" refers to the drifting vapors in the fields;
this serves as a metaphor for the subtle and hidden signs of agitation within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "Gleaming" refers to the light of fireflies;
this serves as a metaphor for the aggregate of formations, which arises and ceases suddenly, like the flickering of firefly light. "Clear agitation" is contrasted with what preceded it.

The *āyus-skandha* (life-faculty aggregate) is heavy and turbid; this reveals its lightness and clarity. In contrast to the subsequent *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate), which is limpid and still, it reveals its agitation.

Regarding its being "the ultimate pivot and socket for the floating sense organs and their objects": the pivot is the door-axle and the socket is the door-hinge. Because of the pivot and socket, the door can open and close;
because of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (formative aggregate), the sense organs and their objects undergo arising and ceasing. This is what is called the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
Within this realm, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is like a great wave; the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is like a subtle ripple;

the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is like flowing water without waves; and the essence of true awakening is like still, unmoving water. Therefore, this aggregate of mental formations fundamentally lacks any real nature;
it is merely a light and clear agitation, like the glow of a firefly that suddenly arises and suddenly vanishes, which is mistakenly taken for its fundamental nature.

If the nature of agitation is extinguished and one returns to the fundamental, limpid, and unmoving essence, then the seeds and habitual tendencies of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) will be exhausted, and one will revert to the original luminosity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Therefore it is said:
"Just as when waves subside and transform into clear water, this is called the sign that the *saṃskāra-skandha* has been fully exhausted. Now, the eighth consciousness is fundamentally suchness...

The nature of the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) is originally pure; however, because the skandha of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) arises and ceases without ceasing, and karmic forces perpetually shift, it results in the turbidity of sentient beings' perceptions, which clouds the true nature.
Now that the skandha of formations has been exhausted, one can naturally transcend this turbidity of sentient beings.
Turning back here to contemplate the origin of the skandha of formations, one finds that its root lies in the subtle, obscure delusions of false imagination.

Because these transitions and subtle shifts are all hidden and minute characteristics, unlike the coarseness of the three aforementioned torrents, they are called "subtle and obscure deluded thoughts" (*youyin wangxiang*).
*Wang* means "non-existent. *Chenxi* refers to habitual tendencies from previous lives.
△ Second, the specific exposition of the works of Māra (ten points). First, calculating two kinds of causelessness:
Ānanda, you should know that this constitutes the attainment of right knowledge [up to] the first heterodox teacher who establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
This demonstrates the ten kinds of false reckonings within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Here, we first clarify two types of causelessness.
Generally, these ten reckonings mostly take the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) of those with sharp faculties as their substance; they comprise sixty-two kinds.

However, when the ancient masters explained the sutras, they primarily focused on resolving the textual phrasing; although they recounted their names, they did not reveal their actual substance. Consequently, this led to...
Later scholars did not know their origin. Now, according to what is taught in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it accords with this sutra;

the categories of dharmas are identical, though the meanings differ slightly from those [other texts]. Thus, these were originally non-Buddhist views, wherein practitioners of the mind erroneously fell into error.

Furthermore, the meanings within these sutras all concern the world and the calculation of the duration of kalpas; therefore, they include the four types of eternalism and the four types of equivocation.
In total, there are sixteen views that constitute the "fundamental views of the kalpa" (*mūla-kalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
From the sixteen views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) up to the five views of nirvāṇa, there are forty-four views in total that constitute the "subsequent views of the kalpa" (*anta-kalpa-dṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the two theories of causelessness (*ahetu-vāda*) are placed between the fundamental and subsequent views, making sixty-two in all. This is the sequence of this sutra and its treatises; thus, each [view] arises according to its own basis.
Furthermore, "attaining right awareness" means that one remains constant whether awake or asleep, never succumbing to deviant thoughts.
Within *śamatha*—that is, within the illumination produced by perfect concentration—one is "congealed," meaning unmoving; "clear," meaning free from doubt;
and "right," meaning free from deviant thoughts. By employing the mind in this manner, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity to exploit them.
Indeed, when deluded thoughts hold sway, the celestial Māras are able to spy upon one’s mental activities and wait for their vulnerabilities to destroy one’s right concentration.
Now that the aggregate of perception has been exhausted, neither ghosts nor spirits can fathom you, and even the celestial Māras find it difficult to enter;
how then could they possibly cause disturbance? Therefore, the ten [delusions] listed below are all merely one's own mind’s perverse interpretations. Self...

This gives rise to erroneous conceptions. Only when one attains refined investigation and exhaustively probes the origin of the various classes of living beings—meaning that conceptualization is exhausted and demonic influences have ceased—can one refine one's study to thoroughly investigate the fundamental source of the twelve classes of beings. Therefore, regarding this fundamental source:

If one investigates each and every point to its ultimate conclusion, then within the twelve categories of beings, the root source of birth and death will be peeled away and revealed from this point on, such that nothing remains unclear.
To observe that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated root is precisely to contemplate the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
In contrast to the superficial, heavy, and turbid characteristics of the preceding *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception), this *saṃskāra-skandha* is therefore revealed as being profound.
The characteristics of profound lightness and clarity contrast with the subsequent aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), which is limpid and unwavering;
therefore, it reveals this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the source of constant flux and the fundamental origin of all collective movement.

Furthermore, within this very source of circular, turbulent movement—the aggregate of formations—those who give rise to conceptual calculations do so through the "original kalpas" and "original views" of non-Buddhists, among which the eighteen views include the positions of existence and non-existence.
From these causes, two views arise: the first is that which comes from the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*), whereby one claims that there was originally nothing and now there is something;

the second is that which results from rapid observation, whereby one falsely claims that things exist without cause. Indeed, these are the fundamental errors of practitioners who seek to cultivate the Path.
They claim to fully know the path to the fruit of enlightenment, yet they fall away into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) due to their false conceptualizations;
thus, they erroneously enter two kinds of causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*). Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern. What are these two kinds of causeless theories?
The first type of person relies on their views regarding the fundamental kalpas to give rise to a calculation. Observing back eighty thousand kalpas, they see nothing but darkness and obscurity;
consequently, they conclude that there has been no cause from the very beginning. Why is this?

Because this person, having succeeded in eliminating the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), has completely penetrated the mechanism by which the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) brings about rebirth. Thus, while in meditative concentration, they rely upon their visual faculty.

With his faculties engaged with the world, through eight hundred merits, he perceives clearly all classes of sentient beings within eighty thousand kalpas as they drift according to their karma, circling and revolving like water in a bay, unable to stop themselves.
Just so, these various classes die here and are born there, transmigrating through those realms without interruption. Furthermore—
There is no difference; this is the characteristic of the shifting and flowing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

However, prior to eighty thousand kalpas, all was dark and nothing could be perceived. Consequently, they falsely calculated that this state of darkness where nothing is perceived was the "Primal Truth" (*tattva*).
This is simply the principle of spontaneous transformation and creation. Such things as the "vast nebula" (*hongmóng*) and the "primordial chaos" (*hùndùn*) are all of this category.
Little do they realize that their own understanding is limited and they are unable to transcend it, yet they instead engage in false conceptualization regarding all sentient beings.
To claim that all things have existed from eighty thousand kalpas ago, being inherently causeless and self-existent—is this not an error?

Because of such false calculations and erroneous measures, one loses right knowledge; by confining oneself to the span of eighty thousand kalpas, one fails to realize that the path of karma is beginningless, and thus loses universal knowledge.
Consequently, one falls into the views of externalists, celestial demons, and heterodox, evil perspectives. And...
They turn back from delusion and attain the true nature of Bodhi. Second, these people rely on views of the final kalpa and give rise to calculations.
They observe that after eighty thousand kalpas have ended, there is ultimately no cause. Why is this?
Because these people see that among all sentient beings, there was originally nothing before the kalpa, yet their faculties exist spontaneously; thus they [conclude] regarding persons...
Humans are naturally born as humans and awaken to this; birds are naturally born as birds.

A crow has been naturally black from the beginning, and a crane has been naturally white from the beginning. Thus, humans and celestial beings are fundamentally natural in that they stand upright and walk;
those born as domesticated animals are fundamentally natural in that they move on their bellies and run horizontally. Therefore, the crane—
Its whiteness is simply natural whiteness; it is not made white by washing. Its blackness is simply natural blackness;
it is likewise not produced by dyeing. All of these are spontaneous and natural, fundamentally having no cause.
Furthermore, since eighty thousand kalpas past, this principle has never shifted or changed. Thus, one knows that from now until the very end, although—
Even when this physical form perishes and one reaches the furthest limits of the future, this principle remains exactly as it is, without change or alteration.
By this, one knows that even after the end of the kalpa, there is no cause [for arising].
Nevertheless, throughout eighty thousand kalpas from the very beginning, I have never seen the twelve classes of beings arise from the nature of Bodhi. Why is this?
After how many kalpas will there again be sentient beings who achieve the matter of Bodhi?
One should know that since all phenomena today already belong to the period before the kalpa and are fundamentally without cause, one knows that the end after the kalpa is likewise without cause.
This calculation holds that after eighty thousand kalpas have ended, there is neither cause nor effect; things naturally cease and perish, returning only to the primordial darkness.
Because of such speculation, one loses right knowledge and falls into the delusions of the external paths (tīrthikas), thereby forming the nature of bodhi.
This is called the first type of external path, which establishes two kinds of non-existence based on the dual views of the fundamental and the derivative.
This is the discourse on those causes. All of these are treatises established by heterodox teachers of former generations who contravened correct principle.

Now, as the *dhyāna-practice* of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to open, they give rise to false conceptualizations and erroneously fall into these views; how can one not lament this?

All this arises from failing to realize that phenomena manifest according to one's karma. They falsely calculate that there was no cause prior to eighty thousand kalpas, and that after eighty thousand kalpas, things exist spontaneously and then cease to be.
Thus, they establish two types of nihilistic theories regarding the fundamental and the derivative as being without cause.
This is subsumed under wrong views.
△ Second, the reckoning of the four kinds of pervasive permanence.
Ānanda, among these virtuous sons within *samādhi*... [up to] "the second non-Buddhist establishes the doctrine of perfect permanence."

This reckoning consists of four kinds of pervasive permanence. Regarding the calculation of "pervasive permanence," it refers to those who, while practicing contemplation within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), perceive a state of pervasiveness and thus designate it as "pervasive" (*pariṇata*); they perceive a state of continuity and thus designate it as "permanent" (*nitya*).
They fail to realize that this pervasiveness and continuity are merely the marks of the shifting, flowing, arising, and ceasing of the aggregate of formations; yet within this [state], they...
They give rise to false conceptualizations, clinging to [the mind] as being all-pervasive, permanent, and eternal; how could this not be erroneous?
For this reason, such a person practicing meditative concentration mistakenly falls into the four types of theories on pervasive permanence established by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The first is that this person calculates both the mind and its objects to be eternal; because they have not yet perceived the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), for this reason—
One penetrates the two natures of mind and phenomena; these are the seeing and image divisions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

Merely attaining the exhaustion of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and the manifestation of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), one relies upon this insight to practice cultivation. Consequently, one investigates from where the two natures of mind and phenomena arise.

However, because the scope of such seeing is limited, one does not penetrate far; one sees only that prior to twenty thousand kalpas there was no cause, and [the two natures] have existed spontaneously.

After ten thousand kalpas, the dark void has nothing to be perceived. Thus, one calculates that within twenty thousand kalpas, all instances of arising and ceasing in the cycle of existence throughout the ten directions have never been lost or scattered.
Therefore, one does not calculate that what exists beyond the kalpas is causeless or subject to annihilation;
rather, one calculates only the continuity within the kalpas as being pervasive and eternal. This is why it differs from the previous calculation and constitutes [the second view].
The first is the doctrine of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*). Second, there are those who reckon that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are all eternal.

These practitioners likewise rely upon their own views and insights to investigate the source of transformation; seeing that all phenomena are formed through the combination of the four great elements, they reckon that the essential nature of these four elements has been eternally abiding from the beginning.
They fail to realize, however, that these are merely manifestations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Its nature is fundamentally empty. Relying upon this for cultivation, one regards it as eternally abiding.

Consequently, one is able to understand that throughout forty thousand kalpas, although sentient beings of the ten directions undergo birth and extinction, the substance of the four great elements is entirely pervasive;
their nature is inherently eternal and has never been lost. This reckoning of what is perceived within a kalpa constitutes the second theory of universal permanence.
Furthermore, thirdly, this person calculates that the eight consciousnesses are all eternal.

This is because they can exhaustively investigate the six consciousnesses inherent within the six sense organs, as well as the seventh manas-consciousness which clings to and sustains the eighth consciousness.

This arises from the practitioner, relying on their own views and understanding, exhausting these three: whether it be the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), or the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), they seek the fundamental source of their arising.

Regarding the place of their arising, they do not realize it is the cause for the continuity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), but instead erroneously speculate that the nature of consciousness is permanent and eternal.

Relying on this, they practice until they can observe how, throughout eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings die here and are born there, circulating and revolving without ever being lost. Thereupon, they claim that from the very beginning, [consciousness] has been omnipresent.

It is eternally abiding because it exhaustively reaches this state and its nature is not lost; yet, based on this, one gives rise to false conceptualization, taking it to be a pervasive and eternally abiding nature.
One fails to realize that this is precisely the continuity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), the nature of incessant arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, within the seventh consciousness, one has not yet even glimpsed the root-source of arising and ceasing, yet one nevertheless clings to it as the perfect, eternal, true nature.
Is this not an error? This constitutes the third theory of universal permanence. Fourth, this person reckons that the exhaustion of thought is itself permanence;
because they have already exhausted the root-source of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), from that point on, there is no further perception-aggregate.

Regarding the principle of birth: one then claims that these movements, gestures, operations, and activities all belong to the cycle of arising and ceasing, the delusive thoughts of the *skandha*-mind.
Now, these have been permanently eliminated. As for this *saṃskāra-skandha*, it is naturally established within the principle as neither arising nor ceasing.
This is because, through the cessation of the conceptual mind, one then [realizes] the delusion...
This means that when arising and ceasing are eternally extinguished, the principle of neither-arising-nor-ceasing is spontaneously accomplished.

One fails to recognize that the root of arising and ceasing precisely lies herein; it is specifically because the characteristics of this process are so subtle and difficult to perceive that one errs regarding arising and ceasing.
To base one’s calculations on the mind’s false conceptualization of a principle that is neither born nor extinguished, yet is all-pervasive and eternally abiding—is this not an error?

This constitutes the fourth type of doctrine of universal permanence. For this reason, although the fundamental nature is not pervasive or perfect, one falsely calculates it to be pervasive and perfect;
although it is fundamentally not truly eternal, one delusively claims it to be truly eternal. Thus, one falls into erroneous views and loses right knowledge.
This is why they fall into external paths and become deluded regarding Bodhi. This is called the second type of external path:
the doctrine of the fourfold establishment of the eternally abiding and all-pervading. All of these are subsumed under the category of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
△ Third, the four kinds of inverted views.
Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) the third type of externalist, the partial doctrine of permanence;
this clarifies the dual calculation of both permanence and impermanence. Furthermore, within *samādhi*, precisely when ideation is exhausted and conduct manifests.

At such a time, those who suddenly give rise to false calculations and engage in vain speculations regarding themselves and their own bodies, others and sentient beings, and the realms of the land—such persons fall into the four kinds of inverted false views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
These are what are called the theory that one part is impermanent and the theory that one part is eternal. The first of these is...

Because people contemplate their own wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions, profoundly still and unmoving, its magnitude equal to empty space, they take this profound stillness to be the nature of the mind and regard it as ultimate.

Consequently, they establish the concept of a "divine self" (*puruṣa*). What is called the "divine self" is the final of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) in the Sāṃkhya system. Those who calculate themselves as being identical to this [self] do so because of that calculation.
There is a true self that pervades the ten directions, lucidly stable and unmoving, without birth or extinction; therefore, it is eternal.
All sentient beings are within my heart, born and dying of their own accord; therefore, they are impermanent.
This is the reckoning of eternity and impermanence regarding one's own and others' states. Second, such a person does not contemplate their own mind, but contemplates only the state of the nation.
The earth [realms] from the third dhyāna downward—where the three calamities reach—are reckoned as impermanent.

From the fourth dhyāna upward—where the three calamities do not reach—they are reckoned as permanent. This is reckoning them as permanent or impermanent based on whether the three calamities reach those places or not.
This constitutes abandoning the observation of oneself to observe others; below this, one abandons the observation of others to observe oneself. (3)
This person, because the body is coarse while the mind is subtle, abandons the world to contemplate their own mind separately. They see only the essence, unmixed;
