it is subtle rather than coarse, minute so as not to be attached to, and dense so as not to be manifest. Its profundity and concealment make it difficult to perceive, like a fine mote of dust.
Nevertheless, though it flows through the ten directions, its nature fundamentally undergoes no transition or change.
It enables this body to reside within the mind, arising and ceasing moment by moment without any alteration;
thus one knows it to be an indestructible nature, which is called the "eternal nature of the self.
As for all bodies subject to birth and death, which flow forth from this nature of the self, these are called the "impermanent nature. This reckons one's own body and mind as—

This refers to permanence and impermanence. Fourth, this person observes the four aggregates collectively and realizes that the three aggregates of form, sensation, and perception have already ceased.

Seeing only the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) currently flowing in transition, they take the uninterrupted continuity of these formations—which appear to flow eternally—and reckon it as a permanent nature. As for the previous three aggregates that have now perished...
This is precisely what is called the nature of impermanence. This refers to the calculation of permanence and impermanence within the four aggregates (*skandhas*).

Due to these four types of conceptualization, although the respective attachments to self, others, and the aggregates differ, they do not, in total, transcend the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
Because they calculate both [permanence and impermanence] simultaneously, this constitutes a perversion; therefore, they fall outside [the Buddhist fold].
To follow such a path while being deluded regarding Bodhi is therefore called the third heterodox school’s doctrine of "one part impermanent, one part permanent.
This is subsumed under the category of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Question: How does this differ from the four doctrines of universal permanence? Answer:

Those [four doctrines] reckon that all things are entirely permanent; this [doctrine] reckons that only one part of oneself, others, and the aggregates (*skandha*) is permanent. Thus, they are not the same.
△ Fourth, the four types of calculations regarding the stages of existence.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi (up to) the fourth non-Buddhist school who establish the theory of finitude:
this calculation regards the stages as being finite or infinite. There are four such stages, namely, the divisions of the three periods of time.
These are the stages: the stage of seeing and hearing, the stage of self and other, and the stage of arising and ceasing.
First, regarding the three time periods below, one calculates whether there is a limit or no limit.

"The mind calculates the source of birth, its flowing function never ceasing" means that one contemplates the root-source of the various classes of beings and the karmic functions of their present flux, which circulate and revolve without end.
He then reflects that the past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; thus, he reckons it as having limits.

He further reflects that the present continues in succession without any interruption; thus, he reckons it as being limitless. This is observing the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) by dividing it across the three periods of time.
Second, regarding the lower [level], this concerns views based on what is seen and heard, through which one calculates whether there is a limit or no limit.
That is to say, when observing within eighty thousand kalpas, because sentient beings can be seen and heard, one calculates that there is a limit;
this is to restrict [the scope] to the number of eighty thousand. When observing beyond eighty thousand kalpas, because no sentient beings are seen and no sentient beings are heard, one calculates...
"It is infinite" because it is immeasurable and thus cannot be seen or heard. The former calculation held that the past and future, being places where there is no seeing or hearing, were finite;
this calculation holds that the present, being a place where there is seeing and hearing, is infinite.
Since both of these views are reversed [from the truth], one knows that the externalists' shifting and inverted calculations fundamentally lack any single, fixed perspective. Third:
The lower [level] concerns the distinction between self and other, based on the calculation of whether there is a limit or no limit.

This arises because the practitioner, observing their own aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), clings to it as a true self; they thus further falsely calculate that "I" am able to pervasively know all things, asserting to themselves that among all phenomena, they alone have attained the nature of boundlessness, while all those sentient beings are merely manifestations of their own nature.
Within this, however, within my own self-nature, I have never known that cognitive nature as something distinct from myself.

Consequently, I reckon that all such cognitive natures do not transcend my own cognitive nature; for this reason, they are not called the boundless mind-nature, but are merely called the limited mind-nature.
This is precisely the grasping at a self within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); how could one know [otherwise]?
Is it not the case that within the state of equality there is fundamentally no distinction between self and other? Fourth, regarding the lower [category], this concerns birth and cessation;

it refers to those who, calculating existence as finite or infinite, exhaustively investigate the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and calculate that there is partial birth and partial cessation.
Consequently, this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) originally lacks a fundamental nature. Previously it relied upon the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) as its root;

subsequently it relies upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as its nature. Thus, now that the aggregate of perception has ceased, the aggregate of consciousness is about to manifest.

Therefore, regarding this aggregate of formations, although its first half ceases along with perception, its second half still arises together with consciousness. For this reason, the practitioner, based on what he himself [perceives]...
Observing the path of mental activity, he falsely devised his own calculations to gauge it.
He then reckoned that within all sentient beings, just as within his own single body, all that exists consists of mind, half of which belongs to arising and half to ceasing.
Furthermore, observing that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) pervades everything, he thereby brought forth an illumination regarding all phenomena within that world.
That which is half-born constitutes "having limits," while that which is half-extinguished constitutes "being limitless.
Based on these four types of conceptualization—whether regarding having limits or being limitless—one falls entirely among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
All such views are delusions concerning the nature of bodhi; for within the nature of bodhi, no divisions, positions, or boundaries can be found. This is so.
This is called the fourth heterodox school’s doctrine of establishing the existence of both the finite and the infinite; it is subsumed within the category of false views.
△ Fifth: reckoning the four kinds of equivocation.

Furthermore, from "the good sons within samādhi" (up to) "the immortal equivocation and pervasive conceptualization of empty discourse," this clarifies the four kinds of equivocal and pervasive conceptualizations of empty discourse.
Regarding these, those who give rise to speculative calculations within their knowledge and views [are as follows].
This refers to how, within that state of meditative concentration, one falsely gives rise to pervasive conceptualization based on what is known and seen.
Regarding "devious and confused speech": it means that these non-Buddhists are unable to make a definitive determination or achieve clear understanding regarding their knowledge and views;
thus, when someone questions them, they all respond with deceptive wisdom and confused answers. Regarding "the doctrine of immortality": it is because the non-Buddhists hold such a view.
The Brahmā Heaven is eternally abiding and is called "the deathless. The Pure Heaven (Śuddhāvāsa) mistakenly claims that one who is born there will never again fall into confusion.
When answering people, if one were to answer while truly not knowing, there is a fear of falling into evasive equivocation (*vibhūka*).
Therefore, when questioned, one says: "This is cryptic terminology; it should not be fully explained," or one employs other expedient means to avoid the matter.
Alternatively, one may respond by following the phrasing of the questioner, or answer in an ambiguous manner that allows for two interpretations. The Buddha’s teachings censure this, saying:

"This is truly the deceptive and confused person who propounds pervasive and empty sophistry. This refers to the latter four types [of sophistry], all of which are pervasive, speculative, and false discourses that lack any real meaning.
The first of these is the sophistry of the life-constituent (jīvitasaṃskāra) based on the cycle of arising and ceasing.
Through discrimination, eight kinds of views are formed, resulting in eight types of erroneous calculations.

"The root of transformation" refers to this aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the fundamental source of shifting changes and illusory transformations. This is observed by examining preceding and succeeding moments of thought.
Seeing that which flows and changes without ceasing, they consequently conceive it as subject to transformation.
Or, observing the preceding and succeeding moments of thought, seeing that which continues in an uninterrupted succession, they consequently conceive it as eternal.
Because they perceive only the present, regarding that which is seen, they conceive it as arising; because they do not see the past or the future, regarding that which is not seen, they conceive...
They consider cessation to be the causal nature of arising, and cessation itself to be the causal nature of arising;

thus, arising and ceasing proceed without any interval of interruption, which they reckon as "increase. Furthermore, they maintain that that which is currently arising does not reach the state of cessation.
Regarding that which ceases correctly: it does not reach the place of birth, yet within the continuity of arising and ceasing, there is a point of departure which is reckoned as "diminution.
At the place where each thought-moment arises, one reckons it as "existence"; at the place where each thought-moment ceases, one reckons it as "non-existence.
Although these eight types are all fundamentally based on the principle of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), when viewed collectively:
However, because there were differences in the mental application of those practitioners, these eight kinds of knowledge and views arose. From that time onward,
as there was no longer any fixed right knowledge or right view, whenever they encountered someone asking about the meaning [of the Dharma],
they would immediately answer with such evasive and confused speech, leaving the person who had come to inquire about the meaning unable to distinguish right from wrong.
They cannot distinguish between things; they cannot resolve what is right or wrong.

Not only are their principles vague and indistinct, such that they lack discernment, but they have also largely forgotten and lost the traditional texts and commentaries, which only serves to increase their confusion and distress.
Second, as for the lower grade, there is no "distortion and confusion. To contemplate the mind is to contemplate the mental states of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Regarding "mutually having no locus": this means that when mindfulness is in the process of arising, there is no characteristic of cessation; when mindfulness is in the process of ceasing, there is no characteristic of arising.
From this, one realizes that all things are non-existent. Therefore, when encountering someone who asks about the meaning [of reality], one answers only that all dharmas are non-existent.
Third, the inferior calculation of existence is a form of evasive equivocation. Regarding "each having its own locus": this refers to mindfulness...
After arising, there must necessarily be the characteristic of cessation; after cessation, there must necessarily be the characteristic of arising. From this, one realizes that all things exist.

Therefore, when encountering people who inquire about the meaning [of existence], one answers only that "all dharmas exist. This is precisely what is meant by "existence. Fourth is the distorted and confused reckoning of existence and non-existence.
Regarding those who perceive both existence and non-existence: it means that they have already perceived the arising of each momentary thought.

Furthermore, one perceives the locus where each thought-moment ceases. Regarding the phrase "because its objects are manifold," this means that the objects of observation are indeterminate, and the observing mind is likewise indeterminate;
it is like a tree with many branches that intersect and diverge in various ways.
Therefore, when someone asks a question, one answers: "It exists, yet it is also non-existent," because that which arises must inevitably return to cessation.

Furthermore, that which is "neither existent nor non-existent" does not mean that it is "both existent and non-existent," because that which has been extinguished can never arise again. As for "evasive equivocation" (*amarā-vikkhepa*):
to be perverse and unyielding while failing to accord with principle is "evasion" (*amarā*); for the mind to lack a central point of correctness is "equivocation" (*vikkhepa*).
Among these, the first and fourth positions are both ambiguous and largely characterized by the sense of confusion; ultimately they do not accord with principle and are also accompanied by evasion.
Furthermore, regarding the second and third types of speech, they consist mostly of one-sided distortions and are ultimately not the primary [truth], as they likewise lead to confusion.
Therefore, it is summarized by saying: "All such distortions and confusions are beyond the scope of thorough investigation or interrogation."
The conclusion here that these are "void and non-existent" means that they are false and erroneous conceptualizations lacking any real meaning.

Regarding "pervasive false theories," this refers to the person who engages in universal speculation—such as grasping at a rope and perceiving it as a snake—all of which are arguments reaching the height of emptiness and falsity, and are thus subsumed under wrong views. These sixteen views above are all [concerning] the primary kalpas and...
[This is] seeing.
△ Six: Calculating the characteristics of the sixteen modes of existence.
Furthermore, among the various sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to) the inverted theories of mind regarding existence after death.
This is based on the views of the final eon (*kalpa*), which calculates sixteen modes of existence regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
"Inexhaustible flow" refers specifically to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); it means that their continuity is inexhaustible and their migration and flux are unceasing.

Because this person perceives that the aggregate of formations flows on without end, they consequently reckon that the three aggregates previously mentioned, which have already ceased, likewise exist after death.
It is inexhaustible. It certainly possesses its own characteristics; thus, one subsequently formulates the "Treatise on the Perverted Mind.
As for those who fortify their own bodies, it is because they reckon the physical body to be the self, and therefore they cling to it with stubborn persistence.

This "self" is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which the seventh consciousness grasps as the internal self. "Form" (*rūpa*), meanwhile, is the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

[The eighth consciousness] differentiates [objects], while the preceding seven consciousnesses grasp them as external realms. All of this arises because the practitioner does not know the root source, leading to successive false attachments.
First, some say that form is the self, meaning that the forms of the four great elements are all the self;
this calculation holds that form itself is the self. Second, others perceive the nature of the self as perfectly interfused, pervading and containing the lands...
Regarding the earth: when one says "I have form," it means that all the pervasive forms of the encompassed lands are entirely my possession;
therefore, this calculation holds that the self is large while form is small, and that [form] resides within me.
Third, regarding those present objective conditions, they all follow me as I turn and move back and forth, saying "form belongs to me"; this means it is "mine."
This is not the same as the self. This [view] calculates that the self is distinct from form (*rūpa*).

Fourth, some perceive the continuity of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and further calculate that the self resides within these formations. To say "I am in form" means that the self is actually within form itself;

this is because the characteristic of the continuity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is identical to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). This calculation holds that form is large and the self is small, and that the self is within form.
This is the middle [category]. All of these are conceptual reckonings that state there are "characteristics" after death; that is to say, although the physical body dies, the self still persists.
As it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), so it is with the other three. Thus, in this cycle, four sets of four together constitute sixteen characteristics.
Since there are already characteristics before birth in the present life, one knows that there will likewise be characteristics after death in the future.
There are characteristics. From this point downward, there is a successive and deluded reckoning:

namely, that since the aforementioned four aggregates are thus identical to the self, they all possess characteristics even after death; it follows that the same principle applies to afflictions (*kleśa*) and bodhi.
For afflictions arise from the aggregates, while bodhi is realized through the self; thus one knows that both of these natures—true and false—possess characteristics. Furthermore...
They may proceed side by side and drive abreast, entering the limits of the future, ultimately never changing; each does not touch the other, yet they do not obstruct one another.
The meaning is this: if it is true, it is ultimately and fundamentally true; if it is false, it is ultimately and fundamentally false. There is absolutely no alteration.
How could there be any principle of returning from falsehood to truth, or transforming the ordinary into the sagely? This...
All of them maintain that after death there must necessarily be a self-characteristic (*ātman*), and they erroneously regard this as permanent and unchangeable.

From this, the conclusion of the non-Buddhist doctrines (*bāhyaka-śāstra*) is formed. Although the text generally clarifies all five aggregates (*skandha*), the correct meaning lies only in the first four;

and although it concerns the first four, it actually refers only to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). All of these are subsumed under the category of extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
△ The seventh [category] consists of eight types of theories regarding the signless (*animitta*).
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to the point of) their death, there are those who propound erroneous views concerning the signless mind after death.
These are the eight types of theories regarding the signless state after death. This arises because they perceive that the first three aggregates (*skandha*) have already ceased and are signless.
From this, one then calculates that the fourth aggregate, the formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), likewise ultimately returns to signlessness (*animitta*).

Its form is like a single body, and its color is like the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Thus, one knows that form exists because of color; if color ceases, then form has nothing upon which to depend.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is like consciousness (*vijñāna*), while the mind (*citta*) is like the faculty of mind (*manas*). Therefore, one knows that the mind is bound by perception; if perception ceases, the mind has nothing to which it is bound.
Form (*rūpa*) precedes feeling (*vedanā*), and the mind follows feeling; with feeling situated between them, form and mind are linked together.
Thus, when there is no feeling, form and mind are no longer linked. These are the natures of the first three aggregates (*skandha*).

Once it has been dissolved and dispersed, it lacks the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*). Even if the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) persists, although it is a physiological process, it is devoid of sensation and perception (*vedanā* and *saṃjñā*).
Thus, even as a physiological process, it possesses no cognition; how does this differ from grasses and trees, which likewise lack sensation and perception?
For this reason, one should know that if this aggregate of formations were separated from the preceding aggregates, it would likewise have no characteristics. This...
Based on the preceding three aggregates, one proceeds to examine the aggregate of formations to ascertain that they are without marks.
Now, when observing this body before us, even the marks of the aggregates cannot be apprehended; how then could there be further marks of the various aggregates after death?
By investigating this, one compares it with what occurs after death: the latent characteristics (*anuśaya*) are fixed, and there is no such cyclical recurrence.

Examining each latent characteristic, one calculates its present and future states; since there are two types of non-existence for each of the four *skandhas*, there are eight aspects of non-existence.
Furthermore, proceeding from this point, one falsely calculates the causes and effects of nirvāṇa and all mundane and supramundane phenomena. All of these...
"Emptiness" is merely a name; it ultimately possesses no substantial reality and, in the final analysis, all things return to annihilation.
From this point downward, the external treatise is concluded. However, this calculation is the opposite of the previous one.

This is because, having previously perceived the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) which has not yet been extinguished, and because it possesses characteristics, one consequently calculated that the preceding three aggregates and all phenomena likewise must possess characteristics; thus, [the former view] was established.

There is the theory of the inversion of signlessness (*animitta-viparyāsa*). Having already extinguished the perception of the three aggregates (*skandha*), one takes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as its basis because it is signless;
consequently, one reckons that all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise signless. Thus, the theory of the inversion of signlessness is established.
All of these are subsumed within the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
△ The eight views on the "neither-nor" of the eight kinds.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within the state of *samādhi* (up to) the post-mortem "neither-nor" theory of inverted minds:

this view maintains that existence and non-existence are both neither-nor across the eight categories. Regarding "while the formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) still persist": this refers to seeing that the aggregate of formations has not yet been exhausted.

The realms still remain. As for the simultaneous cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*), one sees that the three preceding aggregates have already been exhausted and their characteristics are entirely empty.
From this, dualistic calculations arise: one calculates "existence" within what remains and calculates "non-existence" within what has ceased.

This causes the intrinsic natures of the four aggregates to mutually subvert one another; for instance, using the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to subvert the non-existence of the three preceding ones. By means of the former...

The negation of the three [aggregates] destroys the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). By destroying non-existence, one establishes "not non-existent"; by destroying existence, one establishes "not existent.
Such a person falls into the inverted doctrine that after death both existence and non-existence are neither.

Below follows the correct explanation establishing the meaning of the mutual destruction of the essential nature and characteristics. This means that since the preceding three have already ceased, within form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*)—

One perceives existence, yet it is not existence; the latter [aspect] still remains. Therefore, within the flux of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one internally contemplates non-existence, yet it is not non-existence.

By contemplating both the prior and the subsequent simultaneously, one finds that both existence and non-existence are negated; thus, the eight aspects are established. That is to say: it is not that there are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
nor is it that there are no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. For this reason, whenever any one of the aggregates (*skandha*) is mentioned, it is said that after death—

It is neither characterized by existence nor characterized by non-existence. Furthermore, regarding the reckoning of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, it means that they do not merely cease within the four aggregates;
rather, they are entirely beyond both. By inferring from this, the nature of all dharmas is entirely subject to change and transformation:
they exist yet are not existent, and they do not exist yet are not non-existent. To be able to fully know and fully see this, with perfect clarity and without delusion—therefore it is said:
The mind gives rise to penetrating realization. Regarding "losing one's bearings regarding the void and the real": because it is not non-existent, the void loses its footing;
and because it is not existent, the real loses its footing. To engage in such conceptualization is to reckon based on the state of being alive.
For example, regarding the state after death, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
If one were to discuss what occurs after death throughout the bounds of the future, it would be dark and obscure, vast and boundless; one could not say it exists, nor could one say it does not exist.
This clarifies that both existence and non-existence are negated, for neither can be spoken of. This is precisely the eighth heterodox view of perversion.
This treatise is also subsumed under wrong views. △ Ninth:
Calculating the severance and extinction at the seven limits.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*... (up to)... the inverted theory of the mind that [the self] is severed and extinguished after death.

This calculation holds that all seven realms are subject to annihilation. Because one perceives the cessation of every thought-moment within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one claims there is no cause for subsequent states.
This false speculation asserts that after being born in the seven places—namely the human and heavenly realms—one is subsequently annihilated in all of them.
Such a person enters the doctrine of annihilation in these seven places. The seven places refer to the four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the first and second dhyānas.
The third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). "Cessation of the body" refers to all humans and devas of the four continents and the six heavens of desire;

"cessation of desire" refers to the three heavens of the first dhyāna, because defilement of desire has already been exhausted there; "cessation of suffering" refers to the three heavens of the second dhyāna.
This refers to "supreme joy," because there is no sorrow; it is the third dhyāna and its three heavens. This refers to "supreme bliss," because there is a sublime bliss free from joy;

it is the fourth dhyāna, which abandons applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and pleasure (*sukha*). It refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), because they abandon the obstruction of material form.
Thus, the term "supreme abandonment" contains these two meanings. In this manner, one cycles through them until reaching the ultimate limit. Beyond this—
The seven limits manifest before one; there is nothing that does not return to extinction.
Since all seven locations are seen to undergo cessation, one knows that within the future after death, there will be no further occurrence of birth.

This calculation maintains that only the present aggregate exists, while the intermediate and subsequent aggregates are not admitted to exist. This is precisely the view of the Confucian scholars of this land, who loathe hearing of saṃsāra.

The doctrine of cause and effect also falls under this calculation; however, it merely calculates that one ceases to exist upon death in the human realm, and still does not allow for the existence of the other six bases.
This is called the ninth heterodox school’s theory that after death all seven bases return to annihilation, and it is also subsumed within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
△ The tenth calculation: the five types of manifesting nirvana.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to) "the fifth, manifesting nirvana," this refers to the inverted discourse on the mind.
This calculation concerns manifesting nirvana in five locations. Regarding these five locations, they exclude the human realm of the desire realm.
This includes the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Those who do not reckon the human realm do so because they currently dwell within the suffering and affliction of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Those who do not reckon the formless realm do so because they are attached to the physical body; thus, they seek *nirvāṇa* by relying on the six desire realms, the four dhyānas, and the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
"Subsequent existence" refers to the locus where the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) arises moment by moment. This is because one contemplates the formations as arising in every instant.
Because there is continuity as new states constantly arise from old ones, one calculates that there must be a determinate, real fruit; it certainly does not cease into non-existence.

As for the five nirvāṇas, these refer to the desire realm and the four dhyānas. In these five locations, one does not depend upon the extinction of the physical remains (ashes), but rather attains [nirvāṇa] simply by being born in those places.
This refers to *nirvāṇa* in the present life. The term "or" (*huò*) is an indefinite particle; it does not refer to a single individual.

"The desire realm" (*yùjiè*) is a collective term for the six heavens of the desire realm; it does not refer to a single celestial abode. Regarding the phrase "as the primary basis for transformation":
because one perceives the desire realm as the common ground for birth, one comes to believe that all principles of existence are entirely contained therein, and thus [one falls into] delusion.
This is calculated to be the turning away from the basis of birth and death toward the true fruit of nirvana. As for "observing the perfect luminosity":

this refers to the initial breaking of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) mentioned previously. Through the manifestation of perfect concentration, one suddenly attains the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and observes the various heavens, which are pure and majestic, far surpassing the radiance of the sun and moon and transcending the filth and turbidity of the human world; therefore, such thoughts arise in the mind.
Out of attachment, they then reckon this state to be present nirvana. Or, those who rely on the first dhyāna reckon the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion to be present nirvana.
Or, those who rely on the second dhyāna reckon the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration to be present nirvana.
Some say that in the preceding passage, it was stated that the afflictions of the first dhyāna do not oppress [the practitioner], while the second...
In the first dhyāna, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) does not oppress, because suffering (*duḥkha*) is heavy while sorrow is light; this is appropriate for its description.
Now, to say that the first dhyāna is without sorrow and the second dhyāna is without suffering is likely a mistranslation or a textual inversion by the translator.

Alternatively, some may reckon the third dhyāna—the stage of sublime bliss detached from joy—as the present nirvāṇa. That which follows extreme joy is what is called "dwelling in a mind of tranquility."
Joy is fully perfected; this constitutes great compliance. Alternatively, regarding those who rely on the four dhyānas:
they reckon the stage of pure equanimity and mindfulness as the present nirvāṇa. As for the simultaneous disappearance of both suffering and pleasure:

because they have cultivated the samādhi of equanimity, the suffering and pleasure of the lower realms cannot disturb them. As for not undergoing the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra: it is because the three calamities do not reach them.
Consequently, they falsely reckon that not undergoing the cycle of birth and death is itself the true nature of nirvana—neither arising nor ceasing.
These are all instances of being deluded regarding the outflows (*āsrava*) and taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to be so; they mistake saṃsāra for nirvana.
This arises because, having somewhat distanced themselves from the suffering and affliction of the lower realms, they then reckon the five [heavens] to be secure and peaceful.
Having somewhat distanced themselves from the defilements of the lower realms, they consequently reckon these five abodes to be supreme purity.
As for their ultimate view, they erroneously claim that these five higher abodes are all the unsurpassed, most excellent fruit. Thus, this concludes the section on the non-Buddhist treatises.
Regarding the fifth, "attaining nirvana in the present": this reckons that these five locations are all nirvana in the present, wherein one experiences bliss now without waiting for the future.
This constitutes the tenth heterodox and inverted doctrine, which is subsumed under wrong views. Indeed, all views that arise do not exceed the five [wrong] views, namely:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), views regarding precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and views clinging to one's own position (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Thus, the ten chapters above comprise sixty-two views; when considered collectively, none of them transcends these.
Even if one were to further condense their meaning through investigation, they would not exceed the two views of existence and non-existence. This is why the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Whether there is existence or non-existence, all rely upon these views; it is in this way that the sixty-two [views] are fully established."
△ Third: The Exhortation Regarding the Harmful Consequences.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding *dhyāna* (up to the point where they lead one to become a Great Awakened King through pure pointing-out) constitute this exhortation regarding the harmful consequences.
This is because what was previously called "the manifestation of objects within *dhyāna*" is an opportunity seized by celestial Māras.

This refers to manifesting false objects. Such individuals are called those with "mad enlightenment" (*kang-jie*) in *dhyāna*. This is precisely when the mental demons (*citta-māra*) themselves give rise to deep calamities.
Generally, whenever practitioners perceive the Way as not true and harbor various divergent, deluded views, all are termed "mad enlightenment.
These are one's own mental demons and must be guarded against most deeply. "The mind and its application intermingle" means that the application of contemplation...
"Power" refers to the mutual victory and defeat in the struggle against the deluded mind. "Those who have awakened" refers to those with wild, distorted understandings.
"The stubbornly deluded": "stubborn" means dull-witted and ignorant; therefore, they find it difficult to enter into correct awakening. "Deluded" means confused;
therefore, they easily give rise to wild, distorted understandings. This is because they are unable to reflect upon or measure themselves, mistakenly taking their confusion to be [awakening].
With such conviction, they act with self-will and self-assertion to establish various treatises. Furthermore, they falsely claim to have attained the stages of the sages;
this constitutes a great lie and it is only fitting that they fall into the heavy hells. You [the disciples] should correct them and offer proper exhortation.
Those who "awaken to and understand this meaning" refer to those who clearly discern and comprehend this meaning, striving to eliminate all that is heterodox.
This is indeed clear. The term "do not" (*mā*) is a word of prohibition. Regarding "lest you yourself give rise to deep calamity":

this means that although external māras may be unable to disturb you, do not allow the māras of your own mind to arise and produce deep calamity. "Calamity" (*niṣa*) refers to the sprouting of misfortune;
it also carries the sense of arising gradually. The two lines concerning "maintaining" (*dhārayet*) are instructions for when [the affliction] has already arisen.
"Seeing" means causing [delusion] to be extinguished. "Teaching" consists of two phrases; these teach that correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) which has not yet arisen should be brought into being.
Now, as for "true meaning" (*bhūtārtha*), it refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This is the meaning of being free from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*) and transcending the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). "Branching off" refers to these ten kinds of false attachments and pervasive conceptualizations (*parikalpa*) existing within the nature.
Within meditative concentration, it is like the lateral branches of a tree or the winding forks of a road; none of these are the fundamental path of rectitude.
To seek through such means is to encounter branches and forks, whereby one falls into heterodox paths (tīrthika). To take little as sufficient leads one to enter the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Therefore, I entrust this to those present at the assembly, so that it may serve as a pure pointer for all humans and devas, acting as a Great Awakened King.
May they proceed directly upon the path of wondrous adornment, never allowing themselves to stray onto crooked bypaths or enter them, thereby falling into the ways of external paths.
△ Section Three: A General Clarification of the Realm of the Five Skandha-Māras.
Ānanda, that good man who cultivates samādhi... [up to] ...takes inverted false discrimination as its root.

This passage clarifies the beginning and end of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), specifically describing first the signs of the exhaustion of formations (*saṃskāra*) and the manifestation of consciousness.

"The nature of all worlds" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which constitutes the twelve classes of sentient beings in the world—the essential nature of their fluxional arising and ceasing.
"The generative impulse of the common lot" refers to the common basis of birth; it is called the "basis" because it gives rise to life.
The locus: the movement of the awakening faculty (*indriya*) marks the beginning; their intent is one and the same. "Sunk and subtle" refers to the main ropes and the ties of a net:
the large ropes of a net are called *gāṅ* (main ropes), and the places where the collar is knotted are called *niù* (ties). Both serve as metaphors for what is essential.

All beings of the twelve classes within the mundane world are like a net or a garment, and this activity-sky (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—with its characteristics of arising and ceasing—is threaded through them from beginning to end.
It is like the main cord and knots of a net. As for the term "profound and subtle," it refers to that which is deep-seated, obscure, and minute;

this is the characteristic of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Therefore, when the aggregate of formations is exhausted, the knots of the life-force's mechanism will necessarily and suddenly collapse and tear asunder.
*Pudgala* means "one who undergoes repeated rebirth"; this refers to those within the various classes of sentient beings.

Furthermore, because the fundamental threads of the life-force have already been shattered and torn asunder, the deep and far-reaching continuity by which various classes of beings recompense their past karma—those responses arising from karmic inducement—is now all suspended, remote, and severed.
This is the sign that one's course of existence has reached its end. Indeed, the nature-heaven of nirvana is shrouded by the five aggregates, causing one to sink and wallow in birth and death.
It is as if one still dwells in the long night: the first three *skandhas* have come to an end, like the first crowing of a rooster;

though it is a sign of dawn, one still remains submerged in the remaining two *skandhas*, and the refined colors have not yet been distinguished. This indicates that the *saṃskāra-skandha* has already ceased and birth-and-death are nearly exhausted;

thus, for the nature-heaven of *nirvāṇa*, the time for great illumination and great awakening is at hand. It is like the rooster announcing the dawn, crowing for the third time during the fifth watch.
This is the final wailing cry. Thus, one looks back toward the nature of the heavens (*dharmadhātu*), which is like the subtle, bright white color already appearing in the east;
yet it is not yet fully luminous or pure white because it is still shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), and therefore does not penetrate through.
Previously, as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) flowed on and the seven consciousnesses clung to a self, the six sense faculties ran wild and followed after them.

[The mind] pursued the six objects of the senses. Now that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) has also become empty, the six sense faculties are void and still;
they no longer rush toward sensory objects. Therefore, whether internally or externally, everything is profoundly tranquil and luminously pure.

Generally speaking, the faculties are the "entrants" and the objects are the "objects entered. Now that the faculties are stilled and the objects have dissolved, it is said that there is "entry into that which is nowhere to enter."
Once the faculties and their objects have dissolved, the mechanism of the knots breaks of itself; then the eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) manifests from this point.

Only then can one profoundly penetrate the fundamental origins of how the twelve classes of beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions have, since beginningless time, entered the womb and received their life-destinies.
This is fundamentally different from being shrouded by the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), where one cannot comprehend the individual threads of each life’s continuity.

This was the day [he attained realization]. Having been able to observe the origins of his reception of the mandate, and furthermore having thoroughly understood the fundamental source of his grasping and sustenance, from this point forward he developed a profound weariness with his own birth. Thus, the mechanism by which he shared in birth with various classes of beings was exhausted;
he would no longer summon rebirth. By this means, he severed the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) and realized universal practice (*sarvatraga*).

Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the two types of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants—across the ten directions, one has already realized that they are identical, being but the single substance of consciousness manifesting itself;
there is no other dharma to be found. Thus, at this initial seeing of the celestial nature (*dharmadhātu*), there is already a subtle radiance.
Although it is not yet fully bright, it is like the first white light of dawn appearing in the east, revealing what was previously hidden in profound darkness.
It remains as it was; this is still like the break of dawn, when the light-sign has not yet appeared—it is the realm where the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) has not yet been shattered.

If, among the various classes of beings, birth and death do not summon you, and you have already attained a distinct nature that enters into sameness, then within that sameness, apply effort and practice to dissolve, melt, refine, and polish the six sense-faculties, so that when they are brought together, they may—
First, when opened, they become six. To employ the six sense organs as the function of a single organ is called "accomplishment through integration.
To employ a single organ as the function of the six organs is called "accomplishment through differentiation.

However, regarding these six organs, while they appear to be adjacent when discussed in terms of their functional positions, from the perspective of their essential nature, there is fundamentally no distinction between them; all can interpenetrate and mutually function.

Thus, one attains a world-body and mind that are like vaidūrya, transparent and luminous both within and without, being solely the pure and fundamental nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, wherein there is no other thing whatsoever.
This is the sign that the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) has been exhausted.

For the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without birth or extinction, nor does it have the origins of receiving a life-destiny; it is only through the perfuming of the preceding seven consciousnesses that [these appear].
The ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) grasps and maintains all seeds of both the defiled and the pure, thereby turbidizing the true nature.

Consequently, it is led by the牵引 (karmic attraction) of various destinies to undergo birth and life; thus, the essence of life is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha). Furthermore, regarding the triad of warmth, breath, and consciousness:
They evolve simultaneously. Once the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, the characteristics of the turbidity of life-force (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) are likewise transcended.
Turning back here to contemplate the origin of the aggregate of consciousness, one finds it is nothing but illusory and false—appearing to exist yet not existing.

Therefore, it is called "formless" (*wangxiang*). Its essential nature is empty and quiescent; therefore, it is called "void and non-existent" (*xuwu*). To be deluded and turn one's back on the true nature is termed "inversion. Fundamentally, there is no separate dharma.
It is only this deluded thought that serves as the root of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

If one can thoroughly understand that deluded thought has no inherent nature, then since even the root does not exist, how could the aggregate of consciousness exist? Therefore it is said: "The aggregate of consciousness is false and illusory;

its fundamental substance is the Tathāgatagarbha. *Vaidūrya* is fully called *veḍūrya*; here it is translated as "blue-colored gem," and is also rendered as "not distant" (referring to the western direction).
In that region there is a mountain, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī. This treasure emerges from the mountain, and it is named accordingly.
"Wangxiang" (Entanglement) resembles an elephant; it is the shadow within a shadow, a manifestation of unreality.
△ Second, a detailed exposition of the works of Māra (ten points). First, attachment to causes and their underlying reasons:
Ānanda, you should know that such good sons [as these] turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give rise to the seeds of external paths.

This demonstrates the ten kinds of false reckonings regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Herein, it first clarifies the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons. The meaning is this:

once a person has thoroughly investigated how the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is empty, they return to the source and revert to the fundamental within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), thereby being able to extinguish the nature of the flux and arising-and-ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Yet, regarding the quiescence of the aggregate of consciousness—
Although its nature has already manifested, its true essence—wondrous and luminous—has not yet emitted light;
it remains shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and is unable to illuminate the Dharma-realm in its entirety.

It can only cause the opening and closing of one's own body, mind, and six sense faculties without any obstruction, and it likewise functions in conjunction with the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of all classes of beings throughout the ten directions.

One naturally attains unimpeded integration. Whether regarding others or oneself, there is no obstruction whatsoever. This is the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), wherein self and other are one and the same.
Thus, this awareness and cognition above merges with all Buddhas and below blends harmoniously with all classes of sentient beings.
Thus, the very life-force received by ordinary beings and outsiders fundamentally originates from the root of the Path attained by sages and worthies;

none of these exist outside of this *ālaya-vijñāna*. Once one knows that all categories of existence throughout the ten directions are manifested solely by consciousness, and that awakening and cognition are universally pervasive, one can then deeply enter the nature of perfect fusion and primordial stillness.
Below, [the text] clarifies this perfect fusion and primordial stillness, [correcting] errors...
One gives rise to the grasping of dharmas and becomes of the lineage of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). For this perfect source is, in fact, the substance of consciousness.

If, regarding this very locus of refuge, one fails to realize it is consciousness and instead falsely establishes a cause that is truly eternal as the ultimate fruit, thereby generating a resolute conviction and taking it as a permanent reliance, such a person is indeed mistaken.
Grasping at the mind as the dependent, one falsely establishes the objective realm as its support; thus, one falls into the error of taking that which fundamentally lacks a cause as a cause.
This is called the "clinging to cause and what is caused. Here, "cause" (*hetu*) is synonymous with "support" (*āśraya*).
Such a person belongs to the same category as Śabikāra’s ultimate principle (*tattva*), which he sought to reach. The Sanskrit term *Śabikāra* translates here as "Yellow."

The first is the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) school that takes Brahmā as its teacher. They calculate that there is neither form nor emptiness; they identify the *ālayavijñāna* as the "Dark Principle" (*tattva*).

Erroneously, they claim that from the Dark [Principle] arises the Great Self (*mahat-ātman*), from the Great Self arises the intellect (*buddhi*), from the intellect arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), from the five subtle elements arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), and from the five gross elements arise the eleven faculties. Nevertheless, they take the spiritual self (*puruṣa*) as the sovereign, asserting that its essence is real.
It is eternal. The awakened mind abides in the center; it is indestructible and unbreakable, encompassing all phenomena. It takes the *avyakta* (the Unmanifest) as the primary truth.
The twenty-three intermediate factors are all produced from the *avyakta*. The *puruṣa* (Spirit-Self) is that which experiences these twenty-three factors.
To be deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi is not the true awakening of the stage of fruition. One loses the knowledge [of this].
To see [in this way] is not the true mind of the ground; this is called the first type of externalist.

Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), they falsely establish a mind that seeks attainment, thereby accomplishing a fruit of attainment. Previously, when practice was exhausted, consciousness manifested.

The separation and union of the faculties are nearing their perfect penetration. Now, by establishing the distinction between subject and object, you have moved away from that state and become distant from it.
Previously, while in the realm of Nirvana, you were on the verge of great awakening; now you turn your back on it and enter the path of birth and death.
Previously, your awakened mind was about to emerge, making you fit to be a son of the Buddha; now you have instead become a follower of external paths, severing the lineage of the Buddhas.
How tragic this is! △ Second, the attachment to the capable and the incapable.
Ānanda, furthermore, O good man, when one exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned formations (up to) giving rise to the seeds of the Great Arrogant Heaven’s pervasive and perfect selfhood.
This clarifies the grasping at the capacity and the lack of capacity. As for "the object of refuge," this refers back to the preceding chapter;
however, while previously one took the source of consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) to be the place of refuge, now one takes that very source of consciousness as one's own self—this is the distinction.

Furthermore, one conceives that all sentient beings throughout the realms are emanations of oneself, and having developed such a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one consequently clings to the notion of "I" as being capable [of such emanation].
They are born there; yet none of them can arise by themselves. Therefore it is said: "This person falls into the dualistic clinging to 'the agent' and 'the non-agent.
By forming such a view, one becomes a companion to Maheśvara, who claims for himself the power to manifest infinite bodies.
To say "that which can act is the mind" is to cling to the notion that the "I" acts as the cause of the mind; "that which can act" refers to the fruit of the activity.
"Those who reckon that they can produce the fruit of their actions" refers to those who claim that the creation of causes and the attainment of results are entirely due to themselves.

"The gods of great pride" refers specifically to Maheśvara; because he clings to the notion that he can produce all things and thus holds the sages and worthies in contempt, he is called a god of great pride.
"The pervasive and complete seeds" refers to the twelve classes of living beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"All these are created by me and perfected by me. This means that through the cause of "me," I am able to create universally, and I am able to bring them to completion.
If they were separated from me, none of them could arise of themselves. Thus, Maheśvara is the deity at the summit of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu);
he has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white bull, and holds a white fly-whisk. As it is said:

This refers to Maheśvara. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "There are those who maintain that there exists a single Maheśvara whose essence is truly omnipresent and eternal, capable of producing all phenomena. They assert that this deity possesses four attributes: first, his essence is real."
Second, it is all-pervasive; third, it is eternal; fourth, it is capable of producing all phenomena. Furthermore, they calculate that there are three bodies:

first, the *dharmakāya*, whose essence is eternally pervasive, its magnitude equal to empty space, and capable of producing the myriad things; second, the *saṃbhogakāya*, which resides in the Heaven of the Pinnacle of Form (*ākaniṣṭha*);
third, the *nirmāṇakāya*, which assumes forms according to the six destinies to teach and transform sentient beings. Within this [text] it says: "If, regarding the object..."
Returning [to the source], one grasps it as one's own essence; this is the reality of the substance, which is the Dharmakāya.
All sentient beings throughout the realms are its outflow; this is the pervasive and eternal, capable of giving rise to all phenomena, which is the second body (Sambhogakāya).
That which manifests as infinite bodies is the third body (Nirmāṇakāya). This is truly because the practitioner does not understand that their own nature is fundamentally...

The Unborn (anutpāda) is mistakenly misapprehended within the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha); one falsely imagines its own essence to be the cause of all phenomena, and thus falls into this attachment, becoming of the same category as Śiva.
△ Third, the attachment to permanence and impermanence.
Furthermore, "Good son, exhausting the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" (up to) "turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa and producing the seeds of inverted perfection.
This clarifies the attachment to permanence and impermanence. Regarding the phrase "that to which one returns," following the general outline of what preceded, this calculation is also...
Because one takes the source of consciousness as the object of refuge, one suspects that it is capable of producing oneself and all phenomena;
consequently, one reckons that the ground from which they arise and flow forth is the truly eternal substance, forming the understanding that it is neither born nor extinguished.
This is precisely to be in the midst of birth and extinction while prematurely reckoning it to be the true, eternal reality that is neither born nor extinguished.

They dwell [in this state]. Having already confused the true, eternally abiding nature that is neither born nor extinguished, they are further deluded regarding the phenomena of present arising and ceasing.
Moreover, they remain complacent, dwelling in attachment and immersion; within this, they conversely give rise to a superior understanding. Thus, they take the impermanent to be permanent;
hence it is called the "grasping at the permanent in the impermanent. Having formed this interpretation, they then proceed from their previous calculation of a self-existent lord (*īśvara*).

That "Heaven can produce all things" means that they share the same nature as its kind. "Establishing causes based on the mind" refers to taking the fundamental source of consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) as the productive cause and regarding it as the refuge to which one belongs.

"Accomplishing the fruit of false discrimination" refers to taking the false discrimination of arising and ceasing as the fruit of permanence. This and the aforementioned attachments both stem from the same fundamental source of consciousness; however, [the former]...

The calculation differs. The former clings to the self as that which produces the "round-arising" (pariṇāma); this [view] clings to that "round-arising" as the self. Therefore, it is called the "inversion of round-arising.
△ Fourth, the clinging to knowledge and non-knowledge.
Furthermore, "the good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" (up to) "turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.

This clearly refers to the attachment to non-cognition within cognition. That which is "known" is precisely the cognition that is the object of contemplation; it is the fundamental source of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Knowing that it is pervasive and perfect" means that this nature of knowing pervades all phenomena without exception and is perfectly complete.
"Establishing divergent views based on knowing" means that because of this pervasive perfection of knowing, divergent interpretations arise.

In short, seeing that the source of this consciousness inherently possesses cognitive awareness, and that all phenomena arise through the transformation of consciousness, one consequently establishes these divergent views.

This erroneous view holds that plants and trees are no different in nature from humans. Since they are not different in nature, it follows that the sentient and the insentient must mutually undergo saṃsāra.
Thus it is said: "Plants and trees become humans; when humans die, they return to being grass and trees.
If this were so, then both the sentient and the insentient would possess consciousness everywhere, with no distinction between them. To conceive such a view...
Regarding those with wrong resolve: such persons take what is known to be unknown, and again take what is unknown to be known;

they thus fall into the attachment of knowing and not-knowing. This is of one class with the two types of non-Buddhist outsiders, the Pāṭhas and the Sainikas, who cling to the view that all things possess consciousness. They calculate that the perfect mind constitutes [the self].

Regarding "erroneous results": this refers to taking this falsely conceptualized, all-pervading cognition as the causal mind; consequently, its retributive fruit also becomes erroneous. Regarding "inverted cognition":
this refers to taking that which has cognition as being without cognition, and taking that which is without cognition as having cognition;
these are both inverted modes of perception. The Sanskrit term is *vāṭa*, or alternatively *vaśa*; this is translated as [the following].
Pixini (避霰尼), also called Xianini (先尼), is a translation meaning "One with an Army"; these are the names of two non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*). Question:
In the preceding text, it was stated that grasses, trees, metal, and stone all manifest as demons and bring about calamities; does this not imply they possess consciousness? Answer:

This refers to the spirits that rely upon and attach themselves to grass and wood who possess consciousness; it does not mean that the grass, trees, and so forth inherently possess consciousness from the outset. Furthermore...
It is said: "In the world, there are old *feng* trees that transform into feathered immortals (*yuren*), and withered wheat that transforms into butterflies;
these are instances of plants and trees becoming humans. Virtuous women have transformed into chaste stones, and earthworms have transformed into lily flowers;

these are instances of humans becoming plants and trees. Thus, according to the twelve classes of living beings in the fundamental scriptures, even those who have transformed into soil still possess spirit.
As for wood, metal, and stone, what can be said of them? The answer is that these are all merely incidental occurrences and cannot be established as a constant rule.
If one were to insist that sentient and insentient things universally possess consciousness and mutually transform into one another, then one would be profoundly mistaken.
△ Fifth, the attachment to birth and non-birth.
Furthermore, "Good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" (up to) "turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seeds of delusion.

This clarifies the attachment to birth and non-birth. For it is only when consciousness is exhausted and the six sense-faculties are dissolved that the various faculties attain mutual function. Now...
Although these six have been dissolved, one has still not been extinguished; therefore, regarding their mutual functioning, they are not yet entirely wondrous.
One has merely attained that which accords with the mind and follows one's intent, such that there is roughly no obstruction.

Consequently, regarding this principle of perfect fusion and transformation, one falsely gives rise to conceptual calculations, erroneously claiming that all dharmas do not arise from these four great elements.

Therefore, regarding the radiance of fire, the purity of water, the circulation of wind, and the stability of earth, they take these to be the causes of true permanence capable of producing the ultimate fruit.
Thus, their seeking of pleasure and their attachment to contemplation become profound, as they honor and serve them in order to realize the fruit.
Consequently, they regard these four great elements and their sensory characteristics as the source of all arising and creation.
The "Original Source" (benyuan) is established as the true sovereign that eternally governs the creation of all things.

However, this is a false conceptualization; while it is claimed to be able to produce the holy fruit (*āryaphala*), in reality it cannot. Therefore, it is said that one clings to the notion of "producing the unproduced. "Observing the dust" (*chen*) refers specifically to observing the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
"Accomplishment" (*chengjiu*) means being able to accomplish all holy fruits, both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-sambhoga*). "Multitudinous dust" (*qunchen*) refers generally to...

This refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). They claim that the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits are all produced and constructed by these four great elements, which serve as the fundamental cause of birth for all holy ones and ordinary beings, both mundane and supramundane.
The Brahmin Kāśyapa refers to a class of materialists (*cāturmahābhūtika*) who hold such views; it is precisely those who are like this.
They are of the same category. To say that "the deluded mind follows external objects" means that one is confused about one's own true mind and instead follows illusory objects.
Consequently, one regards what is not a cause as a cause and falsely seeks it; one regards what is not a fruit as a fruit and falsely hopes for it.
Furthermore, taking the dust-like phenomena produced by delusive thoughts to be the master who can generate and transform them—is this not a perversion of the principle of transformation?
...of such a kind? △ Sixth, the attachment to non-reliance as a place of reliance.
Furthermore, good son, when one exhausts all conditioned phenomena to find them empty (up to) turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seed of annihilationism.
This clarifies the attachment to "non-return" as a place of refuge. Regarding "perfect clarity" (*yuanming*):

it refers to the point when the preceding aggregates have all vanished and all states of existence are empty, such that one perceives only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), which is perfectly pervasive and profoundly clear, like still water.

Yet, the practitioner does not realize that this is still but a phantom-like, void, and false conceptualization; they instead take this void nature within the perfect clarity to be the ultimate reality.
Having reached the end of the earth, they wish to disparage, destroy, and sever all worldly dust, taking the eternal extinction of emptiness as the place of their ultimate refuge;

having returned to this, they rest and no longer advance. How could they know that this place is merely a realm of voidness and unreality, not a truly existent place to which one can return? If one holds such an interpretation, [it is a grave error].
This attachment to that which is truly non-existent as a place of refuge is a false conceptualization;

it places one in the same category as those in the heavens of Non-conception and the Four Formless Heavens, or as the deities who preside over space. Even after passing through eighty thousand kalpas, one will ultimately fall into emptiness and perdition.
Thus, the present sutra says: "Those who follow the heavens of external paths and exhaustively pursue emptiness without finding a true refuge"—this refers precisely to such people.

Furthermore, regarding "the perfect voidness and mindlessness resulting in the fruit of annihilation": this refers to taking the pervasive, tranquil, and luminous state—yet devoid of thought—as the causal-ground mind;
thus, one achieves the awakening of the resultant ground as a state of total cessation and emptiness. Question: How does this differ from the fixed-nature Śrāvaka?
Answer: In their intent, they are the same: both involve abandoning existence to grasp at emptiness. However, it is merely a matter of their prior mental disposition.
Each has its own distinction. This seed of ordinary outsiders merely suppresses delusions to attain emptiness; that seed of the noble nature, however, cuts off delusions to attain emptiness.
△ Seventh: Attachment to Greed and Non-greed.

Furthermore, "the good man who exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned formations" (extending to) "turning his back on the city of Nirvana and giving rise to the seeds of delusive extension" clarifies that greed is not the grasping of greed.
"Perfect and eternal" also refers to the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

Because he perceives that the preceding aggregates have been extinguished, while the essence of consciousness is lucid and brilliant, profound and unmoving, he consequently falsely calculates it to be perfect and complete.

It is eternally abiding. Furthermore, seeing that the aggregate of consciousness can grasp and maintain the body, preventing it from decaying, one then desires to make the body firm and eternally abiding, identical to the perfect luminosity of the essence of consciousness, seeking long life so as not to fall or pass away.
One does not realize that this body is fundamentally not eternally abiding and truly cannot be clung to as something enduring; now, such false thoughts arise.
Because of greedy attachment, it is said that greed is the clinging to what is not greed. Asita means "Incomparable" (Anupama) in this language;

he is also named Rui-ben (Aśvajit), which refers to the Long-lived Immortal. Regarding "clinging to the root of life": one takes the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) as the root-source for the body's reception of life.

△ II. The Tathāgata’s Explanation and Response (II): A. Fully Answering the Three Questions (III): 1. An Extensive Explanation of the Arising of Conceptualization (III): 1. General Clarification.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "From 'the essence of purity and truth, wondrously luminous' (up to) 'the fundamental causes of the five aggregates are all equally false conceptions.
This passage generally clarifies that the five aggregates all take false conceptions as their root.

When the Buddha told Ānanda, 'I say that the five aggregates are all fundamentally false conceptions,' was this not for a reason? It is because 'the essence of purity and truth' refers to the Dharma-body; 'wondrously luminous'..."
This is *prajñā* (wisdom). "Perfectly pure" refers to *vimukti* (liberation). These three virtues, this secret treasury, are perfectly complete within the single mind;

that is to say, they are the primordial self-awakening that is inherently perfect and pure. Furthermore, as for its essence, it is fundamentally not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and cannot be made to abide.
It is free from the two kinds of birth-and-death—those within and beyond the realms—as well as all conceptualizations and marks.
These are the defilements of the sensory objects and the stains of the conscious mind; they are the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*).
Furthermore, neither the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nor anything such as *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, or even empty space can serve as a resting place for them.

Therefore, both the conditioned and the unconditioned—the very source of these phenomena—are not the original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*). Within the wondrously luminous mind, these are not things that exist inherently; they all arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Thus they arise. Therefore, we know that the five aggregates are nothing but a single deluded mind. This is truly because a single moment of deluded movement occurred within the fundamentally enlightened, wondrously luminous, and true essence of the mind;
thereby, the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as all sentient beings, their environments, and the entire world, were brought forth.
Consequently, there exist the characteristics of the four great elements and the five aggregates of the conditioned. Such is the case for sentient beings.
Deluded, they do not know for themselves that these four elements and five aggregates are fundamentally empty.
Within what is neither a sentient being nor the vessel-world, they falsely reckon them to be true and substantially existent;
this is just like Yajñadatta, who was deluded regarding his own head and mistook the reflection in the mirror for it. Since these five aggregates arise from delusion, they are fundamentally...

It can thus be clearly understood that there is fundamentally no cause for their arising. Now, within the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), because they arise through mutual dependence and interact as false illusions, they successively serve as seeds;

the subsequent establishment of a nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is already a mere expedient means (*upāya*) and possesses no ultimate reality. How much more so for those who do not understand this expedient means and are further deluded?
Based on causes and conditions, the five aggregates are designated as having a "natural nature.
Not only is the nature of the conditioned unreal, but even that unconditioned nature of empty space is likewise unreal.

This is because within the Tathāgatagarbha, a single thought-moment follows conditions and arises through illusory delusion—what is called "dark obscurity becoming space. Thus, one should know that the unconditioned is [unreal].

These emptinesses and the aggregates of conditioned phenomena are all the deluded minds of sentient beings, which engage in pervasive conceptualization, calculation, and the proliferation of names and signs;

they do not possess any true reality. Furthermore, Ānanda, if you and the others can truly know the source from which all these conditioned and unconditioned, false and illusory dharmas arise, then I may permit you to speak.

It may be granted that all delusive phenomena arise from causes and conditions; however, if these delusive phenomena fundamentally have no place of origin, then to insistently claim that they arise from causes and conditions is untenable. Why? Because they fundamentally have no place of origin.
Since it is fundamentally not something that exists, how can it be said to be a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions? Thus, even causes and conditions cannot be spoken of;
how much less so for one who, failing to understand causes and conditions, further speculates that things arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*)?
Therefore, I have now, together with you, clarified each of the five layers of the fundamental productive cause that has been obscured, as we have previously discussed.

It is just as I previously said: "When one thinks of vinegar, saliva flows."

Observing this, one knows that the physical forms manifest before us are all produced by deluded thoughts; this is clearly evident.

through false reception, there is bitterness and astringency, which agitate the substance of your physical form. If you do not awaken to this, you should contemplate what is presently manifest.
Regarding the objects encountered and experienced by the preceding physical body— namely, those which benefit when accorded with and cause harm when opposed—
these two types of sensation currently enslave the mind, driving it back and forth in mutual pursuit without rest.
This constitutes the second delusive thought of "empty luminosity," for sensation has no substantial reality and is nothing more than a hollow manifestation of experiencing luminosity.
This merely distinguishes between the contrary and the favorable. There are, however, three types: namely, suffering (*duḥkha*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

That which is favorable and beneficial is the sensation of pleasure; that which is contrary and detrimental is the sensation of suffering. Should one encounter that which is neither contrary nor favorable, neither detrimental nor beneficial, that is the sensation of equanimity.

If this body of yours were not of the same nature as such deluded thoughts and mental conceptions, for what reason and by what causal conditions would it be employed according to those thoughts?
