All of these arise from the mind through conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Subsequently, the sense faculties (*indriya*) take on form and engage in grasping.
Thus, one knows that the images apprehended by the faculties and the body are necessarily in correspondence with conceptualization.
It is just as dancers, performers, and artisans follow the beat of another: when the beat is slow, their steps are slow; when the beat is rapid, their steps are rapid. And as for the body...
Your perception is likewise so. Thus, when you are awake, it is called discursive thought (*vikalpa*); when you are asleep, it becomes various chaotic dreams.
From this, one knows that your body and your perceptions are never and nowhere dissociated.
This is truly because your thoughts and reflections do not cease, thereby causing deluded emotions to fluctuate; thus, the states of waking and sleeping are in constant turmoil without interval.
Thus one knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the first five sense-consciousnesses are mutually fused and interpenetrating; this constitutes the third false imagination.
Not only are they mutually fused such that the physical body obeys their impulsion, but they also interpenetrate the realm of dreams, all of which occurs because of them.
Thus we know that these aggregates (skandhas) are a dual fusion of matter and mind, pervading both the states of waking and sleeping;
therefore, they are called "pervasive delusive thoughts" (*yōtsū mōjō*). △ Fourth, explaining that conduct is precisely "hidden and obscure delusive thoughts."
The principle of transformation does not abide, shifting and moving in secret; this is called the fourth delusive thought, known as the "profoundly hidden.
This clarifies that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is precisely this profoundly hidden delusive thought. Regarding "the principle of transformation does not abide":

it means that the *saṃskāra-skandha* is the essential substance of the principle of transformation, yet it possesses the functional activity of constant flux and non-abiding. Shifting and moving in secret...
"Shifting" refers to the constant transformation from moment to moment, a subtle and continuous displacement that causes people to remain unaware of it;
it is like the metaphor of a boat being carried away by flowing water. The following section explains the matter of subtle shifting through transformation.

The meaning is that the four characteristics of the *saṃskāra-skandha*—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—never cease, and they are able to cause your body to undergo subtle and continuous transformation from youth... [until old age].
From vigor one reaches old age, and throughout the intervening stages, it is like the growth of nails on the fingertips or the emergence of hair on the head;

physical strength silently wanes and the countenance gradually wrinkles. All of this occurs day and night without ceasing, as the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-vināśa*) succeed one another in constant alternation.
Yet, not a single person is able to awaken to this; all of these are the transformations of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

This is the function of subtle transformation. Ānanda, if this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) were not your own body, how could it cause your physical body to grow old, with its wrinkles diminishing and its features changing?
If this aggregate of formations is truly and necessarily your own body, then since it is your body, it must be constantly replacing itself day and night; for what reason, then, do you...?
Furthermore, because there is no conscious perception, you know that your body undergoes arising, abiding, change, and cessation;
that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) flow on, transforming from moment to moment without ever remaining still—all of this is brought about by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Because these arise and cease without ceasing, right and wrong cannot be distinguished; they are obscure and invisible, hidden and difficult to discern. For this reason, it is called the aggregate of formations.
This constitutes the fourth deluded thought of the dark and obscure.
△ Fifth, it clarifies that consciousness is itself a deluded thought of inversion.
Furthermore, from "the place where your brilliant clarity is tranquil and unmoving" up to "the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined thought."
This clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is precisely this subtle, refined ideation. The Buddha’s intention was as follows:

"Furthermore, your essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous and as still as a pond of water; you take this state of being unmoving and unshaken to be what is therefore called 'eternal' and 'real.
If that were so, then this aggregate of consciousness would be the eighth consciousness, which, within your single body, [is not...]"
The nature inherent in the six sense organs is, if truly pure and unmixed, authentic and not delusive, and its essence is eternally constant;
thus, it cannot admit the defilement of delusive habitual tendencies within the six organs.
For what reason, when you previously beheld a marvelous object, after many years have passed, there is neither memory nor forgetfulness, yet upon seeing it again, you do not remember it?

"Is it left behind, remaining just as it was before? While the initial formation of memory arises from the perfuming of the first six consciousnesses, the subsequent maintenance of these seeds without loss is the function of the eighth [consciousness]. For the first six are like ministers who collect and amass."
The seventh is like an official in charge of transport; the eighth is like a steward of the granaries.
Therefore, as years and seasons pass, when one sees them again as they were before, one realizes that consciousness is concealed within this essence, which is profoundly still and undisturbed within.
Moment by moment, they are perfumed by those delusive habitual tendencies; therefore, there is the occurrence of memories that appear vividly clear.
It is not the case that these arise only after one has engaged in reflection, deliberation, conceptualization, or calculation.
For this reason, Ānanda, you should understand that when these eight consciousnesses—which are otherwise profound and unshakable—are perfumed by the True, then the True perfumes them.
Because it is delusion, delusion itself is not a nature that is truly eternal or immovable. It is merely like a rapid current of water without waves;
when viewed from afar by people, it appears only as something placid and tranquil, yet its flow is swift.
Subtle and minute, its characteristics are not seen; it is not like a clear pond or still water that truly lacks the appearance of flow.

The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* is also like this: it is not truly unmoving. Because it serves as the root-source of the deluded thoughts of the preceding four aggregates (*skandhas*), it receives deluded habit-energies (*vāsanā*).
If it were not the root-source of the deluded thoughts of the preceding four, how could it receive these deluded habit-energies?
How can it be that which is perfumed? Now, since this aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is already not real and is but a deluded thought, when will this delusion finally be extinguished?
If you wish to eliminate and destroy it, it cannot be done during the time when your six sense organs function interchangeably;
rather, at the moment when their opening and closing are separated, this deluded thought may be extinguished. Otherwise—
It is ultimately difficult to block and eliminate, nor is there ever a time when it can be extinguished.

This is because the eighth consciousness and the preceding six consciousnesses serve as mutual roots for one another; if they are true, they are equally true, and if they are delusory, they are equally delusory.

Therefore, it is necessary that the six be resolved before the one can begin to perish. For this reason, you now possess the six faculties—namely, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
These six kinds of essence are perfumed moment by moment within the eighth consciousness, interpenetrating one another.
Although it is said that these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are subtle and few, yet within the *tathāgatagarbha*, if one discusses the nature-consciousness—
within the true consciousness of luminous awareness, the wondrously enlightened, profound, and pure clarity— they nonetheless still appear as if they exist.
The "formless phantom" (*wangxiang*) is not a true emptiness of non-existence; this is the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined conception. As for "inverted":
it refers to being deluded regarding the Truth and clinging to the semblance, abandoning the *cangxing* (store-nature) while clinging to the *cangshi* (store-consciousness);
is this not indeed an inversion? As for "subtle": it is because this aggregate of consciousness (*shishiyin*) is precisely the subtle *ālayavijñāna*. As for "refined"...

Regarding "perception" (saṃjñā): this refers to the substance of this aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha). Although it is the essence of consciousness, it has not yet transformed into wisdom;
it still belongs to the false conceptualization of a phantom-like void.
△ Third, the conclusion:
"Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by the five kinds of false conceptualization.
This summarizes the five aggregates as being constituted by these five types of false conceptualization. The aforementioned five kinds are, namely:
The dharmas experienced as retribution by sentient beings are collectively termed the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
They are also called the five aggregates of grasping because there are no sentient beings who do not grasp these as their own self-substance.
This is truly because sentient beings are deluded regarding the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, giving rise to false form and false mind; based upon this form and mind, the five aggregates are formed.
Therefore, there exists the distinction between the mundane and supramundane, and between the noble and the ordinary.
If one uses the knowledge and vision of sentient beings and clings to these five aggregates as being truly existent, that is the mundane dharma.

If one uses the knowledge and vision of the two vehicles and clings to these five aggregates as being empty and quiescent, that is the supramundane dharma. However, if one is among the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have skillfully attained the Middle Way...
The Way consists in realizing that form is itself emptiness and penetrating that emptiness is itself form;

this is the supreme Dharma of both the mundane and supramundane realms, the realm of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) beyond thought and cognition. Were one to depart from these dharmas of the five aggregates, [one would fall into error].

Consequently, there would be no place for the establishment of the holy teachings of the five vehicles. For this reason, to be deluded regarding it is to be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while to awaken to it is to be a sage (*ārya*).
All these do not transcend the cultivation of meditative concentration by ordinary beings.

If one can, within this, employ the wisdom of Vajra-contemplation to wash away the attachment to the existence of sentient beings and sweep away the views of annihilationism and eternalism, one will realize that the One True Reality is inherently possessed.
When one realizes that all delusions are fundamentally empty, then the mind of delusive thought regarding the five aggregates is, in its very essence, pure;
this is precisely the wondrous true suchness-nature of the original Tathāgatagarbha.
△ Second, the answer that transcends [the literal] regarding the depth of the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus).
"If you now wish to know the depth of the causal elements... [extending to] "...penetrating the profound stillness, merging with the profound, one returns to the limit of consciousness.
This is the answer that transcends the previous question concerning where the five aggregates reach their boundaries and limits. The meaning is: "You now..."

If you wish to know the fundamental cause of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), to what they belong as elements (*dhātu*), and which are shallow and which are deep, you must understand that the earlier ones are increasingly shallow, while the later ones are increasingly deep. Thus, there is only form with shape (*rūpa*) and emptiness without marks (*animitta-śūnyatā*).
Mutually manifesting one another's forms, being both form and emptiness—this is the limit of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Only the two objects of suffering and pleasure, when joined with the body, constitute contact; and that which is neither painful nor pleasant, when separated from the body, constitutes detachment—all these are the limits of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).
Only the recollection during waking and the forgetfulness during sleep are entirely perception (*saṃjñā*).

This is the limit of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Only the cessation that returns to non-existence moment by moment and the birth that becomes existence moment by moment are both the limits of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

Regarding "the profound entry merging with the profound": the upper character "profound" refers to the profound essence of the six consciousnesses, while the lower character "profound" refers to the profound substance of the eighth consciousness. This is because these six profundities are all divisions of the eighth consciousness.

Now that the four aggregates have been exhausted, the six faculties no longer function; hence it is said, "the profound entry. Because the flow is reversed and returns to its entirety as one, it is said, "merging with the profound.
This is the reversal of the six functions to return to the single essence, which constitutes the ultimate limit of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
△ Third, the sequence for pursuing and eliminating [the doubts].

From "These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession" (up to) "What is it that is not clear?"—this is a further response to the previous inquiry regarding the sudden removal and gradual severance of the five aggregates. The meaning is: as you have asked concerning the five aggregates...
Is it through sudden elimination or gradual severance? Generally, these five aggregates originally proceed from the subtle to the coarse;

they arise one upon another in successive order. Thus, birth occurs because delusion conceals the nature, which transforms into the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), subsequently giving rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), sensation (*vedanā*), and form (*rūpa*).
If one wishes to extinguish them, one must first begin with form. If form is extinguished—
When they are eliminated, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are eliminated sequentially. Their arising proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on a garment;
their cessation proceeds from the coarse to the subtle, like taking off a garment. Such is the order of their arising and ceasing.
This is explained in terms of the sequence of entering the womb and forming the body, for there is nothing that precedes the delusion of truth into falsehood.
Ah! Once consciousness has formed the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it ceases not from moment to moment, flowing and revolving according to karma.

Because there is the arising of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) through this drifting and wandering, one gives rise to thoughts of love and hatred toward perceived objects. Because of these perceptions and attachments, there arises the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Due to these perceptions and attachments, consciousness takes refuge therein, grasping it as a self and causing feelings to arise; thus, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) arises. Having experienced [sensation]...
The body is formed; when one falsely seeks to preserve it, there is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). This is the sequence of its arising.

When the sevenfold karma is purified and the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) becomes thin and weak, the aggregate of form dissolves. Once the view of a self-identity has perished, the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, and thus the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) ceases.

Being neither affected by the agreeable nor the disagreeable, one no longer experiences hatred or love. When the perception [of such sensations] vanishes, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) ceases; when the perception of craving does not arise, [the aggregate of mental formations ceases].

When the mind no longer flows outwardly, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is exhausted. When the essence of consciousness returns to its source and reverts to the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness) is exhausted;
this refers to the varying degrees of depth in their eradication.

If one discusses the sequence of these stages of eradication solely in terms of their elimination, there are both principles and phenomena, which are inherently distinct. For, when these five aggregates are analyzed according to principle:

This arises from a single thought of deluded imagination. If one can remain in a state where not even a single thought arises, suddenly severing all攀缘 (pān-yuán, clinging/seeking after objects), one awakens to the vehicle of one’s own nature.
When this mind opens, the five layers of deluded imagination are eliminated all at once, like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace.
How could there be any distinctions of shallow or deep, or any sequential stages to be found? If, however, we discuss it in terms of phenomenal appearances, since they already exist...
Regarding all phenomena of form and mind, one must certainly investigate the truth and sever delusions, proceeding from the shallow to the deep until they are exhausted in succession.
As for these Dharma gates, I have previously tied a cloth for you to demonstrate the knots;

the sequence of the knots being untied and the correspondence between the phenomenon and the metaphor are self-evident. You ought surely to know this through that. Why then do you neglect that [metaphor] and...
I inquire further regarding this: What is the meaning of "sudden enlightenment followed by gradual elimination"?
The answer is: It is like the fierce winds of a great ocean suddenly ceasing; this is sudden enlightenment. The waves gradually subside; this is gradual elimination.
It is like the sense organs of an infant being produced all at once; this is sudden enlightenment. Their capacities gradually become complete; this is gradual elimination. It is like the Great...
The sun suddenly emerges; this is sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*). The frost and dew gradually dissipate; this is gradual elimination (*jianchu*).

It is like the spring bamboo shoots that suddenly grow tall and become equal in height to their mother; this is sudden enlightenment. The branches and leaves spread out, growing upward joint by joint; this is gradual elimination.

If one were to achieve only sudden enlightenment without gradual elimination, there would be understanding but no practice, and one would cling to principle while remaining deluded regarding phenomena.

If one merely eliminates [defilements] gradually without sudden awakening, then there will be practice without understanding; such attachment to phenomena while being deluded regarding principle is, in neither case, the correct cultivation of true samādhi.
△ Second, the summary and exhortation to transmit and demonstrate.
"You should take this root-source of deluded thought... [until] knowing that there is nirvana and not clinging to the three realms.
This generally summarizes the five aggregates and exhorts you to transmit them to future generations. The meaning is: you should take these five...
The fundamental origins of the five kinds of delusive imaginings that constitute the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) are here explained in detail,
one by one, so that the ground of the mind may be opened and cleared of confusion. If one’s path of self-benefit lies herein,

and if this is further transmitted to future generations so that all practitioners in the Dharma-ending age may thoroughly penetrate the essence of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), then the purpose is fulfilled.
Since their nature is illusory, they naturally develop a profound weariness toward birth and death as suffering.
Knowing that there is nirvana as bliss, they resolutely seek liberation and certainly do not remain attached to the three realms; thus, the path of benefiting others also lies herein.
This concludes the second section, the Main Body of the Teaching.
△ Section Three: The Circulation Portion (2) Subsection One: The World-Honored One’s Praise of Merit by Comparison (3) Sub-subsection One: Comparing the Merit of Making Offerings to the Buddha.
Ānanda, if there were someone who filled the ten directions... [up to] how could this merit have any limit?
This clarifies the section on the dissemination [of the teaching]. First, it uses the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*) to determine and compare the merit of making offerings to the Buddha.

Although the phrasing of this comparison is brief, its underlying principles are comprehensive. The phrase "the seven treasures filling the void" expresses the excellence of the gift of material wealth.
The "myriad Buddhas as fine dust" reveals the vastness of the field of merit. To serve them without fail demonstrates the universality of one's virtuous mind.
Furthermore, with a vast mind like the jewels of space, one offers worship to the Buddhas; this foremost state of mind never passes in vain.
With such a constant mind, practicing giving in this manner, both the object of the mind and the mind itself are supreme. How could the merit obtained thereby not be great?
Ah! By offering seven coins to the Buddha, one attains the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). This demonstrates that among all fields of merit, the merit of the Buddha is supreme.
Even the merit of a Wheel-Turning King—who possesses the seven treasures and is surrounded by a thousand sons—is surpassed by one who offers all the rare jewels filling the void to the Tathāgata.
Thus, the material objects bestowed would be inconceivable even throughout kalpas; how could the merit thereby summoned have any limit by which it might be measured?
△ Second, praising the merit of extinguishing evil.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas... [up to] cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.

This clarifies that the gift of Dharma surpasses the aforementioned gift of material wealth, thereby praising the merit of propagating the sutras and extinguishing evil, even for those who possess faults.
The Buddha said, "Below" [refers to the following]. First, it clarifies that the Buddha’s words are true, exhorting one to believe them with sincerity.
"If there should be another person" means that even if such a single individual exists. *Pārājika* in the Sanskrit language means "abandonment," or "that which is not to be enjoyed.
Thus, being currently without the function of a monk and being "not to be enjoyed," one shall immediately enter hell. [This refers to] the four [pārājikas] of the Hīnayāna.
The "grave" offenses refer to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. Regarding the ten abandonments of the Mahāyāna, in addition to these four grave offenses, there are five more:
(5) selling intoxicants; (6) speaking of the faults of laypeople or monastics; (7) praising oneself and disparaging others; and (8) being stingy and miserly.
Ninth is malice; tenth is slandering the Triple Gem oneself and lacking faith in cause and effect.
"In a mere instant" means that within the blink of an eye or a single breath, one immediately falls. "The ten directions of Avīci" refers to the most extreme and evil retribution.
"One who can [do so] with a single thought" means one who can resolve to propagate this sutra for even a single moment; this refers to the extreme brevity of time.
This Dharma-gate points to the Dharma-gate of the nature of meditative concentration (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) as expounded in this very sutra.

"The final age" refers to the latter five hundred years, a season when Māras are powerful and the Dharma is weak. "Those who have not yet studied" refers to beginners who find it difficult to advance and easily retreat.

Furthermore, "this person" refers to one who propagates the sutra for even a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). "Karmic obstacles" refer to the aforementioned four grave offenses and ten heinous acts;
these are all extremely heavy and profound hindrances. "Should be extinguished upon thought" means they are eliminated by the very thought-moment of propagating the sutra.
"Transforming what lies below" means that not only can one eliminate evil karma, but one also transforms extreme suffering.

This is the cause for achieving the fruit of Ultimate Bliss. Regarding the phrase "attaining blessings," it means that one not only leaves suffering behind to obtain happiness, but moreover, the merit one performs surpasses that of previous people;
it is the merit of filling the void with the seven treasures to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as atoms.
This is not merely one or two times greater, but even a hundred, thousand, ten thousand, or ten million times greater, even beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

[This] analogy is such that none can equal it. Question: For a person who has committed the most grievous sins, to preach [the Dharma] for even the briefest moment is not yet sufficient to be called praiseworthy;
why then does it extinguish sin and obtain merit in such a supreme manner? Answer: There are many reasons why one obtains this superior retribution.
First, the sutra being propagated is the Buddha’s ultimate discourse; its teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are all...

Because it is inconceivable. That is to say, it reveals that the dharmas of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind—whether sentient or insentient, possessing nature or lacking nature—all equally attain the Buddha-way.
This principle is inconceivable. The *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-citta-mantra* is relied upon by both those on the path of cause and those on the path of fruition;
through this dharma, they extinguish evil and give rise to good, enter into the principle and transform others, ward off the heterodox and obtain the correct, and advance [in the practice].

The practice becomes ever more rapid, enabling the accomplishment of Bodhi; this teaching is inconceivable. Among the gateways of universal practice, the twenty-five sages of Avalokiteśvara are supreme;
this practice is inconceivable. At the third stage of the sixty stages of sanctity, one immediately realizes non-arising;
furthermore, it speaks of "Dry Wisdom," which can transcend the causal positions and enter directly into Sublime Enlightenment—this is the fruition.
It is inconceivable. Second, in this degenerate age there are many obstacles; that one can, at such a time, propagate this ultimate teaching and possess true faith and understanding is truly rare.
Third, regarding the merit of giving, it usually results only in tainted retribution and benefits oneself alone;
yet, by propagating the Dharma of the sutra, one can attain the untainted and cause listeners to understand without error, benefiting them through successive transmission.

Joy, because it is inexhaustible. The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dharma, the King of Śūraṅgama Samādhis, the Mother of Buddhas, as expounded in the four fundamental sūtras, is capable of giving birth to all Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions.

While those seven jewels filling the void can only serve as offerings to the Buddhas, this person, through a single thought-moment of propagating the sūtra, is able to give birth to Buddhas. For this reason, one...
Although this mindfulness may be slight, its benefit is exceedingly vast; thus, it can surpass the merit of that gift of jewels.
△ Third, describing the virtue of generating wholesome roots:
"Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra... [up to] they will directly attain Bodhi and no longer have demonic activities."
This describes the virtue of generating goodness through recitation and upholding [the teachings] without fault.

Regarding the phrase "according to my words," it means that one must first cultivate the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) by reciting sutras and holding mantras; yet, even though this merit has been spoken of by the Buddha, it cannot be fully exhausted.
How much more so for one who follows the teachings to practice the Way, entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation,

and proceeding from the upward quest for the fruit of Buddhahood to the downward transformation of sentient beings, directly transcending to attain the unsurpassed bodhi of a Tathāgata; for such a person,
there will be no further demonic activities or complications along the way— how could the merit of this even be described?
Is it conceivable?
△ Second, the great assembly attains benefit and rejoices.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, from the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (until) they all rejoiced greatly, paid homage, and departed.

The assembly having heard the Dharma and obtained its benefits, all were filled with joy. This [section] and the introductory section (nidāna) form the beginning and end [of the narrative], both being recounted by the sūtra-compilers.
Regarding the passage "the bhikṣus... and below, the fourfold assembly is first mentioned; regarding "all... and below, the distinction between the noble and the ordinary is explained in detail.
As for the "noble seer-boys" (ārya-ṛṣi-kumāra), they reside in the realm of the seers (ṛṣi-gati); because they have heard the Buddha-dharma, they aspire to join the ranks of the noble ones.

They are those who flow [toward liberation]. As for the powerful spirits and deities, they are those capable of first generating the wholesome mind to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, and who personally dwell beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.
Regarding "great joy," one attains worldly joy in the near term and the supramundane first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) in the distant term.

However, the meaning of joy can be briefly stated to have three aspects: first, the purity of the person who preaches; [the second is the purity of the dharma preached; and the third is the purity of the assembly.]
Second is the purity of the Dharma taught; third is the purity of attaining the fruit by relying on that Dharma.
The one who can teach it is the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who speaks for the sake of delivering sentient beings and not for the sake of fame or profit.
The Dharma taught is the present definitive and ultimate scripture; it is the Perfect and Sudden True Doctrine, and is certainly not a provisional or inferior teaching.
Regarding those who attain the fruit according to the Dharma: first, they do not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* but suddenly obtain the *dharmakāya*.
Next, they gather with the great assembly and attain the purity of the *dharmacakṣus*; immeasurable sentient beings give rise to the incomparable mind.
Finally, they suddenly awaken to the supreme and wondrous principle and sever subtle afflictions; even as they hear the sutra at every joint, they receive benefit in every place.
For this reason, they were all greatly delighted; they paid their respects, took their leave, and departed.
At that time, having composed this commentary, [Puwen] joined his palms, prostrated before the Buddha, and spoke these words:
I look up and address my original teacher, the Great Master, The Dharma King witnessed by the ten directions,
The assembly of holy sages at the Universal Gathering of Śūraṅgama, And the eight classes of devas and nāgas, as well as the Vajra-holders:
May you, out of great compassion, extend your eyes of wisdom, Together observing the heart of this sunflower as it composes these humble verses.
Having encountered this scripture through the legacy of the Bequeathed Teachings, I am deeply moved by my lack of skillful understanding.
For twenty years I have secluded myself in Longcong Cave;
at midnight I investigate and deliberate within, and by day I discourse with the white clouds, while at dusk I remain with the bright moon to propagate the Dharma.
Though I wield the meager tools of a bamboo tube or a small ladle to peer at the Milky Way, I am truly ashamed as a tiny mouse drinking from a river or a pond;
yet, should these superfluous words not contradict the intent of the Sūtras, I hope they may be granted circulation throughout the ten directions,
so that those who practice for perfect penetration will surely attain the Tathāgata’s pure treasury.
Furthermore, I hope that all who see or hear this shall rejoice in it together, ascending to the boundless joy of benevolence and longevity.
*The Precious Mirror Commentary on the Great Buddha-Top Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Ten (End).
